Case Study Title: Addressing Maternal and Infant Mortality in Meghalaya by Building State Capability
Case Study Description:
The case centres on the dilemma faced by Sampath Kumar, Principal Secretary of Health in the northeastern state of Meghalaya, as he strives to reduce the high maternal and infant mortality rates in the region. To address the issue, Kumar implemented a variety of measures, including the use of data and technology for real-time monitoring of high-risk pregnancies, centralising decision-making at the frontline worker level, enhancing communication between citizens and the state, fostering cross-functional problem-solving among government departments, building political support, and addressing systemic gaps.

These efforts resulted in significant progress. However, to fully resolve the challenge, Kumar also needed to address broader societal issues, such as teenage pregnancies and the lack of family planning.
Case Text:
“Every 2 minutes, a woman dies during pregnancy or childbirth, globally. Most of these deaths are preventable with
the right care, at the right time”.

UN report1

It was January 2023. Sampath Kumar, Principal Secretary of Health, Meghalayai

, smiled as he
reflected on the last 2 years. The Rescue Mission’s implementation in Meghalaya had brought about a
significant decrease in both maternal and infant mortality rates. (Infant deaths decreased by over 27%
(between 2020-22) and maternal deaths decreased by 35% (between 2020-23) (see Exhibit 1) with minimal
resources. This caught the attention of the state’s administration. Instilling a sense of purpose throughout
the state’s administrative machinery and equipping them with an approach to problem-solving, which
enabled experimentation and learning-by-doing, had fostered a positive shift in the organizational culture.
However, challenges remained. Adaptive issues—such as a high proportion of teenage pregnancies and a
lack of birth spacing—needed to be addressed if Meghalaya was to reduce maternal and infant deaths
further. Sampath was aware that these issues could be solved only by igniting a change in the attitudes and
behaviours of communities, no easy task.
The challenge that Sampath saw was: “How could the State Capability approach be strengthened to help
tackle these adaptive problems in order to further reduce maternal and infant deaths in Meghalaya?”
MMR and IMR in India
MMR (Maternal Mortality Rate), the number of maternal deaths per 1,00,000 live births as IMR
stands for Infant Mortality Rate, which is the number of infant deaths per 1,000 live births. According to
the latest reports from the Registrar General of India (RGI), the MMR in India had reduced from 130 per
lakh births in 2014-16 to 113 per lakh births in 2016-19 at the national level.2 The IMR in India had reduced

from 39 per 1,000 live births in 2014 to 30 per 1,000 live births in 2019 at the national level3

. However, there
was still a wide variation in MMR and IMR across different states and regions in India. For example, the
MMR ranged from 43 per lakh in Kerala to 197 per lakh in Uttar Pradesh4

, and the IMR ranged from 3 per

1000 live births in Mizoram to 46 per 1000 live births in Madhya Pradesh.

Sampath Kumar’s interventions
Since March 2020, when the Covid-19 pandemic began, Sampath and his team had been working
to develop strategies to address the challenges of testing, tracing, and tracking the spread of Covid 19, as
well as strengthening the healthcare system. Health had been his passion since the beginning of his career.
As District Magistrate - Tura in 2006-07, he had successfully combated & managed the menace of Malariaii
by leveraging the support of the local community and ASHA workers. His commitment to improving the
lives of citizens pushed him to dedicate time to identify steps to tackle the pandemic.
Sampath’s experience dealing with health issues highlighted the significant task ahead, as he was
well aware of the weak health infrastructure in remote villages, poor road connectivity, low social
acceptance of modern medical treatment, and complicated heuristic behaviour. He began daily review
meetings and health officials from all districts to implement required solutions and monitor the situation.
Leveraging review meetings
The Covid-19 pandemic gave him the opportunity to build a unique state capability model.
Meghalaya fostered cross-departmental collaboration, responsive citizen-state relationships7
, and

community-level covid management8

to manage the spread of infection. The success of Meghalaya in
maintaining one of the lowest infection rates during the pandemic led Sampath to try to solve other health
issues through a similar approach.
Recalling that SDG 3.19 aimed to reduce the global maternal mortality ratio to less than 70 per

100,000 live births (211 in Meghalaya in 2015-16) and SDG 3.210 aimed to end preventable deaths of new-
born and children under five years of age (IMR was 33/1000 live births in 2019), he was deeply upset by

the statistics for Meghalaya. Addressing this was a priority.
From June 2020, the review meetings with the district Covid management teams began to be used
for monitoring and analysing health issues, such as maternal and infant deaths in the state. The focus on
maternal health was given impetus due to decline in pregnant women coming to health facilities for seeking
care due to fear of contracting the virus11
.

Initial Steps Towards Local Solutions for Local Issues
Sampath, through the daily review meetings held with the district teams got valuable inputs. He
encouraged district teams to proactively develop solutions on a local level rather than waiting for directions
from state leadership.
To facilitate this, he organized a workshop for district officials on the PDIA12 (problem-driven
iterative adaptation) approach to problem-solving. Additionally, he announced that two districts would be
reviewed each week, to identify areas of concern and [plan] customize interventions accordingly.

ADDRESSING MATERNAL AND INFANT MORTALITY IN MEGHALAYA BY BUILDING STATE CAPABILITY 3

Crisis as an Opportunity
The State leadership in Meghalaya recognized the need for systematic changes as a result of the
pandemic. Firstly, the pandemic highlighted the gaps in the health infrastructure and service delivery.
Secondly, they realized that improving the health system was crucial to prepare for future crises.
In November 2020, the Meghalaya government launched the Rescue Mission to save the lives of
mothers and infants in the state. This mission was developed based on the findings from review meetings
and aimed to operate in a mission mode. The initiative built upon the processes established during the
Covid-19 crisis and institutionalized them within the State Capability Enhancement Project (SCEP)
Framework13. This framework aimed to enhance the public service delivery mechanism in Meghalaya and
make it more capable, robust, responsive, and efficient in achieving the state's development objectives
across all departments. This was when the pillars of the SCEP framework began to be institutionalized.
The SCEP approach called for broad mobilization of all stakeholders, including community leadership and
political leadership, which is essential to address complex challenges. Moreover, SCEP called for a pivotal
role of state leadership in identifying and addressing systemic challenges. The approach of SCEP was
inspired by frameworks such as Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA)14 and Adaptive Leadership15
and has been refined over time through the state’s own experimentation and reflection.
How the SCEP Framework was used to tackle maternal and infant deaths
The pillars of the SCEP framework were used to address different dimensions of maternal and infant
deaths.
Effective Use of Data and Technology
Sampath decided to track key indicators and insights to guide decision-making. The MOTHER APP,
developed by the MD, National Health Mission (NHM) (Ram Kumar, IAS), Meghalaya, with assistance
from the Centre for Digital Financial Inclusion (CDFI), enabled real-time monitoring of high-risk pregnant
women across the state. This data was shared with frontline workers at district and block levels, enabling
them to provide assistance to high-risk pregnant women.
Building Local Leadership through Problem-Solving
State leadership learned that reducing maternal and infant deaths was a complex challenge which
needed people to take ownership at each level: district, block, and community. Sampath realized the
importance of breaking the hierarchy between policy formulation—often understood as the work of senior
bureaucratic leadership— and policy implementation—often thought to be the work of frontline staff at
district, block, or community levels. Frontline workers were given the authorization to experiment and
innovate to come up with solutions to solve maternal and infant deaths at the local level. Successful
innovations were then scaled-up as positive deviance cases across the State.
For instance, in the West Khasi Hills (WKH) district, it was found that postpartum haemorrhage
(PPH) was the major cause of maternal deaths. The district team took various initiatives to address this
issue: ensuring wide availability of Misoprostol tablets; conducting capacity building of healthcare workers
and community members to stop PPH deaths; and engaging influential officials such as Block Development
Officers (BDOs) to change community norms on institutional deliveries, particularly among high-risk
pregnant women.

ADDRESSING MATERNAL AND INFANT MORTALITY IN MEGHALAYA BY BUILDING STATE CAPABILITY 4

Strengthening Citizen-State Relationship
Sampath realized that winning the trust of citizens in the public healthcare system was crucial. This
trust could only be built by making the government responsive to citizens’ needs and concerns, and by
strengthening the connective tissue between the state and citizens.
A system of regular field visits by senior state leadership to communities where maternal deaths had
occurred was institutionalized. Maternal death reviews were conducted with the community to learn about
the causes that had led to a mother dying within the community and to sensitize the community on the
steps they could take to prevent future deaths. Frontline workers were trained to engage with communities
in a more empathetic manner and in adaptive skills such as facilitating behaviour or norm change in a
respectful manner.
Departmental Convergence
The analysis of maternal deaths showed that several causes—severe anaemia; lack of birth spacing;
lack of access to health facilities; the high number of gravidae—could not be solved by the health
department. Sampath’s role as the Principal Secretary of the Community & Rural Development (C&RD)
department and the Social Welfare department (Women & Child Development Department), along with
his role as Principal Secretary of the Health & Family Welfare (H&FW) department, allowed him to drive
collaboration between all the three departments. This arrangement was felt necessary by the Chief Minister
Mr. Conrad Sangma to effectively mobilize all the departments and government functionaries to work with
a greater sense of purpose.
This departmental convergence across all levels enabled for pooling of resources from all three departments
and allowed different dimensions of maternal and infant deaths to be addressed. For instance, existing
schemes under the Social Welfare and C&RD departments were used to address issues such as anaemia
(through nutrition provision).
Political Supportability
Sampath knew that political support was required to build sustained momentum to drive systemic
change. He regularly reported data on maternal and infant deaths to the political leadership, thus making
them aware of the scale of the problem, as well as the systemic issues that needed to be addressed. Quick
wins were regularly communicated to the political leadership. The formation of the Human Development
Council, headed by the Chief Minister of Meghalaya, along with the membership of ministers from relevant
departments and senior bureaucratic leadership, enabled the political leadership to be regularly informed
of both implementation challenges and quick wins.
Addressing systemic Challenges
The regular review meetings led to identification of a major challenge which needed to be addressed
to further reduce maternal and infant deaths. Many villages located in remote regions did not have any
transportation facility. Pregnant mothers who came from a poor socio-economic background, and had
other young children, were uncomfortable with institutional deliveries, as they worried about who would
look after their children. The recognition of this problem by the political leadership led to the formulation
of the Chief Minister’s Safe Motherhood Scheme (CM-SMS)16. The CM-SMS scheme — launched in March,
2022 — provided for the transportation of pregnant mothers to come for institutional deliveries. It also
provides for setting up of transit homes where deliveries can be performed by skilled birth attendants.
Moreover, it financially incentivised Traditional Birth Attendants (TBAs) to accompany pregnant women
to transit homes. The SHGs were put in charge of these transit homes and incentivized to look after the

ADDRESSING MATERNAL AND INFANT MORTALITY IN MEGHALAYA BY BUILDING STATE CAPABILITY 5

pregnant mothers’ other children if needed. This enabled mothers to feel safe in the company of familiar
women from their community and to be assured that their children will be looked after when they came
for institutional deliveries. This led to a rapid uptick in institutional deliveries.
The Way Ahead
Sampath smiled as he reviewed the significant reduction in MMR and IMR achieved in two years,
signed as he thought about the facility-level gaps and infrastructure shortages that still needed attention.
While the Rescue mission's supply-side interventions had contributed to positive outcomes, addressing
teenage pregnancies and lack of family planning required changing the behavioural and cultural norms of
the community. As a seasoned civil servant, he wondered about the long-term sustainability of systemic
changes.

Case Study Title: Ayushman Bharat - Healthy India for Universal Health Coverage
Case Study Description:
The case centers on a scheme to expand access to primary health care services under the Indian central government’s flagship Ayushman Bharat program, a national public health insurance initiative. The scheme aimed to establish 1.5 lakh Health and Wellness Centers across India to provide free and universal comprehensive primary health care. These centers would offer a wide range of services, including health and wellness services, maternal and child health services, treatment for non-communicable diseases, palliative and rehabilitative care, oral, eye, ENT, mental health, elderly care, and emergency and trauma care.

The program manager encountered several challenges in implementing this ambitious project. Key obstacles included obtaining approval to recruit a new cadre of officers, namely Community Health Officers, to serve in these centers. Additionally, there were significant efforts required in capacity building and training these officers and other primary health service personnel, as well as monitoring the performance and effectiveness of these centers.
Case Text:
Universal Access to Equitable, Affordable Quality Healthcare, Accountable and Responsive to the People
It was June 2023. Dr. M.A. Balasubramanya (Dr. Bala), Advisor, National Health Systems Resource
Centre and the then Advisor of Community Processes and Comprehensive Primary Health Care, Ministry
of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India reviewed the progress made since joining India’s flagship
health initiative, the Ayushman Bharat Program, as Advisor in July 2020. As a part of the programme,
1,50,000 Health and Wellness centres spanning all States and Union territories were to be established by
December 20221
.
Set targets had been achieved, and the numbers visiting the centres had increased to a record 600
million2
. Screening for non-communicable diseases such as hypertension, cancer, and diabetes was at an
all-time high. Challenges related to recruitment and certification had been addressed, and the number of
facilities meeting National Quality assurance standards had risen. 2.04 crore wellness sessions covering
over 22.08 crore community members (ibid) had been held. (See Exhibit 1 for Statistics on Ayushman
Bharat Health and Wellness centres). However, much remained to be done. Wider adoption was required,
and funding beyond March 2026 needed to be addressed.
Background: Ayushman Bharat – Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs)
Ayushman Bharat (AB) Health and Wellness Centres aimed to deliver preventive, promotive,
curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care. The first priority was to set up 1,50,000 Health & Wellness
Centres (HWCs) to deliver free and universal comprehensive primary health care with a focus on both
illness and wellness. These centres offered health promotion and wellness services, maternal and child
health services, non-communicable diseases, palliative and rehabilitative needs, oral, eye, ENT, mental
health, elderly, emergency, and trauma care. Essential drugs and diagnostic services were provided free of
cost (See Exhibit 2 for Components of the program).
Dr. M.A. Balasubramanya (Dr. Bala)
Dr. Bala understood the established protocols and processes within the administrative framework
of India. As a trained anaesthesiologist, development interventionist, and trainer, he brought an
understanding of the medical profession, empathy for the people, and administrative skills to the role.

AYUSHMAN BHARAT – HEALTHY INDIA FOR UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE 2

The Indian Healthcare System
The Indian public healthcare system relied on an ecosystem of Primary Health Centres (PHC), a
single-physician clinic equipped to address basic reproductive and child health issues, some communicable
diseases and to perform minor surgeries. This is where citizens first encountered a doctor.
The PHC doctor referred cases requiring advanced treatment to Community Health Centres at the
block level or to district hospitals equipped to provide critical care. Each PHC managed several Sub-Health
Centres, which in turn were manned by Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs). Accredited Social Health
Activistsi
(colloquially called ASHAs) facilitated community access to the health centres. Each ASHA was
selected from amongst the residents of the area.
Ayushman Bharat programme introduced a cadre of Community Health Officers (CHOs) to lead
the Sub-Health Centres and liaise between the PHC doctors and the midwives and ASHAs. It was hoped
that this cadre would reduce the burden on the single physician centres and improve community health
outcomes. This required large-scale recruitment and buy-in from state health departments, as health is a
state subjectii
.

The First Challenge: Recruitment
The Union Government's guidelines suggested the recruitment of BSc (Nursing) graduates
and BAMS graduates (commonly known as Ayurvedic doctors) for the role of CHOs. However, finding
eligible candidates was challenging and made even tougher as CHOs had to complete the “Certificate
Programme in Community Health” (CPCH) after selection but before final recruitment.
State governments were uneasy about introducing a new cadre and had to fix salary levels for
CHO’s at low levels as the nurses in general earned low salaries. Midwives (ANMs) on the government
payroll demanded promotion to this new cadre, and many felt threatened that the CHO cadre would
undermine their authority. They found it difficult to accept CHOs as leaders of the health centres, causing
conflicts between the CHOs and other team members mainly ANMs.
Some lab technicians and paramedics demanded inclusion in the recruitment, leading to legal
battles as petitions were filed in various high courts. One homoeopath argued that they were as qualified
as an Ayurvedic doctor and could manage patients effectively, questioning why they had not been given
the same opportunity. The rural population long trusted and knew the midwives and ASHAs.
Handling the recruitment challenges
States knew the importance and role of CHOs in unburdening the PHC ecosystem and enhancing
range, reach and quality of services to the community. The role of CHOs in independently managing the

trained and supported to function in her own village to improve the health status of the local population,
forming a critical link between the community and the public health system. She is supported by the
community for services rendered, apart from performance-based support from public health programs
ii This means that state legislatures enjoy jurisdiction over it, i.e., the state legislature can pass laws and
govern the said subject - Public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries. Hence the Union
Government has little legal authority to overrule the State.

AYUSHMAN BHARAT – HEALTHY INDIA FOR UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE 3

patient, team, community and public health outcomes was shared. This encouraged acceptance by the
States of the new position, of a salary that was higher than what was for a regular nurse supporting doctors
in hospitals on clinical care.
The Qualification criteria was expanded to accelerate recruitment. States could choose amongst
candidates with either a Diploma in Nursing or BSc Nursing or BAMS graduates or candidates who had
pursued BSc Nursing with an integrated CPCH course. Only these qualifications ensured the candidates
had an understanding of the whole-body functions, drugs and diagnostics; clinical experience in both
medicine and surgery and the ability to manage emergency conditions.
The course on certificate programs for the CHO’s was made available in a blended mode. The
Ministry and IGNOU created a 6-month course, while State health universities were empowered to offer a
four-month course, provided IGNOU stipulated study hours and evaluation were followed. This
accelerated recruitment.
States were providing guidance to argue their case in the courts. The details of the favourable
verdict in Allahabad High Court3 were shared with all other states in need. This helped most states to get
a favourable court verdict.
Further, awards to district authorities for distinguished performance, financial incentivisation of
the States for achieving the set annual target propelled progress towards the goal.
The Second Challenge: Capacity Building
The teams across all levels, ANMs, ASHAs, CHO’s staff nurses, and PHC Medical Officers, needed
training on an expanded range of services quickly for the entire country and different capacity-building
programs tailored to their role. CHOs required an additional 15-day induction training on National Health
Programmes and managerial responsibilities. Online training was not effective.
The Ministry through its technical assistance body – the National Health System Resource Centre
(NHSRC), created training manuals for primary healthcare teams on all the expanded range of services,
and established a pool of 5000 State trainers for face-to-face sessions. NHSRC also created learning
materials on Learning Management System with knowledge content provided ONLINE and skill training
on face-to-face mode. Skill videos were uploaded to YouTube as ready reckoners.
Additionally, a web-based training monitoring system named SASHAKT (Systematic Assessment
of Health Care Providers Knowledge and Training)4 was developed to monitor the pace and the quality of
the training across States/UTs.
The Third Challenge: Mentoring and Monitoring
CHOs needed help understanding their leadership roles and establishing themselves in the
existing ecosystem of village health. They were faced with managing staff, services, and the community.
CMC Vellore provided the technical expertise to launch a national online mentoring program for CHOs.
This offered individual mentoring to CHOs and included technical and managerial inputs in all 35 states
and UTs. The medical officers at the PHC’s were provided with an orientation program to enhance their
monitoring capabilities.
Dr Bala travelled extensively, interacting with all frontline workers, Health officials in Districts and
State and providing clarity of concept of comprehensive primary health care. He visited 24 states, dealing

AYUSHMAN BHARAT – HEALTHY INDIA FOR UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE 4

with language barriers along the way. He was supported by health ministry officials and central officers
who also visited at least two health centres in each State they visited. These frequent field visits helped
execution.
CHOs updated data in real-time on web portals. The Indian Health Ministry reviewed the
performance of the health centres and involved the State Mission Directors and Health Department
Secretaries. (See Exhibit 3 for Monitoring Process).
The Way Forward
Dr. Bala acknowledged that although progress had been made, there was still much to do. The
middle class was reluctant to use the AB-HWCs due to perceptions of poor quality of service and prolonged
waiting time. This discourages the poorer sections of society in using these services. Funding for the
initiative was available till March 2026. The next big question was, how could these services be sustained
after that?

Case Study Title: Jeevika – Didi Ki Rasoi
Case Study Description: This case focuses on JEEViKA, Bihar’s Rural Livelihoods Promotion Society, an initiative aimed at organizing economically marginalized women in the state into self-help groups. These groups empower women to seek employment opportunities and access funding. One notable program conceptualized under JEEViKA is the “Didi ki Rasoi” initiative. Through this program, local women establish institutional canteens at state hospitals, schools, and other community centers to provide fresh, home-cooked healthy meals. This initiative addresses the issue of poor food quality in these institutions while simultaneously generating employment and income for the women involved.
Case Text:
“Before I joined Didi Ki Rasoi, I was just an ordinary woman; I had no real sense of identity or uniqueness. Didi ki
Rasoi has given me a sense of self-respect as I don’t have to ask anyone for money anymore.”

Leela Devi, employee at Didi Ki Rasoi
Mr. Rahul Kumar, the officer in charge of Bihar’s Rural Livelihoods Promotion Society, also known as
JEEViKA, had just finished his field visits and meeting with women from one of the program’s Self-Help
Group (SHG) in that area. The women he met were self-confident and grateful for increased financial
independence since the initiation of the Didi-ki-Rasoi (DKR) program, an initiative to turn community rural
women into entrepreneurs to cook and deliver good quality homely food to local hospitals and schools.
Additionally, Mr. Kumar received first-hand praise on the quality of food from patients admitted at the
local state hospital.
Impressively, the program had continued to operate through COVID-19 pandemic times, with more than
6 lakhs meals1 made and distributed. Mr. Kumar could see that impressive strides had been made under
the program, with 1725 women empowered economically, and 2,26,092 meals served annually.2 But there
was much more to do. Mr. Kumar was concerned about whether the program would continue unhindered?
Would it receive another round of funding? And how would they scale the program across the state and
possibly to other states in India as well?
JEEViKA (Bihar Rural Livelihoods Promotion Society)
Bihar, India’s third most populous state (Census of India 2011)3

, was largely rural and agrarian. The state’s
heavy reliance on agriculture, coupled with the widespread issue of land fragmentation and landlessness,
contributed to significant seasonal migration amongst marginalized households. Typically, male members
migrated to bigger urban centres in pursuit of better opportunities, leaving behind women and children.
Bihar’s social norms were feudal, which limited economic prospects for women. Deep-rooted societal
taboos acted as a barrier to women’s employment.
To address this situation, Bihar’s state government launched the Bihar Rural Livelihoods Promotion Society
(BRLPS) or JEEViKA, in 2006 with a budget allocation of Rs. 1189.15 Croresi

. The goal was to create an
innovative, scalable, and sustainable model to enhance livelihood opportunities for rural households. It
i Budget allocation for JEEViKA in 2006 was a total of Rs. 1189.15 Crores [Rs. 344 crores + Rs. 845.15
(additional financing)]

JEEViKA-DIDI KI RASOI 2

focused on empowering women by helping them form Self-Help Groups (SHGs) to create self-employment
opportunities and gain access to credit, with the ultimate goal of poverty alleviation. The program was
based on the fundamental belief that aggregating rural women into SHGs could help unleash their full
economic potential.
From its commencement as a small-scale project in 18 blocks across six high-priority districts, JEEViKA had
evolved into a state-wide movement, impacting the lives of over 12.9 million families by April 2023.
Presently, JEEViKA operated in more than 44,000 villages across 534 blocks and 38 districts in Bihar.4 As of
April 2020, JEEVIKA had helped create a network of 1.45 million self-managed SHGs.

5 These SHGs had
emerged as a powerful platform for enhancing women’s livelihoods in various ways, including by
facilitating financial intermediation, access to resources from formal financial institutions, and providing
support for agricultureii and livestockiii through community-based extension services. Moreover, they
enabled women to engage with markets on equitable terms by leveraging economies of scale and
improving awareness on access to government schemes and entitlements. It had fundamentally altered
Bihar’s approach to combating poverty by capitalizing on the abilities of rural women and the institutional
capacities of the state.
Conceptualization of Didi Ki Rasoi (DKR)
Inadequate food quality in Bihar’s hospitals and schools was a pressing issue, and upon investigation, Mr.
Kumar of the state government identified a number of problems in the system. The supply chain and raw
material procurement process was mismanaged. The state’s constrained budget meant that tenders were
allocated to the lowest bidders, leading to poor food quality. Additionally, little oversight had also resulted

in a consistent decline in food quality. Finally, financial discrepancies consistently appeared when third-
party vendors were introduced.

Mr. Kumar launched the ‘Didi ki Rasoi (DKR)’ idea in response to these challenges; to enhance the food
delivery system for district hospitals and schools while empowering rural women in Bihar.
DKR- An Institutional Canteen Model

In 2018, JEEViKA introduced DKR, an innovative model for institutional canteens. DKR was a community-
driven initiative that encouraged rural women in SHGs to establish and operate high-quality, hygienic food

canteens within public hospitals and residential schools. The project was created in partnership with the
State Health Department, and received initial funding from JEEViKA.
DKR proved to be a remarkable success, enabling the provision of quality food at reasonable prices while
simultaneously providing livelihood opportunities to disadvantaged rural women. The commitment of
DKR entrepreneurs to serving customers with hygienic and homely food at subsidized rates had been
unwavering, even in the face of the COVID-19 pandemic.

ii JEEViKA empowers through diverse livelihoods, involving over 50 lakh farmers and 3,148 Agri-
entrepreneurs. All-women Farmer Producer Companies, selling 50,121 MT of Agri-produce, play a

significant role in this economic shift, rooted in rural women's culture.
iii Beyond agriculture, livestock programs under JEEViKA impact 6.75 lakh households, with successes
like the 'Kaushiki Women Milk Producers Company' selling 75,127 litres daily and engaging in poultry
and fisheries activities

JEEViKA-DIDI KI RASOI 3

Initiation of the Model
DKR was initiated with the help of seed capital (Rs. 17,00,000) provided by JEEViKA to establish each
enterprise. Cluster Level Federations (CLFs)iv identified women from the local SHGs to participate in the
program. Women identified under the program underwent a comprehensive 7-day training program
focused on technical and managerial skills, including hygiene, book-keeping, and customer service, to
prepare them to work as DKR entrepreneurs (Refer to Exhibit 1).
Procurement of Raw Materials
Under the DKR system, equipment and utensils were procured by the CLFs. Meanwhile, ingredients and
groceries were sourced from local SHG women-run producer groups, producer companiesv, and rural
retail marts, all of which are promoted by JEEVIKA. This approach ensured that the food served maintained
high standards of quality and nutrition.
Quality and variety of food
The DKR model prioritized delivery of affordable, healthy, and varied home-cooked meals. This
encompassed a morning menu featuring eggs, fruits, and milk, an evening snack of tea and biscuits, and a
lunch and dinner menu consisting of rice, roti,

vi pulses, and seasonal vegetables. In the walk-in canteens,
more popular items were offered on the menu, including local snacks such as Littivii and kachori.
viii

Digital Intervention in the Model
Mr. Kumar introduced the Central Process Monitoring System (CPMS), a fully integrated digital system
designed to capture all transactional data, including data on customers and suppliers, DKR-wise purchases,
inventory, and sales, and production of reports on this data, in every DKR, to track and monitor activity
under the scheme. The system also enabled voucher entry to firms’ balance sheets, financial accounts
systems, and analysis reports. Rural women entrepreneurs specifically trained by Institute of Hotel
Management to handle the process, managed the running of the system. Login IDs granted users at
different levels access to comprehensive data on DKRs, including real-time information on sales, inventory,
profit, margin, best/worst performing DKR, and member transactions. This information in turn enabled

Case Study Title: Mission Youth: A Journey to Empowerment
Case Study Description: The case revolves around Dr. Shahid Iqbal Choudhary, an IAS Officer in Jammu and Kashmir, who faces the challenge of high youth unemployment and disenfranchisement in the state. In response, Dr. Shahid launched the Mission Youth initiative in March 2021 with the goal of transforming the state's youth into ambassadors of peace, prosperity, and development. This initiative included a series of interventions aimed at improving employment, empowerment, and engagement among the youth, securing Rs. 200 crores in state funds for the program. The program was a resounding success, resulting in a significant increase in job creation and youth engagement.
Case Text:
“The journey of last two years has been very exciting, arduous and satisfying. We put in efforts for innovations in
every sector and bringing in measures for sustainability while continuing to upscale the efforts on all fronts for youth
empowerment. Prime Minister’s Award for Excellence in Public Administration-2022 conferred for Mission Youth,
in April 2023, recognises our efforts for laying a strong foundation of an institutional mechanism for youth
empowerment in Jammu and Kashmir, and at the same times puts a greater responsibility on the shoulders of the team
members for excellence in plans for youth engagement and empowerment.”

Dr. Shahid Iqbal Choudharyi
Dr Shahid Iqbal Choudhary was both pleased as well as apprehensive. The flagship youth engagement and
empowerment program “Mission Youth” was launched in Jammu and Kashmir in 2020 to tackle the
program of youth unemployment and disenfranchisement had been successful by all measures. The
program had led to the generation of jobs, and the engagement of young people in areas including
livelihood generation, education and counselling, social engagement, and sports and recreation. Dr Shahid
and his team had overcome key challenges in implementing the program. Still, there was much to do. Dr
Shahid wanted to make sure that he was thinking big enough in expanding the program’s reach and scale
over the coming years; he wanted to touch as many young people as possible. Additionally, he wanted to
ensure that the program was genuinely meeting the needs of the youth and not just meeting few stated
objectives. Finally, he wanted to ensure the continuity of the program. He brought his team in to discuss.
Mission Youth
Jammu & Kashmir (J&K), India’s northernmost state bordering Pakistan, was weighed down by a
challenging paradox. The state’s young population constituted a staggering 69% of its inhabitants,1 but yet
the region grappled with an alarmingly high youth unemployment rate. Finding themselves on the fringes
of the system, the state’s youth were disillusioned and marginalised. This sense of detachment pushed
them towards anti-social and illegal activities, further intensifying the region’s turmoil. Social unrest and
economic underdevelopment became persistent shadows looming over this beautiful land.
It was amid this backdrop that the clarion call for change emerged, leading to the launch of project
“Mission Youth” by IAS Officer Dr. Shahid Iqbal Choudhary. The program’s goals were to combat the
state’s pervasive unemployment crisis, bridge the gap between youth and the state, and reignite the flames
of enthusiasm and confidence in the hearts of J&K’s young populace.
i Dr. Shahid Iqbal Choudhary, IAS, assumed the position of Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Mission Youth
in March 2021. Widely acknowledged for his noteworthy contributions to grassroots developmental
activities, he has been duly recognised and honored by the Government of India.

MISSION YOUTH: A JOURNEY TO EMPOWERMENT 2

The abrogation of Article 370ii in August 2019 made Jammu & Kashmir a union territory, thereby
bringing it under the purview of the central government. This paved the way for the implementation of
national-level schemes in the state, which in turn enabled the inception of Mission Youth in the region.
Mission Youth, a state-run program, aimed to offer a vibrant platform for youth engagement and
empowerment. Its overarching mission and strategy were to mould the state’s youth into ambassadors of
peace, prosperity, and development through a structured framework of interventions. These encompassed
the domains of livelihood generation, education, skill development, cognitive psycho-social counselling,
systematic financial assistance, social recognition, and sports and recreation.
Initiation
Although conceived in 2020, with many months of groundwork to identify thrust areas and
possible collaborators, the program only gained full-fledged momentum after its formal registration as a
specialised agency in March 2021. Dr Shahid Iqbal Choudhary assumed the role of the program’s Chief
Executive Officer (CEO) in March 2021,2 and was tasked with the formulation and delivery of relevant
schemes to identified beneficiaries.
The task was daunting given the lack of confidence among the youth in the state government,
heightened by a combination of political and socio-economic factors. Social unrest in the region instilled a
feeling of insecurity and instability among residents, particularly amongst the youth. Prolonged
uncertainty limited the growth of institutional platforms that addressed the aspirations of the youth, and
the limited interaction between the government and the youth led to a sense of disconnect & discontent
among them. Furthermore, there was limited consultation and low participation of the youth in state
initiatives related to socio-economic development and general governance.
However, Dr Shahid and his team, consisting of select officers from the Jammu and Kashmir
Administrative Service (JKAS), were undeterred, and worked diligently on youth-centric policy
formulation and scheme creation. A few months into their dedicated efforts, they convened the inaugural
meeting of the Governing Body, presided over by the Lieutenant Governor of J&K. In this pivotal meeting,
numerous schemes in the realms of livelihood generation, education, skill development, sports, and more
were approved, with the state sanctioning Rs 200 Crore3

towards the initiative. This momentous occasion
marked the commencement of an exciting and enduring journey for Mission Youth. The Annual Action
Plan, a vital instrument, aided the Mission in aligning resource allocation with policy objectives through
the fiscal year, ensuring maximum impact and desired outcomes.
Implementation
To implement the scheme in a seamless, inclusive and target oriented manner the following steps were
taken by the team:
Step 1 - Engaging with the Youth
The team proactively reached out to around 34944 young individuals in Jammu and Kashmir, seeking their
valuable suggestions, feedback, and reviews. The individuals were chosen systematically to represent a
wide socioeconomic, geographical and political range, and included students, professionals, youth with
disabilities, youth from ethnic minorities and also some young victims of the social unrest. Response and
feedback (Refer exhibit 1) from the youth was carefully considered, leading to the launch of Mission Youth’s
ii Article 370: Provision in the Indian Constitution that granted special autonomous status to the state of
Jammu & Kashmir, allowing it to have its own constitution and exclusive rights over certain matters.

MISSION YOUTH: A JOURNEY TO EMPOWERMENT 3

dedicated portal in April 2021. The portal served as a dynamic platform for the exchange of ideas and
feedback. In addition, a robust grievance redressal system was established, which played a pivotal role in
building trust, enhancing efficiency, and improving the implementation of schemes.
Step 2 - Administrative and Policy Initiatives
Mission Youth took swift and proactive administrative and policy measures to empower the youth. The
first was to establish District Level Task Forces (DLTF) composed of key stakeholders from the government.
This move facilitated the timely approval and funding of individual and community initiatives/projects,
creating a youth-friendly administrative setup at the district level. The second was the approval and
notification of an empowered CEO for Mission Youth, with the goal of expediting decision-making

processes. An Executive Committee, headed by the CEO and comprising department heads, ensured inter-
sectoral coordination, prompt decision-making, and real-time issue resolution. This collaborative effort

played a pivotal role in the implementation of meaningful administrative measures for youth
empowerment.
Step 3 - Youth Volunteer Program
Mission Youth launched a Youth Volunteer Program (Refer Exhibit 2), which established youth clubs across
the state, with the goal of increasing youth engagement and instilling a sense of nation-building amongst
the youth (Refer Exhibit 3). These voluntary youth clubs were envisioned as catalysts for change, bridging
the gap between the community and the government. The clubs were designed to take schemes and
initiatives to every household, ensuring equitable opportunity for participation and broad youth coverage.
Furthermore, they served as channels for community feedback and real-time updates on various fields,
including implementation processes. The range of activities organised by these youth clubs spanned
campaigns against drug addiction, sports events, environmental initiatives like plantation drives, and the
celebration of national days. The state encouraged a sense of healthy competition amongst the clubs to
improve outcomes.
These clubs were established across all districts of Jammu & Kashmir, and extended across every Panchayat
and Urban Ward. More than 5000 youth clubs were created under this initiative, boasted over 1 Lakh active
youth members.5 Each club received a Grant-in-Aid of ₹25,000 for community-oriented activities. During
the fiscal year 2021-22, these youth clubs actively engaged in various community-oriented programs and
services, including awareness campaigns regarding government welfare programs. The state granted a
total of ₹7.17 Crores for the operation of youth clubs across all districts of J&K.
6

Challenges
As the proverb wisely tells us, every noble action carries with it its own share of obstacles to
conquer. Dr Shahid and his team encountered their own array of challenges, but the team’s unwavering
determination led to innovative solutions, as outlined below:
Challenge 1: Establishing an effective administrative framework
Solution
The team met this challenge with dedication and meticulous fiscal planning. A series of capacity-building
workshops were organised for Sub-Divisional Magistratesiii throughout Jammu and Kashmir, preparing
them for their new roles as pivotal figures in the youth volunteer network. Subsequently, financial
iii Sub-Divisional Magistrate is an administrative officer in charge for a district’s sub-division

MISSION YOUTH: A JOURNEY TO EMPOWERMENT 4

provisions for grant-in-aid to Youth Clubs received approval. Following this, the mission set up
comprehensive training sessions for youth volunteers across all districts, alongside the development of an
annual calendar of activities tailored to their needs. These collective efforts successfully transformed youth
clubs into well-established institutions within the state.
Challenge 2: Creation of a Youth Portal
Solution
This initial step for this endeavour began with the development of a software, which enabled the
construction of a youth data repository, encompassing crucial parameters essential for informed policy
formulation and a deeper understanding of youth aspirations, challenges, and requirements by the team.
The team introduced the Youth Portal to the masses through electronic media and disseminated
information about it at the village Panchayat level. Thousands of young individuals enthusiastically
registered on the portal, providing information and articulating their needs and suggestions relating to
skill development, education, entrepreneurship, and various other domains.
The initiative yielded a repository of consistent and dependable youth statistics, vital for both short- and
long-term planning and the implementation of youth engagement and empowerment initiatives. As of the
end of FY 2021-22, this database captured over 80 psycho-social parameters (Refer Exhibit 4), and included
data from more than 1.5 lakh youth.7

It also helped the team establish direct communication channels with

the youth, fostering enhanced engagement.
The Mission Youth team set up a dedicated team to meticulously analyse the Youth data repository, which
resulted in the formulation of a range of youth-centric plans – evidence -based youth empowerment policy,
grounded in a wealth of youth-specific data. The ultimate goal is to craft a targeted database encompassing
various aspects, from demographics to psychometrics, enabling the design of specific programs for the
engagement and empowerment of the youth of Jammu & Kashmir.
Challenge 3: The Psychological Impact of Prolonged Conflict on The Youth
Solution
Recognising the psychological impact of armed insurgency, Mission Youth integrated psycho-social
support services into youth engagement initiatives. Schemes implemented to reverse the negative
psychological impact on the youth included target-specific social recognition counselling, de-radicalisation,
and de-addiction and reintegration programs.
Challenge 4: Instilling Confidence Among Youth in the Scheme
Solution
To bolster confidence amongst the youth that their applications for various programs under Mission Youth
would be seamless and transparent, a dedicated website for the initiative was established. This website
served as a one-stop solution for accessing all of Mission Youth programs, eliminating the need for
applicants to physically visit various government departments and endure the manual processing of their
applications. The introduction of online application submission and processing through the portal marked
the first stride in ensuring transparency and time-bound service delivery. Setting specific timelines for
approvals, sanctions, and the establishment of enterprises or benefits under schemes related to education,
skill development, and sports was also pivotal in building confidence. Additionally, the incorporation of a
grievance redressal mechanism was also integral to confidence-building.

MISSION YOUTH: A JOURNEY TO EMPOWERMENT 5

On the administrative front, District Level Task Forces were established in each of the 20 districts of Jammu
and Kashmir in August 2021, with the Deputy Commissioner of the District assuming the chairmanship
role of each task force.

8 These task forces were created to ensure the effective implementation and

monitoring of Mission Youth Initiatives.
Challenge 5: Optimal Resource Utilisation and Regular Progress Monitoring
Solution
The Mission Youth journey highlighted that simply allocating financial resources to various initiatives was
not sufficient to render a scheme successful. Rather it was more important to devise strategies for optimal
resource utilisation and regular progress monitoring against strategic objectives. Seeing that the mission
encountered several challenges on account of rigid and skewed budgetary allocations, the Mission moved
towards formulating an Annual Action Plan centred on strategic objectives rather than on budget.9
The goal was to ensure that the action plan achieved an alignment of efforts & resources with the actual
vision of Mission Youth, long term continuity and sustainability of policy, adaptability to change as per
actual situational demand, prioritisation of strategic objectives without a subservience to financial
constraints, and the ability to innovate without constraints from financial rigidity. The overarching
objective was to ensure that Mission Youth continuously re-strategised its efforts and realigned its
resources in line with demand. The learning was that while budget considerations are crucial for practical
implementation, strategic orientation of an action plan is more important to ensure that policies are not
solely reactive to short-term financial constraints but are instead part of a broader, purposeful framework.
Key Impacts of the Scheme
As a testimony to the effective implementation of Mission Youth, a youth volunteer from Pulwama, shared:
“We had long felt estranged from the system, but upon becoming a part of this initiative, we now embrace a profound
sense of belonging within the system and governance. We are supporting the government in the drug de-addiction
campaigns in every panchayat of the district and we pledge to make Pulwama a drug free district within next few
months.”
Youth volunteers from the Poonch district were jubilant about their participation in socio-economic
improvements in their district, expressing: “The process of developmental planning and governance apparatus
was never as much participatory as made by this novel initiative of the Government. Our youth volunteers organised
scores of community-oriented activities during last year. We were able to plant more than 30000 saplings including
Chinars in the district in a single go.”
In the Budgam district, youth volunteers were participating actively in the state’s welfare programs. The
COVID-19 vaccination and deworming programs in the district were organised by Youth Volunteers in
collaboration with Health authorities. “We ensured to reach every child of every household in every Panchayat”
said one of the lead members of the Youth Volunteer Program.
Dr. Shahid expressed:
“I think, more than the government schemes offering opportunities, it was all about mutual trust and confidence
building, certainly through our words and actions. The proactive policy landscape offered a very youth-friendly
atmosphere where they were heard as stakeholders and their suggestions and feedback acting as the primary force
driving the youth engagement measures. Transparency in the system right from enrolment to selection under schemes
and a very time-bound decision making is another hallmark under the Mission Youth. Making the processes and

MISSION YOUTH: A JOURNEY TO EMPOWERMENT 6

procedures easy and simpler, end to end assisted services, efficient grievance redressal mechanism and a very
responsive coordinate teamwork were the benchmark right from the beginning of this journey which mainly evolved
towards better institutional mechanisms over the period. Community outreach and optimum communication
strategies led to a sustainable response system for youth aspirations.”
Armed with this robust foundation, Dr Shahid and his team embarked on the further implementation of
various Mission Youth schemes in the financial year 2021-22 ( Refer Exhibit 5). Through his relentless
dedication, Mission Youth accomplished the commendable milestone of providing self-employment
opportunities to approximately 35,000 young individuals during the fiscal year 2021-22.10 It successfully
engaged millions of youths in areas including livelihood generation, education and counselling, social
engagement, and sports and recreation (Refer Exhibit 6). The program’s evident success was a testament to
the power of a visionary initiative and the resilience of the youth.
The Way Ahead
Mission Youth was awarded the prestigious Prime Minister’s Award for Excellence in Public
Administration in April 2023,iv in acknowledgement of the team’s remarkable efforts in establishing a
robust institutional framework for youth empowerment in Jammu and Kashmir (Refer Exhibit 7). This
honour also placed greater responsibility on the team to continue to excel in future plans for youth
engagement and empowerment. Dr Shahid and his team set out the following initiatives to enhance the
Mission’s reach in coming years:
• Revitalisation and Strengthening of Youth Clubs: A top priority involved the revitalisation and
fortification of the 5000 Youth Clubs established in every Panchayat and Urban Ward. These clubs,
which served as the eyes and ears of local administration, would receive additional incentives and

• Awareness Campaign Against Drug Abuse: An innovative approach, involving storytelling and

Case Study Title: En Uru – The Tribal Heritage Village of Wayanad
Case Study Description: The case is situated in Wayanad, a Northern district in the state of Kerala, where the scheduled tribe (ST) community comprises a high share of the local population, yet is economically marginalised. The local officer in charge, Mr. Nair, comes up with an innovative way to generate income for the state while also uplifting the members of the local tribal community. He comes up with the idea of setting up En Uru – a model heritage village – a tourist site in which tribes can be employed while generating revenues for themselves and the district. He puts in place training programs to ensure that ST members are able to contribute to the project.
Case Text:
“Purity, perseverance and patience are three essentials of success, and above all love, overcome all obstacles.”
Swami Vivekanandai

Mr. Prasanth Nairii

, sub-collector in the Wayanad district of Northern Kerala, was contemplating. He had
successfully conceptualized and built the “En Uru” project, a model heritage village tourist site to create
employment and income for the marginalized local tribal community. Members of the local tribe had
benefited tremendously, with increase in the number of jobs created with a rise in average annual incomes.
The local community was pleased with the progress, and tourists were flocking to the site. But Mr. Nair
had a number of concerns on his mind. He knew that he had been the champion and driving force behind
the project’s conception and execution. Would it continue to grow and secure funding even in his absence?
What additional steps could he take to secure the livelihoods of the tribal members who worked in En Uru
and their family members? Should they think about setting up affordable housing or a local school for the
children? Finally, how should he think about scaling and replicating the project at other sites within the
state, and possibly across other states in India? For a project to be truly successful, it needed to be scalable.
Project En Uru
Nestled in the Western Ghats of Northern Kerala, Wayanad was a picturesque district, strategically
positioned with robust connectivity. Despite constituting 18.53% of the state’s Scheduled Tribe (ST)
population, well above the 1.45% average across other parts of the state (Refer Exhibit 1), the district’s tribals
faced socio-economic discrimination. The then sub-collector Mr. Prasanth Nair, recognizing this paradox,
delved into the root causes for this issue. He discovered that tribals in the district were exploited as
agricultural labourers, and often trapped in cycles of debt and poverty. Although tourism had boomed in
Wayanad between 2005-10, the ensuing prosperity had largely bypassed the ST community as they lacked
land rights and skills required in the hospitality sector. Mr. Nair, introduced the innovative “En Uru” (My
Place) project with the goal of bridging this gap, addressing the needs of both tourists and tribals by
creating employment opportunities. En Uru, meaning “My Place,” embodied an inclusive development
initiative designed for, by, and of the tribal community in Wayanad, Kerala.
i Swami Vivekananda was an Indian Hindu monk, philosopher, author, religious teacher, and the chief
disciple of the Indian religious leader Ramakrishna.
ii An inquisitive and hardworking Indian administrator, Mr. Prasanth Nair, coming from a law background,
was first posted as a sub collector in Wayanad. He served there in various capacities in diverse sectors
including Tourism, Taxation, Roads, Water supply, Skill Development etc. He also headed two World Bank
Projects, viz. Jalanidhi & Kerala State Transport Project (KSTP)

EN URU – THE TRIBAL HERITAGE VILLAGE OF WAYANAD 2
Initiation of the Project
The core idea of linking tourism with tribal livelihood originated when Mr. Nair, the Sub-Collector in the
area, had the idea of transforming the Managing Director's residence in the local Priyadarshini Tribal
Resettlement Tea-Estate Cooperative, into a tourist resort named “Wayanad Tea-County.” The Bungalow
was converted into rentable rooms, furnished with basic amenities, and adorned with Mr. Nair’s wildlife
photography, and offered to tourists, leading to the creation of a successful revenue-generating model.
Despite its premium pricing, bookings at the Priyadarshini Tea-County thrived, bringing a share of the
booming tourism industry to tribal families for the first time.
Efficient Revenue Utilization
Mr. Nair channelled the revenue earned to the local ST community. The project addressed the nutritional
needs of tribal families through the provision of daily free noon meals to the 300 odd families of the estate
workers from the funds generated from Wayanad Tea County. Mr. Nair also mandated that the project
employ members of the tribal community in roles such as guards, watchmen, guides, cooks, and gardeners,
to ensure employment and income generation for the community. To enable tribals to work in these roles
and interact with tourists, the initiative offered them free English language training and skilling. Apart
from the nutritional improvement amongst the estate workers, employee absenteeism reduced and the
estate made record production and moved into profit after decades.
Development of En Uru Model
In 2010, the non-tribals in Wayanad capitalized upon the booming premium homestay tourism sector as it
was a good source of employment and income, but opportunities for the tribal community were minimal.
The Sub-Collector now wanted to expand the Wayanad Tea County experience and target the rest of tribal
population outside the Priyadarsini Estate premises. Mr. Nair expanded the program’s vision to include a
tribal heritage village project loosely modelled on Dilli Haat concept but on a massive scale. The project
was envisioned literally as a model village site, and included an organic farm, a warehouse, a tribal market,
a cafeteria and restaurant, a hotel, a shopping complex, a community and conference hall, an open stage
with a light and sound system, an art gallery, a museum, tribal huts, and entertainment activities such as
archery.
In November 2010, the project proposal secured funding approval from the Schedule caste & Schedule tribe
Development Department, Government of Kerala, obtaining Rs. 3 crores for its initiation.1 En Uru became
a separate society, operating independently from the Priyadarshini Tea-Estate Cooperative, and was
registered under Section-21 of the Society Registration Act 1860. The society included Urukutam, the Gram
Sabha of tribes. The Sub Collector was the president of the society. Meantime, Mr. Nair completed his
tenure as Sub Collector and moved to Thiruvananthapuram but he continued to champion the cause of
tribal development through En Uru.
Challenges
Mr. Nair and his successors faced several challenges in getting the En Uru project off the ground.
To begin with, construction in Wayanad’s rugged terrain was extremely challenging. The Sub Collector
enlisted an architect to make a plan for the identified land, and appointed a Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
to oversee the project. The survey work commenced in 2012, and construction was initially entrusted to

EN URU – THE TRIBAL HERITAGE VILLAGE OF WAYANAD 3
KRITCO,iii and later completed by Wayanad district Nirmithi Kendra. In 2015, 'En Uru' secured registration
under 12A and 80G of the Income Tax Act.2 The architect’s plans were submitted to the State Tourism
Department, which sanctioned funds in 2016, leading to the resumption of work in 2017.
Unfortunately, project construction faced multiple setbacks. Wayanad’s territory was disaster prone, and
the project faced a major setback in 2018 when a massive flood washed away all construction that had taken
place since initiation in 2010. Another flood in 2019 further stalled progress. Builders were forced to start
the project afresh in 2018.3 Environmental concerns added further complexity to project construction. In
December 2018, the Forest Department issued a Stop Memo,iv citing the project’s proximity to a forest area.
Although this memo was withdrawn in 2019, another resurfaced in 2021, slowing progress once again.
Despite these obstacles, the project was taken forward, thanks to a meticulous study of the topography, the
involvement of the Geological Survey of India, and persistent construction efforts by Nirmiti. In a review
meeting in February 2022, the Chief Secretary of Kerala, revoked all Stop Memos from the Forest
Department.
Securing financing for project construction was another challenge. Funding strategies included seeking
corporate CSR funding for ticket counters, electric rickshaws, waste bins, etc. Corporations like the
Mahindra Group, the Kerala Shipping Corporation, and the Aspirational District Programmev contributed
CSR funds, sustaining the project’s momentum even amid the challenges posed by the Covid-19 pandemic.
The ‘En Uru Tribal Heritage Village’ was formally inaugurated on June 4, 2022, coinciding with Mr. Nair's
transfer as Special Secretary to the SC & ST Development Department. An enthusiastic Mr. Nair said, “It
was like ‘Ghar Wapsi’ for me. I have been nurturing ‘En Uru’ from outside for about a Yug, i.e. 12 years. Now the
project is under my domain of works”
Major Highlights of En Uru
The En Uru project constituted several highlights that made it a unique destination:
1. Interpretation Centre - Replica of Tribal Colony: En Uru's main attraction was its interpretation
centre which featured prototypes of seven types of huts, showcasing the building types and
materials used by early generations of tribes in the region. (Refer Exhibit 2)
2. Tribal Emporium: The largest showroom of tribal products in Kerala, was located in En Uru. This
tribal emporium was owned and operated by the Tribal Cooperative Marketing Federation of India
(TRIFED), under the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Government of India.
3. Cultural Events: En Uru revitalized Wayanad’s fading tribal art forms, providing a platform for
struggling performers to showcase and preserve their traditional culture. The open-air theatre
hosted various performances and art forms by tribes from Kerala (Refer Exhibit 3).
4. Tribal Market: Within the village, a tribal market showcased and sold products such as millets,
wild honey, and bows and arrows, generating revenue for the tribal community.

one person or department to another in an organization

Key Impact
The “En Uru” project created significant positive impact. Firstly, it served as a catalyst for social and human
capital development among the tribal community in Wayanad. Mr. Nair took proactive steps towards
capacity building amongst the local tribal community, providing training in various sub-trades such as
guiding, bird watching, photography, and archery. A government order was issued in 2023 after he took
over as Special Secretary in the Department for skill training for positions like Managers, HR Managers,
Tour Guides, and Marketing Managers within the society. Approximately Rs. 3.00 Cr was allocated for this
capacity-building initiative.
Secondly, the project served not only as a heritage village but also as a source of both direct and indirect
employment for the local tribal community. The village engaged tribal members on a contractual and daily
wage basis. The tribal community managed stalls, cafeterias, and other services. The project generated an
average daily income of Rs 40,000.4 Additionally, approximately 35-40 tribals, equally split between men
and women, participated in daily project activities, earning around Rs.1000 per day.5
Ancillary opportunities including in garages, parking management, and small shops further enhanced
tribal livelihoods and income (Refer Exhibit 5).
By 2023, Mr. Nair’s vision of creating a 25-acre large6 must-visit destination in En Uru had come to fruition,
and come to seamlessly form a vital element of any Wayanad excursion. The project played a pivotal role
in propelling tourism development in the region, augmenting Wayanad’s allure. En Uru had witnessed a
surge in tourist arrivals since its formal opening in June 2022, attracting around 5,000 visitors in initial
months. To date, En Uru has hosted nearly 160,000 visitors,7 a testament to its growing popularity.
The Way Ahead
Looking ahead, Mr. Nair had a few plans and ideas for the projects, and also some concerns. His first
priority was to integrate Public-Private Partnership (PPP) models within the village to ensure innovation
and efficiency while prioritizing local tribal employment. He also planned to introduce initiatives like rope
ways and tent accommodations to provide eco-friendly and economically viable tourist activities. These
projects not only addressed tourist needs but also served as platforms for tribal employment, training, and
engagement, fostering a sustainable and inclusive approach to tourism in Wayanad. But beyond these
projects, Mr. Nair was concerned about the long-term future of the project. What additional steps could he
take to secure the livelihoods of the tribal members who worked in En Uru and their family members?
Should they think about setting up affordable housing or a local school for the children? Finally, how
should he think about scaling and replicating the project at other sites within the state, and possibly across
other states in India? For a project to be truly successful, it needed to be scalable.

Case Study Title: Risk mitigation in public infrastructure projects: The case of Rewa Solar Power Plant
Case Study Description: The Rewa Solar Project (RUMSL) case offers an authoritative example of public-private partnerships in India and helps discern how risk can be mitigated to ensure the success of a PPP model. An innovation by IAS Manu Srivastava, Rewa was financed in a way to ensure that the project did not rely on viable gap funding (VGF), offered by the Government of India while attracting procurers. RUMSL was commissioned on January 3, 2020, and was formally dedicated to the nation by Prime Minister, Mr Narendra Modi, on July 10, 2020. However, right from the beginning, Manu Srivastava faced a spectrum of challenges such as identifying donors, maintaining an attractive tariff rate without VGF, acquiring land, and identifying procurers. By studying these challenges and the solutions adopted by Manu Srivastava, learners can learn the innovative ways through which risk can be mitigated in a large project such as RUMSL.

Challenges & Their Resolution
Letting go of VGF
Many roadblocks obstructed Mr. Srivastava’s path, but with strategic thinking and sturdy planning, he
overcame them as they emerged. The first challenge was the lack of subsidy or VGF from the Government
of India; no solar project had been set up in India without it till then. The Government of India had
authorised RUMSL to make decisions and perform duties that were otherwise in SECI’s domain, on the
condition that RUMSL would be ineligible for VGF. For RUMSL, achieving SECI’s VGF subsidised tariff of
₹ 5.0 seemed feasible as, during an earlier bidding experience, Mr. Srivastava had received a tariff of ₹ 5.05
without any support. Mr. Srivastava thought that, since they were developing a solar park, achieving ₹ 5
would not be too much of a risk. Subsequently, GoI reduced the target tariff to ₹ 4.50/unit, thus setting a
stiff target for RUMSL. Mr. Srivastava made the strategic choice of letting go of VGF, which transferred
decision-making authority for the project to RUMSL, thus enjoying freedom of implementation and doing
innovation in the project from concept to commissioning, as well as bearing the undivided risk of any
possibility of failure.

Plug and play
Solar projects have a huge demand for land - one MW solar project needs almost two hectares of land. In
most countries, including India, land belongs to the sovereign. In view of the same, it reduces the
uncertainties for the project developer if the government provides the land. This was done by developing
a solar park with a ‘plug and play’ facility, wherein the developer just comes, puts the panels in and starts
evacuating power. As a part of the same ‘plug and play’, infrastructure for the evacuation of solar power
was developed by RUMSL. This is crucial since the development of the evacuation infrastructure takes
longer than the deployment of solar panels, and thus the development of the evacuation infrastructure
should start before the developer is chosen.
Land Arrangement
A big challenge was arranging the massive contiguous land parcels and obtaining consent from
landowners for the solar park. Being a time-consuming exercise, that could escalate project costs and create
uncertainties for the project, Mr. Srivastava and his team chose government land on a barren plateau that
was once used as an army firing range. The remaining land, intermittent within the boundaries of the
identified project site, was bought from private landowners as per prevalent government norms on a free
consent basis.
To make the contracts fair and reduce the risk of the developer, it was provided that day zero of the
developer’s commitments would start, not with the signing of the PPA, but with 90% of the land being
handed over to the developer. This was another milestone set by RUMSL for the solar industry in India.
Resource Mobilisation
Existing solar parks required the developers to pay an upfront charge to enable the SPPD to develop the
infrastructure. RUMSL realised that it would be easier for the developers to pay the park development
charges over a period (back loading of costs) from their revenues realised through the sale of solar power,
rather than paying them upfront. Mr. Srivastava decided to mobilise the funds for the development of park
infrastructure, including transmission infrastructure, from the World Bank. After a thorough assessment,
the WB sanctioned a loan of ₹ 7.3 billion (US$ 100 million) at a concessional interest rate for infrastructure
development.

Payment Security
Bidders had legitimate concerns about the regular payment of energy bills being made by the MP
DISCOMs, who were to be the procurers for 3/4th of the energy. To address this challenge, an innovative
Three-tier Payment Security Mechanism was developed, for the first time in India. It constituted as the first
tier – Letter of Credit by DISCOM, as the Second tier - Payment Security Fund (PSF): created without any
budgetary allocation from MNRE with support from IREDA22, and as the Third tier - Guarantee of
Government of MP23

. This gave comfort to the bidders about the payment risk from DISCOMs in spite of

their moderate credit rating.
Contractual terms
The heart of a Public Private Partnership (PPP) is the contract determining the relationship between the
contracting parties for the entire duration of the contract. The terms in the contract need to address all
conceivable situations that might present themselves over the life of the contract and must safeguard
interests of concerned stakeholders. For a project, where the entire investment is being made upfront by
the developer and their only revenue realisation is over a 25-year project cycle, it is extremely important
that the risks and the uncertainties of the developers’ investment are mitigated. This was ensured by
RUMSL by carefully developing the contractual terms. To get better expertise in development of contracts,
IFC was made the transaction advisor which took the services of legal firm Trilegal. The pre-bid meetings
were taken very seriously and the suggestions from bidders were used to strengthen bid documents.
Usually in India, bid documents once issued are considered final, but RUMSL took a conscious decision to
use the pre-bid meetings to take inputs from bidders and make suitable changes in the project documents,
if the changes strengthened the bid structure, were fair to all bidders and were made substantially before
the bidding date.
Addressing Information Asymmetry
In most projects, the bidders suffer a lot of ‘Information Asymmetry’ with respect to the bidding authority.
Sometimes, the information is given in exchange of favours to preferred bidders. RUMSL addressed the

issue of ‘information asymmetry’ pertaining to complete bid process and documentation, especially, with
respect to availability of land by creating a data room which showed the total project boundary and the
land arranged by RUMSL. As the bidding progressed, the map started filling up and, on the day of the
bidding, 97% of the land was available with RUMSL. Interested parties were also encouraged to visit the

To address the concern of the developers regarding the evacuation infrastructure coming up in time with

Structured Planning & Risk Mitigation
The broad aim of the above steps was to mitigate risk. This allowed developers to remove the cost allocation
attributable to these risks from their quoted tariff, leading to a lower tariff. Governments and project
developers bear a responsibility to deliver projects, including inter alia renewable energy projects, where
the developers’ risks are sufficiently mitigated. Setting up such viable projects has multi-fold advantages.
First, they attract serious developers to countries that otherwise would be perceived as too risky. Second,
they encourage sovereign, pension and trust funds to invest in such de-risked projects, since these groups
of investors are keener on assured returns than windfall profits. And third, the low risk profile would allow
debt structuring at lower rates.
Viable renewable energy projects, protected from uncertainties in the host country, would attract
international investors beyond OECD countries. This would boost capital flow from pension, trust, and
sovereign funds that are usually invested in traditional sectors in developed countries with low returns.
Capital becomes available internationally at low rates and for long periods, features that perfectly suit the
RE sector with their typically long-term (25 years) Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). Debt, that
constitutes around 70% of the project finance, would be available for sufficiently de-risked projects at
reasonably low rates; debtors are especially risk-averse since they never get the upside of a project, and
their interest is limited to preserve the repayment of their loan.
Risk mitigation is even more important for the renewable energy sector, since almost the entire investment
in these projects must be made prior to their commissioning and the revenue expenditure is limited to
operation and maintenance. Admittedly, risks can never be completely extinguished, especially for a
period of 25 years, which invites uncertainty. However, it is the responsibility of the project proponent to
anticipate and mitigate those risks and uncertainties to the extent possible, though admittedly all risk and
uncertainties can never be extinguished. This could be largely made possible through careful project
structuring and incorporating appropriate provisions in the PPA, something that RUMSL focused on- and
the success of Rewa is on this account.
