Case Study Title: Mainstreaming renewable energy: The case of Rewa Solar Rooftop Installation Project
Case Study Description: The Madhya Pradesh solar rooftop installation case is a good example to illustrate how to make a project an attractive proposition for key stakeholders. The case can help us understand how de-risking a project, addressing information asymmetry, mitigating risks, and ensuring transparency in the project cycle drives increased and informed participation.The case unfolds against the challenge of increasing solar rooftop installations to meet the state’s solar energy production targets under the National Solar Mission. Mr Manu Srivastava, head of Madhya Pradesh Urja Vikas Nigam Limited, is tasked with resolving the puzzle of why uptake is low despite incentives offered by the government. Through addressing key stakeholder concerns, efficient project structuring, and process innovations in a market-based financing model, the climate agenda is taken forward.
Case Text:
“The Sun has been worshipped as a life-giver for our planet since ancient times. The industrial ages gave us the
understanding of sunlight as an energy source.”

Ministry of New and Renewable Energy1

Introduction
After tremendous success of Rewa 750 MW solar park in spring of 2017, Mr. Manu Srivastava, IAS, sat in
his Bhopal office overlooking lush, green and clean campus, wondering how to deepen the uptake of solar
in smaller segments, i.e., rooftop installations, in his state (Exhibit 1). He was the Principal Secretary of
Renewable Energy in Madhya Pradesh and the Managing Director of Madhya Pradesh Urja Vikas Nigam
Limited (MPUVNL)—the state’s nodal agency for renewable energy. As its head, he was in-charge of the
driving energy generation and use from non-conventional sources across sizes and segments.
Coincidentally, solar rooftop installations were part of the new initiative of the National Solar Mission,
under which MPUVNL had to produce 2.2 gigawatts (GW) of solar power by 20222 aligned to the then
national solar aspiration of 100 GW. Mr. Srivastava’s concern was that if the State targets for solar power
generation were to be met by the set deadline, the adoption of solar rooftop installations had to be ensured
quickly and on a large scale. And that was his problem statement, which he worked on tirelessly over the
next couple of months to create another landmark in Indian renewable industry.
In sharp contrast to the solar projects on rooftops of buildings, Mr. Srivastava had recently successfully
implemented a solar project at the other end of the spectrum, a 750 MW project at Rewa, spread over more
than 15 square kilometres. The project had proved to be the first project in the country to bring down the
price of solar energy below that of coal-based project. He envisioned to promote Solar Rooftop on the
similar principles of risk mitigation3 and project innovation that had led to the pioneering success of Rewa.
The Puzzle of Low Uptake
Mr. Srivastava faced a puzzling situation. Despite the state of Madhya Pradesh having adopted numerous
consumer and investor-friendly measures to promote rooftop solar installations, the uptake was
surprisingly low. Solar installations were exempted from liability of Value Added Tax and entry tax on
solar installation equipment, as also electricity duty on generation of electricity for the first 10 years.
Additionally, solar installations could get a subsidy of 25 per cent from the Government of India and
additional subsidy of 20 per cent from the Government of Madhya Pradesh4

. Thus, on the face of it, the
solar installation policy seemed attractive as it allowed solar installations at a subsidised cost and ensured

MAINSTREAMING RENEWABLE ENERGY: THE CASE OF SOLAR ROOFTOP INSTALLATION
PROJECT

2

long-term savings. Mr. Srivastava, however, identified the limitation of the current financial model of
Capex and the sub-optimal implementation of Opex (Exhibits 2 and 3), as significant barriers to increased
solar rooftop installation uptake.5
1. The Capex model: MPUVNL has been undertaking projects for government institutions under the
Capital Expenditure (Capex) model. In the Capex model, the most common in India, the customer must
pay for the installation, operation, and maintenance costs of the solar installation. The problems with this
model were the requirement of high upfront investment by the customer and regular maintenance. Under
this model, investments were dependent on Central subsidy (25%), State government subsidy (20%) and
customer contribution that accounted for 50-55 percent of the total investment. Consequently, institutions
did not demonstrate much interest, as they were either unable or unwilling to invest the necessary funds.
In projects that were set up, the Operation & Management (O&M) has been a challenge, since solar projects
have a life of 25 years and many Capex projects, especially those with battery, were in disuse beyond the
usual 5-year maintenance period.
2. The Opex model: The alternative Operational Expenditure (Opex) model enables private sector
investment for setting up and maintaining the rooftop solar project by a developer called “Renewable
Energy Service COmpany (RESCO); hence, the model is also called RESCO model. This is a Public Private
Partnership (PPP) model, wherein the consumer pays the developer only for the electricity produced every
month. The Opex model requires no capital investment from the consumer. If the project is structured well,
the bills generated are substantially lower than grid electricity bills and, hence, there are savings from Day
one. O&M of the project is the responsibility of developer for all 25 years. Payment to the RESCO developer
is only on energy supplied, and there is no minimum charge or fixed payment to the developer; this
transaction structure guarantees optimum production from the project and continued benefit to
beneficiaries. The relationship of the RESCO developer and the consumer is behind the meter, implying
that any excess power belongs to the consumer to be sold to the grid at terms decided by the state electricity
regulator. This insulates the developer from the risk of regulatory uncertainty.
National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC), Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI)6 and others had
tried this Opex or RESCO model. However, these projects suffered from ‘information asymmetry’
7 and the
RESCO developers8 knew nothing apart from the name of the state when they got the contract for that
respective state. The project gave the RESCO developer the responsibility of marketing to government
institutions. Thus, the RESCO developer was expected to convince the government institutions to agree to
the RESCO project. Further, the RESCO developers had no idea of the nature of building, assessment of
solar capacity and the requirement of capital investment, before the bidding. Hence, there was poor
investor confidence in these projects, leading to comparatively high tariff during bidding, rendering this
model for solar installations unattractive for customers. Further, conversion of tenders into actual projects
was not very high, since the RESCO developers found it difficult to convince government institutions to
sign-in. It was considered necessary by Mr. Srivastava to adopt a different strategy.
Developing the Solar Rooftop Project: Onboarding Stakeholders
Mr. Srivastava made the decision to move forward with the Opex model, given that it enabled “Zero
Investment, Savings from Day one, Moving towards Net Zero.” However, it was crucial to overcome the
deficiencies9

in the present implementation of the project. There was a dire need to gain customer trust and
investor confidence. Additionally, considering the project scale and the stakes involved, arranging funds
for developers and efficient implementation of the project was crucial. Hence, he reached out to the World
Bank (WB), the Asian Development Bank (ADB)

10 and the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency
(IREDA) for funding. The World Bank and the International Solar Alliance agreed to give technical
assistance for the project. For successful implementation of the project, Mr Srivastava had to bring on board
the key stakeholders (Table 1).

PROJECT

3

the project

The most prominent stakeholders who needed to be onboarded encountered challenges with the solar
rooftop intervention. Both the beneficiaries and the developers had their own set of concerns.
Stakeholder Concerns
1. For RESCO, interactions with the Government were a different experience. Conventional PPP
models gave RESCO the responsibility of convincing government organisations to benefit from the
project. RESCO developers were largely private players and found it challenging to approach and
convince government officers. Some government organisations wanted to change the conditions of the
contract; since the interaction between the RESCO and the government organisation was, by design,
after the bid, this posed additional challenges.
At the stage of the bidding, the developers had no clue as to how many and which projects they would
be getting once they enter the state. They did not know the sizes of the projects or their locations,
leaving them clueless about the capital or effort needed. Further, developers had limited information
about potential beneficiaries, their paying capacity or creditworthiness, or even site suitability and
sustainability, which made financing a major concern and risk. Given that the project had to be
managed for long-term, a guaranteed return on investment was crucial to the developer. The
uncertainties regarding assured returns and the exhaustive process translated into low investor
confidence, high tariff rates, and consequently low enrolment.
2. For potential beneficiaries, there was no RESCO interested. Many government organisations
found the idea of RESCO appealing, since it envisaged no investment and promised savings all through
the project life. It seemed to be a project with no risk and all benefits, but there were no RESCO players

MAINSTREAMING RENEWABLE ENERGY: THE CASE OF SOLAR ROOFTOP INSTALLATION
PROJECT

4

who were willing to take up individual buildings. Developers were interested only in projects with a
certain scale, and they were not keen on individual projects.
Further, two unforeseen scenarios cropped up, that added to the complexity and threatened to shake
investor confidence. Close to the bidding date for the project, the Government of India imposed a safeguard
duty11 on solar panels and cells, a notification which the Odisha High Court subsequently stayed. This
caused ambiguity and led to uncertainty over the existing project cost proposals in the bids. Another issue
that emerged was the timing of the assembly elections, which were close to the bidding dates.
Apprehensions emerged about the electoral Model Code of Conduct coming into force and derailing the
project bids. Mr. Srivastava and his team effectively dealt with these challenges so that bidding and project
implementation could occur successfully. The barriers to take up the project and its implementation
required an urgent resolution. The team introduced several initiatives to improve investor confidence.
Risk Mitigation in the Opex Model
The team implemented the solar project through the Opex model instead of the Capex model used by the

MPUVNL until then. It was realised that government organisations rarely had resources, technical know-
how and the willingness to invest in solar rooftop; in the few cases that the happy coincidence materialised,

the O&M of the project would be a challenge and the project would often be dysfunctional within a few
years. On the other hand, the reward structure was so configured in the Opex or RESCO model that the
project was likely to perform optimally for the project life of 25 years. The revenue stream of the RESCO
developer was only and only on the solar energy generated, and this ensured that good quality panels were
installed, and the project was maintained to ensure maximum production.
Additionally, MPUVNL adopted a hands-on approach to mitigate investor risk in terms of marketing by
identifying government organisations as potential customers and convincing them of the benefits of
RESCO as also the contract terms. This eliminated the marketing effort and risk that developers bore in the
earlier RESCO projects in the country. To achieve this, MPUVNL targeted government organisations with
the capacity to benefit from large-scale solar rooftop projects. It assessed the potential for large-scale
installation and the organisation’s credibility to minimise developer’s risk12. MPUVNL reached out to all
departments with the message13 that the programme would entail no investment by the beneficiary and
there would be assured savings right from the first day. MPUVN also collected data on rooftop availability

and solar energy generation potential at all the selected sites; this eliminated the effort in developing pre-
engineering design that developers had to undertake in the earlier RESCO projects in the country and

facilitated bidding by developers14

. MPUVNL also developed contractual terms that guarded the interests
of both consumers and developers; the contractual terms were substantially modified based on inputs
received from potential bidders during pre-bid meetings organised in Bhopal and New Delhi.
Mr. Srivastava and his team envisioned the RESCO project as an ideal PPP project, wherein there was no
adversarial contractual position between the two parties, rather both the parties worked in their mutual
interest to make the project successful15. The government organisations would need to only pay for the
power consumed through the rooftop solar installations, at substantial discount to the DISCOM rates16
,
during the entire 25-year contract period; their saving would increase by maximising the solar production.
Developers were assured adequate returns, even at lower bid rates, by mitigating their risks. Basis historical
tariff analysis, solar energy tariffs were pitched with an annual increase of 3%, against 4-5% witnessed with
DISCOMs.17 Thus, the contract became an attractive proposition for both the developer and the customer
throughout the project's life cycle18, as a well-structured PPP project should be. The project's operation and
maintenance were the developer's responsibility, who was paid based only and only on the power
generated, and without any minimum charge or fixed payment. Thus, developers had to ensure the proper
functioning of the installations to keep receiving revenue. The developer's investment was safeguarded
through provisions in the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA), which was carefully drafted. It also specified

MAINSTREAMING RENEWABLE ENERGY: THE CASE OF SOLAR ROOFTOP INSTALLATION
PROJECT

5

equitable terms of severance of the contract and the penalties involved. The steps followed while preparing
the PPA included floating the tender, discussions in pre-bid meetings, seeking suggestions from all
stakeholders, and then modifying the tender document accordingly.
MPUVN’s approach to the Opex model was fundamentally distinct from the typical practice prevalent in
the country, which were quite like the proverbial Russian roulette. MPUVNL sought to correct limitations
in this model and the project was initiated by persuading beneficiaries to enrol. Over 690 institutions were
identified by MPUVNL.19 They were presented the concept of ‘Zero investment, Savings from Day one,
Moving towards Net Zero’. When enough government organisations had expressed interest in the project,
a bid was issued exclusively for pre-identified organisations.
Subsequently, project grouping was done based on the profile of ultimate paying entity20, viz., central or
state government and capacity of the project, thereby ensuring that each group has similar projects21. For
example, all government colleges spread all over the state with individual capacity ranging from 8 kW to
80 kW constituted one group, while universities of the state with individual capacity ranging from 1 MW
to 1.5 MW formed another group. Bidding was separately undertaken for each group, and winner had to
implement all the projects in that group. This enabled better risk profiling, good economies of scale,
efficient material procurement, project execution planning and efficient financing22
.

A data-room23 was created with complete details of the project sites, including building layout, rooftop
availability and even a pre-engineering design, so that the bidders, sitting in their offices, were aware of
the costs involved in each project at the click of a mouse, and had the confidence to offer competitive rates.
The development of the data-room was done by the World Bank under its Technical Assistance programme
at no cost to MPUVN or the bidders.
Tied loan was arranged, so that the Selected Bidder would get an assured loan at a pre-determined rate,
subject to due diligence. The tied loan was made available from State Bank of India (under World Bank’s
line of credit), Punjab National Bank (under ADB24 line of credit) and Indian Renewable Energy
Development Agency (IREDA). World Bank and State Bank of India (SBI), Asian Development Bank (ADB)
and Punjab National Bank (PNB), and IREDA pre-cleared the terms of the Power Purchase Agreement, to
ensure that the Project addresses their concerns. The terms and conditions of the loan were added as part
of the RESCO RfP.
MPUVN organised pre-bid meetings in Bhopal and New Delhi to inform the prospective bidders about the
innovations being implemented and to take their feedback on the project documents. Government
organisations usually tend to ignore majority of suggestions received in pre-bid meetings, so that these
become merely formalities. Rather, the philosophy followed by MPUVN was to accept the request for
change in the contractual condition, if it was rational, fair to all bidders and beneficial to the end-user in
the long run. The feedback received from bidders went a long way to ensure that the contractual terms in

the project ensured investment of the developer and enhanced their enthusiasm for the project. The pre-
bid meetings were organised with funding support from the World Bank and assistance of the International

Solar Alliance25
.

Safeguard duty on solar panels and cells was imposed by Government of India on 30th July 2018. With only
a few days left for the last date of submission of the bids, the implementation of the order was stayed by
Odisha High Court. In such a situation, there was lack of clarity if the expected imposition of Safeguard

duty after the bid date would be covered as a ‘change of law’ event. The bidders were concerned if pass-
through would be allowed to them as impact of the safeguard duty on the cost of systems under the ‘change

of law’ provision. MPUVNL promptly came up with a Corrigendum and a Clarification explaining its
impact on tariff and made it clear that it shall be provided as a pass through if safeguard duty is affected
after the bid submission date. The Clarification went on to make it clear that the expected imposition of
25% Safeguard Duty, after the bid due date, would lead to increase in tariff by 5.2%, thus giving clarity to

MAINSTREAMING RENEWABLE ENERGY: THE CASE OF SOLAR ROOFTOP INSTALLATION
PROJECT

6

the bidders26 and consequently they did not consider it necessary to build in the impact of expected
imposition of safeguard duty in their bid price.
Reception & launch
The project met with huge investor enthusiasm; this was an easy litmus for any good tender. MP’s RESCO
- 1 tender attracted 31 international and domestic bidders27 who oversubscribed its rooftop tender capacity
by 700%. MP’s RESCO - 2 tender was oversubscribed by 630%
The RESCO project got the lowest ever tariff in India28. The lowest tariff achieved over all groups was ₹
1.38 per unit, with 3% annual increment. Various categories of government organisations got solar power
at rates substantially lower than DISCOMs tariff, ranging from ₹1.38 to ₹2.35 per unit with an annual
escalation of 3%.
The successful tender results were followed by expeditious signing of PPAs. On 29th September 2018, a
record number of 427 PPAs were signed between various educational institutions and Selected Bidders at
Academy of Administration, Bhopal. The Chief Minister, along with the Director General of International
Solar Alliance (ISA), presided over the PPA signing at the Central Academy of Police Training (CAPT) at
₹ 1.38 per unit, the lowest rate in the country29

. Following the bidding in 2018, the State of Madhya Pradesh
witnessed a change in government twice. Yet, the project continued to enjoy bipartisan support and
remained a priority as its beneficiaries are government institutions.
Among many beneficiaries of RESCO project in Madhya Pradesh, the Indian Institute of Management (IIM)
Indore and Central Academy of Police Training (CAPT) Bhopal pay the lowest rates for rooftop solar power
in the country. IIM Indore, without any investment, saved over ₹80 lakhs from a rooftop project on its
campus that was launched in January 2021. The project thus takes forward the country’s climate agenda
and can help government institutions move closer to achieving the Net Zero target.
Future of the Project and Persisting Challenges
The World Bank has appreciated the project as a model solar rooftop project with balanced risk allocation,
careful contractual drafting, and efficient project structuring. A major limitation in a bigger rollout of solar
rooftop programme is the issue of creditworthiness of the government organisations, as developers feel
confident about regular bill payment by only some categories of institutions. Contract enforceability and

customer default are two major risks of any Opex model. There have been reports of beneficiaries’ non-
payment of dues to developers, thus challenging the solitary revenue stream for the RESCO developer,

which needs to be addressed through appropriate single window mechanism for ease of doing business
(EoDB). Other challenges include perceptional hazard of DISCOMs, who face the competition of lower
rates in the face of paying organisations producing their own power.
Beneficiaries’ willingness to participate in the project is another challenge that requires to be investigated
and resolved. Despite attractive contract terms involving neither investment nor operational costs, various
organisations are yet to realise it holistically and be integrated into the project, which hampers its
scalability. There is also the challenge of scalability regarding residential, micro, small and medium
Enterprises (MSME) and individual units, which lack credibility in the eyes of the developers and have
small project size scattered over geographies.

Case Study Title: Enabling inclusive governance: The case of Rail Divyang Saarthi
Case Study Description: The development and implementation of Rail Divyang Saarthi application by the Ahmedabad Division of Western Railways is a good case to discuss embedding technology into policy solutions effectively for People with Disabilities (PwD). The app helped significantly reduce the number of days applicants had to wait to receive their railway concession cards. Accessibility and inclusion are the principles that resurface throughout this story. It demonstrates how technology is not a one-stop solution and how its effectiveness goes hand-in-hand with clarity in policies, inter-departmental coordination and communication. The app helped significantly reduce the number of days applicants had to wait to receive their railway concession cards.
Case Text:
Introduction
Lengthy queues of Persons with Disabilities (PwD) and their caregivers formed in the office halls of the
Ahmedabad Railway Division daily. The application procedure for obtaining a railway concession card,
i
which offers a subsidy of up to 75 percent on the ticket price for 2nd SL, 1st class, 3rd AC, and AC chair car
compartments, was long and arduous.ii The entire process was demanding for the railway department and
its beneficiaries.2
A Day at the Ahmedabad Railway Division Office
At the Facilitation Centre for Divyangjan or persons with disabilities, an overwhelmed railway commercial
officer, Mr. Arun Dalal, attended to Jignesh, the primary caregiver and younger brother of an applicant,
Kokila Ben. Mr. Dayal patiently answered all of Jignesh's questions and then sent him home with a list of
documents needed to formally register Kokila’s PwD card before he turned to the next applicant in the long
queue ahead of him. This was not an uncommon sight at the Ahmedabad Division Office of Western
Railways. On this day, another officer– the new Assistant Divisional Commercial Manager, Mr. Ashish

citizens, differently-abled persons, and students. These cards offer discounts on railway ticket fares. For
PwD, the disabilities fall under approved categories including visual, hearing, and orthopaedic ailments,
and the degree of disability should be typically above 40%. Concessions are valid for those aged 18 to 64.
ii The Indian Railways trains have various compartment types with differential seating arrangements,
facilities and charges. 2nd SL refers to a non-AC sleeper coach, 1st class is a non-AC lockable
compartment with 4 berths, and 3 AC refers to the 3-tier AC coach.

ENABLING INCLUSIVE GOVERNANCE WITH DIGITALIZATION AT RAIL DIVYANG SAARTHI,
AHMEDABAD

2

Ujlayaniii
, witnessed this exchange and was stunned by the sight. After a long discussion with his team,
Ashish learned that officers were overwhelmed by the sheer volume of daily applicants speaking different
languages or dialects of Gujarati. Additionally, interactions with vulnerable groups like PwD demanded
patience, sensitivity and appropriate training. For potential beneficiaries like Kokila Ben, acquiring the Rail
Travel Concession Card was a long and tiring process.
Application Process for a Railway Concession Card Prior to the App
1. Processing: On Kokila Ben’s second visit, Mr. Dayal filed her application after ensuring that the
applicant had submitted signed copies of all necessary documents.
2. Verifying: Mr. Dayal then cross-checked the authenticity of the supporting documents, including
the disability medical certificate issued by the state hospital. Fortnightly visits were made to the
hospitals to obtain applicants’ medical certificates to verify their proof of disability, after which a
date and time were scheduled for the collection of concession cards.
3. Intermediate visit: If any document is missing or incomplete, the applicant had to visit the railway
office and submit the document.
4. Approving: A final round of cross-checking the documents is done before signing the cards. From
initiation to completion, an applicant like Kokila Ben would need to wait more than 30 days to
receive her concession card.
Mr. Ashish Ujlayan swiftly figured that the time-consuming and laborious process of concession card
application was hurting the beneficiaries it was designed to help. He believed that digitising the application
process via an app/website would solve the issue. Rail Divyang Saarthi thus emerged as a solution in
response to the issues encountered by both his team and the PwD.
Developing Rail Divyang Saarthi
The Rail Divyang Saarthi app was developed for Android and iOS platforms and introduced in July 2020.
The free-to-download application allows people with disabilities to apply for a Western Railway,
Ahmedabad Division disability ID card (Exhibit 1).

iv It enables users to submit the application and relevant
documents online, thus reducing the number of visits to the office, to procure a Railway Travel Concession
ID card. Use of this application has also shortened the period of time required to process applications and
issue the card to 4-5 days (Exhibit 2 lists the accessibility features included in the Rail Divyang Saarthi app).
The architecture of the application was designed in-house after careful consultation with the stakeholders.
Challenges in the Development & Realignment of Institutional Processes
App development and, most importantly, integration of the app into a system accustomed to working in
the old way led to persistent challenges.
iii Ashish Ujlayan is an Indian Civil Services Officer (IRTS, batch of 2017) with over 10 years of experience
in both the public and private sectors. His passion lies in integrating data-driven decision-making into
governmental policy frameworks and daily operations. His areas of expertise encompass public policy,
transportation and logistics, data analytics, artificial intelligence, and blockchain technology.
ivRailway travel concession cards are available for different categories of passengers, such as senior citizens,
differently abled persons, and students. These cards offer discounts on railway ticket fares. For PwD, the
disabilities fall under approved categories including visual, hearing, and orthopaedic ailments, and the
degree of disability should be typically above 40%. Concessions are valid for those aged 18 to 64.

ENABLING INCLUSIVE GOVERNANCE WITH DIGITALIZATION AT RAIL DIVYANG SAARTHI,
AHMEDABAD

3

1. Funding: Working on a shoestring budget, Mr. Ujlayan had to find a way to develop the app without
relying on consultants who charged exorbitant fees ranging from ₹ 50 lakhs to ₹ 1 crore.3
2. Infrastructure and Personnel: The division office had enough computers, but about 60 percent of the
employees were inexperienced with technology. Additionally, most applicants were from low-income
and socio-economically disadvantaged groups without access to digital platforms who preferred direct
interaction with government officers rather than interacting with technology. But mobile access
emerged as a common engaging factor among the various beneficiaries. Every applicant was using a
smartphone either on their own or through a caregiver/family member.
3. Coordination with Other Departments: Digitalization mandated the support of not just the team and
PwD but also the hospitals issuing the medical certificates for PwD. Doctors at these hospitals were
often unaware of the policy compliances required and rarely agreed with the railway department on
defining disability. Consequently, the conflicted staff were unable to provide accurate information.
This problem was solved using the Svavlamban portal of the Ministry of Social Justice and
Empowerment. The Svavlamban card for disability is easily verified on the portal.
4. Financial Support for App Development: To overcome the funding challenge, Mr. Ujlayan leveraged
his contacts from outside the department. He contacted Krish Compusoft Services (KCS), a
multinational IT company that agreed to develop, customise, and maintain the app for a fair price. In
2020, the app was tested internally, before being opened for public use. Department personnel required
about 10 days of intensive training to become accustomed to the technology.
5. Not a one-stop solution: Easing the application process led to a boom in the number of applicants. The
department personnel were trained in technology and soft skills. A new Divyang Facilitation Centre
well-equipped with computers and internet connectivity was built adjacent to the earlier office to be
more accessible to PwD (Exhibit 3). The railway rules still require the card to be issued physically. This
rule position was an inhibition in issuing a digital version of the concession card.
Life after the introduction of the Rail Divyang Saarthi App
The Rail Divyang Saarthi app impacted the lives of the department officers and the beneficiaries. When
Jignesh learned about the Rail Divyang Saarthi app while perusing newspaper advertisements, he wanted
to avail the disability concession card for his parents’ too. With the Railways making long-distance travel
more accessible and affordable for PwD, they could now apply for their cards online with the app. Jignesh
downloaded the application on the one smartphone the family owned and initiated the application process.
He entered his father’s disability ID and chose the authorised hospital closest to their residence to obtain a
medical certificate. He was required to upload digital copies of his father’s medical certificate, disability
ID, proof of birth, ID card, address proof and photo. He did not have digital copies of these documents and
hence needed to visit the hospital. Jignesh then tried to enter his mother’s credentials into the app but
couldn’t create an account with an already registered mobile number. For Jignesh, talking to a government
official seemed more accessible and reassuring. Before visiting the office however, he completed his
parents’ medical examination, procured certificates for them both and carried the originals of all their
documents as listed on the app.
At the Ahmedabad Railway Headquarters, he was directed to the Divyang Facilitation Centre located just
next to the entrance gate. Earlier, people had to walk at least 200 to 300 metres to reach the concerned office
which included walk of stairs or ramp. The centre has a small room with a minimum sitting area. He
assisted his ageing parents up a few steps to the centre and had them sit on a bench on the veranda while
he spoke with an officer. Mr. Arun Dayal, the railway commercial officer, now handles more cases online
than offline. The team after the launch of the application was still overburdened by the face-to-face dialogue
needed to inform and educate every applicant. This has largely stabilised now. Although the staff found

ENABLING INCLUSIVE GOVERNANCE WITH DIGITALIZATION AT RAIL DIVYANG SAARTHI,
AHMEDABAD

4

its motivation in the goodwill and satisfaction of those they helped, these intangibles were insufficient to
support the team entirely. They needed bigger office rooms with ventilation, AC/fans during the summer
season and administrative personnel to make their work easier. Mr.Dayal checked the documents that
Jignesh presented for his parents’ application. He then informed Jignesh that his parents’ application could
not be processed as the mobile number entered was already registered under his sister Kokila Ben’s
concession card. The family had no other smartphone.
To assist Jignesh, Mr. Dayal listed an alternate number that the office reserved for just these situations.
Jignesh was then directed to the nearby cyberhub where he could obtain digital copies of his parents’
certificates. The staff at this cybershop were familiar with the protocol required for railway concession card
applications. Mr. Dayal added the data entries to Jignesh’s parents’ online application while verifying the
document copies. Soon, the system generated a date on which Jignesh could come to receive his parents’
concession cards. The details would have reached him as an SMS on his phone if Jignesh had a mobile
phone number for registration. Mr. Dayal then provided Jignesh with his official phone number to contact
him in case of any queries or concerns. Jignesh revisited the office in three days, but alone this time, and
returned home with his parents’ concession cards.
It was not easy for officers like Mr. Dalal, who had requested to be stationed at the Divyang facilitation
centre without having received additional training. Apart from issuing new cards, the workload of the
small staff increases under two scenarios not addressed by the digital app. The Rail Divyang Saarthi App
only contains two divisions of the Western Railways: Ahmedabad and Baroda. When PwD change
residence to other cities, they must comply with the systems followed by the division under the new
jurisdiction. Similarly, applicants coming to Ahmedabad and Baroda divisions from other towns must
apply for new cards via the app, as their previous cards are null and void under these divisions. Moreover,
for temporary disability in the case of a paraplegic person or an orthopaedic handicap, the certificate must
be renewed after five years or in ten years for people under 25.

4 The hospitals issuing the medical
certificates for PwD are often unaware of the mandated policy compliances that deem an applicant fit for
concession. Hence, hospital staff are often unable to provide accurate information. But the recent
Swavlamban card issued to the PwDs by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is transforming
this problem with the medical certificates.
Discussion
Since the introduction of the Rail Divyang Saarthi app, the waiting period for the concession card for PwD
has been reduced from over 70 days earlier to just 4-5 days. The number of visits made by PwD and/or
their caregivers who had to come to the office has been reduced to just 2-3 from January 2022 to December
2022.5 As of February 2023, Ahmedabad Railways received 6906 railway concession card applications, of
which 4319 cards were successfully issued. About 820 applications were rejected due to non-compliance
with rules, while the rest are pending owing to insufficient data.6 Today, 20-50 concession cards are issued
every day with the support of Rail Divyang Saarthi. No doubt the app has been a much-needed
intervention. However, there is more to be done as some issues remain unaddressed.
The responsibilities of the small team of officers managing the facilitation center have increased following
the introduction of the app as the volume of applications has increased. Also, despite the availability of the
app, many PwD still prefer to visit the Center. Issues relating to inter-departmental collaboration and lack
of clarity about eligibility criteria continue to burden the team and beneficiaries.
The case study of the Rail Divyang Saarthi app raises some key questions for discussion:

AHMEDABAD

external stakeholders?
2. How can technology-based solutions be made more accessible and inclusive to all sections of society?

Case Study Title: Innovative grievance redressal: The case of the RailMadad app
Case Study Description: The Rail Madad Application of Indian Railways is a good case to discuss principles of decentralisation and transparency in large-scale grievance redressal systems. It uses a passenger or benefactor-centric model to achieve maximum customer satisfaction. To create this system, they focus on a bottom-up approach with room for levels of escalation, ensuring speedy service delivery while maintaining full transparency across the board. Rail Madad is the brainchild of Vivek Srivastava, the protagonist of the innovation. Soon after joining the commercial department of Rail Bhawan in New Delhi, Srivastava discovered that the many channels of communication established by divisions across the country were not standardised or centralised to provide real-time grievance redressal for the passengers. He led his team to create a singular platform, Rail Madad, that connected passengers to the last-mile service delivery staff to offer real-time problem resolution while offering full transparency to all stakeholders.
Case Text:
Innovative grievance redressal: The Case of
RailMadad
“Indian Railway has launched RailMadad, the integrated and innovative one-stop solution for customer grievance,
inquiry, suggestion, and assistance, providing passengers the choice to access RailMadad through multiple
channels... 99.93% of complaints received get closed, and 72% of the feedback given by complainants is ‘Excellent’
or ‘Satisfactory’.”

Ministry of Railways, Government of India1

Introduction
The Indian Railways network, which spans 18 railway zones and 68 divisions with 68,000 km of railway
routes across the country, is the world’s fourth largest railway system, catering to over 23 million
passengers and carrying over 4 million tonnes of freight daily.2

It is also the world’s tenth-largest employer,

with over 1.38 million employees powering it around the clock.

3 This complex and dispersed system
maintains one of the country's most complex service delivery systems that cuts across topographical,
geographical, socio-economical, and linguistic boundaries. Given the enormity of India’s rail operations,
complaints and grievances are inevitable. Indian Railways received complaints through multiple avenues,
such as the Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS)
i
; social media
channels such as Twitter and Facebook; COMS, an earlier complaint management system for Indian
Railways; complaint registers kept with Travelling Ticket Examiners (TTE) and station masters; and
multiple customer care phone numbers. Indian Railways however, employed a decentralised approach to
complaint management, with each zone and division troubleshooting their own complaints. This lack of
cohesion and synergy between complaint management systems—even as passengers cut across zone and
division lines during travel—rendered real-time grievance redressal challenging.
Challenges of the Top-Down Grievance Redressal Method
The Commercial Department in each railway division used to gather passenger grievances from the
different channels. The staff identified and matched each complaint to the department responsible for
delivering the service concerned. The complaints were then mostly manually filed as email printouts, call
transcripts, and copies of complaint letters and were then subsequently sent to the divisional heads of the
concerned department (Exhibit 2). From here, it trickles down, from supervisors to frontline officials who
i Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) is a 24x7 online platform available to citizens to lodge
their grievances on any subject related to service delivery. It is a single portal connected to all the Ministries/Departments of the
Government of India and states. CPGRAMS is also accessible to the citizens through a standalone mobile application called UMANG.

INNOVATIVE GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL: THE CASE OF RAILMADAD 2
oversee day-to-day operations. At each level, the officials added their remarks on the complaint to the
original file before forwarding it. Depending on the nature of the complaint, these officials also coordinated
with the vendors/contractors delivered the service. Upon resolution, the file travelled via the same route
back to the commercial department, which communicates to the complainant a response to the grievance.
This multi-level system takes between 7 days and 15 days to resolve a grievance (Exhibit 1). The system
design was focused on fixing responsibility for service delivery failure rather than redressing the grievance.
Consequently, stakeholders could not have their grievances redressed during the period of their travel
under the above-mentioned redressal mechanism.
When Mr. Vivek Srivastava, IRTSii joined the apex body of Indian Railways in 2017 as Executive Director,
Railway Board, he quickly identified the limitations of the top-down approach to producing a real-time
grievance redressal response system. He started working on a system based on “delayering” the
information flow process. He identified the need to streamline these processes into a single entity that
would allow passengers and freight customers to lodge their grievances across various media in a seamless,
customer-friendly manner while ensuring that the information flow to the concerned frontline staff is
immediate, cutting across the bureaucratic layers, and facilitating a prompt resolution. The common issues
highlighted by the Indian Railways pertained to a multiplicity of communication channels (media) without
any coordination mechanism between them, a layered flow of information, addressing grievances on a
moving train and the socio-economic diversity of the users. An extensive examination of the current
customer service channels was conducted to establish a comprehensive remedy. This involved collecting
data on service performance indicators such as the number of inquiry calls, average time to address
complaints, existing complaint resolution methods, customer sentiment towards the service, and staff
proficiency. Collaborative meetings were held with stakeholders from the Railway Board, Zonal Railways,
Divisions and the Centre for Railway Information Systems (CRIS) that was designing the necessary
software, based on valuable inputs provided by Mr. Vivek Srivastava and his team.

iii The innovative
approach centred on creating a framework that unifies the various customer service channels into a single
platform to streamline tasks linked to services. Thus, was born RailMadad, the grievance redressal
mechanism of the Indian Railways with unprecedented reach, speed and efficiency. It allows online
registration of complaints and redressal in real time through multiple channels and languages.
Pre-requisites for a Standardised Platform
Considering the vastness of the railway network and the innumerable stakeholders involved, Mr.
Srivastava realised that specific prerequisites are essential for a platform like RailMadad:
1. An apex body - There was a need to have a centralised entity collecting all the grievances directly
from the customers. This entity should be accessible through various media, without insisting on
any kind of tech-savviness among users. The same entity, using algorithms should be able to
communicate the grievance to the concerned staff of the concerned department on a real-time basis,
for quick disposal of the grievance. Such an entity could operate only at the Railway Board level,
the apex body of the Indian Railways. It also meant the closure of multiple grievance collection
systems across divisions and zones.
2. A neutral coordination and mediation body - The Commercial Department of the Indian Railways
is responsible for customer assistance, provides information and ensures transparency. Though the
ii Mr Vivek Srivastava is a graduate of IIT Kanpur, which he has followed up with a degree in Law. After joining IRTS in 1991, he
has worked extensively on freight and passenger Railways, besides stints in IRCTC & DGCCIL. He developed RailMadad while
working at the Ministry of Railway. His earlier software innovation was Rake Allotment System (2010), which brought
unprecedented transparency in allotment of rakes of iron ore.
iii CRIS (Centre for Railway Information Systems), an organisation under the Ministry of Railways, includes IT professionals and
experienced railway personnel tasked with delivering complex Railway IT systems in core areas.

INNOVATIVE GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL: THE CASE OF RAILMADAD 3
Commercial Department is the customer interface, it does not control all the services being
provided to the customers. The challenge was to reach out to the department concerned with a
service delivery failure and then to its concerned frontline staff. The train itself being a moving
object added to the challenge. The divisional Control Rooms which housed all the service
departments, including Commercial, were roped in. Through an algorithm and by using the
location of the train, the information was passed by RailMadad directly to the concerned divisional
control and through it, to the frontline staff.
3. A robust monitoring mechanism - Such a grievance system that sought to redress the grievance
within hours could not have worked without a robust monitoring system and a complete audit
trail of the complaints. The entire system works through the supervisors and staff who work round
the clock, just like Indian Railways’ trains. No new staff were added for RailMadad at the divisions.
The officers worked through management by exceptions principle, looking only at those cases
where protocols of disposal time or satisfaction levels were breached. The system also maintains a
complete trail of various inputs going into the redressal of each complaint.
4. Ease of use, technical prowess – The system had to be designed in such a manner that it provided
easy access to all rail users. An insistence on smart phones, knowledge of English etc., was ruled
out. The Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation (IRCTC) was roped in to provide
round-the-clock language support in twelve languages. A call from a basic phone would allow the
user to lodge her complaint from anywhere in India in a language of her choice.
RailMadad was thus conceived by the Public Grievance Directorate of the Railway Board. It was introduced
and fully operationalized in July 2019, a proud moment for Mr. Srivastava and his team. RailMadad
transformed the procedural approach to grievance redressal, which became delayered and achieved
convergence of all communication channels. RailMadad provided all the intermediaries involved with
complete visibility of a complaint. The platform was designed to connect the complainant. The new
delayered approach by RailMadad changed the operational methodology and the customer experience,
opening doors for the application of the process to other public utilities and government delivery systems.
RailMadad: Tracing the Journey of a Complaint
To improve passenger facilities, IRCTC introduced Rail Neer, a branded packaged drinking water for train
travellers, that was available on trains and at stations. Pantry car managers and station stall owners are
required to maintain a record of water brands endorsed by the Railways and provide this list when
requested by passengers on their journey from Delhi to Meerut. A passenger named Mahesh noticed that
the water bottles being distributed on the train were not from Rail Neer. Unclear about whether the brand
had been approved by the IRCTC, there was no way to determine if the bottle was safe for consumption.
Knowing that RailMadad was the grievance redressal platform for Indian railways, Mahesh lodged his
complaint using his phone number and an OTP he received via SMS (Exhibit 3). He provided other
identifying details like his PNR number and the incident date. He selected the type of complaint he had -
Water Availability - from the options listed and an additional sub-type of complaint about the Packaged
Drinking Water - Rail Neer. He also uploaded an image of the unauthorised water bottle he had received
on the website. He added a brief description of the complaint, which was however optional, before
submitting it on RailMadad. In a few minutes, Mahesh received an auto-generated SMS from the platform
confirming the registration of his complaint with a promise of action.
On the other end of this complaint was Anupam, a staff member at the Delhi Divisional Office who had
worked with the Complaint Cell, Commercial Department for 6 years. Every day, Anupam attended to the
complaints registered on the RailMadad platform, reached out to them for clarification and forwarded the
grievance to the authority or service provider responsible for addressing the concern. Upon receiving

INNOVATIVE GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL: THE CASE OF RAILMADAD 4
Mahesh’s complaint, Anupam quickly called him to gather more details. It was part of the procedure for
Anupam to confirm the veracity of the complaint before acting. In his experience, sometimes complaints
were unfounded. RailMadad also provides staff like Anupam with real-time information about various
staff and service delivery personnel on a moving train or station. He contacted the TTE present on Mahesh’s
train through their WhatsApp group to bring the matter to his attention. Within 15 minutes of the complaint
being lodged, the TTE visited Mahesh and collected his statement. He also asked the service delivery staff
on board to provide him with bottles of Rail Neer. He further raised the issue with the contractor
responsible and reported the incident to IRCTC management officials. The TTE also informed Anupam
about the complaint’s resolution status and that he had escalated it for further investigation to IRCTC. An
auto-generated SMS reached Mahesh for feedback, followed by a call from Anupam, who closed the
complaint in 25 minutes. Thus, RailMadad takes an average of about 26 minutes from the time of complaint
registration to resolution and feedback, which is well within the team’s target of 30 minutes for grievance
closure (Exhibit 1).
On average, Anupam handles 50-80 complaints on RailMadad, a few complaints received through other
mediums such as complaint registers are manually entered into RailMadad by railway staff such as
Anupam. The redressal of even these complaints must be shared with the complainant via the offline mode
by which they initially lodged their complaints. Serious grievances lodged in RailMadad, such as passenger
security and accidents, follow the offline route to ensure that they are brought to the attention of senior
officials and department heads who appoint someone for investigation. (Exhibit 4)
Persisting Bottlenecks to Speedy Processing and Redressal of Grievances
1. Using alternative channels like WhatsApp for coordination: To facilitate swift coordination
between staff members and receive real-time updates for RailMadad, Anupam also resorts to using
channels like WhatsApp groups. These groups are active around the clock, thus making employees
such as Anupam attend to them even after working hours, which might cause. An effective
implementation of RailMadad will require additional hours and effort from officials in the short
run.
2. Social media complaints: Since the advent of social media, most Railway Divisions have
established their own Facebook and Twitter pages. Railways also receive complaints on such
prominent platforms with greater visibility and the potential to shape public opinion. Thus, special
teams have been set up to feed these complaints into RailMadad and promptly respond to them on
social media. Most complainants on social media are not aware of the RailMadad platform. Upon
being approached, they agree to transfer the grievance to RailMadad, thus bringing it on track
while also adding to the complaint database. (Exhibit 5)
3. Lack of information: Although Anupam could contact the TTE within minutes of receiving the
complaint, this is not always the case. The dynamic nature of operations necessitates constant
updating of information about onboard officials, who may need to be contacted for any specific
complaint, which can sometimes lead to delays. This is being addressed by capturing the layer
comprising of onboard staff through access to their centralised reporting, wherever implemented.
4. Effects of privatisation in railways: Privatisation has complicated matters for railway employees
like the TTE, who in the complaint cited above had to coordinate with the vendors for authorised
water bottles. On the other hand, most vendors are organised and have their own access systems
to their workers. Sending alerts directly to vendors is now increasingly being resorted to.

INNOVATIVE GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL: THE CASE OF RAILMADAD 5
5. Infrastructural facilities and training: Anupam is a key member of the team in the Delhi Division
office with access to a computer dedicated to RailMadad use. He has yet to receive refresher
training for platform operations or its updated features. Staff is also not trained to directly deal
with passengers who may use impassioned language or even hurl abuse, which has a severe effect
on their mental health, a professional hazard in such jobs handling complaints all over the country.
6. Employee experiences across railway divisions: While the staff have uniform training on handling
the RailMadad system, their training in customer care and Customer Relation Management (CRM)
varies across the divisions. Anupam, based out of the Delhi division, expects more, after his
experience, with RailMadad at his office as compared with his colleagues in other divisions, mostly
on account of the lack of exposure given to him so far.
Discussion
For a traveller like Mahesh, RailMadad has been a success and adds to their satisfaction with rail services
as their grievances were resolved during travel.4 The availability of this platform has also led to an
increased number of complaints, a positive development reflecting customers’ trust in railways to
promptly resolve their complaints. Railways have also set up incentives for employees like felicitating
teams with prize shields to reward and acknowledge their efforts and boost employee morale.5 Though a
huge hit with rail users, RailMadad has still to cover some ground in facilitating working of backend teams
under control while IR should plan a systemic exposure to CRM training for them.
1. What other departments or in what contexts can the RailMadad model be replicated for service
delivery?
2. What are the requisites for implementing RailMadad-style solutions in these contexts? What
service-specific changes would this model have to undergo to be effective in these new contexts?

Case Study Title: Leveraging AI for Security: The case of ASTR
Case Study Description:
The ASTR case illustrates the administrative and ethical complexities of employing AI-based facial recognition powered solutions for governance. The case unfolds against terrorism concerns in J&K in 2021. Around the same time, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) under Mr. Naveen Jakhar was working on addressing the increase in cybercrime in Mewat, Haryana, due to the issue of SIM cards based on fake identities.

The use of fake SIM cards is leveraged to propose a solution based on adopting AI-based facial recognition technology to identify fake SIM cards. The case can help us understand how an ecosystem could be developed, to facilitate the smooth interaction of stakeholders needed to incorporate facial recognition technology in governance.
Case Text:
"Artificial intelligence is a tribute to human intellectual power, the power to think enabled humans to make tools and
technologies. Today, these tools and technologies have also acquired the power to learn and think."

PM Narendra Modi at RAISE, 20201

Introduction
In 2021, the State Intelligence Agency (SIA) of the Jammu and Kashmir police was grappling with the
escalating network of terrorism in the valley. One of the key challenges was the use of fake SIM cards by
terrorists, obtained using forged proof of identity/address documents to maintain communication with
their handlers in Pakistan, thereby directly threatening national security.2 Meanwhile, in Mewat, Haryana,
Mr. Naveen Jakhar, the Additional Director General (ADG) of Security at the Department of
Telecommunications (DoT), was working on a technology-based SIM verification system to address this
challenge. It was an Artificial Intelligence and Facial Recognition-Powered System for Telecom SIM
Subscriber Verification, called ASTR, which could help to combat the proliferation of fake SIM cards
across cybercrime hotspots in the country.
Background
The exponential rise of cybercrime in India has drawn international attention and caused significant
financial losses. The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs, highlighted that
India recorded 52,974 cybercrime cases in 2021, a significant increase from 50,035 cases in 2020 (Exhibit 1).
In 2019-20, India lost ₹ 1.25 lakh crore (approximately US$ 16.7 billion) due to cybercrimes alone.3 To
combat this, Mewat in Haryana, the epicentre of cybercrime in India, became the first site for active
intervention by Mr. Jakhar and his team.
ASTR promised to improve the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of SIM subscriber verification. This
verification process otherwise done manually through customer acquisition forms (CAFs), is neither
foolproof nor efficient, with only 0.1 percent of the forms being cross-checked, but without a reliable
method to verify the accuracy of identity-proof documents. The ASTR was designed as an innovative
solution to verify 100 percent of SIM card documents while reducing costs and time on criminal
investigations.
The Core Team Behind ASTR
The core team behind ASTR consisted of four members, each contributing their expertise to address the
issue of fake SIM cards and cybercrime:

LEVERAGING AI FOR GOVERNANCE: THE CASE OF ASTR 2
1. Mr. Naveen Jakhar proposed using AI and facial recognition to tackle the problem of fake SIM
cards. His vision and innovative approach laid the foundation for ASTR.
2. Dr. Mahesh Shukla, Senior Deputy Director-General of Haryana Licensed Service Area (LSA),
helped link security concerns in Jammu and Kashmir with fake SIM cards.
3. Mr. P.K. Singh, Deputy Director-General (Security Assurance) at the Department of
Telecommunications (DoT), provided insights on security measures to be taken after identifying a
fake SIM card involving intervention from law enforcement agencies (LEAs).
4. Mr. Pranay Diwakar, Assistant Director General - AI & Digital Intelligence Unit (AI&DIU) at the
DoT, played a pivotal role in reaching out to telecom service providers (TSPs) to understand how
fake SIM cards impacted different stakeholders.
The Conundrum of Tracking Cybercrime
The conceptualization of ASTR was shaped in late 2020 when Mr. Jakhar, amidst growing cybercrime and
complex cybercrime syndicates, instructed Mr. Diwakar to engage with various stakeholders to gather
information on how to effectively address the issue of fake SIM cards. The anonymity associated with
untraceable fake SIM cards posed a significant challenge, particularly to combat and control cybercrime.
To address this issue, the team proposed developing an algorithm to manage fake SIM cards. Developing
the algorithm however, involved leveraging technology and data analytics to analyse a variety of data
elements, including CAF details, transaction patterns, location data, and other relevant information. The
algorithm was designed to identify suspicious patterns or anomalies in SIM card registrations, transaction
data, and additional information pertinent to flag potential cases. It could also use machine learning and
predictive modelling techniques to identify patterns of cybercrime syndicates and track their activities over
time.
ASTR could be integrated with the existing systems of the DoT and other law enforcement agencies to
enable real-time monitoring and proactive action. It would generate alerts for suspicious activities, which
field units or other designated authorities would investigate and use as evidence in the investigation and
prosecution process. In cases of confirmed fraud, appropriate legal action would be initiated against the
criminals. It would also aim to collect and analyse data on cybercrime syndicates, including their modus
operandi, networks, and operation patterns, to enable authorities to proactively disrupt operations of
cybercrime syndicates'. Implementation of ASTR required robust data security measures to protect the
privacy and confidentiality of user data, as well as regular updates and improvements to keep up with the
evolving tactics of cybercriminals. By leveraging technology, data analytics, and proactive monitoring,
ASTR aims to prevent fraud, track down criminals, and manage the losses incurred by victims more
effectively.
The Genesis of ASTR
The project was initiated with Mr. Jakhar and the team focusing on facial images as a potentially reliable
and readily available data set developed to overcome any gaps left by conventional text-based analysis, an
algorithm for detecting fake SIM cards. The team worked tirelessly to gather and analyse facial images
from various sources, to develop an algorithm to detect information anomalies across submitted facial
images, and to look for discrepancies that might indicate the use of fake identities. The team tested and
refined the algorithm through multiple iterations, continually improving its accuracy and performance, to
ensure it was cost-effective, efficient, and reliable. They were determined to make it foolproof, considering
the complexities of more than 30 different types of documents that can be used to obtain SIM cards in India.
This project served as a proof of concept, to demonstrate the feasibility of using facial images as a data set
to develop an algorithm for detecting fake SIM cards. With its success, the team gained support from
various stakeholders, including government agencies, law enforcement, and telecom service providers.

LEVERAGING AI FOR GOVERNANCE: THE CASE OF ASTR 3

Processes in Integrating Facial Images: By collecting facial images from telecom service providers (TSPs)
and criminal records from the NCRB, the algorithm underwent training to detect changes in age and
demographics that could impact facial features. The algorithm used a 68-point frontal facial landmark
model (Exhibit 2) to quantify facial images and create clusters of similar faces, enabling the AI to reduce
the time to distinguish between different facial images. Additionally, the training data considered different
facial patterns across India to avoid false positives or negatives. A similarity score of 97.5 percent or above
indicated that the faces were identical, ensuring high accuracy in the identification process. These were
crucial in building a robust AI to detect fake SIM cards and identify potential cases of fraud. The algorithm
was designed to be cost-effective, efficient, and reliable, providing a promising alternative to tackling SIM
card fraud.
Using Fuzzy Logic: ASTR used fuzzy logici

to analyse big data available in subscriber forms. It was an
improved approach that attempted to consider the inherent uncertainties and complexities in human
reasoning. By doing so, ASTR combined essential details such as mobile number, CAF number, and
subscriber name with their facial images under one directory, making it a comprehensive and effective tool
to combat SIM card fraud. This directory could be accessed by stakeholders such as TSPs, financial
institutions, law enforcement agencies (LEAs), and point of sale (PoS) of SIM cards to identify similarities
between facial images.
Piloting
In April 2021, Mr. Jakhar conducted a pilot project to test the algorithm’s utility on 5,000 reported mobile
numbers associated with cybercrimes from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and other agencies. The
algorithm successfully identified and disconnected 4800 of these numbers for using fake identity proofs to
procure SIM cards, demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness in detecting fraudulent activities.4 This
success provided Mr. Jakhar the confidence to pitch the algorithm's feasibility to higher-ranking authorities
up the chain of command. He reported to the Deputy Director General, who discussed it with the Senior
Deputy Director General of DoT, LSA Haryana, who would rely on the Secretary of DoT to secure financial
support and the necessary permissions needed for the project. With the pilot project’s success, Mr Jakhar
was optimistic that ASTR would receive the necessary approvals from higher authorities to proceed with
its implementation in Mewat and potentially in other regions.
Navigating the roadblocks for clearances: The core team at DoT consisting of Dr. Shukla, Mr. Jakhar, Mr.
Singh, and Mr. Diwakar, endeavoured to project the impact and importance of ASTR to ensure its support.
Dr. Shukla related the applicability of ASTR to the concerns faced in Jammu and Kashmir; Mr. Jakhar
outlined the technical superiority of ASTR; Mr. Singh highlighted how ASTR could be integrated within
the existing model to effectively address cybercrime; Mr. Diwakar underlined the potential benefits of
ASTR for different stakeholders. Their efforts gained support when the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)
approached the Secretary of DoT to seek a solution to the issue of fake SIM cards in the valley. This backing
by the MHA made it easier for Dr. Shukla's lead team to navigate the bureaucratic hierarchy, and they were
allowed to move forward with a strategy that outlined the framework of the successful pilot study. The
team could proceed with their plan to implement ASTR in Mewat and potentially in other regions.
Achievements of ASTR: The project to implement ASTR at the district level in Mewat received positive
support from the DoT. The team at DoT Haryana LSA worked tirelessly to procure and process the vast
amount of data from 16.69 lakh SIM cards provided by the telecom service providers (TSPs) to train the AI
i Fuzzy logic - Fuzzy logic is a form of many-valued logic in which the truth value of variables may be
any real number between 0 and 1. It is employed to handle the concept of partial truth, where the truth
value may range between completely true and completely false.

LEVERAGING AI FOR GOVERNANCE: THE CASE OF ASTR 4
algorithm. 5 The data from TSPs was then matched against the data available with the Ministry of Home
Affairs (MHA) to identify any fake profiles used to procure SIM cards. The project showed promising
results, and within six months, it had helped to deactivate 4.96 lakh non-bonafide SIM cards in Mewat.
6
This demonstrated the potential of ASTR in disarming the network of cybercrime syndicates in the region
and curbing the problem of SIM cards issued to fake identities. After the successful implementation of
ASTR in Mewat, the DoT collaborated with the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) and State Law
Enforcement Agencies (LEAs). They expanded the use of ASTR in cybercrime hotspots across India in the
states of in West Bengal, Haryana, Odisha, Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, and Jammu & Kashmir. ASTR proved
its effectiveness in these states by deactivating 15 lakh fraudulent SIM cards and disrupting illegal
activities. The collaborative efforts highlighted the importance of technology-driven solutions in
addressing complex challenges related to cybersecurity and fraud.
Stakeholders and their concerns
The next step was expanding the project across the entire country, which involved bringing on board the 3
primary stakeholders—the TSPs, the state LEAs, and financial institutions, which raised a more significant
challenge. TSPs being private entities with differing priorities had reservations about data sharing. The
primary responsibility here was to persuade TSPs to see the value addition generated by bringing together
different stakeholders and the ways in which this action aligned with the interests of individual actors.
1. Telecom Service Providers: Mr. Diwakar and the DoT team took proactive measures to address the
concerns of TSPs and win their confidence in the ASTR initiative. Mr. Diwakar visited TSPs and
leveraged the success of ASTR in Mewat to explain how addressing the issue of fake SIM cards could
help restore trust among TSP customers. To make the integration of ASTR technology easy for TSPs,
the DoT team explained how ASTR could be incorporated at the Points of Sale (PoS), where the data
originates, to address their privacy concerns. Highlighting the legal provisions that allow a maximum
of 9 SIM cards per person, the DoT team explained how ASTR could run facial images to identify
potentially fraudulent SIM card buyers possibly involved in cybercrime. To allay concerns about data
breaches, data was to be stored locally at TSPs' premises, making data collection more convenient
without storing data at a single location. By addressing these concerns, DoT successfully gained
support and cooperation from TSPs to actively participate in the ASTR initiative.
2. State Law Enforcement Agencies: Mr. Singh, recognized the close cooperation between the State Law
Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) and the Field Unit of the DoT, and the potential for this collaboration in
tracking cybercrime cases. By ensuring that the confidentiality concerns of the State LEAs were
addressed, the field units of the DoT assisted the State LEAs in tracking cybercrime cases using the
ASTR technology while being aligned with their operational needs. The strong relationship between
the DoT and the State LEAs fostered mutual trust and cooperation, facilitating a smooth collaboration
in using ASTR to combat cybercrime across different states in India in cybercrime hotspots, leading to
the deactivation of fraudulent SIM cards and tracing of cybercrime syndicates operating in the country.
3. Financial Institutions: The ASTR team recognized the importance of gaining the trust of financial
institutions (FIs) to secure their participation in the project. They highlighted how ASTR's preventive
mechanism could help FIs protect their customers from financial frauds, thereby building faith and
ensuring the safety of their customers' hard-earned money from phishing, identity theft, and other
financial scams. It could provide a robust layer of security to FIs and their customers, preventing
financial losses and safeguarding their transactions. Through effective communication and
demonstration of the benefits of ASTR, the team was able to foster the FIs’ confidence in the project
and garner their support in using ASTR. This collaboration with FIs further strengthened the overall
ability of ASTR in curbing cybercrime across India.

LEVERAGING AI FOR GOVERNANCE: THE CASE OF ASTR 5
Discussion
ASTR leverages AI-based facial recognition technology to significantly reduce the number of fraudulent
SIM cards and associated cybercrime in India. Under Mr. Naveen Jakhar’s tutelage, this tool ushered into
the DoT the use of modern technology to serve citizens. However, critical questions regarding the use of
facial recognition software to solve crime remain.
1. Can ASTR be replicated and scaled up across India? What kind of challenges could arise in the
process?
2. What are the potential drawbacks or risks – ethical and technical, associated with use of facial
recognition technology in governance?
3. How can facial recognition technology be used ethically and responsibly in different governance
contexts?

Case Study Title: Balancing economic growth and sustainable ecotourism: The case of Dhar Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp
Case Study Description: The ‘Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp’ – an ecotourism project in Chamrod, Dhar Kalan in Punjab – is a good case to discuss the principles of participatory natural resource management. The relevant principles include understanding natural resources management mechanism, biodiversity of the ecosystem, livelihood strategies sustained by the ecosystem, and participatory environmental governance.The case set between 2017 and to present day in Chamrod, Dhar Kalan in Punjab was developed in 2017 where Dr Sanjeev Kumar, the protagonist undertakes the task of efficiently using the barren land near the Ranjit Sagar Lake to help bring about economic development in the Dhar Kalan’s villages. Being cognizant of the fact that such ecotourism camp in an ecologically sensitive zone requires a scientific approach, careful planning and participatory support from local residents to assure the sustainability of the ecosystem. Conserving Dhar forest's flora and fauna and spreading awareness about green living to people residing were essential elements to the project’s development.
Case Text:
Balancing Economic Growth & Sustainable
Ecotourism: The Case of the Dhar Nature Retreat &
Awareness Camp
“Let us pledge to collectively work towards conserving precious environmental resources. Let us live in harmony

with nature and keep our beloved Earth clean and green.”

PM Narendra Modi1
The concept underlying the ‘Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp’—an ecotourism project in Chamrod,
Dhar Kalan, Punjab – was developed in 2017 by Pathankot’s Divisional Forest Officer (DFO), Dr. Sanjeev
Kumar Tiwari. He wanted to efficiently use the barren land near the Ranjit Sagar Lake for economic
development in the villages of Dhar Kalan. He and his department colleagues were aware that establishing
an ecotourism camp in such an ecologically sensitive zone would require careful planning and support
from the local community. A scientific approach was crucial to ensuring the sustainability of the ecosystem
and conservation of Dhar forest's flora and fauna, in addition to spreading awareness about green living to
residents, all essential elements to the project’s development.
The Changing Governance System of Dhar Kalan
Dhar Kalan, the site of the proposed Nature Retreat Awareness Camp, is approximately 30 km from
Pathankot district headquarters in Pathankot. Known for its natural biodiversity, Dhar Kalan has the
largest forest cover intensity in Punjab and is situated near Ranjit Sagar Lake. Although Dhar Kalan also
covers some panchayat land for farming, most of its land, approximately 15,771 hectares, is forest land
governed by the Punjab Land Prevention Act (PLPA).2 Enacted in 1900
3
to stop soil erosion and flash floods,
the Act mandated communities to obtain approval from the forest department to gather firewood and

timber for personal use. Thus, most villagers in the region work as daily wage labourers due to the non-
availability of land for agriculture, while the younger generation is migrating to metropolitan areas in

search of employment opportunities. In 2010, the Punjab government modified some PLPA provisions
relating to regulations and coverage areas to usher in livelihood opportunities for communities living near
forests. About 8,600 hectares of forest land in Dhar Kalan were de-reserved for everyday use.

4 A project by
the Punjab Forest Department was launched under the aegis of the National Medicinal Plant Board (NMPB)
in 2017 to offer livelihood opportunities for women through the collection and sale of herbs from the local
forest.
Establishment of the Nature Retreat & Awareness Camp
Acknowledging that environmental sustainability through local participation is the foundation of any
ecological livelihood initiative, Dr. Tiwari emphasised the importance of people’s involvement at every

BALANCING ECONOMIC GROWTH AND SUSTAINABLE ECOTOURISM: THE CASE OF THE
DHAR NATURE RETREAT AWARENESS CAMP

2

stage of the proposed Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp, from design and planning to implementation.
While protection of the Dhar forest and conservation of its biodiversity were key to this project,
simultaneously raising awareness about the preservation of this forest formed an essential element of this
enterprise. The initiative, inaugurated in February 2020, aimed to utilise the abundant natural resources to
generate employment and create a larger ecosystem to address current and future challenges in the area.5,6
As the first-of-its-kind nature retreat, the project offered visitors an unparalleled treasure trove of beauty
with vast views of the Ranjit Sagar Lake and Dhar Forest from the eight all-weather tents with attached
bathrooms and essential amenities. The project generated employment opportunities through boat rides
along Ranjit Sagar Lake, adventure sports facilities like zip lining and hiking, and food trucks operated by
locals. The Nature Interpretation Centre, founded for instructional and training purposes, used augmented
reality to broadcast films and shows about wetlands, climate change, and environmental preservation.
Numerous guided excursions along natural routes with lengths ranging between 2 km and 10 km are
regularly organised for tourists, along with bird viewing activities.i
Upon reflection, Dr. Tiwari was astonished to realise how much of his time as DFO in Pathankot was spent
developing this ecotourism project for launch and preparing for the day of its inauguration. A couple of
years before its inauguration, Tiwari and his team from the Punjab Forest Department engaged with the
villagers and other local communities in Dhar Kalan about developing this initiative. The team from the
Forest Department presented them with the concept of the initiative that would utilise the natural resources
available and transform the region into a thriving tourist destination. It strengthened its presentation by
declaring the plan to convert the abundant natural resources in the region into means of creating
employment for the people of Dhar Kalan, which would also ensure that they retained control of their land
