by preventing it from falling into the hands of private players. However, the Forest Department struggled
to secure approval from the villagers despite many discussions and assurances of giving preference to
locals for job opportunities. The department recognised the villagers as the right holders of the land where
the proposed project was to be built.
The locals, on the other hand, were sceptical about the entry of forest officials and authorities into their
area, which they believed complicated their livelihood practices and restricted their freedom. This belief
was rooted in the long history of restrictions imposed by the forest department in the region until 2010, in
addition to the villagers’ reliance on natural resources from the forest for their livelihood. Furthermore,
some people from the villages were engaged in illicit activities, including smuggling firewood and killing
small animals, which feared the presence of forest officials. The rising tensions between the Forest
Department and villagers needed to be addressed, as one of Tiwari's primary objectives was to encourage
community participation. The turning point came with the decision to address the lack of physical
infrastructure in Dhar Kalan, particularly power-electricity-water. With the involvement of the Forest
Department, concerns regarding a lack of infrastructure were addressed.
A three-phase electricity supply and a 2-inch dedicated pipeline for water supply were installed, replacing
the previously outdated and ineffective infrastructure. A borewell was also constructed to ensure enough
water for everyone in the village. The forest department also focused on the installation of solar panels and
benches in Chamrod to encourage the use of renewable energy. Plans for expanding the width of the roads
and repairing the current ones connecting the villages to the main highway also significantly contributed
to strengthening the rapport between the local community and the Punjab Forest Department. Overcoming
these contrasts was pivotal in gaining the village panchayat's approval to initiate the project's construction.
The availability of ample infrastructural facilities in Dhar Kalan, with continual efforts by the Forest
i The camp also boasts four all-weather resort tents and a state-of-the-art interpretation centre to
showcase augmented reality-based animal shows and other informative multimedia shows. The camp
also trains guides on bird watching and other aspects of floral and fauna cultivation.

BALANCING ECONOMIC GROWTH AND SUSTAINABLE ECOTOURISM: THE CASE OF THE
DHAR NATURE RETREAT AWARENESS CAMP

3

Department, helped to manage concerns about the sustainability and success of the project among the local
community. It had been a long road for the project to reach a stage where everyone involved in the
project—from its development to bringing it to fruition—was satisfied with how the different project
components had been structured.
Management & Financing of the Camp
Tiwari acknowledged the local community and villagers for their knowledge and familiarity with the
region and their expertise in it. The local community and the Forest Department worked together to
maintain the region through the Joint Forest Committee. For instance, it was the neighbourhood that
notified the Forest Department of any forest fires, encroachments, or other offences involving the forest.
Without community support, it is impossible to protect forests. The Joint Forest Committees developed the
infrastructure before turning it over to the Village Forest Committee (VFC) for execution. The Village Forest
Committee consists of nine members, of whom two are women. The Pradhan of Chamrod village serves as
the chairman of the committee, which is responsible for efficient operations and management of the Nature
Retreat and Awareness Camp.
About ₹ 1.2 crores7 were invested in this Nature Retreat. The project proposal was presented to the Principal
Chief Conservator of Forests (PCCF)ii and the Additional Chief Secretary of Forests (ACS)

iii. The Forest
Department made an investment of ₹ 60 lakh, while the District Mining Fund (DMF) contributed the
remaining amount. Additionally, substantial funds for the Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp come from
the outsourced operations of water and speed boats. For instance, the Forest Department received ₹ 1.5
crore for the two boats to be plied in a reservoir area in a tender in 2022.

8 Water sports, which are most
popular with tourists, provide the most profit. The department has also signed a memorandum of
understanding (MoU) with the village forest committee in Chamrod village. Accordingly, 50 percent9 of
the revenue earned from Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp is invested into village development after
paying maintenance costs as per the guidelines of the joint forest management committee. This is an
essential agreement deemed crucial by the President of the Committee, as this fund is significant for
development and for the maintenance of basic amenities in the village panchayat.
The revenue generated from the camp since its inauguration has been utilised to cover operational
expenses. A self-sustainability model has been adopted to run this project. Dr. Tiwari rationalised this
model with the understanding that if payments were handled by the Forest Department, these would then
flow into the treasury of the state government. Consequently, the Forest Department would then need to
first obtain clearances from the Punjab government for conducting any maintenance work, which would
be a drawn-out process. Instead, with the self-sustaining model, the department can withdraw funds with
the president and member secretary's joint signatures. Meetings of the General Body and the Executive
Committee are held periodically as part of consultations to oversee these expenditures.
Success of the Nature Retreat & Awareness Camp
Since the launch of the Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp in February 2020, this ecotourism project in
Chamrod hamlet (Exhibit 1), Dhar Kalan, has been dubbed Mini Goa. Due to its magnificent terrain (Exhibit
2), the region has always had enormous potential to be developed as a recreational location for adventure
ii Principal Chief Conservator of Forests: The Principal Chief Conservator of Forests is the highest-ranking
officer belonging to the Indian Forest Service who is responsible for managing the forests, environment
and wild-life related issues of a state in India.
iii Additional Chief Secretary of Forests: An Additional Chief Secretary of Forests (ACS) is an officer who
helps to protect natural forests by performing important administrative duties in a forest department.

BALANCING ECONOMIC GROWTH AND SUSTAINABLE ECOTOURISM: THE CASE OF THE
DHAR NATURE RETREAT AWARENESS CAMP

4

sports and weekend gateways. A keen focus on sustainable tourism has led to an administrative shift
towards nature conservation, cleanliness, sanitation, clean drinking water, employment, better roads and
connectivity, safety, and security. Ecotourism promises to be a game changer in this region, which has few
other livelihood opportunities. Before the initiative, the land on which this camp is constructed was
occasionally used for herding and grazing livestock. Currently, the people employed within the camp come
from the adjoining villages of Dhar Kalan, such as Chamrod, Badi Dhar, Chhoti Dhar, Hardosar, Chhibarr
and Dalla.10 They are employed in various positions, such as managers, cooks, housekeepers, security
guards and parking attendants. The hills overlooking the lake below the camp have become sites for mobile
food stalls operated by those who earlier worked as daily wage labourers in urban factories and other
commercial enterprises.
Most of the people employed are under the age of 35 years, thereby ensuring that the youth in the village
can now stay and assist their community to thrive instead of migrating to urban areas in search of a
livelihood. In fact, this project has successfully achieved its goal of preventing the migration of local youth
to metropolises cities by promoting entrepreneurship, innovation, and employment generation. Earlier,
many young people from these villages—for want of livelihood opportunities—had turned to alcohol and
narcotics. Today, many village elders credit this project with providing the younger generation with a
lifeline to take up responsibilities and have something to look forward to. The project has also ushered in
infrastructural benefits. Due to narrow and poorly maintained roads, few vehicles could travel downhill to
the villages, which resulted in continued problems for parents with school-going children. With the roads
being maintained, vans and small school buses can enter the villages to collect and drop off children. The
installation of fences and warning signs around the lake's boundaries by the Forest Department has proved
beneficial, as there have been significantly fewer drowning incidents. Thus, most people in Dhar Kalan
acknowledge the Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp for heralding regional growth and development.
The Price of Success: Current Dilemmas Faced by Dhar Kalan
The success of the Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp has not been without challenges. The retreat camp
experiences heavy footfall during peak summer, which are the busiest tourist months, which raises
concerns about law and order in the neighbourhood. Nighttime parties and loud picnics around the
reservoir continue to pose a problem. Moreover, the Dhar Kalan community has undergone several
transformations. The socio-economic shifts in the local community and the changes in livelihood patterns
are significant. A substantial increase in land value around the Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp has
led to many landholding people becoming more affluent and moving to metropolitan areas in the state.
A significant change in the land use pattern in the region has led to most of the pastoral land being lost to
the site of the Nature Retreat and other upcoming private holiday resorts. A marginal increase in household

incomes has led to most villagers producing food grains only for personal consumption. While law-and-
order concerns have been managed with support from the local police force, which has assisted in

regulating parking facilities and controlling rogue elements, the transformation in the community raises
concerns. Questions have emerged about the safety and security of the visitors and the local staff, in
addition to the meaning of livelihood sustainability connected to the camp.
In view of this discussion, the following questions ought to be explored:
1. What could be some policy incentives to motivate villagers to shift their livelihood practices?
2. How can the administration engage villagers in participatory natural resource management?
3. What other synergistic, sustainable livelihood opportunities can be harvested from the ecotourism
project?

Case Study Title: Capacity building in Southern Railway: The case of the IT Cell initiative
Case Study Description: The establishment of an IT Cell in the Chief Commercial Manager (Passenger) office in the Southern Railways is an ideal case to discuss principles of optimal utilisation of limited resources in team building. Relevant principles include capacity building through continuous guided learning, adaptive management through the institutionalisation of innovation, committed leadership and responsive governance.The case is set in December 2017 when Mr. Vinayan was appointed as the Chief Commercial Manager (Passenger) of Southern Railways, headquartered in Chennai. With decades of experience in Southern Railways, Mr. Vinayan is aware of challenges that affect the efficiency of the system for both its employees and passengers. He knows that the solutions to these challenges can be through technological development, but he does not want to outsource the work to external agencies and become dependent on their service. He undertakes the charge to address these challenges internally by developing an IT Cell, using old resources that already exist and harnessing those lying dormant.
Case Text:
“Mahatma Gandhi’s talisman is reflected in the objectives of Mission Karmayogi which aims at “the right person for
the right role at the right time.”

- Mission Karmayogi, 2020

Introduction
In December 2017, Mr. J. Vinayan was appointed the Chief Commercial Manager (Passenger Marketing) at
Southern Railways, headquartered in Chennai (Exhibit 1).1 With over 27 years of service in the Indian
Railways, Mr. Vinayan understood that even the most efficient of units faced challenges that needed to be
resolved to enhance the performance. In his day-to-day work, he was often reminded of a statement made
by a senior colleague upon his initial hire into the Indian Railways: ‘This is a job where one never runs out
of problems to solve.’ Mr. Vinayan’s experience over the years had proved the veracity of this statement.
To anticipate, address and resolve emerging critical issues therefore, Mr. Vinayan had established a
‘Brainstorming’ group. This group consisted of members from across different units of his headquarters
office and more importantly, from the field units. Their discussions led to the creation of a forum for
members across various departments to share experiences about the challenges in their work, and possible
solutions. Before long, a pattern emerged where most discussions centered on issues impacting the
efficiency of services rendered to passengers or feedback on rail employees’ performance and its
improvement.
Southern Railway’s Key Challenges in Passenger Marketing services
In the domain of service delivery by Railway officials in the passenger service domain, a singular recurring
challenge that emerged from the brainstorming discussions was the need for swift and reliable information
dissemination with an efficient mechanism for circulation of orders and regulations to employees. When
notifications were issued, these were required to be individually communicated to the appropriate
departments and officers quickly and accurately, without leaving anyone out. This process often took too
long and was riddled with errors and mistakes, leading to officers often being unaware of the latest rules
and regulations. Mr. P.S.Panchapakeswaran, Chief Commercial Inspector in the office of Principal Chief
Commercial Manager, Southern Railways, recalled that when regulations regarding a specific issue needed
to be identified and used, the entire team would scramble helter-skelter, hoping that someone would know
of it or at least know where to look for it. Here was a need for a new mode of dissemination of rules and
procedures and orders.

CAPACITY BUILDING IN SOUTHER RAILWAYS: THE CASE OF IT CELL INITIATIVE 2
The standard practice prevalent in any Governmental organization including Railways for resolving
technical or commercial work challenges was to reach out to external service providers through floating
tenders. However, in this case, this team decided that it was necessary to incorporate a culture of resolving
challenges internally by leveraging existing resources differently or by harnessing additional resources for
problem resolution from within in-house resources. The Southern Railways offices usually executed its
assigned responsibilities, and employees fulfilled their mandated duties. However, Mr. Vinayan was
perturbed by the absence of an effective information dissemination infrastructure, particularly with regard
to the vital role that the regular release of notifications and rules played in the everyday functioning of a
24x7 all year-round working organization like the Railways.
Further, the brainstorming groups identified additional challenges in the railway system like manual
collection and collation of data on the number of passengers travelling in the trains. Every year on two
occasions (‘lean’ period in November and ‘busy’ period in May) passenger censuses are carried out, when
Railway staff physically stand at the stations when the trains pass and manually take a head count in all
the unreserved coaches on each train. This is crucial management information data for decision making on
infrastructure planning by way of number of coaches on trains, additional services, running of special trains
for festivals etc. (In the reserved coaches, this data is already available from the reservation system database).
Traditionally this used to be a three-to- four-month process. The census station would compile the data of
various trains and send it to the division office which would then collate the division’s details. 2 This data
was then sent as hard copy to the office of the Headquarters of the Chief Commercial Manager (PM), who
would compile and collate and publish the data and send it to the user officers. Consequently, the
collecting, collating, and processing of this data became a long, tedious and error-prone undertaking in
terms of the number of employees involved and the long time required to complete the exercise.
Another such challenge identified was the absence of monitoring mechanisms for use of computer
peripherals like printers, routers, switches, and modems, which are used around-the-clock for Unreserved
Ticketing Systems (UTS) and Passenger Reservation Systems (PRS) that account for generation of some 95
percent of passenger revenue amounting to over Rs 6500 crore every year over Southern Railways.
3 With
thousands of terminals, ticketing counters and crores of tickets printed daily, there was no way of keeping
track of the upkeep, maintenance and life of individual computer peripherals. This often resulted in
protracted delays in equipment maintenance, which could lead to a loss in revenue, and customer
complaints.
Mr. Vinayan also learnt that passengers often faced difficulty in acquiring authentic, up-to-date
information about railway services at a local level, despite several applications and websites to assist them.
Information on various facets of railway services, such as ticket status, train schedules, and contact details
of support services, only available physically at railway stations or on different mobile phone applications
was often inaccurate, out-dated and not authentic, thereby misleading passengers.
To sum up, for Mr Vinayan’s team, four key questions emerged from these discussions:
• How can an efficient and effective information dissemination system be developed for in-house
rules, orders, and circulars for employees?
• How can unreserved passenger census and data processing be made effective and efficient in terms
of time and labour?
• How can a centralized mechanism be established to effectively monitor all peripherals and
accessory equipment across thousands of ticketing counters?
• How can a remotely accessible system be developed to efficiently provide accurate and updated
information about railway services in one centralized location?

CAPACITY BUILDING IN SOUTHER RAILWAYS: THE CASE OF IT CELL INITIATIVE 3
Charting a New Path
Convinced that these issues were critical and needed immediate redressal, Mr. Vinayan, in July 2018,
finalized the technological resolution of these four challenges at the Southern Railways. He was certain that
the solution to these problems was through technical innovation and development of appropriate online
applications and solutions. However, implementation of these ideas according to his plan presented a

hurdle. Mr. Vinayan intended to create these innovative applications in-house as an alternative to the pre-
existing method of floating tenders. He firmly believed that it was possible to avoid the tender route and

break the cycle of dependence through independent initiative and innovation expertise available within
the Railways. Earlier too, the Indian Railways had resolved its information technology challenges through
the successful development of the Centre for Railway Information System (CRIS) within the Railway
Ministry in the past millennium.1
While CRIS is not an external private service provider, it is still an organization independent of the
Southern Railways. This meant that once projects were outsourced to CRIS, these became their prerogative,
and bound to their schedules, priorities, limitations and requirements, thereby minimizing the role of the
Southern Railways in resolving its own issues. Further, CRIS being headquartered at Delhi, brought with
it a possibility of limited utilization of the existing workforce and resources available with the Chennai
based Southern Railways in developing the solutions, thereby depriving them an opportunity to build the
tools necessary to overcome in-house challenges. Mr. Vinayan, driven by the objective of autonomy and
judicious use of existing resources, was determined to resolve the challenges impacting the passengers and
employees of Southern Railways from within the system itself.
Old Systems, Novel Solutions: Developing an In-house IT Cell
Mr. Vinayan’s primary challenge was establishing a team of application developers, or a dedicated IT
(Information Technology) centre focused on evolving IT-based solutions for Southern Railways customers
and staff. As a public sector undertaking, the Southern Railways operated with restricted funding assigned
to each department and individual employee bound by rules and regulations of financial management,
which also limited access to infrastructure and non-human resources.
Mr. Vinayan was however aware that although Southern Railways employees were from diverse
educational backgrounds, after their on-job training, their present roles and responsibilities were restricted
to the demands of their current official role. For example, there may be an Engineering graduate working
as an office clerk or as a ticket examiner; and he/she would have more or less lost touch with their
engineering skills after few years of service as a ticket examiner. To set up an IT Cell and develop
technological innovation in-house, Mr. Vinayan would have to identify how to use the existing staff and
resources differently and find a way to institutionalize this. To establish a sustainable system. Mr V. Anil
Chowdary and Mr. R. Nithyaraj, both Ticketing Supervisors, but with technical qualifications, and
members of the ‘Brainstorming’ group assisted him in this endeavour. It transpired that they were
experienced technical experts with knowledge of application development. Mr. Nithyaraj and Mr Anil thus
began developing an app to resolve the problem of passengers' lack of access to authentic and accurate
information related to railway services, through development of an Android app.
Encouraged by this progress, Mr. Vinayan began to believe he could set up an in-house team and provide
the support needed for them to become adept application developers. In the meantime, he started to devise
1 CRIS (Centre for Railway Information Systems) is an organisation under the Ministry of Railways. CRIS
includes IT professionals and experienced railway personnel tasked with delivering complex Railway IT
systems in core areas. Since its inception in 1986, CRIS has been developing and maintaining software for
the following key functional areas of the Indian Railways.

CAPACITY BUILDING IN SOUTHER RAILWAYS: THE CASE OF IT CELL INITIATIVE 4
strategies to enable the team to exist and function independently, even if he was no longer in the team,
which could endure the vision and objective of the IT Cell as a sustainable model of in-house innovation
and technical development. To avert the possibility of a newly appointed officer, in the future,
discontinuing the innovative efforts, Mr. Vinayan established a distinct, formal, dedicated unit within the
Chief Commercial Manager’s (Passenger Marketing) office that would work solely on providing technical
and innovative solutions to challenges faced by the Southern Railways. Mr. Vinayan says, “Thus, we
started to build our own IT and Innovation Cell” (Exhibit 2).
Today the IT Cell is well established in the CCM-PM office and the members are handling various projects
and applications developments and maintenance. The vacancies arising are filled through the established
in-house practice calling for qualified and willing candidates from multiple backgrounds and selecting the
most suitable ones through a screening process.
Troubleshooting Through Tech Innovations
Following the identification of challenges and the development of a team built through identifying optimal
ways of using existing resources, the IT and Innovation Cell created technological solutions to resolve each
problem plaguing the Southern Railways as identified above. The challenge of information dissemination
was addressed by developing an app titled ‘Rail Dhandora’. Taking inspiration from the common Indian
term ‘dhandora’, meaning an ‘announcement drum’, the Rail Dhandora application provides users easy
access to all extant circulars, rules, procedures and orders issued by the Railways from time to time.
The team devised a mechanism whereby, each time a new circular is issued by the Railway ministry, it gets
automatically uploaded on the application, which triggers a notification that alerts and informs employees
about the issuance of the circular. Besides new circulars, the team worked to collect circulars, rules and
regulations issued between 1999 and 2005, along with important rulings under different categories such as
passengers, freight customers, parcel customers and employees. This database could be easily accessed by
employees and distributed further by simply downloading the circulars and directly sharing these through
mobile applications like email, WhatsApp, and Telegram.
The IT and Innovation team similarly developed the Rail Census application, which automated the
laborious data collection and collation procedure so that data may be ordered through the application and
directly processed through the system. In much the same way, the Ticketing Peripherals Management
System (TPMS) application enables efficient maintenance of computer-based ticketing peripherals and
accessories by employees and allows for their continuous use by the passengers of railways. The
application provides a centralized, computerized information system, which provides real-time
information on the working status of different equipment at the thousands of counters in over 800 locations
in the Southern Railways.
Impact & Continuing Dilemmas
The IT cell has proven to be a great success. Its Rail Dhandora application was awarded the ‘Order of Merit’
SKOCH Certificate 2020 award, that honours people, institutions, and projects that go the extra mile to
make India a better nation.4

It received the award for innovation in the sphere of governance. Inspired by
its accomplishments and support, the team is more determined than ever to sustain its innovation journey
and improve Southern Railways commercial operations. When asked what they liked most about their
work and what keeps them motivated, the team unanimously declared that they enjoyed utilizing their
educational and professional training in performing over and above expectations of their Railway roles.
“Winning accolades, knowing that we are helping our beloved passengers and dedicated staff ease their
struggles, getting requests for replicating the technology elsewhere and positive feedback from passengers
are all motivating factors,” they chimed in. Mr. Vinayan believes that the success of the IT Cell is to be

CAPACITY BUILDING IN SOUTHER RAILWAYS: THE CASE OF IT CELL INITIATIVE 5
attributed to the people constituting it and the railway institutional environment which encourages
innovation and problem-solving attitude. He believes that creating a space dedicated to collective learning
and innovation, with minimum interference except to provide support, is the real reason for its success. He
does not worry about the future functioning of the IT Cell. As he mentioned, “I realized that what is most
important are the people and not innovations.” Now that the people have stayed, the innovations will
continue.

But lurking beneath the exuberance are some rarely voiced team concerns. The biggest concern is their ad-
hoc status. Each member belongs to a different railway department and is still governed by its rules of

conduct despite being a part of the IT Cell for over five years now. This often causes a clash in their duties
and expectations. “We have been performing work for which we have received educational training, but
are not required to do as per our original designation in the Railways. We worry that if the IT Cell and our
designation as its members changes, we will have to return to our old work, with which we have lost
touch.” Even though the IT Cell continues to work efficiently and create more unprecedented technological
innovations, it is perhaps pertinent to look closely at the need to sufficiently institutionalize the Cell's and
its members' existence to prevent uncertainty and promote complete dedication to the work and its visions.
All things considered, nevertheless, at the heart of all these initiatives is the spirit of the message now
painted on an office wall at the spanking new CCMPM office in Southern Railways Chennai. “The best
teamwork comes from men and women who are working independently towards one goal in unison”.
Discussion
This case demonstrates the need for committed and innovative leadership that serves to identify and utilize
resources when additional means are scarce. To set up a new IT Team, Mr. Vinayan had to find ways to
reconfigure existing resources to identify and hire members. The struggle also lay in providing the
inspiration and guidance so they would go beyond their immediate work tasks and be driven by the
broader vision of developing technological innovations to improve the efficiency of the existing system at
Southern Railways. Some key challenges that merit reflection include:
1. How can a new IT Cell be established within the existing infrastructure and resources of the CCMPM
office?
2. How will the IT Cell and its members be institutionalized?
3. How can a reliable and stable set-up be built for IT Cell members to ensure continuity and commitment?
4. What other factors may be considered while investing in team building and capacity building when
operating with limited resources, and laid down rules in a purely Governmental environment?

Case Study Title: Adopting an ecosystem approach to groundwater recharging: Pond rejuvenation project in Udham Singh Nagar
Case Study Description: The pond rejuvenation project in Udham Singh Nagar, Uttarakhand is a good case to discuss the principles of applying an ecosystem approach to governance. Relevant principles include focusing on relationships and processes within the ecosystem of key players' economic and political activity, benefit-sharing, adaptive and responsive management, including change management practices, appropriate decentralisation of tasks and responsibilities, and intersectoral cooperation. The case is set between 2019 and present-day Udham Singh Nagar, Uttrakhand, where Mayur Dixit, the protagonist, undertakes the task of rejuvenating ponds that have been encroached upon to recharge the district’s groundwater table. Apart from hydrogeological reasons, Udham Singh Nagar, a district located in Uttarakhand’s Terai region, is on the verge of a general water crisis resulting from water-intensive farming and rampant industrialisation. Mayur Dixit is aware of the limits of simply recharging ponds via desilting and other conventional pond rejuvenation methods. He understands the need to develop a holistic approach that takes into account the underlying causes of the lowered groundwater levels.
Case Text:
“India’s development and self-reliance is dependent on water security and water connectivity.”
1

Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri. Narendra Modi
“This is necessary and should be easy enough”, muttered Mr. Mayur Dixit, Chief Development
Officer (CDO), to himself as he surveyed a silted pond in the district of Udham Singh Nagar, Uttarakhand
in northern India. His optimism was tempered by the reality of Udham Singh Nagar’s impending water
crisis. The influx of farmers cultivating water-intensive crops and growth in the number of industrial units
were key contributing factors. Over the years, the naturally occurring water bodies had been levelled in
many places to house livestock or store cow dung. At other sites, permanent shops or houses had been
built on the drained lands.
To stave off a water crisis, Mr. Dixit spearheaded an initiative in 2019 to recharge the district’s
groundwater table by rejuvenating and removing the encroachments on traditional ponds. However, as
work to clear up the ponds got underway, Mr. Dixit and his team quickly realized that these ponds'
encroachments, silting and drying were only symptoms of a wider, multifaceted problem. Much more
work was needed to recharge the groundwater table, including close collaboration with the local
community and the industries. Therefore, before launching the pond rejuvenation exercise, Mr. Dixit
understood he had to first address the primary factors that had caused this situation in the first place.
Key Factors Contributing to the Depleting Groundwater in Udham Singh Nagar
Geographical Sensitivity
Carved out of Nainital district in 1995, Udham Singh Nagar is located in the terai, a lowland region
between the outer Himalayas and the Indo-Gangetic plain. Lying in the discharge zones of the perennial
rivers flowing through the region, it has ample fertile soil ripe for crop cultivation. The district's geology
(Exhibits 1 & 2) shapes the groundwater scenario, ideally sustained and recharged by direct infiltration and
percolation of rainwater. However, due to its flat or level terrain, there are few opportunities for
replenishing the groundwater table here. Consequently, artesian wells—the region’s primary source for
drawing groundwater—have drastically depleted.2

In 2016, the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB)
reported that the district witnessed a 40 percent decline in the district’s artesian land, where water rises to
the surface naturally without a pump.3

This statistic is alarming as it takes more than one century for
artesian land to recoup. This situation is further compounded by the advent of tube wells—commonly used

ADOPTING AN ECOSYSTEM APPROACH TO GROUNDWATER RECHARGING: POND
REJUVENATION PROJECT IN UDHAM SINGH NAGAR

2

for irrigating fields—that use 89 percent of extracted groundwater.4

Udham Singh Nagar had thus become
one of the most water-deprived regions in the country according to the CGWB report, which experienced
a 61 percent decline in groundwater levels between 2007 and 2017. Over-exploitation of groundwater was
attributed to rapid urbanization, deforestation, water-intensive agricultural practices, and
industrialization.
Water-intensive Agriculture
The district has a high concentration of agriculture, with migrants from the neighbouring states of
Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal being attracted by the seemingly fertile land. Often called the food
bowl of Uttarakhand, the district produces half of the state’s wheat production. Called the ‘chawal ki
nagari’ (land of rice), the water-intensive cultivation of rice thrice a year has resulted in an onerous
dependence on groundwater. An official representative from the state’s irrigation department mentioned
that 200 litres of water were needed for every kilogram of nonseasonal paddy. To further impair the
region’s water woes, there has been a growth in the cultivation of poplar trees, which are water-intensive
and used by the paper pulp and board industries in the district.i

The situation became worse with state
government initiatives like free power and subsidized borewells and tube wells, which resulted in
uncontrolled exploitation and wastage of resources (Exhibit 3) that increased the pressure on the
groundwater table. Groundwater levels have come down to below 250 ft, especially when monsoons do
not deliver sufficient precipitation.
Growth of Industries
Rapid urbanization has led to the emergence of major industries in the district. This industrial
boom—an unavoidable aspect of economic development and employment generation—has caused heavy
reliance on groundwater. In 2014, Mr. Vinod Singh from the Uttarakhand Environment Protection and
Pollution Control Board (UEPPCB) disclosed that industries like paper and pulp, sugar, and distillery
companies consume the maximum amount of water. It was reported that close to 7000 KL of water were
used daily by the district’s 22 paper pulp units, which has significantly contributed to the adverse impact
on the groundwater table and now calls into question the future of nearly 1,500 companies based in Udham
Singh Nagar.
Lack of Awareness & Encroachment of Traditional Water Bodies
Interestingly, many villagers and officials do not view water scarcity as an imminent problem and
consider it as hype propagated by the media and state administration to ensure water security through
futureproofing. This indicates a certain level of ignorance about declining water levels and the urgent need
for water conservation. Furthermore, village ponds, called Common Property Resources (CPR), have
deteriorated and become unusable due to various reasons like village politics turning ignorant to
encroachments and lack of awareness about the need to protect natural resources. While some of these
encroachments were temporary—sheds to store cow dung or use as animal shelters—others like
construction of homes and shops over the dried pond lands were more permanent.
Consequently, the challenges facing Udham Singh Nagar district were multi-fold. The diminishing
groundwater levels due to lack of groundwater recharge opportunities, heavy reliance on groundwater for

industries in Rudrapur.

3

agriculture and industry, compounded with rising urbanization, besides encroachment of traditional water
bodies had placed this district on the verge of a serious water crisis.
Recharging Groundwater - National & State Government Initiatives
Groundwater depletion is widely prevalent and pond rejuvenation is accepted as a low-cost
method to recharge the groundwater tables. The National Institute of Hydrology has accordingly
established a standard operating procedure (SOP) via a Natural Treatment System to support states. The
Government of India additionally offers technical support and financial assistance under various welfare
schemes identified under the Repair, Renovation and Restoration of Water Bodies component of the
Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY)—Har Khet Ko Pani (HKKP) program.
5
In 2019, Jal
Shakti Abhiyan was launched in some of India’s water-stressed districts to introduce interventions for the
rejuvenation of traditional water bodies/ tanks besides removing encroachments. Revival of water bodies
was also covered under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) scheme
and the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA).ii Under the newly
launched Mission Amrit Sarovar, authorities aim to develop and rejuvenate 75 water bodies in each district
across the country as part of the 75th year of Independence (Azadi ka Amrit Mahotsav).iii
Preparing the Ground
Planning Field Surveys for Pond Identification
Following consultations with experts in 2019, Mr. Dixit (CDO), Dr. Neeraj Kherwal (District
Magistrate), and other district authorities decided to conserve and harvest rainwater by rejuvenating
encroached ponds. The primary goal of rejuvenation was to accomplish the dual outcomes of recharging
the groundwater table and reducing dependence on tube wells. The project began by first creating a roster
for new works before the start of the financial year at the Gram Panchayat level in a khuli baithak (open
discussion). This roster was collated at the block and then approved at the district level.
A funding plan was devised, and the project was approved and passed at each level. For the pond
rejuvenation project, Mr. Dixit spoke to the SDM and the tehsildarsiv to collect data along with revenue
records. The revenue records contained a list of 546 ponds which had various types of encroachments
including structures for farming use (temporary and permanent).6 Between 2019 and 2022, revenue and
block teams used these records to survey and demarcate the encroached ponds through traditional
methods like lime powder or ‘chuna’ to mark territories. This was an intensive exercise which required
close collaboration with the Revenue Department and the Irrigation Department, which provided guidance
on the appropriate digging depth after due consideration of the soil's water retention capacity.
Developing Buy-in
Mr. Dixit and other senior officials recognized the need to bring local residents on board before
launching the pond-clearing operation as there were homes and shops built on many of the identified

government land and their obligation to vacate. This initiative was converged with other government
schemes whereby members of the affected families were hired to help in the clearance of these ponds and
earn a compensatory wage. This proved to be a wise decision as it generated employment and fostered
support from residents and the impacted parties, rendering the project operations eco-system sustainable.
Convergence with Government Policies
Following the identification of ponds that were silted, polluted or encroached, district authorities
initiated the pond rejuvenation work through MGNREGA, which guarantees employment to unskilled
rural labourers and paid workers a daily wage of ₹ 213. Under the scheme, up to ₹ 2 lakhs were assigned
to remove encroachments from each identified community pond. The villagers most impacted were
preferred for hire. Sourcing labour entirely from within the villages, eliminated the need for external
contractors. Vegetable production and planting of fruit trees in the areas surrounding the ponds was also
conducted under MGNREGA. Animal shelters were designed and constructed for residents who needed
alternative spaces for their livestock. Convergence with government schemes like the National Rural
Livelihoods Mission (NRLM)

v was employed for the construction of polyhouses and duck rearing to benefit
those involved in the pond rejuvenation (Exhibit 4). Occasionally, this was done before the commencement
of the pond-clearing project to allay potential resistance.
Unfolding Challenges: Double Whammy for Farmers
Kishan Lal, a migrant from Punjab and a marginal farmer who had built his house on the
encroached land, was going to be doubly affected by the administration's interventions. He was sceptical
of the administration's promises and unwilling to give up the land on which he had built his house. He
also shared the preference of the majority of farmers to cultivate paddy all through the year due to its
higher gross returns per acre (nearly ₹ 14,000) as against maize.
By May 2021, following the growing pressure to resist 'encroachers', Lal, along with other farmers
from three villages, approached the then CDO’s (Chief Development Officer) office for a sunwai (public
hearing). CDO accompanied by two other senior district officials and the local public representative
conducted the sunwai. The Gram Pradhans (Head of the village) represented the residents and farmers.
Both factions presented their sides vociferously. The local public representative attempted to convince the
residents about the common good and the benefit from recharging the ponds, in addition to the
administration’s plans to compensate everyone. Lal was concerned about the administration’s push to set
up drip/micro irrigation systems, which in Uttarakhand, with its sloping and terraced land,

7 requires an

investment of ₹ 1-2 lakhs even after a 50 percent rebate under the Prime Minister’s Krishi Sinchayee Yojana-
Per Drop More Crop (PMKSY-PDMC) scheme. Thus, the proposed irrigation systems were viable only for

large farmers with 2 to 3 hectares of land. The administration's push for cash crops like sugarcane, with a
long cultivation period of 10 to 18 months, reduced the land’s productivity. Farmers were lured to growing
poplar trees for the medium density fireboard (MDF) industry, even at the cost of the depleting
groundwater table.

Community Involvement & Shifting Perceptions
The next few weeks remained tense, particularly in areas where people had built structures like
houses and shops. Despite the ongoing opposition, CDO directed the authorities to commence work in and
around demarcated ponds with temporary encroachments. Permanent constructions however, remained
untouched and tricky to approach amidst the prevailing issue. In addition to pond rejuvenation, fishing
rights were granted to self-help groups (SHGs) under the NRLM scheme in an effort to create livelihood
opportunities. The project slowly gained traction with the villagers as money flowed directly into the
village. Media coverage of the project's initial success increased the momentum of work and traction
amongst residents in neighbouring towns. On the broader issue of groundwater depletion due to intensive
agriculture practices, the Irrigation Department conducted workshops to educate farmers and incentivize
a shift to maize cultivation. However, concerns raised by farmers like Kishan Lal continued to prevent this
shift. CDO and his team were keenly aware of the challenge of having to convince farmers to shift practices.
Yet, they were clear that to ensure sustainable benefits for everyone, a broader ecosystem had to be
developed to facilitate this transition.
Challenges of Pond Maintenance and Sustaining Efforts
The work on demarcated areas that extended beyond village boundaries could not be undertaken
under MGNREGA and presented a key challenge. Additionally, there were initial hurdles in sourcing
labour, as wages under MGNREGA were only ₹ 213 per day while private contractors and projects paid
between ₹ 500 and ₹ 600 per day. However, when COVID-19 struck the district, MGNREGA, despite low
wages, allowed families to sustain themselves during the pandemic.
Maintenance of the rejuvenated ponds by various self-help groups posed another challenge. The
SHGs had been promised ownership and exclusive fishing rights. However, out of over 350 rejuvenated
ponds, only about 100 have been handed over to the different SHGs (Exhibit 5). Additionally, maintaining
the depth of 10 ft for a pond, the size of 1 acre, became difficult due to continual silting, collapsing bunds
and rapid growth of grass. It was also challenging to conduct maintenance work in winters due to the bitter
cold and snakes as well as during the monsoons, when the fish tend to escape the ponds with the rise in
water levels and spill over as the boundaries are not solid. Furthermore, if the ponds were away from
homes in the village, it would be challenging to stop thieves from stealing fish from the pond, leading to
losses.
Implementation of an Ecosystem Approach to Manage Groundwater
Pond rejuvenation projects have been undertaken across the country with varying degrees of
success. Under Azadi ka Amrit Mahotsav (Exhibit 6), nearly 93,300 sites have been identified countrywide.
In Udham Singh Nagar alone, 75 ponds were initially identified, and work is already underway. There are
differences, though, between Mission Amrit Sarovar and the pond rejuvenation project. The ponds
identified under the Amrit Sarovar program had to be community-owned and of a minimum size of 1 acre,
while the pond rejuvenation project had no such ownership or size criteria. Additionally, alternative
methods are also being used. As administrative officials in Rudrapur block mentioned, reboring of already
dug borewells and tube wells allows for water to be directly injected into the ground. These recharge shafts
serve to increase groundwater levels significantly and are more effective for the terai region with slower
recharge through percolation.8
This case demonstrates that natural resource-driven projects are vulnerable to failure over time as
the challenges are complex and interwoven. Work had to be conducted on multiple fronts simultaneously

to address changes in perception and behaviour, consumption patterns and usage, besides overall
implementation and monitoring with close supervision by Mr. Dixit and his team. He notes that out of the
546 identified ponds, only 351 have been rejuvenated to date while work on the remaining has been going
on. However, these ponds remain vulnerable to encroachments and silting once again. Mr. Dixit states that
“regular monitoring of the ponds is required”, which can be accomplished only through a larger
institutional mechanism to ensure the project’s sustainability. Additionally, while rejuvenating ponds is an
effective approach to recharge the groundwater table, emphasis on water conservation through rainwater
harvesting is still low and makes for greater dependence on groundwater. Mr. Dixit is acutely aware that
even government buildings lack a rainwater harvesting plant.
Discussion
This case illustrates the need to think holistically about the multiple factors that can contribute and serve
to solve a pressing problem. Mr. Dixit and his team realized the need to apply an ecosystem approach to
address the challenge of pond rejuvenation. It was therefore necessary to establish a ‘win-win’ situation for
all players to the extent feasible. Almost three years after the first few ponds were de-silted, the district
administration continues to battle major and minor obstacles arising from the project. Some of these key
challenges merit consideration:

Case Study Title: Combating the Covid-19 Pandemic in India
Case Study Description: The Har Ghar Tikakaran campaign is centred on the remarkable efforts of Dr. Veena Dhawan and her dedicated team, who spearheaded one of the largest vaccination drives ever conducted in India - the National Covid-19 Vaccination Program, amidst the throes of a pandemic. This campaign reflects upon the myriad challenges and obstacles encountered by the team and illuminates their triumphant journey in surmounting these hurdles through unwavering unity, unyielding determination, and exemplary cooperation.
Case Text:
“In more than three decades of my experience, I found this to be quite a rare experience where multiple stakeholders
and community were always willing to contribute. This went a long way to fulfil the national aim of successfully

Dr. Veena Dhawan
On January 3, 2023, Dr Veena Dhawan, a qualified medical professional, serving as an Additional

resolved to reevaluate the existing strategies, identify any shortcomings, and enhance the implementation
of proven best practices.
Nonetheless, her confidence remained unshaken. Drawing inspiration from the lessons learned during

would provide valuable insights to tackle the threat posed by the novel variant.

hospitalisations and it was clear that it would need to initiate a nationwide vaccination programme.
By January 2021, India approved the use of indigenous vaccines, namely 'Covishield' and 'Covaxin,’ for
restricted emergency use. This milestone set the stage for the launch of the national Covid-19 Vaccination

vaccination programme had been initiated.
The Universal Immunisation Programme had several well-established systems in place, including
supply-chain management using a dependable IT platform, cold-chain infrastructure, and partnerships
with multilateral organizations such as United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), United
Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF), and World Health Organization (WHO).
Nevertheless, the officials encountered numerous challenges during the implementation of the
programme. The existing assets under the programme were well tapped and improvised to build a
strong Covid vaccination delivery system.
Challenges during the Implementation of the Programme
Challenge 1: Overcoming Vaccine Manufacturing, Supply, and Delivery Barriers
India's Covid-19 vaccine manufacturing capacity was limited to the existing domestic manufacturers who
faced bottlenecks in the development of the vaccines required for the nation. Vaccine introduction
typically took 10 to 15 years

3 due to rigorous scientific research, safety testing, efficacy trials, and quality
assurance before mass production can begin. Even in cases of expedited development, indigenous
vaccines still couldn't be produced in large quantities in such short time due to manufacturing capacity
constraints.

v Measles is a highly contagious disease caused by a virus. It spreads easily when an infected person
breathes, coughs or sneezes. It can cause severe disease, complications, and even death.
vi Rubella, also called German Measles is a contagious disease caused by a virus.

COMBATING THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC IN INDIA 4
Furthermore, the simultaneous distribution of indigenous vaccines across the vast country could have
been hindered by the inadequate cold-storage infrastructure at distribution points need to accommodate
the quantities of vaccine required for the ambitious campaign. India's diverse geographic landscape,
encompassing snow-clad hills, raging rivers, and scorching deserts, added complexity to the delivery
process. To address these challenges, a scientifically calculated demand-supply equation was required to
ensure prudent vaccine distribution.
Solutions
I. Ramping up Production of Indigenous Vaccines
Recognizing the need to vaccinate its vast population within a limited timeframe, India decided to
quickly ramp up production of indigenous vaccines:
• Covaxin: Developed by 'Bharat Biotech' in collaboration with Indian Council of Medical Research
(ICMR) and National Institute of Virology (NIV).
• Covishield: Developed by 'Serum Institute of India' in partnership with Oxford University.
Support was provided to the manufacturers during the production period for these vaccines while
ensuring all essential protocols were met. The Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Government of India,
provided substantial financial support of INR 900 crore under Mission COVID Suraksha- The Indian
COVID-19 Vaccine Development Mission4

. These manufacturers were further supported by facilitating
technology transfer, advance payments against the orders to enable them to procure the necessary
components for vaccine production to expedite the process.
II. Logistic and Supply Management
A well-defined supply chain was established for vaccine delivery, from manufacturers to the Covid
Vaccination Centres (CVCs). Starting with allocation on a pro-ratavii basis approach, a dynamic demand
supply equation was created for each session site or CVC. This dynamic approach, based on daily
assessments, proved challenging but prevented vaccine wastage and reduced vaccines stranded in
pipelines. (Refer Exhibit 5)
III. Multi-modal Delivery Partners
To maximise vaccine delivery to remote areas, the states/UTs used various transportation methods, as
per the geographical region in question, using boats, camels, and drones in difficult or hilly terrains, and
last-mile delivery was done on foot by the front line workers.
IV. Structured Governance Mechanism
A core group, 'National Expert Group on Vaccine Administration for COVID-19 (NEGVAC),' was
established to manage the overall operationalisation of the vaccination programme. A network of
empowered committees and task forces was set up at various federal levels, including National/Centre,
State, District, and Block. Information and feedback were exchanged at each level to ensure a smoother
process. Additionally, the 'National Technical Advisory Group on Immunization (NTAGI),' was
responsible for providing technical recommendations to NEGVAC by evaluating all available evidence
for inclusion of the vaccine approved by the regulator into the National Covid vaccination programme.
This structure ensured a consultative approach and smooth information flow. (Refer Exhibit 6)
vii Pro-rata: Pro rata is a Latin term used to describe a proportionate allocation

COMBATING THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC IN INDIA 5
Challenge 2: Administering and Universalising Vaccination
The programme officers faced multiple challenges while adapting to adult vaccination, universalising
vaccination, and maintaining routine immunisation.
• No prior experience with Adult Vaccination: The division lacked prior experience in vaccinating
adults at such a large scale, making the transition from child to adult vaccination complex.
• Age-Related and Co-Morbidity Challenges: Each age group of adults presented unique challenges
due to age-related factors and co-morbidities, necessitating a more specific vaccination approach
keeping the uniqueness of the beneficiaries in mind.
• Accessibility Issues: Some adults may not be able to travel to vaccination centres, requiring a
special and customised approach.
• Digital Divide: Many adults were not proficient with digital vaccination platforms like CoWIN and
needed offline or onsite registration options.
• Complexities of Vaccinating Pregnant Women: Administering vaccines to pregnant women was
intricate due to concerns over minor adverse effects and their potential impact on both the mother
and the unborn child.
• Challenges of Diverse Populations: Unique strategy required for vaccinating foreigners residing in
India, migrant labourers, individuals without valid government-issued identification cards, and
those living in isolated institutions like jails, mental asylums, or rehabilitation homes etc.
• Ensure smooth running of routine immunization programme: Targeting children under five and
pregnant/lactating mothers continued seamlessly under the Universal Immunisation Programme
alongside the new mandate of COVID-19 vaccination. The division had to allocate its existing
resources, including capacities, physical infrastructure, institutes, systems, and manpower,
effectively to maintain both responsibilities.
The team worked tirelessly to mobilise the necessary resources to ensure the uninterrupted functioning of
the regular immunization programme and the commencement of the new National Covid-19 Vaccination
programme.
Solutions
I. Content Development and training of stakeholders
A very clear Covid-19 Operational Guidelines and a Communication Strategy was formed by the
National Covid-19 Vaccination Programme. The vaccination programme proved to be significantly more
complex than initially anticipated. Training was provided to various stakeholders, including:
Operational Guidelines and Communication Strategy for Covid-19 vaccination
• At National level, training for Principal Secretary (Health) and Mission Director (NHM) of all States,
District Magistrate/District Collector of all Districts, State Programme Managers, Finance officers
and other administrative officers, Municipal Commissioners, Urban Nodal Officers, State Senior
Official, SEPIO, State Cold Chain Officers, State IEC officer, State data in-charge, Partners, National
representatives of professional bodies such as IMA, IAP, AEFI Nodal officers, Defence Institutions.
• At State/UT Level, Chief Medical Officer, District Immunization Officer, Urban Nodal Officers,
Corporation Health Officer, District Programme Managers (NHM), District AEFI Nodal Officer,
District Data manager, State IMA, IAP societies, Nodal officers of medical colleges, Other
Departments including Supervisors, ICDS, Medical Colleges, Private practitioners.

COMBATING THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC IN INDIA 6
• At District Level: District Level Officers, Block Medical Officer, staff of Municipal Corporations,
Nodal officers of Municipal health institutes, Block Programme Managers, staff of NUHM, Block
Supervisors, Cold Chain Handlers, Data Entry Operators, District IAP societies, ICDS and other stake
holders.
• Use of Co-WIN platform: All level of officers from States/UTs, Central Health Institutes and other
Nodal Ministries, Inter Ministerial Nodal Person. Training of the vaccinator and the vaccination
teams on use of the digital platform was done repeatedly as the platform evolved with the
programme. For the beneficiaries there were clear SOPs, Videos available on CoWIN for them to
use the platform easily
These training programs were conducted on an extensive scale, utilising a combination of virtual and
classroom training. The training efforts were supported by appropriate training partners, enabling
rapid implementation. (Refer Exhibit 7)
II. Corona Warriors- The Protectors in Shining Armour
Dedicated Health Care Workers (HCWs), including the ANMviii, Nurses, played a pivotal role in mass
vaccination. They received thorough training on COVID-safe practices for administering the vaccine and
recording vaccination but also protect themselves while vaccinating others. The ASHAix

, Anganwadi and
other link workers were involved in mobilizing the eligible beneficiaries. These Corona Warriors
conducted special drives to track and mobilize those due for vaccine doses.
III. Vaccination-Centre Partnerships with Govt. Organizations
Collaborations were established with various government organizations possessing existing
infrastructure, including Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) dispensaries, Railways’
dispensaries, certain private players, and defence and police forces. United Nations International
Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF) partnered with the Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MOTA) for
advocacy in tribal areas. These partnerships decentralized the vaccination process, expanding its reach.
The private sector was also involved.
V. Partnership for designing CoWIN.
The existing partnership with UNDP was leveraged to enhance the existing Electronic Vaccine
Intelligence Network (eVIN) system, the vaccine logistic monitoring platform and creating a ‘beneficiary
module'. CoWIN served as a comprehensive platform for beneficiary registration. It offered both digital
and non-digital registration options, ensuring each vaccination event was digitally recorded. CoWIN
generated individual QR (Quick Response) code -based certificates for recording and facilitating national
and international travel. The success of the national programme owed much to the CoWIN platform, that
was integrated with ‘Aarogya Setu’x

to improve access. (Refer Exhibit 8). The platform was built under the

overall guidance of National Health Authority and the MoHFW.

viii ANM: Auxiliary Nurse Midwife
ix ASHA: Accredited Social Health Activist

VI. Rural and Gender Inclusivity
Most of the vaccination centres, 74%, were situated in rural areas, where 71% of the total doses were
administered5

. Public vaccination centres were well-stocked with vaccines, leading to 97.5%6 of
vaccinations taking place there. Gender equity was a priority, with nearly equal numbers of males and
females vaccinated. Comprehensive measures were ensured so that every intended beneficiary,
regardless of their location, gender, difficult geography, received their vaccination on schedule. (Refer
Exhibit 9)
Challenge 3: Spread of Misinformation about the Vaccine
The universal vaccination programme faced significant challenges due to the spread of misinformation.
Some citizens in remote areas were unaware of the pandemic and the vaccination programme. Others,
though aware, were reluctant to get vaccinated, doubting modern healthcare technology. Misinformed
individuals with no expertise began spreading opinions about the vaccine, leading to an info-demic.
xi
Some beneficiaries grew complacent about the pandemic's severity, avoiding the second vaccine dose.
This presented the division with a dual challenge- mobilizing and convincing one group to get vaccinated
while addressing the eagerness of another group to break vaccination queues.
Solutions
1. Innovative Campaigns
To boost vaccination rates, the 'Har Ghar Dastak' (Door-to-Door Vaccination) campaign was launched,
focusing on individuals like the bedridden, very old, specially-abled and institutions like mental health
institutions, old age homes etc. This initiative led to an increase in daily vaccinations, averaging 6.9
million per day in January 2022.
Following a decline in vaccinations from February to mid-July 2022, the 'Amrit Mahotsava' campaign was
introduced. This 75-day campaign set up special vaccination camps at various locations, contributing to a
sustained vaccination pace. During this period, over 76.18 lakh first doses, 2.35 crore
second doses, and 15.92 crore precaution doses were administered, with an average of 24.73 lakh doses
per day, including 20.68 lakh precaution doses per day7
.

2. Partners for Designing & Conducting Public-Sensitization Drives
To combat misinformation, it was crucial to educate vaccine recipients through user-friendly awareness
campaigns and multilingual sensitization drives. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)
designed informative displays and posters, targeting the eligible beneficiaries including pregnant women
and their families to make informed vaccination choices. Collaboration with the Ministry of Information
and Broadcasting facilitated public awareness through digital citizen engagement platforms. The
Division also partnered with the Press Information Bureau (PIB) for fact checking campaigns during their
telecasts and myth-buster series. The Division worked diligently to address vaccine misinformation and
ensuring timely and correct information.

topics/infodemic#tab=tab_1, Accessed October 2023
