Several innovative measures using mass and social media platforms were adopted, including:
• Regular media briefing was adopted throughout the pandemic by MoHFW. It was key to address
media queries, clear misconceptions and keep public updated on the future strategies.
• Communications National Media Rapid Response Cell was established at MoHFW to swiftly identify
rumours/incorrect information circulating on various platforms.
• FAQs for general public and healthcare & frontline workers were developed & uploaded on MoHFW
website.
• Media Channels, Radio Jockeys, Producers & Programming Heads of AIR, Doordarshan, FM
Channels, Regional PIB Heads etc. were oriented on COVID-19 vaccination
• Experts were identified to write op-eds and articles to build vaccine confidence. Fact checked videos
by key experts were prepared and disseminated to provide correct & factual information for general
public.
Key Impacts of the Programme
The National Covid-19 Vaccination drive turned out to be a success story, overcoming all obstacles to
ensure that India’s population was vaccinated and protected against Covid-19. September 2021 marked
a significant milestone in the vaccination programme, with the highest daily vaccination rate recorded at
an impressive 7.9 million doses (Refer Exhibit 10). The most remarkable achievement was on September
17, 2021, when a staggering 25.1 million doses were administered in a single day across approximately
100,000 Covid Vaccination Centres (CVCs). (Refer Exhibit 10). As of October 2023, approximately 2.2
billion people in India have been vaccinated with Covid-19 vaccines.8
Reflecting on this accomplishment, the protagonist expressed deep emotion, stating, “During that time,
everyone shattered the glass ceiling and transcended conventional human limits to ensure the success of
this programme.
Conclusion
The National COVID-19 vaccination programme unravelled a new policy path for India to address the
needs and aspirations of its population. It faced unprecedented challenges which were surpassed through
a series of unconventional ideas far beyond the conventional bureaucratic way of working. The
programme is a shining example of success in the face of an unprecedented global public health
challenge. This programme may inspire many imitations to achieve ‘well-being for all’ - both in the
country and around the world. After all, it is India which is a pioneer in believing:

Case Study Title: Improving Revenue Department performance through LAKSHYAM
Case Study Description: In rural India, Lekhpals are crucial in safeguarding property rights and facilitating various administrative tasks. Despite their significance, there has been a lack of an objective performance management system to track their effectiveness. This deficiency hinders the government's ability to identify strong performers, support those needing improvement, and ensure accountability. To address this, UP Govt. developed a comprehensive performance management system named LAKSHYAM (Lekhpals Actionable KPI System for Holistic Assessment and Management) and piloted it in Prayagraj. LAKSHYAM operates on three pillars: Objective KPIs, Direct Supervisor Feedback, and Stakeholders & Feedback.
Case Text:
Lekhpals, also known as Patwaris, are frontline revenue officials who play a vital role in upholding
property rights in rural India. They help demarcate land boundaries, settle land disputes, ensure that public
land is free of encroachments, and process important applications such as income and caste certificates.
These issues, which matter most to rural citizens, are often raised in public meetings with bureaucrats and
elected representatives. Therefore, for most rural citizens, the work of Lekhpals is crucial for shaping their
perception of governance in the state.
The Need for a Performance Management System
Mr. Sarthak Agrawal is a 2021 batch IAS officer. During his training in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, he
was posted as Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) of Soraon tehsili

in March 2023. The tehsil has 452 revenue
villages and around 55 Lekhpals, which is nearly half of the sanctioned strength. As the SDM, Mr. Agrawal
learned that despite the importance of Lekhpals’ work for the functioning of the state, there is no objective
performance management system to track their performance. The government has several scheme-level
portals that measure scheme performance at various administrative levels: district, block, tehsil, and
village. However, these systems do not provide a holistic assessment of the individual employee’s
performance. Therefore, in the tehsil leadership’s regular review meetings with Lekhpals, they had no
systematic approach to identify officials who were consistently underperforming across different tasks and
differentiating them from those who were only behind in implementing a certain initiative. Consequently,
employees' assessments relied on arbitrary criteria, leading to ad-hoc and subjective evaluations. This
adversely affected overall performance and service delivery and undermined the department's
accountability to citizens.
Mr. Agrawal realized that in order to understand how a Lekhpal performs across all tasks, it was
necessary to integrate different data systems, which led to the conceptualization of LAKSHYAM—
Lekhpals' Actionable KPI System for Holistic Assessment and Management. Through this performance
management system, the district and its tehsils could measure and improve the performance of Lekhpals
by celebrating strong performers and managing poor performers more effectively.
While the government was considering key performance indicators or KPI-based objective
performance management for employees with well-defined, specialized roles (for example, ANMsii), it has

i Tehsil - It is a local unit of revenue administrative division in India– the subdivision of a district.
ii ANMs – Auxiliary Nurses and Midwives

IMPROVING REVENUE DEPARTMENT PERFORMANCE THROUGH LAKSHYAM 2
been challenging to establish KPIs for 'generalist' public sector workers like Lekhpals, who have to perform
a wide variety of tasks. LAKSHYAM seeks to bridge this gap.
Scoping
Mr. Agrawal reached out to the IDinsight team, a data analytics and research organisation, to develop
LAKSHYAM. As part of the scoping exercise, Mr. Agrawal and his team shadowed and interviewed a few
Lekhpals to understand their work and responsibilities. A comprehensive inventory of services delivered
by the Lekhpals to citizens and government departments was compiled. This list included over 30 distinct
activities, including their everyday core tasks, work streams, and ad hoc work from the district and state.
The first version of LAKSHYAM focused on only a subset of permanent tasks that form the core of
Lekhpals’ responsibilities. This selection was primarily based on
(1) the ready availability of data for these workstreams and
(2) feedback received from tehsil administration members (Tehsildariii, Naib Tehsildarsiv, Revenue
Inspectorsv) as well as the District Magistrate and the Chief Revenue Officer.
The team then collaboratively drafted the KPIs with other tehsil officials to design and pilot a
measurement strategy to assess Lekhpals’ performance.
Data Systems for Creating Performance Management System

iii Tehsildar - The chief government officer in a tehsil– the executive magistrate in charge of the collection
of revenues, taxes, etc., in a tehsil.
iv Naib Tehsildar - The immediate subordinate of a tehsildar.
v Revenue Inspector - The Revenue Inspector (RI) is the executive assistant to the Tehsildar. They are the
direct supervisors of Lekhpals.
A New Digital Data System for IGRS: A Success Story from Soraon Tehsil,
Prayagraj
An example of an online system is the IGRS platform - Integrated Grievance Redressal System, UP.
Citizens submit their land-related grievances on this portal, and the Lekhpals then need to investigate
the case and submit a report to higher authorities in a time-bound manner. The due date of an
application is usually ~30 days from the date of receiving the application. However, if a Lekhpal fails to
conduct this investigation timely and submit the report, the Tehsil administration is asked for
clarification on the defaulted applications. There is no way to provide feedback to specific Lekhpals, and
even if the tehsil leadership provides immediate feedback, there is no way to record it and monitor their
performance over time.
Soraon tehsil’s IGRS data entry operator underwent training to track all applications received through
the IGRS and compile them in an online Google sheet connected to a dynamic automated IGRS
Dashboard (Exhibit 1), which summarized Lekhpals’ performance in resolving complaints. The
dashboard provides details on the following indicators:
● Summary of IGRS applications received, pending, defaulted, and close to defaulting in the
tehsil.
● The average number of days taken by a Lekhpal to submit the report for an application.

IMPROVING REVENUE DEPARTMENT PERFORMANCE THROUGH LAKSHYAM 3

The KPIs were determined using the department’s existing digital and offline data systems, including
digital data portals and the physical registers maintained by the tehsil and the revenue courts. When
scoping out the data sources available within the tehsil, the team recognized a pressing challenge: the lack
of standardization and absence of uniformity in the register and report formats. This led to poor data
quality, which rendered evaluation of Lekhpals’ performance difficult. New standard templates for
uniformity in registers and reports had to be designed. Mr. Agrawal then released an official order in the
tehsil that mandated everyone to follow the new templates to ensure consistency in data format and quality.
LAKSHYAM also requires application programming interface (API) access to other portals, data from
which can be used to compute Lekhpals’ KPI scores. The team is pursuing these requests with the state
government and UP’s Board of Revenue.
The 3 Pillars of LAKSHYAM
LAKSHYAM2

follows a 360-degree feedback system with three components, viz.
1) Objective KPIs
2) Direct supervisor feedback
3) Stakeholders’ feedback.
1. Objective KPIs: These include objective indicators to measure Lekhpals’ performance in select
workstreams. The KPIs focus on action within Lekhpals' control, such as ensuring the timely
submission of investigation reports, rather than relying on outcomes that may necessitate support
from other team members.
2. Direct Supervisor feedback: This component captures the subjective feedback of Lekhpals’ direct
supervisor, the Revenue Inspector (RI), and their verbatim comments on the Lekhpals’
performance. Six key competencies that every Lekhpal must possess were identified and defined.
They are:
a. Technical Knowledge: The Lekhpals understand their responsibilities, processes, and
systems and follow the due process to complete an assignment. They know how to resolve
various types of cases, requests, and complaints.
b. Internal Communication: When collaborating with other Lekhpals or departments, the
Lekhpal can clearly communicate the assignment and the support needed. They produce
good quality reports and are respectful and open to communication and feedback.
● Percentage of reports received within the last three days of the deadline—last-minute
submission of reports by Lekhpals does not provide the tehsil leadership enough time before
the deadline to provide feedback on report quality.
● Lekhpal and village-level summary of applications received—allows the leadership to observe
which Lekhpals and villages receive the most applications and follow up accordingly.
The tehsil leadership can use this dashboard to monitor the tehsil’s performance in real-time and
monitor the past performance of Lekhpals. The data entry operator uses the new online sheet to send
reminders to Lekhpals and follow up with those whose applications are close to defaulting.
An improvement in the average processing time of IGRS applications was observed, which was
reduced from 27 to 20 days within two months of implementing the new system.1

IMPROVING REVENUE DEPARTMENT PERFORMANCE THROUGH LAKSHYAM 4
c. External Communication: The Lekhpals are courteous towards applicants and citizens in
response to the receipt of requests/grievances. They can represent the department
positively and build a positive image in the community. They are not ruffled easily under
pressure, particularly when handling difficult/sensitive situations on the field.
d. Responsiveness: The Lekhpals can resolve assignments and grievances in a timely manner
without compromising the quality of the report and resolution. They are responsive and
enthusiastic about ad hoc tasks and rise to the occasion.
e. Ownership of Work: The Lekhpals can perform their tasks and complete their assignments
almost independently, without much support from their supervisors. They can flag
bottlenecks, foresee delays, and take measures to avoid them.
f. Time Management: The Lekhpals can efficiently manage all workstreams and meet
deadlines.
The rubrics for each competency were developed in Hindi, and training was provided to the
supervisors—the Revenue Inspectors (RIs)—on conducting these evaluations. The feedback was
collected through paper forms and subsequently digitized.
3. Stakeholders’ feedback: This component captures feedback on the quality of Lekhpals’
performance from their colleagues, peers, and stakeholders, which includes Registrar Kanungosvi
,
Naib tehsildar, and data entry operators. These officials routinely interact with Lekhpals in their
professional and personal capacities. Competencies assessed under stakeholders’ feedback
include:
a. Responsiveness: The Lekhpal is responsive to the stakeholder’s requests/complaints.
b. Politeness: The Lekhpal is polite during interactions with the stakeholder.
c. Positive attitude: Lekhpal's attitude is positive and helpful during work interactions.
d. Technical knowledge: The Lekhpal is knowledgeable about how the system operates and
how a particular complaint is to be resolved.
e. Adherence to systems and protocols and due diligence: The Lekhpal follows prescribed
procedures, including all the required steps and protocols to complete an assignment.
Upward accountability for Lekhpals, ensured by tracking KPIs and collecting feedback from their
supervisors, becomes less significant if downward accountability towards citizens does not exist. In the
spirit of Jan Bhagidarivii, surveys were set up to collect feedback from citizens who have interfaced with
Lekhpals and query them about their experience of interacting with Lekhpals. The protocols were designed
to emphasize objective attributes to build credibility for the new performance management tool. For
example, one of the questions posed to citizens is whether the Lekhpal assigned to their case at least spoke
to them over the phone or visited them before submitting an investigation report.
Lekhpals receive a score out of 5 on each KPI and competency. The score is compiled in a tehsil-level
Lekhpal Scorecard (Exhibit 2), which summarizes the performance of each Lekhpal across the three
components and ranks them based on their overall performance score. The overall score is calculated by
giving 50 percent weightage to the objective KPI scores, 30 percent to the supervisor feedback scores, and
20 percent to stakeholders’ feedback scores. The dashboard and Lekhpals’ ranking allow the tehsil
leadership to identify the strong and low-performing Lekhpals and monitor their performance across
different areas.

vi Registrar Kanungos – An administrative role with the responsibility of maintaining registers and
records in the tehsil office.
vii Jan Bhagidari – The term translates to people’s participation. In the case study, it refers to the spirit of
citizen centricity.

IMPROVING REVENUE DEPARTMENT PERFORMANCE THROUGH LAKSHYAM 5
In Soraon Tehsil, Mr. Agrawal implemented the administration of the first round of performance
assessment. The first round of rankings that emerged aligned closely with senior officers’ subjective
perceptions of the Lekhpals’ performance, reflecting the robustness of the system.
After the completion of Mr. Agrawal’s training in Prayagraj, the new SDM in Soraon tehsil has
continued with this evaluation system. He felicitated LAKSHYAM’s top 5 performing Lekhpals during the
annual Independence Day ceremony on August 15, 2023. The Lekhpals and Revenue Inspectors who
attended the ceremony offered positive feedback and expressed gratitude that and felt motivated that the
leadership recognized their hard work. Soraon tehsil plans to conduct a similar felicitation ceremony for
the top performing Lekhpals on Gandhi Jayanti, October 2, 2023, which can thereafter be repeated every
quarter. Currently, another tehsil in Prayagraj, Bara, is also implementing LAKSHYAM along the lines of
Mr. Agrawal’s implementation.
Lessons and Reflections
The effectiveness of any performance management system is contingent upon the leadership’s
deliberate use of it to conduct deliberate exercises and then provide feedback to the employees and their
next steps towards continual improvement. An understanding of the factors that function as enablers and
impediments to institutionalization can help us identify new ways to nudge the leadership in tehsils to use
performance management systems, make data-informed decisions, and engage in discussions and
feedback sessions with Lekhpals.

LAKSHYAM is far from being a perfect system yet. The lack of data integration across multiple scheme-
related portals renders the list of KPIs incomplete. Moreover, the true test of a performance management

system is its longevity; whether it can overcome the behavioural and political challenges in implementation
of changes over a sustained period of time and prove its usefulness. Nevertheless, it is a good starting point.
Mr. Agrawal’s team continues to refine LAKSHYAM further by including more workstreams and ad hoc
responsibilities of Lekhpals to capture their performance holistically.
The ultimate objective of this initiative is to propel a shift from a culture that relies almost exclusively
on continual negative feedback to one that relies on constructive feedback. Instead of merely reprimanding
employees for poor performance, such systems can enable senior officers to identify the underlying reasons
for underperformance and provide support to help Lekhpals overcome the challenges.
One of the key learnings from this initiative is that if young bureaucrats pursue an innovative idea with
an open mind, they will receive the necessary support from their colleagues and seniors. While designing
and piloting LAKSHYAM, Mr. Agrawal constantly received valuable feedback and support from the
Divisional Commissioner, District Magistrate, Chief Development Officer, and the Chief Revenue Officer
of Prayagraj, among other officials.
The invaluable insights from this pilot can be used to expand the scope of performance management
for human resources within the government to more departments and geographies. As the system expands
across Uttar Pradesh, it has the potential to transform personnel-based decisions, encourage constructive
feedback, and reward excellence.

Case Study Title: Operation Parivartan: Societal change through transformational leadership
Case Study Description: Ms. Tejaswi Satpute, Mumbai's Deputy Commissioner of Police spearheaded Operation Parivartan, targeting the long-standing issue of illicit liquor consumption in Solapur, rooted in illegal brewing and hazardous ingredients. Facing challenges in conventional raids, Ms. Tejaswi adopted a scientific strategy to address the entire brewing cycle, aiming to disrupt the production and distribution of illicit liquor. The 72-hour brewing cycle was a critical focus, requiring post-raid actions for a lasting solution. Her dedication to ethical principles in public service guided her efforts to combat the multifaceted issues associated with the illicit liquor trade.
Case Text:
“Dedication is belief transitioned into action, transforming into change.”

Byron Pulsifer

On September 30, 2023, Ms. Tejaswi Satputei

, serving as the Deputy Commissioner of Police in the
Recruitments Division, Mumbai, Maharashtra, received a call on her cell phone from a prominent
educational institution. She was invited to address a group of students, to share her experience regarding
the recent success story of Operation Parivartan in Solapur. She accepted the invitation with the belief that
sharing her experience might act as a nudge towards empowering future leaders to fearlessly pursue their
goals. The opportunity prompted her to reflect on her journey with "Operation Parivartan."
Issues in the Solapur District
Solapur, located in the south-western region of Maharashtra near the Karnataka border (Refer
Exhibit 1), grappled with a century-old problem of illicit liquor consumption across 10 districts. The root
of the problem lay in the illegal brewing of liquor, with the use of spurious and hazardous ingredients,
putting the lives of both producers and consumers at risk. The illicit substance was transported from
Solapur to various districts, leading to widespread issues such as violence against women, domestic
violence, and severe health complications due to consumption.
The allure of easy money had driven manufacturers to brew liquor in rural areas and establish a
distribution network to transact and earn profits. The affordability of this illicit product attracted the
economically disadvantaged and exacerbated the law-and-order problem. Without effective intervention,
this unethical practice visibly caused more harm than the economic profits, being in contradiction with the
general virtues of public service (Refer Exhibit 2).
Ms. Tejaswi became familiar with the problem of illicit liquor during her probationary stint in
Solapur and the challenges confronted by the department. When appointed as Superintendent of Police in
20201
, she decided to systematically address this longstanding issue. Instead of trying to resolve the
problem through conventional raids only, which often provided limited results only and partially
addressed the problems of brewing, equipment, and storage, as demonstrated by previous attempts, she
opted for a scientific strategy.

i Ms. Tejaswi Satpute is an IPS (Indian Police Officer) officer from the batch of 2012, who is currently serving
as the Deputy Commissioner of Mumbai, Maharashtra. She has been recognised by bodies like the National
Commission for Women, Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry etc. felicitating her
efforts under the Operation Parivartan.

OPERATION PARIVARTAN - SOCIETAL CHANGE THROUGH TRANSFORMATIONAL
LEADERSHIP

2

Typically, police raids faced two possible outcomes: either locals, supported by henchmen
thwarted the operation, that further strained relations between law enforcement and the public, or if
successful, the raids only scratched the surface of the brewing operation. The 72-hour duration2 of a
brewing cycle allowed illicit brewers to recover from losses incurred in one production cycle before the
next police raid. Any lasting solution to the problem of production and distribution of illicit liquor would
need to address post-raid actions.
Kickstarting a Transformation - Operation Parivartan
In her visionary approach to societal transformation, Ms. Tejaswi aimed for a long-term solution
to eradicate illicit liquor rather than conduct mere raids on village breweries. Recognising that the
conventional raids were not enough, she developed a four-pronged action strategy3

involving - frequent
raids, counselling, rehabilitation, and awareness of the social and personal consequences of illicit liquor
production, purchase, or consumption.
Before spearheading the implementation of Operation Parivartan, she sought strategic support
from her reporting officers, peers, and colleagues. She acknowledged the organization's challenges, and
emphasized the need for a fresh, effective approach. Her confidence in the transformative power of the
strategy and her ability to lead the change inspired her team.
The Four pillars of the Strategy
• Frequent Raids
Ms. Tejaswi assembled a police force squad. As against the small-scale raids done previously, she shifted
to conducting larger raids on production centres with 200-250 members. Raid frequency was also increased
to every third day or twice a week4

, which disrupted the brewing cycle. Her leadership on the front lines

boosted team confidence and facilitated an organizational transformation.
• Counselling
Ms. Tejaswi recognized a pattern in the illicit business with the involvement of families across generations
and the plight of women trapped in the trade. To address the victims, she introduced counselling as the
second pillar of the Operation Parivartan strategy. Together with the police team and professional
intervention from a Pune-based institution - Kala Krida Sahitya Shantidoot Parivar5

, this operation aimed
at deep-rooted behavioural change while providing an alternative path for affected individuals. This
demonstrated an impact on the root causes rather than temporary suspensions.
• Rehabilitation
Ms. Tejaswi initiated rehabilitation through skill development, for which she used government resources,
policies, and financial institutions facilitated by Udyog Mahamandal6

through MITCONii7
. Skill
upgradation and vocational training programs, including stitching, sewing, embroidery, and handcrafts,
were conducted to empower women (Refer Exhibit 3). Beneficiaries were encouraged to open retail shops,
with support from the 'Umed' government scheme for raw material capital. Many started outlets for

ii MITCON Centre for CSR & Skill development is a part of Maharashtra Industrial and Technical
Consultancy Organisation Limited which acts as a catalyst to industrial & entrepreneurship
development.

OPERATION PARIVARTAN - SOCIETAL CHANGE THROUGH TRANSFORMATIONAL
LEADERSHIP

3

retailing clothes, others established general format stores, including home needs and provisions, etc. A few
beneficiaries also set up tea- shops.
• Awareness
Having addressed issues of supply, Ms. Tejaswi implemented Awareness Drives. These drives served as
the fourth pillar of Operation Parivartan. These awareness drives were organized to convince those who
consumed illicit liquor to abstain from doing so. Public meetings and small gatherings were organized by
the police teams to communicate the poisonous effect of illicit liquor. An action plan with effective
communication strategies was designed. The police force was urged to practice compassion and spread the
message of change.
Ms. Tejaswi's comprehensive strategy not only disrupted the illicit liquor trade but also focused on societal
transformation by addressing the root causes, which demonstrates a holistic and impactful leadership
approach in Operation Parivartan.
Key Impacts
Positive Transformation of 714 Families
Operation Parivartan resulted in a positive shift for more than 714 families8

, by steering them towards
alternate livelihoods, which not only provided them satisfaction and dignity but also served as a deterrent
to keep them away from the illicit liquor trade in the future.
Adoption of Sewing as a Profession
Provision of vocational training helped many to pursue a career. For instance, out of the 41 individuals
trained in sewing, a substantial 30 chose to make sewing their profession.9

Industrial sewing machines were

made available to them through loans from the lead bankiii

. Women involved in producing illicit liquor
earlier are now manufacturing shirts, school uniforms, aprons, and several other products for their
livelihood. They have proudly named their small unit ‘Parivartan Udyog Samuh’ (Refer Exhibit 4).
10 This
outcome illustrates the successful integration of skill development into sustainable livelihoods. (Refer
Exhibit 5)
Significant Reduction in the Problem
Although complete eradication was not achieved under Operation Parivartan, the strategic action led to an
80 percentiv 11 reduction in the illicit liquor problem. Additionally, there were also fewer incidents of crime,
social conflicts, and domestic violence associated with illicit liquor. The total number of body offenses
registered by the local police reduced by 5.19 percent. When considered separately, crime against women
has come down by 8.14 percent.12 This marks an accomplishment, demonstrating the effectiveness of the
implemented measures.

increase the flow of credit to agriculture, MSE and other economic activities with the district being the basic
unit in terms of geographical area.

same

LEADERSHIP

4

The Way Forward
Ms. Tejaswi is optimistic about the sustained effectiveness of the initiative. Her confidence in its
replicability across India, considering the widespread issue of alcoholism in many districts, particularly
affecting women and children through domestic violence, crime, and loss of male lives, underscores the
initiative's potential impact.

Case Study Title:
Tribal Telehamlet: Project Punnagai Transforms
Healthcare Delivery & Education in Erode
Case Study Description:
Kathirimalai, a remote tribal hamlet in Erode district of Tamil Nadu, was inaccessible due to its location on a high mountain top in the Bargur Hills and deep within the Channampatti forest reserve. Also, home to 400 members of the Sholaga tribe, these inhabitants of Kathirimalai Village needed to travel several hours along a rough trail and through the forest to access medical facilities at the nearest primary health centre. Severe malnutrition, stunting, and communicable diseases were prevalent among these tribals as they mostly avoided visiting the medical centre for regular health reviews. Even the availability of educational facilities in a single-teacher local school was minimal. Poor learning outcomes and absenteeism among school-going children was common.

A young IAS officer, Mr. Krishnanunni led a coordinated effort under Project Punnagai (Project Smile) to transform this hamlet. The Wi-Fi facility, set up in the school premises, essentially to establish telemedicine facilities in Kathirimalai was used as a convergence platform to bring other facilities to the community viz., learning resources for improving education, skill development programs for enhancing employability of youth, livelihood enhancement by better agriculture and animal rearing practices. Today Project Punnagai is being replicated across multiple villages of Tamil Nadu.
Case Text:
Mr. H. Krishnanunni, a young IAS officer, reminisced about his early years as a sub-
collector of Gobichettipalayam in Erode district of Tamil Nadu while perusing the newspaper on

May 21, 2022.
He recalled the period in 2019 when Kathirimalai, the most remote region in Erode district, hit
news headlines with videos of donkeys transporting modern electronic voting machines and
other electoral equipment to ensure democratic processes for the residents of this tribal hamlet,
in the absence of motorable roads. Currently, Kathirimalai village is connected to a long-distance,
high-speed Wi-Fi network via Project Punnagai, which translates to ‘Smile’ in the local Tamil
language. This network has been utilised to provide telemedical consultation and innovative
educational resources for the tribal residential school. Mr. Krishnanunni, while serving as the
Collector of Erode district from June 2021 to May 2023, initiated and implemented Project
Punnagai, which has completely transformed the tribal hamlet of Kathirimalai.
Erode and its Hinterland
Erode district of Tamil Nadu, while known for its economic progress in agriculture and industrial
growth, struggled with disparities on the Human Development Index (HDI)1. The blocks with
the lowest HDI were Thalavadi, Bhavanisagar, and Nambiyur, followed by Sathyamangalam and
Anthiyur, which also lagged in Child Development Indices and Still Birth Rate. (Refer Exhibits 1
and 2).
Kathirimalai is a remote tribal hamlet in the Bargur Hills of Anthiyur Panchayat Taluk. Located
on a high mountaintop, deep within the Chennampatti forest reserve, Kathirimalai village is

home to about 400 members of the Sholaga—a scheduled tribe of India—community. This forest-
bound, Dravidian-speaking tribal group practically lived in isolation, practicing subsistence-level

agriculture under primitive conditions.2 The hamlet lacked basic amenities, including all-weather
i BOD- Board of Directors
ii ATA- American Telemedicine Association

TRIBAL TELEHAMLET: PROJECT PUNNAGAI TRANSFORMS HEALTHCARE DELIVERY &
EDUCATION IN ERODE

2

roads, electricity, health, and education infrastructure. Getting medical treatment from the
nearest primary health centre (PHC) took an entire day because it took at least 3 hours to just
reach the centre by a 9 km mud track, meet the physician and then trek back up to the hamlet.
Hence, these tribals largely avoided a visit to the PHC unless the illness was life-threatening.
Change through Convergence
Mr. Krishnanunni’s visits to this tribal hamlet—as a District Collector and earlier as a Sub
Collector of Gobichettipalayam, a revenue division of Erode district, had familiarised him with
the terrain, its people, and their challenges. It was evident to him that connectivity with the
outside world was Kathirimalai’s primary demand. He had witnessed the devastation caused by
the COVID-19 pandemic in this community—serious health problems, robbing others of their
livelihood, and leaving them vulnerable to a long-lasting negative impact on their physical, social,
and economic wellbeing. He had also seen firsthand how technology might bridge geographical
distances. Classes were conducted online, courts held online hearings, and work was happening
from home. He believed in the power of collective action to combat the impact of the pandemic
on this community. He felt it was time to act.
Project Punnagai is Born
Mr. Krishnanunni built a team of experts, each bringing a specific skill set essential for creating,
maintaining, and sustaining the changes that he envisioned.
1. Mr. Ashok Kumar, District Development Manager (DDM) of the National Bank for
Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), suggested avenues to finance the
project.
2. Dr. Jithendranath, a medical officer in Wayanad, Kerala, had more than forty years of
experience in handling healthcare for forest dwellers in his area. He became a
telemedicine expert.
3. Mr. Roshy K. Falgunan, the managing partner of a private technology firm, provided and
maintained the technology solution.
Mr. Ashok Kumar informed Mr. Krishnanunni that NABARD had earmarked funds from the
Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) to be used for building roads and facilities to
connect the tribal hamlets of Anthiyur, including Kathirimalai. Mr. Krishnanunni realised that
while better roads would reduce the number of hours of travel and support the youth in seeking
education and employment, they would not make healthcare accessible. Roads alone would not
solve the issues of prevalence of malnutrition and stunted growth among tribal children as
women, children, and the elderly could not afford to commute several hours with a caregiver to
seek routine healthcare. Thus, Project Punnagai (Project Smile) was born to bring telemedicine to
Kathirimalai.
Challenges in Making Telemedicine Work
Dr. Jithendranath, the medical professional who joined Mr. Krishnanunni’s team, understood
that a long trek through dense forests, sightings of elephant herds browsing the jungle close to

TRIBAL TELEHAMLET: PROJECT PUNNAGAI TRANSFORMS HEALTHCARE DELIVERY &
EDUCATION IN ERODE

3

the mud tracks, besides rains and landslides were common reasons for patients to avoid or
postpone essential treatment for their ailments.
While seeking a solution to overcome the distance barrier, Dr. Jithendranath developed
numerous options. Previously, he had used a wireless telephone powered by batteries that were
recharged using solar panels. He had trained a local person from the community to operate the
telephone during a telemedicine consultation and relay the patient’s responses to his questions.
Once the diagnosis was made, he recommended the appropriate medication.
This solution involved four major components. One was a systematic clinical protocol to diagnose
the disease based on patient responses. This was the easy part, as the doctor was a skilled clinician
with many years of experience treating his patients. Besides, it was observed that only 20-25
different diseases would be present in roughly 80 percent of the patients.3 Furthermore, Dr.
Jithendranath regularly visited the hamlets at least once a month and was familiar with his
patients and their household information. The community trusted him.
The second challenge was to systematically organise the medication in ways that made it easy to
identify and locate. Using his creativity and expertise, Dr. Jithendranath designed a 5-foot by 3-
foot cabinet with shelves for storage. Three boxes in the shape of a bread box were placed on each
shelf. Each storage box and its lid were distinctly colour-coded and contained medicines for a
specific set of symptoms—fevers and body pain; cold and coughs; stomach-related ailments;
ointments and so on.
The third and most difficult component was to train a local person to serve as the physician’s
aide. Dr. Jithendranath trained a tribal person to be his eyes and ears, listen to the questions he
posed, transmit the responses, confirm that the symptoms were not serious enough to warrant an
urgent visit to the local hospital, hand over the medication and review the patient’s condition 3
days later. Patients were instructed to rush to the hospital if the symptoms persisted or worsened.
The final and most crucial element was the technological solution. The forest presented numerous
challenges: poor network connectivity in dense jungles, elephant attacks, monkey menace and
nesting birds that wrecked telephone wires, besides prolonged and heavy monsoon rains that
prevented the use of solar panels. Thus, telephone was thus not a viable or sustainable option.
The Connectivity Challenge
Following multiple unsuccessful attempts, Dr. Jithendranath enlisted the assistance of a skilled
engineer, Mr. Karthik Iyer, who had found ways to connect his home in the mountains of
Kodaikanal to the telecom tower located in Palani Hills, about 65 km away by road. Mr. Karthik
designed a technological solution to overcome the challenge of long-distance connectivity and
agreed to train the two persons identified by Dr. Jithendranath to implement this solution. Three
months later, the team was prepared to weave their technological magic and realise the vision of
providing telemedicine for remote tribal communities.
Technology Service Provider

TRIBAL TELEHAMLET: PROJECT PUNNAGAI TRANSFORMS HEALTHCARE DELIVERY &
EDUCATION IN ERODE

4

Mr. Roshy K. Falgunan, the third member of Mr. Krishnanunni’s team, served as the technology
provider. His company, Computer for Social Computing Infrastructure LLP (C4S), had
indigenously developed the technology to provide long-distance Wi-Fi connectivity to remote
villages. The hardware required to connect remote areas to towns already existed. The gap was
bridged by the necessary software to transmit sound and images across users. The team trained
by Mr. Iyer used open-source software to code and recode the computer programme required to
transmit audio and video images via the distant communication networks.
Mr. Falgunan had successfully completed several projects for the Government of Kerala,
including the installation of transmission towers in inaccessible forest terrains connected with
various citizen services ranging from education to health.
Project Punnagai was soon off to a great start once NABARD had approved the funding proposal.
Bringing Wi-Fi to Remote Villages
Once the project was approved, the C4S team sprung to action under the guidance of Mr.
Krishnanunni. Mr. Falgunan and his technical team made multiple reconnaissance visits to
Kathirimalai to understand the topography of this region. Braving the severe monsoon rains that
had washed away the mud tracks, heavy equipment had to be manually transported across the
jungle, to set up the Wi-Fi connection at Kathirimalai in line with the tower at Anthiyur. The team

installed solar-powered lithium-ion batteries with sufficient backup capacity to ensure that Wi-
Fi connectivity had uninterrupted power to provide a 100 GBPSiii internet connection around the

clock. The C4S team trained the local youth to operate the system and then visited Kathirimalai
regularly to ensure the upkeep and maintenance of the system. The team was only a phone call
away to troubleshoot any issues.
Community Support
Kickstarting Project Punnagai still required the support of key local elements to launch the
education and telehealth facilities for the tribal population of Kathirimalai.
Teacher
Kathirimalai’s residential school for students of the Sholaga Scheduled Tribe is a single-teacher
school. Mr. Gunaseelan Srinivasan, the sole teacher-cum-headmaster, served as the only resource
person for teaching all subjects across all classes, along with managing the administrative
responsibilities of running the state-owned school. Any teacher posted to Kathirimalai was
expected to traverse several hours each day across rough terrain to reach the school. Absenteeism
and school dropout rates were both high. The students were barely literate. Most could neither
recognise letters nor numbers, let alone read or carry out simple arithmetic functions.
This school was designated to play a key role in Project Punnagai. Located within Kathirimalai,
easy-to-access infrastructure was installed on the school premises. A desktop monitor in the
classroom became the focal point where the Wi-Fi connection was provided to connect
iii GBPS: Gigabyte Per Second

TRIBAL TELEHAMLET: PROJECT PUNNAGAI TRANSFORMS HEALTHCARE DELIVERY &
EDUCATION IN ERODE

5

Kathirimalai to the world. The Vadhiyaar—meaning teacher in Tamil—was happy to support
any initiative that would benefit the students and the community.
Doctor
Dr. N. Parthiban had treated members of multiple Kathirimalai households. He worked as the
medical officer in the Primary Health Centre (PHC) nearest to Kathirimalai village. Nonetheless,
his patients visited him only in cases of major ailments or emergencies such as complicated
pregnancies. Common ailments such as fever, cough, and body pains were either neglected or
treated with home remedies. Communicable diseases such as scabies were rampant as several
generations of family members—from newborn babies to the elderly—shared living spaces in
cramped huts. Poor nutrition, lack of running water, and lack of proper sanitation facilities
exacerbated the ill health of the residents. Though he was initially hesitant to diagnose without
physically meeting the patients, the pandemic had demonstrated the effectiveness of telemedicine
across the world. Dr. Parthiban came onboard to be trained by Dr. Jithendranath’s team and
practice telemedicine to impact Kathirimalai residents.
Community Health Worker
Ms. Roja was a rarity among Kathirimalai residents. As a young lady who had completed her
education up to class eight, she was chosen to work as the local community health worker to
assist Dr. Parthiban at the primary health centre in diagnosing, handing over the medication, and
reviewing patient conditions. She underwent rigorous training in the clinical protocols of seeking
information from patients by observing and inquiring about their symptoms and sharing these
with the physician. She was trained to carefully follow the doctor’s instructions to select the right
medication and dosage and to repeat the doctor’s usage instructions regarding the medication.
The Master Coordinator
The team was prepared, and Mr. Krishnanunni’s Project Punnagai was ready for launch. Several
departments and several layers of bureaucratic hierarchy had to work in unison to get the project
underway. Mr. Krishnanunni’s role as the master coordinator was to motivate and support his
team to ensure the project’s successful execution on the field. He travelled and camped on-site
in person for several days to resolve the emanating issues, be it delays in execution, conflicts
arising across departments, taking executive decisions, or smoothening the process. His presence
ensured that the project received priority despite the administration's demanding routine work.
Convergence for Community Benefit
The launch of Project Punnagai and its coverage by media houses provided the impetus for other
departments to explore the Wi-Fi platform for social change. Improving educational outcomes
was a top priority, along with health. A Chennai-based Civil Society organization, Lokalex, was
involved in improving students' learning outcomes. The Lokalex team worked closely with the
schoolteachers and community youth to bring online educational resources and tutors across the
world to help the students. Gone were the days of a single teacher managing the entire school.
With the use of Wi-Fi connectivity, students could access an extensive range of educational
materials and engaging activities. A review of their education outcomes conducted two years

TRIBAL TELEHAMLET: PROJECT PUNNAGAI TRANSFORMS HEALTHCARE DELIVERY &
EDUCATION IN ERODE

6

later showed remarkable improvement in their reading, writing, and arithmetic abilities. Lokalex
also worked with school dropouts to provide them with skill training to enhance their
employability. Both State and National level Skill Development Corporations supported these
trainings by offering educational resources, certification, and enrollment for employment
opportunities.
Women, youth, and children were frequent users of the Wi-Fi facilities. Men, too, were not
excluded either. The agriculture department was eager to use Wi-Fi facilities to train farmers in
increasing productivity. The local community, involved in sustenance agriculture, had small
plots to farm millets (Ragi) for their consumption. The department offered these farmers training
to increase productivity and cultivate vegetables around their homes to provide their families
with a more nutritious diet. The Wi-Fi platform was ready for use by multiple departments, from
doctors to disaster management teams, to inform people of ways to protect themselves during
monsoon rains and landslides.
Sustenance and Way the Forward
Most significantly, connectivity provided citizens with a secure and rapid way to reach officials
to communicate their demands. They were no longer isolated in a remote jungle, unable to seek
help. They could reach the nearest hospital without having to spend hours commuting on muddy
trails or riding a donkey. The physician was available for consultation on most days every week
at a fixed time. Students could access educational resources for their lessons. Employment and
livelihood opportunities for youth were created through agricultural extension services and skill
development workshops. Wi-Fi was their gateway to the world. Residents realised that they were
responsible for its maintenance and usage, even though support was available from government
departments, civil society organisations and technology service providers. Mr. Krishnanunni’s
vision for the transformation of Kathirimalai, the donkey-connected village, into a development
model was a resounding success.
A Year Later
Mr. Krishnanunni, as the Joint Secretary for the State Finance Department, was happy to read this
news in the local newspaper.

July 22, 2023. “The state tribal welfare department will soon provide free long-range
wireless Internet connectivity in selected tribal areas in Erode and Tirupathur districts using
which telemedicine and smart study centres will be introduced in these remote areas. The facility
will be provided in 33 tribal hamlets in Nelli Vasal Naadu, Pudur Naadu and Pungampattu Naadu
in Jawadhu Hills in Tirupathur district at a cost of Rs 3.25 crore and three tribal settlements at
Anthiyur taluk in Erode at a cost of Rs 2.96 crore, according to an order issued by the tribal welfare
department. The scheme has been introduced to improve the locals’ connection with the outside
world and offer them better opportunities for growth.”
Now, Project Punnagai is ready to spread its smile to other locations also.

Case Study Title: Initiative for Digitalization of Land Information (IDLI) at Delhi Development Authority
Case Study Description: The Delhi Development Authority (DDA), as a regulatory body, is responsible for the management of land resources under the Master Plan for Delhi, India’s capital city. It controls the planning, acquisition, development, and allotment of land for private, public, and government needs. Following his appointment as Commissioner (Land Disposal), Mr. Subu recognised an urgent need to develop a digital information system for the effective processing and management of land records and activities. Previous efforts by DDA to implement digitalisation through data outsourcing to leading software development companies had failed and tracking documents was difficult. Mr. Subu initiated the development of the information system named Initiative for Digitalisation of Land Information (IDLI), which is an online cloud-managed information system for the workflow of land-related activities. It provides transparency and improved turnaround time for service delivery.
Case Text:
Initiative for Digitalisation of Land Information at
Delhi Development Authority
Mr. Subu R.1 was pensive when he received notification of his new posting with the Railway Board in the
first quarter of 2021. He had just completed five years of central deputation with the Government of India
as Commissioner (Land Disposal) at the Delhi Development Authority (DDA). Despite challenges, he had
been able to initiate some positive changes during his tenure at DDA. He had focused on objectivity,
transparency, and honesty to ensure appropriate land valuation and inventory in accordance with DDA's
charter.
ii As he reflected on his accomplishments, what stood out notably was the successful implementation
of the Interactive Disposal of Land Information (IDLI). He hoped his approach could motivate others to
improve service delivery.
Delhi’s Land Disposal Management Dilemma
Each working day at the DDA, Mr. Subu allocated a specific time slot between 2:30 p.m. and 5:30 p.m. to
address public grievances. During these sessions, he received numerous complaints from beneficiaries about
land allotment and related matters. He learned that applying for a transfer of lease was a lengthy process as
it involved the movement of physical documents, which made it difficult to track. He recognised that there
was a nexus among some stakeholders, particularly brokers (touts), users, and prospective rightful users
vulnerable to fraud. He wondered if the existing land records data accurately reflected the correct
information, namely, the rightful owners, lease rentals to be collected, and the appropriate levy of penal
interest on late or non-payment of charges for renewals and transfers.
Mr. Subu sensed the scope for improvement in DDA operations. He was determined to trace the origins and
perpetuation of this information asymmetry that led to multiple grievances and hardships for citizens. He
knew that all files in the DDA existed in physical form, leaving room for inefficiencies, mishandling of
premium property valuations, and improper transactions. He was clear about the need for computerisation
to track land information. He first decided to investigate the initiatives to computerise land records

1 Mr. Subu R., a 2001 batch Indian Audit and Account Service (IA & AS) officer, who has served across the
country in different capacities, played a pivotal role in the conceptualisation and implementation of IDLI.

INITIATIVE FOR DIGITALIZATION OF LAND INFORMATION (IDLI) AT DDA 2
undertaken by the DDA over the last 20 years. Apparently, several IT service contracts to develop and
implement software to create an inventory of DDA’s land holdings had been outsourced to India’s top
companies. The contract values were substantial, with software development and deployment costs being
as high as ₹ 300 crore. However, all these IT companies had either abandoned the contracts or been dismissed
by the DDA. Mr. Subu initially believed that his work environment may not be receptive to resolving this
problem. However, with the government focused on ‘The Ease of Doing Business’ and making India the
destination of choice for business investment, he was confident that he could implement change.
Given his prior experience in leading capability-building initiatives, he was committed to crusading this
change in DDA’s functioning. The challenge was to convert the information he had gathered into an
opportunity to establish a reliable and robust information framework.
A Career in Capacity Building
Mr. Subu was not new to the digitalisation process in government. In 2005, he was a part of a team which
had successfully implemented the digitalisation of database of pension schemes in Tamil Nadu and
Pondicherry, which was subsequently replicated by Auditor Generals in other states. He was also
Chairperson of a committee for digitising the Accounts & Entitlement (A&E) offices of the entire country in
2011. To be successful, the digitalisation process required a comprehensive one-to-many engagement portal
with participation by the significant stakeholders (government, citizens, businesses, etc.).
The Delhi Development Authority
Delhi used to be the second-largest urban area in India—after Mumbai—and among the largest urban areas
in the world. Delhi’s population began to grow significantly in the 1970s, and surpassed Mumbai. According
to population estimates from the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI– Aadhaar), the population
of Delhi Union Territory was approximately 33,807,000 as of May 31, 2024iii. Delhi covers an area of 1484 sq.
km. (573 sq. mi.).
The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) was established in 1957 and pioneered the city's development
process.iv The DDA formulated a Master Plan in 1962 to ensure the balanced development of Delhi through
the creation of new, self-contained residential extension areas that provided healthy, secure environments.
The DDA acquired vast tracts of land and developed the city of Delhi (See Exhibit 1). Tasked with ensuring
a fair and equitable existence, the DDA put this land, a critical public resource, to the best use considering
long-term urban needs and a sustainable revenue model. As the DDA mutated and redeployed land,
tracking these changes became particularly important. If the user did not adhere to the intended land use,
the DDA—an autonomous body under the Central Government—was empowered to sublease, repossess,
and redeploy the land.
Consequently, managing land record information was one of the most crucial activities of the DDA.
However, handling physical records over time was challenging primarily due to the prevalent operational
processes and the organisation of the DDA. Property transactions were first registered as per law by the
Delhi Government’s Department of Revenue, which was a separate department. Upon the DDA’s
confirmation of the freehold, Department of Revenue officials registered or permitted transactions on the
property, already inventoried by the DDA. The involvement of two authorities complicated the land
management process.
As the city expanded, the demand for land increased. The limited supply of land coupled with skyrocketing
land prices raised constant conflicts relating to freehold ownership of land between DDA and its allotted
rights holders. These conflicts highlighted the issue of land as inventory and the allocated rights of

INITIATIVE FOR DIGITALIZATION OF LAND INFORMATION (IDLI) AT DDA 3
landowners. Improper and inaccurate documentation for recordkeeping and management of land resources
was a severe issue that threatened the very existence of the DDA.
Stumbling Blocks
As DDA was the landowner, the land was issued/allotted in the Commissioner's name. Consequently, Mr.
Subu, as DDA’s Commissioner (Land Disposal), had access to the land files. He found that some properties
were leased and could be purchased for industrial and commercial purposes and by hospitals. Leases were
granted for a period of 99 years. Naturally, land mutations had occurred. Further, numerous regulations
implemented by the Government of India to manage the land appropriately, worked differently in Delhi.
Unlike other states where land was a subject on the state list, in Delhi, land was on the central list. In this
scenario, land management was a top priority. In 2016, when Mr. Subu commenced his posting at DDA, the
freshly elected central and state governments were relatively new and focused on exercising their powers to
develop Delhi. He had to operate amidst delicate socio-political scenarios.
Action, Reaction, and Crusade
Mr. Subu found that most of the documents scanned into the computer system over the past 20 years could
not be put to any use. The documents needed to be systematically organised, tracked and checked for
validity.
Setting Up Processes
His first task was to create a flowchart of different processes for handling multiple categories of land
information. Working alone, he allocated time from his busy schedule to develop process maps and
flowcharts. His goal was to design an appropriate system based on his prior experience. This was a
challenging task. He had to find extra time and motivation while continuing to address day-to-day setbacks
and challenges. After accomplishing this task, he decided to track transfer of information in a simple Excel
spreadsheet. To establish a trackable field, each piece of land allocated for a specific use (residential,
institutional, or commercial) was identified with a unique number.
Establishing Linkages
He then scanned the available documents to update the linkages in the system. He assigned four computer
operators in his department to create records in their desktop systems. However, acquiring data files quickly
for upload turned out to be a challenge. Therefore, they decided to begin with properties that did not
command a premium in the market and would not invite scrutiny. He also mandated that all properties
undergoing a decision, such as renewal or lease payments, be routed through the newly established
procedure, so that their movement could be tracked. When a file moved or was modified, it was tracked by
the information system, thereby reducing the risk of malpractice. With IDLI software Mr. Subu empowered

the public with the information about files at their fingertip totally reversing the philosophy of being Officer-
controlled culture to a Citizen-Oriented service delivery system at public offices using technology.

Shifting to Cloud Storage
One Monday morning, a few weeks after having initiated the new process, the four operators rushed to Mr.
Subu to report that their systems had crashed. There was no option, but to reset the IT system whereby no
records could be saved. Mr. Subu was not worried as he had anticipated this issue and consequently created
backups of all systems on a hard disk every Friday evening. He did not however, restore the system on the
desktops immediately as he now recognised how pervasive the problem was. Instead of assigning blame to

specific individuals, he decided to develop a practical solution to prevent such incidents from happening in
the future. He transferred the entire back-up of the records to cloud storage and shared access with his four
operators. Shifting processes to the cloud eliminated opportunities for malpractice and possibility of
information loss due to negligence. Additionally, the cloud service provider would automatically back-up
the information, enabling data recovery in case of accidental record deletion. The only challenge remaining
was to formalise the system and make it mandatory.
Hard Work and Good Intentions Pay Off
Mr. Subu named the system ‘Interactive Disposal of Land Information (IDLI)’. He chose this acronym
because it was unusual and being a popular food item in South Indian cuisine, it was easy to remember.
From his experience at the Indian Institute of Management, Bangalore (IIM-B), he knew this title would also
facilitate branding. The system would improve the flow of transactions and the transparency of information.
Previously, when transactions were initiated, there was no basis for fees, liability, default charges, or any
other levies, including penal interest.
He wanted to make the system official but understood that formalising the system would not be welcomed
in the existing scenario. However, an appropriate opportunity presented itself during an official visit of the
Lieutenant Governor (LG) of Delhi, who was also the DDA Chairman. Mr. Subu demonstrated IDLI to the

LG who was impressed with the transparent working and recommended the immediate adoption for day-
to-day use and institutionalisation (See Exhibit 2). This marked the culmination of his mammoth efforts

since first conceptualising IDLI in 2017. The e-Capture, a module for capturing the details of any file,

was created in 2019. Other modules, such as e-Conversion, e-EoT2

Appointment, were launched for the public on August 13, 2020. Mr. Subu had finally achieved an interactive

land information tracking system that was transparent, objective and citizen oriented. This system has
served to eliminate suspect practicesv. This accomplishment took four years of dedicated effort from
conceptualisation to adoption.
Key Impacts
Mr. Subu was recognised for his work in the public system and commended for his strengths. Given that
one of the original contracts for development and implementation of a similar system by the IT companies
quoted a price of ₹ 300 crores, he estimated that development of IDLI by a team of four under his guidance
had saved the government at least that amount. IDLI was made available on a simplified cloud platform and
required only regular updates and maintenance. It ensured that crores of revenue were received by the
exchequer of DDA instead of leaking out from the system. More significantly, the end beneficiaries were
satisfied and appreciated the fairness in the Land Disposal function of DDA. By utilising DDA’s existing
hardware and software, Mr. Subu had saved resources and time, with zero cost to the exchequer, thus
personifying Atma Nirbhar Bharat in the Civil Services.
The Way Ahead
The government has been proactive in promoting digitisation of land records. The DDA's completely online
interface for conversion, mutation and time extension for all types of land has successfully eliminated the

Case Study Title: Leadership Interventions and Succession Planning at Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited
Case Study Description: The case highlights the positive impacts of Leadership Intervention and Succession Planning at HPCL through Various Strategies- T20 Strategy, T25 Strategy, HP Possible Model. Case Text:
Dr. Pushp Kumar Joshi, Chairman & Managing of Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL), one
of India’s largest integrated public sector undertakings operating in the refining and marketing of crude
oil and other transport fuels, was faced with an urgent dilemma. With the Indian government committing
to net-zero by 2070 and setting out ambitious goals for the transition to electric mobility, the demand for
fossil-fuel based transport fuels was likely to come under pressure over the coming years and decades.
HPCL’s HR team had put in place a series of impressive HR interventions to sensitise not only senior
leadership but also mid and junior management to these changes. These programmes had focused on
mentorship, leadership building and succession planning, and building the business and behavioural
competencies that executives needed to lead the firm through the energy transition. A comprehensive
impact assessment revealed a favourable organisational impact on employee behaviours because of these
interventions. But Mr. Joshi was convinced that more needed to be done. What more could be done to
improve the exposure of the senior leadership team, which could then, in turn, take decisions that drove
change? What kind of new capabilities needed to be developed? Further, how could HPCL ensure that each
worker, including those out on the field, was prepared for the transition?

and environmentally friendly opportunities, and the minimization of portfolio risks. (Refer Exhibit 4)

investments in green opportunities, capital efficiency, operational excellence, risk management, and
building resilience and agility among employees. This was a reaction to the changing global geopolitical
environment, continuous technological innovation, and significant regulatory uncertainty, factors which
were impacting all aspects of the economy, but particularly the fossil-fuel industry. Changing consumer

continuous learning and greater agility within the firm.
