Case Study Title: Leaving No One Behind: Leveraging the Power of Collaboration to Vaccinate the Most Vulnerable
Case Study Description: The Chikkaballapur district administration in Karnataka was working hard to scale up COVID-19 vaccinations, but without much success. Under the leadership of Dr. C.N. Satyanarayana Reddy, Taluka Health Officer of Chikkaballapur district, strategic collaborations were initiated to accelerate vaccinations for the most vulnerable populations across India in line with the government's mandate of leaving no one behind. Following an understanding of the causes underlying vaccine resistance and implementation challenges in the district, appropriate measures were undertaken to raise awareness and design effective vaccine delivery systems.
Case Text:
In early August 2021, the Chikkaballapur district administration in Karnataka was working hard to scale
up COVID-19 vaccinations, but without much success as motivation at the ground level was low. Change
was, however, just around the corner under the leadership of Dr. Satyanarayana Reddy C.N., Taluka
Health Officer, Bagepalli, Chikkaballapur District, Karnataka. Although COVID-19 vaccination fell under
the purview of the state government, Dr. Satyanarayana initiated strategic collaborations and leveraged
multi-sectoral partnerships to accelerate vaccinations for the most vulnerable populations across India. The
VaxNow1
initiative, launched in Bagepalli Taluk of Chikkaballapur District, Karnataka was featured in the
‘promising practices library’ created by India COVID SOS (ICSOS) and Exemplars in Global Health (EGH).
2

Covid-19 Vaccination and the Indian Health System
In January 2023, the Economic Survey 2022-233 declared that more than 220 crore Covid-19 vaccine
doses were administered under India’s National Covid-19 Vaccination Programme by December 2022. In
addition to meeting programme goals, 97 percent of the eligible beneficiaries had received at least one dose
of the vaccine. India’s National Covid-19 Vaccination Programme, which is the world’s largest vaccination
programme, began on 16 January 2021, initially with the aim of covering the adult population of the country
in the shortest possible time. The programme was expanded to include all persons aged 12 years and above,
and the precautionary dose was for all persons aged 18 years and above.
As per the Economic Survey 2022-234

this success was achieved by overcoming some major
challenges, such as research and development for the introduction of new Covid-19 vaccines; training of
more than 2.6 lakh vaccinators and 4.8 lakh other members of the vaccination team; optimum utilisation of
vaccines available in stock; reaching populations that lacked access to vaccines, and ensuring the provision
of essential health services along with scaling up the vaccination programme. These measures helped the
programme to meet its goals within a short time frame.
The emergence of the Covid-19 pandemic presented the world with a humanitarian crisis, the likes
of which had not been witnessed in decades. Nonetheless, the Government of India responded to the
pandemic with the development of policies based on recommendations from experts and the
implementation of standardised measures (Exhibit 1). This was complemented by proactive efforts at the
local level in the Chikkaballapur district of Karnataka, to fulfil the government’s mandate of leaving no one
behind.

LEAVING NO ONE BEHIND: LEVERAGING THE POWER OF COLLABORATION TO
VACCINATE THE MOST VULNERABLE
Dr. Satyanarayana’s Actions
The Government of India set out to accelerate vaccinations across all states and districts in the
country with the understanding that delays could cause the Covid-19 virus to mutate, create new
outbreaks, and cause further sickness. For Bagepalli’s Taluka Health Officer, Dr. Satyanarayana, and his
team in Chikkaballapur district, this was a call to action. The Bagepalli block was facing challenges in terms
of vaccination uptake, which was a cause of concern for the district officials.
To vaccinate at least 70 percent of the population in each village of the block, Dr. Satyanarayana
deployed a team of three Auxiliary Nursing Midwifery (ANM) experts to conduct a vaccination drive in a
different village each day. However, by early August 20215

, he noticed that despite the team’s best efforts,
vaccination penetration had not increased as expected. Team motivation was also low, related to
vaccination hesitancy and other access related issues including mobility and safety of health workers.
Determined to protect his block from Covid-19, Dr Satyanarayana dedicated time to understand the
challenges and needs of his team and the community. He then actively engaged with the Covid Action
Collaborative to accelerate vaccination efforts for the most vulnerable populations who faced hurdles in
accessing healthcare. This segment of the population was also least likely to be able to afford life-saving
medical interventions, and remained at higher risk of contracting COVID-19 due to a predisposition to
acute illnesses and chronic diseases.
VaxNow, endeavoured to address these challenges by raising awareness and designing vaccine
delivery systems to overcome access challenges. This initiative integrated routine immunisation with the
administration of the Covid-19 vaccine to ensure that the most vulnerable do not fall through the cracks.
VaxNow segmented the community based on their sentiment towards vaccination (vaccine eager but not
getting access; vaccine indifferent, but can be convinced; mobilised; hesitant; and unwilling) and then used
a layered approach to reach the unreached vulnerable groups through a set of operational tactics specific
to each segment.
From Scattered to Saturation approach - Pivoting to Ensure No One is Left Behind
Dr Satyanarayana studied the routine vaccination approach, in which one Auxiliary Nurse
Midwife (ANM) would spend an entire day in an assigned village, vaccinating every individual who
appeared at the vaccination drive. The next day, she would move on to the next village among the 40-45
villages assigned to her. She was able to then return to the first village for the second vaccination drive only
40 days later. From the ANMs and community members, Dr. Satyanarayana learnt that this approach,
termed the “scattered approach,” was ineffective and translated to only 10-15 persons receiving
vaccinations on the day of the drive. Recognising the need for change, he worked with his team to deploy
the “saturation approach,” wherein a team of 3 ANMs visited the same set of neighbouring villages for 4-
5 consecutive days, to create vaccine awareness, debunk myths and misconceptions, and generate vaccine
demand. They remained in the region to administer vaccines until at least 70 percent of the village was
“saturated.” Only then did the ANM team move on to the next set of villages to repeat the exercise. The
implementation of this approach in Bagepalli led to a 25 percent increase in administration of the first dose
from 50.4 percent to 75.37 percent; a rise of 12 percent in the 2nd dose, while vaccination reach increased
from 14.33 percent to 26.24 percent in just 4 weeks between August 11, 2021 and September 10, 20216
.

LEAVING NO ONE BEHIND: LEVERAGING THE POWER OF COLLABORATION TO
VACCINATE THE MOST VULNERABLE
A Community-Centric Approach to Vaccination
Overturning Perceptions
There was the general perception that Bagepalli, being home to a large tribal population, was
largely sceptical of modern medicine, which accounted for the poor vaccination rates in the block. Dr
Satyanarayana however, refused to accept this unvalidated claim and instead, organised a visit to the
homes of individual community members for himself and his team, and government health officials
(Exhibit 2) to better understand the barriers to vaccination. (Exhibit 3).
Changing Vaccination Timings for Community Convenience
House visits with community members made it evident that a significant section of the population
relied on agriculture as their primary source of income. Farmers had to leave early in the morning to tend
their farms and returned late in the evening. This information helped Dr. Satyanarayana and the team to
realise that to accommodate these populations, vaccination camps had to be conducted outside of regular
working hours. Accordingly, supported by Dr. Satyanarayana, the vaccination team made the decision to
run the vaccination camp from 7:30 am to noon and then between 5:30 pm to late night until 70 percent
coverage was attained in the village.
Involving Local Leaders & Influencers in the Vaccination Programme
At a district level, Dr. Satyanarayana leveraged review meetings to communicate the impact of the
VaxNow initiative and how it supported the frontline workers’ continual efforts to vaccinate communities
en masse. Satisfied with the outcomes at Bagepalli, the District Health Officer instructed other blocks to
follow Dr. Satyanarayana’s lead and implement the VaxNow initiative to boost vaccine penetration in their
own blocks. At the community level, Dr. Satyanarayana and his team spent long hours helping local leaders
and influencers (i.e., Gram Panchayat members) understand the cost and consequences of not getting the
Covid-19 vaccine. After gaining the leaders’ support, Dr. Suryanarayana leveraged their social capital with
the community to generate awareness and demand for the vaccination camps. He recognised that obtaining
support from local leaders was key to VaxNow’s success in the block because the community would
contemplate vaccination only after they saw their trusted leaders receiving it. He was instrumental in
generating awareness and helped to dispel the fears of the vaccine-hesitant people, thereby developing
community champions who mobilised and enlisted their friends, neighbours, and family members for
vaccination.
Empowering Community Health Workers
Dr. Satyanarayana dedicated time and made the effort to understand the challenges his team was
facing in vaccinating all residents in every village in the block. Apart from the challenge of locals not being
available for the vaccination drives during working hours, additionally, to avoid wastage, the ANMs
would not open the vials unless they had 10 (Covishield) or 20 (CoVaxin) individuals present to receive the
vaccine. Due to the long wait, many individuals would leave the drive without receiving the vaccine. Dr.
Satyanarayana thereby assured the ANMs that he would assume responsibility for any wastage but that
the vaccines must be administered to everyone who attended the drive. Under his leadership, the ANMs
were equipped with safe, private transportation which enabled them to visit a single village repeatedly
until maximum coverage was attained before moving on to the next village.

LEAVING NO ONE BEHIND: LEVERAGING THE POWER OF COLLABORATION TO
VACCINATE THE MOST VULNERABLE
Unlocking the Power of Collaboration
Dr. Satyanarayana had the foresight to combine resources and expertise as the only way to combat
the Covid-19 pandemic. Recognising the importance of multi-stakeholder collaboration, he was receptive
to the VaxNow initiative that delineated responsibilities for (i) the private sector organization (ii)
government officials (iii) NGOs and civil society (iv) media. Under the VaxNow initiative, every
stakeholder played a critical role in addressing vaccine supply and demand barriers, facilitating operations
and system delivery besides overcoming accessibility concerns in a time of crisis (Exhibit 4).
The implementation of VaxNow at Bagepalli perfectly demonstrates the dynamic operation of a
multi-stakeholder collaboration between the community, healthcare workers, and government officials for
achievement of positive outcomes that ensured timely delivery and smooth administration of vaccines. Dr.
Satyanarayana leveraged his position as Taluka Health Officer to highlight these outcomes from VaxNow
during his regular review meetings with the District Health Officer and Taluka President. He was thus
instrumental in facilitating trust and collaboration between the Taluka Health Officers. By using his
significant social capital among the community, Dr Satyanarayana was able to generate support for
VaxNow among local leaders and influencers who then inspired the emergence of community champions.
He worked with the ANMs to ease their operational challenges and empowered them to run vaccination
camps and administer vaccines with transparency.
Becoming an Agent of Change in a Time of Crisis
Although the COVID-19 pandemic evolved into a crisis, it proved to be a disruptor that provided
humanity an opportunity to reimagine systems and solutions, particularly for the most vulnerable
populations. Dr. Satyanarayana’s actions demonstrate how VaxNow catered to the needs of the village
community in the entire block and thus emerged successful.
Inspired by the VaxNow results, other blocks in the Chikkaballapur district approached Dr.
Satyanarayana to support the implementation of a similar vaccine drive in their communities. Dr.
Satyanarayana’s actions demonstrates the power of leveraging networks to bring about community and
ecosystem-level changes even after the Covid-19 crisis. His willingness to collaborate in an open and
transparent manner continues to serve as an example for other government health officials who require
pooled resources to implement lasting changes in their own jurisdictions.

Case Study Title: New Age Learning Centre- Transforming the lives of the students of Changlang
Case Study Description: NALC is a Free of Cost Service which enables flexible, state of the art, futuristic and leisure learning space which enables people from all age groups to learn and improve every aspect of their personality through free Wi-Fi (24x7), online training through tablets, e-reading through kindle, etc, in an environment furnished with modular furniture. It converges resources that are rendered unused viz. libraries of government schools are marred with a lack of dedicated library teachers, library infrastructure and books and transforms these existing libraries into NALC helping in optimum utilisation of unused resources of libraries run by the library department which acts as cluster libraries for nearby schools wherein children from all schools may access this space as their library.
Case Text:
All the students at a government school in Vijoynagar, located in the Changlang district of Arunachal
Pradesh (Refer Exhibits 1& 2) who appeared for their 10th Board exams in 2023 passed with flying colors.
It was for the first time in the history of Vijoynagar that a government school infamous—since it was
established—for a 100 percent fail rate of students had achieved a 100 percent pass record!1 For Mr. Sunny
K. Singhi
, a young bureaucrat who played a key role in this turnaround, it was a day to cherish and reflect
on this journey.
Hope Rises in Changlang

Changlang was rated by the Ministry of Education, Government of India, as being among India's worst-
performing districts in terms of school education. With its undulating mountainous terrain and high

altitudes, Changlang district had minimal all-weather roads. Vijoynagar—the easternmost inhabited land
in India shared its borders with the neighbouring country of Myanmar, (which is burdened with a troubled
past and insurgency). This posed some unique challenges for Changlang District, especially with the
development and maintenance of public infrastructure, including schools. The population consisted of
several tribal communities, Tibetan refugees, and settlers from nearby districts, such as Assam, and
neighbouring countries, like Bangladesh and Nepal.2
When Mr. Sunny K. Singh was posted as the Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC), Miao (about 157
km west of Vijoynagar in Changlang district) in 2021, the youth wing of the local tribal community and the
Women’s Welfare Society apprised him of their grievances in the hope that this young bureaucrat would
initiate much-needed administrative change in Changlang.

i Mr. Sunny K. Singh, an IAS officer from the 2018 batch, is currently serving as the DC of Kra-Daadi.
Awarded the Prime Minister’s Award for Excellence in Public Administration-2022 for his innovative
New Age Learning Centre initiative, he previously served as DC Changlang. An engineer by
qualification, he is also a passionate sports enthusiast.

NEW AGE LEARNING CENTRE: TRANSFORMING THE LIVES
OF THE STUDENTS OF CHANGLANG

2

The youth of Changlang aspired for better education and employment prospects, while the women desired
for their children’s safety and better job prospects, not much different from the dreams of a million other
Indians.
Discerning the Dilemma
As the ADC, Mr. Singh initiated communication with all sections of society to gain insight into the complex
development and security issues in Miao. The primary occupation of the communities in this district was
agriculture, besides other allied vocations like goat rearing or the collection and sale of forest products,
including timber. Hunting wild animals was also part of their tradition and culture.
In the context of academic education, school dropout rates in the district were high, as was teacher
absenteeism. It was also difficult to hire and retain teachers. The school buildings were old, the classrooms
were not well maintained, and the libraries were dark and dingy.
Students’ homes were also not conducive to learning. The children enrolled in government schools came
from economically weaker households and resided in shared living spaces. Although most families owned
mobile phones as a source of communication and entertainment, power outages were frequent, particularly
during monsoons, and could extend for more than 12 hours a day. Changlang district’s location, too, added
multiple layers of complexity. Cultivation of opium and processing of opium into derivatives, cross-border
trade, and smuggling of psychotropic narcotics were prevalent. Substance abuse was rampant among
young adolescents, who were trapped in a vicious cycle of drug usage and then coerced to partner in drug
networks to meet their addiction needs.
Determination and Design for Success
Before starting his journey as an IAS officer, Mr. Sunny K. Singh, raised in Gopalganj, Bihar, had obtained
his engineering degree from Delhi College of Engineering and then worked as a design engineer for Hero
MotoCorp. He had experienced the life of a village lad with minimal infrastructural support, which shaped
his dream of becoming an IAS officer. With grit and determination, he prepared for the UPSC exam while
exercising the power of creativity and design during his time in the private sector. It was now time to
combine these experiences.
With unwavering support from youth and women’s associations, Mr. Singh made the decision to engage
the young people of Changlang in activities that build their competencies and could shape their future.
Considering that the youth in Changlang were avid soccer fans, an indoor football or futsalii

court was set
up in Miao (Exhibit 3). A basketball court (Exhibit 4), a skateboard rink, and a well-equipped gym were
also established. The players could play until late in the evening, after school hours, between 5 p.m. and 9
p.m. These sporting facilities were the first of many spaces that attracted the youngsters Miao. To honour
the hunting tradition of the communities, a shooting range was also established in local Kendriya
Vidyalaya school in March 2022iii. Mr. Singh enlisted the support of the Indian Armed Forces, which
donated professional guns and trained participants to sharpen their inherent marksmanship skills. Further,
following the state government's successful gun surrender campaign in 2021, the weapons surrendered by

iii As of January 2024, the following facilities have been established in Changlang, Miao and Diyun

NEW AGE LEARNING CENTRE: TRANSFORMING THE LIVES
OF THE STUDENTS OF CHANGLANG

3

the tribal communities were also used to train school children.iv The shooters from Changlang district went
on to win several national-level gold and silver medals in the rifle and pistol competitions conducted for
school-level cadets. The youth of Miao now had access to a trendy sports arena to hone their physical
capabilities.
A shift towards Books & Meaningful Activities
It was now time to move focus from the playground to the classroom and address the academic challenges
faced by the students of Miao. The youth did not find the libraries appealing. The existing libraries were
dull racks of books, staffed by strict librarians who only wanted to maintain discipline and silence. The
libraries instilled a sense of dread in those struggling with studies and textbooks. Mr. Singh decided to
make some drastic changes.
He envisioned the library as "a fluid, well-lit space” where students and young people were encouraged to
visit, read the books and periodicals, and develop their life skills. Browsing through online resources for
ideas, Mr. Singh shortlisted 12 design concepts for a library, which were presented to the youth leaders for
finalisation. They were unanimous in their choice. They favoured a structure that did not constantly impose
restrictions. They wanted a space to be student friendly. Thus, the “New Age Learning Centre (NALC)”
was designed and inaugurated on May 7, 2022, in the Miao sub-division of Changlang district.
The NALC was split into multiple sections to meet the demands of its different users. Quiet, well-lit nooks
and cubicles for those who sought a peaceful space to focus on their studies (Exhibit 5); an area with swings,
cushions, and bean bags for those who preferred reading as a fun activity (Exhibit 6); or even a space lined
with chess boards, Rubik's cube, jigsaw puzzles, and board games for those who wanted to spend time
with friends. (Exhibit 7)
The NALC housed plenty of books, ranging from textbooks for different classes, study materials to prepare
for competitive exams, and even Kindles for those who preferred to read online. (Exhibit 8) It also included
a centrally mounted smart television set with 10 GB/day internet access, which was available 24x7 for
watching educational channels and sports matches. The NALC additionally made available Virtual Reality
(VR) headsets, which quickly became popular among the youth of Miao; the kids who had never crossed
their district could now take a tour of India within the safe comfort of the NALC. What more could the
youth aspire for their future needs? The NALC had plenty more to offer.
The library had an elevated stage and a podium, which served as an epicentre for several activities. Various
public speakers were invited to train the youth on disaster management during emergencies and
calamities. Medical practitioners provided training on cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) using
dummies and other first-aid techniques. Career counselling sessions were conducted for students aspiring
to undertake higher studies.
Promoting peer learning was another critical initiative. Groups of children sharing similar interests joined
clubs to acquire and impart skills ranging from yoga to public speaking to drone piloting methods.

2459187.html (Accessed: 29 January 2024).

OF THE STUDENTS OF CHANGLANG

4

Challenges and Solutions
Funding the Dream
“Financing a project is not difficult if you are determined and committed,” claims Mr. Singh. “I had ideas for NALC,
but no fund was budgeted for the same I was, however, certain that if the idea is noble, the pathway to success would
emerge” he added.
He convinced the local Chief Engineer of Border and Roads Organisation (BRO)v, a department of the
Government of India, that Miao’s youth needed a library. The officer graciously agreed to donate bricks
and other building materials, such as cement, steel, and rods, for the project. Mr. Singh then met the
panchayat president and the local traders. Local timber merchants and the traders who ran stone crusher
units agreed to support the initiative by contributing to the NALC in purchase of wood, bricks, sand, and
other construction materials.
The project design incorporated construction of the floor, wall units, and stairs from locally available
materials like wood and plywood. Tree trunks discarded by timber units were repurposed as reading
tables. The community generously donated books and other supplies.
The project leaders negotiated with Jio Telecom to provide a 24x7 internet connection with 100GBP speed
in perpetuity in exchange for a lease of a plot of land to construct their telecom tower.
When the project stopped due to a paucity of funds, the support of the Member of the Legislative Assembly
(MLA), an elected representative of the district, along with the deputy Chief minister, provided INR 50
lakhs that was available under the untied for the project. Within 8 months thereafter, the construction was
completed, and NALC was ready to welcome its users.
Onboarding the Naysayers
The librarian, as part of the old library system, was in shock. Mr. Singh recalled the words of the shocked
librarian- “How can a library not be silent? How can you run a library without a ledger to input the borrower's
details? What if the children steal the books or never return them? I shall lose my job.”
Mr. Singh’s perspective was different. He felt, "If a child wants a book bad enough to steal, that is the best form
of thievery. Besides, these books are donated by the public and belong to their children. I had to explain to the librarian
that the books in NALC were not owned by the state library, so he would not be held accountable if the books went
missing. However, we held several meetings with youth club members and the librarian to guide the handling of books
and maintain them in good condition. We also ensured that all schools had access to the library, as it was well-stocked
with textbooks, reference materials, video lessons, and learning guides. I convinced school principals to assign one
period per week as a library period, in which students could use the library resources during school hours. Most
teachers were enthusiastic and urged their students to use these facilities. I sent a letter of appreciation from my official
letterhead to laud them for their efforts and encourage others to join in.”
Key Impacts
Since its establishment, NALC has functioned as a state-of-the-art, futuristic, and leisure learning facility
that is free and accessible to people of all ages. It also focuses on e-learning and conducts activity-based
learning during its extended hours up to 9 p.m. The children have watched the Republic Day parade and
v The BRO constructs and maintains road networks in border areas and in friendly neighbouring
countries, including Myanmar.

NEW AGE LEARNING CENTRE: TRANSFORMING THE LIVES
OF THE STUDENTS OF CHANGLANG

5

celebrated India’s space vehicle, Chandrayaan-3 landing on the moon. Sitting in Miao, they can participate
in events across the country. Mr. Singh recounted the wonderment of several dignitaries who visited the
facilities. They were amazed to see a well-lit, state-of-the-art, world-class facility in a remote area.
The second surprising aspect has been the enthusiastic participation by the youth of Changlang. They used
every opportunity to highlight their talent before the visiting dignitaries. During a visit by the Chief
Secretary of Arunachal Pradesh, the students demanded details of the state government’s strategy for tiger
conservation in their National Park and even about the Israel-Palestine war.
Project Safal
While the students enrolled in schools located near Miao benefitted from the NALC, the students of
Vijoynagar, located 157 km away from Miao Town, were still isolated. During that time, it took about 2
days of trekking in hilly terrain to reach Miao.
In 2020, 12 students of Vijoynagar’s single state government run secondary school—who were enrolled in
the 10th grade had no expectation of clearing the board examination. Until an innovative intervention
changed their prospects, Project Safal, launched under Mr. Singh’s administration in consultation with local
parents and schoolteachers, presented these students with an opportunity to overcome their isolation and
change their fortunes.
As a District Collector, Mr. Singh had access to a helicopter meant to airlift patients facing medical
emergencies. He used this chopper to airlift the twelve students and one parent to Miao.
Two houses were prepared to accommodate them during their three-month visit. The teachers of Kendriya
Vidyalaya in Miao were ready to undertake the challenge of helping these students pass the board
examination. They devoted the first month to improving students’ basic reading and writing skills. The
following two months were devoted to preparing them to pass the exams. They were carefully coached to
solve the previous year’s exam papers. They were provided with textbooks and materials for self-study
and peer learning. The NALC provided them with reference books and the ambiance for self-paced
learning.
The parent—a student's mother—who accompanied the children—ensured that they were provided
nutritious home-cooked food and comforted them when they felt homesick. The three-month boot camp
concluded with the students appearing for their exams.
Soon, the results were declared, and all Vijoynagar students had passed the grade X board exam.
Additionally, Vijoynagar was the only school in Changlang district with a 100 percent pass ratio, whereas
the state average was 39.72%. The entire Vijoynagar community celebrated their students’ success with a
grand feast.
The NALC was also pivotal to other notable achievements. Mr. Ankit Chauhan was the first student from
Changlang district to get selected to AIIMS (All India Institute of Medical Sciences), a prestigious medical
college in New Delhi; two more students were accepted into other colleges to pursue medicine; two
students passed one of the difficult competitive entrance exams, to study at the Indian Institute of
Technology (IITs). All these winners who became role models for their communities, visited every local
school and shared their journey. They spoke to students about the support NALC offers to students in
classes 11 and 12. Students in Changlang district have formed online groups to support and learn from
their seniors and each other.

NEW AGE LEARNING CENTRE: TRANSFORMING THE LIVES
OF THE STUDENTS OF CHANGLANG

6

The Way Ahead: Maintaining the Momentum
The NALC and the sports arena had a great start. But the question is, will it be able to sustain the initial
enthusiasm and energy?
The inauguration of the NALC, Miao (Exhibit 9) in May 20223 created a publicity buzz in both print and
social media. Community leaders, parents, and teachers were curious and eager to learn more about this
knowledge hub. The community donated materials during construction and contributed to buying books,
musical instruments, and other amenities. Consequently, they would visit the NALC to monitor the
facilities' functioning and use. Often, they would take photos that highlighted their involvement and
contribution to NALC, which is like a prized treasure and their responsibility to maintain for their children.
Furthermore, SEED (Society for Education and Environmental Development) a local voluntary
organization, established by the local residents, came forward to ensure governance and guidance of
NALC, Miao.
Soon, a second NALC was inaugurated in the district headquarters of Changlang on September 23, 2023.
And the third NALC was inaugurated on March 6, 2024, at Diyun (Exhibit 10). As part of their CSR
initiative, Oil India Limited, Duliajan provided support for replenishing supplies and adding to the books
collection as did several other civil society organizations.
Lessons Learnt
A worthwhile takeaway from NALC is to involve users, in this case, youth, in the design stage and consider
their bright ideas that are relevant and practical to make the space come alive.
Public spaces designed and built by the government focus on efficiency, that is, the completion of the
project at the lowest cost and time. Users seldom participate in these processes. Children and youth are
almost never consulted when building infrastructure like schools, libraries, or sports facilities for their use.
Traditional libraries are anachronistic for the new generation of learners with different aspirations and
learning styles.
Secondly, when communities contribute to development, it creates a sense of ownership among
community members and ensures that they remain accountable for the use of facilities and their upkeep.

Case Study Title: Bikes of Bijnor: A waste to wealth public bike sharing programme
Case Study Description:
This case documents the innovative and collaborative efforts by the Bijnor administration to create wealth from the bicycles—abandoned by the migrant workers during the COVID-19 pandemic—to birth the inclusive Bikes of Bijnor ride-sharing program. The bicycles left as a heap of iron waste outside the police stations of Bijnor in Uttar Pradesh were utilised in the ridesharing program with significant social and environmental benefit. Under the program, the bicycle owners were first identified and then compensated to obtain legal possession of the bicycles. Bicycles were then refurbished, and bike stands were set up at 10 spots in Bijnor town. The bicycles were then made available for hire at a minimal cost.

The ridesharing program—the brainchild of the Bijnor Joint Magistrate, Mr. Vikramaditya Singh Malik, in 2020-21—brought together the civil service and the municipal administration. Both collaborated to fund the project and formally registered “Bikes of Bijnor “as a society headed by the Sub-divisional Magistrate (SDM) Sadar, while the Head and the Executive Officer of the Nagar Palika functioned as its secretary.
Case Text:
One morning in July 2023, Mr. Vikramaditya Singh Malik (IAS)i

, the Chief Development Officer of
Ghaziabad received on his phone the video of a yellow-coloured bicycle with the message, “Sir, your bikes
are still plying around the town.” The message forwarded by an acquaintance from Bijnorii

, revived some
memories wherein Mr. Malik recalled the days of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, when the world battled
for survival.
In April 2020, when the first wave of COVID-19 started to spread, Mr. Malik was posted as the Sub
Divisional Magistrate (SDM) of Raja Talab at Varanasi. Due to the severity of the pandemic, when
nationwide lockdowns were announced, migrant workers from the northern states of Punjab, Haryana and
Uttarakhand had poured into Bijnor and Varanasi, on the way to their hometowns and villages in Eastern
Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Many labourers had arrived by foot, others by bicycle or by whatever means they
could manage. The district administration immediately sprang into action, to provide food and makeshift
shelters for these migrant labourers besides arranging for trains and buses to transport them to their
hometowns. For the workers being transported by road, their bicycles were also loaded onto the buses to
be retrieved at their destination. The number of migrant workers returning to their hometowns was huge.
In Mr. Malik’s Varanasi tehsiliii

, between 80,000 and 85,0001 persons rode on buses in two weeks.

The Abandoned Bicycles of Bijnor
A few months later, Mr. Malik was posted as the Joint Magistrate of Bijnor. During a field visit in the tehsil
bordering Haridwar district, Mr. Malik observed a huge stack of bicycles outside a police station, partially
submerged in the monsoon waters that had overflowed from the river Ganga. Upon enquiry, he learned
that most of these bicycles had been abandoned by the migrant labourers, who had left the district for their
i Mr. Vikramaditya Singh Malik (IAS) is an Indian Administrative Service officer, 2018 batch. He is a law
expert and an alumnus of NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, and Oxford University (UK).
ii Bijnor is a town in Western Uttar Pradesh, with a population of 3.68 million (36.7 Lakhs), located 185 km
northeast of the National Capital, New Delhi.
iii Tehsil is a revenue sub-division within a district.

BIKES OF BIJNOR: A WASTE TO WEALTH PUBLIC BIKE
SHARING PROGRAM

2

hometowns. In contrast to Varanasi, where the district administration had arranged buses to transport the
workers, the Bijnor administration had arranged special trains for travel as they hailed from faraway towns
in Eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Unlike buses, their bicycles could not be loaded onto the trains and
had to be abandoned. These unattended, unused bicycles remained unutilised. The numbers were huge, in
hundreds, and without any name tag to identify the owners. While some claimants called back from their
hometowns to enquire about the bicycles, they had left behind at Bijnor, others did not. How could one
trace the owners?
An Out-of-the-Box Idea

Mr. Malik ideated some creative uses for the abandoned bicycles and discussed his ideas to clear the pile-
up with his superior, the then-district magistrate, Mr. Ramakant Pandey (IAS), who was supportive. Some

of the options they discussed were to get the bicycles refitted to be either presented as awards to students
or given to local labourers.
Mr. Malik however, had another innovative idea drawn from his experience in cities like Chandigarh,
Hyderabad, and London, where public bike-sharing programs are popular as a sustainability measure. He
thus developed a workable model of a “waste to wealth bike sharing program.”
Mr. Pandey too was upbeat about the idea and encouraged him to explore it further. Funding the program
during the COVID-19 pandemic presented a major obstacle. With limited availability of government
resources, Mr. Malik’s idea needed divergent solutions for execution.
Releasing the Restraints
Implementation of the idea required a hundred bicycles in the initial phase, to be refurbished and deployed
across town for ridesharing. However, before the reuse of the bicycles could be deemed legally valid, the
owners of the bicycles needed to be traced, tracked, and compensated. Their consent for reuse was also
required. It was a gargantuan task, like searching for a needle in a haystack. However, a solution was soon
found. In 2020, the city administration had meticulously adhered to a best practice of listing the names,
Aadhaar card numbers and contact mobile numbers of the migrant labourers who were sent to their
hometowns in trains during the chaos and uncertainty during the pandemic. This proved useful when the
city administration sought to call these individuals for their consent.
Mr. Malik formed a three-member committee that included members from civil society and the Industrial
Training Institute, to conduct a systematic valuation of the bicycles. Based upon the age of the cycle, the
value varied between INR 200 and INR 1500. A new bicycle in the market cost INR 3000. Following the
valuation exercise, the average value of the bicycles was processed at INR 599.The administration therefore
made the decision to provide a compensation of INR 600 per bicycle to the owners. This was much higher
in contrast with other districts like Saharanpur, where the abandoned bikes were auctioned for an average
amount of INR 225/- per bike.2
Unexpected Challenges
Mr. Malik established a control room to make calls to the bicycle owners. The team was tasked with calling
each bicycle owner to request consent to use their bicycle for the public cause. If they agreed, the team
obtained their bank account information and effected the transfer of INR 600 into their accounts. However,
some unexpected challenges were encountered and had to be resolved. Some phone numbers were
unreachable.

BIKES OF BIJNOR: A WASTE TO WEALTH PUBLIC BIKE
SHARING PROGRAM

3

Many phone numbers were changed or not in use any longer. Some call recipients either disconnected the
call or refused to provide the information. They were wary of online scams—well circulated through news
reports—in which con artists called random numbers and requested their bank account information and
ATM numbers etc. to defraud unsuspecting people. So, when the Bijnor team called the bicycle owners,
some call recipients did not believe it was a call from the government team, others considered it a scam,
and refused to provide any information.
Finally, the team could only locate about one hundred people and obtain their consent and bank account
numbers. Money was transferred into their account, and the team received legal possession of the bicycles
(hereafter referred to as bikes or bicycles in this case study). The beneficiaries were astonished that the
government system had called them personally and were pleased to receive the compensation. About ten
people, when contacted, returned to Bijnor, and collected their bicycles. Unclaimed bicycles were stored in
safe custody.
Urban Mobility Moves Forward with Collaboration
The administration then worked with the Municipal Corporation of Bijnor to identify ten locations for
bicycle stands in Bijnor town. The team considered the general pattern of people’s movement across the
town geography, and identified the following areas:
1. The Collectorate
2. The Tehsil offices
3. Roadways junction
4. Nagar Palika office
5. Ramlila Maidan
6. Qazipara
7. District Hospital
8. Bijnor Club
9. Chandpur Chungi
10. Kotwali City Thana
These spots are mostly located at crucial points where Bijnor’s primarily used roads intersect. People from
the nearby rural areas would typically travel by bus to reach Bijnor and then mostly commute from the bus
station to the places listed above for their intended work. Mr. Malik’s team collaborated with the Nagar
Palika to identify the spot to set up a bike stand at each of the 10 locations and then sought their assistance
in establishing the bike stands. As some of these spots were dilapidated, the team employed local resources
to renovate the rundown areas, performing civil works such as cleaning, covering the drains, painting and
other tasks (Exhibit 4B). "Bikes of Bijnor Society” was formally registered as a society and headed by the
Sub-divisional Magistrate (SDM) Sadar while the Executive Officer of the Nagar Palika functioned as its
secretary. A logo for “Bikes of Bijnor” was also indigenously designed through a local competition. It was
painted across the city and proved instrumental in the effective branding of the project (Exhibit 1). To
enable payment of compensation—a COVID-related expense—to the migrant workers and facilitate the
legal possession of the bicycles, funds were transferred from the District Magistrate's COVID fund to the
society. The Collectorate and Nagar Palika also contributed to the project as did local industry associations.
Refurbishing of the bikes was done at a minimum cost. The team contended that the total cost of gaining
ownership and refurbishing the old bike should not exceed INR 1500 considering that the cost of a new
bike was INR 3000. As INR 600 was already paid to the bicycle owners, the cost of refurbishing was capped
at INR 900. While some bikes did not need too many repairs, others needed more work like replacement of
worn-out tires, rims, and bell or addition of road-safety reflectors, etc. The average spending still worked
out around INR 900 per bike.

BIKES OF BIJNOR: A WASTE TO WEALTH PUBLIC BIKE
SHARING PROGRAM

4

Finally, all the bikes were repainted a bright yellow colour to give them a distinct identity and numbered
from 1 to 100 for identification. The total refurbishment cost of INR 90,000 for the hundred bikes was borne
by the Collectorate. The Nagar Palika bore the cost of establishing the bike stands. Excluding the expense
incurred on refurbishing the bike stands, the total cost of the entire project was just around INR 5 lakhs.3
Some funding as CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) contribution was also received by the Bikes of
Bijnor Society through industry associations, Vyaapaar Mandals(Commerce Chambers), and organizations
like HDFC Bank.
The stands were painted with large maps, instructions for renting a bike and the terms and conditions of
hire (Exhibit 2). Bike Stand managers to man the bike kiosks were chosen from a spectrum of people from
diverse, economically weaker backgrounds, such as tea shop owners, helmet sellers, and physically
challenged cycle mechanics. This inclusive, community-level ‘Atmanirbharta'iv action benefited many
people, both at the financial and social levels. Some Nagar Palika water pump operators were also assigned
the role of stand managers as some bike stands were located next to the municipal water pumps. The stand
managers received 60 per cent of the revenue, and the balance, 40 per cent was deposited into the society
account4
to meet continual maintenance expenses. Each stand manager also received a free air pump to
maintain correct air pressure in the bikes.
Project Launch
Noble works are usually tested with hurdles. For the Bikes of Bijnor, when all systems were in place, the
deadly Delta wave of COVID-19 pandemic began and delayed the project’s launch. The project was finally
launched when the impact of the delta wave started to recede. On April 5, 2021, the project was officially
inaugurated by Mr. Ramakant Pandey, District Magistrate of Bijnor and Mr. Dharm Veer Singh,
Superintendent of Police, Bijnor. All the officers, including Mr. Malik, rode the refurbished bikes on the
streets of Bijnor on the day of the launch.
Service Pricing and Operations
For the initial month, the service was offered completely free, to allow the public to get accustomed to using
it. To familiarize people with the concept of bike sharing, one day per week was allocated for officers to
ride these bikes to their workplaces. Postal personnel, dak runnersv, and sanitary workers were also
encouraged to use the bikes. People from rural areas were also urged to use the new mode of transport.
These efforts served to develop much traction for the bike project among the public.
From the second month onwards, INR 5 was charged for four hours and INR 10 for 12 hours, considered a
full day’s usage. To use the bicycles, every user had to make an advance payment of. INR 5, and submit
their name, mobile number, and a government-issued identity card number. The user was then issued the
bike token with a timestamp and could return the bike to any of the ten stands along with the token. For
the user, a payment of INR 10 for the use of a bike over a 12-hour period was very affordable when
compared with a single ride on an auto rickshaw, which also cost INR 10.
For example, people from the villages who worked in the shops in the inner-town area would commute by
bus and spent INR 20 per day for the auto-rickshaw ride from the bus station to their workplace. The “Bikes
of Bijnor” service allowed them to save a significant amount of money and became popular. This facility
also helped them to use the bikes for multiple trips during the day without any additional expenditure.

Many street vendors—beneficiaries of the PMSVANidhivi program—also found the bike service affordable
and useful for the commute between their homes and the vending spots.
The fitness culture in Bijnor also served to propel the bike project. Besides providing residents an option to
expand the range of fitness activities, the bikes bridged the affordability gap for those who could not buy

Key Impacts
The impact was positive and widely reported in the media (Exhibit 4). The reach was expansive to the

As pointed out by the minister, this project has the potential to impact innovative waste management,

Initiatives like the Bikes of Bijnor project are critical for India's carbon emissions and strengthen India's

The "Bikes of Bijnor" project illustrates how positive civic changes could be initiated by government and

Case Study Title:
SOTTO: Transforming Lives through Organ
Transplantation in Gujarat
Case Study Description: In the heart of Gujarat, the transformative impact of cadaver organ transplantation unfolds through powerful narratives. These stories highlight the profound effect of the State Organ and Tissue Transplantation Organisation (SOTTO), established in 2019 to revolutionise cadaver organ procurement and transplantation across government and private hospitals. Guided by rigorous protocols and the 2020 Brain Stem Death Declaration guidelines, SOTTO ensures ethical and efficient practices. Its online platform, launched in May 2020, enhances transparency and coordination, matching organs with recipients to maximise life-saving impacts. These efforts underscore Gujarat's commitment to fostering a sustainable healthcare ecosystem through the generosity of donors, breathing hope and life into countless individuals.
Case Text:
In the heart of Gujarat, a symphony of generosity and resilience unfolds through the narratives
of individuals whose lives have been intertwined by the transformative power of cadaver
transplantation. Among them stands Aaradhya, a young dancer whose graceful movements echo
the rhythm of a transplanted heart, which was once beating in the chest of 14-month-old Somnath.

This connection between the two souls-one departed and the other embracing a legacy-
encapsulates the essence of organ donation in Gujarat. Alongside Aaradhya's story, the tears of a

Syrian family bear witness to the gratitude and relief afforded by the gift of breath from a brain-
dead patient in Gujarat. These narratives, among the countless others, bear testament to the

genesis of cadaver transplantation in the region and the founding of the State Organ and Tissue
Transplantation Organisation (SOTTO) Gujarat. —a legacy woven by the generosity of donors,
breathing hope and life into countless others.
Background of Organ Transplantation in India
There are two types of human organ donation:
1. Living Donor Organ Donation: People can donate organs during their lives without which
they can continue to survive, such as a kidney, a portion of the pancreas, or part of the
liver.
2. Deceased Donor Organ Donation: People can donate multiple organs and tissues after
(brainstem or cardiac) death. This is also known as cadaver organ donation.
The former process restricts the kinds of organs available for donation, as one could donate only
those without which one can still survive. Also, live donations can be done by near relative
donors or non-near relative ones in special cases. On the other hand, the Cadaver method opens
the doors to donating multiple and numerous organs for transplantation from a single patient
who is brain dead and saves multiple lives. The cadaver method is the embodiment of the
statement that a single life has the potential to save many lives.
With the rising burden of non-communicable diseases and a growing number of patients who
suffer from irreversible organ ailments involving the kidney, liver, heart, etc., their health
indicators can be improved with the opportunity of organ transplant surgery. However, only 2-

SOTTO - TRANSFORMING LIVES THROUGH ORGAN TRANSPLANTATION IN
GUJARAT

2

3% receive such lifesaving transplants and more than 5 lakh people die due to shortage in organ
donations.1 To bridge this gap, in 2005, the state of Gujarat started laying down some procedures
to structure organ donation, strictly for transplants performed in the government sector hospitals
(Refer Exhibit 1). The state developed a cadaver transplant programme, which was further
strengthened by augmenting the entire ecosystem in 2019 with the establishment of SOTTO
Gujarat. Gujarat was the first state to have structured cadaver transplants restricted in the
government run public hospitals. For better regional and national coordination, the Gujarat state
aimed to establish SOTTO.
NOTTO Regulatory Guidelines
The National Organ and Tissue Transplantation Organisation (NOTTO) is the national-level
organisation that functions as the apex centre for coordination and networking, for the
procurement and distribution of organs and tissues and maintaining the registry of donations
and transplantation in the country. But the number of cadaveric organ donations were not rising.
Hence, the state of Gujarat sensing the benefits cadaver transplants could bring, decided to look
out for the limitations restricting the spread of cadaver organ donation and transplantations.
There existed a complex scenario in the case of cadaver organ donation: the patient must be
declared deceased either through cardiac death or brain stem death. But doctors were
apprehensive about declaring a person brain dead because there is a theoretical chance that the
patient might get revived, making it difficult to explain and convince the patient’s family as there
is no 100% certainty in the medical domain of the person not reviving. Doctors needed some kind
of reassurance in the form of guidelines or regulations to be able to convince their families.
Therefore, certain guidelines were laid down by Gujarat, which gave legal assurance to the
doctors to declare patients brain dead following certain criteria and to perform cadaver organ
transplantation with the family's consent.
SOTTO: As a Solution
In 2019, the Gujarat Deceased Donor Organ and Tissue Transplantation (G-DOT) Guidelines were
enacted to address issues surrounding organ procurement, transplantation, and governance,
setting the stage for significant developments in the field. A pivotal advancement came in 2020
with the introduction of the Brain Stem Death Declaration guidelines, establishing protocols for
identifying potential cadaveric donors among brain stem death patients. These guidelines
provided a foundational framework upon which the State Organ and Tissue Transplant
Organisation (SOTTO) could be established in Gujarat, marking a milestone in the region's
healthcare landscape.
SOTTO, established in 2019, prioritises the promotion of transparent and sustainable cadaver
transplants, aiming to save more lives while upholding ethical standards. Functioning as a
regulatory and administrative entity, SOTTO oversees organ transplantations in Gujarat,
operating through a web application designed to support cadaver organ harvesting and
transplantation across registered government and private hospitals in the state. The
implementation of SOTTO's online platform in May 2020 revolutionised the organ
transplantation process, streamlining tasks such as hospital and patient registration, donor

SOTTO - TRANSFORMING LIVES THROUGH ORGAN TRANSPLANTATION IN
GUJARAT

3

identification, and allocation procedures. By adhering to NOTTO guidelines and adapting to the
specific requirements of cadaver transplantation, SOTTO ensures efficient and transparent
governance, making strides towards a more sustainable healthcare ecosystem in Gujarat.
Process followed under SOTTO
The process followed for cadaver organ transplantation under SOTTO, encompasses several
crucial steps aimed at ensuring efficient and ethical organ transplantation procedures.
• It begins with the declaration of a patient as brain dead, following stringent criteria
outlined in G-DOT guidelines, brainstem death guidelines and other medical guidelines.
• Once brain death is confirmed, trained medical professionals approach the patient's
family to discuss the possibility of organ donation. This sensitive conversation involves
explaining the significance of organ donation and seeking the family's consent to proceed
with the donation process.
• Upon receiving the family's consent, the details of the donor, including any specific
criteria or conditions, are recorded, and entered into the SOTTO system. These criteria
may include factors such as the donor's medical history, organ compatibility, and any
preferences or restrictions specified by the donor or their family. The information is
meticulously documented to ensure accuracy and compliance with regulatory standards.
• Subsequently, the SOTTO software initiates the critical task of matching the available
organs with recipients on the waiting list. This automated matching process considers
various factors, including the medical urgency of the recipients, compatibility of organs,
and other relevant criteria established by medical professionals. Through advanced
algorithms and database management, the software efficiently identifies suitable matches,
optimising the chances of successful transplantation and maximising the impact of
donated organs.
• Once a compatible recipient is identified, arrangements are swiftly made to retrieve the
organs from the donor and transport them to the respective hospitals where
transplantation procedures will take place. This phase of the process involves high
coordination among medical teams, transportation providers, and hospital staff to ensure
timely and safe delivery of the organs.
• Throughout each stage, stringent protocols and guidelines are followed to uphold patient
safety, confidentiality, and ethical standards, reflecting the commitment of SOTTO to
facilitate transparent, compassionate, and life-saving organ transplantation practices.
Challenges Addressed by SOTTO
Challenge 1: Registration and Paperwork Assistance
Solution: The introduction of the SOTTO Portal (Refer Exhibit 2), known as the Gujarat Network
for Cadaver Organ Sharing (GNCOS), revolutionised the registration process for donors and
recipients. Through this online platform, extensive paperwork and registration procedures are
now streamlined. The software developed specifically for SOTTO Gujarat facilitates transparent
e-governance by managing tasks such as hospital and patient registration, organ donor and
recipient identification, and approval processes. This transition from manual to online

SOTTO - TRANSFORMING LIVES THROUGH ORGAN TRANSPLANTATION IN
GUJARAT

4

management has significantly reduced human effort and improved efficiency in implementing
SOTTO across Gujarat. Moreover, the establishment of state-of-the-art, NABH-accredited
facilities like IKDRCi and UNMICRCii further exemplifies the government's commitment to
equitable access to organ transplantation services. These facilities, particularly IKDRC, offer
dedicated facilitation centres that provide comprehensive assistance to patients, including
information dissemination and paperwork support.
The Gujarat University of Transplantation Sciences (GUTS), established in 2015, stands as the
world's first and only university dedicated to transplantation and allied sciences. Through its
structured courses and training programmes, GUTS ensures the availability of skilled medical
and paramedical professionals, thereby enhancing the sustainability and effectiveness of organ
transplantation infrastructure in the state.
Challenge 2: Addressing Doctors' Apprehensions Regarding the Brain Death Declaration
Solution: To address the doctors' concerns regarding brain death declaration, the state
implemented the G-DOT guidelines, which govern organ procurement, transplantation, and
governance. These guidelines provide clear criteria for scoring and organ allocation, ensuring
transparency and effective outcomes in the transplantation process. Furthermore, the resolution
related to Brainstem Death Guidelines specifies procedures for identifying cadaveric donors,
offering reassurance to medical professionals and families alike.
Challenge 3: Convincing Families and Ensuring Timely Organ Retrieval
Solution: Proactive media engagement and the deployment of grief counsellors have facilitated
communication and decision-making processes with the families of potential donors. This
proactive approach helps minimise delays in organ retrieval, ensuring that organs are harvested
within the critical time frame for transplantation. Additionally, measures such as stringent
regulations against illegal organ extraction and initiatives to increase organ donation rates
through social awareness campaigns contribute to a more sustainable and transparent organ
transplantation system.
Challenge 4: Timely Organ Retrieval and Preservation
Solution: Infrastructural development and specialised training for ICU teams ensure the timely
retrieval and preservation of organs. By enhancing capabilities and resources in donor centres,
the state mitigates the risk of organ deterioration and maximises the viability of donated organs
for transplantation.
Challenge 5: Transportation of Organs
Solution: To address challenges related to organ transportation, the state has invested in
additional vehicles and established green corridors for expedited transportation. Budgetary

i
IKDRC: Institute of Kidney Diseases and Research Centre
ii UNMIRC: U.N. Mehta Institute of Cardiology & Research Centre

SOTTO - TRANSFORMING LIVES THROUGH ORGAN TRANSPLANTATION IN
GUJARAT

5

provisions enable the use of special air ambulances or chartered planes for airlifting organs,
ensuring rapid and efficient transportation to transplantation centres. (Refer Exhibit 3)
Challenge 6: Financial Assistance and Accessibility
Solution: The state has taken comprehensive measures to address financial barriers to
transplantation, including inclusion under the PMJAY-MAiii scheme and the provision of grants
from PM (Prime minister) & CM (Chief Minister) Relief funds. By expanding coverage and
accessibility to transplantation services, particularly for low-income and marginalised
communities, the state ensures equitable access to life-saving transplant procedures, irrespective
of financial constraints. Additionally, provisions prioritise vulnerable groups such as women and
children, ensuring that they receive timely and affordable access to transplantation services when
needed.
Impact of SOTTO Gujarat
Service, Education and Research Integration
The establishment of the Gujarat University of Transplantation Sciences (GUTS) in 2015 marks
the world's first and only university dedicated to transplantation sciences. It offers various
medical and paramedical courses related to transplantation, thereby creating a skilled workforce
that promotes organ transplantation across healthcare facilities.
Medical Impact
• Before SOTTO, the live organ transplant to cadaver organ transplant ratio in Gujarat
government hospitals was 4:1, which has significantly improved to 1.35:1 post - SOTTO
implementation, indicating a paradigm shift towards cadaver transplants.2
• Public sector hospitals in Gujarat lead in organ retrieval (47%) and cadaveric transplants
(65%). Over the last five years, 1,290 organs from 464 donors were received by those in
need.3
Social Impact
SOTTO ensures access to state-of-the-art lifesaving transplant services for marginalised
populations, with a two-fold increase in cadaver kidney transplants in women and children.
Affirmative discretion provides additional points to children and women, prioritising vulnerable
groups for needed services.
Economic Impact
The otherwise expensive treatment becomes affordable or free for the needy through various
schemes and funding mechanisms. Over 1,428 transplants worth over Rs. 8 Crore were conducted
iii PMJAY-MA: Pradhan Mantri Jan Aarogya Yojana - Mukhyamantri Amrutum

SOTTO - TRANSFORMING LIVES THROUGH ORGAN TRANSPLANTATION IN
GUJARAT

6

under the PMJAY-MA scheme4. Additionally, over 250 paediatric transplants5 were carried out
free of charge under the RBSK-School Health scheme. Grants, relief funds and CSR further
support and aid transplant costs.
Conclusion
In the remarkable journey of SOTTO, organ transplantation in Gujarat has transcended mere
medical procedures to become a symbol of hope and renewal. Through its unwavering
commitment to saving lives while upholding ethical standards, SOTTO embodies the ethos of
giving the ultimate gift—the gift of life.
With its dedication towards transparency and sustainability, SOTTO has not only enhanced the
availability and accessibility of state-of-the-art care but has also championed the cause of the
marginalised, ensuring that no life is left behind. The recognition bestowed upon SOTTO with
the PM’s Excellence in Innovation Award in 2023 (Refer Exhibit 4) underscores its remarkable
contribution and innovative approaches in the field of organ transplantation, heralding a future
where every life holds the promise of renewal and vitality.
Way Forward
Moving forward, SOTTO can collaborate with NOTTO and other state organ transplantation
organisations to scale its model nationally, sharing best practices, advocating for policy reforms,
and establishing standardised protocols. Leveraging its expertise, SOTTO can shape a cohesive
national framework for organ transplantation, saving countless lives across India.
SOTTO in Gujarat should also focus on sustained advocacy efforts to raise awareness about organ
donation, expand transplantation infrastructure to reach underserved areas, invest in continuous
training programs for healthcare professionals and integrate technology into administrative
processes to ensure equitable distribution and transparency.
Moreover, fostering a culture of research and innovation, along with international collaboration,
will further enhance transplant outcomes and contribute to saving more lives while upholding
ethical standards, ultimately advancing the field of organ transplantation in Gujarat and beyond.

Case Study Title:
Andhra Pradesh Pioneers Energy Demand
Forecasting Using Artificial Intelligence/Machine
Learning Techniques
Case Study Description: The case revolves around Andhra Pradesh Transmission Corporation (APTransco) efforts to advance India's electricity grid management with the introduction of the country's inaugural AI-driven day-ahead electricity forecasting model. This innovation predicts electricity consumption and demand in precise 15-minute intervals, thus optimises grid operations, minimising costs, and extends its forecasting capabilities to include wind, solar energy, and market prices. With an aim to establish a low-cost dispatch model for electricity generation, APTransco underlines its commitment to efficient grid management.
Case Text:
Dr. Srikant Nagulapalli,1 as the Secretary for Energy in the Government of Andhra Pradesh (AP), recalled
his thoughts from 2020 when he spearheaded the Energy Demand Forecasting initiative at the Andhra
Pradesh State Load Despatch Centre (APSLDC). For the first time in India, artificial intelligence and
machine learning were used to forecast the next day's electricity consumption, which led to efficient power
management and reduced the power purchase cost for the state.

ii The mission demonstrated the potential
for capability building within the public sector by using available resources, effective leadership and
without the need for extravagant investments.
Electricity Generation in India
In India, utilities, especially electricity, are mostly managed by the state and central governments, with
limited private participation. Although most of the power generation and transmission is undertaken by
public sector undertakings, the last-mile distribution, in most states, is the responsibility of the state
government. The state electricity distribution companies (discoms) distribute power from the transmission
network to ensure power availability for domestic, business, and industrial consumption. In case of any
shortfall in electricity production, discoms purchase power from producers in the open market.
While power supply is prone to fluctuations due to uncertainties in production conditions, especially for
wind and solar energy, the demand for power also fluctuates from day to day due to factors such as the
time of day, temperature and weather patterns, even festivals, days of the week, etc. To successfully meet
customers' power demand and plan its power purchases more prudently, the State Load Despatch Centre
(SLDC), as the grid operator responsible for the supervision, monitoring, and control of the integrated
1 Srikant Nagulapalli, a 1998-batch IAS officer from the Andhra Pradesh cadre, is currently the Additional
Secretary, Ministry of Power. As a seasoned administrator in the domain of power and energy, he has held
key positions in state and central governments.

ANDHRA PRADESH PIONEERS ENERGY DEMAND FORECASTING USING ARTIFICIAL
INTELLIGENCE/MACHINE LEARNING TECHNIQUES

2

power system in a state, needs to be able to make accurate energy forecasts for the distributing companies
(discoms). Reliable predictions of short-term energy demand and changes in power generation factors can
be beneficial to ensure efficient operations and save costs.2
Energy Demand Forecasting
Typically, power demand estimates are provided for a grid on a day-ahead basis. Consequently, the
generating plants required to meet this demand are scheduled for the next day. These plants operate within
specified upper and lower bounds, determined by the technical capabilities of each plant. The grid operator
or the SLDC adjusts the generation from different power plants to align with real-time demand, much like
a vehicle driver controls the speed of his car to match traffic flow. This proactive management prevents
overloading the grid or falling short of meeting demand, thereby preventing power outages. However, this
system of matching supply with demand involves costs and needs to be reliable.
The Naïve Model
Traditionally, all Indian states have sought to forecast their daily electricity demand hour by hour, typically
prepared a day in advance. This simplistic model, known as the naïve model, entails using the previous
day's demand as the forecast for the following day. Use of this method, however, often results in a
significant mismatch between the projected demand for power and actual daily consumption. These
inaccuracies posed operational challenges, including blackouts, until Andhra Pradesh developed a new
model of energy demand forecasting.
AP State Load Despatch Centre
The Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation (APGENCO) is engaged in the business of power
generation, while transmission and distribution come under APTRANSCO and its three distribution
companies—Andhra Pradesh Southern Power Distribution Company (APSPDC), AP Central Power
Distribution Company, and AP Eastern Power Distribution Company that supply electricity to the state’s
domestic, agricultural, industrial, and commercial sectors to meet the increasing power demand (Refer
Exhibit 1).
The Andhra Pradesh State Load Despatch Centre (APSLDC) was established in 2014iii under APTRANSCO
to operate the power grid when AP’s north-western area separated as the newly formed state of Telangana.
The APSLDC became responsible for optimum scheduling and dispatch of electricity within the state, in
accordance with contracts with generating companies.
Renewable vs Conventional Power
In accordance with the demand, power must be optimally sourced from different power generation projects
within the state, be it thermal, hydro, electric, solar, wind, or nuclear. Power can be sourced from the open
market too. However, the total power supply in Andhra Pradesh includes a sizeable share of energy
derived from renewable energy sources, which must be consumed on priority as the state purchases all the
available contracted renewable energy. Any deficit is fulfilled by conventional power stations.

Renewable energy accounts for approximately 40-50% of the installed energy capacity in the state, while
contributing around 25% to the total power consumption. Managing renewable energy production,
however, presents complexities due to limited control over natural weather fluctuations, while maintaining
and operating conventional power generation units incurs high costs.
Simultaneously, there is ample availability of power in the market at more affordable rates. The APSLDC
therefore identified a strategic opportunity to reduce production from the more expensive conventional
thermal power units and procure energy from the market, which led to significant cost savings. This
strategy became more expedient as power distribution companies were facing severe financial constraints
at the time.
Uncertain Demand and Supply
In Andhra Pradesh, renewable energy sources such as wind and solar energy contribute significantly to
the total energy supply. On the supply side, while generation of wind energy exhibits seasonal fluctuations,
typically increasing from June onwards with the onset of monsoons, day-to-day variations are also
common, occasionally resulting in significantly lower-than-expected power production when forecasted
strong winds fail to materialise.
On the demand side, the occurrence of significant fluctuations is mostly correlated with the time and day
of the week. For instance, Sunday's demand differs from Saturday’s. Holiday demand patterns also vary
widely. Extraordinary circumstances like COVID-19 lockdowns also influenced demand patterns.
Consequently, simplistic assumptions under the naïve model proved inadequate.
Uncertainties in renewable power generation compounded the demand-supply imbalance and caused
fluctuations in cost as rates are contingent on specific procurement contracts. The cost of renewable energy
generation, however, has demonstrated a significant downward trajectory over time, even though initial
costs were higher. In this situation, energy demand forecasting was a boon.
Effective Leadership
Dr. Srikant Nagulapalli headed the power sector in the state of Andhra Pradesh. Trained as a mechanical
engineer, he furthered his expertise with a master’s degree in industrial engineering and then a Ph.D. in
economics. His curiosity led him to explore the frontiers of technology through diverse online platforms,
including free courses from various universities and academic YouTube videos. He also encouraged his
team to learn and continually update their skill sets.
He actively sought opportunities to apply the latest advancements in technology to solve real-world
challenges. His exploration of state-of-the-art forecasting techniques, like the bicycle-sharing application
successfully implemented in Australia, led him to discover the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and
machine learning (ML) models to reliably estimate energy demand. He was confident that the technical
talent available in the state’s power sector was capable of implementing and scaling complex energy
solutions within the state.
Solving the Uncertainty Puzzle
Dr. Srikant understood that an advanced demand forecasting system could enable the APSLDC to
efficiently manage the power plants as well as the grid and enhance its service delivery.

The APSLDC implemented AI and ML-based demand forecasting for the next day’s grid supply or
distribution. With demand estimates generated for every 15-minute time window, the solution provided
four power demand estimates within each hour, resulting in a total of 96 power demand estimates for the
following day.
This in-house initiative by APSLDC resulted in the development of a sophisticated model capable of
predicting the required electricity generation and dispatch. Leveraging this predictive capability, APSLDC
could balance the operation of generating stations, primarily coal-fired and those operating at different
variable costs, with the procurement of power from external sources. This optimisation served to minimise
the overall cost of energy procurement while ensuring seamless grid operation.
The Solution
APSLDC’s energy demand forecasting model using AI and ML was developed to fulfil the following
objectives:
i) To mitigate demand variability and achieve precise predictions. Uncertainties in estimating wind
and solar power production from the supply side also had to be resolved.
ii) To capitalise on cost-saving opportunities through short-notice market purchases of electricity,
which would reduce intake from high-cost contracts for thermal power generation.
In this decision-making process, fixed costs like plant and equipment, financing, project management, and
grid connection, for instance, were considered sunk costs, meaning the expenses already incurred would
not influence the choice between energy production and purchase. Instead, the focus was on comparing
the variable cost of production with the market cost, which meant if the variable cost of production
exceeded the market cost, it would be economically prudent to reduce power generation from coal-fired
power plants and purchase from the open market.
Implementation Challenges
There were multiple stumbling blocks in implementing this solution, be it assembling an expert team
trained in AI and ML procedures or even the development process, including data sourcing, data gathering,
and management, besides establishing a robust computing infrastructure with the required hardware and
software for AI development.
The Team: Strategic Staffing
The APSLDC’s initial task was to set up a team with the technical capability as well as expert knowledge
on the AI and ML fronts. A blend of domain expertise and proficiency in cutting-edge AI and ML
methodologies is a rare combination to find in a single individual. Typically, domain experts with
experience spanning 25-30 year lack the bandwidth to stay updated with the latest advancements in rapidly
evolving fields like AI and ML. APSLDC adopted an innovative method to staff the team.
• In-house domain expertise was tapped by two senior engineers each with over 25 years of
experience.
• The core team was supplemented by a group of 7-8 recently recruited bright engineers, to inject
fresh perspectives and enthusiasm.
• The APSLDC additionally enlisted the services of two external experts, specialising in statistics,
artificial intelligence, and machine learning, on a contractual basis.
