This strategic staffing approach ensured a balanced blend of seasoned expertise and contemporary
knowledge to facilitate effective problem-solving and innovation within the team.
The Day-ahead Energy Demand Forecasting Model
Following a typical AI/ML project lifecycle (Refer Exhibit 2), the development process was iterative and
interactive, characterised by trial-and-error experiments to refine the model parameters. The initial phase
focused on the selection of the variables, which are essential for forecasting. This crucial step unfolded
through multiple brainstorming sessions, with seasoned employees leveraging their extensive 25+ years’
experience with APSLDC to make a significant contribution to identifying the model variables.
The first goal was to comprehensively define the factors influencing the following day’s demand. Through
collaborative efforts, the team identified an extensive range of key factors contributing to energy demand,
including the weather forecast, temperature data from across the state, and essentially 74 relevant locations
that correlated with high energy demand. Typically, temperature from a forest area would not apply to the
model; rainfall measurements from 272 carefully chosen locations; humidity, cloud cover, etc.; seasons:
summer, winter, monsoon; cyclone and hurricane warnings; agricultural seasons like kharif and rabi,
which determine the energy demand from the agricultural sector; lift irrigation; sunset and sunrise timings;
and any situation expected to impact energy demand, like the COVID-19 lockdown, and release periods
with four parameters specific to COVID-19.
Variable selection and its inclusion in the model were influenced by the availability of data. Thus, for a
variable to be considered relevant, it should be available in historical data and next-day predictions. The
team continually refined the model by considering new factors and approaches for increased accuracy. The
addition of a new factor impacted the model's accuracy. Multiple models with diverse model parameters
were developed and deployed in this iterative process. If a model's performance in terms of accuracy in
energy demand prediction was high, it was deployed and operated for a while, typically a month or two,
before being replaced by a better model. The team was continually enhancing the forecasting models to
obtain better performance.
Open-Source Software
The APSLDC team initially used Facebook’s Prophet, an open-source library, to create quick,
accurate time series forecasts. Subsequently, however, they switched to the open-source package “Keras”,
more suited to a deep learning model, which presented another challenge—the development of an
appropriate architecture. The team tested multiple hyperparameters, including the number of layers,
neurons per layer, the activation function, etc. They eventually observed that increasing the number of
layers or neurons per layer did not significantly improve performance beyond a particular point. The
results were promising in terms of accuracy. The Mean Average Percentage Error (MAPE) of the AI model
was less than 2%, compared with less than 3% for ML and 4% for the naïve model. (See Exhibit 3).
However, the deep learning model presented a "black box" approach to machine learning, which provides
a result without explanation of the internal processes, or the weighted variables used. Without process
transparency, the team could not figure out how the model obtained the specific results.
Sourcing Data for the Model
Deep Learning Models typically require large amounts of data. Sourcing and making data available at the
right time can be challenging, especially when multiple state government agencies are responsible for the
data collection. For instance, the model uses weather data as an input, which is sourced from multiple
departments, including the AP Space Applications Centre (APSAC) and Disaster Management

INTELLIGENCE/MACHINE LEARNING TECHNIQUES

6

Department. Securing the necessary permissions and access privileges from government departments can
be challenging. However, most of the necessary data inputs were readily available within the state.
Consequently, obtaining the requisite permissions proved to be a relatively straightforward process. The
only remaining challenge was to link the servers of these departments with the forecasting system in SLDC.
This task was accomplished by means of an application programming interface (API) system, which was
developed to routinely source the forecasting data. The development and testing of the API interfaces
required one month for completion.
Initial Results
The deployment of the deep learning model yielded encouraging results. The model provided the team
with forecasts for the next day's energy demand. With these projections, the team could accurately estimate
the cost of generating one unit of energy from their power plants. Based on the predicted demand and their
available capacity, the discoms could bid for specific quantities of power from the open market. If the open
market cost was less than the per-unit variable cost of production in their plants, the team preferred to
purchase power from the market. This led to significant savings of about ₹ 3 crore/day and between ₹ 300
and ₹ 400 crore during the period in which this model was deployed. iv The savings on some days were as
high as ₹ 8 crore/day. Compared with the expenses incurred on this project—the hiring of 2 experts from
the market—the savings represented a significant benefit.
Major Benefits
The transition from the naïve model to a sophisticated forecast model, which uses artificial intelligence and
provides predictions every 15 minutes, was transformative. This advanced approach facilitated a seamless
balance in power procurement between internal sources and the market. When the forecast was right, but
demand was slightly higher, discoms could buy more power from the market at competitive rates without
either exceeding the budget or overloading the internal power plants. This experience underscored the
efficacy of procuring electricity at more economical rates, thereby optimising operating costs.
The shift towards a more scientific approach to generation and procurement also marked a significant leap
from previous reliance on daily perceptions or naïve estimates. Forecasts, particularly beneficial during
holidays and periods of peak demand, served to enhance operational efficiency. The improved demand
estimation methodology introduced a greater level of scientific rigour into public policy management,
thereby mitigating reliance on individual discretion. This initiative instilled confidence in the energy sector,
dispelling the notion of haphazard management of demand fluctuations and bolstering perceptions of
managerial competence. Ultimately, it served as a compelling argument for the digitalisation of public
policy and the adoption of modern techniques like AI across various sectors, resonating with stakeholders
across the board.
The Way Ahead
The Andhra Pradesh Energy Department is working on two more innovative tools for optimal resource
mobilization. The development and implementation of the Intra-state Open Access Settlement project using
various computer programming languages enables the purchase of wind and solar power from different
consumers when the pricing is not uniform. It has served to lower the complexity and time required for
purchase, besides reducing the expenditure incurred. The other tool, which is under development and
being fine-tuned for use, will enable solutions in cases of surplus and deficit production.v The success of
the energy forecasting project has also elicited inquiries from other states seeking to replicate the model.

the integration of AI into real-time public policy management without an extravagant investment. This

Case Study Title:
Vehicle Tracking to Ensure Cradle to Grave
Disposal of Hazardous Waste in Gujarat
Case Study Description: The Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) launched an innovative Vehicle Location Tracking System (VLTS) developed in collaboration with NIC Gujarat and NIC Uttarakhand to enhance the monitoring and management of hazardous waste transportation. This project aims to ensure the safe and compliant movement of hazardous materials by leveraging advanced GPS technology, real-time tracking, and robust data analytics. By implementing the VLTS, GPCB seeks to mitigate environmental risks, improve regulatory oversight and promote sustainable waste management practices across the state. This case study delves into the technical aspects, implementation challenges and anticipated benefits of this groundbreaking initiative, underscoring its potential to set new standards in environmental regulation.
Case Text:
The Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) launched an innovative Vehicle Location Tracking System
(VLTS) developed in collaboration with NIC Gujarat and NIC Uttarakhand (See Exhibit 1) to enhance the
monitoring and management of hazardous waste transportation. This project aims to ensure the safe and
compliant movement of hazardous materials by leveraging advanced GPS technology, real-time tracking,
and robust data analytics. By implementing the VLTS, GPCB seeks to mitigate environmental risks,
improve regulatory oversight and promote sustainable waste management practices across the state. This
case study delves into the technical aspects, implementation challenges and anticipated benefits of this
groundbreaking initiative, underscoring its potential to set new standards in environmental regulation.
On June 5, 2022, also World Environment Day, the GPCB became the first state pollution control board in
India and possibly the world, to launch the Vehicle Location Tracking System (VLTS) to track the
transportation of hazardous waste from industrial sites to the waste management facility for its safe
disposal. The VLTS is a comprehensive web-based application that facilitates real time tracking of these
vehicles, which has served to curb environmental pollution and ensured the cradle to grave disposal of
hazardous waste. Additionally, the platform has yielded a ready inventory of hazardous wastes, which has
enabled GPCB to facilitate the recycling or reuse of hazardous waste for greater environmental protection.
An Idea Evolves
‘In January 2022, a tanker illegally discharged chemical waste into a drain. Toxic fumes emanating from the drain
led to the death of six persons working at a factory premises nearby.’
1

The GPCB had to ensure the environmentally safe disposal of hazardous waste from industries including
chemicals, dyes, and pesticides—from the generator to the end user—which was a critical challenge despite
the imposition and implementation of the Hazardous & Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary
Movement) Rules, 2016, which provide for the safe transportation of hazardous waste across the nation.
Gujarat, as an industrialised state and the nation’s industrial hub with more than 40,000 industries, has the
largest number of hazardous waste generating industries in India.2 Naturally, hazardous waste generation
is huge. In 2022, Gujarat generated over 4.2 million metric tons of hazardous waste,3 which has today
increased to 5 million metric tonnes annually, according to the GPCB.
As the regulator, it was therefore important for the GPCB, to be able to monitor the movement of hazardous
waste to ensure that the vehicles transporting this waste reach the safe disposal or reuse destination along
a pre-defined route. As Mr R.B. Barad, Chairman, GPCB states: ‘With the implementation of the Vehicle

VEHICLE TRACKING TO ENSURE CRADLE TO GRAVE DISPOSAL OF
HAZARDOUS WASTE IN GUJARAT

2

Location Tracking System, the Gujarat Pollution Control Board is taking a significant step forward in
ensuring the safe transportation of hazardous waste. This will not only enhance our monitoring capabilities
but also reinforce our commitment to environmental protection and public health. We are dedicated to
setting new standards in waste management and fostering a sustainable future for Gujarat.’
Waste Management
Under the Hazardous & Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016,
hazardous waste needs to be treated, stored or disposed in an environmentally sound manner. Treatment
facilities use various processes like incineration and oxidation to alter the character or composition of the
hazardous waste before its disposal. Or even use processes to dramatically reduce the amount of hazardous
waste. Storage facilities temporarily hold hazardous wastes until they are treated or disposed. Disposal
facilities for hazardous wastes use carefully constructed units to protect ground water and surface water
resources.4
The state of Gujarat provides industries common environmental infrastructure including Treatment,
Storage and Disposal Facilities (TSDF) as well as common incinerators. (See Exhibit 2). The industries or
generators of hazardous waste hold the responsibility to transport the waste to the TSDF sites or to the
common incinerators for safe disposal under the regulatory eye of the pollution control board. However,
the process to register each transportation of hazardous waste was being manually managed and therefore
complicated.
A Convoluted Process
The hazardous waste rules provide for a manifest system, which is actually a movement document
designed to track hazardous waste from the generator unit through its transportation to the final waste
management facility to ensure that hazardous waste reaches its destination. The erstwhile manual manifest
or Form 10—a document—contained details about the sender, the transporter and the receiver of waste in
addition to information about the nature and quantum of waste being transported. The generator or sender
of hazardous waste prepared and signed the manifest and its copies. No transporter could accept waste
from the sender unless it was accompanied by Form 10 and its seven colour coded copies meant for the
sender, transporter, receiver and the regulator. (See Exhibit 3).
• The transporter accepted the signed copies from the generator
• The transporter then submitted to the receiver, the relevant copies of the manifest for
acknowledgement along with the consignment of hazardous waste
• The transporter then returned three copies of the manifest to the generator after acknowledgement
• Both the generator and the receiver of hazardous waste then sent an acknowledged copy of the
manifest to the regulator for manual reconciliation
This was a cumbersome manual process while reconciliation was a herculean task for the GPCB,
considering that nearly 700 manifests are generated each day. End of the year reconciliations were almost
impossible. Manifests were required to be kept on file for three years. A workable solution had to be found
urgently.
Birthing an Online System
The GPCB put on its thinking cap and implemented a re-engineered manifest followed by a GPS-powered
VLTS system to ensure the environmentally safe and better management of e-waste and hazardous waste
in the state. To do this, it used its existing e-governance platform called Extended Green Node (XGN),
which was already operational and used in the day-to-day working of the GPCB, including issue of online
environmental permits or licenses to set up an industrial unit or even expansion of a unit. (See Exhibit 4).

HAZARDOUS WASTE IN GUJARAT

3

The XGN, developed by the National Informatics Centre (NIC), Gujarat had been operational in the state
since 2008. Piggybacking on this system, the GPCB introduced an e-manifest system which would
transform the manual system of Form 10 with its seven colour coded copies.
E-manifest for E-governance
To participate in the e-manifest system to transport hazardous waste, each industrial unit is required to
register with the GPCB. Even the vehicles to be used for transportation, usually provided by a private
transporter, are required to be registered with the GPCB. As a registered user, an industrial unit can access
Form 10 online and provide the requisite details, including a self-declaration professing responsibility for
the safe delivery of the consignment, in addition to sender and receiver details, the nature and quantum of
hazardous waste to be transported, besides details of the registered vehicle which will transport the waste.
Most of the details are auto fetched from data stored in the system during registration. Even the description
of hazardous waste may be selected from options provided under a drop-down menu, which provides a
choice of different types of hazardous wastes under the prescribed Schedules I and II, under the Hazardous
& Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules. There are more than 35 categories
under Schedule I and sub-categories too, which are already defined in the system and the sender simply
has to choose the right menu option. This means there is minimal manual input which limits the scope for
errors. Online instruction manuals on how to generate an online manifest are also available online, in
addition to human assistance through helpline numbers.
Prior Consent

Besides the ease of doing business through an e-manifest, the GPCB also wanted to introduce a simple, self-
monitoring tool for industries on its e-governance platform. A new element was therefore added into the

system to make even the receiver of the waste more responsible. ‘We embedded into our online system, the
principle of prior information consent (PIC), which is an international tenet in the movement of hazardous
waste,’ Mr Thaker informed. This means that a manifest for transportation can be generated only when the
sender has obtained an in-principle online approval from the designated receiver of the hazardous waste
Once the recipient unit has given its prior information consent or in-principal approval for accepting the
hazardous waste—for treatment, storage, reuse, disposal or incineration, only then the sender is able to
generate a uniquely numbered manifest for transport. This element of prior information consent provides
a self-monitoring tool to industry and serves to make both the generator and the recipient responsible
throughout the transportation of the waste. This was the first step towards implementation of the VLTS
system. As the system was online, the manifest was generated online, and even the vehicle was registered
with the GPCB and transportation details were logged into the system. It was now possible for industry to
self-monitor the transportation routes to ensure that the hazardous waste reached its destination.
VLTS Tracks Transport Trucks
The GPCB pioneered the development of the Vehicle Location Tracking System (VLTS) to monitor the route
of the vehicle transporting the hazardous waste. (See Exhibit 5) This technological intervention ensured
that these vehicles would follow the route pre-decided at the time of manifest generation, from source to
the waste disposal destination. Any deviation from the route logged into the system would sound a system
alert which could be investigated by the industrial unit and the GPCB.
To enable the implementation of the VLTS, the GPCB mandated all the industrial units registered with the
Board to ensure the installation of the AIS 140 Global Positioning System in all the vehicles being used for
the transportation of hazardous waste. The AIS 140 is a GPS protocol adopted and standardised by the
Ministry of Road Transport for the transportation industry in India. The e-manifest portal was then

HAZARDOUS WASTE IN GUJARAT

4

integrated with the Vehicle Location Tracking System. Depending on the disposal destination, travel routes
from source to destination are logged into the system. The GPCB has also set up a command-and-control
room with two personnel to monitor the vehicles and any alerts about route deviations in real time. The
Board also enabled the sender and recipient of the hazardous waste, to track the vehicles from source to
destination in real time.
There are more than 12,000 vehicles registered on the VLTS platform. About 600 trips are noted daily, while
the total number of vehicles carrying hazardous waste which are being tracked and monitored in real time,
number between 1300 and 1400 vehicles at any given moment, considering an average trip length of 1.5
days.
Technology Development
The GPCB partnered with the National Informatics Centre (NIC), Gujarat, to develop the VLTS module, a
system, the likes of which had never been attempted in the country’s regulatory domain. The NIC, Gujarat
associated with a team from NIC, Uttarakhand, which had some experience in GPS and vehicle monitoring.
The NIC teams developed the VLTS as a web-based application for real time tracking of vehicles
transporting the hazardous waste from industrial sites to the waste management facility. The application

provides a dashboard through which the GPCB Control Unit can monitor any deviations from the pre-
determined route and ensure that the waste reaches its designated facility. (See Exhibit 6).

VLTS Features5
• Integrated with GPCB’s XGN portal for creation of e-manifests online
• Purchase of software licenses and Google Map Service by GPCB
• Data hosted on servers of Gujarat State Data Centre

• The entire journey is recorded and specific trip history can be replayed

Funding the VLTS Project
For the GPCB, the implementation of the VLTS was largely completed in-house, in partnership with NIC,

Gujarat and Uttarakhand. As it is being managed in-house, the GPCB has not worked out the micro-
detailing of the costs. However, there were largely three components to it. Costs were incurred towards

supporting manpower expenses for NIC during development of the software, in addition to purchase of
software licenses and the Google Map Service. The GPCB regards these expenses as minimal costs relative
to achieving compliance with pollution prevention regulations and environmental protection standards.
The GPCB has also not imposed any fees for registration of hazardous waste generating industrial units or
the vehicle tracking facility, as it first wants to make the system inclusive and bring all hazardous waste
