HAZARDOUS WASTE IN GUJARAT

5

producing industrial units under its ambit for compliance. This may change however, when the system is
stabilised and strengthened. ‘Even if we do charge industrial units in the future, it would be based on
manifest generation,’ Mr Thaker commented.
Key Impacts
With the implementation of the VLTS, the GPCB has successfully developed a perfect closed-loop system
to monitor the cradle to grave transport of hazardous waste to the designated disposal site for environment
safety. Additionally, it has introduced e-governance for industrial units and enabled them to self-monitor,
thereby introducing transparency and accountability into the system. For the GPCB, the online generation
of manifests eases record-keeping and there is no need to manage multiple copies of Form 10.
However, an unforeseen benefit of online manifest generation has been the preparation of a detailed
inventory of hazardous waste, which has facilitated the recycling and reuse of this waste, while also
reducing the amount of waste sent for treatment, storage, or incineration.
Co-processing: Waste to Wealth
Under the able state leadership, the concept of co-processing was initiated by Mr Hardik Shah, IAS, former
Member Secretary of the Board. Gujarat became the torch bearer for this concept which later on proliferated
in other states. Taking his efforts forward, with the VLTS and the online manifest system, the database of
hazardous waste products has become very robust.
As Mr Thaker states, ‘In our parlance, waste is nothing but a resource in the wrong place. What is waste
for one industry, could be a resource or raw material for another. I now know through my inventory, which
industry generates what waste and which industry utilises this waste. So GPCB has become a facilitator
between industries and promotes co-processing or use of waste as a resource, for environmentally sound
management of hazardous waste within the state and out of Gujarat too.’
Inorganic waste, for instance, is commonly sent for disposal to the Treatment, Storage, Disposal Facility
(TSDF) while waste with high calorific values is disposed through incineration. Having observed this,
GPCB came up with an out-of-the-box idea. It considered that a stage in cement production involves
burning of raw materials in a high-temperature kiln and then grinding the burned product known as
‘clinker’ with gypsum. GPCB thus emerged with a novel proposal to use industrial wastes such as crushed
concrete or lignite fly ash or paper ash as raw material for clinker production and high calorific waste such
as tyres or paint sludge as an alternative fuel in the cement industry.
GPCB made available to the cement companies a waste characterisation report to identify suitable waste
for co-processing. The Board also facilitated a series of B2B meetings between cement plants, waste
generators and other stakeholders like major industry associations etc in its own offices and convinced
them to adopt co-processing. (See Exhibit 7). The message was clear: Conventional disposal methods

induce an unnecessary demand on natural resources and land requirement. Diverting waste for co-
processing provides a solution for reducing fossil fuel dependency and contributes towards lowering

atmospheric emissions. This concept eventually became popular and has also been replicated in other
Indian States. GPCB has also permitted registration of industrial units in the neighbouring states to enable
transportation to out-of-state co-processing facilities.
Pre-processing for Co-processing
GPCB further strived to reduce the quantum of waste disposal by taking co-processing one step back to
pre-processing, which enables the conversion of a wide variety of waste into a homogeneous mix to make
it suitable for co-processing as a raw material or alternative fuel in cement kilns. ‘It is a pre-step of co-

VEHICLE TRACKING TO ENSURE CRADLE TO GRAVE DISPOSAL OF
HAZARDOUS WASTE IN GUJARAT

6

processing where various wastes are collected and blended in a quality that is required for co-processing,’
Mr Thaker explains. For instance, TDI tar, a waste product from the agrochemical industry, that is normally
sent to the incinerator, is now co-processed and channelised to the cement industry to be used as an
alternative fuel. For the cement industry, the advantage is reduction in the use of fossil fuel. For the industry
that used to pay for disposal, is now getting paid for its waste. ‘It is a win-win situation, environmentally
benign, economically advantageous and leads to reduction in pollution,’ Mr Thaker states.
Less Waste for Disposal
One of the biggest advantages of the VLTS and e-manifest platform has been the reduction in the quantum
of waste through its diversion into pre-processing and co-processing. The GPCB has become a bridge
between the generator of hazardous waste—who does not know where its waste could be reused—and the
recipient of this waste—who doesn’t know where the waste is being generated—as it seeks to increasingly
recycle and reuse hazardous waste in an environmentally sound manner as an alternative to its disposal.
Consequently, about 40,000 hazardous waste producing industrial units registered with the GPCB in
Gujarat produce 50 lakh metric tonnes of hazardous waste per annum. Of this waste, about 25% goes to
TSDF while 50% is recycled. Formerly, waste meant for incineration, which constituted between 5% and
10% of the total waste, has now been reduced to less than 1% due to the GPCB’s continual efforts to move
waste from incinerations to co-processing. About 20% of the waste is being co-processed.
Waste-Exchange
The GPCB’s promotion of co-processing has extended to neighbouring states too. Consequently, industries
generating hazardous waste in Gujarat are sending their waste to cement companies in other states,
including Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and even Tamil Nadu. Already, about 40 out-of-state
cement and other actual user and recycling industries have registered on the VLTS platform.

Challenges
The VLTS is a first of its kind system to have been developed by any regulatory body in India and possibly

in the world. It was challenging to build as there was no precedence available, which made it a time-
consuming process.

Brick by brick approach
Any transformation from a manual system to e-governance is always challenging. The VLTS platform was
built module by module with some trial and error. It was deliberately kept simple so it would not be a
deterrent for industry. Small video clips of how the system would work were made to encourage industry
to feel comfortable enough to adopt the system.
A series of seminars and awareness programmes were conducted in every region, in each of the 27 districts,
to familiarise industry with the VLTS system, which promised ease of use and a user-friendly interface. It
was emphasised that what they were doing manually could now be done on a computer screen. Helpline
numbers were generated and the team swiftly resolved emerging queries. Significant challenges included
persuading the industry to overcome resistance and shift its mindset. Changes and improvements
demanded by industry were also implemented. ‘It was a process of continual learning and we are still
learning,’ Mr Thaker comments.

VEHICLE TRACKING TO ENSURE CRADLE TO GRAVE DISPOSAL OF
HAZARDOUS WASTE IN GUJARAT

7

Convincing Transporters
Another obstacle was to convince the transporters, mostly in the unorganised sector to register their
vehicles with the GPCB and install the AIS 140 device on its vehicles. However, transporters followed when
the GPCB made registrations mandatory. Industry could only use registered vehicles failing which it was
deemed illegal transportation.
Illegal Dumping
A measure of success of the VLTS platform is industry’s willingness to register on the GPCB. Most
industrial units in Gujarat have stepped onto the VLTS e-governance platform. However, despite having
made the registration of industrial units producing and transporting hazardous waste, mandatory in
Gujarat, the primary challenge before the GPCB is to bring small-scale industrial units into its fold. ‘The
VLTS is a preventive tool and provides a platform for the right-doers. The black sheep who won’t use my
system until they are caught, may still be resorting to illegal dumping of hazardous waste,’ says Mr Thaker.
However, the VLTS is a good monitoring and audit tool and it’s only a matter of time before the small-scale
waste generators are also brought into the fray and illegal transportation of hazardous waste can be
controlled.
The Way Forward
The GPCB seeks to first strengthen the platform. It also seeks to use it to effectively address any violations
by applying smart analysis to the various alerts generated by the VLTS. The system has already assisted
GPCB regional officers in co-ordination with the police department to trap many illegal movements of
hazardous waste in Gujarat. In case of a grievous violation, there is a penalty mechanism and the
registration of the offending vehicle may be cancelled.. The GPCB may also consider embedding a guardian
officer for the waste generating industry with responsibility for monitoring and overseeing the safe
transportation of waste to the designated facility.
Linkages
The GPCB is exploring linkages with other government agencies like the Regional Transport Offices (RTO),
state government facilities etc. for greater impact including identification of vulnerable hotspots on the
map to spot illegal movement of hazardous waste and integration with tools using artificial intelligence.
It is also exploring possibilities to expand the use of the platform in the future to transportation of
hazardous chemicals or even green credits through optimization of set trips. This will help industry to have
alternate routes and arrangements for sustainable hazardous waste management.
Replicability
The VLTS platform has a high potential for being replicated across the nation. Meanwhile, the pollution
control boards in states like Maharashtra and Karnataka have sent inquiries to adopt the VLTS platform,
which is under progress.
In May 2023, the GPCB’s VLTS platform won the SKOCH GOLD award under the environment category,
which was shared with NIC, Gujarat and Uttarakhand.

Case Study Title:
Socio- and Techno-Economic Upliftment of Tribal
Population with Bioresource-Based Entrepreneurship:
A Case Study from Arunachal Pradesh
Case Study Description: Dr. Debajit Mahanta and his team, aimed at uplifting the socio-economic status of the tribal population through bioresource-based entrepreneurship. Leveraging the state's rich biodiversity, the CoE, supported by various national and international institutions, focuses on research, innovation, and capacity building to create sustainable livelihoods and promote economic growth. It addresses challenges like unemployment and limited market access, striving to preserve cultural identity while adapting to modern advancements. The initiative exemplifies a holistic approach to biodiversity conservation, sustainable development, and techno-economic empowerment, aspiring to serve as a model for the entire Northeast region of the country.
Case Text:
Arunachal Pradesh, known for its rich cultural diversity, is home to a significant tribal population (see Exhibit 1), comprising numerous indigenous communities with distinct languages, customs, and traditions. The tribal population in Arunachal Pradesh predominantly relies on agriculture, horticulture, animal husbandry, and forestry for their livelihood.1 These livelihood activities also form the backbone of the state’s economy. Traditional farming practices, including shifting cultivation (jhum cultivation), are common among the tribal communities.2 Land ownership and access to natural resources are crucial aspects of tribal life in Arunachal Pradesh. Despite their rich cultural heritage, tribal communities in the state face various challenges, including limited access to education, healthcare, infrastructure, and market opportunities. Preserving their cultural identity while adapting to modern changes poses a constant challenge. While agriculture remains a key sector providing livelihoods for a significant portion of the population in Arunachal Pradesh, efforts are being made to diversify the economy, create sustainable employment opportunities, and address the unique challenges faced by the state in terms of its employment scenario.3

Northeast India comprises two (the Indo-Burma and the Himalayas) of the four biodiversity hotspots in India.4 It is abundant with rich endemic flora, fauna, and microbes. This region is home to 51 forest types, 5,000 flowering plants, 800 endangered floral species, numerous medicinal plants, and countless species of fauna5 making it the perfect cradle for bioresource-based development solutions. Arunachal Pradesh contains 40% of the floral and faunal species of India. Orchids form a dominant group of plants with their attractive and unique blooms. There are more than 600 species of orchids, 52 species of rhododendron, 18 species of Hedychium, 16 species of oak, 18 species of canes, and 45 species of bamboo in addition to many medicinal and aromatic plants.6 About one-third of the 105 species of Indian bamboo are found in Arunachal Pradesh


Bioresources refer to biological materials or substances derived from living organisms that have the potential to be utilised for various purposes.8 They offer sustainable alternatives to traditional resources by promoting eco-friendly practices and reducing reliance on non-renewable sources. Bioresources are thus believed to be a significant component of natural resources and occupy a central position in human culture and economy.9 Bioresource-based entrepreneurship can contribute to environmental sustainability and promote the conservation of biodiversity. It can stimulate economic growth by creating new business opportunities, generating employment, and fostering investment in research and development.10 It contributes to the growth of industries such as biotechnology, biofuel production, natural product manufacturing, and sustainable agriculture.11 Bioresources play a vital role in the development of pharmaceuticals, nutraceuticals,12 and functional foods that contribute to human health and well-being. 13 Entrepreneurs in the bioresource sector can innovate products that promote health, address nutritional deficiencies, and offer alternatives to synthetic compounds. Utilising bioresources efficiently can help in waste reduction, recycling, and circular economy practices.14 Bioresource-based entrepreneurship encourages the responsible use of natural resources and minimises environmental impact through sustainable practices.15

As someone who belongs to Northeast India and has been actively involved with the Department of Science & Technology since 1995, Dr. Debajit Mahanta wanted to leverage the untapped natural advantage bestowed upon Northeast India to promote bioresource-based entrepreneurship and research. This case study explores the journey of Dr. Mahanta and his team in establishing a Centre of Excellence (CoE) for Bioresources and Sustainable Development at Kimin in Papum Pare district of Arunachal Pradesh (see Exhibit 2) with the support of the Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science & Technology, Govt. of India, and the Arunachal Pradesh State Council of Science & Technology (APSCS&T).16 The genesis and rationale behind the establishment of the Centre reflect a holistic approach to addressing the complex challenges of biodiversity conservation, sustainable development, and socio- and techno-economic empowerment or upliftment of the people in the region. Through research, innovation, capacity building, and partnerships, the Centre strives to contribute positively to the well-being of both present and future generations through bio-economy growth, while conserving and preserving the rich bioresource heritage of Arunachal Pradesh and the Northeast in general. The DBT-APSCS&T CoE for Bioresources and Sustainable Development is the result of Dr. Mahanta’s strong vision and equally stronger implementation. As he reflected on how much the centre has achieved, he stated that there is a lot more he would like to achieve. His vision for the centre is to make it a prototype for the entire Northeast India to follow. 

The Initiative and the Key Consorts in the Creation of the Centre of Excellence

The state of socio-economic conditions in Arunachal Pradesh with high unemployment rates motivated the need for an intervention for alternative livelihood generation. Dr. Mahanta and his team conceptualised the theory of change (see Exhibit 3) to develop an intervention to foster entrepreneurship development in the state through the optimum utilisation of bioresources, which culminated in the establishment of a Centre of Excellence for Bioresources and Sustainable Development. Through this intervention, Dr. Mahanta aimed to provide employment opportunities for the state's educated youth and offer sustainable livelihood options for local populations and farmers, thereby addressing pressing socioeconomic challenges and fostering economic sustainability.
 
In the quest to establish a dedicated centre for bioresource-based entrepreneurship development and research, various steps were taken by Dr. Mahanta, and many factors played an important role. Firstly, to identify gaps and determine the need for the establishment of the centre, expert consultations were held. Many research & academic institutes of repute such as the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), the DBT-North East Centre for Agricultural Biotechnology (DBT-NECAB), the Assam Agricultural University, the Govt. of Assam and Jorhat were taken into confidence for insights along with state government consultants, analysts, eminent researchers, and academicians from state and central universities. All these expert consultations acted as strong support for the initiation of the project. Moreover, Dr. Mahanta also relied on successful models of similar interventions undertaken in other parts of the country such as the Northeastern States and the Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Tsukuba, Japan for inspiration and learning.

The founding institutions that helped in the establishment of the CoE are the Department of Biotechnology, Ministry of Science and Technology, Government of India, and the Department of Science and Technology, Government of Arunachal Pradesh. Assam Agricultural University, Jorhat, Assam has provided mentorship to the CoE. In addition collaborative ties have been established to seek technical support, guidance, and collaboration in joint programmes with institutions such as the Cellular and Molecular Biotechnology Research Institute, Department of Life Science and Biotechnology, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), Tsukuba, Japan; the ICAR-National Research Centre for Banana, Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu; the ICAR-Central Institute of Agricultural Engineering, Regional Centre, Coimbatore; the ICAR-National Research Centre for Orchids, Sikkim, and many others.
 
The objectives of the DBT-APSCS&T Centre of Excellence for Bioresources and Sustainable Development, which reflect the holistic approach of bioresource-based entrepreneurship development through research, skill development, and collaboration or partnership, are as follows: 
 
To set up state-of-the-art biotechnology research facilities in Arunachal Pradesh for work on sustainable development of bioresources, using tools of modern biology (see Exhibit 4). 
To study and document the unique biodiversity and bioresources of Arunachal Pradesh. 
To undertake biotechnological interventions for sustainable development and utilisation of bioresources in Arunachal Pradesh (see Exhibit 5).
To generate technological packages for employment generation and the economic progress of the state (see Exhibit 6-9).
To undertake capacity building (human resource development) in bioresources conservation, development, and utilisation (see Exhibit 10).17
To collaborate with National and International institutions/organisations/universities in further research pursuits in bioresources.

Steps Taken to Overcome Challenges faced by the Centre
In setting up the Centre of Excellence, Dr. Mahanta and his team went through various challenges. Some of these challenges are of an enduring nature too. These challenges include the areas of garnering institutional, technical, financial and community support.
Institutional Support
In the establishment of an institute of this stature, institutional support from government agencies, academic institutions and other relevant stakeholders was crucial. Garnering such support involves obtaining official approval and endorsement, and securing partnerships and collaborations with key institutions. Various challenges were faced by Dr. Mahanta in acquiring support such as delays in obtaining approvals, negotiating agreements with multiple stakeholders and ensuring alignment with government policies and priorities. To overcome the challenges faced in gaining support, Dr. Mahanta took various steps. These include actively engaging with government agencies and academic institutions to advocate for the importance of the CoE and its potential benefits. Regular meetings, presentations, and communication efforts to raise awareness and build consensus among stakeholders were held. Dedicated personnel were appointed to oversee efforts to streamline the approval process and negotiate agreements with multiple stakeholders. In addition, efforts were made to conduct thorough research and consultation to identify areas of mutual interest and synergy so as to ensure alignment with government policies and priorities.
 
Technical Support
As an institution involving a lot of research in the area of bioresources, large-scale technical expertise and infrastructure were needed. Human resources specialised in specific skills play a very important role; hiring qualified researchers, technicians, and support staff with expertise in various disciplines relevant to bioresources and sustainable development was crucial. However, challenges were faced in attracting and retaining talent, considering the state has limited access to skilled professionals. To overcome challenges relating to acquiring technical talent, it was ensured that competitive salaries and benefits were offered to attract qualified researchers, technicians, and support staff. Additionally, the CoE established partnerships with academic institutions and industry partners to leverage their expertise and resources. Efforts have also been made to provide ongoing training and professional development opportunities to enhance the skills and capabilities of staff members. As a technology-driven Centre, its success depends on ensuring the availability of state-of-the-art equipment and facilities and keeping pace with rapidly evolving technologies which can pose a challenge. Therefore, the CoE regularly evaluates and updates its equipment and facilities to keep pace with advancements in technology.

Financial Support
As a state-of-the-art Centre of Excellence, the Centre needs adequate financial support for infrastructure development, research projects, capacity-building activities and day-to-day operations. There are various challenges attached to ensuring financial support such as competing for limited funding resources, navigating complex funding application processes, and ensuring financial sustainability in the long term. Additionally, economic uncertainties and fluctuations in funding availability also pose a challenge to the CoE's financial stability.

To acquire funding, Dr. Mahanta and his team applied for grants from government agencies, research funding organisations, and private sector partners by preparing detailed project funding proposals and collaborating with stakeholders to demonstrate the potential impact and value of CoE activities. In addition, efforts were made to explore innovative financing mechanisms, such as public-private partnerships and crowdfunding, to supplement traditional funding sources and ensure financial sustainability in the long term. The CoE was fully supported by the DBT, Govt. of India from March 2018 to September 2023. After the completion of the project as per the signed terms and conditions with the DBT, the state government took over the CoE.


Community Support
As a Centre focused on instilling entrepreneurship development among the people in Arunachal Pradesh, the participation of communities in the region is pertinent. Without, community participation, the Centre will not be able to fulfil its mission. However, ensuring community engagement involves building trust and fostering partnerships which is difficult due to challenges such as cultural and linguistic barriers, lack of awareness or interest in scientific research among community members, and addressing concerns related to land use, resource management, and environmental conservation. Moreover, one of the main aims of the Centre was to ensure the equitable distribution of benefits from the CoE activities and promote social inclusion and empowerment. To overcome these challenges, outreach events, workshops, and focus group discussions were organised to gather input, address concerns and involve community members in decision-making processes. Efforts were also made to tailor the CoE activities to meet the specific needs and priorities of local communities, such as conducting research on issues relevant to the community and providing training and capacity-building opportunities.

Other Challenges
Apart from the above challenges, the Centre also faced logistical challenges associated with operating in remote or rural areas, such as limited access to transportation, communication infrastructure, and basic amenities and most importantly, the continuous power supply. Additionally, regulatory compliance, ethical considerations, and risk management were important factors to consider in carrying out research and development activities. Fostering collaboration and coordination among diverse stakeholders, managing conflicts of interest, and maintaining transparency and accountability in decision-making processes are challenges that the CoE faces regularly. To address these varied challenges, the CoE established efficient systems and protocols for operating in remote or rural areas. This includes establishing remote work capabilities, implementing robust communication networks, and providing logistical support for staff working in field locations. It also prioritised regulatory compliance, ethical considerations, and risk management by adhering to relevant laws and regulations, implementing ethical guidelines and protocols, and conducting thorough risk assessments for its activities. Furthermore, efforts were made to foster collaboration and coordination among diverse stakeholders by establishing formalised governance structures, such as advisory boards and steering committees, and promoting a culture of transparency and accountability in decision-making processes.

CoE’s Journey of Success so Far
Since its inception (October 2018), the CoE has significantly established technical linkages, and academic collaborations with national and international institutions for achieving the CoE’s objectives of research and development, techno-skilling of various stakeholders towards sustainable utilisation, conservation of rich bioresources for socio-techno-economic development of indigenous populace of the state.

The CoE signed Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with several national and international institutions, viz., (i) ICAR-National Research Centre on Orchids (NRCO)18, Pakyong, Sikkim for garnering technical support and training in different areas of orchid research and conservation; (ii)  ICAR-Central Institute of Agricultural Engineering (CIAE)19, Bhopal through its Regional Centre20 at Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu for technical support, training in the area of Banana fibre extraction and its processing and value addition, etc.; (iii) Fragrance & Flavour Development Centre (FFDC)21, Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, Government of India, Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh and the Institute of Horticulture Technology (IHT)22, Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh for the development of aroma sector in Arunachal Pradesh through technical hand-holding, support and training on aromatic plant cultivation and entrepreneurship development; (iv) Letter of Intent (LOI) was signed with Cellular and Molecular Biotechnology Research Institute, Department of Life Science and Biotechnology, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST)23, Tsukuba, Japan for developing and undertaking collaborative research programmes, information sharing and exchange of education, teaching, researchers and students for limited periods; (v) Academic collaboration has been established with Dibrugarh University24, Dibrugarh, Assam towards pursuing collaborative R&D and Academic activities. 

Successful implementation of the Skill Vigyan Program25 in Life Science and Biotechnology by the CoE with the support of Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Govt. of India led to signing of Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with three Skill Development Councils of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, Government of India namely (i) Life Sciences Sector Skill Development Council (LSSSDC)26, (ii) Agriculture Skill Council of India (ASCI)27, and (iii) Food Industry Capacity & Skill Initiative (FICSI)28 and with four knowledge partners, i.e., (i) CSIR-North East Institute of Science and Technology (NEIST)29, Jorhat, Assam, (ii) North Eastern Regional Institute of Science and Technology (NERIST)30, Nirjuli, Arunachal Pradesh, (iii) College of Horticulture and Forestry, Central Agricultural University (CHF-CAU)31, Pasighat, Arunachal Pradesh, and (iv) Tezpur University32, Napaam, Tezpur, Assam towards developing trained and skilled graduate students, technicians, prospective entrepreneurs and teaching faculties in various selected fields of Life Sciences and Biotechnology.

The CoE has extended infrastructure and technical facilities, training to farmers, Self-Help Groups (SHGs), Non-Governmental Organisation (NGO) members and prospective entrepreneurs of Arunachal Pradesh for conservation, sustainable utilisation of bioresources through processing, value addition for their livelihood and income generation. Forty-one training programmes have been organised, in which One Thousand Eight Hundred Fifteen (1815) researchers, students, progressive farmers, and prospective entrepreneurs of the state have benefited from the CoE’s initiatives.

The CoE has fostered entrepreneurial spirit among prospective entrepreneurs in Arunachal Pradesh by encouraging aroma-based business ventures. Through the programme "Establishment of Aroma Unit for Promotion of Cultivation of Aromatic Crops and Entrepreneurship Development”16, the CoE has successfully supported two start-ups. The first, M/S Jeevan Sathi LLP, led by the CEO Shri Gyamar Sikap originating from the Jeevan Sathi Self-help Group, Kakoi of Kimin Circle, and the second, M/S Cher Enterprise Pvt. Ltd., headed by CEO Shri Pil Tadap in Hawa Camp, Kimin, Papum Pare district, Arunachal Pradesh are now thriving enterprises in the aroma industry. These start-ups exemplify the potential of aroma-based businesses to drive local bio-economy-based growth and entrepreneurial development in the State.  

Impact Evaluation Process for the Success of the Centre
For the success of any Centre, periodic process and impact evaluations are necessary to assess the effectiveness of its strategies in alignment with the Centre’s mission. Several committees and mechanisms are involved in this evaluation process:

Project Monitoring Committee: This committee is constituted by the Department of Biotechnology, Ministry of Science & Technology, Government of India. It oversees the overall progress of the CoE, its projects and initiatives, ensuring they are in line with the defined objectives.
Technical Evaluation Committee (TEC): Also constituted by the Department of Biotechnology, Ministry of Science & Technology, this committee evaluates the technical aspects of the CoE's activities, providing insights and recommendations for improvement.
Evaluation Committee by Arunachal Pradesh State Council for Science and Technology: At the state level, this committee evaluates the impact of the CoE's initiatives on the local communities, environment, and overall development of Arunachal Pradesh.
Internal Evaluation by Experts: The CoE conducts internal evaluations where experts in relevant fields assess the progress and impact of the initiatives. These experts provide valuable feedback for course correction and improvement.
Internal Evaluation through Presentations and Reports: The CoE presents periodic reports and presentations detailing its activities, achievements, challenges, and outcomes. These materials are reviewed internally by the CoE's management and stakeholders to gauge progress and effectiveness.
By involving multiple committees and mechanisms in the evaluation process, the CoE ensures comprehensive assessments of its strategies and activities, leading to continuous improvement and better outcomes aligned with its objectives.

Steps taken towards ensuring the Sustainability of the Centre
Towards ensuring the sustainability of the Centre, it has outlined a roadmap that focuses on efficiently utilising limited resources to establish itself as a reliable service provider in consultancy and state-of-the-art instrumentation facilities. It aims to generate revenue through Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) on processes and products with commercial viability. Key revenue-generating avenues of the Centre include offering contract research & development, training, and consultancy services for entrepreneurship development across sectors such as medicinal and aromatic plants, cultivation of aromatic and medicinal plants and important horticulture crops, orchid production and conservation, banana fibre products, rice germplasm, biofertilizers, and value addition services like primary and secondary processing of medicinal plants, solvent extraction, rectification of essential oil, research and development for scaling up the developed process, etc. and many more.

Replicability- The Way Ahead
Replicability or scaling up this successful model of a Unit fostering bioresource-based entrepreneurship across other parts of the country can be possible and depends upon the following criteria:

Regional Potential: Identification of regions with abundant bioresources and significant potential for sustainable development is crucial. According to Dr. Mahanta, areas rich in biodiversity, such as tropical rainforests, coastal regions, or agricultural heartlands, are prime contenders for having similar interventions.
Research Infrastructure: As access to research infrastructure, including laboratories, equipment, and technical expertise, is essential for conducting advanced research and development activities. Therefore, areas with established research institutions, universities, and industry clusters are well-suited for setting up such a CoE.
Government Support: Strong support from government agencies at the national, state, and local levels is critical for providing funds, regulatory oversight, and policy guidance. Regions with proactive government policies and initiatives promoting research, innovation, and sustainable development are ideal for establishing such a CoE.
Community Engagement: Engaging with local communities and stakeholders is vital for ensuring the relevance, acceptance, and success of the CoE's initiatives. Areas with active community involvement, support networks, and a culture of collaboration are conducive to setting up a CoE.
Economic Viability: Assessing the economic viability and market potential of bioresource-based products and technologies is essential for long-term sustainability. Regions with strong market demand, industry partnerships, and access to funds and investment opportunities are attractive for establishing such a CoE.
Environmental Considerations: Evaluating the environmental impact and sustainability of proposed activities is necessary to mitigate risks and ensure responsible resource management. Areas with a commitment to environmental conservation, sustainable practices, and eco-friendly policies are well-suited for hosting such a CoE.

Based on these criteria, Dr. Mahanta and team identify regions such as the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, Northeast India, coastal regions like Kerala and Gujarat, and biodiversity hotspots like the Western Himalayas and Eastern Himalayas as potential avenues for similar interventions. In addition, these regions possess diverse ecosystems, rich biodiversity, and significant opportunities for bioresource utilisation and sustainable development. By leveraging local strengths, resources, and expertise, CoEs can play a pivotal role in catalysing innovation, driving economic growth, and fostering environmental stewardship in these areas.

Case Study Title:
Developing a Sports Ecosystem in Odisha: The
Role of Private Public Partnerships
Case Study Description: In the past few years, Odisha has emerged as a hub for sporting activities in India. It has hosted international sporting events such as the Asian Athletics Championship (2017) and two hockey World Cups (2018 and 2023), besides having built the largest seated hockey stadium in the world and laid 22 artificial hockey turfs in a single district. By the end of 2023, Odisha had 90 multi-purpose indoor stadiums, 25 hockey training centres, 314 rural mini stadiums and 149 urban mini stadiums . During the same period, there was a significant increase in Odisha state’s representation in national and international sports events, improvement in athlete performance besides large-scale participation from the grassroots in numerous sports disciplines. Odisha’s transformation as a leader in sports was led by a multitude of factors such as an inspired and involved leadership, a committed bureaucracy and a well-orchestrated public-private partnership that complemented each other. This case study covers in depth how multitude actors from diverse organisations and institutions came together to create an ecosystem of sporting excellence in Odisha, which has hitherto never been seen in India.
Case Text:
In the past few years, Odisha has emerged as a hub for sporting activities in India. it has hosted international sporting events such as the Asian Athletics Championship (2017) and two hockey World Cups (2018 and 2023), besides having built the largest seated hockey stadium in the world and laid 22 artificial hockey turfs in a single district. By the end of 2023, Odisha had 90 multi-purpose indoor stadiums, 25 hockey training centres, 314 rural mini stadiums and 149 urban mini stadiums.  During the same period, there was a significant increase in Odisha state’s representation in national and international sports events, improvement in athlete performance besides large-scale participation from the grassroots in numerous sports disciplines. Odisha’s transformation as a leader in sports was led by a multitude of factors such as an inspired and involved leadership, a committed bureaucracy and a well-orchestrated public-private partnership that complemented each other. Multitude actors from diverse organisations and institutions came together to create an ecosystem of sporting excellence in Odisha, which has hitherto never been seen in India. 
Sporting Potential
With 1.4 billion people, India as a nation has the gene pool to become a sporting superpower. During the past few decades, there has been a notable surge in the nation’s aspiration to replicate the triumphs of cricket and erstwhile Indian hockey across multiple sporting disciplines. However, such aspirations did not transform into the reality of sustained performance on the international stage, largely because India lacked organisational and institutional systems and processes essential to the development of a vibrant sporting ecosystem. 
The Odisha model of development offers a blueprint for establishing such an ecosystem, which can be replicated in other states in India so that the country’s diverse talent pool can be honed and harnessed to elevate the level of sporting performance. This case study describes how a partnership between the government and private organisations contributed to the development of a sports ecosystem in Odisha. 
Developing a Sporting Ecosystem
Historically, Odisha has never been known as a sporting powerhouse. Neither did it have any track record of hosting national or international sporting events. The breakthrough came in 2017, when Odisha received a request to host the Asian Athletic Championship, just a few months ahead of the scheduled event, due to challenges faced by the original hosting state. 
Driven by the enthusiasm of the Chief Minister, the Odisha administration embraced the 90-day challenge. The infrastructure necessary to host the event was built during the next three months and the event was successfully conducted. This achievement provided the organising team confidence in its capability to host an international sporting event. In 2018, Odisha hosted the Hockey World Cup. 
With the success of hosting two major sports events, the government realised that to sustain high performance in sports, it needed to develop a sporting ecosystem, which could be sustainably built and managed through partnerships with private organisations. Private enterprise was considered essential because while the state government could  orchestrate the system of development,  private organisations had specific advantages which could complement the efforts of the state government. For instance, the rigid systems of compensation under the public system can be a hinderance to attracting the best talent. These fiscal constraints are more easily overcome within a private setup.  Further, project management under private enterprise can guarantee the adequate maintenance of infrastructure. Although there were multiple institutions such as the state associations and national federations within the government setup, even these needed to work together with private enterprise, if Odisha wanted to make a mark in the intensely competitive, scientific, and multidisciplinary world of sports. 
The Public Private Partnership Model 
India is a vast country and its diverse talent base presented Odisha with an enormous opportunity. However, this same diversity made it challenging to make smart choices from among the nearly 40 sports disciplines. Therefore, the involvement of multiple stakeholders was required for the selection of sporting disciplines and to establish high standards within it. 
The strength of the government, it was realised, was in making long term investments, typically in infrastructure. Private organisations were not in a position to make such huge investments which did not provide immediate returns. Further, the government and federations had the organisational capability to conduct competitions at multiple levels, which was essential for improvement of performance standards. Additionally, the government had the credibility to provide rewards and recognitions to sportsperson for their achievements in national and international competitions. Apart from cash awards, some government organisations also provided employment to sportspersons. 
Private organisations on the other hand, were deemed to be more effective in the procurement of products and services. Programmes for elite sportspersons for instance, necessitates procurement of expensive equipment and high-quality nutrition for sustained performance. The government system of procurement, which is often oriented towards obtaining the lowest price for products and services was deemed unsuitable. Sometimes, products and services need to be customised to the specific needs of a sportsperson and require a fast turnaround time. These objectives are difficult to achieve within the constraints of the government system. Human resource management comprising selection, recruitment and monitoring of coaches are also important for running a successful coaching programme, yet another area where private organisations are more effective due to their flexibility and faster responsiveness. Elements of human resource management such as variable compensation, and performance linked tenure, which are an essential part of any private organisation, are difficult to deploy in government organisations.  
Having considered the advantages and disadvantages of both government and private organisations, a model of private public partnership establishing the specific criteria for partnerships was developed.  A broad framework providing for a division of activities and responsibilities between private organisations and the government was also created. (See Exhibit 1). Under this partnership model, the Odisha government invited private organisations to set up high performance centres (HPC) for various sporting disciplines. 




High Performance Centres 
The state government first approached organisations who were already present in Odisha for business reasons and had a track record of investing in sports. Business houses such as the Tatas and JSW were already operating in Odisha and already known for their contribution to Indian sports. The government signed Memorandum of Understandings (MoUs) with these organisations to set up high performance centres that would be professionally managed like the ones in advanced sporting nations such as China, Japan, or the USA. Apart from establishing a state-of-the-art facility with equipment for training, recovery, and rehabilitation, the HPCs also recruited specialised professionals to manage multiple aspects of an elite sportsperson’s development. Unlike the erstwhile model, wherein only the coach was responsible for the well-being of an athlete, the HPCs had dedicated professionals such as physiotherapists, nutritionists, masseurs, sports scientists and psychologists besides video analysts who worked alongside the coach for athlete development and performance improvement. Many of these professionals would travel with the sportspersons during competitions to ensure their best output for the events.  Numerous HPCs were established in partnership with private organisations. (See Exhibit 2). 
The Odisha Naval Tata Hockey HPC was established in Bhubaneswar in August 2019, in partnership with Tata Steel and Tata Trusts. Its purpose was to impart scientific and structured coaching for budding talent which could then represent Odisha and subsequently India and earn laurels for the state and the nation. The centre was equipped with all the necessary sports infrastructure—both soft and hard—to provide athletes complete support through sports science. 
The centre conducted for the players specialised camps under the supervision of able coaches and former Indian players with international experience, in addition to education workshops and certification programmes for coaches by qualified foreign instructors. The HPC paid significant attention to the development of sports at the junior and sub-junior level, so that a steady stream of talent could be trained and developed for the future. 
HPC Regional Centres
The Odisha Naval Tata Hockey HPC also established three regional centres and 14 grassroot centres across the state. The centres were built and maintained by the Odisha government while Tata Steel deployed coaches to conduct the training programmes. About 3000 boys and girls have undergone training under the watchful eyes of more than 40 coaches at these centres. Grassroot leagues were regularly conducted to introduce a competitive spirit among the players. Summer camps, organised for young children across the state to introduce hockey in a fun and playful way, received more than 2500 registrations. In tandem with such grassroot level initiatives, Odisha government also built Astro turfs in several districts to expose players to this surface at an early age. To ensure the all-round development of sportspersons, the HPCs also provided them with education, yoga sessions, recreational facilities, and opportunities for celebrating festivals. 

Success and Expansion
Cadets from the Hockey HPC have already made a mark. 20-year-old Jyoti Chatri and 16-year-old Suneilta Toppo were among the probable candidate selected for the senior national team. Odisha’s junior women’s team were champions of East Zone in 2023 and the senior team were national champions in 2022. Satisfied with the progress achieved, the Odisha government initiated other partnerships with Tata Steel for setting up HPCs for Archery and Sports Climbing.
The Odisha government also established the swimming HPC in partnership with JSW Sports. Located at the Biju Patnaik Swimming Pool Complex at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar, this HPC is also modelled like the other HPCs.  JSW Sports manages the coaching programme at the HPC and at 16 swimming centres across the state, training close to 7000 budding swimmers. The Odisha administration’s objective is to establish 30 swimming centres in addition to developing a network with other privately owned swimming pools in the state where the JSW coaching programme can be replicated. The early success of the HPCs is demonstrated by swimmers such as Srishti Upadhya, Pavan Gupta, Pratashya Roy and Mannata Mishra who have begun to win in the national and international competitions at multiple levels. 
Efficient Use of Resources
To optimise the utilisation of resources, flexibility was integrated into the partnership model template. For instance, while the weightlifting HPC had the Ahluwalia Group as a corporate partner, Tenvic Sports was engaged to manage the coaching programme. Speaking with media on the occasion of the centre’s inauguration, the Tenvic spokesperson explained: 
We take care of their (athletes) accommodation, food, diet and coaching. We also handle procurement of stuff like weights and jerseys. At the same time, we understand that only lifting weights all day can be stressful and tiring, both physically and mentally and try to ensure they have other interests to relax. Tenvic would also be taking care of their education and most of them would be admitted to schools and colleges soon.   
Apart from the swimming HPC in Bhubaneswar, the Odisha government created subcentres in two other districts and built 47 training centres in different locations in the state across varied sports such as gymnastics, athletics, football, tennis, shooting etc. Under each of these sports project, the state government has built the infrastructure while the corporate partner commits to nurture the operations through providing the coaches and imparting scientific training to athletes. 
Forays into Multiple Sports
In April 2023, sensing the potential for development of gymnastics in Odisha, the government partnered with Arcelor Mittal Nippon Steel India (AM/NS) to set up HPCs for gymnastics in three locations. Speaking on the occasion of signing the MOU, a government spokesperson explained: 
The state government will create and maintain the infrastructure for the HPC and academies while AM/NS India will operate and manage these centres. They will train the gymnasts, in particular women gymnasts, and provide coaching, development and certification, and judge certification.  .
Indigenous Sports
Earlier, AM/NS had been the Principal sponsor of the Odisha Juggernauts, the state’s Kho Kho franchise—in the Ultimate Kho Kho League, wherein the Odisha Juggernauts emerged as the champions of the league.   In November 2023, the government signed an MOU with AM/NS for setting up a Kho Kho HPC. Speaking on the occasion, Chief Minister Mr Naveen Patnaik said: 
We want to support our indigenous sports like Kho Kho. The partnership with AM/NS to establish the Kho Kho HPC will set a new benchmark for support towards Indian sports.   
Mr Vineel Krishna, Special Secretary to Chief Minister and Secretary, Sports and Youth Services Department explained why the government had considered it important to develop indigenous sports such as Kho Kho: 
‘Western sports such as football and athletics are expensive, requiring large infrastructure and regular maintenance. Compared to that, indigenous and Eastern sports such as Kho Kho, Yoga or martial arts do not need much infrastructure. How many athletic tracks can we construct to cater to our large population? The aim of the government is to promote sports at a societal level. Therefore, sports needs to become easily accessible, affordable, and scalable. Indigenous sports are more suitable for that.’  
Use of Sports Science
Elite athlete management integrates injury management, rehabilitation and recovery wherein the contribution of Sports Science becomes critical. The Odisha government therefore partnered with the Abhinav Bindra Foundation to set up Sports Science HPC at Kalinga stadium in Bhubaneswar, where sportspersons from multiple disciplines could come for support and recovery. Inaugurated in December 2023, this is the largest Sports Science centre in India. It has specialised laboratories such as a biomechanics lab, para-athlete performance lab, altitude training centre, cryotherapy and floating therapy.  As Abhinav Bindra commented, 
‘Sport is something that champions inclusivity and gender equality. It is marvellous to see how Odisha is using sport to imbibe these values in society. I haven’t personally seen a state-of-the-art para-training facility anywhere in the world. The entire facility is very thought-through, inclusive, and accessible in nature.’ . 
Governing the Partnerships 
The Odisha government deliberately kept the MOUs signed with partner organisations, broad based and flexible so that a wide variety of activities could be incorporated within their scope. Government officials worked closely with the partners on the ground, and specific monitoring mechanisms were introduced that were mutually agreeable and suitable for the operations. Outsourcing and contracting mechanisms have ensured that numerous activities could be conducted during the past few years, without any corresponding increase in the number of government employees involved with these initiatives.  
Challenges
Governing the partnerships, however, has brought its own challenges. 
Multiple Agencies:  It was a complex task to deal with multiple agencies, including the sports associations of the State, the coaches, their support staff, and the athletes. 
Talent Retention: It was not always easy to attract and retain high performance national and international coaches and their support staff in a place like Bhubaneswar, which is not as well-known as metro cities like Mumbai or Delhi. 
Expectations: Setting expectations was also a challenge. As the focus of most of the initiatives was to develop the sports ecosystem, results would consequently take some time to materialise. There was a certain minimum time required for athletes’ career progression, especially when they were at the sub-junior and junior level. One therefore had to be patient, instead of expecting immediate podium success. 
All these challenges had to be addressed through extensive discussions with various stakeholders to gradually set the right expectations.
The Way Ahead
Odisha's emergence as the sports capital of India is based on its development as a responsible hub of grassroots centres, providing the necessary sports infrastructure, facilities and the necessary training from the best coaches to young talent all around the year.  Odisha's unique private-public collaboration model, guided by a common vision, has served to develop a sports ecosystem, which when adopted by Indian states can serve to identify and nurture talent, an essential step towards promoting sports at an early age in India. 
Reflecting on Odisha’s journey during the past five years, Mr Vineel Krishna commented:
‘Odisha today is in a strong position to make investments in sports. It is one of the best fiscally managed states in the country and has the largest sports budget at ₹ 1300 crores. The private organisations present in the state are also the ones who were already connected to sports. However, sustainability of these programmes depends on leadership that is visionary and stable. There was a clear signal from the Chief Minister regarding the importance of sports. For example, as a Chief Secretary, I held additional charge of sports. As I worked in the CM’s office, it was easy for me to coordinate with various other departments, which a stand-alone sports secretary would otherwise not have been able to do.’

Case Study Title:
Land Resource Inventory Boosts Farm Yields in
Karnataka
Case Study Description:
The Land Resource Inventory (LRI) was developed as a new approach to enhance the impact of the watershed programme. It is an inventory of five physical factors—rock, soil, slope, erosion type and severity and vegetation—which form the basis for assessing land resources. The Land Resource Inventory (LRI) technology—developed under Sujala III in 2013-14 and implemented in 11 districts—empowers farmers with site-specific information to make crop choices and boost farm incomes.

It was designed for execution through a consortium of partners to develop a site-specific land resource database through use of state-of-the-art remote sensing (RS) and geographic information systems for data collection and interpretation. A Land Resources Portal for information dissemination was then established by developing a digital library through pooling all the spatial and non-spatial data, containing both site-specific farm information and generalised data about land. A mobile application was developed to enable farmers to access the LRI portal. The Watershed Development Department (WDD) of the Karnataka state government spearheaded the project.
Case Text:
Farmers would often confront the officers of the Watershed Development Department (WDD) of the state
government of Karnataka during their field visits about soil, water and crop-specific information of their
own fields to enable higher productivity. While the state government's decade-long efforts through various
watershed programs, particularly Sujala I and Sujala II led by the WDD since 2001, have made strides in
land conservation, there was an opportunity to further enhance the positive impact on farmers' yield and
livelihoods.
Officers of the WDD, unable to provide farm-specific information relating to soil characteristics and water
availability of their farms, would instead provide generalised macro-level data pertaining to the entire
block and taluka. This data was mostly irrelevant considering the wide variation between neighbouring
fields and within each field itself.
Watershed Development for Farm Productivity
Karnataka, predominantly an agricultural state, suffers from low and uncertain rainfall. It is ranked as the
second highest drought prone state with the highest percentage (79%) of arid land in the country, after
Rajasthan.1 Considering that soil erosion, droughts, erratic rainfall and depleting ground water had
impacted potential productivity, the government of Karnataka had introduced watershed development
programs in the semi-arid regions to improve agricultural production. These programs however, did not
achieve the desired impact. This was primarily attributed to not being based on a site-specific land
resources database, which could provide farmers with the scientific base for increasing productivity. The
farmers demand for farm-specific data could no longer be ignored. Thinking minds at WDD worked to
plug the information gap.
Launch of LRI Technology
The development of a Land Resource Inventory (LRI)—was initiated under Karnataka Watershed
Development Project-II—also known as Sujala III—in 2013-14. Under this program by 2022, the LRI
technology is mainstreamed by scientifically integrating micro and macro data about land, water, climate
and other resources into a digital portal, which will assist farmers with critical interventions and livelihood
decisions. This one-of-its-kind LRI technology singularly empowers both planners and farmers with
unique, farm-specific information to make correct crop choices, conservation measures, nutrient
management to boost farm yield and incomes.
An outcome of a convergence of diverse skills of planners and domain experts, LRI technology has been

implemented across 14 districts in Karnataka state, covering 14 lakh hectares of land, 2531 micro-
watersheds and benefiting about 7 lakh households.2 The key innovation of this project was to bring

LAND RESOURCE INVENTORY BOOSTS FARM YIELDS IN KARNATAKA 2
together a consortium of scientific and technical partners and harness state-of-the-art technology towards
scientific soil and water conservation and sustainable farming.
Shaping the Land Resource Inventory System
Determined to make a difference in farmers lives, WDD led by the Commissioner and nodal officials, Mrs
Geeta Halli and Dr K.J. Parmeshwarappa with specialisations in agriculture and rural development,
explored the feasibility of creating an inventory of each individual farmer’s field. It was opportune, that
they were led by Dr A. Natarajan, a former scientist of the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use
Planning (NBSS&LUP), posted as a consultant with the World Bank. He not only possessed the technical
knowhow, but also the persuasive skills to ensure the funding, required to materialise the technology. This
team showcases how intention met initiative, to birth and shape Sujala III, a World Bank (WB)-funded
project in 2013, followed by REWARD in 2022.
Building on Sujala I and II
Earlier in 2001, the WDD—supported by the World Bank—had implemented Sujala I, which introduced
for the first-time active community participation in designing the land use plan in seven districts. Titled
Karnataka Watershed Development Project (KWDP), both farmers and local non-governmental
organisations (NGOs) worked together to improve the productivity of natural resources and boost rural
livelihoods. Spread across 12700 villages, its target was four lakh households.3 This project concluded in
March 2009. Close on its heels, followed Sujala II, also under the KWDP, and financed by NABARD. Smaller
in scale, its mandate covered five districts of Karnataka.4 The WDD continued the work with a focus on
developing community resilience and environmental protection. The lessons learnt under these
programmes mandated the need for site-specific land information.
The Land Resources Inventory (LRI) was developed as a new approach under Sujala III to enhance the
impact of the watershed programme. Highlighting the significance of LRI technology, lead scientist Dr
Natarajan explained, ‘Larger questions of protecting the environment are embedded within the issue of
soil and water conservation. Contrary to common perception, soil contains twice the amount of carbon
content than trees and serves as a crucial carbon sink for our planet.’5
Sujala III: Project Design
The mandate of Sujala III was to bridge the farm-specific information deficit so that farmers could
effectively use the site-specific database to plan and implement agricultural activities through the LRI
technology portal. The larger objective was to persuade farmers to adopt a science-based approach toward
watershed management, i.e., arrest soil degradation, conserve water in their farmlands and enhance
livelihood opportunities. The LRI technology consisted of three distinct parts:
A. Data Collection: The project was designed for execution through collaboration with a consortium
of partners to develop a site-specific land resource database on soil and other resources at the
watershed level with use of state-of-the-art remote sensing (RS)i and geographic information
systems (GIS)ii for data collection and interpretation.
B. Land Resources Portal: A Land Resources Portal for information dissemination was then
established by developing a digital library through pooling all the spatial and non-spatial data,
containing both site-specific farm information and generalised data about land.

i Remote sensing is the process of detecting and monitoring the physical characteristics of an area by
measuring its reflected and emitted radiation from a distance (typically from satellite or aircraft).
ii A geographic information system (GIS) can capture store, check and display different kinds of data
relative to positions on the earth's surface, like fields and vegetation, or even streets and buildings.

LAND RESOURCE INVENTORY BOOSTS FARM YIELDS IN KARNATAKA 3
C. App-based Decisions: A mobile application was developed to enable farmers to access the LRI
portal. The WDD provided a dynamic decision support system to promote the sustainable
management of farmer resources.
The total budget for developing the LRI technology and making it farmer-ready was estimated at ₹ 8,359.12
lakh to cover an area of 14 lakh hectares across 14 districts. The WDD, Karnataka, received a total ₹ 412
crores, with 70 per cent of the project financing from the World Bank to implement LRI based watershed
program as Sujala III project.
Challenges in Implementation
There were multiple challenges confronting the core team involved in the planning and execution of LRI
technology under Sujala III. Forming workable collaborations, raising funds, ensuring scientific data
collection and its integration under the LRI portal, development of mobile application and then training
the farmers in its usage were some key stumbling blocks.
Collaboration
The team’s first challenge was to put together a collaboration—hitherto never attempted—across 13
different government organisations and institutions, identified through their respective domain expertise
in land use, soil, hydrology, crops, water resources, GIS mapping systems, cartography etc. (See Exhibit 1)
This initiative involved breaking down the silos that government departments and organisations routinely
inhabit to foster a collaborative culture where knowledge and expertise is shared across domains and
working together is valued. This effort ensures scientific data collection relating to farmers’ land, both
above the surface and below it.
Funds
The next obstacle before the team was to convince government to invest on developing dedicated
laboratory, field facilities and on human resources at partner institutions in the state. Hitherto government
is accustomed to allocating funds on tangible initiatives like building bundsiii or infrastructure. However,
finances were allocated to partner organisations to conduct their domain-specific work under the three
broad categories of generating LRI data sets, thematic outputs and portal development.
Data Integration
The third challenge was to integrate the extant and newly generated data post collection and collate the
information on site-specific farms to be made available on a common platform for real time use by the
farmers and planners. Once the LRI portal was activated, a mobile app had to be developed and more
importantly, farmers were required to be trained in its usage.
Strategic Implementation of LRI
Operations under Sujala III were based upon the twin pillars of collaboration and communication. The
WDD was uniquely poised to anchor the collaborative project for effectiveness as its core functions relied
on its existing connect with a host of line departments like agriculture, horticulture, forestry, and irrigation.
To convince and stitch together a collaboration among 13 partner organisations including government
departments and agriculture institutions, the WDD of Karnataka, as the anchor institution and the 14th
member of the collective, relied upon the following strategies:

iii Farm bunds, which are 'walls' along the boundary of fields, serve to retain rainwater and soil moisture
for a longer time, thus reducing soil erosion during heavy rains.

LAND RESOURCE INVENTORY BOOSTS FARM YIELDS IN KARNATAKA 4
Institutionalising Organisational Cooperation
Collaboration was demanded on two fronts. One, to collate the available, extant data on soil and water
from 7 different government departments onto a single platform. Two, to collaborate with multiple
government departments and 6 universities for science research, to generate the much-needed farm specific
micro data, which farmers could apply to make effective farming decisions.
To enlist the cooperation of 13 organisations under a consortium, WDD initiated memorandums of
understanding (MoUs) with each partner organisation. The consortium approach of Sujala III was extended
to REWARD program i.e., Rejuvenating Watersheds for Agricultural Resilience through Innovative
Development, in Karnataka and Odisha from 2022-23 onwards with the support of World Bank. Each
partner organisation assigned a dedicated team of scientists to collect fresh field data from both above and
below the land surface.6 To ensure cooperation within the consortium, and its smooth operation, Directors
and Vice Chancellors of the participating organisations were kept informed of progress at every stage.
The MoU’s worked to provide funding and establish institutional bonding. For instance, under the
REWARD programme, under which the LRI technology is mainstreamed, both Karnataka and Odisha
jointly receives Rs 1100 crores, of which 70% is financed by the World Bank. Funds were provided for
partner organisations to conduct various LRI-related tasks like data collection and soil assessment on each
farmer’s field. The financing was welcomed by the cash strapped universities as it infused much-needed
financing for infrastructure and personnel, the primary prerequisites for an enabling research environment.
Institutional cohesiveness was fostered by reinforcing the notion that each partner organisation contributed
in a distinct way.
Fostering a Shift in Mindset
Collaboration within the consortium involved two distinct processes. The first process involved
deliberations and discussions within the consortium to establish uniform work protocols to cull out field
data. The other was training scientists and field researchers for data collection. In some instances, those
with limited technological capability had to be schooled in the new frontiers of digital technology for data
collection and processing.
In this scenario, the core WDD team had to instill confidence among the teams that the data being generated
by them was valuable and no single team’s work was more important than any other team. A silo mindset
had to be replaced with a sense of shared responsibility to underline the equal importance of each partner
organisation that contributed to make LRI technology a success.
Educational institutions in the consortium were also compelled to acknowledge that to become meaningful,
research outcomes had to be shared with farmers for everyday use. Members of partner institutions were
also incentivised to present the project findings on special forums like conferences and seminars.
To maintain progress, the WDD needed to keep track of those organisations unable to keep pace with the
schedule. WDD was able to identify the laggard institutions through members’ attitude and behavioural
approach characterised by a marked lack of responsiveness and use of flimsy justifications for incomplete
tasks. The WDD used the techniques of persuasion and appeal to provide some hand holding for such
organisations.
Communication Strategies to Navigate Challenges
The LRI technology project integrated communication at multiple levels. The project’s success rested as
much on communication endeavours as it did on its scientific implementation. Consequently, WDD
designed a comprehensive strategy to maintain open lines of communication among partner organisations
and stakeholders. The team resorted to some common, yet effective communication tactics:

LAND RESOURCE INVENTORY BOOSTS FARM YIELDS IN KARNATAKA 5
Core Messaging
The core team worked to inculcate and steadfastly maintain a positive attitude among all partner
organisations. The core message that ‘every organisation was an equally important contributor to make
LRI technology a reality for farmers to use constructively’ set the consortium on a sound foundation. The
same message was leveraged for individuals too, who were encouraged to ‘break the shackles of working
in silos and collaborate for directly impacting India’s development.’ This notion was reiterated at every
opportunity including online or in-person monthly or review meetings.
Interpersonal Communication
As a nodal department, WDD relied heavily on one-on-one meetings for mission implementation. In the
early phases of onboarding, it communicated individually with each partner organisation to perceive the
value of their contribution. These meetings also served to resolve any specific challenges faced by partners
within their organisations. For instance, some organisations faced an uncooperative finance department
reluctant to release funds on time in view of concerns about project feasibility. Or members who were not
punctual about attending meetings or unresponsive to online mails and messages had to learn that ‘there
was no other option but to participate and collaborate with other team members.’
Group Communication
To overcome systemic institutional barriers, WDD resorted to persistent group communication—online
and offline—through frequent follow ups and review meetings.
To bring all knowledge partners on board, it was essential to facilitate information sharing, develop
manuals, disseminate digital tools and produce the output needed to mainstream the LRI approach.
Training programmes were designed to cover all activities involved in LRI management. Review meetings
and monthly meetings were routinely organised to stay updated on project status and address any
emerging challenges. Group discussions were conducted through e-mails and social media applications
like WhatsApp. These virtual communities were named ‘Reward Sujala’, or ‘Reward District Group’ and
so on.
Data collection being an arduous task, monthly review meetings were held to discuss progress and gather
feedback on specific issues. For instance, LRI technology uses a combination of remote sensing imagery
and field mapping techniques. So, when field researchers complained about the lack of clarity in the printed
cadastral mapsiv and remote sensing imagery, the problem was immediately addressed by providing prints
with high quality resolution.
Birth of LRI Technology
It took the consortium 3 years—from 2014 to 2016—to establish the protocols for completion of individual
tasks. From 2017 onwards, the project gathered momentum in terms of gathering and collating farm
specific information.7
Data analysis formed a crucial link in the development chain as micro data of soil moisture in a particular
farm field had to be linked and integrated with macro data about weather and climate conditions. Further,
scientists had to provide farmers innovative farm specific solutions regarding water balance and the
corresponding water budget. For the micro data to be truly integrated with the macro information,
scientists needed to establish protocols on the basis of a uniform methodology and models of interpretation.

iv Cadastral Maps are digital land records maintained by the state government for all cities, villages and
towns.

LAND RESOURCE INVENTORY BOOSTS FARM YIELDS IN KARNATAKA 6
By 2022, the consortium had completed the data analysis and developed the LRI technology, a one stop
digital portal that hosted 14 lakh hectares of LRI database in Karnataka.
Project Outcome
The LRI technology project has been a game-changer. Through a scientific analysis of each patch of land,
including its soil, slope, erosion, depth, structure, soil reaction and drainage etc. , LRI technology has been
able to provide advisories and options to farmers, planners, researchers and other land users.
Farmers have benefitted from rain water harvesting and diversification of crops moving from traditional
low-value crops to high value crops through suitable crop selection and judicious use of fertilisers and
other inputs. It has also aided government departments—as a single-stop data resource—in the
management of natural resources. (See Exhibit 2).
Shorter Timeframe to Plan Rural Schemes
The planning period for rural development projects pertaining to land and agriculture in the villages has
been substantially shortened from 2 years to 3 months. Additionally, generation of Detailed Project Report
(DPR) and implementation time by the WDD has been reduced by half from 6 years to 3 years.
Huge Cost Savings
Limited budgetary resources earlier squandered away on obtaining informative inputs can now be solely
focused on project implementation, thereby increasing cost effectiveness and sustainability. Consequently,
budget expenses incurred on planning and DPR preparation has been significantly reduced.
Acceptance of Technology
The implementation of LRI technology fostered the adoption of this technology by watershed and other
line departments, and consortium institutions that relied extensively on digital tools, communications and
mapping technologies for planning interventions and as well as the beneficiary farmers who used it to hone
their farming practices. (See Exhibit 3).
LRI Cards and Using the App
The increasing popularity of LRI technology since 2022 showcases Indian farmers positive disposition to
scientific knowledge. Farmers have been issued LRI cards containing information like land survey number
of their farm plots, characteristics of surface and sub-surface soils, crop suitability and required nutrient
inputs, etc (See Exhibit 4). Accessing LRI technology through a specially designed mobile application,
allows each farmer to enquire about the soil characteristics and water quality of a specific farm field.
Farmers can request a scientific response for queries across 9 expert systems fed into the LRI portal (See
Exhibit 5).
Farmers Mr Sudhakar Gaikwad from Bhalki Taluk and Mr Santosh Reddy from Aurad Taluk who
benefitted from LRI technology likened it to a ‘ray of hope’. 8 The LRI technology informed Mr Gaikwad of

the shallowness of his acreage at 15 cm deep, which helped him to switch to farm-appropriate multi-
cropping of ginger, tomato, and watermelon, after a decade of managing an unprofitable mango plantation.

Mr Reddy replaced cultivation of papaya with drum stick, based on the crop suitability advisory issued by
scientists from College of Horticulture at Bidar. The LRI technology thus marks the arrival of ‘digital’ in
rural India.
Gendered Learnings
Women farmers have responded positively to LRI technology. While shy of public speaking, women
farmers opened up to officers during farm visits. They were keen to learn about the nutrient requirement
