of their land through LRI technology for gauging cost of inputs such as fertilisers. In Geeta Halli’s
experience, women tend to be highly receptive to recommendations from the WDD, whereas some men
may need more encouragement. Even landless women labourers have benefited significantly. The
Horticulture College in Bidar, a partner organisation within the LRI consortium, collaborated with the local
Zilla Parishad to organise a series of trainings on cashew processing, benefiting landless women like Ms.
Renuka of Shahapur and her self-help group. To rejuvenate fallow land, the concerned department
allocates it to landless labourers for cultivation, offering them new opportunities for growth.9
These women could thus grow cashew plants and custard apple in Bidar district. For the first time,
scientists like Dr P.K. Naikodi and Dr P. Jholgiker, inspired by the accurate classification of land through
LRI Technology, introduced plantations to cash crops like cashew and custard apples suitable for degraded
laterite and black soils in Bidar. According to Dr Naikodi, ‘the roots of these plants can burrow through the
rocky layer of sub-soil to reach out for water and other nutrients found deeper in the soil.’10
The Way Forward
LRI technology has emerged as a successful, replicable, scientific and technology-driven watershed
management model.11 Building on the momentum, Team REWARD Sujala has set an ambitious target to
bring an additional 20 lakh hectares across 21 districts of Karnataka, within the ambit of LRI technology
prior to the expiry of its term in June 2026.
To harness LRI’s full potential, the team is presently engaged in introducing the dynamic element in the
form of agro advisories factoring in climate change, unseasonal rains, etc. for farmers to meet any weather
and crop related exigencies in real time.

Case Study Title: GST: The Story of India’s biggest tax reform
Case Study Description: The case explores how the multiple stakeholders in the GST project were finally able to work together to implement GST. How is consensus built when so many parties are involved? How are the diverse interests of these stakeholders safeguarded in the process? The case also examines the complexities of the Indian taxation system pre-GST and thus, delves into the inherent consequent complexity of such a massive tax reform as GST. How did the centre get the states on board with the idea of GST? How was a rapport of trust and understanding established between the centre and the states? Finally, the case looks briefly at the challenge of bringing a new technology-driven system into a nation that was just beginning to accustom itself to the concept of digitalization. The case explores how all these factors tied in to making GST possible, and a major success, at that.
Case Text:
Introduction
June 2024. The Government of India was gearing up to celebrate six successful years of implementing the
Goods and Service Tax (GST). Over the years, GST had brought in significant revenue for the government,
demonstrating an unprecedented year-on-year increase. The gross GST revenue collected in June 2024 was
INR 1.74 lakh crorei

, a 10% increase from collections recorded in May 2023. The indirect tax revenues had
steadily grown over the years – the GST implementation had caused no major disruptions (Exhibits 1 and 2).
The tax base more than doubled from 60 Lakh in July 2017 to 1.46 Crore in June 2024.
i

GST was the Indian government’s unified tax solution that subsumed all previously levied indirect taxes. It
was implemented in 2017 after years of discussion among multiple stakeholders. Despite multiple challenges,
the Indian government forged ahead with implementing GST, which yielded visibly positive results from its
early days. India’s biggest tax reform to date, GST, managed to eliminate several issues under the previous
VAT (Value Added Tax) system, such as cascading taxes, non-compliance, and lack of uniformity in tax rates.
While several countries have attempted to move to the GST system, a few have failed to implement it (British
Columbia in Canada) or have retained their previous tax systems (the USA). How did GST thrive in India,
winning against the myriad reservations different stakeholders held about its potential effectiveness? How
was a project of such scale, with so many diverse stakeholders, designed and steered to successful
implementation efficiently and effectively?
History of Tax Reform in India
India’s taxation system has a rich history of substantive reform. Governments broadly levy two types of taxes
on citizens: direct taxes (charged on the incomes, profits, and assets of individuals and economic entities, such
as personal income tax, corporate income tax, and property tax) and indirect taxes (charged on the production,
trade and consumption of goods and services). Direct taxes are generally seen as progressive taxes (since the
tax incidence increases with the taxpayer’s income or capability to pay taxes, and it is often easier to exempt
low earners from paying income taxes). Indirect taxes, on the other hand, are often regressive (in that tax
incidence decreases as a proportion of income with an increase in taxpayer’s ability to pay taxes). Indirect
taxes are, however, a big part of total tax revenues raised by the government (Exhibit 3).
Given its federal nature, India has a dual-structured taxation system. Only the central government can levy
direct taxes, and the Centre and the states can levy indirect taxes. Indeed, indirect taxes constitute a major
chunk of discretionary revenue for states. Indirect taxes in pre-independence India primarily comprised
customs duties and excise duties. After the country’s independence in 1947, the system of indirect taxes
became increasingly convoluted (Exhibit 4). While the central government taxed the production of goods
through excise duty (and later services through the services taxes), the states taxed trade through the
octroiii/entry tax and sales through the sales tax.

GST: THE STORY OF INDIA’S BIGGEST TAX REFORM 2
Each government decided which commodities to tax and which it wanted to exempt. Lists of exempt goods
changed over time, and goods that were taxed were taxed at different rates. This was true for excise duty and
state taxes such as the octroi and sales tax. What was taxed, and at what rate changed from state to state. This
resulted in a different tax base in each state, which differed from the central government. Information was
often outdated, unverified, and incomplete, so an accurate, comprehensive tax base could not be developed.
The differing governance levels between states and state tax departments did not help. This also led to
numerous disputes between businesses and governments, made further challenging by the lack of clarity
regarding goods classification and unclear definitions, because of which firms sometimes ended up in court
under charges of tax evasion. D P Nagendra Kumar, Member GST, Central Excise, Service tax and Legal,
recalled:
“Since a lot of classifications and definitions were unclear, it caused confusion for some regarding the kind of tax filing
they were required to do. For others, it was easy to misuse these ambiguities to evade taxes. Approximately 3,00,00 crore
fake invoices have been detected by the government till date. Over 1700 individuals were arrested for tax evasion.”
Introduction of MODVAT
The 1986 union budget recommended introducing a new system to attempt to resolve the issue of commodity
classification. This Modified Value-Added Tax (MODVAT) scheme would apply to all commodities covered
by 37 specified chapters of The Central Excise Tariff Act of 1985ii. MODVAT was meant to relieve the multiple
excise duties paid by final manufacturers.
Under the existing systems, before any commodity was produced, inputs were first taxed. Then, after the
commodity was produced, output was taxed again, including the input tax load. This caused a burden of
multiple taxation (i.e. “tax on tax”) with a cascading effect. Moreover, in the sales tax structure, whenever
there was a system of multi-point sales taxation, the burden of sales tax paid at each level of purchase was
added to subsequent levels of distributive trade, along with input tax load, thus further aggravating the
cascading effect (See Exhibit-5 for an illustration of cascading taxes and their effects in the pre-GST regime).
Such a complex system made tax compliance challenging and influenced business decisions.
MODVAT was introduced at the Central level for a select number of commodities to combat the growing
burden of multiple taxations, as was the case with the pre-existing Central excise duty and the State sales tax
systems. The primary benefit of introducing MODVAT as a replacement for central excise duty would be the
set-off, i.e., a deduction from the overall tax burden for input tax. In the case of MODVAT, a set-off was given
from the tax burden, not only for input tax paid, as was the case with the sales tax system, but also for tax paid
on previous purchases. With MODVAT, the problem of “tax on tax” and the related burden of the cascading
effect was, thus, removed.
Another issue that MODVAT aimed to address was the lack of uniformity among states regarding taxation
rates for various commodities and categories. Sales tax in many states was often significantly high, and states
were engaged in a competitive environment, imposing higher entry taxes. Since the Constitution granted
states the sovereignty to make these decisions independently, the union government needed to approach the
situation delicately. They had to find a way to harmonize state taxation rates while respecting the sovereignty
of the states.
Disadvantages of MODVAT
While implementing MODVAT addressed certain issues, it also introduced new challenges. One notable issue
was the matter of exemptions; there were numerous exemptions for specific industries and small businesses,
adding complexity to the tax structure. Additionally, the percentage of input credit as part of total tax revenue
increased substantially after MODVAT's implementation. This raised the need for careful monitoring of
MODVAT credits by manufacturers, as there were instances of credit being claimed multiple times,
submission of inadmissible inputs, incorrect documentation, missing invoices, and credits availed on falsified
documents. Addressing these discrepancies was challenging due to the lack of consensus on qualifying items
for MODVAT creditiii. The various ambiguities made it difficult to determine whether there were actual issues

GST: THE STORY OF INDIA’S BIGGEST TAX REFORM 3
or merely miscommunication and misinformation due to classification and definition inconsistencies.
Furthermore, there was ongoing discussion about whether MODVAT effectively eliminated the cascading of
taxes, as input credit remained unavailable for several commodities.
Introduction of CENVAT
In 1991, the Raja Chellaiah committee recommended replacing MODVAT with VAT, as VAT would help
lower the overall tax burden. As the name suggests, a Value Added Tax (VAT) is imposed on the value added
in each stage of production rather than the total value of the good, which will include the earlier taxes paid.
MODVAT was a modified version of VAT since, for a true VAT, no goods or services can be exempt from
taxation. MODVAT had too many exemptions. Indeed, MODVAT was an interim response to the challenges
in implementing VAT in one go. In a significant meeting of all the Chief Ministers, convened on November
16, 1999iv by Shri Yashwant Sinha, the then Union Finance Minister, two important decisions were taken.
First, before state-level VAT could be implemented, the sales tax rate war among the states would have to end,
and sales tax rates would need to be harmonised by implementing uniform floor rates of sales tax for different
categories of commodities with effect from January 1, 2000. Second, basis achievement of the first objective,
steps would be taken by the States for the introduction of State-level VAT after adequate preparation. A
Standing Committee of State Finance Ministers was formed to implement these decisions, which was then
made an Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers with the West Bengal Finance Minister and noted
economist, Asim Dasgupta as the chairperson. The committee’s efforts yielded near success in terms of their
first objective, which gave them the go-ahead to effect steps that different states would take for harmonization
of tax rates. The committee engaged in numerous discussions with stakeholders from each state as they
attempted to find a middle ground that would enable the state to accept certain common points of convergence
across states with regard to VAT while allowing for a measure of federal flexibility that was aligned with the
unique local characteristics of each state.
With adequate training, computerization of processes, and interaction with trade and industry, the states were
finally prepared to adopt VAT, which would come into effect beginning April 1, 2005. After its initial success,
VAT was introduced in a phased manner for all commodities as CENVAT (Central Value Added Tax) in 2002-
03. Subsequently, after a Constitutional Amendment empowering the Centre to levy taxes on services, these
service taxes were added to CENVAT in 2004-05.
CENVAT, an improved version of MODVAT, was meant to eradicate the problem of double taxation. Under
CENVAT, tax liability was to be significantly lower and easier to understand and adhere to - a precise set of
CENVAT rules (the CENVAT Credit Rules) were shared with manufacturers and consumers alike. CENVAT
aimed to simplify the taxation process further and eliminate cascading taxes.
Disadvantages of CENVAT and the conception of GST
Although CENVAT was meant to eliminate multiple taxation and simplify the system, it was difficult to
ascertain the tax breakdown on a certain product at its sale stage, as CENVAT applied taxation at every
production stage separately. The tax burden, instead of becoming lighter, had begun to vary quite wildly, as
every product went through a different number of production stages and hence came with differing rates of
taxes. Yet again, given that some exemptions continued under CENVAT, the classification issue came up: for
instance, how should a particular commodity be categorized in its raw material form if its potential use and
distribution was ex-ante unknown?
In the interim, however, while VAT was still a matter of discussion, alternate taxation systems were also
considered. Some felt strongly that even deeper reform than VAT was the need of the hour—and this was
reflected clearly in 2000 when the Kelkar Task Force, headed by renowned economist Dr. Vijay Kelkar,
proposed one tax to eliminate the need for all other indirect taxes: the GST. Dr. Kelkar explained:
“Rather than struggling with multiple taxes, the simplest solution would be a nationwide unified taxation system that
we hoped would reduce - even eliminate potentially - the cascading effect of taxes, simplify compliance for taxation, and
to create a common tax base for the whole country. However, not everyone believed this to be the best solution...”

GST: THE STORY OF INDIA’S BIGGEST TAX REFORM 4

By 2003, the task force had prepared and published a list of recommendations for the GST system, how it
would operate, what would be taxed and what kinds of exemptions would be made, and other relevant
details. The proposal itself, and the ensuing recommendations, countered varied responses, most expressing
uncertainty as to how a single taxation system could possibly work in India, across all states and union
territories.
Early responses to recommendations of the Kelkar Task Force
The Kelkar Task Force shared a set of recommendations regarding indirect tax after many rounds of debate,
discussion, and revision through the early 2000s. Some of the proposed tariff proposals gained popular
approval, but critics felt that many prior suggestions needed to be considered. In a 2003 Economic and Political
Weekly commentary paperv, Sukumar Mukhopadhyay critiqued some of the recommendations.
While Mukhopadhyay agreed with the report that CENVAT led to cascading taxes and that one unified tax
structure would be much more helpful in eliminating them, he noted that the task force’s recommendations
did not account for the revenue loss that might likely be incurred with such a taxation system. Kelkar
suggested 14 per cent as the standard indirect tax rate, with food items being taxed at 0 or 6 per cent and 20
per cent for motor vehicles, air conditioners and aerated water. This was lower than the average tax rate
prevailing at the time. The committee argued that lower rates and tax rationalization would sufficiently
expand the tax base to make up for the loss in tax revenue due to lower rates. Mukhopadhyay was
unconvinced and believed that the tax on items of conspicuous consumption – like cars and ACs – need not
be lowered.
Additionally, Mukhopadhyay’s paper pointed out the administrative difficulties of a fully computerized
system—like the committee was proposing—without simplifying the tax regime. Both these concerns
foreshadowed future discussions on GST.
The Kelkar task force report also encountered some political opposition. Many of the recommendations
presented were opposed, with parties stating that they were largely in favour of corporates and large
businesses and completely sidelined the country's larger population, i.e., the working middle class, senior
citizens, and farmers.
The evaluation of the GST was placed alongside growing recognition of the issues with VAT. Meanwhile, after
that was implemented country-wide in 2005, issues with the system, including, but not limited to, the
continued cascading of taxes, emerged.
Although VAT had proven to be a far superior replacement for the erstwhile taxation system, it was not
without its flaws. One issue that emerged was related to the non-inclusion of some central taxes in CENVAT,
such as additional customs duty, surcharges, etc., which meant that manufacturers and dealers would have
to go without benefits like service tax set-off. At the state level, several indirect taxes on goods and services,
such as luxury tax, entertainment tax, etc., had not yet been subsumed in VAT. Thus, the CENVAT load on
goods and services remained, and the cascading tax problem emerged again. The VAT system was lacking
and needed to be improved upon.
GST: Challenges in Driving Adoption
GST was meant to be the new tax system that had learned from its predecessors’ mistakes and improved upon
the same. An improved version of VAT, all indirect taxes would finally be included under GST, and the
CENVAT load on goods and services would be eliminated since VAT itself would be replaced. Several other
problems would be solved with GST as well: while under VAT, different rates of VAT applied in different
states, and each state had its own tax rules, GST would have every state follow the same rate and structure,
for uniform taxation. (See Exhibit-6 for key components of the tax regime)

GST: THE STORY OF INDIA’S BIGGEST TAX REFORM 5
Although the purpose of GST was to simplify the taxation system in India, implementing GST itself proved
to be a complicated task. Given that multiple stakeholders were involved, the needs and issues of each
stakeholder needed to be considered and resolved to some extent to get their buy-in for GST implementation.
Further, several administrative constraints emerged at the Centre and State levels. The challenges faced by

GoI in GST implementation were nuanced and not easy to tackle, and more would emerge post-
implementation.

Getting state Buy-in
Under GST, some states worried that they would incur revenue loss, particularly those involved in many
inter-state transactions, as the distribution of revenue between the states had yet to be clarified. Rajasthan,
Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Maharashtra, Jharkhand, and Chhattisgarh, as well as Tamil Nadu and
Karnataka (manufacturing states), were unhappy about GST because of this.
Further, getting the state governments’ buy-in for GST was tough because they each had different incentives
that appealed to them. Each state had its own distinct tax structure, taxation rates, and systems, which had
been designed, for the most part, to benefit the state itself above others. Naturally, states disagreed on a
uniform tax structure and system because each felt that their benefits were being taken away.

To get the states completely on board with GST, the GoI and the GST Council also engaged in a series of wide-
ranging dialogues and discussions with stakeholders from each state, aiming to understand their grievances

and to try and offer incentives they would not want to refuse. This was immensely challenging, as it would
not be feasible to meet each state’s widely differing demands, and yet, failing to meet any of them at all would
turn the states further against GST.
To resolve these issues, the government declared that compensation funds would be given to the states that
lost out on indirect tax revenue. To that end, the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act 2017
was introduced to compensate the states for their revenue loss due to GST. This compensation would apply
from the date GST had come into effect, covering five years or a period as determined fit by the GST council.
[See Exhibit 6]
Reservations over compliance
Under the previous tax regime, assesses would have to file 13 tax returns in a financial year. However, under
the GST regime, the assesses would have to file up to 37 returns in a year, including an annual return and
three-monthly tax filings. For businesses and service providers that operated in multiple states, this meant
filing multiple returns across the states and maintaining documentation accordingly. According to GST laws,
businesses must register separately in every state they operate in. This, in turn, meant compliance and
logistical issues. The introduction of GST also meant that many businesses that had never paid taxes would
come under the tax net.
To ease businesses' compliance burden, the government decided to roll out the changes in a phased manner
so that there was plenty of time to get used to them. Taxpayers were informed of ways to contact the
government for assistance, and several campaigns were launched to raise awareness about the new practices.
Administrative and Technological issues
Rolling out an entirely new taxation system in a country as vast and diverse as India also carried its share of
administrative difficulties. The GST system came with Goods and Service Tax Network’s new digital taxation
platform, which, for the first time, attempted a feat of great complexity: to create a unified platform for indirect
taxes for all taxpayers, shared by the Centre and the states. The multiple IT systems used previously by the
States and the Centre would have to be integrated into one interface, to create a virtual ecosystem for all the
stakeholders to interact. However, this was much easier said than done. Kumar recalled:

GST: THE STORY OF INDIA’S BIGGEST TAX REFORM 6
“Pre-GST, there were about 65,00,000 taxpayers registered in the database. Since multiple taxation was the norm at the
time, many of the taxpayers might also have been availing different tax credit, but as they transitioned to GST from 2017,
these tax credits would have to be transitioned- and translated accurately- into the new system as well. This posed a huge
challenge.”
In many states, the existing IT infrastructure was insufficient to take on the new platform and its requirements.
This led to systems crashing and myriad technical issues. Further, and a larger issue was that this was among
the firsts for India’s digital economy. Upender Gupta, IRS Chief Commissioner CGST (retd.) recalled:
“The states were all in different situations. In some states such as Maharashtra and Karnataka, VAT had already been
automated a while ago, and so they did not have much trouble with GST’s online system. However, in contrast, states
like Bihar and Jharkhand had not even considered automation and were completely at sea. Yet other states like Punjab
and Haryana were primarily agricultural states, whose produce was paid for by FCI (Food Corporation of India) and
hence taxes were levied on FCI as well- many of the farmers were thus not even in the database.”
Most people working in banks and government administrative offices had never worked or interacted with
this level of technology before. For businesses and taxpayers as well, the new platform was an alien way of
interacting with the tax system. This meant that relevant individuals and teams would have to undergo
thorough training to understand and utilize the system in question.
To address existing technical issues, GSTN continuously monitored the activity on the platform, engaged in
active troubleshooting, and made improvements where and when required.
Driving Transformation
In 2006, the then Minister of Finance (MoF) for India, Mr P. Chidambaram, announced that the Government
of India (GoI) aimed to roll out the GST soon over the subsequent years. At this point, the MoF emphasized
a) the challenges encountered in the rollout of VAT in the past and b) the collaborative efforts already
underway between the states and union territories under the VAT regime. This knowledge would prove
valuable as the government attempted to anticipate the challenges; they would face in implementing GST.
That is, the VAT implementation offered lessons to get states to work together under GST.
Thereafter, the central government began holding detailed discussions with the state governments, which
resulted in the first GST discussion paper in 2009, a key recommendation of which was the dual structure for
GST in India. The government had to consider how best to introduce the dual tax structure so that all the states
and union territories were in harmony. Another key consideration was the matter of tax exemptions. Since the
challenges posed by exemptions under the previous taxation systems had accumulated and grown over the
decades, it was time to revisit them, too. Kumar said:
“In the pre-GST era, we were operating with more than 4,000 exemptions at the central tax level, and nearly 600
exemptions within state-level VAT taxation. It was a major challenge to sort through these exemptions and identify
which ones we would have to necessarily keep under GST, and which to eliminate.”
The first discussion paper also noted that dual jurisdiction on taxation and other required reforms would be
possible only if certain amendments were made to the Constitution to accommodate GST.
Constitutional Amendment
GoI aimed to launch and implement GST in a manner that allowed both the Centre and the states the right to
levy and collect GST and that GST laws applied uniformly across the Centre and the states. It became evident
that a constitutional amendment would be required to make this possible. In 2011, the Ministry of Finance
introduced the Constitution (115th Amendment) Bill (GST Bill)vi to the Lok Sabha.
The bill proposed amendments to the Constitution to introduce the GST and grant authority to both the Centre
and the states to frame GST laws. However, due to resistance from some states over perceived potential
revenue loss, the bill lapsed, and the Lok Sabha was dissolved as the reins of the government changed hands

GST: THE STORY OF INDIA’S BIGGEST TAX REFORM 7
in 2014. As soon as the new government had settled in, the new MoF for India, Arun Jaitley, began the steps
for reintroducing the bill and was successful soon after.
Once the bill had been passed, the actual amendments to the constitution were made, referred to as the
Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016; the Act led to the insertion, deletion, and
modification of specific articles in the Constitutioniii. The changes made included-
● Formation of the GST council: The President would now have the authority to form a committee
comprising legislative representatives from both the Centre and the States, referred to as the GST
Council. To foster a spirit of mutual trust and promote shared responsibility, the Council's voting
process to decide gave a weightage of one-third of the total votes to the Centre and two-thirds to the
states. The council would be in charge of making, modifying, and addressing changes related to the
GST in India.
● The power to make laws under the IGST Act (dealing exclusively with inter-state supplies) would be
solely with the Parliament on the recommendations of the GST council. The state and union territory
legislatures would still be able to make laws on their own GST impositions, except for IGST. Until the

GST council gave its recommendations, certain goods, such as natural gas, crude petroleum, high-
speed diesel, motor spirit, and aviation turbine fuel, would be excluded from the scope of GST.

● The distribution of revenue collected from inter-state supplies between the Centre and the State was
modified. Marking a significant change from the proposition in the 2011 GST Bill (that only the
Parliament would have the authority to levy taxes on the import of goods), the Amendment stated
that the import of goods would now also come under inter-state supplies, and the GST council could
make laws regarding this. Further, it bestowed upon the Centre the power to levy IGST on the import
of goods, which was beneficial for the taxpayer, who could now enjoy the credit of IGST paid upon
import in the current stage of the supply chain.
● States would not be allowed to tax goods purchased or sold outside their territory, including import
sales and purchases. A further amendment included services along with goods, according to which
services rendered outside the state territory could no longer be taxed by the state.
Representation from Key Stakeholders
Since GST was to be the largest tax reform initiative in Indian history, multiple stakeholders were involved in
the initial discussions, and more would join as the project progressed toward completion and implementation.
At the helm was the then MoF, Arun Jaitley. Jaitley, who led the GST project from 2014 to its launch in 2017,
was widely credited with shepherding the GST reform through.
The 2011 version of the GST Bill envisaged an external judicial body to manage any dispute resolution related
to GST implementation. This was changed in the 2014 draft. Jaitley declared that the GST council would have
the authority to resolve disputes and frame laws regarding GST. However, the Council would only begin
operating at full capacity by September 2016, until which time an Empowered Committee of State Finance
Ministers would engage with other stakeholders.

The key parties that were part of the Council and involved closely in the GST project included-
The central government and the state governments: Officials from the central government and each state

government came together to facilitate the planning and subsequent roll-out of GST. From the central
government, the Union Finance Minister, representatives from the Ministry of Finance, and the Department
of Revenue played an active role in discussions with the state governments and negotiations. Finance
ministers from each state joined in the policy dialogue and shared their inputs as well as respective concerns
regarding GST- they formed the Empowered Committee of the State Finance Ministers and led much of the
project in terms of drafting the GST laws from 2014 to 2016. The GST Council, consisting of state and central

Customs (CBIC) participated throughout the project as India’s largest recognized indirect tax authority.
GSTN: To digitalize the tax-filing process, GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) was given the onus of
creating an online GST portal on which users could register themselves or their businesses, file taxes easily
and paper-free, and manage other compliance-related activities. The Central and State governments and
taxpayers would use this platform. It was to be a unified digital platform encompassing all tax-filing
requirements previously scattered across different systems.
Tax professionals: Tax professionals and legal advisors played a significant role in assisting the GST council
with the legal aspects of implementing GST and overall compliance. Their input helped draft the GST laws,
implement them, and transition into the GST system. Legal firms also helped raise awareness about GST and
its uses and benefits.
Businesses: Businesses large and small would be greatly affected by the roll-out of GST; as such, it was
necessary to get them involved in the project right away. Several businesses and industry experts joined in to
share their insights and began to work on updating their processes and systems so they would comply with
GST. Being hands-on with the process, these businesses could also pilot-test the GST system early on and
share their experiences regarding any hiccups or issues they observed with the system.
Legislative representatives: The Parliament of India and representatives from each state legislature played a
key role in GST implementation, primarily in the constitutional amendment made for GST.
Trade unions across industries: Trade unions and authorities from various industries chipped in to offer
industry-specific knowledge and raise issues about how GST might impact their specific industries. This
helped the government make more informed decisions regarding each industry.
Steps in the process of Implementation
The Union budget was announced in early 2014. At once, Jaitley urged the GST council to fast-track the GST
project, which had already faced delay due to several restrictions, most of which had now been eliminated.
As first steps, he suggested that the Council focus primarily on two key tasks: one, to gather and combine all
taxable events (manufacturing, sale or purchase under VAT, excise provisions, etc.) under the broad head of
supply; and two, to identify best practices used internationally in other nations following GST like systems,
study them and take inspiration from a few to draft GST laws for India.

Next, the Empowered Committee for State Finance Ministers was tasked with rounding up resources-
government officers with significant experience with tax, policy planning and research were handpicked by

the committee. They were then grouped into three sub-teams, which would each focus on drafting designated
sections of the GST law and would work in tandem in the interest of time. The three teams would then meet
to share their progress and discuss any emerging points of conflict regarding differences in the laws proposed.
Consensus-building was of utmost importance at this point. Kumar, who had been part of two sub-committees
one after the other, said:
“One of the primary drivers behind GST’s success today is the way we worked together to build consensus. Whenever
there was disagreement regarding some part of the law being drafted, it was up to the rest of us as committee members to
have a dialogue with the objecting member(s) and come to a middle ground. If the subject matter was non-negotiable, we
still would not push it further, but would instead put it away to discuss at a later point. Consensus was that important
to the GST exercise, because we held that the Centre and the States were to be equal partners under the GST regime.”
Meanwhile, as the committees worked on drafting GST laws, the process of automating the entire tax system
and database commenced alongside. It had already been decided early on that GST would be completely
computerized and an online tax filing system, for which GSTN was to be developed as a platform, but this
presented a major challenge. This complete digitalization was a first for the country’s tax system. To address

this and to build the tax department’s capacity to handle GSTN, a mass training programme for government
officers was launched in 2016. Kumar added:
“Over 50,000 officers required training. Many of us who had been part of the GST law drafting committees, were selected
as resource trainers this time, and were tasked with training about 1500 officers who would be referred to as ‘master
trainers. These master trainers would then impart training to officers across the country, spanning both the Centre and
the States. For this, we prepared a lot of structured training material, from FAQs to presentations and capacity-building
workshops. The entire exercise, a massive investment in itself, took us seven to eight months.”
Additionally, to raise sector-wise awareness among trade associations, businesses, and consumers alike, the
committees prepared and launched mass campaigns regarding GST across the nation, with advertisements
and other informational materials circulated from 2016 through 2017 until the launch of GST. Gupta recalled:
“We conducted over 10,000 workshops for traders and representatives from various industries. Every week, there were
three to four of these workshops in progress across the country. We travelled all over India to make this happen. The then
Revenue Secretary, Dr. Hasmukh Adhiya, came up with this idea: GST ki Masterclass (A Masterclass for GST), a
televised segment in which viewers all over India could watch officers like me discuss GST and the issues surrounding
it. We kept our language and our points simple and clear, so knowledge around GST would become as accessible as
possible for the whole country.”
This helped establish a sense of transparency and cleared up misconceptions the general populace had about
GST.
Lessons Learned
GST, as an exercise in tax reform, took over a decade to implement and ushered in a unique set of learnings
for all stakeholders involved.
Accommodating the views of all stakeholders
Since GST involved multiple stakeholders, it quickly became clear that not all would agree on every matter.
The opposite was truer: very rarely would there be immediate agreement, and sometimes there would be
none. However, the idea that any individual or party’s opinions would be valued above the rest was discarded
almost at once, and Jaitley clarified that no decision would be taken without total consensus. This meant a
series of dialogues and discussions over quite possibly every topic related to GST and the GST laws. Still, the
committee was ready to oblige- because taking the route of conflict resolution and discussion meant that the
outcome, the GST system, would result from all the stakeholders’ input, with no one left behind. All would
have a stake in the outcome. Gupta stated:
“Taking collective responsibility for the project was of paramount importance. We wanted to make sure every stakeholder
was involved and encouraged them to participate in the project. The number of clarifications issued before and during
the implementation of GST is unprecedented. Till date, over 211 circulars, 538 non-tax notifications, and 533 tax-related
notifications have been released by the GoI during the course of the GST project: the aim was to ensure everyone was in
the loop. The project would never have succeeded otherwise.”
Building Trust
The GST project commenced in earnest around the time when there was distrust between the States and the
Centre. One of the key reasons behind this was that when VAT was introduced, the states had been promised
compensation owing to the decrease in the rate of CST (Central Sales Tax), but they believed they had not
received this compensation. Gupta explained:
“The states perceived that they had not received the promised compensation- in reality, they may not have received it yet
at that point of time due to a delay, or other factors such as wrong documentation or technical issues. But in their minds,
they had been lied to by the Centre and could not trust the Centre again. Although the central government under Jaitley’s

GST: THE STORY OF INDIA’S BIGGEST TAX REFORM 10
helm had promised to compensate the states for any anticipated revenue loss in the coming months post-implementation,
the states remained wary of whether this promise would be upheld.”
It became clear that a certain level of trust had to be built between the Centre and the States- and among the
states themselves. To try and foster this rapport, a system of co-convenorship was established. Under this
system, a state government officer and a central government officer would be grouped to handle matters
relating to a singular aspect, for instance, payments. Several such groups were made to handle different
aspects and, this way, officers from each state were involved in at least one of these groups. This move played
an essential role in winning the confidence of the states. The system of co-convenorship became a system of
cross-empowerment, wherein the Centre and the States could actively support each other’s efforts, put their
differences aside, and trust one another as they moved towards a unified goal: the GST.
Continually learning and adapting
Given the multiple levels of opposition and criticism GST faced before implementation, it seemed like it might
never be a good time to launch the system. Kumar recalled,
“New hitches emerged in the place of ones we had already resolved. We were not ready, it was said, there was too much
to be handled and there was not enough time. How could so many lakhs of taxpayers be onboarded to a wholly digital
platform in such little time? How would they learn how to use it? How would the system take the load? How would we,
the committees, come up with the perfect GST framework, in total consensus? These were the questions plaguing us. But
Mr. Jaitley said that we had waited long enough, and if we kept waiting, the correct time to launch would never arrive,
there would always be some or the other new issue. ‘Let the issues emerge’, he said. ‘We will learn from them and improve
again and again.’ So, we went ahead with it. It was always fast-paced, we did not know if and when we would see the
finish-line, but the learnings from this initiative are parallel to no other. The sense of satisfaction is immense- as we knew
right from the start, however long it took, we were making history.”
Post-GST implementation, the GST Council continued to note the issues cropping up within the system and
made sure to meet at least once every three months for further discussion, possible changes, and resolutions.
Thus, the learning process continued far beyond the launch of GST.
Conclusion - The way forward
GST was a nearly two-decade-long dream that had finally turned into reality and had now completed five
years successfully. While data and the consensus proved that GST had been the right reform for India’s
taxation system, the council knew the road ahead was still long. Could the existing GST system be improved
for efficiency and ease of use? What improvements could be made? How could compliance be further
simplified? Could the technological capabilities be built upon for a more robust IT infrastructure supporting
GSTN’s platform?

Case Study Title: Implementation of Poshan Abhiyaan in Kokrajhar district, Assam
Case Study Description: This case study highlights the innovative approach of Ms. Varnali Dekha in addressing nutrition-related challenges faced by children in Kokrajhar district, Assam. Under the broader “Poshan” initiative, Ms. Dekha employs a multifaceted six-pronged strategy designed to tackle these issues comprehensively. Her approach integrates various creative interventions aimed at improving nutritional outcomes, enhancing community awareness, and fostering sustainable practices. Through this case study, we explore the effectiveness of her strategies and their impact on the well-being of children in the region, providing valuable insights into the practical application of targeted nutritional interventions.
Case Text:
Ms. Varnali Deka reflects deeply on her journey with the Poshan initiative in Kokrajhar, where one memory
from the Jwthwn initiative stands out vividly. During a visit to the home of a malnourished little girl she
was assigned to care for, she discovered that the child’s parents, tea estate workers reliant on daily wages,
had been asked to stay home for her visit, resulting in a loss of income for the day. This realisation was
heart-wrenching for her. Although she immediately compensated the family for their lost wages and
provided additional support for the child, the incident highlighted the severe struggles faced by the tea
estate workers. From that moment on, she made it a priority to personally connect with parents before her
visits, ensuring that her presence would not disrupt their livelihoods.
Caring for this malnourished child and witnessing her gradual transformation became a cherished
milestone in Ms. Deka’s journey. The Jwthwn initiative, as part of the larger Poshan program, transformed
the lives of 719 such children. Each child was assigned a volunteering government official who provided
crucial support to the children and their families in their fight against malnutrition. Through her work, Ms.
Deka found not just a role, but a calling—one that left a lasting impact on both her heart and the lives of
those she served.
Background
During her tenure as Deputy Commissioner of Kokrajhar, Ms. Varnali initiated a year-round campaign
focused on children's nutrition. Inspired by the positive outcomes she observed during the annual Poshan
Maahiand Poshan Pakhwadaii, she was determined to make "Poshan" a continuous, year-long activity.
Additionally, the poor performance of Kokrajhar on the NFHS-5

iii indices further motivated her to prioritise

nutrition as a key area of focus. (See Exhibit 3)
The primary challenge Ms Varnali encountered was not the availability of nutritional resources but rather
how to motivate the community to integrate proper nutrition into their daily lives. She recognised that the

(https://poshanabhiyaan.gov.in/)
ii Poshan Pakhwada celebrated as a part of Poshan Abhiyan is a 15 day-long event, celebrated to build

resources in a number of cases. The objective was to foster a deeper awareness among parents and children
about the importance of their dietary choices, aiming to instil lasting behavioural changes that would
prioritise nutrition
To tackle this, Ms. Varnali focused on building awareness and encouraging community ownership of the
issue. She strategically utilised existing resources from various departments, collaborating with
stakeholders to brainstorm and develop initiatives designed to improve Human Development Index (HDI)
indicators for young children. By emphasising sustainable, community-driven efforts, she aimed to create
long-term, impactful changes in nutritional habits that would benefit the community as a whole.
Kokrajhar’s child nutrition indicators
The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) is a vital, multi-round survey conducted across India to collect
essential data on population health and nutrition. Overseen by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
(MoHFW), the survey serves as a critical tool for monitoring and improving various health indicators
nationwide. However, the NFHS-5 report for Kokrajhar district revealed an unexpected decline in several
key indicators related to child feeding practices and nutritional status compared to NFHS-4. Indicators such
as breastfeeding rates, nutrition, height-for-age, and weight-for-age—crucial factors for the mental,
emotional, and physical development of children—showed alarming gaps, particularly during the critical
"1000 days" or golden window of early childhood, indicating a pressing need for better child care practices
in the region.
The "1000 days" window, which constitutes the nine months of gestation and the first two years of an
infant's life, is the most important phase for determining the mental, emotional, and physical growth of a
child. Nutrition provided to both mother and child during this period significantly influences the Infant
Mortality Rate (IMR) iv and Under-5 Mortality Rate (U5MR)v, which are essential indicators of nutrition
and health in India. The decline in these indicators in Kokrajhar highlighted the need for targeted
interventions to improve maternal and child nutrition during this critical developmental phase.
Jan Bhagidari Concept
Jan Bhagidari as a term was introduced to us by our Honourable Prime Minister in the year 2016, to invite
citizen participation in the governance processes. Literally translating to “people’s participation” this term
ever since became an essential cornerstone for the Indian democracy.
Community ownership and demand were identified as critical factors for the initiative's success and

sustainability. By promoting, Jan Bhagidari from within the community, the initiative aimed to ensure long-
term impact and meaningful change in addressing nutritional needs.

Case Study Title: Chandrayaan 3
Case Study Description: This case explores the Indian Space Research Organisation’s (ISRO) landmark achievement with Chandrayaan-3, which made India the first country to land near the lunar South Pole on August 23, 2023. It highlights the strategic leadership, structured failure analysis, and risk management that defined the mission — along with ISRO’s hallmark strengths in cost-effective innovation, organizational culture, and a balanced approach to collaboration and self-reliance. The case offers insights into how ISRO’s inclusive, learning-driven ecosystem enabled a bold leap in space exploration, setting the stage for even more ambitious missions ahead.
Case Text:
‘Anyone who goes to space tries to look at his own country first, but soon it appears that there is no boundary between
the countries and the entire world is one family where our destinies are integrated.’

—Rakesh Sharma1
It was 5:43 pm on August 23, 2023. The atmosphere at the Mission Operations Complex at ISRO Telemetry,
Tracking, and Command Network (ISTRAC) in Bengaluru, India was electric. It was a mix of confidence
laced with some apprehension. Anxiety was palpable as scientists bore the weight of their nation's
expectations. Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) Chairman, Dr S. Somanath, and his colleagues,
had their eyes glued to the large consoles as Vikram, the lander, began its descent. The Automatic Landing
Sequence (ALS) was initiated. All four throttleable engines were activated for a powered descent. With
everything working seamlessly, India was poised to create history in the next 20 minutes.
Rewind to September 7, 2019, when the situation was no different. Every parameter was on target during
the first phase of the descent, called the Rough Braking Phase. Scientists cheered as the Vikram lander
successfully descended to 2.1 km above the lunar surface. However, the jubilation was short-lived. Tense
moments followed as everyone witnessed Vikram deviating from its path while transitioning between the
final two critical phases—the Absolute Navigation Phase (also known as the camera coasting phase) and
the Fine Braking Phase. What unfolded next shattered the dreams of 1.4 billion people. Earlier that day,
while addressing journalists, then ISRO Chairman, Dr K. Sivan’s description of the last phase of Vikram’s
landing as ’15 minutes of terror’ became prophetic. The nation stood silent, yet resolute, as it witnessed
a teary-eyed Dr Sivan being consoled by the Prime Minister.
Four years later, India once again stood on the cusp of scripting history. Would everything go as planned
tonight? Considering the vast number of landing tests and simulations completed before the launch of
Chandrayaan-3 Dr Somanath felt confident. However, such odysseys into unknown realms were always
fraught with uncertainties. No number of successful tests could guarantee the success of such hugely
complex missions. Just three days earlier, the Russian Luna 25 had crash-landed near the lunar south polar
region, a sobering reminder of the mission's risks. (See Exhibit 1).

1 Rakesh Sharma is the first Indian astronaut to orbit in space. In April 1984, he flew aboard Soyuz T-11,
as part of the Soviet Interkosmos programme.

CHANDRAYAAN 3: ISRO’S INCREDIBLE ODYSSEY INTO SPACE 2

India held its breath as Vikram entered the terminal descent after completing the Fine Braking Phase.
Schools across the country were live streaming the event. Finally, at 6:03 p.m., young school children of
Bharat witnessed the nation’s moment of glory as they watched the dust rise from the lunar surface. Vikram
had achieved a perfect touch down on the lunar south pole. Spontaneously, scientists, engineers, and
technicians at the Mission Operation Complex (MOX) erupted in joy. The smile on Dr Somanath’s face as
he rose from his seat to shake hands with his team members captured the nation’s elation. As the first
country to land on the challenging region of the lunar south pole, India had achieved a milestone hitherto
unaccomplished by mankind.
The Genesis
The legacy of ISRO since its inception in August 1969—or even earlier when the Government of India set
up the Indian National Committee for Space Research (See Exhibit 2) under the Department of Atomic
Energy in 1962—has been shaped by the vision of legendary leaders like Vikram Sarabhai, MGK Menon,
U.R. Rao, and Satish Dhawan.

2 Each of these individuals contributed not just to the space programme but
also to the national cause, propelling India to the global high table through soft knowledge power.
‘ISRO's future is no longer a future for India alone. It is a future for humanity. It is a future for humankind, how it
will move out of the planet called Earth’, proclaimed Dr K. Kasturirangan, former Chairman of ISRO.3
The journey of ISRO, becoming a beacon of hope and dreams not only for Indians but for all of mankind,
has been arduous. The nature of challenges might have changed, but the determination to overcome them
remains steadfast. This resoluteness is now an inherent characteristic of the organisation embedded in its
very DNA. Time and again, this persistence has left the world enthralled by ISRO’s ability to manoeuvre
complexities despite resource constraints.
‘Add up all the money that we have spent on ISRO since its inception, and still, it would be less than the annual
NASA budget,’ said Dr A.S. Kiran Kumar, former Chairman of ISRO. Even the cost of launching
Chandrayaan-3, at approximately US $74 million, was considerably lower than production costs of many
Hollywood or Bollywood blockbusters.
Resourcefully Reimagining Restraints ISRO’s innovative thinking has been an enabler in transforming
its dreams into reality. Where else could one see rockets meant for transportation into space being carried
on bicycles and old, creaking bullock carts?
i
(See Exhibit 3). In 1981, the American magazine NEWSWEEK
published a picture showing APPLE, India’s first indigenously built experimental communication satellite,
which was developed in ‘just two years, with limited infrastructure in industrial sheds’,

ii being transported on a
bullock cart from a hangar to the test centre (See Exhibit 4). The photograph was captioned: ‘Collision of
Centuries’.iii
Even today, this spirit of overcoming resource limitations through ingenuity endures. The absence of a

powerful rocket did not deter ISRO scientists from launching the Mars Orbiter Mission and Chandrayaan-
1. They overcame the shortcoming using the sling-shot mechanism (See Exhibit 5), to harness Earth’s

gravity in transferring the orbiter to the lunar or Martian gravitational field. Inventive thinking and
2 All these personalities are former Chairmen of ISRO.
3 This quotation by Dr K. Kasturirangan, and other subsequent quotations attributed to Dr Kasturirangan,
Dr A.S. Kiran Kumar, and Dr S. Somanath—all of whom have headed ISRO as Chairman—have been
sourced from the interviews conducted by Dr R. Balasubramaniam, Member—Human Resource, Capacity
Building Commission, Govt. of India.

CHANDRAYAAN 3: ISRO’S INCREDIBLE ODYSSEY INTO SPACE 3
resilience in the face of technology or resource constraints have been ISRO’s hallmark, a legacy instilled by
its founding leaders.
Chandrayaan 3: India Rises like a Phoenix
‘Nobody gets Mars right on the first try. The US didn’t, Russia didn’t, the Europeans didn’t. But on September 24,
2014, India did. That’s when the Mangalyaan...went into orbit around the Red Planet, a technological feat no other
Asian nation has yet achieved.’

– ‘Time’ American News Magazineiv
ISRO, however, did not always get everything right on the first try. No space agency does. A failure study
conducted by NASA observed that 41.3% of all small satellites launched by space agencies between the
years 2000 and 2016 were unsuccessful.v The study implies that almost one out of every two modern small
satellite missions will result in either a total or a partial mission failure. ISRO’s success rate was better.
From 2000 until February 2024, out of 83 launches, ISRO succeeded in all but five, which equates to a failure
rate of only 6.02% (See Exhibit 6), which is comparable with NASA. However, the pressure on ISRO to
deliver is significantly higher, given that India, a developing country, is often criticised for investing in
expensive space programmes when countrymen living below the poverty line are struggling to make ends
meet.
Failure Analysis: ‘Everything will Fail’
The criticism was unforgiving when, in 1979, the satellite launch vehicle, SLV-3 failed to place the Rohini
satellite into orbit. It plunged into a watery grave instead. The harshest criticism, nonetheless, was
encountered in 1987, when, after a gap of four years, ASLV-1, described as a ‘quantum jump’ in space,
plunged into the Bay of Bengal. The cash loss was assessed at ₹6 crore.
‘It is only a setback in time. It is only when you stumble that you can get up and walk better,’ the then Prime
Minister of the country said.vi

However, within 15 months, when the Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle
(ASLV-2) could not achieve orbit, it was the toughest time for ISRO, as India also faced an embargo from
the developed nations.
ISRO set up high-profile failure analysis committees each time after a mission failure. These committees
included not just ISRO scientists but multiple external experts too. A thorough diagnostic examination was
undertaken, and each time, India rose like a phoenix. The ambitious launch vehicle ASLV-3, in which ISRO
introduced the ‘closed-loop guidance system’, was finally successfully launched in 1992.
‘For any organisation, especially a space agency, success and failures are an integral part. How the organisation deals
with that success and failure is very important. This is where culture plays a role. At ISRO, we have looked for what
caused the failure rather than who caused the failure’, explained Dr Kiran Kumar.vii
ISRO uses the same analysis process even today. With refinements and enhanced follow-up actions, the
possibility of failure is reduced over time.
‘Moon cannot be created on earth, especially the gravity field cannot be replicated. One cannot create the absence of
atmosphere or other perturbations like radiation. When Chandrayaan-2 was executed, there were certain shortcomings
in terms of the absence of sufficient data. ISRO had no data about the moon other than what Chandrayaan-1 had sent.
But someone must take the first steps into unknown realms. So, the process began with the help of various other
players. Even the gravity model of the moon was borrowed,’ elaborated Dr Somanath. Yet, there will always be
a certain level of uncertainty in such missions, which one can only attempt to minimise.

CHANDRAYAAN 3: ISRO’S INCREDIBLE ODYSSEY INTO SPACE 4
To increase the probability of success for Chandrayaan-3, ISRO initiated reviews at multiple levels,
including peer-level reviews. Greater participation from academia was facilitated to elevate the rigour of
understanding a complex problem in its entirety. Global experts were invited to review the scientific
approaches and scrutinise the entire scenario sceptically. Software rigour testing, like helicopter drop tests
and crane-based testing, was conducted on a large scale across domains.
‘This is the culture that we have created internally: we do not assume everything will succeed; we rather assume that
everything will fail. Many failure modes were addressed, but none occurred in the real flight. This is the beauty of this
system: Your ability to visualise numerous possibilities of failure saves you from real catastrophe,’ Dr Somanath
contended.
Using Failure as a Springboard
The analysis of what went wrong during the soft landing of the Chandrayaan-2 mission went on for almost
a year. This understanding was synthesised into a case where success could be achieved under all possible
conditions. After the first year of understanding, scientists considered the necessary design modifications.
Additional sensors were included, and more fuel was added to effectively manage various scenarios while
simultaneously decreasing the number of throttleable engines from five to four. The entire model was
rigorously tested in the third year, considering numerous perturbations. Test cases were increased, and the
boundaries of performance were extended. Newer assessments like ground tests and simulations, on orbit
testing, and evaluations were introduced and extensively implemented. These evaluations were a game
changer and marked a clear improvement over Chandrayaan-2.
For the first time, ISRO also introduced a cross-functional review system. Satellites were built in the satellite
centre, and rockets in the rocket centre. The new review system ensured that the scientists at the rocket
centre analysed the work of the satellite centre, and vice versa. Simulation test beds were created in other
centres, and data was cross verified to ensure no mistakes were made.
As India celebrated the success of Chandrayaan-3, Dr Somanath reflected on the capacity-building process
undertaken over the past three years, a classic example of using failures as springboards to success. He also
attributed the achievement to a culture of continual learning and being in sync with the overarching
purpose of ISRO.
A Strong Sense of Purpose
‘There is a larger purpose that drives people in ISRO...everybody who is working, whether he is working for a satellite,
working for a rocket, or working for an application; all of them see the big picture of space technology serving specific
national requirements. And that itself is a great motivator, affirmed Dr Kiran Kumar.
Dr Sarabhai, as the first ISRO chairman and a visionary leader, was convinced that space science had
immense societal applications in a developing nation like India where agriculture was the mainstay. As Dr
U.R. Rao, former ISRO Chairman mentioned:
‘When remote sensing was unheard of in the country, Sarabhai got us to get into a helicopter to record visuals of
wilting coconut trees in Trivandrum. He showed it to Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and told her, 'See, a satellite
picture can show you much more about agriculture.' He convinced her.’
viii

Dr Vikram Sarabhai not only laid down the vision but also secured approval at the national level. The
country accepted the national blueprint with a broad agenda covering remote sensing, scientific, and
communication satellites at the August 1972 seminar. ix

A book about ISRO titled ISRO, A Personal History, documents the long-term vision of planetary
exploration laid down two decades ago.x Every mission, every capacity-building effort is aligned with
ISRO’s ubiquitous vision: to ‘harness, sustain and augment space technology for national development while
pursuing space science research and planetary exploration.’xi
‘We were the only country that started the space programme for a purpose other than military,’ said Dr Kiran
Kumar.
Thus, at ISRO, it is not only about being strongly aware of the vision in every single mission but about
living it every day, in every moment, in every decision.
Collaborate Globally, Build Indigenously for Self-reliance
‘Dr Sarabhai was a well-known figure internationally. He approached NASA with a bold request, ‘I want to move the
Advanced Technology Satellite, ATS 6, to the Indian Ocean region. Give it to us as a loan for two years; we would
like to use it for our developmental purposes.’ recollected Dr Kasturirangan.
Whether for communication or remote sensing, building a satellite at that point in time was a formidable
challenge for India. Hence, the strategy adopted was to procure what was available, collaborate with
willing global players, and simultaneously build ground systems. This is evident throughout the history of
ISRO, starting from the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment that enabled India to broadcast
television to an audience of millions of viewers4

to ISRO joining hands with the USSR to launch its first

experimental satellite, Aryabhata, in 1975. (See Exhibit 7).
During Chandrayaan-1 for instance, several payloads like the Near Infrared Spectrometer (SIR-2) and

was an entirely indigenous endeavour. Most of the instruments on board, including all the sensors, were
Indian, designed, built and tested in India. ISRO was determined to carve its own path in the cosmos.
‘From 2019, India’s space power has seen a remarkable surge, attributed to both striking scientific missions and

NASA and ISRO, in February 2014, entered into an agreement for a joint Earth-observing mission ‘with the

Mission Mode at ISRO
During ISRO’s formative years, Prof. Dhawan (former Chairman of ISRO) instituted a stringent review
mechanism, holding the entire organisation accountable to the chairman periodically. Every three months,
he reviewed design documents, critical designs, secondary critical designs, flight readiness, and many
other parameters of a programme’s progress within the context of technology, maturity, and development.
These reviews were never closed-door affairs.xviii Anyone could attend and raise an issue, regardless of
seniority. The person presenting was bound to answer and offer the necessary explanation. Youngsters, in
particular, have a voice at ISRO. Such openness ensured that fresh ideas and critical feedback were always

cornerstone of ISRO even today.
Given the complexity and multi-disciplinary nature of space missions, Prof. U. R. Rao, who succeeded

Case Study Title: Raj Kisaan Saathi
Case Study Description: India’s agriculture sector continues to be a mainstay of the country’s economy, supporting millions of livelihoods and is the backbone of rural development. Despite its importance, the sector continues to be plagued by poor public investments, limited access and uptake of technology, and outdated practices. The Raj Kisan Sathi Portal is a novel effort by the Government of Rajasthan to modernise agricultural practices in the state using IT solutions. Initiated in 2019, the portal simplifies farming processes, provides vital information, and improves service delivery for farmers. In this policy and technology integration case, students will learn about the design, implementation, and challenges associated with executing and scaling a state-wide initiative. Studying this initiative offers valuable insights into leveraging technology to address systemic challenges in the agricultural sector to improve efficiency and social equity.
Case Text:
Introduction
Until recently, Krishan1

, a farmer from Barmer, had to travel 20 KM just to apply for a fertiliser subsidy. Now,
with a few taps on his phone, he can not only complete his application process in a jiffy, he also receives updates
about the latest subsidies, all without leaving his village. He could not have dreamed of this till recently. But now,
thanks to a phone application created by the Government of Rajasthan, he worries less about administrative
hassles and can focus more on his farming practices.
India's agricultural sector is vital to the national economy, supporting millions of livelihoods and ensuring rural
development. However, the sector continues to suffer from myriad challenges, including outdated agricultural
practices, low public investments, and restricted access to modern technology. However, in recent years, the
Central and state governments have introduced policies and programmes aimed at modernising agricultural
services for better service delivery and enhanced farmers' incomes. One such initiative is the Raj Kisan Sathi
Portal, which aims to uplift farmers and modernise agricultural practices by increasing the uptake of IT in
Rajasthan. The aim was to create a single online portal for farmers based on the idea of “ease of doing farming,”
(see Exhibit 1a) similar to “ease of doing business.” [1]

Challenges Faced by Farmers Availing Agricultural Services in the Past
In the past, Krishan faced a host of issues in availing agricultural services. Some of these are listed below:
1. Time-consuming and inefficient processes: In the past, he would have had to make multiple rounds of
government offices to submit forms, verify documents, track the progress of his applications, and receive
disbursements. This led to delays and confusion. For instance, it took anywhere between 30 and 45 days to apply

for and receive Direct Benefit Transfers (DBTs), due to the need for physical inspections (pre- and post-
verifications) and departmental approvals. [2]

2. Lack of transparency and higher chances of corruption: For a typical subsidy application, he had to fill out as
many as 40 fields in a form and submit multiple documents, including affidavits and certificates countersigned

2

by local authorities such as the Patwari2

. These required more visits to additional offices, and so to save time and

reduce the hassle, Krishan would seek the help of paid intermediaries.
3. Absence of a unified database leading to miscommunication and data duplication: Krishan had to visit multiple
offices with different departments, including the Departments of Horticulture, Agriculture, and the Rajasthan
State Department, for his needs. As each department maintained its own records, he had to furnish the same
information in different formats, leading to unnecessary administrative burdens.
4. Opaque inspection processes: To be eligible for many of the services and entitlements, physical inspections had
to be conducted. Due to the opacity and lack of objectivity in inspections, Krishan was essentially at the mercy of
the officer inspecting his land. He had no idea how long it might take for the officer to clear him to the next stage,
nor did he have a clear point of communication for updates, unless he went pillar to post.
5. Information asymmetry: Earlier, Krishan and other farmers relied on word of mouth to exchange news about
new schemes, subsidies, entitlements, and changes in market prices. They learnt from each other about new
farming practices through discussions and observations. This led to delays and sometimes a lack of information,
and the spread of misinformation, leading to losses.

Features of the Raj Kisan Sathi Portal
The Raj Kisan Sathi Portal is a web portal, and along with it, over 11 mobile applications have been created (as of
July 2024) to deliver over 150 services. [3]. These pertain to G2C (government to consumer), G2B (government to
business) and G2G (government to government). The project is based on the pillars of e-governance laid out by
the Government of Rajasthan, namely, “transparency, citizen-centric, social inclusion, and ease of service.” These
apps offer a wide range of facilities to farmers, including:
1. Online application and verification: The application process has been simplified with pre-loaded information
and shorter forms linked to Rajasthan’s Jan Aadhaar card for authentication.3 Since the system is integrated
with Jan Aadhaar, verification is faster, and farmers receive timely SMS updates on their application status.
Simplified application procedures with pre-loaded information and shorter forms tied to Rajasthan’s Jan
Aadhaar card for authentication. Since its integrated with Jan Aadhaar, verification takes less time, and
farmers get timely information about the status of their applications through SMS updates. Information is
also available offline, as the apps sync to the databases whenever the phone reconnects to the internet or to
any network, making the apps work in even the most remote areas.
2. Information on agricultural subsidies and schemes, farming advice, weather updates, and market price
information: The portal provides all the relevant information that farmers and buyers need. It also contains
information on schemes spanning multiple allied departments, including Krishi Vibhag (Agriculture
Department), Udyan Vibhag (Horticulture Department), and Rajasthan Rajya Vibhag (Rajasthan State
Department). By providing weather forecasts, the apps help farmers plan their activities around weather
patterns, potentially mitigating crop loss from adverse conditions. By providing up-to-date market prices,
farmers can decide exactly where and when to sell their produce to maximise their returns. Farming advice
mentioned on the portal and apps is from experts on farming techniques, pest control, and other agricultural
best practices to aid farmers.

are eligible for.

4. Online license registration: The Department of Agriculture requires sales licenses for seeds, pesticides, and

Development of the Raj Kisan Sathi Portal and Allied Applications
The state’s political leadership and top bureaucrats were aware of the issues plaguing farmers and decided that
they had to come up with a holistic tech-based solution for them. [6] The Government of Rajasthan initiated the
project in 2019 as a Budgetary Announcement, which helped garner visibility and secure funding. [7] The work
then began in phases.
Phase 1: The portal and the apps were developed in-house by the Department of Information Technology and
Rajcomp Info System Limited (RISL). A Project Management Unit (PMU) was set up to ensure that farmers’ exact
needs were being addressed by the tools being developed. This PMU was established in the Agricultural
Department and consisted of business analysts, designers, project leads, and nodal officers from all allied
departments to ensure smooth coordination. The whole initiative had high support from the state’s political and
bureaucratic leadership; as a result, progress was made quickly. The Agriculture Commissioner and the Principal
Secretary of Agriculture helped monitor this process and conduct video calls with other departmental heads
when the PMU members faced resistance from members of their departments.
The PMU was led by Ms. Monika Chaudhary, Joint Director, Dept. of IT & Communication. Being an IT
professional from the private sector in the past, she introduced a workflow similar to product development. Her
team organised multiple meetings with all stakeholders, including frontline functionaries, to discuss all the
paperwork that farmers had to submit. They identified redundancies and eliminated them. For example, farmers
now no longer had to submit countersigned affidavits and certificates. [8] They mapped user requirements,
created wireframes, conducted multiple rounds of testing, and incorporated feedback at all stages. In the first

Improving Farmer Lives with Technology: The Case of Raj Kisan Sathi

4
phase, high-volume services were identified, such as subsidy disbursement. The portal, as well as other mobile
apps were first developed for DBT-related services. By August 2021, 46 out of the 144 planned modules were
completed. [9]
The focus was firmly on the users’ requirements. Many of the digital services offered through the Raj Kisan Sathi
platform were customised to the distinct requirements of district-specific farmers. For instance, the facility
supported local languages, which helped cater to a larger number in the rural region. Niche apps catering to
specific produce for farmers and sellers also increased the initiative’s appeal. The government also ensured that
the information available on online weather forecasts, market prices, and agriculture advisories were locally
relevant to enhance the platform's utility. Such localisation of services made the platform more relatable and
useful to the farmer and helped overcome initial hesitations regarding adopting digital tools.
Phase 2: By ensuring the work was done entirely through departmental staff and repeated experiments,
institutional memory and trust were strengthened. It also reduced the time to modify these tools. By 2020, the
focus had also turned inwards. A challenge that any state portal or application faces is mapping the jurisdiction
of the people assigned to process a request or application being submitted by users. Ideally, the officer responsible
for fulfilling the request should instantly receive the data or application. But given the number of overlaps in
functions across the allied departments (example, Agriculture, Horticulture, Rajasthan State Department), there
were delays in assigning the right file to the right officer. This was complicated further when officers were
transferred to other departments for various reasons. To address this, the PMU created a jurisdiction mapping
software module. Officers could now sign in using their Single Sign On ID4 and self-declare their jurisdiction,
which would then be approved by their supervisors. Thus, the information was updated in real-time in the
system, and this ensured that the right file went to the right officer. The officers’ transfer, leave and joining
requests would also be generated through this system.
At this stage, emerging technologies like AI-enabled tools were also introduced. For this, an external private
vendor was roped in to develop the solution. Farmers could now upload pictures of their crops and receive
feedback on pest and disease control. The team collaborated with agricultural universities to refine this model,
which had over 90% diagnosis accuracy as of 2024. [10]
During the second phase, the team started bridging market players with farmers and the state. They started
roping in manufacturers and dealers of agricultural inputs (such as seeds, fertilisers and pesticides) onto the

platform. This was a Government-to-Business (GTB) process, which would allow farmers to find a list of pre-
approved dealers and manufacturers on the portal. The Raj AgriQC app also facilitated quality checks of the

samples provided by these manufacturers and dealers. Another app called “Manufacturer GeoTagging” was
introduced that would allow manufacturers and dealers to tag their institutions and manufacturing units.
Phase 3: In the third and ongoing phase, the team is working on refining their GIS integration processes and
adopting blockchain. GIS will be useful in estimating crop yield using satellite images, while the blockchain
module is being developed and tested for tracking seed supply. Under a PPP model, the government is engaging
various private sector forms for specialised services in critical areas such as cloud computing, analytics, and
cybersecurity to bolster the platform. [11]

via WhatsApp, and online training modules were created for employees as well as the farmers. Video calls were
set up with field staff and farmers separately to update them about new developments, identify and troubleshoot

Next Phase and Lingering Questions for Raj Kisan Sathi
As of June 2025, the Raj Kisan Sathi project has reportedly onboarded over 73 lakh farmers and over 2500 buyers
and sellers. [12] It has been used to disburse over Rs 2900 crore in DBTs. [13] Over a lakh licenses/certificates

Despite its widespread adoption, Raj Kisan Sathi initiative leaves some unanswered questions that the state will
