1. Digital inclusion and equity
Though digital infrastructure has improved tremendously, not all farmers enjoy equal access to smartphones,
reliable internet connections, or adequate digital literacy. Disparities in access would continue marginalising
groups, so questions are raised around the programmes’ inclusivity.
2. Scaling while adapting to evolving needs
Agriculture is a dynamic sector, constantly in flux due to changing climate and market influences. Safeguarding
against these shifts remains a question.
3. Monitoring mechanisms and feedback
As the programme scales, its user-friendliness and responsiveness may become increasingly difficult to maintain.
In addition to finding robust mechanisms to collect, analyse, and act upon feedback, identifying and following

4. Data privacy and security
Handling personal and financial data online exposes users to data privacy and security risks. Strong safeguards
are important factors in maintaining users' trust. So, what kind of best practices in data protection could be
adopted to protect users and stay proactive against misuse and breaches will be a key challenge.

Case Study Title: PM SVANidhi – Turning Adversity into Opportunity through e-Governance
Case Study Description: The PM SVANidhi Scheme has emerged as a catalyst for inclusive urban entrepreneurship, breaking barriers that previously limited access for marginalized micro-entrepreneurs. With a notable rise in female participation, the scheme has advanced women’s entrepreneurial empowerment, contributing to broader gender equality in urban markets. PM SVANidhi has strengthened the sustainability of small urban businesses. This caselet explores the scheme’s implementation, the challenges faced in reaching its objectives and outlines the path ahead to further enhance its role in fostering resilient and inclusive urban livelihoods.
Case Text:
The Covid-19 lockdown came down harshly on street vendors, as it did for many other workers in
India’s informal microeconomy. An empty city meant street vendors losing their livelihoods and
income source, confronting hunger, deprivation and even reverse migration1

from the cities back into

their shanty towns and villages.
To support street vendors who had experienced significant losses during the pandemic, the
Government of India launched a welfare initiative offering affordable, collateral-free microloans to
foster their financial inclusion and economic recovery.
On 1 June 2020, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs launched the PM Street Vendor’s Atma
Nirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi) scheme—an innovative e-governance initiative featuring digital
approval mechanisms. The scheme was designed to provide micro-credit facilities to urban street
vendors, enabling them to sustain and grow their businesses. By facilitating access to formal credit, the
PM SVANidhi scheme aimed to integrate street vendors into the formal financial system, thereby
fostering their economic empowerment and promoting digital inclusion.
The Marginalised Class
Street vendors, constitute a vital segment of India’s informal economy, offering essential goods and
services at affordable prices. Owing to the low entry barriers, their numbers have grown substantially,
1 Reverse migration, also known as return migration, refers to the phenomenon where
migrants return to their place of origin after having migrated to another place for a certain period. It’s
a common occurrence worldwide but gained significant attention in India due to the large-scale
reverse migration prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic.

3

making them one of the most prominent groups of self-employed individuals in urban areas. However,
considering that street vending was illegal in India for almost six decades since Independence, street
vendors have historically faced livelihood challenges including harassment, eviction, and confiscation
of goods by authorities. It is estimated that there are nearly 10 million street vendors in India, whose
livelihoods remain insecure and vulnerable despite the legal recognition and protection of their rights
offered under the Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014.
This Act—to regulate the activities of street vendors—provided a consultative framework under which
Town Vending Committees (TVCs) were constituted to facilitate the registration of vendors and the
allocation of designated vending zones. However, inconsistent implementation by States and Union
Territories had limited its impact. The situation worsened during the COVID-19 lockdowns, which
severely disrupted their earnings. Even after the lockdowns were eased, they lacked the capital to
procure goods and rebuild their businesses. Banks refused to offer them loans without collateral. The
only options available to them for raising capital were borrowed funds, which could push them
towards debt traps. Their survival in business needed swift and contactless intervention at the national
level.
Timely Intervention
The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) considered that the existing Street Vendors
(Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act of 2014 had all the provisions required
for the rehabilitation of street vendors that just needed to be enforced to bridge the implementation

gaps. So, without crafting new laws, the Ministry introduced the PM SVANidhi scheme, not as a one-
time financial intervention, but as a centralised e-governance initiative to be implemented by the

Government of India with the states across India.
On June 1, 2020, the Ministry launched the Prime Minister’s Street Vendor Atma Nirbhar Nidhi (PM
SVANidhi) to protect the livelihoods of street vendors. The scheme’s vision was not just to rehabilitate
and revive the vibrant street vending economy, but also to ensure a scalable framework in which street
vendors could thrive with dignity and access opportunities. The achievement of this outcome
mandated going beyond the Act to motivate state governments to notify the scheme and rules in line
with the Act.

Navigating Emerging Challenges
Some of the evolving challenges that the Ministry faced included identification of eligible street vendors
across India, facilitating their access to credit and managing the loan repayments. These issues that
were compounded by the inherent complexities of the informal economy, and the need to integrate
street vendors with limited financial literacy into formal financial systems in collaboration with states.
A Collaborative Approach
PM SVANidhi was designed to promote long-term financial discipline and sustainable inclusion for
street vendors. The scheme offered interest subsidies for timely repayments, cashback incentives on
digital transactions, and higher loan eligibility for those who repaid their first loan on time.
Its success relied on a collaborative approach, involving nodal agencies, state governments, Urban
Local Bodies (ULBs), and banks to ensure effective implementation and nationwide reach.
The PM SVANidhi platform was developed to provide a completely digital journey that allowed
beneficiaries to register and avail of a loan with only a street vending certificate or a letter of
recommendation issued by the urban local bodies (ULB)

2 or the Town Vending Committee. A ULB
included the Mahanagar Nigam, the Municipal Corporation, the Nagar Palika, the Municipality, and
the Nagar Panchayat, or the Notified Area Council.

2 ULBs are the local government bodies responsible for various administrative functions
delegated by state governments, including identifying and assisting street vendors.

4

Notification by States
The significant loss of livelihoods during the pandemic made the PM SVANidhi scheme an extremely
sought after initiative. However, access to the benefits under the scheme was restricted only for street
vendors in states, which had implemented the PM SVANidhi scheme and notified the rules under the
provisions of the Street Vendors Act 2014. This conditionality served as an effective leverage to
encourage States and UTs to fulfil the compliances under the Street Vendors Act. Consequently, all
states and UTs have since met this requirement.

Inclusivity of Street Vendors
The PM SVANidhi scheme evolved to overcome obstacles. It was primarily based on recognition of
street vendors, which required the ULBs to conduct an identification survey of street vendors working
in their jurisdiction. However, only about half the ULBs had conducted the identification survey of
street vendors. The top-down approach for recognition of street vendors was therefore eliminated in
favour of a demand-based model. To ensure no vendor was excluded, the scheme introduced the Letter
of Recommendation (LoR), to be issued by a ULB or Town Vending Committee (TVC) to verify vendors

even if no prior survey had been conducted. This eliminated delays as surveys could be a time-
consuming process. The PM SVANidhi scheme also permitted a significantly expanded list of

documents that could be submitted by street vendors for obtaining the LoR. The impact of this
intervention was evident over three years. As of 16 May 2025, over 81.25 lakh LoR applications were
received, with 76.29 lakh street vendors approved for enrolment under the scheme. Without this, nearly
60% of street vendors might have been denied access to crucial financial support.
Devising Hassle-free Processes
Lenders were hesitant to provide loans to informal workers due to the high credit risk. To address this
institutional hesitation, the PM SVANidhi scheme guaranteed up to 31.8% of the borrowed amount
through the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE), thereby
mitigating lender concerns. A dedicated online portal and mobile app streamlined the entire process—
from application and e-KYC to sanction and disbursement—to ensure efficiency. The results highlight
its success: Until 23 April 2025, more than 114.6 lakh eligible applications were received of which 98.37
loans were sanctioned, and over 96 lakh disbursements were made to more than 68 lakh beneficiaries
and the total disbursed amount is 13,780 crore loans.
This fully digital approach also enabled the Ministry to monitor progress in real time and implement
timely interventions.
Bridging the Digital Divide
Street vendors typically engaged in a large number of small-value transactions daily, whether related
to buying stock or receiving payments. The nature of the transaction like selling vegetables or street
food, created a heavy reliance on cash. This scheme was able to empower street vendors to increasingly
make and receive payments digitally, thereby decreasing their reliance on cash. Besides, with the digital
data being captured, a credit history was established for the vendor, thus opening up further financial
possibilities.
Securing the Future
To ensure sustainable business growth, the PM SVANidhi initiative makes a provision for disbursal of
higher loan amounts to street vendors who have made pre-payments or timely payments of their first
loan. For instance, a vendor who has availed a loan amount of ₹10,000 and subsequently demonstrated
a consistent track record of payments, will be eligible to avail ₹20,000 as a second loan. On repayment
of the second loan, a street vendor would be entitled to avail a loan of ₹50,000 as a third loan.

5

Promoting Timely Repayment Practices
The PM SVANidhi scheme addresses the apprehension of loan default by incentivising street vendors
with an interest subsidy of 7%, which is , directly transferred to beneficiaries' accounts upon timely
payment of the equated monthly instalments (EMI). If a vendor repays all EMIs on time and completes
the prescribed number of digital transactions, the cashback incentives can offset the interest, effectively
making the loan interest-free.
Building a Safety Net
The PM SVANidhi scheme addresses socio-economic needs. The ‘SVANidhi se Samriddhi’ initiative
was designed to connect not only the street vendors but their families too, to social welfare schemes
offered by various ministries. These schemes related to healthcare, insurance, maternity benefits,
education etc. to provide a holistic safety net for street vendors.
Expanding the Customer Base
The Government of India partnered with private companies like Swiggy and Zomato to offer a platform
for street vendors to significantly expand their customer base and income. To facilitate this process,
street vendors were provided training relating to the digitisation of menus, FSSAI (Food Safety &
Standards Authority of India) licencing procedures and the use of mobile applications.
A Strong Sense of Belonging
Street vendors are often considered disruptive and threatened with eviction. To provide immediate
legitimacy and protection to the PM SVANidhi beneficiaries, they are provided with a ‘Parichay Board’,
that prominently displays the vendor's details, including their photograph and Certificate of Vending
(CoV) Number, thus affording them recognition and security. PM SVANidhi Beneficiaries are also
given Udyam Assist Certificates and Udyam Registration Numbers by the Ministry of Medium, Small
and Micro Enterprises, thereby registering them as Micro Enterprises in the informal sector.3
Major Impacts
The scheme has achieved nationwide success in both volumes and geographic spread. For many, PM
SVANidhi was a lifeline during their lowest moments post-pandemic. Beneficiaries not only appreciate
the restored dignity and financial independence but also find great value in the cashback incentives for
digital transactions. Most importantly, they report sustainable growth, having repaid their initial
₹10,000 loan and successfully moved on to the ₹20,000 loan, paving the way for a stable future.
The PM SVANidhi scheme has ensured the sustainability of inclusive entrepreneurship. It has
dismantled barriers to seamlessly connect marginalised urban micro-entrepreneurs. Considering the
increased number of female beneficiaries, it has served the entrepreneurial empowerment of urban
women besides creating a wider impact on gender equalisation, rise in consumption levels among loan
recipients, improved spending pattern among the street vendor demographic indicating a rise in
income levels, increase in persistency ratio for repayment of loans, and greater acceptability for digital
transactions.
Way Ahead
PM SVANidhi has transformed the lives of millions of street vendors, providing financial stability,
digital empowerment, and business growth opportunities. By breaking down barriers to credit access,

PM SVANidhi (Prime Minister Street Vendor's AtmaNirbhar Nidhi) is part of Government of India’s
“Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan”, aimed at providing financial assistance to street vendors. Research has

Vendors who once struggled for recognition now enjoy financial independence, digital literacy and

Case Study Title: Udyam Assist Platform – A Key Differentiator for Informal Micro Enterprises (IMEs)
Case Study Description: Micro enterprises play a critical role in India’s economy, contributing to GDP, exports, and job creation. However, over 99% operate informally, limiting access to finance and government benefits. To address this, the Ministry of MSME launched Udyam Registration in 2020, but many informal micro enterprises (IMEs) remained unregistered due to lack of awareness, documents, and digital skills. To bridge this gap, the Ministry introduced the Udyam Assist Platform (UAP) on January 11, 2023, developed and managed by SIDBI. Unlike the self-registration Udyam Registration Portal, UAP enables banks and microfinance institutions to register IMEs on their behalf, using Aadhaar-based verification and bulk data uploads. The platform enhances reach, ensures data security, and issues an Udyam Assist Certificate, allowing IMEs to later self-register fully.
Case Text:
The Micro enterprises in the organised sector have the ability to boost jobs and economic growth in
India. Many such small businesses - street vendors and home-based workers- operate informally
without legal recognition. To help them, the Ministry of MSME launched the Udyam Assist Platform
(UAP) on January 11, 2023. The platform made it easier for these microenterprises to register formally.
With registration, they could access loans, government schemes, and new market opportunities. This
move aimed to empower small businesses and support their growth.
The Challenge of Informal MSMEs in India
Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are vital to India’s economy. They contribute around
30% to the GDP and account for nearly half of India’s exports. MSMEs also create millions of jobs across
rural and urban areas. However, over 99% of these businesses operate informally, without formal
registration. This limits their access to finance, increases borrowing costs, and exposes them to tough
market competition and operational challenges.
To address this, the government introduced Udyam Registration in July 2020. This online system aimed
to make MSME registration easier. Despite this, most informal micro enterprises (IMEs) remained
outside the formal sector. Many IMEs lacked awareness, the necessary documents, or digital skills to
register.
Recognising these barriers, the government launched the Udyam Assist Platform. This new platform
that helps informal micro enterprises register with support, making formalisation easier. Formalising
these businesses is crucial for boosting productivity, ensuring inclusive growth, and creating more jobs.

3

Roadblocks to Formalisation
The Ministry of MSMEs had to enable the registration of the informal micro enterprises (IMEs) on its
Udyam Registration Portal, but faced several challenges in launching its formalisation initiative. The
primary hurdles were:
1. Identification and Outreach
• Large Unregistered Base: Crores of IMEs operated without legal recognition, making it
difficult to identify and reach them.
• Lack of Legal Frameworks: Their informal status meant that there were no official records or
databases to track these enterprises.
2. Digital Literacy and Access
• Limited Digital Skills: Most IMEs lacked digital literacy, which hampered their ability to use
online registration platforms.
• Choosing the Right Approach: The Ministry had to decide between direct registration (e.g.,
through E-Seva Kendras), an assisted model (via designated agencies), or third-party
campaigns to facilitate registration.
3. Motivation and Incentives
• Low Awareness of Benefits: Many microenterprises were unaware of the advantages of formal
registration.
• Perceived Compliance Burden: The benefits of registration clearly outweighed the costs and
effort of compliance to motivate IMEs to formalise.
4. Access to Finance and Growth Opportunities
• Dependency on Registration: Without formal registration, IMEs missed out on access to
finance, government schemes, and growth opportunities.
Discussions with Industry
The Reserve Bank of India recognised MSMEs under Priority Sector Lending. This helped registered
MSMEs access credit and other benefits. However, MSMEs without registration could not avail these
benefits.
The Ministry of MSME consulted key industry stakeholders. These included the Ministry of Finance,
Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI), Indian Banks’ Association (IBA), and the
Association of Community Development Finance Institutions (Sa-Dhan). They shared that lending
institutions faced challenges. Many micro-enterprise loans lost priority sector status because borrowers
lacked Udyam Registration.
There was a clear consensus that formalising MSMEs, especially informal micro enterprises (IMEs), is
crucial. Formalisation would support their growth and integration into the formal economy. It
improves access to financial services, government schemes, and skill development opportunities.
Based on this, the Ministry focused on the Udyam Assist platform. This platform aimed to close the
registration gap for informal micro enterprises and promote their formalisation.
Empowering Regulated Agencies
The Ministry of MSME authorised the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) to build the
Udyam Assist Platform (UAP). SIDBI, already the nodal agency for MSME registration, now managed
and maintained this new portal.
There were two separate portals for MSME registration. The Udyam Registration Portal (URP) allowed
MSMEs to self-register online. The Udyam Assist Platform (UAP) was designated for agencies, like
banks and microfinance institutions, to register their customers as informal micro enterprises (IMEs).
Both portals worked in parallel to bring more businesses into the organised sector.

4

The registration process seemed simple. Designated agencies collected and submitted the IME’s data
and documents on the UAP. After verification, the IME received an Udyam Registration Number and
a Udyam Assist Certificate through the agency. With this certificate, the IME could register on the main
Udyam Registration Portal.
SIDBI designed the UAP with an Assist Methodology1. This approach used Aadhaar identity and the
support of designated agencies to help IMEs get registered and receive their Udyam Registration
Number and certificate. This process made formalisation easier for small, informal businesses.
Technology Solutions
The Ministry of MSME authorised SIDBI to maintain the Udyam Assist Platform (UAP) and collect
IME data—including Aadhaar details—from designated agencies using Bulk Upload through Smart
Excels. SIDBI built the UAP on a robust web application architecture, following industry best
practices. This ecosystem allowed regulated agencies to register their existing IME customers quickly,
solving problems of reach, penetration, and speed. The platform is lightweight and has minimal entry
barriers, making it easy for agencies and IMEs to use.
Key Technological Features
• Speed: Bulk Upload was chosen over APIs for efficiency, given the scale of registering up to 6
crore IMEs. This method maintained data security while allowing rapid processing.
• Data Security: The platform uses public key encryption during file uploads, ensuring data is
secure while in motion.
• Data Protection: Aadhaar numbers were not stored on the main UAP database. Instead, they
were kept in a separate, quarantined Aadhaar Data Vault, protecting sensitive information at
rest.
• De-duplication: The UAP enforced Aadhaar-based de-duplication, ensuring each IME
receive a unique Udyam Registration Number and Assist Certificate.
• Cloud Community: The platform was hosted on a secure Government Cloud Community
(GCC) managed by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, ensuring
reliability and security.
Design Elements
• Removal of Entry Barriers: IMEs registered using documents they already have, rather than
being required to provide new or unavailable documents.
• Digital Platform: The fully digital process replaced manual touchpoints, increasing agility,
scale, and reach.
• Onboarding and Incentivising Agencies: Designated agencies introduced their customers as
a value-added service and classified their loan books under Priority Sector Lending.
• Bridging the Digital Divide: The assisted model agencies handled data submission, ensuring
data integrity and informed consent, and overcoming IMEs’ digital literacy challenges.
• Seamless Process: Registration through UAP required only minimal documentation, making
the process smooth for agencies and IMEs.
The Udyam Assist Platform’s technology-driven approach had made formalising informal micro
enterprises faster, more secure, and more accessible, supporting India’s goal of inclusive economic
growth
Future Outlook
1 Assist Methodology in the context of the Udyam Assist Platform (UAP) refers to a supportive and
simplified process designed to help Informal Micro Enterprises (IMEs) transition into the formal economy. It
was developed by SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India)

5

Over one crore informal micro enterprises received Udyam Registration Numbers and Udyam Assist
Certificates. This showed the platform’s strong impact on formalising and empowering India’s
microenterprise sector. With identification, recognition, and registration of IMEs now at a critical
stage, the focus shifted to new benefits. Plans included creating a marketplace for collateral-free and
low-interest credit schemes, offering free credit reports, and providing credit counselling for IMEs.
There was also targeted support in regions with low MSME penetration.
Conclusion
The Udyam Assist initiative has removed major barriers to MSME formalisation through clear
policies, digital solutions, and industry partnerships. By bringing IMEs into the formal economy, the
government was able to make a big step toward economic inclusion and sustainable growth for
millions of small businesses. This initiative continued to strengthen India’s MSME sector and support
the country’s economic progress in the long run.

Case Study Title: PM PvTG
Case Study Description: The Pradhan Mantri PVTG Mission, a flagship program of the Indian Government, is dedicated to enhance the socio-economic conditions of the Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) in the country. This case delves into the assessment and resolution of challenges faced by the mission, which has been allocated a budget of Rs. 15,000 crore over three years, commencing in 2023-24. The mission aims to provide critical support in the form of housing, water, sanitation, education, healthcare, and livelihood opportunities, while respecting the cultural integrity of PVTGs. This case offers a comprehensive understanding of the issues faced by PVTGs, and the effectiveness of the mission in addressing these concerns, aligning with broader governmental objectives in accordance with United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs). The case encourages adoption of an empathetic approach and devising of impact-oriented execution strategies.
Case Text:
Introduction
It was a warm day on 9th August 2023; the two-day all-hands meeting on Pradhan Mantri Particularly
Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PMPVTGs) had just concluded in New Delhi. The meeting was organized by
the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to brief the District Magistrates (DMs) of 18 states and a union territory on
the urgent need for the sustenance and development of the rapidly diminishing 75 PVTGs in India.
Showcasing the successful implementation of schemes associated with the Kamar tribe of Chhattisgarh as
a benchmark, the meeting highlighted that the Pradhan Mantri PVTG Mission was initiated with the aim
to enhance the socio-economic conditions of the tribal groups in India. The top priority of the mission was
the sustenance of these tribes through the development and implementation of schemes aligned with UN’s
Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs), particularly those focused on livelihood, survival, health,
habitation, education, and infrastructure.
However, the condition of PVTGs, with some having only about 17 people, raised serious questions about
the validity and effectiveness of government schemes. Although rife with challenges, DMs had their task
cut out, as they were the ones responsible for ensuring practical implementation of the PVTG schemes.
They had to navigate between the needs of the target group, existing policy framework, and the
overarching sustainable development goals; they had to often deal with budget constraints, conflicting
interests, and various administrative bottlenecks. The District Magistrates had to balance and align efforts,
as well as budget allocation across various policies and schemes with multiple ministries and their different
agendas.
PRADHAN MANTRI PVTG MISSION: ADVANCING SUSTAINABILITY AND SAFEGUARDING VULNERABLE TRIBAL
3
COMMUNITIES
Concluding the meeting, the Secretary of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs said:
I am sure you understand the gravity of the situation. We expect you to expedite the ground-level execution of the on-
paper PM PVTG schemes. The mission targets saturation of benefits over five years, aiming for the comprehensive
development of PVTG households. The ministries involved in the mission have relaxed norms to accommodate the
unique needs of PVTGs. The goal is to integrate PVTGs into mainstream society while respecting their unique
cultural and livelihood needs.
About PVTGs
In 1973, the Dhebar Commissioni recognised the need to identify the most vulnerable and marginalised
tribal communities in India; it categorised them as ‘Primitive Tribal Groups’ (PTGs). The objective for this
categorization was to pinpoint tribal groups that were significantly behind other tribal communities in
terms of socio-economic development. From 1973 to 2013, the Indian government implemented a series of
initiatives aimed at improving the socio-economic conditions of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups
(PVTGs). At the outset (i.e., in 1973), the government initially recognised 52 Primitive Tribal Groups (PTGs),
laying the foundation for targeted interventions. Over the following decades, several key programs were
introduced, including the Tribal Sub-Plan in 1975, which allocated specific funds for tribal development,
and the 1992 Scheme for Development of Primitive Tribal Groups, focusing on improving housing,
infrastructure, healthcare, education, and income generation. In 1998, the term PTGs was changed to
PVTGs to reflect a more inclusive and sensitive approach. This shift was followed by more focused
strategies, such as the Revised Scheme for Development of PVTGs in 1999, which allowed direct funding
to state governments for specific projects.
India had 705 Scheduled Tribes (STs), out of which 75 were identified as PVTGs due to their declining
populations and lack of development. The process of identifying PVTGs began in 1975, when the
government initially recognised 52 such groups. By 1993, an additional 23 groups were added, bringing
the total number of identified PVTGs to 75.
The identification of PVTGs was based on several criteria, including the preservation of pre-agricultural
practices, economic backwardness, a decreasing or stagnant population, and relatively low literacy levels
compared to other tribal groups. These criteria were used to ensure that the most vulnerable groups
received the necessary attention and support. Notably, PVTGs lived across about 15% of the country’s
landmass in various ecological and geo-climatic conditions, ranging from plains to forests, hills, and
inaccessible areas. They encompassed a wide diversity of cultures, systems of self-governance, and
livelihood systems, and were provided special protection under Schedules V and VI of the Indian
Constitutionii (see Exhibit 1). While some tribal communities had adopted a more mainstream life, others
remained on the periphery, characterised by (a) forest-based livelihoods, (b) pre-agricultural levels of
existence, (c) stagnant and declining populations, (d) extremely low literacy, and (e) subsistence economies.
Notably, PVTGs living in forest areas faced threats from both forest authorities and the environment. They

PRADHAN MANTRI PVTG MISSION: ADVANCING SUSTAINABILITY AND SAFEGUARDING VULNERABLE TRIBAL
COMMUNITIES
had a migratory lifestyle and lacked permanent housing, education, and healthcare. Traditional
livelihoods, such as hunting and shifting cultivation, were becoming unsustainable.
According to the 2001 census, 75 PVTGs had a total population of 2,768,322; among these groups, the
Sahariyas had the highest population (about 450,217). The Sentinelese and the Andamanese, on the other
hand, were among the smallest PVTGs. Largely, PVTGs resided across 17 Indian states and a Union
Territory. Geographically, around 77% of their total population, covering 38 out of 75 PVTGs, was spread
across five states (see Exhibit 2).
Each of the 75 PVTGs was unique; they had their own distinct characteristics. These groups included the
Shompens, Jarawas, Sentinelese of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Bondos of Odisha, Cholanaickans of
Kerala, the Abhujmarias of Chhattisgarh, and Birhors of Jharkhand. Because of their customary habitats
being altered, their traditional rights were often overlooked. This, in turn, affected the livelihood resources
they had relied on and led to significant concerns about food security, health, and sustenance of traditional
occupations. PVTGs needed focused and dedicated support to enhance their well-being, given their unique
living conditions, distinct socio-economic circumstances, and the importance of sustaining their
communities for future generations. In the early 2000s, the government introduced key support measures

The Problems Persist
Despite concerted efforts, PVTGs continued to encounter challenges that highlighted the importance of
tailored support. Their geographical remoteness and strong cultural traditions at times limited their access
to government services, owing to which, they primarily relied on subsistence activities, which were
impacted by environmental changes. Health services and education access remained limited in some areas,
with barriers like infrastructure gaps and administrative challenges affecting program implementation.
(see Exhibits 4a & 4b). Additionally, it may be noted that traditional livelihoods, often tied to forest
produce and shifting agriculture, were affected by environmental shifts and changes in land use.
Recognising the importance of their ancestral lands, there was a growing focus on aligning land
management policies with the needs of PVTG communities.
Education was a key area for lending support, as improved access to schooling and transportation would
expand literacy, and possibly increase participation in development opportunities. Physical remoteness, a
part of the PVTGs' unique heritage, meant that connectivity improvements required thoughtful design to
balance preservation with access to resources. Development projects had to increasingly consider the
specific needs of PVTG communities to minimise disruptions, especially in cases involving land use for
initiatives, like mining or infrastructure. Addressing these considerations required a community-centred
approach that respected the distinct cultures, needs, and aspirations of each group, with a focus on creating
sustainable and inclusive progress that integrated these valuable communities into the broader fabric of
development, while preserving their unique identities.

Case Study Title: Third Party Inspection
Case Study Description: On April 25, 2022, Mr. Arun Mehta, Principal Chief Materials Manager of Western Railways, launched a transformative Third-Party Inspection (TPI) initiative to modernize quality assurance in Indian Railways. The program aimed to enhance efficiency, build capacity, and create a competitive inspection ecosystem focused on quality over cost. Presented to top Railway Board officials, it received strong support from the Chairman, Member Finance, and RDSO. On May 8, 2022, the Board authorized Western Railway to engage private TPI agencies for 2–3 years. Tasked with designing the empanelment system, Mr. Mehta sought to integrate private efficiencies without disrupting inspections while reflecting on fairness and possible stakeholder conflicts.

In a meeting with the Chairman and CEO of the Railway Board, along with the Director General of RDSO,

round the clock, 365 days a year, Mr. Mehta underscored the urgent need to rethink traditional approaches
to inspection and quality assurance; in the process, he proposed setting the stage for a transformative shift

is expected to significantly
enhance the quality of incoming materials, raising product standards to international levels. This, in turn,

Genesis of Third-Party Inspection (TPI)
The Third-Party Inspection (TPI) program was aimed at enhancing the quality of goods, spares, input
materials, sub-systems, and manufacturing processes, ultimately improving asset reliability and
maintenance, while reducing failure rates. By implementing statistical sampling plans, the program aimed
to shorten the inspection cycle times, and facilitate the adoption of new processes and systems through
process inspections. Additionally, it sought to build capacity to meet growing demands, and foster a
competitive market to drive greater efficiencies. Integrating third-party inspections would not only enable
more efficient and reliable service operations, but would also expand product inspection capacity within
the supply chain. In other words, it was meant to encourage innovation, enhance quality control, and drive
continual improvements in technical specifications and process capabilities, ensuring higher standards and
operational excellence.
ROLLING OF TPI
Both the concept and methodology of this initiative received endorsement from the Chairman of the
Railways Board, who further emphasized the importance of quality over mere cost reduction. The concept

the Railway Board issued a directive and appointed the Western Railway (WR) to finalize a private contract
with reputable agencies for a duration of 2 to 3 years.

the vast and intricately managed railway system, which encompassed nine production units, a fleet of
13,000 locomotives, 86,000 coaches, and 330,000 wagons, all ably supported by a workforce of 1.3 million
employees. Importantly, given the extensive inventory, and the ongoing need for maintenance, and new
locomotive production, implementing changes to the inspection process posed significant risks that
included potential impacts on business continuity, inspection integrity, and operational stability. There
