prevailed. In fact, there were numerous complaints raised regarding frequent cancellations of inspection
calls, particularly when deadlines were under 15 days.
Mr. Mehta observed: “although RITES is our own organizationv and technically very strong, they often lack
professionalism in their inspections, leading to numerous complaints directed to the Chairman of the Railway Board
(CRB).” He further noted, “RITES charged a fixed fee of 0.9% of the purchase order. They would delay inspections,
requesting 15 working days to complete them, only to not show up. Firms would continuously complain that RITES
wasn’t showing up.”
Concerns of material suppliers were also significant; for example: if there was an inspection delay by RITES,
the railways imposed liquidated damages by deducting 2% from vendors of their purchase orders, which
served as a strong deterrent for them. As a result, suppliers often felt compelled to cut costs on products
and services to offset these financial penalties. In turn, this led to compromises in quality and service,
ultimately affecting the overall reliability of the supply chain. Noticing these inefficiencies within RITES,
Mr. Mehta believed that involving private players in third-party inspections would enhance efficiency and
leverage top-tier expertise. This approach would also help in improving the quality of goods, spares, input
materials, and manufacturing processes. Ultimately, it proposed to lead to more reliable and efficient
services, strengthening the Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Safety (RAMS) of assets in the
process. Mr. Mehta believed that once RDSO and Chittaranjan Locomotive Works approved suppliers,
including their manufacturing processes and Quality Assurance Plans (QAPs), it would be wise to use
Third-Party Inspectors (TPIs) for product and process verification. This approach could be more effective
in preventing conflicts of interest. For example: during process inspections, materials could be accepted
based on internal inspections and an approved test plan. A system of regular process inspections conducted
by TPIs at the firms' premises, field units, and user locations at random intervals could be implemented,
similar to the Bureau of Indian Standards approach for ISI-marked products, which was recognized as an
internationally accepted practice.
Building on this idea, Mr. Mehta believed that a more competitive and accountable inspection framework
would be essential for achieving long-term improvements in quality and efficiency. He was convinced that
involving third-party agencies in the inspection process would introduce much-needed competition and
accountability. By adopting globally recognized inspection practices, Indian Railways could foster stronger
collaborations with vendors and streamline operations for greater reliability.
INITIATING EVALUATION PROCESS AND SELECTION OF THIRD-PARTY INSPECTION (TPI)
The decision to engage private third-party inspection agencies marked a significant departure from the
inspection practices that had been in place for the past five decades. This transition prompted several
internal brainstorming sessions. The goal was to have a comprehensive and holistic approach. An
introductory meeting, or pre-notice Inviting Tender was held with potential private TPI agencies to gather
v RITES is a subsidiary of Indian Railways, providing engineering consultancy and project management service

THIRD-PARTY INSPECTION IN RAILWAYS: A GAME CHANGER 6
insights into market trends, and the specifics of the inspection process. Additionally, a thorough risk
analysis was conducted; this led to strategy formulation to mitigate the identified risks (see Exhibit 1).
Following the risk analysis, the selection system for TPIs was established; it included an assessment of the
users' ability to manage and oversee the implementation of the proposed assignment. Moreover, the
evaluation process of TPIs was structured into three stages:
1. Pre-Qualification Stage: agencies were pre-qualified based on their ability to meet minimum technical
criteria, a mandatory requirement. Agencies that did not meet these criteria were eliminated from further
consideration (see Exhibit 2).
2. Technical Evaluation Stage: agencies that successfully passed the pre-qualification stage were evaluated
based on their technical scores. Notably, a minimum score of 70 was required to qualify. If more than four
bidders achieved the necessary technical score, only the top four agencies based on their scores were
eligible for financial evaluation.
3. Financial Evaluation Stage: the financial bids of the four shortlisted bidders were assessed. These bids,
expressed as a percentage of the Purchase Order (PO) value, were categorized into four slabs, with
weightage assigned based on historical data regarding value proportions. For Purchase Orders exceeding
INR 500 crores, the financial bids from the empaneled list were also subject to process inspection based on
man-days.
This structured evaluation process aimed to ensure that the selection of TPI agencies was thorough and
transparent. Moreover, it was aligned meticulously with the objectives of enhancing inspection quality and
efficiency.
SELECTION PROCESS OF THIRD-PARTY INSPECTION (TPI)
The TPI selection process began with the assessment of those that met the minimum technical criteria for
pre-qualification. The Technical Evaluation Parameters were carefully chosen, based on the specific
requirements of the work, with relative importance assigned to each criterion. The parameters used to
determine the technical score included:
1. Experience of the TPI Agency: evaluated through turnover and previous project involvement.
2. Geographical Presence: the agency's ability to operate in relevant locations.
3. Technical Competence: assessed by the number of graduate engineers, certified inspectors, and their
areas of expertise.
4. Registration with Statutory Bodies: compliance with necessary regulations and standards.
5. Infrastructure Facilities in India: availability of adequate facilities to support inspection activities.
6. Inspection and Response Time: efficiency in conducting inspections and addressing queries.
7. Complaint Redressal: effectiveness in handling and resolving complaints.
Based on these criteria, four agencies with the highest technical scores (all exceeding 70 marks) were
shortlisted; and their financial bids were subsequently opened. The Weighted Financial Score was
calculated based on the weightage assigned to four different slabs. The financial bids had to be quoted as
a percentage of the Purchase Order value, categorized into the following slabs:
i) Greater than ₹5 lakh and up to ₹1 crore
ii) Greater than ₹1 crore and up to ₹25 crore
iii) Greater than ₹25 crore and up to ₹100 crore

THIRD-PARTY INSPECTION IN RAILWAYS: A GAME CHANGER 7
iv) Greater than ₹100 crore and up to ₹500 crore
The work was then allocated according to a ratio of 40:30:20:10, with majority of the work assigned to the
agency that had the lowest Weighted Financial Score. For process inspections, the evaluation was based on
daily manpower rates; the distribution of work too followed the same ratio.
The financial evaluation criteria for the agencies utilized either Least Cost Selection (LCS)vi, Quality and
Cost-Based Selection (QCBS)vii, or a hybrid approach. The choice of method was determined through a
comprehensive analysis of risk and corresponding risk mitigation strategies. A decision matrix was created
considering LCS, QCBS, Shortlist + LCS, and Shortlist + QCBS (see Exhibit 3). Importantly, the regulatory
framework permitted all these options in selecting the TPIs with Shortlist + LCS identified as the most
effective selection method within the regulatory guidelines (see Exhibit 4).
Further, in conjunction with the three stages of the evaluation process, key features of the inspection policy
were documented to facilitate the smooth integration of TPI within Indian Railways (see Exhibit 5).
THE WAY FORWARD
Mr. Mehta noted that engaging reputable private Third-Party Inspectors (TPIs) led to significant cost
savings—up to 80% in inspection expenses, amounting to approximately ₹500-600 crores annually. This
was achieved through a slab-based inspection fee system and competitive bidding for high-value orders;
this resulted in greater financial efficiency. The Inspection Test Plans recommended by TPIs were also
expected to enhance product reliability and reduce costs by eliminating redundant testing.
Nearly two years after the introduction of TPIs in the railways, Mr. Mehta reflected on their crucial role in
advancing the Government of India's vision for world-class manufacturing, and improving the global
competitiveness of Indian products. This reform increased inspection capacity, ensured efficient warranty
management, and facilitated better vendor assessments.
In reviewing the reports, he wondered if Railway benefited from TPIs and whether this initiative could be
expanded to other railway zones or Public Sector Units like Metro or Rapid Metro. He acknowledged that
while process inspections were now part of the new inspection policy, product inspections remain vital.
The challenge now, was to shift focus towards process inspections, which covered everything from raw
materials to finished products, allowing for early recommendations on replacements and potential cost
savings.

Case Study Title:
The Hunt for Benami Property:
A Data-Driven Approach
to Financial Investigation
Case Study Description: A retired senior civil servant, living a quiet post-service life, drew attention when the Benami Unit in Delhi spotted unusual property records. Quiet checks began—silent, precise, unnoticed. Clues pointed to hidden wealth. A secret search was planned across four cities. When the Income Tax teams struck, they uncovered a web of unreported assets and benami properties worth over ₹240 crores. Behind the calm facade lay a story of evasion—now exposed.
Case Text:
Introduction
When Ritu Singh Sharma took over as the head of a Benami Prohibition Unit (BPU) in New Delhi in June 2017,
she found that this new role was unlike any of her previous positions in the Income Tax Department. Typically,
a predecessor would provide a detailed “handing-over note” listing the pending tasks in the office. However,
this time there was none, as she was the first occupant of a newly created office.
It had been less than a year since Parliament passed the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act,
aimed at revitalizing a defunct law designed to prohibit and penalize benami transactions. The term “benami”
refers to a transaction in which property is acquired in the name of a person other than the actual beneficiary
owner. Benami properties, particularly land and other real estate, have long been identified as a favoured avenue
for criminals and tax evaders to conceal their ill-gotten wealth.
The newly amended legislation now empowered the Income Tax Department to establish special offices—
BPUs—to implement the benami law. While the existing investigation units focused on detecting and recovering
due taxes, the newly created BPUs were tasked with invoking provisions of the benami law to ultimately
confiscate benami properties and prosecute the beneficiaries of those properties.
The primary function of the BPUs set up across the country was to investigate allegations of benami properties
and issue show-cause notices to the accused beneficiaries, which would then be adjudicated by an independent
authority. As one of the first heads of a BPU, Singh Sharma had to be cautious, as her team’s interpretation of the
law would set a precedent for future cases. However, she faced a challenge with limited resources, having only
one junior officer and one staff member, both untrained in the new law.
Another issue was sourcing information on benami properties. One method was for an investigation unit to send
a “reference” to the BPU. This reference would contain detailed information about the property, the individuals
in whose name the property was acquired (the “benamidars”), and the actual beneficiary owner. Since the benami
law was new, not all investigation officers were aware that they were required to send references to the BPU. To
address this, Singh Sharma’s team held conferences and training sessions to encourage investigation officers to
share information on benami properties for further processing.

The Hunt for Benami Property – A data-driven approach for financial investigation

2
Relying on second-hand information through references made the BPU entirely dependent on the investigation
units. Was there any possibility for fresh approaches that would allow the BPUs to independently detect benami
properties?

The Data-Driven Approach
Unlike what she had expected, Singh Sharma’s BPU office was not overwhelmed with references of benami
properties from the investigation units, which were generally overburdened with their primary work. However,
after processing a few references, her team gained insight into how benami properties were acquired and
managed. A common trend was that these properties were owned by shell companies. Shell companies, or paper
companies, are lawfully registered on paper but, as their name suggests, are hollow inside and carry out no real
business activities. They are incorporated solely for the purpose of owning real estate.
Singh Sharma’s BPU office believed they could identify benami properties owned by shell companies if they had
access to data on companies incorporated specifically for that purpose. As a law enforcement agency, they had
access to the national company registrar database, where they could search for companies with no revenue that
simply held properties. However, this would have been a cumbersome approach, given that there were more
than 2 million registered companies. A simpler method would be to access a property database to identify
properties held by shell companies.
The real estate property database is usually maintained by a local government official known as a “sub-registrar.”
Although her office could have officially requested specific data from the local government under provisions of
the Income Tax Act, the process would have taken considerable time. The sub-registrar officials likely would not
have sufficient knowledge about the new benami law and its potential impact. To expedite the process, Singh
Sharma identified two senior officers in the local government who were her “batchmates”—they had joined the
civil service and trained together in the same cohort. This informal network of batchmates helps connect officers
and break down silos within the government. Singh Sharma specifically requested data on immovable properties
registered in the past 3 years in their districts of South and South-West Delhi. With some persuasion, she was
able to convince them to direct their subordinates to provide the property registry data for her investigation.
Once the data was obtained, Singh Sharma tasked her deputy, Pitamber Kumar, with analysing the South Delhi
property data to identify properties purchased by potential shell companies. Certain criteria were established to
narrow their search. First, the property had to be purchased by a company. Second, a transaction limit of a
minimum of Rs. 100 million was set, which reduced their set to around 1,000 properties. By scanning through the
names of the owner companies, they were able to easily identify those owned by large listed or blue-chip
companies, which were most likely genuine transactions. The remaining properties were privately held
companies, which were further examined through the companies database to determine whether they actually
conducted any business activity or merely held properties.
Ultimately, their list of potential suspects was narrowed down to a small set of properties owned by private
companies that conducted no business but appeared to have been incorporated solely for the purpose of owning
property. Among these was a property held by Prism Trades (name changed), a company registered in Kolkata.
Although Pitamber was a newcomer to the BPU, he had spent enough years in the tax department to know that
Kolkata was the hub for shell companies in the country. Prism Trades was a Kolkata registered company with no
annual revenue, its only asset being a property in the upscale area of Greater Kailash in South Delhi. Two
individuals became directors of this company at the time the property was acquired. Further checks into the
national company registry revealed that these directors were an octogenarian couple in Delhi who had assumed
directorships in 16 companies in a short span of time.
Profiling these 16 companies showed that many had also acquired residential or commercial properties
coinciding with the time the couple became directors. Were they the true beneficiary owners of these properties?
Singh Sharma considered this possibility, but a team she dispatched for discreet field inquiries reported that the

The Hunt for Benami Property – A data-driven approach for financial investigation

3
couple’s middle-class lifestyle did not align with the profile of someone who could own properties in the affluent
South Delhi suburb. The octogenarian husband was noted to have been a one-time legislator in 1977, but seemed
unlikely that he would suddenly come into wealth and purchased properties 40 years later.

Finding the beneficiary owners
Singh Sharma’s team of inspectors conducted discreet inquiries around the heavily guarded house in Greater
Kailash. The guards and caretakers, usually tight-lipped, revealed that the house belonged to one “Mr. Lal,” an
influential man in his sixties. He did not permanently reside there but visited once every couple of months with
his wife and family. However, there were no photographs or further descriptions to help identify the mysterious
Mr. Lal. The team needed more clues to track him down.
The breakthrough came when Pitamber, while reviewing the tax and regulatory filings of various companies,
discovered that one company owned a commercial property leased to a banking company. The monthly rent
from this property was deposited into a bank account listed in the tax return. Unlike residential properties with
anonymous occupants, this situation presented a clear case of pecuniary benefit from a benami property.
Exercising his authority under the Income Tax Act, Pitamber requested the details of the authorized signatories
for the bank account. He opted to obtain this information from the bank’s head office rather than the branch office
to prevent any leaks from bank employees familiar with the account holders.
The reply that reached him late one evening introduced new names: the siblings Mr. Krish (aged 30) and Ms.
Pragya (aged 33) from Lucknow, who were the authorized signatories of the bank account and, therefore, the
actual controllers of the companies. Had they found the beneficial owners they were looking for?
Pitamber did not want to wait until the next day to share this information and rushed to Singh Sharma’s office in
excitement. His superior acknowledged that they had made a breakthrough— Krish and Pragya could indeed be
the beneficial owners of the benami properties. She felt it was the right time to escalate this information to her
superior, Ramesh Yadav, Principal Director (Investigation).
A veteran tax investigator, Yadav had worked on investigation policy matters and had drafted the guidelines for
the benami law. He was eager to see the law implemented as intended. His current role as the head of
investigations allowed him to test the legislation outside laboratory conditions. When the case findings were
presented to him, Yadav smiled upon seeing the address where Krish and Pragya were reported to live.
“How well do you know Lucknow?” he asked his juniors. They shook their heads.
Yadav was familiar with Lucknow, having worked in the state government before joining the Income Tax
Department.
“Krish and Pragya are young and live at a Kalidas Marg address. This is the same street where the Chief Minister
of the state lives. It is a VIP area where ministers and top civil servants live, and no private citizens will have a
residence there. We must find out who Krish and Pragya’s parents are.”
It did not take Pitamber long to look up their father’s name and obtain his tax return filings.
“Nek Chand, retired as the senior-most civil servant of the state, is the father of Krish and Pragya. The Kalidas
Marg address was his official residence during his service; now he lives in a different area,” he reported to his
superiors.
Singh Sharma was thrilled. “Well done, Pitamber! We have identified the beneficiary owner!” She thought it was
an open-and-shut case. Turning to her superior, she asked, “Sir, we have our benami case ready. We have at least
four properties owned through shell companies, with the benamidars being the Delhi couple and the beneficiary
owner being Nek Chand. Shall we send him a show cause notice?”

The Hunt for Benami Property – A data-driven approach for financial investigation

4

“No, Ritu, we will conduct a search action.”
“But sir, we have all the data; we have identified the individuals...”
“No, we must launch a search,” Yadav insisted, speaking from his experience.
“The civil servant in question held many powerful positions and likely consolidated his earnings—no doubt from
dubious or illegal sources—into properties in Delhi just before his retirement, intending to leave a pot of wealth
for his children. He has used intermediaries in Kolkata and has carefully built the structure of companies to
conceal his involvement. If we send him a notice asking for an explanation, he will only provide minimal
information. He will engage accountants and lawyers to delay the process. It will be difficult for us to penetrate
the layers involved, some of which extend to other cities like Kolkata. Without sufficient information, we won’t
be able to establish a strong benami case. I firmly believe that we cannot achieve our desired outcome through
open inquiries; only a search action will lead us there.

Preparing for the search
Yadav discussed the matter with his superior, the Director General (Investigation), who promptly agreed that a
search should be initiated. With general elections approaching, both men sensed that there would be no political
obstacles or resistance in this case. They had all the necessary information to proceed with a search action.
Singh Sharma, who also headed an Investigation unit in addition to the Benami unit, was given a target of 3 days
to launch the search. Sachin Kumar, her deputy in the Investigation unit, was tasked with preparing for the search
with the assistance of Pitamber. The two deputies worked through the night, compiling and consolidating the
information at hand, mapping the layers of company structures, identifying all the properties held, and
pinpointing the key individuals they planned to search.
The search was to be executed at 18 locations in Delhi and Lucknow, including the residences of the suspected
benamidars, the suspected beneficiary owners, the offices of the shell companies, and the suspected benami
properties. They also added Vikas, an accountant in Kolkata whose email address appeared in the tax returns of
the shell companies and who seemed to have helped establish the company arrangement. Throughout the
planning process, the strictest levels of secrecy were maintained, ensuring that only a few officers knew the
identities of the individuals and locations to be searched.

The search action
Teams from the Investigation Wing in Delhi arrived at 18 locations early in the morning on the scheduled date.
The standard procedures for such an operation include serving search warrants, calling in two witnesses for each
location, recording preliminary statements from the individuals being searched, and searching the premises for
evidence.
As expected, Nek Chand denied ownership of the South Delhi house or any other property not in his name. He
claimed that the South Delhi house belonged to his friend, Pankaj Kapoor from Bareilly, and that he only used
the place for occasional trips to Delhi. Consequently, a new team of officers with a fresh search warrant was
immediately dispatched to Bareilly to investigate Kapoor.
Singh Sharma and Sachin Kumar coordinated the search from the control room in their Delhi office. The four
teams in Delhi, Lucknow, Kolkata, and Bareilly now needed to work together to gather and share evidence and
corroborate the statements of the suspects.

The Hunt for Benami Property – A data-driven approach for financial investigation

5
It emerged that the directors of the Kolkata shell companies were none other than Nek Chand’s parents-in-law.

The elderly couple from Delhi admitted that the companies and properties were actually owned by their son-in-
law and that they were merely name lenders for the companies.

In the vacant South Delhi house, the team discovered a large amount of cash. However, with no one to claim
ownership or provide an explanation, the cash was promptly seized.
In Bareilly, Kapoor testified under oath that he had been instructed by Nek Chand to acquire shell companies
holding various properties and that he acted as a middleman to facilitate these acquisitions with the help of Vikas,
the Kolkata-based accountant.
In Kolkata, Vikas, the accountant, admitted under oath that he assisted Nek Chand in acquiring shell companies
and explained the entire layered ownership structure, which ultimately vested in Nek Chand’s son, Krish.
The admissions made were significant developments for the search teams. However, despite the admissibility of
these statements as evidence, Singh Sharma believed they were insufficient. The teams directed to search for hard
evidence persisted and uncovered two crucial pieces of incriminating information.
First, a diary was found in the South Delhi house containing neat entries that listed all properties held through
various companies. These entries included names of companies and details of properties that were not known to
the investigation teams prior to the search. Although Nek Chand denied that the diary entries were in his
handwriting, a subsequent examination by a forensic laboratory confirmed that the handwriting matched Nek
Chand’s.
The second important piece of evidence was a mobile phone hidden in Nek Chand’s wardrobe, which was
exclusively used for communication with Kapoor and Vikas, the Kolkata accountant.
Singh Sharma identified a pertinent issue that needed resolution: establishing the identity of Mr. Lal, named by
the caretakers of the South Delhi house as the ultimate beneficiary. This did not take long, as the teams now had
access to photographs of Nek Chand, his family members, Kapoor, and Vikas. The truth was finally established
when the caretaker of the South Delhi house admitted under oath that Mr. Lal was the person whose photograph
was shown to him—Nek Chand.

Conclusion
A search action is “concluded” when a record of the proceedings, known as a panchanama, is signed by the
searched individuals in the presence of two witnesses referred to as panchas. The seized documents, cash, and
other valuables, along with the panchanamas from each premises, were brought to the control room in Sachin
Kumar’s office. In the following months, he examined the seized documents and prepared a detailed report
estimating the tax evaded by Nek Chand. More importantly, documentary evidence established that Nek Chand
was the actual beneficial owner of the properties identified during the investigation. His properties worth around
₹2.4 billion were attached by the Income Tax Department. The information gathered during the search was used
to create a comprehensive reference for the Benami Prohibition Unit, which would pursue a prosecution case
under the Benami law.
“A property is considered benami when it is acquired through funds owned by the beneficiary owner, who often
is the individual that actually enjoys the property. Establishing the identify of Mr. Lal was crucial for building a
strong benami case,” said Singh Sharma. “Nek Chand had acquired numerous properties for the benefit of his
family. His family members either resided in these properties or earned rent by leasing them out. Although he
had involved his in-laws as proxy directors in the Kolkata shell companies, he did not trust them with the bank
account; their purpose was to sign documents. Our investigation also revealed that his friend Kapoor introduced
him to Vikas, the accountant who helped conceal the ill-gotten wealth through a network of Kolkata shell
companies. This not only aided us in detecting the properties but also in establishing them as benami.”

The Hunt for Benami Property – A data-driven approach for financial investigation

6
For Ritu Singh Sharma, whose tenure began without a handover note or prior case precedents, this case
underscored the potential of data in effectively conducting financial investigations. Analyzing property records
was the starting point, followed by meticulously tracing ownership through company registry documents, and
finally conducting discreet yet patient inquiries, which led to the astonishing detection of an offense by a
significant person. This experience demonstrated that enforcing a complex law requires leadership and
collaboration.
Epilogue
Nek Chand’s desire to leave a grand empire for his son was unfulfilled. Tragically, his son, who struggled with
alcoholism, died of cirrhosis just a few months after the search.
The benami law faced challenges in the courts, and in 2022, the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional.
However, in 2024, this ruling was reversed, reviving the case.
A significant portion of the black economy in the country, particularly proceeds from crime or funds that have
evaded taxation, is tied up in benami properties. Despite administrative and legal obstacles, the Income Tax
Department continues to combat the issue of benami properties. ek Chand’s desire of leaving a grand empire for
his son was not met. Unfortunately, the son who was battling alcoholism died of cirrhosis a few months after the
search.

Case Study Title:
Institutionalizing Community
Engagement to Tackle Malnutrition:
A Case Study of the Tithi Bhojan Initiative
Case Study Description: This case study explores the institutionalization of Tithi Bhojan under the PM POSHAN scheme as a model of community-led action to address child malnutrition. It highlights the shift from government-led service delivery to community-enabled participation, examining how diverse stakeholders collaborate to integrate the initiative into policy. The case raises key questions about sustaining community engagement, building multi-stakeholder partnerships, and embedding participatory governance in public nutrition programs for long-term impact.
Case Text:
Introduction
In the 113th episode of Mann Ki Baat on August 25, 2024, Prime Minister Narendra Modi stated, “आपके एक छोटे
सेप्रयास सेकु पोषण केखिलाफ इस लडाई मेंबहुत मदद ममलेगी.” (“Your little effort will go a long way in this fight against
malnutrition.”)
This message conceptualizes the essence of Tithi Bhojan, a community-driven initiative under Pradhan Mantri
Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN) aimed at addressing malnutrition through collective effort and societal
accountability.
India has long struggled with child malnutrition. At the time of independence in 1947, an estimated 50% of
children under the age of 5 suffered from severe malnutrition and related illnesses due to poverty, food
insecurity, and inadequate healthcare infrastructure (World Bank 1998). Over the decades, significant efforts have
been made to combat this crisis through interventions such as the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS),
launched in 1975, and the Mid-Day Meal Scheme (MDMS), rolled out nationwide in 1995. These programs
provided critical support, including supplementary nutrition, health check-ups, and immunization under ICDS,
as well as school meals aimed at improving both education and nutrition through MDMS.
Despite these efforts, progress has been uneven. Recent data show that nearly 35% of children under 5 are stunted,
19% are wasted1

, and 32% are underweight, according to the National Family Health Survey – 5 (NFHS-5) (2019–
2021). While this marks an improvement from earlier decades—such as the NFHS-3 (2005–2006), when 48% of
children were stunted and 43% underweight—malnutrition remains a persistent challenge. A significant factor
contributing to this persistent challenge is the gap in implementation. Challenges in implementation stem from

1 A child is considered wasted if their weight-for-height is significantly below the expected standard, meaning
they are thin for their height.

Institutionalizing Community Engagement to Tackle Malnutrition: A Case Study of the
Tithi Bhojan Initiative

2
inadequate infrastructure, transmission losses, and a shortage of trained personnel. Moreover, these programs
have been limited in reach due to a lack of community ownership and engagement.
Child malnutrition is not only a government challenge but also a societal issue that demands collective action.
Government programs like ICDS and MDMS provide fundamental support, but they often fall short because of
resource constraints, logistical challenges, and the sheer scale of the problem. Strengthening community
participation is essential to bridging these gaps. Local stakeholders, including parents, teachers, community
leaders, and civil society groups, have a better understanding of their needs, cultural practices, and challenges.
Their involvement can ensure that nutritional programs are more relevant, effective, and sustainable. Scholars
such as Elinor Ostrom have demonstrated that coproduction—the joint effort of government agencies and citizens
in designing and delivering public services—can dramatically enhance both the reach and quality of those
services (Ostrom 1996). In her analysis of sanitation systems in Brazil, Ostrom emphasized that activating
community involvement from the planning stage led to better outcomes, lower costs, and greater accountability.
Similarly, Archon Fung’s work on participatory governance highlights the power of inclusive, deliberative
processes, where ordinary citizens engage in shaping policies that affect their lives, leading to more equitable and
responsive governance (Fung 2006). Inculcating a sense of ownership among communities enhances
accountability and transforms malnutrition from a distant policy issue into a shared responsibility. When
communities actively participate, they bring innovative solutions, mobilize local resources, and build trust in
government initiatives.
Recognizing the need for community-driven solutions, Gujarat pioneered the Tithi Bhojan program in 2014,
encouraging individuals and communities to contribute meals on special occasions to enhance school nutrition.
This innovative approach demonstrated how involving local stakeholders could fill gaps in government
programs and strengthen the fight against malnutrition. The success of Gujarat’s model laid the foundation for
scaling it nationwide. In 2018, guidelines for integrating Tithi Bhojan into broader nutritional frameworks were
developed. By 2022, the program was officially incorporated into the revised PM POSHAN guidelines, promoting
community involvement across states. Between April and July 2024, the initiative was launched as a Jan Andolan
(people’s movement) through the Ministry of Education’s 100 Days Program. Community members, local groups,
and civil society organizations organized events on significant dates, symbolizing a unified effort to improve
child nutrition.

The Driving Forces Behind Tithi Bhojan
The origins of Tithi Bhojan trace back to a simple yet transformative vision articulated by Prime Minister
Narendra Modi—to make malnutrition a shared societal responsibility rather than just a government mandate.
What began as a localized experiment in Gujarat quickly gained national attention, leading to its policy
integration into PM POSHAN and adoption across multiple states. However, as Tithi Bhojan scaled up, it raised
fundamental governance dilemmas—balancing government oversight with community leadership, sustaining
contributions, and ensuring quality and safety in donated meals. Recognizing the potential of community-driven
nutrition, the Ministry of Education institutionalized Tithi Bhojan within the PM POSHAN framework,
formalizing guidelines for implementation. As emphasized in a letter dated 29 November 2023:
“Tithi Bhojan is a community participation program in which additional food items/full meal is provided on
special occasions such as festivals, anniversaries, birthdays, marriages, and days of national importance to school
children by community.”
This initiative was designed to supplement the MDMS with fresh, locally sourced, and culturally relevant food
contributed by the community. To ensure nutritional adequacy, meals provided through Tithi Bhojan must align
with the nutritional norms outlined under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013—delivering 450 calories
and 12 grams of protein for primary students and 750 calories and 20 grams of protein for upper primary students.

Institutionalizing Community Engagement to Tackle Malnutrition: A Case Study of the
Tithi Bhojan Initiative

3
The Ministry of Education has also included Tithi Bhojan in its 100 Days Programme, urging states and union
territories to organize at least one event during this period with active community participation. A letter dated
26 June 2024 (Exhibit 1), issued by Anandrao V. Patil, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Education, Government
of India, to the additional chief secretaries/principal secretaries/secretaries (Education) and PM POSHAN
commissioners/directors of all states and union territories, emphasizes the importance of using these events to
“inculcate and promote healthy eating habits and best hygiene practices among students.” The guidelines
mandate the inclusion of green leafy vegetables, legumes, millets, and seasonal fruits in the menu while strictly
prohibiting junk and stale food. The involvement of school management committees (SMCs)2

is critical in

planning menus, identifying donors, and ensuring smooth execution.
The initiative is implemented under various names across states, such as Sneh Bhojan in Madhya Pradesh and
Maharashtra, Sampriti Bhojan in Assam, and Anna Dhanam in Puducherry, reflecting its adaptability to local
cultures. The ministry emphasizes the need for states to collaborate with farmer producer organizations, women’s
self-help groups (SHGs), and corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives to sustain the program. To ensure
food safety and hygiene, the guidelines specify that meals must be tasted by a teacher or cook before serving and
prepared according to standard cleanliness protocols. States are also encouraged to conduct training programs
for cooks and volunteers through institutions like the Institute of Hotel Management to maintain quality.
The ministry has further directed states and union territories to provide a comprehensive action plan and submit
reports detailing the number of schools and students covered during Tithi Bhojan events. By embedding
nutritional guidelines into community participation efforts, the government aims to bridge implementation gaps
in existing school meal programs while fostering a sense of local ownership and accountability. However, as
states began adapting Tithi Bhojan to their unique sociocultural contexts, questions arose about how best to
institutionalize this model for long-term sustainability. Would standardized administrative oversight help scale
and sustain the initiative, or would a fully decentralized approach, empowering local governance structures, be
more effective?

The Actors Behind Tithi Bhojan: Governance, Challenges, and Decision Points
The Tithi Bhojan initiative relies on diverse stakeholders, each playing a crucial role in its implementation,
sustainability, and governance. At the policy level, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Ministry of Education
act as policy architects, positioning Tithi Bhojan not merely as a welfare scheme but as a Jan Andolan (people’s
movement) to promote collective accountability. Policy integration into PM POSHAN guidelines ensures a
national framework while granting states flexibility in execution, leading to variations in implementation across
regions.
District education officers and school committees serve as the nodal agencies at the administrative level,
overseeing the initiative’s coordination, school participation, contribution tracking, and food safety compliance.
However, they face a governance dilemma—should they tighten regulations to ensure uniform meal quality and
distribution, or allow greater autonomy to communities, even if it risks inconsistencies in implementation?
Panchayat leaders and religious institutions act as mobilizers within the community, integrating Tithi Bhojan into
local traditions to encourage sustained participation. Their primary challenge lies in institutionalizing
community engagement so that meal contributions remain consistent and inclusive, rather than being driven by

2 The school management committee (SMC) is a statutory body in government schools that includes parents,
teachers, and local authorities, responsible for planning, monitoring, and supporting the implementation of
school activities.

Institutionalizing Community Engagement to Tackle Malnutrition: A Case Study of the
Tithi Bhojan Initiative

4
sporadic or elite-dominated donations. Meanwhile, Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA) workers3
,

Anganwadi staff4

, and schoolteachers serve as the frontline implementers, directly connecting parents, students,
and donors. They must decide whether to expand their role in actively coordinating meal contributions or limit
their involvement to avoid overburdening their already demanding responsibilities.
Finally, nongovernment organizations, SHGs, and CSR entities serve as resource enablers, providing logistical
support, funding, and training to scale Tithi Bhojan. However, their role remains a strategic consideration: should
they become direct food suppliers to ensure meal consistency, or should they focus on capacity building,
equipping local governance structures to take ownership of the initiative? These intersecting roles and decision
points define the governance scope of Tithi Bhojan, highlighting the tensions between centralized oversight and
decentralized community- driven ownership.

From Government-Led Programs to Community- Driven Governance
To enhance food safety, several states have actively involved Mothers’ Committees in the monitoring and
implementation of the MDMS. In Assam, mother groups play a significant role in overseeing meal preparation
and quality, ensuring adherence to safety protocols. Similarly, in Uttarakhand and Jharkhand, the involvement
of mothers in the scheme’s implementation is recognized as a best practice, fostering community ownership and
vigilance in maintaining hygiene standards. These collaborative efforts between government bodies and
community members, particularly Mothers’ Committees, are crucial in preserving the integrity of meal programs
like Tithi Bhojan, ensuring that children receive safe and nutritious food.
“The strength of Tithi Bhojan lies not in policy directives but in the collective will of the people,” said a school
headmaster in Gujarat, who has witnessed the program evolve from a one-time meal donation to a deeply
ingrained community tradition. “When parents and local leaders take ownership, children receive nutritious food
and feel a sense of belonging.”
Public welfare programs often struggle with long-term sustainability due to an overreliance on government
mechanisms. Tithi Bhojan challenges this norm by shifting the focus from ”government as the provider” to
“community as the enabler”—a model where governance is not just about policies but about participation. The
initiative operates on the philosophy that while the state provides the framework, the true custodians of child
nutrition are local stakeholders—community leaders, grassroots mobilizers, civil society, and private players—
who collectively institutionalize governance at the community level.
The success of this model is evident in villages where local panchayats have institutionalized Tithi Bhojan as a
community responsibility. In some districts, panchayat members have passed resolutions ensuring that every
household contributes at least once a year, embedding the initiative into local traditions rather than treating it as
an externally imposed program. Religious institutions have also played a catalytic role, with temples, mosques,
and gurdwaras integrating Tithi Bhojan into their charitable activities, making community meal-sharing a
spiritual and social obligation.
“We started by organizing meals on festival days,” explained a village priest in Rajasthan, “but now it has become
a part of our identity. Feeding schoolchildren is as much a duty as performing rituals in the temple.”

3 ASHA workers are community health volunteers under the National Health Mission, who act as a bridge
between the community and the public health system, promoting maternal and child health, nutrition, and
sanitation.
4 Anganwadi staff includes Anganwadi workers and helpers who run centres under the ICDS scheme,
providing basic healthcare, nutrition, and preschool education to children under six, and support services to
pregnant and lactating women.

Institutionalizing Community Engagement to Tackle Malnutrition: A Case Study of the
Tithi Bhojan Initiative

5
Institutionalizing such an initiative requires more than goodwill—it demands structured mobilization. In this
regard, Anganwadi workers, ASHAs, and schoolteachers have emerged as the linchpins of decentralized
governance. They ensure that Tithi Bhojan is not perceived as charity but as a community duty. Their role extends
beyond mobilization to facilitating logistics, ensuring food safety, and integrating Tithi Bhojan into school health
programs. In some villages, ASHAs and Anganwadi workers have mapped households based on dietary
diversity, suggesting meal contributions that complement school meals rather than duplicate them. This
scientific, structured approach to community-led nutrition ensures that Tithi Bhojan is not merely a one-day event
but a continuous, well-balanced intervention.
“We are not just collecting food,” said an ASHA worker from Madhya Pradesh, “we are ensuring that the
donations meet the nutritional needs of the children.” This shift—from ad-hoc donations to strategic, need-based
meal planning—demonstrates that successful welfare programs do not require increased government
intervention but rather stronger horizontal linkages between existing community structures.
At the heart of this movement is a growing network of youth groups and women’s SHGs, which have
transformed Tithi Bhojan into more than just a meal-sharing initiative. Women’s SHGs, recognizing the
nutritional gaps in children’s diets, have donated protein-rich foods such as lentils, eggs, and dairy products.
Youth groups have leveraged social media to raise awareness and mobilize micro donations. In some districts,
former students have formed alumni networks that fund periodic Tithi Bhojan events, creating an
intergenerational model of community responsibility.
“We don’t wait for funding,” said a young volunteer from Karnataka. “We create it. Our former schoolmates
working in cities contribute a small amount every month, and that is enough to ensure our school has a Tithi
Bhojan event every fortnight.”

Unlike traditional public welfare models that rely on continued state funding, Tithi Bhojan leverages market-
driven solutions through CSR partnerships. Several corporate groups have adopted schools, providing long-term

infrastructure support rather than one-time meal donations. “With the support of the government and society,
this initiative is succeeding. We need to expand it further,” noted a CSR head from a leading business firm that
has partnered with government schools in Telangana. This shift toward public–private–community partnerships
ensure sustainability, reduces financial dependence on government budgets, and strengthens localized
ownership.
Ultimately, the success of Tithi Bhojan lies not just in feeding children but in demonstrating how governance can
move beyond government. The initiative has blurred the lines between policy, philanthropy, and personal
responsibility, proving that collective accountability—when institutionalized—can outperform conventional
welfare models.
“We don’t need rules to tell us to feed our children,” reflected a school committee member in Uttar Pradesh. “We
just need a platform to do it together.” The initiative has transformed from a policy intervention into a societal
movement, embedding local leadership, decentralized decision- making, and social accountability into Tithi
Bhojan.

Key Dilemma and Implementation Challenges
Tithi Bhojan is emerging as a promising community-driven solution to address child malnutrition by encouraging
local participation in enhancing school meals. However, the key dilemma lies in institutionalizing community
engagement for sustainable and scalable impact. While the initiative has demonstrated its potential, several
challenges must be addressed to ensure its long-term viability and success.

Institutionalizing Community Engagement to Tackle Malnutrition: A Case Study of the
Tithi Bhojan Initiative

6

1. Coordination and Supply Chain Issues
Effective implementation of Tithi Bhojan requires seamless coordination among multiple stakeholders, including
school management committees, panchayats, local donors, and government departments. In many cases,
overlapping responsibilities and the absence of a clear operational framework lead to delays and inefficiencies.
The supply chain for sourcing fresh, nutritious, and culturally relevant food often encounters logistical hurdles,
particularly in remote and underserved areas. Ensuring a steady flow of quality ingredients while minimizing
wastage requires significant planning and monitoring, which is not consistently implemented across regions.
2. Resource and Capacity Challenges
Despite the community-driven nature of the program, many regions face resource constraints that hinder
effective execution. Schools often lack basic infrastructure, such as storage facilities for food and functional
kitchens for meal preparation. Furthermore, there is a gap in the capacity of local stakeholders, including school
staff and community members, to organize and manage Tithi Bhojan events. Training programs for food safety,
logistics, and nutritional requirements are either insufficient or inaccessible, particularly in rural areas. These
gaps limit the ability of schools and local bodies to fully capitalize on community contributions.
3. Program Operator Issues
The individuals and organizations responsible for managing Tithi Bhojan—such as headmasters, schoolteachers,
and panchayats—face numerous operational challenges. Many program operators struggle to balance the
administrative workload of organizing Tithi Bhojan events with their existing responsibilities. The lack of a
standardized monitoring framework often results in inconsistencies in implementation, making it difficult to
track progress or identify areas for improvement. Ensuring accountability and maintaining transparency in
resource utilization remains a persistent challenge, further complicating the institutionalization of the program.

Policy Options for Institutionalizing Tithi Bhojan
Strengthen Administration at the District Level
One approach to institutionalizing Tithi Bhojan is to strengthen administration at the district level. This strategy
empowers district-level officials, such as district education officers, SMCs, and other administrative bodies, to
oversee and monitor the program’s implementation. Enhanced capacity- building efforts for these “street
bureaucrats” and the introduction of robust monitoring systems would ensure compliance with program
guidelines and maintain accountability.
The advantages of this approach include a structured and consistent framework, as district-level authorities can
standardize processes across all schools, ensuring uniformity and reducing the potential for errors. It also enables
effective capacity building, as district officials and school staff receive targeted training in resource management,
food safety, and community engagement. This model strengthens monitoring mechanisms, allowing the
administration to track contributions, measure outcomes, and address issues such as food safety violations or
logistical inefficiencies. However, this approach has notable drawbacks. It requires significant administrative
investment, including training programs, IT systems, and additional personnel to support monitoring and
reporting. Centralized oversight can lead to bureaucratic inefficiencies, resulting in delays in decision-making
and a lack of responsiveness to local challenges. Most critically, a top-down model may reduce community
ownership, as local stakeholders may feel less involved or empowered, undermining the program’s goal of
fostering grassroots participation.
Decentralize Efforts to Local Governance

Another approach is to decentralize the implementation of Tithi Bhojan by empowering panchayats, community-
based organizations (CBOs), and SHGs to take the lead. This strategy places decision- making power in the hands

Institutionalizing Community Engagement to Tackle Malnutrition: A Case Study of the
Tithi Bhojan Initiative

7
of local governance structures, allowing them to plan menus, mobilize resources, and organize events based on
their unique cultural and regional contexts.
This approach offers significant advantages, particularly in encouraging local ownership and responsibility.
Communities are more likely to engage actively when directly involved in decision- making. Additionally, local
governance bodies have a better understanding of local preferences, customs, and needs, enabling them to design
culturally relevant menus and events. Decentralization can also be more cost-effective, as it reduces dependency
on higher-level administration and taps into existing community resources and networks.
However, this approach is not without challenges. The capacity of local bodies varies widely across regions,
leading to uneven implementation. While some panchayats and CBOs excel, others may lack the resources,
leadership, or experience to manage the program effectively. There is also a heightened risk of resource misuse
due to weak accountability mechanisms, which can result in inconsistent food quality and safety. Furthermore,
coordination challenges between local bodies, schools, donors, and administrative authorities can complicate the
program’s execution.

Epilogue: Measuring the Impact and Future of Tithi Bhojan
By the end of 2024, data from Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha highlighted both the successes and
challenges of institutionalizing Tithi Bhojan as a community-driven school nutrition initiative.
In Gujarat, where the program first originated, 97% of schools reported regular and sustained contributions from
the community. The panchayats took ownership of the initiative by integrating it into village governance
structures and establishing formalized donation schedules. This systematic approach ensured that meal
contributions were not sporadic but rather structured and reliable, creating a self-sustaining model of collective
responsibility.
In Madhya Pradesh, the integration of Tithi Bhojan with the state’s Mere Bacche Abhiyan (My Children
Campaign) demonstrated the potential of SHG-led nutrition programs to enhance meal diversity and nutritional
quality. This approach also empowered women at the grassroots level, reinforcing the link between community
engagement and decentralized governance in public welfare programs.
The national challenge emerging from these state-level experiences was twofold: Should high- performing states

serve as models for others, replicating their best practices and governance structures? And how can low-
performing districts be supported and incentivized without introducing excessive bureaucratic oversight that

could deter community ownership?
As policymakers and stakeholders deliberated on these questions, one fact remained clear—Tithi Bhojan had
transcended its origins as a policy initiative and evolved into a people’s movement, redefining participatory
governance in India’s nutrition programs.

Reflection and Future-Oriented Questions
The Tithi Bhojan initiative illustrates the transformative potential of community-driven governance in addressing
malnutrition. Yet, its sustainability depends heavily on institutional frameworks, continuous community
motivation, and the ability to adapt and scale effectively. Reflecting on this case, readers are encouraged to
consider:

strengthened to maintain sustained community engagement and ownership in the long term? How might
these structures balance local autonomy with necessary accountability?
2. Leadership and capacity-building: How should capacity-building efforts be structured to equip local
leaders, frontline workers, and community volunteers to sustain engagement and respond effectively to
evolving nutritional challenges?

Case Study Title: Ticket to Transformation:Digitalizing Human Resourcesin Indian Railways
Case Study Description: This case explores the ambitious digital transformation of the Human Resources function in Indian Railways, one of the largest public sector employers in the world. It follows the shift from a manual, paper-based system to an integrated Human Resource Management System (HRMS) developed by CRIS, the IT arm of Indian Railways. The case outlines why the change was needed, how it was implemented, and the challenges faced along the way, from managing legacy data and ensuring cybersecurity to handling change in a hierarchical system. It also touches on stakeholder engagement, training, and the wider impact of digitisation in government. This is a story of transforming scale with strategy, and legacy with leadership.
Case Text:
Introduction
“Thank you, Madam. Your system just saved me 6 months’ worth of effort, which I had never imagined.”
Bhooma recalled these as the most satisfying words she had heard from a junior railway technician in the
northernmost corner of the country during her inspection tour. As the leader overseeing human resources (HR)
management for over a million personnel in India’s largest government organization, she felt a sense of relief
and pride as her team’s efforts to leverage technology for transforming HR processes began to yield tangible
results.
In the vast expanse of India’s nationwide railway network, efficient human resources management is
paramount for smooth operations. However, HR in Indian Railways is not like that of any other organization.
Indian Railways is one of the largest employers in the world under a single management, with a workforce of
over 1.2 million employees spread across the country, in addition to another half a million pensioners and
counting. Beyond the sheer numbers, Indian Railway’s employee base is highly diverse, reflecting India’s
multifaceted nature. It employs individuals from various social, cultural, economic, and educational
backgrounds, distributed throughout the vast railway network. This diversity not only ensures inclusivity but
also brings varied perspectives and skills, enabling Indian Railways to effectively serve a diverse population.
The Personnel Department manages the HR needs of this large workforce. Most functions have been performed
manually for decades, including recordkeeping and employee services. Being a government organization, all
processes are rule-based, adhering to specific codes, manuals, and circulars. Any change or process
reengineering is complex, as it involves multiple levels of approval followed by actual implementation across
all units. The system required constant human intervention and was replete with shortcomings such as a lack of
standardization in processes, oversights, leakages, misuse, and weak monitoring. Additionally, employees
found it inconvenient to access many of HR services, leading to numerous grievances. Thus, the need for a
technology-based solution became imminent.

Introduction to Human Resources in Indian Railways
The Personnel Department in Indian Railways ensures that major HR functions such as recruitment,
promotions, transfers, retirements, payroll, welfare, training, industrial relations with employee unions, and
legal matters are conducted in accordance with established rules and policies. It also serves as the custodian of
employee records, service books, and personal files for the majority of the workforce. These functions can be
broadly classified as follows:
1. Employee-centric activities - These are services provided to individual employees, including applications
for leave, free travel passes, requests for transfers, and withdrawals from the Provident Fund (a retirement
fund). All employee-centric activities involve a paper-based application and approval process, which is lengthy,
non-transparent, and inconvenient, often requiring employees to travel long distances to the headquarters for
applications or status updates. Attempts have been made to streamline these processes, but they remain mostly
paper-based and prone to petty corruption.
2. Administrative processes - These activities are necessary for the HR Department to perform for all
employees. Promotions, for instance, may include departmental exams or selection processes for specific
employee categories. Other examples include processing payroll, completing performance appraisals,
conducting training, managing employee service records, addressing grievances, overseeing retirement

Ticket to Transformation: Digitalizing Human Resources in Indian Railways

3
processes, and handling disciplinary actions. All these processes in Indian Railways are highly rule-bound,
requiring various levels of approval and involving significant file movement and paperwork. While some
processes, like payroll, have been partially digitalized, others, such as grievance handling, have only been
brought online in a few units. Most tasks, however, remain manual and file-based.
3. Organizational setup - Certain core HR functions in Indian Railways pertain to Cadre Management and
maintaining Industrial Relations with active and vital employee unions. As a large employer, Indian Railways
has employees across various categories and skill sets. It is critical to maintain the right balance between the
number of staff required for safe and efficient operations and to redeploy redundant staff—those affected by
technological advancements, work closures, or medical unfitness—into different skills sets. Additionally, to
ensure personnel availability, recruitment must occur nationwide, gathering requirements for various skill sets
from different units. All these activities are part of Manpower Planning, a vital function of the HR Department.
These processes were always confined to files, with the closest brush with technology being Excel sheets and
Word documents. Despite the critical importance of the data and reports generated— essential for informed
decision-making—the methods of data collection and recordkeeping across the HR Department of Indian
Railways remained outdated and fragmented. The potential to harness this data for strategic, analytics-driven
HR was immense, but manual, file-based systems hindered any meaningful insight or analysis. Each divisional
and zonal headquarters maintained a large storehouse of files and records, staffed by record-sorters and
recordkeepers who assisted employees in locating specific documents. Interestingly, the R&D section in the
office did not involve research and development; rather, it referred to the Receive and Dispatch section that
managed the movement of files and papers across the bureaucratic hierarchy for approvals and processing.
As evident from the above, digitization would not only provide reliable, fast, and convenient access to services
but also enhance data analysis and information management. The first attempt at technology integration came
in the form of the Personnel Management Information System (PMIS), which primarily covered some
administrative processes. While basic employee data was digitized in a database, it remained locally accessible
within individual units and the system lacked integration across all units. Consequently, organization-level
data was unavailable, with only isolated applications and employee databases implemented. Nevertheless, this
marked the first IT implementation involving human resources in Indian Railways. This was followed by
applications related to some employee-centric activities, but these too were limited to local units and lacked
integration among different units of Indian Railways.
A major IT advancement was the implementation of the Integrated Payroll and Accounting System (IPAS),
which reengineered legacy payroll application to create a system accessible over the internet [1]. Developed by
the Centre for Railway Information System (CRIS), the IT wing of Indian Railways, this web-based application
utilized a centralized architecture with a single application and database. Based on functionality, the various
modules of IPAS basically perform two functions: payroll and accounts. It enables the preparation, processing,
bill passing, and accounting of salaries, allowances, loans, etc. Additionally, it includes provisions for
budgetary control, as well as the preparation of current accounts, appropriation accounts, and other financial
statements. While these changes in IT applications primarily focused on the accounts side and 4 Ticket to
Transformation: Digitalizing Human Resources in Indian Railways transformed payroll processing, a major
part of HR processes remained manually executed. There were isolated attempts to create applications
specifically for grievance redressal and for storing and sharing scanned service records, but these attempts were
highly localized, each with its own database and limited functionalities. Throughout this period, the need for an
enterprise-level HRMS application encompassing all aspects of human resources and employee-centric business
processes was increasingly felt and envisioned for Indian Railways.

Ticket to Transformation: Digitalizing Human Resources in Indian Railways

4

The Road Before the Map – Early Challenges
Crafting the Core – Built or Bought?
HRMS in Indian Railways, envisioned by the senior-most leadership in the Ministry of Railways, is an
enterprise-level application. While its necessity and advantages were widely acknowledged, considerable
debate arose regarding its execution and scope. Much of the discussion centered on whether the project should
be handled by the home-grown IT wing, CRIS, or outsourced to an external IT company. Another dilemma was
whether to opt for a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) application or to develop a bespoke in-house solution
from scratch. Major factors influencing this decision included cost and the availability of a more affordable
solution within the system. Numerous off-the-shelf products exist for implementing HR functionalities at an
enterprise scale, typically referred to as Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) applications. These products come

with built-in functionalities that support best practices in the domain, along with extensive reporting and data-
sharing capabilities. However, implementing these solutions would require significant customizations to meet

the specific requirements of HR processes in Indian Railways. This would involve hiring an IT partner to
conduct requirement gathering for a fit-gap analysis and to make necessary adjustments to align the product
with the organization’s existing processes. Extensive training would also be required for users before the
system could be tested and rolled out to all units. Such products require ongoing support and upgrades from
the vendor, similar to other software applications, which significantly increases the overall cost.
In contrast, a home-grown IT solution might be less expensive but would require development from scratch.
This would involve substantial work in gathering functional requirements, designing data flows, and
converting them into technical specifications. The technical team would also need to determine the appropriate
technology platform. One fundamental requirement for HR application would be a comprehensive employee
database. The existing payroll system already contained a wealth of employee data that could be used.
Consequently, senior management considered building HR functionalities around the existing payroll
application to minimize the effort involved in creating a new product.
However, a major issue with the payroll data was that it identified employees based on accounting and billing
units related to salary preparation, lacking a unique identifier for each employee. The identification number
used for salary preparation was not of standard length and had been replicated from a legacy payroll system.
While this number could be used for processing payroll, it was unsuitable for many HR processes. HRMS needs
to uniquely identify employees, record all possible attributes, and maintain real-time data updates through the
integrated business processes. Therefore, rather than using payroll data, it was deemed more appropriate to
create an employee master record within HRMS that would integrate all HR processes, including the existing
payroll system. Ultimately, the Employee Master in HRMS adopted a six-letter HRMS ID defined in the
database to uniquely associate with each employee.
The employee database, now featuring an HRMS ID for each employee, became so significant that, since its

launch, several other railway applications using their own employee data have switched to using the HRMS ID-
based employee details from the Employee Master of HRMS. This data proved very helpful in identifying

employees and their dependents during vaccination efforts during the COVID pandemic. It also played a
crucial role in the swift implementation of Mission Karmayogi, a national initiative launched by the
Government of India aimed at providing nationwide training and skill development for civil servants, with a
substantial number coming from the Indian Railways cadres.

Ticket to Transformation: Digitalizing Human Resources in Indian Railways

5

Unequipped and Unprepared: Missing Hardware, Missing Skills
To create a centralized database covering all employee-related attributes, it was crucial for data to be accurately
entered into the system. The Digital Transformation of HR, a greenfield project, aimed to convert a manual
paper-based ecosystem into a technology-driven online system based on Information Technology Enabled
Services. In this context, a legacy system typically refers to an older way of working; however, here, no such
system exists. Employee records were maintained on paper, and files had to be manually entered into the
system. Service records were kept in a standard booklet, with each entry manually signed by custodians.
Similarly, biographical, educational, medical, and family details of employees, starting from their recruitment,
were stored in files managed by a clerk who ensured they were preserved, updated, and transferred to new
custodians as needed. Data related to seniority, promotions, and manpower planning was also kept on paper.
All this information needed to be digitized for further processing. Manual data entry was the only option, as
scanning or image processing of records was not possible, which presented additional challenges.
The data to be entered was distributed across many offices nationwide. Each of these units required
appropriate hardware and skilled personnel to complete the job, highlighting two major gaps that the HRMS
team needed to address: the lack of adequate infrastructure and the absence of necessary skills among most
users involved in data entry. Although computers had been in use for a long time, they were not available to all
Personnel Department users responsible for data entry. Many machines were shared, some were isolated, not
connected to the office network. Any implementation strategy had to address this major concern because digital
transformation could not occur without proper access to technology and hardware.
Most employees in the HR Department, who would be pivotal in adopting the new HRMS system, lacked basic
computer skills, as they primarily worked on paper and files. While payroll processing was online, exposure
was limited to a few users, leaving a large number unaccustomed to online processes. In fact, the skill gap
extended beyond a few employees in the HR Department. Several senior officials and trade union leaders
expressed concerns that if basic employee services were offered online, many employees will struggle to access
them due to a lack of computer knowledge. They noted that older workers, some of whom were not sufficiently
literate, would depend on others to access the HRMS online. Additionally, the language barrier was a concern,
as the online system would be in English, which could alienate some employees who were not comfortable
using the language.
It was suggested that data entry work could either be outsourced or that data entry operators could be hired for
the task. This practice is common in many government offices, where data entry operators are engaged on a
contract basis to input data into the system. This would be a onetime activity for the HRMS. Once the data was
entered, it could be utilized for processing and generating additional data to update records online. However,
this one-time job was sensitive for two reasons: first, the data had to be entered accurately and verified at two
levels to ensure its correctness; second, the information was sensitive, containing actual employee details such
as personal information, family data, bank accounts, and medical records. Sharing this data with unauthorized
personnel would be inappropriate. Even if one level of data entry was outsourced, verification and approval
could only be performed online by internal staff. The digital backbone of the entire system needed to be
carefully curated and could not be compromised. Therefore, the basic IT skills of the involved staff became
crucial.
The hardware challenge was addressed by allocating a special budget for computers and related accessories as
part of the total project cost. These equipmnts were provided early on, soon after the first module was
deployed, to enable users to complete the data entry exercise more efficiently. To bridge the skill gap, both

Ticket to Transformation: Digitalizing Human Resources in Indian Railways

6
online and offline training sessions were conducted, and units were encouraged to direct all new users to utilize
the HRMS system exclusively. Some frequently used processes, such as issuing free railway passes and
applying for provident fund money were made mandatory, ensuring that all employees engaged with and
learned the system. Most units designated at least one nodal person to coordinate HRMS needs for all other
users, including those in the HR Department. Their roles became increasingly important each time a new
