Case Study Title: Defeating the Black Fever: India’s strategic win against Kala-azar
Case Study Description: India’s long-standing battle against Kala-azar persisted despite substantial resources and strategic programmes under NKEP. In 2021, Mr. Rajiv Manjhi identified that program success hinged on behavioural change and direct community involvement. Through innovative, locally adapted solutions—such as mud-house crack sealing, intensified surveillance, targeted vector management, health worker training, and rural evening awareness sessions—the programme enhanced effectiveness and public engagement. These measures significantly strengthened disease control efforts and marked a pivotal shift toward achieving national Kala-azar elimination.
Case Text:
Introduction
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Kala-azar, or visceral leishmaniasis, is a life-threatening
and neglected tropical disease that remains a significant public health concern in parts of India. The term was
coined in late nineteenth-century. It is also called ‘black fever’, referring to the greyish or blackish
discolouration of the skin during infection. It is derived from the Hindi word kala (black) and the Persian word
azar (disease/fever). It is the second deadliest parasitic disease after malaria. It is prevalent in four major
states—Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, and Jharkhand which together account for over 90 percent of
reported cases. This fatal disease has posed persistent health challenges in these regions, contributing
significantly to both morbidity and mortality. Globally, Kala-azar affects around 200 million people and
imposes a severe health and socio-economic burden. According to WHO [1], “India accounted for 18 percent of
the global burden of kala-azar in 2020.” The disease is especially widespread among poorer communities,
making India one of the most affected endemic countries.
Kala-azar is a vector-borne disease caused by a parasite transmitted through infected female sandflies. It
remains endemic in parts of India, especially Bihar, with outbreaks common during the monsoon [2]. The
disease thrives in areas with poor sanitation, inadequate housing, and limited healthcare. Such conditions are
often found in mud houses and cattle sheds that support sandfly breeding. Proximity to endemic regions in
Nepal and Bangladesh further increases vulnerability. Kala-azar presents with symptoms like prolonged fever,
weight loss, splenomegaly3

, and anaemia which are often mistaken for other illnesses. Diagnosis typically

involves rK39 tests4

, splenic or bone marrow aspiration5

, or Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)6 assays.
Generally, these are not always available in rural areas, leading to underdiagnosis and delayed treatment.
The National Kala-azar Elimination Programme (NKEP), a centrally sponsored scheme, was launched in 2002
by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India. The primary objective of the scheme was
to eliminate Kala-azar as a public health problem in the country. The National Health Policy 2002 aimed at
eliminating the disease by 2010. Elimination meant when no block in the country reports more than 1 case per
10,000 population. Under this scheme, the Central government met all the operational costs of state
governments, such as insecticidal sprays, drugs, diagnostics, monitoring, supervision, and community
mobilisation.
Unfortunately, the disease could not be eliminated by 2010, and the target was missed. A new target was set for
2015, and the situation was reviewed. It was found that despite persistent efforts of the government, success
could not be achieved as targets were missed. Over the years, multiple targets were set to eliminate Kala-azar,
but deadlines were missed in 2017 also. Although, 95% blocks had achieved benchmark elimination level, yet
5% blocks had been posting challenge. This was largely due to challenges such as inadequate surveillance,
difficult terrain, limited healthcare access in endemic areas, and vector control issues. Hence, the target was
revised, and the goal was extended to 2023. As a result of rigorous government interventions and by

Delivery Challenges
Soon after taking charge of National Vector Control Programme, Mr. Manjhi called a meeting of the entire team
of NVBDCP, headed by, Dr. Tanu Jain, the Programme Director. Dr. Jain apprised Mr. Manjhi about NKEP,
progress made over the years and the difficulties the team had faced. Mr. Manjhi asked Dr. Jain to prepare a
report on identification of challenges faced in disease control along with evaluating the impact of existing
government interventions and policies on elimination of disease after visiting the prominent endemic areas.
While tracking the progress of NKEP, it was found that despite taking several measures such as ensuring
availability of effective drugs, construction of several pucca (brick) houses and due usage of Indoor Residual
Spray (IRS), cases of Kala-azar did not go down. It continued to pose significant public health challenges in
endemic areas due to poverty, malnutrition, and weak healthcare infrastructure. Although the government had
implemented NKEP, gaps in coverage, infrastructure limitations, and underreporting of cases persisted. Mr.
Manjhi asked Dr. Jain to re-analyse the prevalence and transmission dynamics of Kala-azar in Bihar, Jharkhand,
Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal. He asked her to find out the reasons for not achieving the last mile success,
particularly in Bihar and Jharkhand. During her study, Dr. Jain highlighted some issues which needed to be
addressed.
One of the primary obstacles was the adaptability of the sandfly vector. It breeds in a wide range of
environmental conditions, making vector control difficult. High population density and the seasonal mobility
of agricultural labour in rural areas further increased transmission risk. The reach of the NKEP was limited in
remote regions where healthcare access remained uneven, and vector control measures often failed to reach
every household. Moreover, Primary Health Centres often lacked diagnostic kits and drugs. Public awareness
about the disease, its transmission, and prevention was low in rural communities. Many patients delayed
seeking medical care due to limited knowledge and due to fear of social exclusion or discrimination if their
illness became known in the community. There was reliance on unqualified quacks
7
in the absence of trained
medical professionals. Misdiagnosis and mistreatment were common which led to severe cases and preventable
fatalities. Another challenge was that despite the availability of effective treatments, there was less demand
from the infected people since patients were not following due treatment regimen. The initial drug regimen
required the patients to consume drugs for twenty-one days. This was not effective at all due to poor
compliance.

IRS is a key vector control strategy used globally to reduce the transmission of vector-borne diseases like Kala-
azar by applying insecticides to the interior walls of homes. The villagers did not allow the spray workers to

spray the insecticide inside their homes because of their peculiar odour and colour. Local health authorities
distributed insecticide-treated bed nets and IRS, but people were not using these vector control strategies. IRS
were to be used till 2017, but their efficacy was not checked. Another technical challenge in IRS implementation
was the dilution of insecticide solutions. Incorrect dilution had resulted in an inadequate concentration of
insecticide being applied to walls. If excessive dilutant was added, the efficacy of the spray was compromised,
reducing its ability to eliminate disease-carrying sandflies. Additionally, the hand pumps used for spraying
were old and required maintenance. These pumps had to be properly calibrated to ensure they deliver the
correct pressure and dilution ratio. Since the insecticide was provided in wettable powder form, proper mixing
was critical to maintain the required concentration for effective household coverage. Mr. Sartaj, NCVBDC team
member mentioned, “Indoor residual spray was adulterated since health care workers did not know about the extent of
dilution needed in sprays. Moreover, they were not using adequate pressure while spraying the insecticide leading to
ineffective vector control.”

Ratri Choupal (Meetings at Night)

hard-to-reach areas where television and other sources of entertainment were absent. It served as an effective

Housing Improvements and the Role of Gerard Soil
Under the PMAY, many households in endemic blocks were transitioning from kaccha houses to pucca houses.

type of soil at the local level called Gerard Soil as an alternative sealing material. This soil, when mixed with
water, formed a cement-like hard layer within hours, effectively sealing wall crevices. Communities were
convinced to use this soil as plaster for their houses. This innovative approach was recognised at the G20
meetings [3] and internationally appreciated for its impact on Kala-azar elimination.
Strengthening IRS through Administrative Measures and Quality Monitoring
The effectiveness of IRS in eliminating Kala-azar was dependent on achieving comprehensive household
coverage. Administrative interventions focused on community sensitisation. Rather than using coercion, efforts
were made to communicate the importance of complete spraying. District administrations played a key role in
reinforcing these messages and supporting field teams, lending legitimacy to the campaign and improving
public cooperation. Moreover, Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane (DDT) which was used as an insecticide was
now replaced with synthetic pyrethroids which was more effective. It was better accepted by the households
since it was odourless and colourless. Simultaneously, monitoring framework was established to enhance the
quality and efficacy of IRS. Pre-IRS monitoring was conducted ten days prior to spraying. It evaluated
personnel training, logistics such as availability of insecticide, equipment, and functional hand pumps, and
micro-planning to ensure that spray teams were well-prepared and organised. Spray workers were trained
using Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). Monitoring teams used geo- tagging and real time dashboards to
ensure quality and coverage. Mobile based IRS monitoring tools were also used.
Post-IRS monitoring occurred one to three months after spraying. It involved checking for the continued
presence of sandflies and assessing whether the spray remained effective for at least three to six months. An
additional obstacle was the prevalence of raw, un-plastered walls in rural homes, often coated with cow dung,
which reduced the insecticide's longevity. To counter this, IEC campaigns were launched to shift behavioural
practices, encouraging residents to maintain treated wall surfaces to preserve the impact of IRS.
Government Interventions
Government agencies provided technical oversight to improve dilution processes, repaired and calibrated hand
pumps, and ensured that proper spraying techniques were followed to maximise the impact of IRS
interventions. Disease surveillance was done through integration of data systems. The management

information system was integrated with the Health Information Platform to ensure real-time reporting of Kala-
azar data. The Kala-azar Management Information System streamlined data collection and analysis. Data

accuracy in the post-elimination period and enhanced disease surveillance helped in NKEP. Real-time reporting
systems facilitated rapid response to outbreaks and ensured timely interventions.
Mr. Manjhi played a catalytic role in the elimination of this disease by ensuring that all activities were
systematically implemented, monitored and evaluated. He facilitated direct coordination between programme
teams and district administrations, ensuring that challenges were addressed promptly through fortnightly
reviews. Field visits were made to remote areas in Jharkhand. This targeted and systematic approach
significantly contributed to the reduction of high-burden blocks in Jharkhand and strengthened the
sustainability of Kala-azar elimination efforts.

Defeating the Black Fever: India’s Strategic Win against Kala-azar

7

Lessons Learned
Reflecting on the journey to Kala-azar elimination, Mr. Rajiv Manjhi learnt some key lessons that shaped the
programme’s ultimate success. Real progress required moving beyond top-down directives and focusing on
deep, sustained engagement with local communities. Awareness campaigns, especially those tailored to local
languages and customs, proved vital in changing behaviours and encouraging early health-seeking actions. The
gap between policy intent and on-ground realities, such as villagers’ reluctance to move into pucca houses,
underscored the importance of understanding social and environmental contexts. Implementation of the
scheme depended on aligning interventions with community preferences and infrastructural realities.
Sustained elimination was achieved by fostering trust, dispelling stigma, and promoting behaviour change
from seeking qualified care to adhering to treatment and adopting preventive practices.
Local innovation techniques like the use of Gerard soil for wall plastering and the Ratri Choupal night meetings
highlighted community needs and addressed local challenges. These innovations became game-changers in
vector control and awareness generation. Moreover, simply rolling out resources and interventions was
insufficient. Persistent gaps in surveillance, quality control, and programme follow-up, frequent staff transfers,
reflected the need for robust and adaptable monitoring systems. The journey reaffirmed that determined
leadership, inter-sectoral collaboration, and empowering frontline workers were essential for overcoming
public health challenges.

Sustaining Kala-azar Elimination and WHO Certification: The Way Forward
These efforts collectively led to progress in the fight against Kala-azar, particularly in high-burden areas. After
failing several times since 2010, the programme finally achieved its benchmark elimination target in 2023. By
2024, all blocks (633 blocks in 54 districts of endemic states) successfully reported fewer than one case per 10,000
population, meeting the elimination threshold [4]. This was a nearly two-decade-long dream that had finally
turned into reality well ahead of the 2030 global Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) target. India's success
was highlighted on the global stage, with progress showcased at the G20 exhibition. As Hon’ble Prime Minister
Shri Narendra Modi stated in his "Mann Ki Baat" address in December 2022, “The elimination of Kala-azar is a
testament to the collective resolve and tireless efforts of our health workers and communities.” This statement
underscored the importance of community participation and dedicated public health initiatives in achieving
national health milestones.
However, sustaining this achievement until 2027 is crucial for securing WHO’s official elimination certification
and being eligible for their validation. The process involves maintaining low case incidence for three
consecutive years (2024–2026), preparing comprehensive documentation of the elimination progress, and

undergoing WHO’s external verification process, including field inspections. If successfully sustained, Kala-
azar would become the eighth disease to be officially eliminated from India, marking a major public health

milestone. The programme’s success demonstrates the effectiveness of targeted interventions, administrative
coordination, and innovative solutions in combating vector-borne diseases.

Case Study Title: Transforming Housing in Ganori through PM Awaas Yojana
Case Study Description: This case study showcases the transformation of 20 Scheduled Tribe families in Ganori Gram Panchayat who, after years of living in forest encroachments without housing rights, gained secure homes through collective action. Led by Sarpanch Mrs. Saralataai Tandale, with support from the Block Development Officer, DRDA Project Director Ms. Sangeetadevi Patil, and others, land was purchased under the Pandit Dindayal Upadhyay Gharkul Scheme. Villager Mr. Dadasaheb Jadhav sold 20 gunthas at a fair rate, and Ms. Anuradha Chavan covered registration costs. Using MGNREGA labour, houses were built with sanitation, LPG, and tap water under national schemes. The initiative demonstrates how convergence between local leadership and administration fosters inclusion, dignity, and lasting empowerment.
Case Text:
Introduction
In India, shelter holds a strong place in society, often acting as the base for social and economic stability. Since
independence, the Government of India has introduced several schemes to provide housing to the underserved,
beginning with the Community Development Movement, the Village Housing Program, and House Site cum
Construction Assistance Schemes, followed by the National Rural Employment Programme and the Rural
Landless Employment Guarantee Programme. A major shift came in January 1996 with the launch of the Indira
Awaas Yojana, a dedicated programme for Below Poverty Line rural households. This effort was taken forward
through the Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana–Gramin (PMAY-G), launched on 1st April, 2016, yet in Ganori, a
village in Maharashtra, families identified as homeless remained without homes for three consecutive years.
The reason was not exclusion, but a missing piece of land.
The PMAY-G was launched by the Government of India with the promise of a pucca (brick) house and basic
amenities for every eligible rural household and set a clear national goal: ‘Housing for All by 2026’. Its primary
objective was to provide pucca houses to families living in kutcha (mud) or dilapidated structures by 2024, along
with basic amenities such as electricity, water, sanitation, and clean cooking fuel by 2026. The scheme aimed to
improve transparency in beneficiary selection by using data from the Socio-Economic and Caste Census 20111
,
issued by the Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India and reducing discretionary decisions at the
local level. Under the scheme, financial assistance of ₹1.20 lakh (~$1400 USD) was provided for houses in plain
areas and ₹1.30 lakh (~$1560 USD) for homes in hilly or difficult terrains which was released in three instalments.
1 SECC-2011 is a study of socio-economic status of rural and urban households and allows ranking of households
based on predefined parameters.

From Forest to Foundation: A Housing Transformation in Ganori Gram Panchayat

2
The PMAY-G encouraged the use of local materials and traditional designs, and supported training and
deployment of skilled rural masons to ensure quality construction. It also converged with other national schemes
such as Swachh Bharat Mission2

, Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana3

, and Saubhagya Scheme4

to offer a more
comprehensive improvement in rural living conditions. The scheme was monitored through digital platforms
like AwaasSoft5 and AwaasApp, which helped track construction progress and ensured accountability at each
stage.
While the scheme laid out a clear national framework, its impact was depended on how it was implemented in
specific local contexts. The Ganori Gram Panchayat had a population of 6,230 residents across 1,240 households.
A Permanent Waiting List6 was created using the census data. It comprised a total of 79 families among which 33
belonged to the Scheduled Tribes7 category. Among them, 20 families had been residing on forest land for
generations, living in temporary shelters with grass roofs and fragile walls. Although they aspired to build pucca
houses, their financial situation did not allow them to purchase land on their own. The local authorities identified
them as homeless and landless households eligible for PMAY-G. Their names were included in the Priority
Waiting List8

from 2016–17 onwards. To qualify for housing assistance, beneficiaries were required to register on
the AwaasSoft portal by uploading photographs that reflected their current living conditions and the proposed
construction sites. This step was crucial to demonstrate land availability, which was a criterion for inclusion in
the housing scheme. But due to unavailability of land, they could not receive housing assistance during the
financial years 2016–17, 2017–18, and 2018–19. This delay in accessing housing benefits pointed to deeper
implementation challenges.
Delivery Challenges
The 20 families lived in precarious conditions for generations without any formal ownership or legal recognition.
Although they were eligible for housing assistance under the PMAY-G, but due to lack of legally titled land,
construction of permanent homes was a challenge. This critical gap left them in continued uncertainty, and in
search of a stable and secure housing solution. The beneficiaries also had an emotional attachment to the forest
land where they lived for generations. While they wanted to own proper homes, the idea of moving made them
feel like they were losing a part of who they are. Leaving the place, they had known all their lives was difficult,
which made them unsure about relocating.
Financial constraints further compounded their struggles. As the scheme provided ₹1.20 lakh to each beneficiary
for constructing a 25 sq. mt. house, the rising cost of building materials and labour rendered this amount
insufficient. The beneficiaries were economically vulnerable. They lacked the means to contribute additional
funds or access bank loans to bridge the gap. The financial aid provided to these 20 families under the Pandit

Deendayal Upadhyay Gharkul Land Purchase Financial Assistance Scheme9 was insufficient. The banking
institutions also proved to be a weak support system. The beneficiaries were frequently denied supplementary
loans to purchase land or materials due to a lack of collateral or formal assets. A Preliminary sale agreement had
been signed by a land owner who gave a portion of her land to beneficiaries, but the registration was still pending.
The beneficiaries faced burden of additional stamp duty, registration charges etc. This unexpected financial strain
created a significant hurdle. With limited resources and little savings, gathering the necessary funds to cover the
extra charges became a struggle for them.
Their concerns extended beyond housing structures to the availability of basic amenities. Many expressed
uncertainties about access to clean drinking water, the timely development of internal roads, and the provision
of indoor toilets. These factors influenced their willingness to participate in the scheme and created
implementation hurdles for local officials.
Another key challenge stemmed from employment-driven seasonal migration. Most beneficiaries worked as
migrant labourers, particularly during sugarcane harvesting seasons. They prioritised income generation over
housing construction. Their frequent absence delayed construction timelines and made coordination difficult,
turning the goal of a stable home into a distant dream. The shortage of skilled construction labour in Ganori only
added to the difficulties. Reliance on workers from the block level drove up costs and caused delays. This
prolonged the construction process and diminished hope for timely completion.
In the financial years 2016–17 and 2017–18, two beneficiaries received partial funds of ₹55,000 (~$660USD) each.
One of them halted construction after completing the plinth level and used the remaining amount for their
wedding. The other diverted the funds entirely for personal use. Consequently, both houses remain incomplete.
In another instance, a beneficiary approved in 2019–20 under the land purchase scheme passed away before
construction could begin. Although heirs existed, their relocation made coordination unfeasible, thus leaving the
project in limbo. These cases underscored the complex realities that disrupted development efforts. The resulting
incomplete housing structures reflected multifaceted challenges present on the ground. Recognising these
barriers was essential to understand the limitations of past implementation and to formulate resilient and
responsive solutions in future.
Tracing the Implementation Processes
In 2019–20, Sarpanch10 Mrs. Saralatai Tandale, along with Gram Sevak11 Mr. Suresh Choudhari and other officials,
engaged with the beneficiaries to understand their socio-economic conditions. It was discovered that no
government land was available in the village for housing, even after consultations with the Talathi12 and
Tehsildar13
.
Community Collaboration to Secure Land for Homeless Families
Since the village had no land available and no government land was accessible, the group decided to find
individuals within the village willing to offer land to the beneficiaries. The Sarpanch began talks with socially
conscious individuals to support the beneficiaries. Mrs. Parasyagbai Jadhav, an elderly landowner, and her son,
Mr. Dadasaheb Jadhav, agreed to provide land for the 20 homeless families. They recalled that some members of
these families worked on their farmland for years. Understanding their prolonged struggle with homelessness,
they offered 20 gunthas (21,780 square feet) of their roadside farmland at a reduced price.

Support from Administration and Elected Representative
During registration of land the beneficiarieswere burdened with additional costs such as stamp duty, registration
charges, bid handling, and document preparation fees. Mrs. Anuradha Chavan, member of Zilla Parishad assured
the beneficiaries that she would personally cover all additional charges. Her timely intervention ensured that the
land registration process moved forward without delays. Following the payment of these charges, the registration
documents were successfully prepared. Mrs. Chavan reflected, “If these 20 long-homeless families, who have remained
isolated from mainstream society, receive permanent housing, it will help future generations integrate into the social fabric.”
Her involvement resolved the financial bottleneck and brought renewed trust, confidence, and collaboration
within the community. Sarpanch Tandale stated, “With the unwavering cooperation of our public representative, the
intricate land purchase process has been completed to everyone's satisfaction.”
Implementation of the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Gharkul Land Purchase Assistance Scheme
A district-level meeting with Ms. Jyoti Kavaddevi, the Block Development Officer14, Ms. Sangitadevi Patil, Project
Director of District Rural Development Agency; and Ms. Anuradhatai Chavan was convened to address the land
purchase execution. They decided to leverage the benefits of the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Gharkul Land
Purchase Financial Assistance Scheme for the beneficiaries. On 18th March 2021, land registration documents were
uploaded to the AwaasSoft platform as part of the scheme’s implementation process. The Gram Sevak had
outlined the steps to access the scheme, emphasising accurate bank details, proper documentation, and timely
application. Ms. Jyoti Kavaddevi coordinated closely with Ms. Sangeetadevi Patil to facilitate and finalise the
land purchase for the beneficiaries.
With all required documentation in place, Fund Transfer Orders were generated through the Public Financial
Management System15

. Each beneficiary received ₹50,000 directly into their bank accounts. The timely
disbursement allowed the beneficiaries to take a significant step toward securing stable housing. After buying
the land, the families planned the layout, setting aside space for vehicle parking, a community temple, and
residential houses.

As per the Maharashtra Government Resolution dated 27 May 2016, the Rural Development Department had
also deployed Rural Housing Engineers (RHEs) to support the implementation of PMAY-G. These engineers
provided continuous supervision, ensured timely financial disbursements to beneficiaries, and offered guidance
on construction technology and materials. Mr. Vijay Gawli, appointed as the RHE for Ganori in February 2020,
prepared a colony layout featuring ten homes arranged to face each other. He also developed cost estimates,
listed the required construction materials, and calculated per-unit housing costs. His guidance helped the
beneficiaries understand the structure and financial details of the project and encouraged a sense of collective
ownership and community living. (Exhibit 1)
Mr. Santosh Wakhare, the Block Data Entry Operator managed the digital inputs. Mr. Sudesh Rokade, the District
Programmer supervised overall project execution. Together, they ensured that photographs showing
construction progress were accurately uploaded to the AwaasSoft portal and that Fund Transfer Orders were
generated without delay. Their collaboration improved administrative efficiency, strengthened community
participation, and enhanced accountability throughout the project lifecycle.
Following the Dussehra festival, many beneficiaries migrated to other districts in search of work, which slowed
progress on some housing projects. The RHE observed disrupted planned masonry training programmes. To
ensure effective oversight, the RHE systematically uploaded stage-wise construction photographs to the

AwaasSoft portal. This enabled real-time monitoring. After each upload, the Data Entry Operator generated Fund
Transfer Orders at the block level, facilitating timely disbursement of funds directly into beneficiaries' bank
accounts. Beneficiaries supported the effort by voluntarily guarding construction sites at night. In accordance

instrumental in improving online monitoring, offering a user-friendly platform that streamlined implementation.
‘AwaasSoft has made online monitoring much easier and more efficient, allowing us to focus more on the needs of the
beneficiaries’, stated Mr. Santosh Wakhare.
Updating Gram Panchayat Records
After the completion of house construction, the Gram Panchayat updated official records in Form No. 8, in
accordance with the Maharashtra Gram Panchayat Act of 1959. This documentation captured key details for each
beneficiary, including the owner’s name, property description, area of the property, applicable property and
health taxes, and other relevant information. By maintaining accurate and transparent records, the Gram
Panchayat reinforced accountability within the community and facilitated smoother governance processes. This
meticulous approach to data management ensured that residents could easily access necessary services and
support.
Empowerment through Beneficiary Meetings
After the completion of house construction, the Sarpanch and Gram Sevak organised meetings with the families
of beneficiaries to discuss important topics aimed at improving their quality of life. One key focus was the
importance of education. During these sessions, the Sarpanch emphasised importance of education in shaping
individual futures and strengthening communities. By sharing success stories of educated individuals from
similar backgrounds, she inspired parents to prioritise education for their children. As a result, many children
from the beneficiary families enrolled in local zila parishad schools. ‘When local representatives take the lead to change
beneficiaries' mindsets and inspire discussions, we can make sustainable rural development clearer and more achievable,’
the Sarpanch of Ganori Gram Panchayat noted.
Convergence of Various Schemes
To maximise the benefits for beneficiaries, the implementation team coordinated the integration of multiple
welfare schemes through a well-structured convergence approach. They provided drinking water under Jal
Jeevan Mission16

. Under PMAY-G scheme, each beneficiary was required to contribute 90 days of unskilled
labour, which was remunerated through MGNREGA17, ensuring both employment and income support during
the construction process. The Gram Rojgar Sevak18 maintained records and musters (attendance registers) which
were uploaded to the MGNREGA portal for processing and ensuring timely wage payments directly into
beneficiaries’ accounts. The wages were calculated based on attendance records submitted during different
phases of house construction. This upheld transparency and accountability in payment disbursement. The
Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana was leveraged to provide gas stoves and LPG connections to households. This
intervention reduced the reliance on traditional biomass fuels, thereby promoting a healthier home environment
and reducing the risks associated with indoor air pollution. The initiative also addressed the need for proper
sanitation under Swachh Bharat Mission, which led to improvements in public health and hygiene across the
community. There was a decline in sanitation-related illnesses and increased awareness around cleanliness and

hygiene practices. These combined efforts strengthened the economic situations of the beneficiaries and enhanced

Lessons Learnt
The construction of these homes began in June 2022 and was completed by December 2023. To complete all homes
on time, the Sarpanch, Gram Sevak, and RHE coordinated their efforts. The local administration provided
beneficiaries with more than just walls and roofs. They ensured the inclusion of essential amenities to enhance
their overall comfort, convenience, and quality of life.
The successful implementation of the housing initiative was underpinned by coordination between beneficiaries,
elected representatives, administrative units, and technical platforms. Local administrations recognised the
importance of actively engaging with beneficiaries to better understand their socio-economic circumstances.
Through open dialogues and community meetings, they gathered valuable insights into beneficiaries' needs,
aspirations, and mental well-being. This participatory approach helped identify specific challenges and enabled
the tailoring of housing support to meet the unique needs of each household. Collaboration between public
representatives and administrative officials further strengthened the process. Elected leaders such as the
Sarpanch and Zilla Parishad members worked alongside Gram Sevaks, Block Development Officers, Project
Directors of District Rural Development Agency, and Chief Executive Officers at the district level. Their combined
efforts fostered trust, facilitated cooperation, and ensured the housing schemes reached the most marginalised
communities.
Interdepartmental coordination played a critical role in streamlining activities across village, block, and district
levels. The key functions like allocation of beneficiary targets, registration under the housing scheme, financial

disbursement, uploading construction progress photos, and managing fund transfers were carried out in a well-
synchronised manner by administrative and technical teams. A central component of monitoring was the use of

the bilingual, web-based platform AwaasSoft. The platform enabled real-time updates on beneficiary registration,
fund disbursement through PFMS, and photographic documentation of each stage of construction. This digital
system brought transparency, increased accountability, and made implementation easier to track for all
stakeholders, including beneficiaries, officials, and local leaders. The Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Gharkul Land
Purchase Assistance Scheme was monitored using AwaasSoft for better coordination, timely fund release, and
efficient reporting. The then Director of the State Management Unit – Rural Housing, Mr. Bharat Shendage, along
with his team, in consultation with the Ministry of Rural Development and National Informatics Centre19
,

adopted this digital platform to strengthen oversight and implementation.
The vision of the initiative extended beyond constructing houses. It aimed at holistic habitat development and
social integration. Beneficiaries were connected with other welfare programmes. The Colony Project led to
significant cost savings by utilising shared walls between houses. This reduced the overall construction expenses.
It also enabled the development of new habitations in previously unused areas, addressing the shortage of
affordable Gaothan (village settlement) land. By promoting the construction of colonies or multi-storeyed
housing, the initiative allowed beneficiaries to secure permanent shelter while supporting the broader goal of
rural development.
The project highlighted the importance of empowering local administrations within the three-tier Panchayati Raj

implementation, and ensure timely fund disbursement. Empowered grassroots governance proved essential in
fostering accountability, transparency, and sustainable community development.

Case Study Title:
The ORMAS Model: Leveraging Community 
Cadres for Rural Youth Engagement in Odisha
Case Study Description: Odisha revitalized India’s flagship skill development program, DDU-GKY, which initially struggled with low enrolment, weak awareness, and high dropouts. The Odisha Rural Development and Marketing Society (ORMAS) introduced a structured mobilization model by incentivizing Community Cadres (Gram Rojgar Sevaks, Community Resource Persons, Master Book Keepers) and using mobilisation camps, IEC tools, and community engagement. This approach boosted enrolment, improved training outcomes, and enhanced job retention, demonstrating how community-driven strategies can make national missions more effective.
Case Text:
Introduction
"Sahib (sir), am I sending my son into slavery?" The trembling voice of an anxious father echoed in the dimly lit
Gram Panchayat office. Across the wooden table, Rajesh Kumar, a senior project officer overseeing the Deen
Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY) in Odisha, met the man’s weary eyes. The father, a
farmer struggling to make ends meet, had heard rumors—stories of village boys leaving for city jobs only to
return penniless and disillusioned.
Unemployment in rural Odisha had reached critical levels, with thousands of young men and women either
trapped in low-paying, seasonal agricultural work or leaving their villages in search of uncertain livelihoods.
The lack of marketable skills further compounded the problem—many rural youths, despite their aspirations,
were not well equipped for formal employment. The Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana
(DDU-GKY) was designed to bridge this gap, offering free skill training, job placements, and financial support
to uplift rural youth. On paper, it was a life-changing opportunity. However, in practice, several barriers kept
potential candidates from enrolling. Deep-seated mistrust, fueled by past exploitative experiences, led families
to question whether these training programmes would truly benefit them. Stories of trainees returning home
jobless, struggling to adapt to city life, or being placed in exploitative work conditions further discouraged
participation. In addition to these, lack of awareness, rigid social norms, and family pressures made rural youth
hesitant to step outside their comfort zones, leaving DDU-GKY struggling to fulfil its ambitious promise.
Awareness about the programme remained low, enrolment was sluggish, and even those who joined, often
dropped out midway due to financial constraints or lack of interest. The job placements, though promising on
paper, rarely aligned with local industry needs.
The problem in the programme was a broken mobilisation strategy. Government campaigns alone could not
reach the last mile. Rural youth, sceptical and bound by familial and societal constraints, were reluctant to take
the leap into training programmes. The challenge was clear: How could Rajesh and his team bridge the trust
gap between rural communities and the programme? How could they make skilling aspirational?

The Turning Point: Mobilizing Through Community Cadres
Realizing that traditional outreach methods were failing, the Odisha Rural Development and Marketing Society
(ORMAS) decided to pilot an innovative approach. Instead of relying on government officials alone, they
tapped into the existing grassroots networks of the Community Cadre.
"When an outsider comes and tells a father that his daughter will be trained in a city, suspicion is natural. But
when I, a familiar face from his own village, tell him that my own niece has completed the training and is
earning well, he listens." – Pratima Nayak, a Community Resource Person said. ORMAS decided to incentivize
these local cadres to work as mobilizers. A staggered incentive model was introduced which provides the
following amount to the community cadres upon each enrolment:
● ₹250 (≈ $3.00) per candidate for enrolment.
● ₹150 (≈ $1.80) for training completion (ensuring that candidates did not drop out).
● ₹250 (≈ $3.00) (for job placement tracking up to 3 months post-placement.
● ₹350 (≈ $4.20) for continued retention up to 12 months in the job.

Innovation in Awareness: Taking Skilling to the People
While mobilizers played a crucial role in gaining community trust, ORMAS recognized the need for a broader,
more dynamic approach to reach the most remote and sceptical populations. To ensure widespread awareness

Case Study Title: Women-led Entrepreneurship and Empowerment: Impact of Mission Shakti in Odisha
Case Study Description: The case study examines the impact of Mission Shakti, a government initiative launched in Odisha, India, to promote women-led entrepreneurship and empowerment. The programme has enabled women to engage in income-generating activities, access financial services, and build leadership skills. It has strengthened women’s self-help groups (SHGs) through capacity building, skill development, and financial inclusion. Mission Shakti has empowered women to start and scale businesses, boosting their confidence, financial independence, and participation in social and political spheres. It further emphasizes the importance of community support, policy backing, and sustainable practices in ensuring long-term success, positioning Mission Shakti as a potential model for broader replication.
Case Text:
Introduction
Odisha grappled with poverty, unemployment, and gender inequality, which affected women in rural areas.
They faced exclusion from economic and decision-making spheres. Economic dependence on male family
members further limited their potential.
On 8th March 2001, as the world celebrated International Women’s Day, the Government of Odisha launched
Mission Shakti, a flagship programme aimed at empowering women through SHGs. Former Chief Minister Mr.
Naveen Patnaik, in his speech at the launch, said, "The Government of Odisha is committed to empowering women in
every aspect of their lives, from economic independence to leadership roles in their communities.” His vision was clear and
was reflected in the mission statement: “Mission Shakti will help construct a society which is self-reliant, conscious of
socio-economic issues, where there is a spirit of cooperation, where women are appropriately skilled to undertake their choice
of activities without hindrance or dependence, where there is leadership development while maintaining gender equity, and
above all, each having a respect for the values of others and striving for the good of the greater society.”i
Mission Shakti was conceived to tackle the dual challenges faced by women: their exclusion from the formal
economy and their marginalisation in decision-making processes. The programme focused on organising women
into SHGs, providing them with financial literacy, skill development, and access to resources. Through this
initiative, women across the state were to gain financial independence, leadership opportunities, and the
confidence to venture into businesses which were traditionally dominated by men. Over the period of 24 years
since the commencement of the scheme, Mission Shakti supported over 6 lakh (0.6 million) SHGs, reaching more
than 70 lakh (7 million) women across rural and urban Odisha.
In May 2019, the Government of Odisha took a significant step towards the financial and social upliftment of
women by passing a Cabinet resolution that involved SHGs in the procurement of goods and services worth
₹5,000 crores ($598 million USD) over five years. This initiative prioritised SHGs as suppliers in government
procurement thus ensuring a stable market for their products and services. While it did not provide direct
government employment but it created income opportunities for SHG members by ensuring a steady demand.
As most of the SHGs comprised women entrepreneurs engaged in sectors such as food production, textiles, and
handicrafts, the move supported their economic empowerment. It also enabled women to assume important roles
in areas like paddy procurement, pisciculture, Mid-Day Meal1 management, and healthcare support, thereby
increasing their participation in critical decision-making processes and economic activities.

Organizational and Community Structure of Mission Shakti in Odisha
In Odisha, the community structure of SHGs under Mission Shakti was a powerful network designed to empower
women through collaboration and support. It followed a structured, multi-tiered approach to its organisational
framework. The planning and implementation of SHG activities across the state were efficient, coordinated, and
impactful. This structure included three levels: District Level Federations (DLF), Block Level Federations, and
Gram Panchayat Level Federations (GPLF). (Exhibit 1)
At the village level, the GPLF acted as a platform where SHG members came together to share experiences, solve
problems, and strengthen their groups. The GPLF played a key role in financial intermediation, receiving grants,
and resolving conflicts. It also focused on empowering women by providing training and ensuring the financial
sustainability of SHGs. Above the GPLF, the Cluster Level Forum (CLF) connected multiple SHGs within a
village, fostering mutual support and shared learning. The CLF consisted of an Executive Committee made up
of representatives from each SHG. It mobilised marginalised groups, trained SHG members, and ensured that

programme in India that provides free lunches to school children.

the entitlements reached those most in need. The CLF also helped SHGs prepare pro-poor plans and linked them
with higher-level federations for resources and support.
The activities were managed efficiently at all levels and addressed the needs of the women and communities
involved in the SHG network. Each level was interconnected and worked in close coordination to advance the
overarching objectives of financial inclusion, livelihood development, skill enhancement, and the social
empowerment of women across the state.

Delivery Challenges: Real-Life Examples and Insights
While Mission Shakti was a groundbreaking initiative in promoting women’s empowerment and
entrepreneurship in Odisha, there were several delivery challenges that hindered its full potential.
A major challenge faced by the women was limited financial literacy. Although the initiative provided access to
financial resources such as loans and savings schemes, many women lacked the knowledge and skills to manage
these tools effectively. In rural areas, traditional financial practices often conflicted with modern banking systems,
making the transition particularly difficult. One such example was that of the Maa Durgabahini SHG which took
a loan to start a small poultry business. However, due to inadequate financial training, the group struggled to
manage income and expenditures. Without proper budgeting or planning, they were unable to set aside funds
for loan repayment, ultimately defaulting on the loan. This not only created financial strain but also eroded
community trust in the group and in the broader SHG model.
Many SHGs excelled in creating unique local products like handmade crafts, organic produce, or processed food
items. However, they often lacked the marketing skills, infrastructure, and distribution networks to take their
products to a broader market. The Maa Vaibhav Laxmi SHG of Nuapada district in Odisha started a handmade
business making nameplates, mementoes, key chains, and boards on teak wood. Despite producing high-quality
products, the group had limited access to customers beyond their village. They struggled to market their products
and gain visibility outside the local market. They faced fierce competition from established companies.

Coordination among key stakeholders, including government departments, financial institutions, and Non-
Governmental Organisations (NGOs), involved in the implementation of Mission Shakti, was often slow and

inefficient. Many SHG members reported delays in receiving loan approvals, training programmes, and other
necessary resources due to bureaucratic hurdles or lack of coordination. The Gangajamuna Producer Group,
comprising women from three villages of Odisha—Karanja, Melkajaba, and Boriguda—faced a six-month delay
in securing a loan to expand their agricultural business due to poor coordination between the local bank, the
district office of Mission Shakti, and financial service providers. As a result, they missed crucial planting seasons,
leading to income loss and low morale.
Even when women successfully ran businesses or engaged in entrepreneurial ventures, they often continued to
bear the weight of traditional domestic responsibilities, which limited their ability to fully invest time and effort
into scaling their enterprises. In rural households, this dual burden of managing both business and household
chores led to exhaustion and reduced productivity. In Rayagada village of Odisha, the Gupteswar SHG operated
a grocery business, but its members continued to shoulder the full responsibility of household duties, including
childcare, elder care, cooking, cleaning, and farming. As a result, many women experienced burnout. They were
unable to devote sufficient time to grow their business.
Another significant challenge was the initial resistance to women taking on leadership roles in SHGs, particularly
in patriarchal communities. In some villages, the cultural and social fabric was so deeply rooted in gender biases
that women faced reluctance from their families and communities to assume leadership positions. In Kandhamal
district, an SHG called Maa Tarini was led by Sabitri, who was actively involved in community development.
Despite her success, many male members of the village initially resisted her leadership, and felt uncomfortable
with a woman in charge. The SHG struggled with low participation rates, and some women even hesitated to
attend meetings or contribute financially.

shifting social norms, which offered valuable lessons for women’s empowerment initiatives across India and

Tracing the Implementation Process: A Detailed Overview
The implementation of Mission Shakti in Odisha unfolded through several distinct phases, each characterised by
specific objectives, strategies, and outcomes. This process was shaped by a combination of government initiatives
and collaborative efforts involving NGOs, financial institutions, and other local stakeholders.
Initiation and Foundation (2001–2005): In its initial phase, the programme focused on raising awareness about
SHGs and mobilising women, particularly in rural areas. The Odisha Rural Development and Marketing Society
(ORMAS)2 was appointed as the nodal agency to oversee its implementation. The early strategy emphasised
forming SHGs across districts to promote savings, credit access, and collective action. Basic training in financial
literacy, leadership, and group management was provided to build capacity among the members. To address the
widespread issue of financial exclusion among rural women, the programme facilitated initial banking linkages
and small-scale loan opportunities. The ORMAS initiated mandatory financial literacy workshops for SHG
members by focusing on budgeting, accounting, and financial planning. Government-led awareness campaigns
educated women on the importance of savings, financial discipline, and collective action. Mission Shakti was first
launched in Lanjigarh, a village in Kalahandi district, one of the poorest regions of Odisha. Initially, women were
hesitant to join due to mistrust of financial institutions. However, after a series of sensitisation workshops
conducted by local officials and NGO partners, women began forming SHGs and pooled small savings. The first
group used their funds to launch small ventures like poultry farming, which generated a steady income. This
early success became a model, paving the way for wider SHG adoption across the district.
Expansion and Integration with Financial Systems (2006–2012): Between 2006 and 2012, Mission Shakti entered
a critical phase of expansion by integrating SHGs with formal financial systems. Moving beyond basic group
formation, the programme focused on credit linkage with banks and financial institutions to empower SHGs as
active economic units. To support this, the Government of Odisha introduced various financial initiatives under
Mission Shakti. These included seed money of ₹15,000 ($174.46 USD) for eligible SHGs without prior microcredit
or revolving funds to enhance creditworthiness and reduce dependence on high-interest loans. A revolving fund
of ₹25 lakh ($29,900 USD) per Block Level Federation was provided in two phases to strengthen financial
autonomy and support lending based on business plans. Financial literacy and digitisation efforts were also
scaled up. The Financial Literacy and Counselling Centres programmes educated women on financial
management and digital recordkeeping for improved transparency. During this period, Mission Shakti aligned
itself with national initiatives like the National Rural Livelihood Mission3

, further broadening its reach. A major
shift occurred as SHGs began to access affordable loans and transform into micro-entrepreneurial hubs. Women
diversified their livelihood by taking up businesses in agriculture, food processing, handicrafts, and services. The
Reserve Bank of India and the Government of Odisha played a key role in facilitating partnerships between SHGs
and commercial banks, ensuring smoother loan disbursement and transactions. In Ganjam district of Odisha, this
transformation was evident in the success of the Sri Baladev Swami Tailoring Unit. What began as a small savings
group evolved into a thriving enterprise after accessing credit from a nationalised bank. The SHG expanded into
manufacturing school uniforms and secured contracts from nearby schools. It provided employment to women

was not sufficient for true empowerment, Mission Shakti expanded to include access to health, education, and

, which provided health insurance, as well as housing and pension programmes that bolstered their

connections. This not only improved their quality of life but also freed up time for entrepreneurial activities. With

Lessons Learned: Insights and Takeaways from the Mission Shakti Experience
The Mission Shakti initiative in Odisha provided valuable insights and lessons on promoting women’s
entrepreneurship and economic empowerment, especially in rural areas. Through its successes and challenges,
the programme helped shape a more inclusive environment for women.
Economic empowerment proved to be a powerful catalyst for social transformation, particularly for women
involved in Mission Shakti. It provided a platform for women entrepreneurs to enter various sectors such as
handicrafts, textiles, food processing, and agriculture. The initiative allowed access to markets, both locally and
nationally, enabling them to showcase and sell their products. Through strategic partnerships and collaborations,
the programme ensured that women entrepreneurs gained better access to resources, networking, and platforms
that enhanced their visibility and marketability. As women gained financial independence through
entrepreneurship, their roles within the family and society evolved significantly. Women-led businesses not only
enhanced self-reliance and household decision-making power, but also elevated women's social status and
challenged gender stereotypes. A cornerstone of this progress was access to credit and financial inclusion.
Traditionally, limited access to credit hindered women’s entrepreneurial ambitions. However, Mission Shakti’s
SHG model bridged this gap by offering microfinance, low-interest loans, and government grants, enabling
women to start and expand businesses and achieve economic stability.
In addition to financial support, the programme emphasised skill development as a means to ensure business
sustainability. Vocational training in areas like handicrafts, food processing, tailoring, and digital marketing
equipped women with the tools to enhance their product quality and competitiveness. The programme’s
community-led approach was instrumental in fostering inclusivity. Through SHGs, women collaborated, shared
resources, and built resilience, with peer learning enabling even those with limited education to benefit from
collective knowledge. This sense of community reinforced their ability to face economic and social challenges.
Government support played a critical role in this ecosystem. The Government of Odisha strengthened women’s
entrepreneurship by providing infrastructure, funding, training, and market access. Policies promoting SHGs
and rural enterprises were central to this growth, although regular policy evaluation was essential to adapt to
changing economic dynamics. Furthermore, Mission Shakti tackled the challenge of limited market access by
facilitating participation in trade fairs, online platforms, and networking events. The integration of digital tools
like online marketing and digital payments broadened customer reach, though digital literacy continues to be an
area requiring attention.
While awareness campaigns and community sensitisation began to shift mindsets, continuous efforts were
needed to dismantle deep-rooted biases. The long-term sustainability of women-led businesses was dependent
upon diversification and innovation. SHGs and entrepreneurs who diversified product lines, adopted digital
services, and implemented sustainable practices such as eco-friendly production and the use of local resources
were more likely to thrive. In essence, Mission Shakti’s multifaceted approach not only empowered women
economically, but reshaped societal structures and paved the way for inclusive and sustainable development.
The impact of Mission Shakti went beyond just economic empowerment. It played a pivotal role in challenging
societal norms and prejudices surrounding women’s roles. By fostering leadership and entrepreneurship, it
opened doors for women to occupy spaces traditionally dominated by men. Many women who benefited from
Mission Shakti emerged as leaders, not just within their families but also in their communities. As one local
entrepreneur remarked, “When I succeed, my community succeeds. We all rise together.” This spirit of collective
growth became a defining characteristic of Mission Shakti, as women supported each other in their
entrepreneurial journeys.
