Education and health were key drivers of this transformation. Mission Shakti promoted better educational
opportunities for children and improved healthcare standards in communities. The women invested in their
families, resulting in better living conditions, healthier lifestyles, and a brighter future for their children. As the
impact of Mission Shakti continues to unfold, the empowerment of women has become a key pillar in the state’s
development.
At its core, Mission Shakti, embodied by the word SHAKTI, symbolised the primal, transformative energy of the
feminine. This energy was not just about individual empowerment but about transforming societies,
communities, and entire nations. As Odisha led the way, the stories of resilient, confident women empowered by
Mission Shakti served as an inspiration to all, proving that when women rose, they not only uplifted themselves
but also transformed the world around them. The success and ongoing transformation driven by Mission Shakti
was captured in the coffee table book Mission Shakti – Building Identities, Transforming Lives. The initiative became
a living testament to the immense potential of women. The rise of women in Odisha was not just a triumph for
the state but a clarion call for women everywhere to claim their space in the world.

Conclusion
The implementation of Mission Shakti offered valuable lessons for future empowerment initiatives aimed at
fostering women’s entrepreneurship and leadership. Its strength lies in a holistic approach combining financial
inclusion, skill development, market access, and institutional support to enable women to take charge of their
economic and social futures. However, persistent challenges such as entrenched gender norms, limited market
reach, and the need for a more enabling policy environment require consistent focus and innovation. To build on
its success, the programme must further strengthen support systems for women entrepreneurs, enhance
coordination among stakeholders, and invest in digital literacy, leadership training, and infrastructure. These
efforts will not only deepen the impact in Odisha but also position Mission Shakti as a replicable model for other

regions in India and beyond. Ultimately, Mission Shakti has helped women to redefine their roles as decision-
makers, community leaders, and agents of change. It exemplifies how targeted, inclusive interventions can break

the cycle of poverty and exclusion, creating a future where women's leadership becomes central to resilient,
equitable development.

Case Study Title:
Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi
Pearl Farming Story
Case Study Description: The Asomi Pearl Farming Project in Nagaon, Assam, demonstrates how grassroots innovation can enhance rural livelihoods by integrating freshwater pearl cultivation with traditional aquaculture, creating additional income streams and environmental benefits. Despite technical and market challenges, the initiative succeeded through skill development, cooperative financial support, and buy-back assurances. With the global pearl market exceeding USD 10.5 billion and India’s presence still limited, the project highlights Assam’s potential to become a key player in global pearl value chains. Scaling the model will require advanced training, improved grafting techniques, stronger cooperative governance, branding, and policy-backed market linkages, enabling its transformation into a sustainable, market-driven rural enterprise that strengthens economic resilience.
Case Text:
Introduction
In the Nagaon district of Assam, an innovative initiative is steadily reshaping rural livelihoods. The Asomi
Pearl Farming Project is not merely an experiment, but an evolving model of sustainable aquaculture aimed at
providing an alternative income stream while promoting environmentally responsible practices. At the
forefront of this endeavor is Rulen Hazarika, a farmer-entrepreneur pioneering freshwater pearl farming as a
viable supplement to traditional fish farming. He serves as the Vice Chairman of the Assam Pearl Development
Cooperative Society and hails from Besamari village in the Dhing area of Nagaon district. Rulen Hazarika
became intrigued by the dual benefits of pearl farming: a high-value product coupled with the environmental
advantage of water purification. Determined to explore its potential, he sought specialised training in mussel1
selection, pearl grafting2

, and market integration. After initially learning about pearl farming through social
media platforms like YouTube, Rulen Hazarika deepened his expertise by undergoing formal training at the
Central Institute of Freshwater Aquaculture in Bhubaneswar in 2018. Upon his return, he conducted small-scale
trials in his pond, experimenting with grafting techniques to evaluate the feasibility of integrating pearl farming
with conventional fish farming. Equipped with both practical knowledge and scientific insights, he began
actively encouraging local farmers to explore pearl farming as a viable and sustainable livelihood option.
For years, aquaculture in Assam has largely revolved around fish farming, a sector that despite its importance,
has faced numerous constraints. Rising input costs, unpredictable market conditions, and environmental
concerns have made it increasingly difficult for small-scale farmers to sustain profitability. Many have
struggled with seasonal income fluctuations and financial instability, prompting a search for diversified and
1 A freshwater mussel is a bivalve mollusc used in pearl farming as the host organism. In Assam, native species
like Lamellidens marginalis are commonly used. Mussels filter water and help the environment, but require clean
conditions and care to successfully produce pearls.
2 Pearl grafting is a precise procedure where a small nucleus is surgically implanted into a mussel to trigger
pearl formation. The mussel coats the nucleus with nacre, forming a pearl over 12–18 months. Skilled training is
essential to perform grafting correctly and ensure quality.

Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi Pearl Farming Story

3
sustainable livelihood opportunities. Pearl farming has emerged as a promising alternative, offering potential
benefits not only to individual farmers but to entire communities.
The concept of pearl farming in Assam is still in its early stages, but it has begun to gain momentum thanks to
early adopters like Rulen Hazarika. However, introducing a novel practice to rural communities steeped in
traditional aquaculture was no easy task. The unfamiliarity of pearl cultivation techniques, lack of awareness
about its market potential, and the long gestation period before returns made many farmers apprehensive.
Rulen soon realised that for pearl farming to take root on a larger scale, it could not remain an individual
experiment. What was needed was a structured, institution-backed approach that would provide technical
training, reduce perceived risks, and build trust through demonstration and peer learning. This recognition
marked a turning point in his efforts, leading him to focus on creating a more enabling ecosystem for
community adoption.

Building Institutional Support: A Collaborative Effort
In early 2023, Rulen’s efforts gained the attention of Biswajit Chakraborty, the then Deputy Registrar of
Cooperative Societies (DRCS) in Nagaon. Recognising the potential impact of pearl farming on rural
livelihoods, Biswajit identified it as a scalable initiative suitable for cooperative development. He introduced
the idea to the District Commissioner (DC) of Nagaon. The District Commissioner played an important role in
institutionalising pearl farming as a sustainable livelihood option.
Recognising its economic potential, the DC facilitated discussions at the District Development Committee
(DDC) meeting, bringing together key officials such as the DRCS, the District Fishery Officer (DFO), and
representatives from the Assam State Rural Livelihoods Mission (ASRLM). This collaboration led to the
formation of the Assam Pearl Development Cooperative Society (APDCS), which provided technical training,
financial support, and structured market access to farmers. The DC’s endorsement ensured sustained
institutional backing for the project.
At this meeting, key stakeholders—including the District Fishery Officer (DFO), the District Project Manager
(DPM) of the Assam State Rural Livelihoods Mission (ASRLM), and Rulen Hazarika—engaged in discussions
on the potential and challenges of launching a structured pearl farming initiative. The outcome was a landmark
decision to establish the Assam Pearl Development Cooperative Society (APDCS), a dedicated entity tasked
with supporting pearl farming in the region.
APDCS was formed with a clear mandate to provide technical training to farmers, facilitate financial support,
establish structured market linkages, and promote sustainable aquaculture practices. By early 2024, the project
had moved into its initial implementation phase, launching pilot farms and introducing 100,000 mussels across
multiple ponds.
Initial Challenges and Responses
When the Asomi Pearl Farming Project was first envisioned, it was clear that building a new livelihood model
from scratch would not be an easy task. Freshwater pearl farming carried immense potential but transforming
that potential into reality meant tackling multiple challenges head-on.
From technical hurdles and farmer skepticism to financial constraints and concerns about market access, every
step required careful planning, innovation, and continuous adaptation. The first and most immediate challenge
was getting farmers to believe in the concept. Unlike fish farming, which had been a part of their lives for

Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi Pearl Farming Story

4
generations, pearl farming was a foreign idea. Most farmers in Nagaon were hesitant to invest time and effort
into something unfamiliar, fearing it would not yield enough returns to justify the additional work.
The idea of pearl cultivation seemed daunting, especially when they learned about the intricate process of pearl
grafting. This delicate procedure involved implanting a tiny nucleus inside a mussel to trigger pearl formation,
a skill that required precision and training. Unlike traditional fish farming, which was relatively simple to
manage, pearl farming demanded patience and technical expertise. The fear that this new skill would be too
difficult to master discouraged many from even considering it.
Another major concern was the market, or the lack thereof. Fish farming had long been an integral part of the
local economy, with a well-established supply chain that assured farmers they could sell their produce without
difficulty. Pearls, on the other hand, were not traditionally traded in the region. The big question lingered in the
minds of many: if there were no guaranteed buyers, why take the financial risk? For small-scale farmers already
facing economic uncertainty, the thought of investing in pearl farming without a clear return on investment
seemed like a risky gamble.
The waiting period also played a crucial role in their hesitation. Fish could be harvested and sold within six
months to a year, ensuring a relatively quick cash flow. Pearls, however, required a much longer gestation
period, anywhere from 12 to 18 months. For farmers who relied on shorter income cycles to sustain their
households, this delay in returns was a significant concern. Many wondered if they could afford to wait that
long before seeing any financial benefit, especially given their already precarious economic conditions.
Recognising these challenges, the APDCS and its partners took proactive steps to bridge the knowledge and
trust gap. A comprehensive capacity-building initiative was launched, focusing on skill development and
practical training. Collaborating with the College of Fisheries, Rural Development and Self Employment
Training Institute (RUDSETI), and aquaculture experts from Madhya Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh, APDCS
organised hands-on training sessions that allowed farmers to witness and practice pearl grafting themselves.
Demonstration farms were set up, offering a real-time glimpse into the process and building confidence among
hesitant farmers.
In addition to technical training, mentorship programs played a crucial role in easing the transition. Farmers
who had already begun experimenting with pearl farming, such as Rulen Hazarika, were paired with
newcomers to share their experiences and provide reassurance. These peer-to-peer interactions proved to be
invaluable, as firsthand success stories helped alleviate doubts and foster trust in the new practice. Despite
these efforts, the shift remained gradual. Pearl farming required precision and patience, qualities that not all
farmers were eager to adopt. Interestingly, it was the younger generation and women’s self-help groups (SHGs)
that showed the greatest willingness to embrace this opportunity, bringing fresh enthusiasm and adaptability
to the initiative.
Beyond training and mindset shifts, financial constraints emerged as another major hurdle. While pearl farming
required less daily maintenance than fish farming, the initial investment in mussels, grafting tools, and training
programs posed a challenge for small farmers. Many simply could not afford to take the risk without external
support. Understanding this, the project tapped into institutional funding to provide financial security for those
willing to give pearl farming a try. The Assam State Rural Livelihoods Mission (ASRLM) played a pivotal role
in facilitating financial linkages, encouraging SHGs to pool resources and invest collectively. The District
Administration also stepped in, securing small grants to subsidise first-time farmers and reduce their financial
burden.
To further minimise risk, APDCS implemented a cooperative model, allowing farmers to buy mussels in bulk at
lower costs. This ensured a steady supply while making the initial investment more affordable. Despite these
measures, financial access remained a challenge for those looking to scale up beyond small-scale production.
Recognising this, APDCS and its partners are actively exploring additional funding avenues, including

Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi Pearl Farming Story

5
microfinance schemes, cooperative bank loans, and potential private-sector collaborations to make pearl
farming a more financially sustainable endeavor in the long run.
Even as financial challenges were addressed, the uncertainty surrounding market access continued to loom
large. Farmers remained unsure whether there would be buyers for their pearls, given Assam’s lack of prior
experience in pearl production. Unlike fish, which had a readily available market, pearls had no established
value chain in the region. Selling them seemed like a daunting task.
To counter this concern, APDCS introduced a buy-back guarantee, ensuring that farmers would not be left with
unsold pearls. This assurance played a crucial role in encouraging first-time participants, giving them the
confidence to invest in the new venture. However, APDCS understood that long-term success would require
more than just a guaranteed buy-back, it would need a thriving market ecosystem. Efforts are now underway to
establish direct partnerships with jewellery manufacturers, creating a seamless link between farmers and
buyers in the jewellery sector. The project is also exploring online sales channels, recognising the increasing
demand for sustainable, naturally cultivated pearls in niche markets. Furthermore, discussions with
government agencies are in progress to integrate Assam’s pearl farming industry into state and national
aquaculture policies, ensuring continued institutional support as the initiative scales up.

Lessons from the Nascent Stage: Learning and Adaptation
The initial phase of the Asomi Pearl Farming Project has been a remarkable journey filled with learning,
adaptation, and perseverance. Introducing an entirely new livelihood model in rural Assam was never going to
be simple, and every milestone, from persuading sceptical farmers to securing financial support and
developing market linkages, has brought invaluable insights. These experiences have reinforced key lessons
that will shape the next phase of the project and provide a roadmap for future rural economic diversification
efforts.
1. Demonstrating Success Increases Participation
One of the most crucial takeaways from the early phase is that farmer participation grows when they witness
real results. Initially, scepticism ran high, with many unsure about the feasibility of pearl farming. However, a
shift occurred when the first group of adopters successfully cultivated pearls and earned financial returns.
Seeing their peers succeed broke down psychological barriers and encouraged others to explore the
opportunity.
Demonstration farms played a pivotal role in changing perceptions. Many farmers who had initially dismissed
pearl farming as risky or unrealistic, reconsidered after observing mussels producing pearls in real-world
conditions. This highlights a fundamental truth about rural livelihood programs: new initiatives gain traction
more effectively when farmers can directly witness success rather than relying on abstract training sessions.
Looking ahead, scaling up pearl farming will require more demonstration farms, well-documented success
stories, and structured farmer-to-farmer interactions to reinforce confidence and participation.
2. Training and Mentorship Are Essential for Skill Adoption
While seeing successful outcomes sparked interest, transforming that interest into actual adoption required
intensive training and mentorship. Pearl farming involves technical skills, particularly in the delicate grafting

Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi Pearl Farming Story

6
process, which directly affects the quality and value of the pearls. Unlike fish farming, which requires minimal
technical intervention, pearl cultivation demands precision and expertise.
Early experiences revealed that without hands-on guidance, many farmers struggled with pearl grafting,
leading to low mussel survival rates and frustration. This underlined the need for ongoing, structured training
rather than one-time workshops.
Mentorship programs proved highly effective in overcoming these challenges. Farmers who were hesitant at
first became more comfortable when paired with experienced trainers and early adopters who could walk them
through the process step by step. This peer-to-peer learning method reduced the intimidation factor and
provided real-time solutions to technical difficulties.
For pearl farming to expand successfully, there must be sustained investment in training programs that
prioritise hands-on learning, expert mentorship, and personalised guidance over traditional classroom
instruction.
3. Cooperatives Reduce Risk and Strengthen Support Systems
One of the most striking observations from the early phase was the vital role cooperatives played in making
pearl farming a feasible livelihood option. The establishment of the APDCS ensured that farmers were not left
to navigate this new venture alone.
By working collectively, the cooperative helped:
• Lower input costs by enabling bulk purchases of mussels at reduced rates.
• Facilitate financial access, securing grants and subsidies to ease initial investment burdens.
• Provide a structured marketing network, reducing dependence on middlemen and ensuring farmers had
direct buyers.
The cooperative model also acted as a safety net, preventing early failures from discouraged farmers. In
contrast, independent farmers who experimented with pearl farming outside the cooperative struggled to
sustain their efforts, reinforcing the importance of collective support structures in scaling up new livelihood
models.

Moving forward, strengthening cooperative governance, ensuring transparency, and maintaining farmer-
friendly policies will be crucial in keeping APDCS an effective institution that continues to provide technical

and financial support to farmers.
4. Market Integration Remains the Biggest Challenge
While financial support and training have laid a strong foundation, the long-term success of pearl farming in
Assam hinges on developing robust market linkages. Unlike fish, which has a ready market in Assam, pearls
cater to a niche audience and require targeted sales channels. Without structured market access, farmers may
struggle to sustain their investment in pearl cultivation.
The introduction of a buy-back guarantee through APDCS was a critical first step in easing farmer concerns
about market risks. Knowing they had a guaranteed buyer allowed early adopters to embrace pearl farming

Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi Pearl Farming Story

7
without fear of financial loss. However, relying solely on buy-back guarantees is not a sustainable long-term
solution.
To ensure market viability, the next phase must focus on:
• Building strategic partnerships with jewellery manufacturers to integrate Assam’s pearls into national and
international markets.
• Developing branding initiatives to establish Assam’s freshwater pearls as a distinct and high-quality
product.
• Leveraging online sales platforms to tap into the growing demand for sustainable, ethically sourced pearls.
• Encouraging local value-added industries, such as pearl-based jewellery making, to retain more economic
benefits within Assam rather than exporting raw pearls for processing elsewhere.
A key realisation here is that market creation must evolve alongside production capacity. If a structured value
chain is not established in parallel, farmers may become disillusioned once initial buy-back mechanisms are
phased out.

The Core Takeaway: Adaptability and Institutional Support Drive Innovation
If there is one overarching lesson from the Asomi Pearl Farming Project so far, it is this; introducing a new
livelihood model requires both adaptability and continuous institutional support. Farmers who had no prior
experience with pearl cultivation have shown remarkable determination in learning this craft, but without
financial backing, technical training, and market access, even the most promising initiatives can falter.
The journey of pearl farming in Assam is still unfolding, and it is evident that this is not a static process but a
dynamic one. Every challenge faced, whether related to training, financing, cooperative organisation, or market
development, has provided critical learning opportunities that are now shaping the next phase of the project.
As efforts continue to expand pearl farming across Assam, these early lessons will serve as guiding principles,
ensuring that the initiative does not remain a short-lived experiment but transforms into a self-sustaining,
scalable livelihood model for the future.

Scaling Up and Future Prospects
The Asomi Pearl Farming Project has witnessed remarkable growth, with substantial advancements in mussel
cultivation and farmer participation. At present, the project cultivates 91,000 mussels, expecting a total pearl
yield of 182,000. Accounting for an anticipated 20% mortality rate, the final projected yield stands at 163,800
pearls by July 2025. Looking further ahead, by 2030, Nagaon is set to emerge as one of India’s largest freshwater
pearl-producing districts, firmly establishing pearl farming as a thriving industry rather than just an
experimental livelihood option.
One of the major drivers behind this expansion is the well-structured economic model implemented by the
APDCS. The cultivation cost per mussel stands at ₹40, covering all essential expenditures, including mussel

Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi Pearl Farming Story

8
seeds, nuclei, pond preparation, feeding, and labour. Since each mussel is capable of producing two pearls, and
market rates range between ₹70 and ₹200 per pearl, the revenue prospects for farmers are highly promising.
With an average selling price of ₹140 per pearl, the projected revenue from the current yield amounts to an
impressive ₹11.47 crore. The buy-back guarantee provided by APDCS further strengthens financial security,
allowing even first-time farmers to confidently participate, knowing that a reliable market awaits their produce.
The project’s scalability is closely tied to financial sustainability and ongoing investment. To drive this growth,
22 Cluster Level Federations (CLFs) have been established across 13 blocks, with pearl farming operations now
spanning 33 ponds. To date, 368 Self-Help Group (SHG) members have undergone specialised training,
conducted at RUDSETI, Nagaon, and through hands-on village-level sessions. Ensuring the long-term success
and expansion of pearl farming in Assam requires continued investments in training, equipment procurement,
and operational support, actively pursued through both government and cooperative funding mechanisms.
To assess the financial feasibility of pearl farming, a breakdown of the current investment landscape is outlined
below:
• Mussel seeds: ₹3,640,000 (91,000 mussels at ₹40 each)
• Training programs: ₹150,000
• Equipment and supplies: ₹200,000
• Operational costs: ₹100,000
• Total: ₹4,090,000
This cost analysis highlights the financial commitment required to sustain pearl farming operations and expand
training initiatives. Given the increasing interest from farmers and the rising demand for natural pearls,
securing a continuous flow of financial support is vital for long-term viability. The cost-benefit equation of
pearl farming is highly favourable, an investment of ₹40 per mussel allows farmers to break even within 15
months. For example, a farmer cultivating 100 mussels (requiring an investment of ₹4,000) can expect to
generate ₹24,000 in profit per cycle, based on an average selling price of ₹140 per pearl.
To achieve large-scale expansion, an additional ₹5 crore investment is needed to support the cultivation of
200,000 mussels. Several key support mechanisms are essential for scaling up operations:
• Subsidised mussel supply: Lowering entry costs to make pearl farming accessible to more farmers.
• Interest-free credit schemes: Encouraging wider farmer participation by reducing financial barriers.
• Direct-to-market linkages with jewellery industries: Maximising profitability and ensuring fair pricing by
connecting farmers directly with buyers.
With these strategic investments and policy-driven initiatives, pearl farming in Assam is on track to become a
key driver of rural economic growth and a sustainable livelihood option for thousands of farmers across the
region.
Conclusion and Policy Recommendations
The Asomi Pearl Farming Project has grown from an ambitious idea into a well-structured model for
sustainable rural livelihoods in Assam. By blending traditional aquaculture with pearl farming, the initiative

Integrating Tradition and Innovation: The Asomi Pearl Farming Story

9
has demonstrated both economic promise and environmental benefits. However, ensuring its long-term success
will require ongoing financial backing, technological innovation, and deeper market integration.
A major contributor to the project's success has been the buy-back guarantee model, which has provided
farmers with much-needed economic security. Looking ahead, expanding cooperative funding mechanisms,
securing policy support for subsidies, and establishing direct connections with jewellery manufacturers and
global retailers will be crucial for sustainable growth. While initial risk mitigation measures have been effective,
enabling farmers to access independent markets will ultimately help them maximise profits and reduce
dependency on institutional buy-backs.
For the project to scale effectively, strengthening cooperative governance and ensuring financial sustainability
are key. APDCS has already made strides in lowering financial barriers through bulk purchases and
microfinance linkages, but evolving toward a self-sustaining reinvestment model will be critical. Additionally,

training programs must advance to include specialised techniques in grafting, pearl processing, and value-
added product development. Establishing mobile training units and regional training hubs will allow broader

participation, particularly benefiting farmers in remote areas.
Technology and sustainability will play defining roles in the industry's future. Enhancing grafting precision,
investing in hatcheries, and improving post-harvest processing techniques will elevate pearl quality and boost
market value. Moreover, leveraging the natural biofiltration properties of mussels can integrate pearl farming
with water conservation efforts, strengthening its environmental impact alongside its economic viability.
Market integration remains the most pressing challenge. Establishing a certification system for Assam’s pearls
and positioning them as a premium product will enhance their credibility and value. Efforts are already in
motion to forge partnerships with jewellery manufacturers, online marketplaces, and export networks to extend
the reach beyond local trade. By developing a distinct brand identity, Assam’s pearls can compete more
effectively in both domestic and international markets.
Policy support will be instrumental in sustaining long-term growth. The formal inclusion of pearl farming in
state and national aquaculture policies will facilitate access to essential resources such as subsidies, loans, and
tax incentives, making it easier for more farmers to participate. Recognising pearl farming as a viable livelihood
within broader rural development frameworks will ensure continued institutional support and investment.
The project’s journey so far has highlighted several key lessons: farmer engagement increases when economic
benefits are clearly visible, continuous skill development is essential for adoption, and cooperative models
significantly reduce financial risk. However, securing market access remains the most crucial long-term
challenge, necessitating a multifaceted approach involving branding, certification, and industry linkages. The
road ahead will be shaped by how effectively these lessons are applied.
If scaled strategically, Assam has the potential to emerge as a major hub for freshwater pearl farming, setting a
precedent for other rural economic diversification initiatives. The Asomi Pearl Farming Project is not just an
isolated success, it represents a growing movement towards sustainable rural entrepreneurship. The next phase
of this journey will be defined by innovation, financial resilience, and supportive policy frameworks, ensuring
that pearl farming continues to transform lives and contribute to Assam’s rural economy for years to come.

Case Study Title: India's Dam Safety Act: From Risk to Regulation
Case Study Description: India, home to over 6,000 large dams—many aging and vulnerable—faced longstanding challenges in ensuring dam safety due to fragmented practices and federal complexities. The 1979 Machchhu-2 dam disaster underscored the urgency, but legislative efforts stalled for decades. The Dam Safety Act, 2021 marks a historic shift by establishing a uniform, legally binding framework for dam safety across India. Overcoming constitutional hurdles, inter-state tensions, and institutional inertia, the Act was enabled by sustained bureaucratic advocacy, legal innovation, and broad stakeholder engagement. Key features include a four-tier safety structure, mandatory inspections, real-time monitoring, and clear accountability mechanisms—balancing national oversight with state autonomy. This case highlights how long-term reform is possible through persistence, adaptive policymaking, and cooperative federalism. It offers lessons for future legislation involving complex governance and public safety systems.
Case Text:
Introduction
11 August 1979, Morbi, Gujarat
Following intense monsoon rainfall and the inadequate capacity of its spillway, the Machchhu-2 dam collapsed at about 3:15
p.m. A massive surge of water swept through the town of Morbi, inundating homes and businesses, sweeping away people
and livestock. Within 15 minutes, the entire city was submerged, with water levels reaching up to 30 feet in certain areas.
The sudden and catastrophic flood triggered widespread panic. Survivors sought refuge on rooftops, trees, and available high
ground. Others clung to floating debris as they were carried downstream. The aftermath was one of immense devastation
with bodies of victims and livestock littering the city. A stench of decay and destruction hung in the air. The once-distinctive
European architecture of Morbi lay in ruins. This disaster was recorded in the Guinness World Records as the worst dam
failure.

The collapse of the Machchhu-2 dam marked a turning point in India’s history of dam governance that elevated
dam safety as a matter of national concern. Implementing uniform dam safety standards in India, however,
proved challenging, primarily because dams are owned and operated by state governments. While international
dam safety practices evolved over time, India's approach, until recently, remained fragmented in the absence of
a cohesive national framework of dam safety procedures.
This case study examines the successful enactment of the Dam Safety Act (DSA), 2021, by the Indian Parliament,
nearly four decades in the making. The Act, a landmark central legislation that establishes a nationwide dam
safety framework, represents a significant milestone in building consensus and resolving complex jurisdictional
issues. The Act reflects the persistence and solution-oriented approach of a dedicated group of protagonists, who
skilfully navigated the valid concerns of multiple stakeholders with the overarching national goal of establishing
standardised dam safety practices and protocols.
The study also traces the evolution of dam safety governance in India, examines the complex legislative
challenges that delayed reform, to distil the key lessons drawn from the prolonged policy process. These insights
are relevant not only for domestic policymakers and administrators engaged in consensus-building initiatives,
but also for international audiences seeking to enact or strengthen dam safety legislation in similar governance
contexts.
‘Transformative change happens when persistence meets opportunity — not always by design, but through ownership,
courage, and the refusal to let setbacks define the final outcome,’ reflects Dr B.R.K. Pillai, former Chief Engineer at the
Central Water Commission who also served as a long-time director in the Dam Safety Organization in the CWC
and played a key role in the Dam Safety Bill of 2019.
He attributes the successful passage of the DSA in 2021, to the unwavering determination and sustained efforts
of techno-bureaucrats in the Central Water Commission and the Department of Water Resources, River
Development & Ganga Rejuvenation, Ministry of Jal Shakti, and the Government of India.

Evolution of Dam Safety Discipline in India
Mr A. B. Pandya, former Chairman, of the Central Water Commission, and former Secretary-General of the
International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage, welcomed the passage of the DSA, 2021 in the Rajya Sabha
3
in December 2021. He reflected on the historical neglect of dam safety in India, by construction-focused state
government departments, observing that ‘Dams are public structures

4 for the public good—and because they were

everybody’s property, they were nobody’s property.’
Mr Pandya has had a long-standing association with the evolution of the dam safety discipline in India. He traces
the roots of India’s dam safety efforts to both global and domestic disasters. The 1976 Teton dam failure in Idaho,
USA, for instance, prompted the United States Bureau of Reclamation to initiate the ‘Safety Evaluation of Existing
Dams’
5 programme. A similar momentum followed India’s Machchhu dam disaster in Gujarat in 1979. Reflecting
on the magnitude of the Machchhu tragedy, Mr Pandya remarks, ‘I would say it was one of the biggest disasters—not
only in India but in the world—in terms of the sheer destruction, the loss of lives, the complete wiping out of Morbi town,
and the total collapse of its economy. It was nothing short of a nuclear bomb disaster.’
Coincidentally, a few months before the Machchhu dam disaster, there were growing concerns about the
importance of dam safety in India. Consequently, pursuant to the directives of the state ministers’ conference, the
Dam Safety Organisation was established within the Central Water Commission in May 1979. In 1982, the Central
Government constituted a ‘Standing Committee on Dam Safety’ to review existing dam safety practices and
evolve unified procedures. The committee's 1986 report recommended the enactment of a legislation on dam
safety and a draft bill was prepared in 1987. However, jurisdictional disagreements relating to division of
legislative powers between the centre and the states stalled progress. Later that year, the committee was
reconstituted as the ‘National Committee on Dam Safety (NCDS)’ with representatives from various state
governments and headed by the Chairman of the CWC. Technical assistance from the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation
and trainings provided by the United Nations Development Programme helped to lay early foundations, but the

NCDS lacked enforceable authority and dedicated funding. The 1990s witnessed the launch of the World Bank-
funded ‘Dam Safety Assurance and Rehabilitation Project’, which emphasised risk-based dam safety frameworks

and legislative reform,ratherthan only rehabilitating identified dams . In 2002, the central government circulated a
model bill for dam safety among all states for adoption and enactment through their respective legislatures.
However, only the state of Bihar enacted a law based on the draft bill in 2006, while the state of Kerala
incorporated dam safety provisions into its existing ‘Irrigation and Water Conservation Act.’
Other states like Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal supported the enactment of a central legislation on dam safety
by the Indian Parliament under Article 252

6 of the constitution, with its application initially limited only to the

consenting states and the union territories that passed similar resolutions.

Repeated efforts to pass the draft, and even finalised, bills in Parliament were, however, stalled each time,
essentially due to reluctance of states and political upheavals in the country. The issue regained urgency in 2010
when the Parliamentary Standing Committee (PSC) on Water Resources reviewed the Dam Safety Bill, 2010.
In 2017, a novel central legislative strategy was championed for a uniform legal dam safety framework across
India through a national legislation applicable to all states. This time, extensive far-reaching consultations were
undertaken with other central ministries, state governments, technical experts, and other stakeholders to build
consensus, address stakeholder concerns and incorporate suggestions into the draft legislation.
Ultimately, after years of groundwork, incorporating incremental capacity-building, crisis response,
deliberations, policy initiatives and legislative learnings, the unified DSA, 2021, was enacted to establish a robust
legal and institutional framework across India. The Act provides clearly defined responsibilities and mandates
at both national and state levels, aligning India’s approach with international best practices.
Dilemmas in Execution
India's journey towards enacting a comprehensive and unified dam safety legislation spanned over four decades,
marked by significant challenges, ranging from political disagreements and differing priorities to complex
jurisdictional concerns between the centre and state governments. Some of the major dilemmas that shaped
India’s journey to dam safety are outlined below:
State Legislation vs. Central Legislation
In the initial years, dam safety efforts in India primarily focused on organisational reforms, issuance of guidelines,
and rehabilitation of identified dams, often supported by externally funded projects. However, these efforts were
limited in scope and lacked a strong legal framework to ensure accountability among dam owners, minimise
risks, and safeguard public safety. Further, institutional mechanisms at the centre and the state-level, were largely
advisory in nature, lacking statutory authority. It soon became evident that statutory provisions were necessary
to effectively enforce continual surveillance and monitoring of dams.
Under the Indian Constitution, water supply and the management of related infrastructure falls within the
purview of states, that own and operate dams, bearing responsibility for their upkeep and safety. Consequently,
early thinking on dam safety, guided by constitutional norms and political realities, favoured state-specific
legislation.
In this context, the central government circulated a draft model bill to encourage states, to enact their own
legislation. However, most state governments displayed limited interest, citing no immediate need to assume
stricter legal obligations. This reliance on state-level legislation significantly delayed the establishment of a
unified national framework. The shift came about when international funding agencies involved in dam
rehabilitation programmes highlighted the need for legislative compliance.
In 2007, the states of Andhra Pradesh and West Bengal formally requested the centre to enact a central law on
dam safety under Article 252 of the Constitution.

7 For the first time, the centre had the constitutional basis to draft
and pass a central dam safety law, initially applicable only to the consenting states but open for adoption by
others. However, the limitations of a voluntary, opt-in approach soon became evident. It could undermine the
goal of establishing unified dam safety procedures. As a result, the call for a comprehensive central legislation
strengthened. This legislation was meant not just for consenting states, but for the entire country. From this
demand to ensure consistency in dam safety standards, a legal hurdle emerged.

Parliament’s Jurisdiction to Enact Unified Central Legislation
A central legal challenge was whether Parliament had the jurisdiction to enact a central legislation on dam safety,
given that water is primarily a state subject.

8 Following the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014,
9
the Ministry
of Law & Justice concluded a legal review holding that the earlier resolution passed by the undivided Andhra
Pradesh legislature in support of central dam safety legislation was no longer valid. This meant that only the
resolution from the West Bengal legislature was remaining as a basis for action, as no other state expressed formal
support for the central dam safety legislation. This meant that the initiative could not proceed under Article 252
of the constitution, which requires support from at least two states for Parliament to legislate on a state subject.
This impasse led to a broader exploration of legislative competence. While states oversee the planning and

implementation of water resource projects, the centre has authority over the regulation and development of inter-
state rivers through entry 56 of the Union List. Further, entry 97

10 of the Union List grants Parliament residuary

powers to legislate on matters not specified in any of the three lists.
Nonetheless, the real issue was that many states perceived the unified central legislation as an encroachment on
their autonomy and feared loss of control over dams within their jurisdiction.
Engaging Diverse Stakeholders
Stakeholder engagement throughout the dam safety legislation process was complex and challenging due to
differing priorities and, at times, conflicting interests. The Dam Safety Bill was introduced in Parliament three
times over nine years, and each time, inter-ministerial consultations and sustained engagement with state
governments proved arduous and time-consuming.
When the bill was first introduced in August 2010 under Article 252 of the Constitution, it was referred to the
PSC on Water Resources for detailed examination. The PSC conducted wide-ranging stakeholder consultations.
It issued newspaper advertisements inviting public feedback, circulated the draft bill to all state governments,
consulted domain experts and held detailed deliberations. These discussions led to substantive modifications and
recommendations to strengthen the bill's framework.
However, additional concerns emerged and persisted, ranging from increased compliance costs and resource
limitations to financial burdens, shortage of trained manpower, and other operational challenges related to
implementation of the new dam safety framework. Another major hurdle was the high level of coordination
mandated among multiple agencies. Defining clear roles, responsibilities, and protocols for inspection,
maintenance, and accountability across the proposed 4-tier institutional setup proved to be complex and a
demanding task.

Managing Inter-State River Water Issues
Inter-state river water disputes posed a major challenge in advancing dam safety legislation.

11 Many inter-state
river water conflicts are closely connected with surrounding dam construction, operation, and regulation.
Several dams in India lie in one state but are owned or operated by another, raising concerns about control,
safety and accountability. For instance, there are dams serving Tamil Nadu and West Bengal but are physically
located in Kerala and Jharkhand, respectively. The Mullaperiyar Dam, over 130 years old, is located in Kerala but
operated and maintained by Tamil Nadu. While Kerala has repeatedly raised safety concerns, Tamil Nadu insists
on retaining operational control, as the dam is essential for irrigation and drinking water and serves as a lifeline
for its five southern districts.
Similar challenges exist in the case of dams that span inter-state borders, where issues related to reservoir levels,
flood regulation, and operational control have caused friction between neighbouring states, such as the Srisailam
and the Nagarjuna Sagar dams on the Krishna River, involving shared control between the states of Andhra
Pradesh and Telangana. Although the dam safety legislation aimed to establish uniform safety protocols
relating to inspection, maintenance, and emergency preparedness, it required a delicate and collaborative
approach to avoid aggravating inter-state tensions.
Given that 92% of India’s dams are located in inter-state river basins, a unified national dam safety framework
was imperative.
Insights from Execution
In the absence of an enforceable legal framework, dam safety practices varied widely across states, sometimes
even within the same structure straddling the inter-state borders. Such inconsistencies were highlighted during
discussions on the Dam Safety Bill, 2019 in the Lok Sabha when a Member of Parliament referenced an audit
report showing that only two out of seventeen audited states had conducted both pre-and post-monsoon dam
safety inspections.
Exploring Alternatives through Persistent Advocacy: Recognising these gaps, the protagonists pursued a
solution-oriented approach that led to legislative reform and the establishment of robust institutional
mechanisms at the national and state levels. Earlier drafts of the bill had notably lacked provisions for establishing
statutory bodies with clearly defined roles and responsibilities—an omission that was later addressed for setting
up stronger institutional mechanisms at both the national and state levels. One of the key protagonists reflecting
on the legislative journey said, ‘The only thing which happened was persistence from our side....’ This insight captures
a vital lesson: meaningful policy reform in complex and sensitive sectors demands sustained advocacy,
collaborative effort, and institutional commitment to overcome systemic inertia.
Stakeholder Engagement: The passage of the DSA, 2021, demonstrated the critical importance of inclusive
stakeholder engagement and consensus-building. The Parliamentary Standing Committee played a pivotal role
in this process by facilitating detailed deliberations and providing a platform for open dialogue that provided
firm clarifications and dispelled misconceptions while the exchange of views proved transformative. Two
detailed rounds of discussions with the PSC enabled thorough scrutiny of the provisions of the bill, helping to
refine and align them with broader national interests.

This experience underscored an important lesson: in complex and sensitive areas like dam safety, sustained
stakeholder engagement, transparent communication, and the willingness to directly address concerns are crucial
for achieving meaningful legislative outcomes.
As one key protagonist observed, ‘We tried to provide proper answers and give comfort to their doubts, rather than
dismissing them—because many of those concerns were genuine.’
A significant challenge in passing the DSA, 2021 was addressing states' concerns about preserving their
autonomy over water resources and dam operations. Consequently, the Act ensured adequate representation for
the States in the National Committee on Dam Safety (NCDS), and mechanisms for meaningful participation in
decision- making. This structure enabled national safety priorities to be achieved without undermining the
state government’s authority over dams under its jurisdiction or operational authority.
Legislative Competence of Parliament: While reviewing the Dam Safety Bill, 2010, the Parliamentary Standing
Committee had supported the view that Parliament has jurisdiction to enact central legislation on dam safety
under entry 56 of the Union List. However, this idea gained traction only after the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh
and the subsequent closure of the Article 252 route, prompting key protagonists to return to the drawing board
to revisit legislative strategy. Despite initial hesitation from the Ministry of Law and Justice, sustained efforts by
the protagonists led to securing a legal opinion from the Solicitor General of India who affirmed that the bill
could be legally and constitutionally introduced in Parliament under Article 246 read with entries 56 and 97 of
the Union List. Insistence on obtaining this legal opinion by Dr Amarjit Singh, then Special Secretary, Ministry of
Water Resources, River Development & Ganga Rejuvenation proved to be a decisive move which ultimately
strengthened the case for a unified central legislation. The legal argument was further bolstered by drawing
parallels with the National Disaster Management Act, 2005 enacted under Parliament’s residuary powers. This
phase thus demonstrates the significance of individual leadership, goal ownership and initiative within the
system. At key junctures—whether in PSC deliberations or in inter-ministerial consultations—the progress was
driven by the willingness of committed individuals to stand up, challenge institutional inertia, and advocate the
need for systemic reform. This sense of ownership, rather than procedural compliance, proved to be the true
driver of DSA, 2021.
Negotiated Solutions to Manage Inter-State Water Disputes: The DSA, 2021, highlights the importance of robust
institutional mechanisms to address inter-state issues, especially where trust deficits persist. For instance, Tamil
Nadu’s objection to Kerala’s State Dam Safety Organisation overseeing its dams located within Kerala, reflects
complexities and sensitivities, that could not be resolved solely through legal provisions.
Prior to tabling the unified central dam safety bill in Parliament, the Ministry of Law and Justice insisted on a
fresh round of state-level consultations, noting that earlier deliberations had included only a few consenting
states. A scheduled meeting of the National Committee on Dam Safety, convened alongside the 3

rd National Dam
Safety Conference in Roorkee, became the platform to address remaining concerns. While most states submitted
technical feedback, Tamil Nadu raised jurisdictional objections.
Behind the scenes, Dr Amarjit Singh, who had by then become the Secretary, Ministry of Water Resources, River
Development & Ganga Rejuvenation, emphasised the need for a constructive and amicable resolution through
consensus. He remarked, ‘I don't want Tamil Nadu to go unhappy from this meeting.’ In response, Dr B. R. K. Pillai
proposed a pragmatic solution. He said that in instances where a dam is owned by one state but located in another
state, the National Dam Safety Authority could assume the responsibilities of the State Dam Safety Organisation,
without impinging on ownership or operational control. This proposal was quickly accepted, and central public
sector undertakings subsequently requested similar oversight by National Dam Safety Authority, reinforcing the
credibility of this model.
This breakthrough demonstrated the power of adaptive policymaking and institutional innovation. In India’s
complex federal landscape, legislative success often depends not on asserting authority, but on accommodating
legitimate concerns through institutional flexibility, dialogue, trust-building, and professional neutrality.

Alignment with SDGs, Citizen-Centricity, and Digital Governance: The DSA, 2021 aligns with India’s
international commitments, particularly the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation)
and SDG 13 (Climate Action), by promoting sustainable water resource management and enhancing resilience to
climate change impacts. Key provisions within the Act include penalties, compensation mechanisms and legal
accountability to ensure compliance with safety regulations. The inclusion of phrases such as
‘desired/satisfactory level of safety assurance’ reflects a commitment to continually improve dam safety practices
while holding dam owners accountable for maintaining prescribed safety standards.
Recognising the critical role of technology in modern dam safety management, the Act promotes the adoption of
technology-driven monitoring systems like real-time surveillance, instrumentation and data analytics to track
dam conditions, predict potential failures, and ensure timely interventions.
Innovations beyond Technology: Innovation in dam safety is not limited to technological advancements. The
Act introduces modern structural governance, including standardised risk assessment methods, and institutional
reforms. The DSA,2021 represents a shift from reactive crisis management to a proactive approach centred on
risk mitigation, accountability, and regulatory enforcement.
Incremental Approach: The prolonged process of drafting the legislation and engaging with stakeholders proved
to be both an advantage and a limitation. On the positive side, the extended timeline allowed for extensive
consultations, enabling state governments and other dam-owning entities to express their concerns—particularly
on sensitive issues such as autonomy, jurisdiction of Parliament and institutional roles. This inclusive,
participatory approach ultimately fostered a more comprehensive and balanced law. On the other hand,
however, delays in enactment meant that known vulnerabilities that may have contributed to avoidable dam
failures—the Tiware Dam failure (2019) in Maharashtra and the Annamayya Dam failure (2021) in Andhra
Pradesh—remained unaddressed. Ironically, both incidents were cited during parliamentary debates on the Dam
Safety Bill, highlighting the urgent need for a robust legal and institutional framework.

Conclusion
The Dam Safety Act, 2021, is a critical milestone in India’s journey toward ensuring dam safety and water security.
Its impact, however, will depend on its effective implementation, continual regulatory refinement, coordination
between States, and integration of emerging technological innovations. While the process remains a work in
progress, the lessons learned underscore the importance of institutional strengthening, stakeholder engagement,
and a balanced approach to governance in achieving long-term water security and dam safety.
The enactment itself provides several key lessons that can be applied to other pending legislations and reforms
seeking to establish institutional/regulatory framework, particularly those involving complex governance
structures, multi-stakeholder engagement, and Central-State coordination such as the proposed River Basin
Management Bill and water pricing reforms through regulatory authorities.
India’s experience in enacting the DSA, 2021, can serve as a model for other countries seeking to strengthen their

Case Study Description: This case presents the policy design and implementation journey of MJPSKY, Maharashtra’s flagship farm loan waiver scheme (2019–20), crafted in response to the operational failures of an earlier waiver (CSMSSY, 2017). Introduction
In late 2019, the corridors of Maharashtra’s Department of Cooperation buzzed with urgency. The Principal
Secretary and administrative head of the department, Ms. Abha Shukla, convened a series of intense meetings
to dissect the persistent limitations of the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Shetkari Sanman Yojana (CSMSSY) — a
farm loan waiver scheme launched in 2017.
“We must identify why our farmers are unable to access the relief they are rightfully entitled to,” she stated firmly,

2
determined to restore dignity to an agrarian community battered by years of hardship and distrust. Farmers
from drought-hit Vidarbha embodied this distress. “The portal kept crashing, and even bank officials were as lost as
we were,” many recalled, frustration evident after waiting two years for the loan relief that never materialized.
Meanwhile, a newly elected government had pledged to waive all eligible loans within 100 days, dramatically

Background: Maharashtra’s Agrarian Crisis

Maharashtra’s farming sector faced several difficult years. Around 68% of its cultivable land was drought-
prone, and the state made up 24% of India’s drought-affected areas [1]. Between 2019 and 2021, floods damaged

over 1.2 million hectares of Kharif crops, leading to large economic losses across rural communities. Irrigation
covered only 18.2% of cultivable land, so most farmers depended on rainfall, which became more unpredictable
over time [2]. Small and fragmented land holdings, averaging 1.34 hectares by 2015–16, limited productivity
and made it hard for farmers to benefit from economies of scale [3]. Poor access to markets meant many relied
on middlemen, often selling their produce at low and unstable prices.
Debt levels continued to rise. Between 2015–16 and 2020–21, outstanding farm loans in Maharashtra grew by
116%, reaching ₹5.5 lakh crore ($660 billion), the highest rate of growth among Indian states [4]. Nationally,
agricultural loans rose by 53%, and the number of farmer loan accounts increased from 6.9 crore to over 10
crore [iv]. More than 50% of agricultural households were in debt, many borrowing from informal lenders who
charged high interest [5]. The pressure took a heavy toll. In 2019, 2020, and 2021, Maharashtra reported the
highest number of farmer suicides in the country, making up over 40% of the national average during these
years [6]. As a temporary relief measure, farm loan waivers were introduced, though the approach remained
widely debated.
The Debt Cycle and Its Impacts
The debt cycle in Maharashtra had become a relentless trap. Crop failures—caused by drought or flooding,
often left farmers unable to repay their loans. This made them ineligible for fresh credit from formal institutions.
In desperation, many turned to private moneylenders who charged interest rates that often exceeded 30% per
annum [7]. In regions like Marathwada, for instance, a farmer borrowing ₹50,000 (around $600 USD) might
find himself owing ₹65,000 (around $780 USD) within a year, as interest compounded quickly. To cope, many
were forced to sell off assets—land, livestock, or household goods—gradually losing the very means by which
they earned a living. In the most extreme cases, the burden proved too much, contributing to Maharashtra’s
high number of farmer suicides. The lack of incentives for timely repayment made things worse. Farmers who
repaid diligently found no benefit or recognition for their discipline, weakening the overall financial culture in
the sector.
Historical Context of Loan Waivers
Farm loan waivers had a long history in India and were often used as emergency relief during agrarian crises.
The first major initiative, the Agricultural and Rural Debt Relief (ARDR) scheme of 1990, had cost ₹7,825 crore
(about $939 million USD) and set a precedent for later state-level interventions [8]. Maharashtra’s own efforts
built on this legacy. Schemes like CSMSSY and MJPSKY reflected not only the scale of the crisis but also the
way implementation strategies had evolved over time. Critics argued that waivers were politically motivated,
often announced close to elections, and did not address deeper structural problems such as irrigation shortages

or inefficient markets. Still, their continued use showed just how widespread and persistent rural distress had
become, and how limited the short-term options were for relief.
The agrarian crisis also brought social challenges. Migration from rural areas to cities like Mumbai and Pune
increased, as farming became less viable, adding stress to urban infrastructure. Women, who often stayed back
to manage farms when men moved away in search of work, bore increased responsibilities without additional
support. Children's education was also affected, as families focused on survival over schooling. These
overlapping hardships made the need for immediate relief measures like loan waivers all the more urgent.
The Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Shetkari Sanman Yojana
(CSMSSY) Launch and Objectives
In June 2017, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis launched the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Shetkari Sanman
Yojana (CSMSSY), with the objective of waiving farm loans up to ₹1.5 lakh ($1,800 USD) for farmers who had
defaulted by 30 June 2016 on loans taken after 1 April 2009 [9]. With a budget of ₹34,022 crore ($4.08 billion
USD), the scheme aimed to support 8.9 million farmer families, covering loans from nationalised, private, rural,
and district cooperative banks [10]. Following a surge in applications, with over 56 lakh farmers registering by
September 2017, disbursements began on 18 October 2017 [11]. The scheme sought to provide urgent relief to
a farming sector strained by debt and recurring natural disasters.
To support disbursements, the Maharashtra government used the MahaOnline portal, a digital platform
designed to streamline farmer access to government schemes and benefits. Benefits were credited directly to
Aadhaar-linked bank accounts, ensuring transparency and minimising leakages. The portal also allowed
farmers to check application statuses, update profiles, and receive official updates. By consolidating services
into a single system, the platform reduced paperwork and improved accessibility for farmers across the state.
Implementation Challenges
Despite its ambitious vision, the implementation of CSMSSY faced several operational hurdles that significantly
slowed progress on the ground.
• Technological Failures: The MahaOnline portal, developed by the Government of Maharashtra in
collaboration with Tata Consultancy Services (TCS)1

, was riddled with technical issues. Frequent server
crashes, limited capacity, and corrupted data frustrated users across the state [12]. A major IT platform
migration in 2018 led to the corruption of 6.5 lakh farmer accounts, leaving ₹5,975 crore ($717 million USD)
undisbursed [13]. In Nashik, a server outage lasted three days, halting the application process throughout

Case Study Title: Anchoring Global Efficiency: Visakhapatnam Leads India’s Entry into the World’s Top 20 Container Ports
Case Study Description: This case study examines how Visakhapatnam Port Authority (VPA) achieved a remarkable turnaround by entering the World Bank’s Global Top 20 Container Port Performance Index (CPPI) in 2024, rising from rank 115 to 19 within a year. Located strategically on India’s eastern seaboard near the Malacca Strait, VPA leveraged strong rail-road connectivity to strengthen its competitive position. The transformation was led by Chairperson Dr. M. Angamuthu, appointed in May 2023, at a time when the port faced ageing infrastructure, procedural delays, and intense competition from private ports. Using the autonomy provided by the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, the leadership implemented reforms focused on operational efficiency, digitalization, and stakeholder coordination. A long-standing PPP with Visakha Container Terminal Pvt. Ltd., along with ecosystem-wide collaboration, enabled capacity upgrades, improved turnaround times, and greater environmental sustainability.

Located on India’s eastern seaboard near the Strait of Malacca and supported by strong rail and road

Institutional Rigidities and Legacy Inefficiencies
Vizag Port was, in many ways, a textbook example of a legacy government institution. Until the early

federal government. This limited the port’s legal ability to make independent decisions regarding
operations, private partnerships, and tariff setting. Even basic commercial discretion— such as offering
a discount to attract more container traffic—was subject to scrutiny. “If I subsidize a rate,” one senior
official explained, “the audit will question whether I am showing undue favour. We are not a private
enterprise—we are a government board.” This fear of audit overreach bred inertia and made risk-taking
virtually impossible.

Even as the port worked to address internal limitations, its location posed unique logistical challenges.
Many ports are built on isolated coastlines, but the Vizag Port is embedded within a growing urban

port, bypassing intermediate handling at container freight stations, were underutilized. The
classification of “trusted clients” was restrictive, and shipments often required cumbersome “stuffing
and de-stuffing” at container freight stations, especially for Less-than-Container Load cargo.8 For
exporters, these delays translated into missed shipping windows and rising costs.
A Tipping Point
“It was a question of surviving the business with competitiveness,” reminisced Angamuthu. It was not just
about cranes and berths. It was about shifting mindsets, digitizing processes, attracting new industries,
and proving that a government-run port could match the agility of its private-sector rivals. For the
VPA, the challenge was clear: how to accelerate the transformation of a legacy bulk port into a modern,
container-focused gateway, overcoming institutional inertia and stakeholder scepticism, while
ensuring Vizag could compete in a rapidly evolving logistics landscape.

Implementation Process: Operational Excellence Rooted in Measurable Outcomes
Before 2022, container operations at Vizag Port were limited in scale. As trade volumes increased and
shipping lines demanded quicker turnaround, it became clear that the existing setup would not be
enough. The need for faster, more reliable operations brought both VPA and its private partner,

Visakha Container Terminal Private Limited (VCTPL), to the same table. They understood that
operational excellence required greater synergy—where VPA provided policy and infrastructure
support, and VCTPL delivered on-the-ground execution and technology upgrades. Both sides
recognized their roles in shaping a more capable and competitive port.
Enhancements Done by VCTPL
Operating since 2003 under the Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer Model (DBFOT),9

the VCTPL
invested in transforming the container terminal’s infrastructure, improving container cargo handling
and supporting service delivery. For them, investing heavily in Vizag Port meant clear long- term gains.
More capacity meant more containers and larger ships, which brought in more revenue.
In December 2021, a major transformation began at the VCTPL. The quay10 at Terminal 1 was extended
from 450 m to a massive 895 m, making it the longest continuous quay on India’s east coast. This
expansion enabled larger ships to dock simultaneously, boosting throughput capacity. With a draft11of
16.5 m—deepest in the country—Visakha Container Terminal can now accommodate container vessels
up to 390 m in length overall, meaning ships nearly four football fields long can berth safely.
But lengthening the quay was only part of the story. Three super post panamax rail mounted quay
cranes12 were also added. Each of these cranes has an outreach of 65 m, allowing them to reach across
a ship’s width, and a safe working load of 65 tons, enabling the efficient lifting of heavy containers. The
addition of these cranes increased the total number of quay cranes at the port from four to seven,
significantly improving cargo-handling speed. At the same time, the number of rubber-tired gantry
cranes nearly doubled, with nine electric units fitted with GPS-based position detection, in addition to
10 electric ones at Terminal 1. In addition to this, five new electric reach stackers were added in the fleet
replacing diesel reach stackers. These upgrades meant containers could be moved faster within the
yard, improving overall workflow and reducing congestion, while reducing port’s carbon footprint of
about 80 tons annually.
The container storage yard13 was upgraded with an additional 41 acres, enabling 2,600 more ground
slots and raising the daily handling capacity to 18,000 TEUs, thereby further reducing the congestion
and improving yard productivity. To facilitate seamless cargo evacuation, a new six-lane kiosk-enabled
gate complex was commissioned in August 2022, alongside the existing three-lane facility, streamlining
trailer movement and reducing turnaround time for cargo vehicles.
To support the increasing volume of refrigerated cargo, Terminal 2 added 300 new reefer plug points
with 24/7 diesel generator backup, complementing the existing 350 plug points at Terminal 1. These
upgrades strengthened the port’s capacity to handle India’s expanding marine export trade.
Together, these infrastructure improvements—particularly the use of advanced twin-lift crane
technology, which enables lifting of two containers simultaneously, and the extension of berths—
helped reduce vessel turnaround times significantly. Ships could now dock, unload, and depart faster
than before, increasing the port’s throughput and productivity.

VPA’s Operational Drive
Operational efficiency at Visakhapatnam Port was not achieved through infrastructure upgrades alone.
A series of ecosystem-level interventions, both within the container terminals and across the wider port
area14 and ecosystem, enabled smoother, end-to-end coordination. The VPA board agreed to bring bold
reforms in pricing. Premium charges for priority berthing were scrapped by August 2023. This move
was strategic: while it involved a short-term revenue dip, the objective was to attract greater cargo
volumes in the long run.
The Custom Bound Area15 was expanded from 160 acres to 339 acres in 2024, allowing better cargo flow
management across terminals. Supporting these operational changes, the team analysed over a decade
of the port’s performance data—tracking cargo trends, shipping line behaviour, and trade flows. This
deep dive generated valuable insights for targeted improvements. By benchmarking against leading
global ports, Visakhapatnam was able to align its performance indicators with international standards,
ensuring every decision was grounded in robust, comparative data.
These efforts culminated in VCTPL’s investment in the adoption of NAVIS N4, a fully integrated digital
platform and the latest generation Terminal Operating System that unified all port stakeholders—
shipping lines, customs, importers, and exporters—through a single-window interface. By streamlining
documentation, enhancing real-time visibility, and reducing the human interface in customs
compliance, this digital transformation not only boosted operational efficiency but also fostered greater
transparency, accountability, and faster service delivery.
This required the adoption of new technology-driven processes by port users. Hence, VPA and VCTPL
shared frequent circulars, conducted multiple training and awareness programs (including shipping
and customs agents, truck drivers) to demonstrate new digital processes (including NAVIS N4 and the
RFID gate system). This helped address any grievances or issues faced by stakeholders and incorporate
their feedback. Further, VPA took measures to strengthen its communication and relation with various
port stakeholders.
Empowering Public–Private Partnership Operators
The partnership with private players strengthened after the Major Port Authority Act, 2021, gave VPA’s
board the legal freedom to act. As the chairperson explained, “Private players do require flexibility as they
come with their own autonomy, processes, and specialized skills.” With this, the chairperson initiated the
practice of conducting monthly meetings with each public–private partnership (PPP) operator16
(separately), along with all heads of departments of the port to review and understand their work and
requirements at one table. To attract more business, the port increased its trade meets, stakeholder
conclaves, and outreach with industry players across India. These engagements resulted in assurances
from participating container liners to increase their cargo volumes through Vizag Port, helping build
robust industry partnerships.
During this period, Visakhapatnam Port also began transitioning to a landlord model. Under this
model, the VPA became responsible for providing all necessary infrastructure, particularly facilities
beyond the port gates, such as roads, truck parking stations, and railway connectivity. For VCTPL
specifically, a designated four-lane road was constructed in 2023 from the city’s busy common junction
road to the container terminal to ensure the continuous movement of containers. As the owner and

regulator of the land and assets, VPA focused on strategic oversight, while private companies managed
the daily operations. This shift marked a significant change in port management, as it separated
regulatory oversight from day-to-day activities. It also created opportunities for private operators to
invest directly in infrastructure upgrades and technology.
Introducing Additional Incentives with a Win-Win Approach
To encourage volume growth and reward long-term commitment, the VPA introduced measures to
support transshipment activities with a discount of up to 80% for the transshipment containers to boost
movement. As a result, operating costs decreased for both the port and its partners. To further boost
cargo volumes, the board approved a policy offering financial concessions to stakeholders who
increased their cargo volumes beyond their own 3-year historical average. This “incremental cargo”
scheme was designed to recognize and incentivize consistent performance rather than one-off
transactions. Under the scheme, logistics providers, shipping lines, and other cargo handlers who
demonstrated growth above their previous average were eligible for rebates on port charges. The more
cargo they brought in over their baseline, the greater the concession they received.
This approach marked a shift from short-term, transactional engagements to a more strategic focus on
sustained partnerships. It created a clear and predictable incentive structure that motivated
stakeholders to expand business through the port.
Creating a Seamless Multimodal Ecosystem and Stakeholder Coordination
Coordination within the Port Working Committee—which included the VPA, VCTPL, exporters,
customs clearing and forwarding agents, the Vizag Stevedores Association,17 the Vizag Steamship
Agents18 and other port users—was strengthened. Regular meetings, supported by clear action reports
and a dedicated WhatsApp channel, enabled swift issue resolution and ensured accountability
In addition to this, the VPA and VCTPL deepened engagement with Customs, CONCOR, Indian
Railways, and more than 65 container lines to improve coordination and efficiency. Plans for a 100- acre
logistics hub and cold storage facilities were proposed, and a new truck parking terminal was
inaugurated. These measures ensured smooth cargo movement and prevented congestion at the
container terminal.
Strengthening Internal Monitoring and Strategic Planning
Angamuthu constituted a unique Port Infrastructure Committee to break down silos and strengthen
cross-departmental coordination. The committee—comprising heads of department, deputy heads, and
senior port officials—was organized into five-member teams to conduct monthly, on-site inspections
across port zones, including visual documentation of any improvements or upgrades required in these
areas. Every month, the general administration department consolidates the reports from all teams, and
a review meeting is held under the chairpersonship of Angamuthu. A senior official from the civil
department commented: “This monthly meeting keeps us on our toes. The teams have become more proactive
and competitive in their work. The best part is that members with desk jobs get to visit the port operations on site.
This was not possible earlier due to their nature of work. Now, the sanctions and approvals of various projects
over e-files are faster as departments are better coordinated and understand the various port operations more
logically.”
