In parallel, the chairperson mandated each department to craft annual action plans with clear targets
and business strategies, integrating feedback and suggestions from both internal teams and external
stakeholders. This collaborative process began each January and culminated by late February or March
with an annual stakeholders’ meet, where the chairperson personally unveiled the unified action plan
and vision for the year ahead.
According to Angamuthu, there was no resistance from staff or port users to the changes. He said,
“Whatever we were doing was not just business for the port; it was incremental business with human perspective
where everyone felt included in the decision-making process.” He added, “They were our ‘partners in progress.’
Everyone benefited, and that was why we face no resistance.”

Impact
Between FY 2022–2023 and FY 2024–2025, Vizag Port demonstrated measurable progress across
multiple performance indicators. Cargo throughput increased from 73.75 million tons in FY 2022–2023
to 81.09 million tons in FY 2023–2024, and further to a record 82.62 million tons in FY 2024–2025,
indicating consistent growth in trade volumes and port-handling efficiency (VPA 2025a). This was
accompanied by a sharp rise in container traffic, which grew from 0.52 million TEUs in FY 2022–2023
to 0.67 million TEUs in FY 2023–2024, reflecting the port’s growing appeal to shipping lines and
exporters (VPA 2024). Vizag also contributed around 314,199 metric tonnes of marine and aqua cargo
in FY 2023–2024—about one-third of India’s total in this segment— highlighting its sector importance
(MPEDA 2024). In parallel, private partner VCTPL, operating under the landlord port model, invested
₹720 crore across four new terminal projects aimed at automating operations and enhancing handling
capacity, underscoring the transformative role of PPPs in the port’s evolution (VPA 2024).
From Eastern Shores to Global Score: Way Ahead
No port operates in a vacuum. From customs clearance to rail logistics, from cold chain to container
tracking—each piece of the system matters. Vizag treated port efficiency as a shared outcome, not an
individual metric. Going ahead, VPA aimed to accelerate the infrastructure upgrades: the port’s
highway was being expanded from four to ten lanes under Bharatmala,19 with four dedicated lanes for
port traffic. Flyovers were under design to bypass 11 railway crossings20 in and around the city, thereby
decreasing traffic congestion, in collaboration with the Rail Vikas Nigam Limited, a PSU under the
Ministry of Railways. Stockyards21 were being redeveloped in a phased manner, with proper drainage
systems, hardscaping of open cargo areas, and improved access roads to cargo zones and railway
sidings, in partnership with MECON,22 to ensure safe, efficient cargo storage— even during monsoon
season. This would further enhance operational efficiency at the port. Further, the VPA aimed to
transform into a landlord model port by 2030 with 100% cargo handling by PPP terminals. This sent a
strong signal to other major ports in India, and aligned closely with the Maritime India Vision 2030,
which aimed to move the majority cargo at major ports through similar PPP models.

However, Angamuthu also raised a critical concern—underutilization. The VPA was still operating at
only 60% capacity, mainly held back by competitive pressures. Many nearby private ports were
performing even below this level. Despite this, new ports were under development, raising a larger
question for the VPA and VCTPL: Are they building faster than they are scaling demand?
At this point, Angamuthu advocated for a regional port coordination authority that spanned 400–500
km of coastline, encompassing major, minor, private, and state ports. “We compete for the same cargo. But
sometimes I can handle cargo X better, and my neighbouring port is better for cargo Y. Why not share
infrastructure, optimize capacity, and build a win-win model?” said Angamuthu.
In his opinion, a regional authority could manage vessel rerouting, berth scheduling, and shared
evacuation logistics. This cooperative model could drastically reduce anchorage delays and logistics
costs—the key friction points in global shipping.
Sudeep Banerjee, Senior Vice President and Terminal Head of the VCTPL, highlighted the urgent need
to anchor port operations in a stronger local and regional cargo base. He suggested strengthening the
hinterland and logistics base. “A port should be fed by its own hinterland. Vizag is still dependent on far-off
states. That is risky and unsustainable,” explained Captain Sudeep Banerjee.

Lessons Learned
Three key lessons stood out from Vizag’s journey
First, institutional transformation was rooted in collaborative partnership. VPA’s turnaround
demonstrated how strategic public–private collaboration—when backed by clear roles, trust, and
accountability—could deliver operational excellence at scale. The outcome of the synergy between the
VPA and VCTPL under the PPP was visible:
• VCTPL’s quay expansion, digitization, and adoption of NAVIS N4 helped reduce port call
duration to 19.1 hours and berth idle time to under 1.5 hours, far exceeding global averages.
• Vizag became India’s largest marine and aquaculture cargo hub, handling nearly 30% of the
country’s seafood exports in 2023–2024.
• The port had been attracting some of the world’s largest vessels like MSC Monica Christina
and later a 15,486 TEU Trans-Pacific mothership in June 2025
As affirmed by Venugopal M. Harbour Master, VPA: “Despite being nearly a day-and-a-half off the main
international shipping lanes like the Colombo–Singapore corridor, vessels are consistently calling Vizag Port. The
preference proves that companies trust the quality of services and the operational efficiency that we offer.”
Indeed, Vizag’s location on the Upper Bay of Bengal could position it as a natural transshipment hub
for the eastern subcontinent, including ports such as Kolkata, Haldia, and even extending to Myanmar.
As argued by Sudeep Banerjee, this required greater investment in supporting infrastructure such as
large-scale logistics parks, cold storage networks, and multi-user distribution centres that could
catalyse trade, especially in value-added cargo like fruits and electronics— cargo that currently
bypasses Vizag for Chennai due to superior ecosystem support. “If we create the critical mass through
enhanced rail links and transshipment planning, more mother vessels will come. Vizag can become northern
India’s preferred eastern gateway,” noted Banerjee.
Second, policy autonomy must be matched with agile and inclusive leadership. The VPA board
leveraged the autonomy provided by the Major Ports Authority Act, 2021 to recognize bottlenecks and
act decisively on infrastructure, incentives, and revenue models that enabled rapid modernization. The
chairperson institutionalized monthly inspections, multi-stakeholder planning, grievance redressal

channels, and transparent performance reporting. As a senior VPA official said, “Our leadership wants
to hear everybody and promotes an open communication with port users. You explore our website. You can see
every big or small information. You can access the existing and ongoing port infrastructure projects (with
timelines and completion rate), port performance data, business plan, and development initiatives—all in one
place.” This shows that empowered boards and clear legal mandates must be activated by participatory
leadership that intrinsically motivates the teams to excel toward shared progress.

Third, modern ports must balance operational growth with environmental responsibility and a citizen-
centric approach. In line with Harit Sagar Green Port Guidelines, 2023,23 sustainability became a central

theme of Vizag Port’s transformation:
• Over 650,000 trees were planted on 650 acres of port land, with a million more pledged across
Vizag city by 2028.
• Landscaping and illumination were done around port roads, and a public promenade road is
being developed leading up to International Cruise Terminal to provide a close-up view of
vessels coming into the port.
With this, the VPA aimed to turn port spaces into shared civic zones and foster a sense of shared
ownership among local residents, thereby reducing community resistance. For the VPA, strengthening
public support is a crucial factor for port-led development. Angamuthu explained this vision, “The port

spans over 7,618 acres of the Vizag city. We aim to change the citizens’ perception that the port is a pollution-
emitting industrial area. Today, we have families doing morning and evening walks alongside the landscaped

roads, clicking pictures at selfie-points, etc. People should feel part of the port ecosystem with pride, especially my
own employees and partners. After all, before anything else, they are the citizens of Vizag.”
Vizag has redefined its role—not just as a port but as a driver of “ease of business” and “ease of living”
for the entire region.
This shift from a busy port to an ecosystem enabler is the next chapter. As Angamuthu said, “It does not
matter whether it is a private or government port. As long as we are building the economy together, it is the right
direction.”

Case Study Title:
The DigiYatra Initiative: Harnessing Technology
for Hassle Free Air Travel
Case Study Description: In Dec 2022, the Government of India launched the Digi Yatra initiative at three airports (Delhi, Bengaluru, Varanasi)—a first-of-its-kind digital transformation program that aimed to streamline air travel processes and enhance passenger experiences at airports across the country. The program aimed to eliminate long queues, reduce paperwork, and improve security checks by leveraging biometric technology and digital identification. The Airports Authority of India (AAI), along with other airport operators, took on the task of implementing this ambitious project. Starting with three airports, the government rolled out the initiative in a phased manner, and by the end of 2024, it had implemented Digi Yatra across various airports in the country, significantly improving passenger convenience and operational efficiency.
Case Text:
Introduction
The festive season was on and the winter holidays were around the corner as the year 2022 was about to end.
People in huge numbers were traveling, either for their homes or holiday destinations. The Indian civil aviation
sector was in prime-time news, but not for very good reasons. There were news reports of chaos at major airports
like Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru. Long queues could be seen outside terminal buildings as well as at counters
for obtaining boarding passes. Many passengers were missing their flights due to the congestion. Videos and
pictures of the crowded airport terminals, resembling bus stands, were being shared widely by electronic media
and passengers on social media portals.
Perturbed by the prevailing chaotic situation at airports, the Ministry of Civil Aviation assigned Mr. P. K. Thakur,
Deputy Director General, Aviation Security, the task of implementing a technology-driven solution to ensure a
hassle-free and health-risk-free travel experience for passengers. He was to take into consideration the work of
the Technical Working Group, which was formed during the years 2017–18. Along with Mr. P. K. Thakur, the
Digi Yatra initiative was tasked to other several key figures in the Indian aviation sector. One such figure was
Mr. Suresh Khadakbhavi, the CEO of the Digi Yatra Foundation, the organisation behind the Digi Yatra service.
Mr. Suresh Khadakbhavi, an electronics and communication engineer by training, had a 15-plus-year stint with
Bengaluru International Airport Ltd before joining Digi Yatra. As described by Mr. P. K. Thakur: "Digi Yatra is
not only changing the way people experience air travel but is also a win-win for airport operators and airlines."
Reasons Behind the Unprecedented Chaos at Major Airports
Air travel worldwide came to an abrupt halt in early 2020 due to the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. The
aviation industry had "the worst year in history for air travel demand." While the year 2021 was still mired by
travel restrictions, turbulence gradually eased in 2022 as more and more passengers returned to the skies. Indian
domestic air travel had touched a new high just before the onset of COVID-19, when 1.3 crore domestic
passengers flew in the month of December 2019. However, soon after, due to lockdowns and travel restrictions,

The DigiYatra Initiative: Harnessing Technology for Hassle Free Air Travel

2
it shrank considerably. During 2022, air travel in India largely revived and reached pre-pandemic levels, with
1.27 crore domestic passengers taking to the skies in December 2022. There were instances where the number of
passengers traveling on a particular day crossed previous records on a day-to-day basis, and thus created chaotic
scenes at major airports such as Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru. Revenge travel1 was also one of the reasons for
the increased number of air travellers. While on one hand, it was a positive sign for the aviation sector, which
needed something like this to boost the confidence of the airlines and airport operators after COVID-19, on the
other hand, there was unprecedented congestion and rush at airports (Exhibit 1). There was also data to support
and show high traffic of domestic passengers in scheduled carriers. (Exhibit 2 and 3)
In addition to above, the government's big push on regional connectivity through UDAN2 Scheme has also played
a role in the steady surge in domestic air travel since 2017.
Response To the Chaos
Union Civil Aviation Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia monitored the chaotic situation prevailing at major airports.
He made a surprise visit to the congestion-prone Terminal-3 (T-3) of Indira Gandhi International Airport, New
Delhi, on 7th December 2022. (Exhibit 4) After detailed deliberation with various stakeholders of the Indian
aviation sector, he decided to adopt several measures, both immediate and longer-term. Among these was the
decision to accelerate the implementation of the Digi Yatra initiative of the ministry, which had already
undergone various stages of trials since 2017. This single decision pushed Digi Yatra from the incubation phase
to the accelerated implementation phase.
Digi Yatra Working Concept
Digi Yatra represents a flagship digital initiative spearheaded by the Ministry of Civil Aviation to modernize the

passenger journey through Indian airports. At its core, it leverages facial recognition and blockchain-based Self-
Sovereign Identity (SSI) technology3

to offer a secure, paperless, and highly personalized travel experience. The
system ensures passengers can move through various airport checkpoints—entry gates, security, and boarding—
without the need for physical ID or printed tickets.
Designed to be inclusive and adaptable, Digi Yatra currently serves all domestic passengers and remains entirely
voluntary. Its framework accounts for diverse passenger types:
(i) First-time flyers
(ii) Frequent travellers
(iii) Families/Large groups
(iv) Foreign nationals
The Digi Yatra ecosystem is built around four strategic pillars: Connected Passengers, Connected Airports,
Connected Flying, and Connected Systems. These foundational elements are intended to create a digitally unified
1 A term coined to signify people trying to make-up for the loss of mobility due to lockdown and travel
restrictions necessitated by COVID-19
2 UDAN, or Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik scheme launched in 2017, is a government initiative to enhance regional
connectivity and make air travel affordable by incentivizing airlines to operate from underserved and unserved
airports, particularly in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities.
3 Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) is a decentralized digital identity model that allows individuals to own, control,
and share their personal data without relying on a central authority. Digi Yatra utilizes blockchain technology
to enable secure, tamper-proof identity verification, ensuring passenger data remains private, consent-based,
and accessible only to the individual and authorized stakeholders.

3
air travel environment, where data security, operational efficiency, and passenger convenience go hand in hand.
By decentralizing data4 control through blockchain and minimizing the need for physical interaction, Digi Yatra

not only addresses concerns around health safety and efficiency, but also sets the stage for a future-ready, tech-
driven civil aviation infrastructure in India.

Enrolment On Digi Yatra App
Enrolling on the Digi Yatra App requires the passenger’s mobile number and an OTP for verification. The system
then retrieves facial data from a trusted source like the Aadhaar5 number, including the passenger’s name and a
digital image. It sends this data to the biometric matching algorithm, which performs a one-to-one match with
the selfie taken by the passenger’s mobile phone. The system checks the date of birth, Aadhaar, face, name, and
gender. Once matched, it stores the passenger’s selfie in the identity credential within the passenger’s phone’s
digital wallet and discards the image of the Aadhaar card.
Instead of storing personal data centrally, the system stores ID credentials solely on the user's smartphone in a
secure wallet. It then generates a unique hash value from the user's credentials and securely stores this hash on
the blockchain to ensure data integrity and detect any tampering of the user's credentials.
Self-sovereign identity offers passengers greater control over their personal data while ensuring a seamless
journey. The Digi Yatra app eliminates the need for physical documents, allowing travellers to move through
airport touchpoints using facial biometric technology. Instead of presenting a government-issued ID and a
boarding pass separately, passengers authenticate their identity once through the app, streamlining the
verification process. This approach reduces wait times, enhances security, and minimizes the risk of document
loss. With over 11 million downloads and 48 million users across 24 airports, Digi Yatra has become one of the

largest successful implementations of decentralized identity. The platform ensures privacy through a self-
sovereign model, where personal information remains securely stored on the user's device—making the process

faster, safer, and more efficient.
Self-sovereign identity (SSI) leverages blockchain technology for certificates and digital signatures on Verifiable
Credentials (VCs)6

. Blockchain provides a decentralized and tamper-proof ledger, ensuring the authenticity and
integrity of digital identities and credentials. This approach enhances security and gives individuals full control
over their personal data without relying on centralized authorities. (Exhibit 5)
Technology That Drives Digi Yatra
The Digi Yatra Foundation (DYF) designed and developed the Digi Yatra mobile app on Amazon Web Services
(AWS), using Amazon Cognito7—a secure, frictionless customer identity and access management service that
scales to authenticate passengers with an access token. This feature signs in users by sending them an SMS
message through Amazon Simple Notification Service8

(Amazon SNS) with a one-time verification code. After

enhancing privacy and user control.

to residents, based on their biometric and demographic data.

allowing recipients to present them for verification without compromising data privacy.

this step, passengers use their Aadhaar—a 12-digit unique identification number—for an Aadhaar ID validation
process. They can do this either through direct Aadhaar validation or the Digi Locker Aadhaar e-Know Your

(e-KYC) document. Once the e-KYC document is received, the Digi Yatra App extracts the face

a serverless, event-driven compute service that manages the generation and verification of the user's verifiable
credentials.
The system operates as a paperless, contactless solution, where the passenger's face effectively becomes a
boarding pass. The selfie serves as the single token throughout the entire boarding journey. The Digi Yatra app
also integrates seamlessly with Digi Locker to fetch the Aadhaar e-KYC data. Only minimal and necessary data
is fetched from the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI)—image, name, gender, date of birth, and
masked Aadhaar10

. All collected data is encrypted and securely stored on the passenger's smartphone in a wallet
as verifiable credentials. After completing this step, travellers simply upload their boarding pass, either by

Digi Yatra Foundation
Digi Yatra Foundation (DYF) is a not-for-profit entity established under Section 8 of the Companies Act12, 2013,

airport operators, and government agencies. DYCE ensures interoperability across all participating airports while
maintaining stringent data privacy and security standards. It facilitates end-to-end passenger processing through
facial biometrics and enables a consistent, paperless travel experience across the country. DYF’s purpose is not to
generate revenue or profits; the sole motive is to provide a seamless travel experience. Founded in February 2019,

Airports Authority of India (AAI) (26% share) and the airports of Bengaluru, Cochin, Delhi, Mumbai, and
Hyderabad (14.8% share each). The foundation operates as a non-profit, with its shareholder airports covering
operational costs. A board of directors—comprising CEOs of public-private partnership airports and a
representative from AAI—oversees its governance. This board reports to the DYF board. The governance
framework follows policies set by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, including data privacy guidelines under the
Digital Personal Data Protection Act13. Regular audits ensure compliance.

The Background Work
"The idea of Digi Yatra was conceived as far back as 2015, when I was working at Bengaluru Airport. I was brainstorming
a passenger experience, where the passenger would pass through all the checkpoints at the airport terminal without being
stopped by anybody"
-Mr. Suresh Khadakbhavi, CEO, DYF
From the outset, the Digi Yatra initiative placed a strong emphasis on user-centric design. The goal was not only
to enhance efficiency and security but to deeply consider the real-life challenges faced by diverse categories of
travellers. During the development of the user journey, the team focused on creating an experience that addressed
the needs of the most vulnerable and convenience-sensitive users. One such example shared by Mr. Suresh
Khadakbhavi is:
"When we were defining the user flow, the fundamental reference point for the passenger that we staged was a woman who
was travelling with two young children. Managing two kids along with their identity cards, showing it to CISF and security
check-in was a major hassle. The vision of Digi Yatra was to enable such convenience that you don't have to bother about all
those things. You can just take care of your kids, mind your luggage and walkthrough"
Taking the idea forward, during 2017–18, the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) formed a Technical Working
Group comprising airport operators from Bengaluru International Airport Limited, Cochin International Airport
Limited, Delhi International Airport Limited, Mumbai International Airport Limited, and GMR Hyderabad
International Airport Limited, along with AAI, to develop a system leveraging technology to provide a seamless,
hassle-free experience for passengers from entry to the boarding gate. MoCA assigned Bengaluru Airport the
task of providing the technological solution for the same. This led to the conceptualization of Digi Yatra. Later,
under the aegis of MoCA, the non-profit organization—DYF was formed, consisting of AAI (26% share) and
airports from Bengaluru, Cochin, Delhi, Mumbai, and Hyderabad (14.8% share each), with the mandate to
oversee the implementation of Digi Yatra by providing technological solutions to airports. A senior official from
AAI acts as the Chairperson of the Foundation and holds decision-making authority.
Framing The Response
Empowered by the faith of the Ministry and entrusted with the responsibility, Mr. P.K. Thakur embarked on the
challenging journey to find a solution to the prevailing chaotic air travel situation. Banking on the work of the
Technical Working Committee, Mr. Thakur began the daunting task of policy formation and implementation.
Reflecting on his experience, he clearly outlines the challenges encountered in the following categories:
(I) Policy Formation
The first challenge he faced was regarding the type of data to be used for verifying and authenticating identity.
After days of deliberation and discussion, the stakeholders decided to use Aadhaar data for the authentication
process. Aadhaar, being widely available across age groups, was preferred over Driving License and Passport
data, as passports are available to only a small portion of the population.
Another moot point was whether to go for centralized or localized storage of biometric data. Initially, a
centralized data platform with MoCA for travel data storage was finalized. However, latency in fetching data
from centralized servers prompted the decision to shift to localized storage at the Airport Verifier Node.

Mr. Thakur further explains that, to access Aadhaar data, UIDAI initially suggested utilizing the DigiLocker
database for creating a unique passenger identity. The bottleneck in using DigiLocker was that not every
passenger had access to it. To resolve the issue, the decision was made to develop the Digi Yatra App, which
would act as an intermediary between passengers and UIDAI.
(II) Technological Integration
Airports in India vary widely in terms of infrastructure and technological readiness. While major airports like
Indira Gandhi International Airport (Delhi), Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (Mumbai), and
Kempegowda International Airport (Bengaluru) had the resources to adopt advanced systems, smaller regional
airports lagged behind. The AAI had to ensure that the Digi Yatra system could be seamlessly integrated across
all airports, regardless of their size or technological capabilities.
However, a one-size-fits-all approach was not practical in this case, and certain sections had to be customized
based on local requirements at each airport. Therefore, airport operators were given the autonomy to select the
hardware type and quantity of systems to be installed at their respective airports.
This non-uniform standardization has, at times, led to hardware malfunctions and frequent failures in the facial
identification process. These hardware issues caused problems such as tailgating14 and errors in biometric
detection. To address the facial recognition issue, the system lowered the threshold for identification purposes to
80 percent (from the original 100 percent biometric match with Aadhaar data).
Another significant operational hurdle involved managing passenger flow at biometric boarding gates. The
introduction of facial recognition systems brought with it new challenges, particularly related to crowd behaviour
and sequencing. As Suresh Khadakbhavi, CEO of DYF, pointed out, "Unstructured flow at the e-gates can lead to
multiple faces being presented at once, creating a challenge for the system to validate documents." The system, designed
to authenticate one face at a time, struggled to process multiple inputs when passengers rushed in clusters.
To address this, airport authorities gradually implemented procedural changes to guide passenger movement
more effectively. Passengers were instructed to pause at a designated point before entering the e-gate zone,
allowing the system to capture and verify their credentials one at a time. Reflecting on the improvement,
Khadakbhavi remarked, "Now, we have a systematic, methodical flow at every touchpoint." This structured approach
has played a critical role in improving accuracy, reducing errors, and streamlining the boarding process.

Civil Aviation Security15, airport operators, airlines, the Central Industrial Security Force16 and other security

integration process.
(V) Regulatory and Legal Challenges
The use of biometric data raised legal and regulatory questions, particularly concerning India's Personal Data
Protection Bill 17 and compliance with General Data Production Regulation18-like data security measures. The
government had to ensure that the system adhered to both national and international data protection standards
to prevent misuse. Regular Forensic Audits have been conducted by Ministry of Electronics and Information

(VI) Passenger’s Scepticism
The launch of Digi Yatra met with scepticism regarding data privacy and the potential misuse of personal
data. The first and foremost resistance that came from passengers was regarding the unauthorized use of
personal data by service providers (in this case, Airport Operators) for business purposes. As the concept
was new, there were concerns about how to install and use the app and the security of their personal
information. News of passenger data leaks from various national and international airlines on the dark web
added to the concern of data privacy and security. To handle the scepticism, the team conducted an extensive
advertisement campaign to raise awareness regarding Digi Yatra. Banners and electronic advertisements,
combined with a social media campaign regarding the data privacy of the Digi Yatra App, somewhat helped
in dealing with the issue.
In the whole system, the data is not stored on anyone's server or repository. That's how self-sovereign identity
works—there's no personally identifiable information on the distributed ledger. Mr. Khadakbhavi explained:
"What we do is create a signature. When we create the credential, a data string is generated, and a hash value21 is created.
We add that signature, and then the data is stored on your phone, in your wallet. When you travel, you upload your boarding
pass, and the name match happens. The two data points—your identity credential and boarding pass—are sent to the airport.
This is similar to the current process, where you scan your boarding card, which is manually verified with the airline's
departure control system... [but] we allow you to share this data in advance. The only additional data we collect is your face,
which is stored in the credential and sent to the airport's back-end system."
"Self-sovereign identity means you are in control of your data. Passengers' credentials, verified against their Aadhaar
information, are stored on their phones—not on Digi Yatra's servers. We consciously decided not to store any personally
identifiable information," he said, emphasizing a Privacy-by-Design 22 approach.
Mr. Khadakbhavi further goes on to explain the Privacy-by-Design approach and how it deals with privacy
concerns. The Privacy-by-Design principles and decentralized storage model significantly enhance security by
minimising the risk of data breaches, identity theft, or unauthorized access. Passengers retain their data solely on
their mobile devices, giving travellers full control over their credentials. Digi Yatra also follows a strict data
retention policy, wherein it automatically purges any information shared with the Airport Verifiers within 24
hours of the scheduled time of departure of the flight. Through these measures, Digi Yatra reinforces its
commitment to data privacy and minimal data exposure. This decentralized model makes large-scale data
breaches almost impossible. Mr. Khadakbhavi says:
"Imagine if I had a database of 5 million users. One hack could expose all that data. But with Digi Yatra, every passenger's
data is on their phone. To hack five million phones is five million times more difficult than hacking one database. What we're
trying to do is build a much more privacy-preserving ecosystem where data sharing is controlled by the passengers
themselves.”

To tackle scepticism surrounding data privacy and the misuse of personal data by operators for commercial

electronic advertisements in and around RGIA were used to dispel doubts and concerns of passengers.
Along with advertisements, 24 Digi Buddies were deployed at the entry gate to assist passengers onboarding

passengers through the Digi Yatra registration and boarding process. These individuals are well-versed with the
technology and application, acting as on-ground facilitators to ensure a smooth and informed transition for
travellers.
These 24 Digi Buddies, grouped into 4 teams of six each, provided round-the-clock assistance to passengers,
especially first-time users. At times, they had to demonstrate the process multiple times to a single passenger to
help them understand the entire procedure. Once grasped, it became a piece of cake for the passengers to board
using Digi Yatra. (Exhibit 7)
Another issue was the inertia of passengers towards adopting new technology. Many were comfortable
maintaining the status quo. For them, downloading the Digi Yatra application from the mobile play stores and

the Aadhaar server didn’t help either. Here, the patience and perseverance of Digi Buddies paid dividends, and
gradually, adoption of Digi Yatra began to rise. To further nudge passengers towards using Digi Yatra, various

acted as incentives, especially for first-timers, not only to adopt Digi Yatra but also to explore shopping while
waiting for their flights.
The technical bottleneck arising from some passengers not having smartphones was addressed by installing Digi
Yatra kiosks at entry gates. These kiosks allow passengers to use Digi Yatra services through mobile OTPs.
Overall, the collective efforts yielded strong results. Such was the success that, on some days during a month,
around 43 percent of identity check-ins were being done through Digi Yatra.

Case Study Title:
Reviving Ordnance Factory Balangir: Strategic
Shifts in Defence Manufacturing
Case Study Description: In a landmark reform, the Government of India restructured the century-old Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) into seven Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) on October 1, 2021, to tackle longstanding inefficiencies in defence production. Triggered by repeated CAG reports and expert committee recommendations, the move aimed to improve agility, accountability, and responsiveness to the Armed Forces’ needs. Within this transformation, the Chief General Manager of Ordnance Factory Balangir (OFBL), Shri P.K. Dash, faces a key challenge: enhancing output without compromising on quality or safety, requiring strategic, balanced decision-making.
Case Text:
Background of Erstwhile Ordnance Factory Board
The OFB has a deep historical legacy that dates back to colonial India, symbolizing the country's journey towards
self-reliance in defence manufacturing. Established to cater to the military needs of British India, OFB initially
comprised 18 factories before independence. Post-1947, the government expanded this network significantly,
adding 23 more factories to meet the growing defence requirements of independent India. These factories played
a pivotal role during major conflicts involving the Indian Armed Forces, contributing to the country's defence
preparedness and strengthening its industrial base for strategic production.
Under the erstwhile OFB, the factories were organized into functional groups based on their areas of
specialization. These included the Ammunition and Explosives group, which focused on producing a range of
ammunition and explosives; the Armoured Vehicles group, responsible for tanks, infantry combat vehicles, and
armoured platforms; the Weapons, Vehicles & Equipment group, which dealt with small arms, artillery, and
military vehicles; the Troop Comforts group, producing uniforms, tents, and protective clothing; the Materials
and Components group, specializing in manufacturing critical industrial components; the Optical and
Optoelectronics group, focusing on optical and night vision equipment; and the Parachute group, which catered
to parachutes and aerial delivery systems. Each group was vital in meeting the operational needs of the Indian
Armed Forces and other security organizations.
The product portfolio of these groups reflected the diversity and scale of India's defence manufacturing
capabilities. From battle tanks, artillery guns, and infantry combat vehicles to small arms, ammunition, and
explosives, the factories under OFB addressed the entire spectrum of land-based defence requirements. They also
produced specialized products such as parachutes, optical devices, and troop equipment like uniforms and boots.
However, as state-owned enterprises4

, OFB factories were not mandated to operate on a profit-maximization
basis, even in their non-defence segments. This lack of a profitability requirement influenced investment and
production decisions, often leading to inefficiencies or misaligned priorities compared to market-driven firms.
Consequently, their participation in civilian markets was sometimes seen as unfair competition by private sector
players, who had to operate under stricter commercial and financial constraints.
Despite its extensive infrastructure and diverse product range, the OFB faced several systemic challenges that
hindered its performance. Critics highlighted issues such as inefficient production processes, leading to delays

context, they are often fully or majority-owned by the central or state governments and may operate in strategic sectors such
as defence, energy, and transportation. Unlike private firms, these are not necessarily driven by profit maximization, as their
objectives often include social, strategic, or developmental goals.

Ordnance Factory Balangir’s Shift towards Efficient Production and Procurement

3
and cost overruns in delivering critical defence equipment. The inefficiency of production processes within the
OFB stemmed from multiple systemic and structural issues that hampered its operational effectiveness. One of
the primary concerns was the outdated manufacturing technology and equipment, which resulted in lower
productivity and higher defect rates. Despite having a vast infrastructure, many factories relied on legacy systems
largely due to chronic underinvestment in modernization by the OFB, which prioritized immediate operational
needs over long-term capacity upgrades. The bureaucratic nature of decision-making also led to delays in
adopting new technologies and implementing process improvements. The organization's rigid hierarchical
structure and lack of financial autonomy manifested in the requirement to obtain Ministry of Defence approval
for large capital expenditures and the involvement of the Defence Accounts Department5

for financial
concurrence in routine procurement decisions, impeded its ability to respond swiftly to technological
advancements and market dynamics.
The rigid procurement policies and lack of flexibility in sourcing raw materials further contributed to
inefficiencies, as factories were often constrained by lengthy approval processes and limited vendor options. A
pattern was observed across several OFB factories, where despite having substantial annual procurement
budgets, a significant proportion of components and raw materials had to be sourced from outside their
respective states. This was primarily due to the lack of adequately equipped local vendors capable of meeting the
stringent quality, certification, and technological standards required for defence manufacturing. As a result,
factories remained heavily dependent on a small number of approved suppliers located in select industrial hubs,
limiting competition, increasing logistical complexity, and reducing flexibility in procurement planning.
Workforce-related issues also played a role, with employees operating under government service conditions such
as fixed tenure, time-bound promotions, and standardized pay scales, regardless of individual performance. This
system, unlike private-sector norms, discouraged accountability, created resistance to change, and offered few
incentives for innovation or productivity gains. There were also concerns about the quality and reliability of
certain products, which did not consistently meet the evolving standards required by the armed forces.
Furthermore, the absence of a competitive environment within the OFB and lack of external competition led to
complacency, affecting innovation and overall productivity. For instance, in many product categories, private
sector players were either barred due to strategic restrictions (e.g., small arms and ammunition were long
reserved for public sector production) or deterred by procedural hurdles and lack of level playing field in defence

undermining its overall productivity.
The OFB was not an absolute monopoly but had a dominant position in several defence supplies, particularly in
ammunition, small arms, and certain armoured vehicles. While it was the primary supplier for many critical
defence goods, competition existed in specific areas from public-sector undertakings like Bharat Electronics

procure certain high-tech equipment from foreign suppliers when OFB’s products did not meet modern
standards. Despite this, OFB enjoyed a largely protected market with guaranteed government orders, reducing
competitive pressure to improve efficiency and innovation. This lack of external competition led to complacency,
affecting product quality and responsiveness to technological advancements, ultimately highlighting the need
for defence manufacturing reforms.

These persistent issues underscored the need for comprehensive reforms to revitalize India's defence
manufacturing sector. In a landmark reform, the Government of India reorganized the OFB into seven
independent DPSUs to enhance efficiency, accountability, and global competitiveness in defence production.
Effective October 1, 2021, the seven new DPSUs were aligned with the legacy groups of OFB: Munitions India
Limited for ammunition and explosives, Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited for armoured vehicles, Advanced
Weapons and Equipment India Limited for weaponry, Troop Comforts Limited for troop equipment, Yantra
India Limited for industrial components, India Optel Limited for optoelectronics, and Gliders India Limited for
parachutes and aerial delivery systems. Ordnance Factory Balangir (OFBL) is one of the factories under Munitions
India Limited.
The corporatization of the OFB was a crucial step in advancing the "Atmanirbhar Bharat" (Self-Reliant India)
initiative, aimed at making India self-reliant in defence manufacturing. This was significant step towards
addressing the long-standing inefficiencies within the organization. The transformation aimed to create a more
accountable and performance-oriented environment, where each of the newly formed entities could operate with
greater autonomy and flexibility.

About Ordnance Factory Balangir
The Ordnance Factory Balangir (OFBL) was situated in Badmal, a remote location 44 km from Balangir, a town
in western Odisha renowned for its rich cultural heritage, temples, and tribal traditions. Spanning 11,971.03 acres,
the facility comprised both residential estates and production units. The nearest town, Titlagarh, lied 20 km away,
with connectivity to the rest of India facilitated by a small railway station at Badmal, along with larger stations
at Titlagarh and Balangir. The closest airports were Jharsuguda (210 km) and Raipur (220 km). Established as
India’s 39th Ordnance Factory, its foundation stone was laid by Late Smt. Indira Gandhi on October 29, 1984.
Initially authorised for ₹610.11 crores ($160.55 million), the project commenced operations in 1997-98 with an
actual expenditure of ₹544.95 crores ($143.41 million)

Key Issues Affecting Production Output
A) Manpower Problems
The manpower at OFBL consist of officers (Group A11 and Group B12), staff and workmen (industrial employees).
The Group A form the top and senior management of the factory. The Group B consists of junior works managers
and chargemen and form the middle and junior management levels of the factory. The Non-industrial
employees13 are involved in support activities. The industrial employees14 are the main production workers and
are involved in production activities.
OFBL being a remote location, had a dearth of qualified and skilled manpower. The recruitment process is
stringent with certain mandatory conditions like Group A are selected only through Union Public Service
Commission15 – civil services, and Engineering services examination. The industrial workers handling explosives
must have attendant operator of chemical plant qualification (Exhibit 3). Also, being a hard station, postings
always remained contentious with transfer policy rarely being followed. When a tenure of 5 years was mandated
for Group A officers, many continue to be kept here for much longer durations. Also, there was dearth of senior
officers at this location and mostly junior officers fresh out of training were posted here to keep the factory
running. A Group A officer joins at the junior time scale16 either through direct recruitment of UPSC civil services
or engineering services, or is promoted into Group A from Group B level and was designated as assistant works
manager17. The hierarchy then ran from junior time scale to senior time scale or works manager to – senior time
scale non-functional (deputy general manager)18 to junior administrative grade or joint general manager to senior
administrative grade or additional general manager/general manager. The senior-most Administrative Grade
Level officer headed the factory. Lack of transparency in transfers and low qualification levels amongst junior
staff resulted in demotivation amongst the officers. There has been no recruitment after corporatization as HR
policy is still under finalization.

A) Machinery Issues
Another issue that plagued the factory was the old machinery. Whenever any machine broke down, it was very
difficult to get spare parts. Many original equipment manufacturers’ (OEMs)19 of the machines, some of which
were purchased when the factory was originally started in the year 1998 about 27 years ago, have updated the
software, that resulted in incompatibility with newer software updates, modern control systems, and replacement
parts. Since many OEMs had upgraded their technology, the factory’s older machines could no longer integrate
with newer digital systems, making repairs and automation difficult.
Such machines also required manual handling by workers which result in fatigue and tiredness. Consequently,
the labour productivity was also affected. Workers performance at OFBL was measured using piece work
profit20. Each task is assigned a standard time allowance through meticulous time and motion studies. If a worker
completes a task in less time than the standard, they earn a profit proportional to the time saved. This profit is
expressed as a percentage and added to their base wages, serving as a motivation for increased efficiency. Piece
workers are paid based on their output, recorded in piece work cards.
The workers failed to meet the PW criteria that required them to work overtime. The failure to meet PW criteria
at OFBL or similar factories was despite working overtime, primarily due to systemic and logistical issues,
resulting from machine breakdowns and many a time due to non-availability of raw materials in the shop floor.
Any work done under proper orders outside the normal working hours or on a sunday or a paid holiday is
treated as overtime. For work beyond 44 3⁄4 hours per week, overtime allowance was paid. The units in the factory
had low piecework profits as output was lower than estimated time decided by time and motion studies and
overtime was required to compensate and maintain production (Exhibit 4 shows the PW Profit of the factory
from 2017 till 2024).
B) Other Issues
Research & Development was also practically non-existent in the factory with very few innovations either in new
product development or improvements in existing products. However, recently 8 patents have been granted in
year 2023-24 for patents filed earlier for innovation in work done in the factory since its inception.
Safety factors that were required to be maintained at OFBL, being an explosive filling ammunition factory, also
contribute to loss of productivity and efficiency. The process safety parameters21 required workers to wear
personal protective equipment’s (PPEs)22 such as masks, gloves, safety shoes and helmets. Violation of these
standards results in chemical hazards. As workers are required to wear this equipment continuously while
working on a process, the result is excessive exertion and workers requiring breaks, which lowers their actual
working time.

C) Input Material Non-Availability
A key factor contributing to OFBL's inability to meet production targets was the delayed availability of quality
raw materials. Each OFBL product comprised multiple sub-parts, typically requiring 40-60 components.
Effectively managing such a vast array of raw materials necessitated a robust and diverse vendor base to ensure
a steady and reliable supply chain.
In a government department, the procurement system was typically intricate, governed by rigid procedures and
stringent compliance requirements at every stage. At OFBL, the procurement process followed the L-1 system,
wherein the vendor submitting the lowest bid was awarded the contract, provided they met the minimum
technical specifications. This cost-centric approach applied to all procurement transactions, with an additional
requirement for tenders when the value of a single order exceeded a certain threshold value. For such
procurements, a Tender Enquiry was issued, which could take one of two forms. If there were already recognized
and approved vendors for the required item, the factory issued a Limited Tender Enquiry, inviting bids only
from these pre-qualified suppliers. Conversely, if no pre-approved vendors existed, a source development open
tender enquiry was floated, allowing a broader range of suppliers to compete. However, in both cases, the L-1
system encouraged vendors to quote the lowest possible price to secure the contract, sometimes at the cost of
long-term feasibility. Since the contract execution period typically ranged from 6 to 12 months, vendors often
struggled to fulfil their commitments if there was even a slight increase in raw material costs over time.
This rigid price-based selection mechanism, while ensuring initial cost efficiency, often led to supply chain
disruptions, as vendors found it financially unviable to deliver at the agreed-upon rates. Consequently, delays,
contractual defaults, and procurement inefficiencies became recurring challenges within the system.
OFBL operated with a relatively limited vendor base, where suppliers often lacked a strong commitment to
quality. Additionally, the procurement manual did not specify a structured process for ancillary development or
long-term supplier onboarding, restricting efforts to expand and strengthen the vendor ecosystem. Ancillary
development referred to the strategic initiative of nurturing and supporting small or medium-sized enterprises
to become reliable suppliers or vendors for a larger organization. These ancillary suppliers received technical
assistance, financial support or skill training to meet the quality and production standards required by the parent
organization. At OFBL, the absence of a structured ancillary development program meant that smaller vendors
were not actively guided or supported to improve their quality and production capabilities. Without structured
support, suppliers might have struggled to meet the required standards, leading to quality and supply chain
inefficiencies.
Long-term supplier onboarding was a structured process of selecting, evaluating, and integrating new suppliers
into an organization's supply chain with a focus on long-term collaboration. Unlike short-term procurement
practices that relied solely on competitive bidding, long-term onboarding included assessing supplier capabilities
beyond just price competitiveness; providing them with guidelines, training, and support to meet required
quality standards; and entering into longer-term contracts or partnerships to encourage investments in
technology, process improvement, and capacity expansion. The absence of a long-term vendor development
framework, including investments and capacity-building support, further compounded the issue, as orders were
mandated to be placed solely through competitive bidding.
The procurement process at OFBL was highly complex and multi-staged, leading to significant delays in
finalizing supply orders. From the initial generation of material requirements to the actual receipt of supplies,
the process was time-consuming, often extending up to 150 days. The procurement cycle began with the creation
of the Store Holder’s Inability Sheet23, based on which tenders were floated and bids invited. After submission,
the technical bids were evaluated for compliance with specifications, and only those meeting the criteria
advanced to the price bid stage. The contract was awarded to the lowest-priced technically qualified bidder.
Further delays arose due to vendor lead times for delivery. Compounding the challenge, the Army occasionally

D) Eliminating Sub-Par Vendors
Enforcing penalties such as Earnest Money Deposit24 or Performance Security Deposit25 forfeiture, debarment
and other punitive measures is often difficult due to several systemic, procedural, and regulatory constraints.
OFBL products involved specialized items and worked with a pool of suppliers that are selected through multiple
stages and new vendors are reluctant to be onboarded due to L1 system and initial setup costs required to start
component production. If stringent penalties are imposed frequently, vendors may become reluctant to
participate in future tenders, reducing competition. In such cases of few approved vendors, blacklisting or
debarment could further shrink the supplier base, making procurement even more challenging. Even when
alternative vendors exist, the time required to qualify and onboard new suppliers through the Source
Development Open Tender Enquiry26 process can be long, causing procurement delays.
Procurement at OFBL is bound by the General Financial Rules27, Manual for Procurement of Goods and
Services28, and guidelines from entities like Central Vigilance Commission29. Any penalty enforcement must
strictly adhere to these regulations, making the process legally intricate. Debarment or forfeiture of security
deposits often requires multiple levels of administrative approvals, show-cause notices, hearings, and
justifications, making it a lengthy process. Vendors can legally challenge penalties in courts or administrative
tribunals, leading to prolonged disputes that delay procurement even further.
Procurement officers also hesitate to enforce strict penalties due to the risk of facing vigilance inquiries or
departmental audits, as stringent actions against vendors can attract scrutiny from oversight agencies.
Government officials often operate under the fear of post-facto investigations by agencies like the CVC or CAG.
If a penalty is later deemed unfair or excessive, the responsible officers may be held accountable. Apart from fear
of such issues, decision-making in government setups being hierarchical and involving multiple layers of
approval, also make swift action difficult. Vendors at OFBL also operate on thin margins under the L-1 system,
and any increase in raw material costs can make contract execution unviable. Forfeiting their deposits might force
them into financial distress, leading to long-term vendor attrition. The system of vendor rating was also not
developed and mature, so that subpar vendors could be eliminated from the system. However, vendors not
performing had been debarred in the past.

Impact of Corporatization
Many of these challenges remained after the transition from a government department to a corporate entity. The
factory still had to navigate a complex landscape of regulatory requirements, legacy systems, and entrenched
practices. The shift required a cultural transformation, with a focus on efficiency, accountability, and
performance. The factory management had to balance the need for immediate improvements with the long-term
goal of building a sustainable and resilient production system. Chief General Manager of OFBL, Shri P.K. Dash
noted a critical issue: “There is a depletion of skilled manpower after corporatization, as no recruitment is taking place,”
which is impacting productivity and knowledge continuity on the shop floor.
The corporatization aimed to streamline operations by removing certain bottlenecks. For instance, the finance
function, which refers to managing all financial activities of the factory, including budgeting, expenditure
approvals, and fund allocation, earlier handled by the defence accounts department, was transferred to the
factory to speed up decision-making. This empowered factory management to control finances directly, enabling
quicker and more efficient operations. A new procurement manual was also introduced. These changes were
intended to empower the factory management, giving them greater control over financial and procurement
decisions. Now with all members of TPC from within the factory, decision making became faster and more
efficient. A new procurement manual was designed by Munitions India Limite to simplify and expedite the
procurement process, reducing delays and ensuring the timely availability of quality materials. However. the
manual borrowed most of its provisions from the procurement manual of erstwhile OFB.
The quality inspection process has been further streamlined and now SQAE inspection is being done only after
packing. SQAE draws sample of assembled ammunition after the packing process has been completed and does
a final inspection to pass or reject the ammunition. To address concerns around product quality, inspection
mechanisms have been strengthened. As per chief general manager of OFBL, Shri P.K. Dash - “Inspection is now
strict but fair, and where defect trends are noticed, joint inspections are being carried out with increased sample sizes.” For
exports, self-certification by factory is the only required criteria resulting in considerable savings in time and costs
as well as enhanced accountability. However, although customer complaints have declined, they are still received
with defective ammunitions being backloaded by army depots for reissue, particularly old ammunition which

Choices and Priorities Post-Corporatization
During a high-level strategic discussion at OFBL, factory leadership reviewed several bottlenecks affecting
output. While challenges like manpower constraints and outdated equipment were on the radar, the most
pressing concern was ensuring the timely availability of quality raw materials, as procurement delays were
undermining productivity. Management believed that long-term supply chain reliability could be improved by
shifting from the rigid L-1 system to a more strategic vendor management approach. However, is such a shift
feasible within the current government procurement framework? Could pilot projects, revised vendor evaluation
metrics, or local sourcing flexibility offer a way forward? Could steps like creating pre-qualified vendor panels,
promoting rate contracts, or leveraging GeM more flexibly offer practical interim solutions?
Similarly, what factory-level steps could be taken to initiate modernization or ease manpower shortages,
especially when formal policy changes must come from the corporate headquarters? How can the factory build
a strong case to MIL headquarters for phased modernization support, and what data should be collected to justify
the investment? Whether the factory should recommend relaxed recruitment norms or propose corporate-level
transfer policy reforms for long-term sustainability. What recommendations should the factory submit to MIL to
start addressing these interlinked issues without losing momentum? These deliberations highlighted the need
for balancing urgent operational fixes with broader systemic reforms, without allowing these concerns to divert
focus from the factory’s core mandate of timely and quality production.

Case Study Description: PARAM Shavak is an indigenous high-performance computing (HPC) desktop system developed under the National Supercomputing Mission by CDAC, MeitY, and VVDN Technologies. Powered by Rudra, it represents a major step forward in making advanced supercomputing accessible to academic and research institutions across India. Compact, energy-efficient, and cost-effective, PARAM Shavak enables institutions with limited resources to undertake cutting-edge research. By democratizing access to HPC, it helps overcome challenges such as low awareness, funding limitations, and a shortage of skilled professionals. This case study explores the system’s development, implementation challenges, and its contribution to strengthening India’s research ecosystem and advancing digital transformation.

This case study traces the transformative journey of PARAM Shavak—from its ideation and design to
development and deployment—highlighting the strategic role of indigenous HPC technologies in strengthening
national capabilities. It underscores how PARAM Shavak empowers India’s scientific and academic communities
of Tier–II and Tier-III cities to address complex challenges in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence,
machine learning, and big data analytics, thereby contributing to the broader agenda of technological self-reliance
and national development.

Senior scientists Smt. Sunita Verma5 and Dr Prashant Dinde,6 present at the pivotal meeting in January 2017,
nodded in agreement with Dr Saraswat’s call for India to achieve self-reliance in HPC. They recognised that
supercomputing systems were essential to computational science, enabling the processing and analysis of vast

Rudra is Born
From 2018 to 2020, MeitY and the C-DAC, Pune, put in intense research and development efforts to foster
homegrown HPC technologies under the aegis of the National Supercomputing Mission (NSM) of India.7 A
foundational outcome of these intensive efforts was the ideation of the motherboard, Rudra. Building upon this
innovation, India’s first native HPC server was developed using the Rudra architecture. Remarkably, within just
one year, from 2021 to 2022, approximately 6000 rack-mounted Rudra servers were designed, manufactured, and

Affordable HPC-in-a-Box Solution: In October 2022, during the National SemiCon-2

power enabled by NSM to fuel our AI research, but the prevailing costs and requirements of HPC systems are
out-of-reach for our smaller institutes’, particularly situated in Tier-II and Tier-III cities.
This appeal highlighted a critical and previously underrepresented computing requirement—the demand for
‘affordable and easily accessible HPC solutions’ for researchers in Tier-II, Tier-III and remote academic institutes.
The MeitY and C-DAC delegation took note of this challenge, recognising it as a new dimension of India’s HPC
roadmap—one which would undoubtedly have to be addressed through development of indigenous systems.
From October 2023 onwards, MeitY, C-DAC, and VVDN Technologies, under the visionary leadership of Dr
Saraswat, spearheaded a collaborative effort to redefine India’s HPC capabilities to make it more accessible,
manageable, and affordable for academic institutes located across the country. These joint efforts led to the birth
of India’s first indigenous All-in-One HPC-in-a-Box solution, powered by the Rudra motherboard. This compact,
self-contained supercomputing solution was aptly re-christened ‘PARAM Shavak’ powered by Rudra and
successfully demonstrated before the NSM’s Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) on January 10, 2024. This
PARAM Shavak exemplifies a holistic approach to the development of indigenous HPC technology.

India launched its HPC endeavours in 2015, under the NSM, jointly led by the Government of India's Department

Alignment with Global and National Development Goals
Through its ability to address various complex governance and scientific challenges, PARAM Shavak aligned
with several United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (UN-SDGs) such as SDG-4 (Quality Education),
SDG-7 (Affordable & Clean Energy), SDG-9 (Industry, Innovation & Infrastructure), SDG-11 (Sustainable Cities

In the face of these complex technology, regulatory, and infrastructural challenges, the successful design,

collaborative approach, that now stand as ‘best practices and a model for indigenous technology development in

Birth of HPC Lion Cub
PARAM Shavak represents a landmark achievement in India’s quest for technological self-reliance. The transition
from manufacturing PARAM Shavaks with foreign components—amidst volatile geopolitical conditions and the
risk of external sanctions—to a path of self-reliance was achieved by overcoming complex design, regulatory,
and user-adoption challenges through strategic partnerships, innovation, and inclusive capacity-building efforts.

The project not only delivered a world-class indigenous HPC desktop but also set a precedent for future public-
private collaborations in advanced technology domains and the birth of an exclusive HPC Lion Cub. Up to March

2025, a demand for 80 PARAM Shavaks had been raised; 50 of which were supplied to academic institutions under
AICTE, and 30 were provided to research laboratories and private organisations.

As India looks toward a future defined by AI, semiconductors, and quantum computing, PARAM Shavak
powered by Rudra provides the foundational infrastructure to ensure inclusive, sustainable, and self-reliant
growth. Some of the cornerstones of its success story, worth emulating across India are as follows:

experienced leadership and sustained continuity of a strong technical team in ensuring the success of a
complex national project. The successful design of the indigenous avatar of the ‘HPC-in-a-desktop’
system was inspired by leaders like Dr Saraswat, who championed this ‘Make-in-India' vision during
his long DRDO tenure, ‘where home-grown technologies were always the first choice.’ Additionally, the

Case Study Title:
Bridging the Last Mile: Nidhi Aapke Nikat 2.0
and the Quest for Human Centric Governance
Case Study Description: This case explores how the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation transformed service delivery through Nidhi Aapke Nikat 2.0, a decentralised, human-centred outreach model that brings services to remote districts, resolves grievances on the spot, and builds trust through direct engagement. As the programme effectively reaches citizens often excluded from digital reforms, EPFO now faces a strategic challenge: sustaining this high-touch model while meeting pressures for digital scale, automation, and cost efficiency. The case highlights the governance trade-offs between AI-enabled systems and personalised interfaces to ensure inclusion.
Case Text:
Introduction
‘Recall the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen,’ said Mahatma Gandhi, urging public
servants to use the welfare of the most vulnerable as a moral benchmark for every policy decision. This talisman
is more than ethical advice—it is a call to reimagine governance not as a transaction, but as a relationship between
the state and the citizen.
For the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO)1

, one of the world’s largest social security institutions,
this principle gained renewed importance as the organisation faced rising public grievances, low field visibility,
and limited digital access in underserved regions. EPFO had made progress in automation and expanding its
service reach, yet many citizens continued to view it as a distant institution—effective in statutory work but less
connected with people during service delivery. As a result, a large segment of end-beneficiaries, particularly
digitally-challenged blue-collar workers, had not fully experienced the benefits of these improvements.
This perceived institutional disconnect emerged at a time when India was advancing its Digital India vision,
aiming to streamline government services through digital platforms. However, the simultaneous need for human

In 2023, EPFO launched Nidhi Aapke Nikat 2.0 (NAN 2.0)—a bold experiment in citizen-centric governance that

The Institutional Landscape: EPFO’s Role in India’s Social Security Framework
EPFO was one of the largest social security institutions in the world. Established in 1952, it operated as a statutory
body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, Government of India. Its core mandate was to provide
retirement income and social protection to India’s formal workforce through the administration of three flagship
schemes: the Employees’ Provident Fund Scheme2

, Employees’ Pension Scheme3 and Employees’ Deposit Linked

Insurance Scheme4

As of March 2025, EPFO managed over 320 million accounts, with a corpus exceeding ₹28 lakh crore (approx.
$330 billion USD), covering workers from more than one million establishments across sectors, served more than
80 lakh (8 million) pensioners (much more than all central government pensioners in India). During financial year
2024-25, it settled more than 6 crore (60 million) provident fund (PF) withdrawal/pension related claims. Its
governance was overseen by a tripartite Central Board of Trustees, comprising representatives from employers,
employees, and the government, ensuring participatory and representative oversight.
EPFO had been a pioneer in the digital transformation of service delivery, integrating Aadhaar-based
authentication, real-time claim settlement, and mobile-enabled grievance portals via the e-Sewa platform,
UMANG app, and DigiLocker linkage. This combination of institutional scale, legal mandate, and evolving
digital architecture made EPFO a critical anchor in India’s broader welfare and labour protection ecosystem.
Historical Evolution – From Bhavishya Nidhi Adalat to Nidhi Aapke Nikat 2.0
For decades, the EPFO had operated primarily through regional and sub-regional offices, and while it managed
an enormous volume of social security funds and claims, its interface with stakeholders remained distant, formal,
and highly procedural. Beneficiaries who encountered problems with Aadhaar mismatches, name discrepancies,
pension delays, or employer defaults often faced long delays and minimal clarity on resolution pathways. The
experience was especially challenging for rural, tribal, or semi-literate workers, who often found the system
complex and not easily navigable.
In response to growing feedback and the government’s broader emphasis on 'citizen-centric governance,' EPFO
revamped its monthly interaction program with its members ‘Bhavishya Nidhi Adalat’ in 2015, marking the
beginning of the first version of Nidhi Aapke Nikat (NAN). The concept was straightforward: every regional office
would host a monthly public meeting where stakeholders could present their grievances directly to EPFO
officials. These sessions brought a degree of visibility and accountability to the organisation, breaking through

Delivery Challenges
The first-generation NAN remained primarily an urban and office-based platform, accessible mainly to those
who lived near regional centres or could afford to travel. It did not systematically cover districts without an EPFO
office, leaving vast areas—often inhabited by vulnerable populations—outside its purview. Furthermore, it was
mostly reactive in approach. Stakeholders had to be aware of their rights, prepare formal complaints in advance,
and attend the hearing on their own initiative. For many informal sector workers, this was an unrealistic
expectation. The outreach rarely included education about entitlements, and language barriers and digital
illiteracy often compounded the problem.
In terms of service delivery, the earlier version of NAN was still dependent on manual processes, paper files, and
centralised escalation mechanisms. This meant that even when grievances were acknowledged, they were not
always resolved on-site. Field officers at times operated with limited decision-making authority or access to
digital tools necessary for on-the-spot resolution. Over time, the outreach began to resemble a symbolic grievance
window rather than a transformative interface.
Recognising these systemic shortcomings, and driven by the broader administrative ethos of Ease of Living, Ease
of doing Business and Minimum Government, Maximum Governance, the EPFO leadership began work on a
structural overhaul. The need for a high-impact, scalable, and equitable delivery mechanism was more urgent
than ever. Many of India’s 500+ districts without a full EPFO presence remained unreached, even as the demand
for social security awareness grew in a post-pandemic labour economy.
This internal policy review culminated in the launch of Nidhi Aapke Nikat 2.0 (NAN 2.0) in January 2023,
envisioned as a mass outreach mechanism that would decentralise EPFO’s services down to the district level on
a uniform, recurring basis. The model drew lessons not only from the limitations of earlier grievance mechanisms
but also from the successes of public-facing initiatives such as the Jan Abhiyan and the Aspirational District
Programme. It was built around a monthly calendar, with each district holding a full-day camp on the 27th of
every month, ensuring predictability and public awareness. The annexure 1 depicts timeline of NAN Evolution
(2015–2023).
Unlike its predecessor, NAN 2.0 was designed to be proactive, educational, and participatory. It emphasised not
only grievance handling but also stakeholder empowerment, convergence with other labour institutions such as
the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (ESIC), and on-the-spot service delivery. Most importantly, it

represented a cultural shift within EPFO—from a file-based administrative mindset to a field-oriented, citizen-
first approach.

By establishing a uniform delivery framework—complete with district nodal officers, reporting formats, digital
kiosks, and multilingual public communication— EPFO sought to evolve a previously decentralised interface
into a more cohesive model of participatory governance.
Operational Architecture of Monthly Outreach: From Planning to Field Execution
The launch of NAN 2.0 in January 2023 marked a significant strategic shift in how the EPFO approached its core
mission—ensuring social security for millions of Indian workers. Rather than serving as a reactive grievance
forum, NAN 2.0 was conceived as a district-level public interface platform, combining service delivery including
handholding, awareness and redressal in a single, predictable, and inclusive format. The program’s design

At the heart of NAN 2.0 lied a carefully designed monthly outreach architecture. On the 27th day of every month,
EPFO would hold a simultaneous camp in each district of India, including those without a permanent EPFO
office. These camps would function as mobile service centres—delivering critical services, resolving grievances

Infrastructure for these camps was largely mobilised through local convergence—including use of district

associations. Camps often included help desks, biometric-enabled Aadhaar verification units, claim-processing
counters, and pension grievance corners. The most common grievances included KYC-Aadhaar mismatches,
pending pension claims, employer contribution delays, and Universal Account Number activation issues.
Importantly, this decentralised, face-to-face model shifted a significant portion of the digital grievance burden—
previously routed via e-Sewa portals—into the physical domain, allowing for more empathetic, immediate

architecture over time.
In remote locations such as tribal districts in Jharkhand or hilly regions of Uttarakhand, local vernacular signage
and informal social networks became critical tools of outreach. Officers innovated within limited means—
sometimes preparing hand-written banners or conducting camps under trees—to ensure last-mile delivery was
not a rhetorical promise, but a lived reality.

Crucially, NAN 2.0 was designed not only as a grievance platform but also as an educational and empowerment

Invitations were extended to employer bodies, trade unions, women’s SHGs, pensioners’ forums, and district

From January 2023 to March 2025, approx. 18,000 district-level camps were conducted under NAN 2.0, with more

public institutions among workers, especially those in India’s less developed regions.
Perhaps one of the most notable operational shifts was the convergence achieved through the inclusion of
Employees’ State Insurance Corporation, under the Ministry of Labour’s broader labour welfare umbrella. In
many districts, NAN 2.0 became a one-stop convergence point where social security issues—spanning health,
pensions, insurance, and digital access—were handled collectively. This kind of cross-departmental synergy was
often cited as a benchmark for effective federal governance.

NAN 2.0, in its short operational life, touched hundreds of thousands of lives across India. For many, it

dignity.
One such example was Ramesh Munda, a 62-year-old retired factory worker from Khunti district in Jharkhand,

in a cement factory on the outskirts of Ranchi, contributing regularly to the EPF. However, after retirement, he

in the EPFO database. Attempts to resolve the issue were futile. The nearest EPFO office was over 125 miles (200
kilometres) away, and the cost and physical toll of multiple trips were beyond his means.

morning, carrying a plastic folder filled with old salary slips, photocopies of IDs, and a handwritten grievance
note. Within two hours, his documents were verified, the discrepancy corrected, and his digital life certificate
submitted. On the same day, he received confirmation that his pension application had been reprocessed. For
Ramesh, this was not just a financial solution—it was an institutional acknowledgment of his working life. “Pehli
baar laga sarkar sun rahi hai” (For the first time, it felt like the government was listening), he said.
In the same district, a local employer association representing small-scale garment units had previously struggled
to get their workers enrolled in EPFO due to procedural delays and limited outreach. During the NAN 2.0 event,
they brought a list of unregistered employees, many of whom were first-time formal workers. EPFO staff guided
them through UAN creation, Aadhaar linkage, and nomination processes. By the end of the day, it paved way
for hundreds of new workers being brought into the social security fold—marking a meaningful step toward
encouraging formal employment within predominantly informal sectors.

In Namsai, Arunachal Pradesh, where mobile connectivity remained patchy and distances from district
