Achievements and Outcomes
Over a brief operational period, NAN 2.0 demonstrated how public institutions can deliver impactful, inclusive,
and responsive governance when anchored in field realities. The initiative, which began as a response to
persistent stakeholder dissatisfaction, has now become a recognised national model for decentralised service
delivery in the social security domain.
Between January 2023 and March 2025, EPFO conducted approx. 18,000 outreach camps across districts of India—
many of which had previously seen minimal or no direct EPFO engagement. These monthly events witnessed
participation from more than 586,000 individuals, spanning a wide range of stakeholders: factory workers,
pensioners, construction labourers, contractual employees, employers, trade union representatives, and members
of civil society. This figure represents not just footfall, but the emergence of trust-based relationships between
citizens and an institution often perceived as distant and rigid.
One of the most significant quantitative outcomes has been in the area of grievance redressal. Across these camps,
EPFO received approximately 240,000 grievances, with a remarkable 85 percent grievances resolved on-the-spot,
thanks to the presence of empowered field staff, digital tools, and simplified protocols. In many cases, resolutions
were delivered in real time—such as Aadhaar linkage updates, digital life certificate processing, or UAN
activation. The remaining cases were typically resolved within days through follow-up from the concerned field
office. This marked a dramatic shift from previous experiences where grievances remained unresolved for weeks
or even months, often lost in hierarchical channels.
Another notable achievement was the increase in social security coverage, particularly in informal and
transitional labour markets. Employers in sectors such as garments, retail, manufacturing, and construction
reported better enrolment figures as a direct result of participation in NAN 2.0. Thousands of first-time workers
were enrolled in the EPFO system through walk-in registration facilitated by the camps. For workers, this
translated into financial security, pension eligibility, and insurance coverage—a crucial shift from informal
employment to formal benefits.
The initiative also made substantial gains in terms of awareness generation and digital empowerment. In every
district, stakeholders were exposed to simplified demonstrations of key services—how to download a passbook,
update nominations, submit life certificates digitally, or raise queries through the grievance portal. Pensioners,
many of whom had relied on middleman or agents in the past, were educated about free online services now
available through mobile phones or Common Service Centres. In tribal and rural districts, volunteers and EPFO
staff used regional languages and audio-visual tools to overcome literacy and technology barriers. As a result,
EPFO observed an uptick in voluntary compliance and a reduction in procedural errors in claims filed after NAN
events.
Collaboration emerged as a key institutional outcome. Through NAN 2.0, EPFO developed closer coordination
with district administrations, labour departments, and the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (ESIC). In
many camps, joint desks were set up where grievances related to health insurance and employment benefits
could be resolved together. This convergence model demonstrated how institutional silos could be bridged to
provide citizen-centric, integrated services at the grassroots level. The success of such coordination was
particularly evident in remote regions like Garchiroli in Maharashtra and Namsai in Arunachal Pradesh, where
infrastructure constraints had previously blocked access to any direct social security engagement.
Perhaps the most meaningful achievement, however, lies in the shift in institutional culture within EPFO itself.
Field officials who were once confined to administrative tasks in regional offices now had a direct interface with

Challenges and Limitations
While NAN 2.0 has made significant strides in improving the outreach and responsiveness of the EPFO, the
program also exposes several structural and systemic challenges that remain unresolved. These limitations are
important to understand—not as criticisms of the initiative, but as guideposts for institutional reform, resource
planning, and future design choices.
Logistical Coordination
One of the foremost challenges lied in logistical coordination, particularly in remote and infrastructure-deficient
districts. Organising a full-fledged monthly outreach in over 700 districts strained existing administrative
bandwidth—requiring not only infrastructure readiness but inter-agency coordination in regions often lacking
both.
In regions with poor road access, frequent power outages, or lack of administrative bandwidth, the delivery of
services was often delayed or restricted. EPFO’s ability to deploy laptops, biometric devices, and digital service
kiosks consistently each month across 700+ districts demanded a scale of logistical reliability that stretched
current institutional capacities.
Human Resource Limitations
A second constraint stemmed from human resource limitations. Many regional and district-level EPFO offices
operated with a lean staff. Besides many such officials who were deputed for the purpose were neither
adequately equipped nor trained to handle the multifaceted role that this initiative demands. Assigning officials
to district camps every month not only increased their workload but often diverted attention from regular office
functions. In several districts, the designated district nodal officers reported difficulty in conducting effective
stakeholder segmentation or awareness campaigns due to the sheer breadth of responsibilities they manage. In
high-demand districts, limited personnel often resulted in rushed delivery, queues, or unresolved cases—
undermining the promise of timely service.
Variation In Quality and Consistency
Another persistent barrier was variation in quality and consistency across regions. While some districts emerged
as exemplars—with strong attendance, seamless digital services, and timely resolution—others struggled with

These disparities often arose from differences in administrative leadership, local governance culture, digital

Technological Illiteracy and Limited Access
Technological illiteracy and limited access, particularly in tribal and rural districts, remained serious hurdles.
Many stakeholders—especially elderly pensioners, migrant workers, and low-income employees—continued to
face difficulties in using digital tools like the EPFO portal, UMANG app, or Aadhaar-based verifications. While
EPFO staff and volunteers assisted during camps, the absence of digital literacy beyond the event means that
long-term engagement remains low. There was also the concern of over-dependence on biometric verification
tools in regions where Aadhaar data errors or fingerprint mismatch issues were common, particularly among
elderly or manual labourers.
Furthermore, although NAN 2.0 attempted to bridge service delivery gaps through decentralisation, it did not
fully address the root causes of stakeholder grievances. Many complaints stemmed from outdated employer
records, systemic data mismatches, or legacy administrative issues that couldn’t always be resolved on-site. In
such cases, grievances required multi-level coordination across departments or follow-up with employers who
were unwilling or unaware. This revealed the limitations of a camp-based model in addressing deeper structural
and procedural inefficiencies within the system.
An emerging concern was the sustainability of the program’s intensity. Monthly camps across all districts require
recurring budgetary outlays, coordination with multiple local bodies, and constant mobilisation efforts. As the
novelty of the initiative wears off, maintaining momentum, attendance, and administrative energy could become
increasingly difficult. Moreover, without clearly defined roles for follow-up, monitoring, and cross-learning
between districts, there is a risk that the platform may become just ritualistic rather than transformational.
The Faceoff Between Digital Scalability and Human Engagement
Tension between digital scalability and human engagement remained persistent. While EPFO increasingly
invested in AI-powered chatbots, mobile applications, and centralised grievance portals to handle queries and
automate claims, the very success of NAN 2.0 stemmed from its human-centric, empathetic approach.
Stakeholders who felt neglected by faceless portals were now being served face-to-face. Balancing these two
models was a challenge that would shape EPFO’s future strategy and is central to the case dilemma.
Institutional Learning and Evaluation: Building a Feedback-Driven Model
A distinguishing feature of NAN 2.0 was not just implementation at scale, but its adaptive governance design.
EPFO institutionalised a feedback loop to monitor impact, diagnose weaknesses, and replicate success. Feedback
forms were collected at most sites, and qualitative insights—such as empathy of officers, waiting time, and
signage clarity—were compiled into monthly learnings.
Moreover, NAN 2.0’s alignment with the ‘Good Governance’ indicators of the Ministry of Personnel, as well as
select Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 1 – No Poverty, SDG 8 – Decent Work and Economic Growth),
positioned it as a candidate for horizontal replication across other welfare departments. Rather than a one-time
reform, NAN 2.0 laid the foundation for a citizen-responsive bureaucracy, demonstrating that decentralisation,
when married with data and empathy, can reconfigure legacy institutions.

Dilemma and Strategic Decision Point
The success of NAN 2.0 brought EPFO to a critical crossroads. While the initiative was widely appreciated for
restoring trust and improving service delivery through physical, decentralised outreach, it also raised a profound
strategic question: How can a high-touch, human-driven public interface be sustained and scaled in the age of
artificial intelligence, automation, and digital governance?
At one level, the answer seemed self-evident. The digital transformation of government services had been a core

policy priority under India’s ‘Digital Bharat’ mission. Platforms such as the UMANG app, Digi Locker, Aadhaar-
based e-KYC, and AI-enabled chatbots promised seamless, contactless, and paperless interactions. For an

institution like EPFO, which handled claims and contributions from over 320 million workers and managed funds
of over $330 billion USD, digital systems were essential for operational efficiency, fraud prevention, and
transparency.
Indeed, EPFO’s own architecture moved in this direction. Online claim settlement, e-nomination, passbook
access, and mobile-enabled grievance filing were now standard features. As more employers and employees
joined the formal sector, there was a growing pressure to consolidate services through centralised digital
infrastructure that reduced cost, increased automation, and eliminated redundancy. This digital-first model also
appealed to younger, tech-savvy users, especially in urban and semi-urban clusters.
Yet, the evidence from NAN 2.0 told a more complex story. The overwhelming majority of participants in the
monthly outreach camps came from rural, tribal, and aspirational districts, where digital access remained uneven
and digital literacy was low. Many workers and pensioners who attended these camps were unable to navigate
online portals, did not possess smartphones, or face biometric mismatches due to physical labour or age. Their
experience with digital-only grievance mechanisms was often frustrating, impersonal, and alienating.
Moreover, stakeholders repeatedly cite trust, empathy, and immediate feedback as the key benefits of NAN 2.0.
For someone like Ramesh Munda, who waited years for his pension due to an Aadhaar mismatch, the
opportunity to speak directly to an officer and have his grievance resolved on the spot was transformative. It
gave him not just procedural relief but also emotional reassurance that he mattered to the system.
This dichotomy between scale and sensitivity, between automation and accessibility, lied at the heart of EPFO’s
strategic dilemma. Should the organisation double down on the momentum created by NAN 2.0, possibly by
increasing frequency/ location, while institutionalising human touchpoints in its service architecture? Or should
it gradually pivot toward a digital-first model, investing heavily in AI-enabled grievance redressal, predictive
service delivery, and portal-based claim resolution, thereby conserving resources and aligning with global best
practices?
The dilemma was further complicated by regional diversity. In metros like Bengaluru or Pune, digital interfaces
were widely accepted and often preferred. In contrast, in areas like Khunti (Jharkhand) or Dhalai (Tripura), the
very idea of a digital-only system risked deepening exclusion. A one-size-fits-all solution was unlikely to work
in a country as complex and demographically layered as India.
Additionally, questions of institutional capacity and sustainability persisted. Could EPFO’s workforce support a

monthly physical outreach in perpetuity without fatigue or mission drift? Could budgetary allocations and inter-
agency coordination keep pace with rising expectations? And if the physical outreach was scaled back, would

the gains in public trust and grievance redressal quickly erode?

The cost-benefit analysis was also required to be considered. While physical camps built inclusion and goodwill,
they required significant logistical investment, staff mobilisation, and coordination efforts. Digital tools, once
developed, promise cost-effective and standardised delivery. Yet they lacked the nuance and responsiveness that
human interaction provided, especially for vulnerable populations navigating complex entitlements.
Ultimately, the EPFO was faced with the classic policy puzzle: How to integrate the efficiency of digital
governance with the equity and empathy of field-based engagement? Could it design a hybrid model that
adapted to regional contexts, segmented stakeholders based on their digital readiness, and ensured no citizen
was left behind?
The resolution of this dilemma would shape not just the future of Nidhi Aapke Nikat, but the broader trajectory of
social security governance in India.
Policy Options and Strategic Pathways
The dilemma before EPFO was not one of abandoning success but of choosing its future direction wisely. NAN
2.0 demonstrated that public service delivery could be both empathetic and effective when grounded in
decentralisation, predictability, and field-level engagement. However, to ensure long-term institutional
sustainability, EPFO needed to consider how best to integrate this success with the imperatives of scale,
technology, and efficiency. Several strategic pathways would emerge, each with its own logic, trade-offs, and
implementation challenges.
Option 1: Hybrid Engagement Model
The most balanced option might had been to adopt a hybrid engagement model that evolved over time. Under
this approach, EPFO would continue to hold monthly outreach camps in all districts while simultaneously
enhancing its digital ecosystem. Dedicated grievance kiosks, regional helplines, AI-driven chatbots, and mobile
apps could complement the physical outreach by providing stakeholders with continuous support between camp

dates. This model would respect the diversity of India’s demographic and digital landscape. It would allow tech-
literate users to rely on self-service systems while preserving the human interface for those who remain digitally

excluded. The advantage of such a model would lie in its flexibility and inclusiveness, but it would also demand
greater resource allocation and sustained administrative coordination across both digital and physical domains.
Option 2: Digital-first Transition Model
An alternative pathway would have been the digital-first transition model, which would prioritise technology as
the main vehicle of service delivery. Here, EPFO would gradually scale down physical outreach, replacing it with
mobile applications, enhanced portal functionalities, and real-time AI-assisted grievance redressal systems. This
model would promise cost-effectiveness, uniformity, and automation at scale. It would align closely with global
trends in social security administration and reduce dependency on human resources. However, the trade-off
would be significant. In regions with low connectivity or limited literacy, such a shift risks marginalising
vulnerable populations. Additionally, the absence of face-to-face engagement could reverse the trust EPFO has
built in recent years, especially among workers and pensioners in remote areas.
Option 3: Targeted Physical Engagement Model
A more ambitious but resource-intensive strategy would be the targeted physical engagement model, wherein
EPFO deepens its commitment to the field-based approach by increasing the frequency / location in industrial
clusters/areas requiring more intervention. This approach would aim to deepen outreach, particularly in states
with large informal workforces or tribal populations. It would also allow for more granular problem-solving,

Balancing Digital Scale and Citizen-Centric Governance: The EPFO Case

12
close monitoring, and integration with other welfare schemes. The benefit of this model is its high visibility and
local impact, but the cost—both financial and administrative—would be considerable. Scaling up physical
engagement may stretch the already lean EPFO workforce and create operational fatigue unless accompanied by
parallel staffing reforms and technology augmentation.
Option 4: Regional Customisation
A fourth and more decentralised option would involve a regional customisation, allowing different zones to
adopt outreach strategies suited to their specific demographic and digital contexts. For instance, districts in Kerala
or Karnataka with high digital penetration could move toward digital-first systems, while districts in Jharkhand,
Chhattisgarh, or the Northeast could continue with a strong physical interface. This model encourages adaptive
governance and local innovation, potentially improving relevance and responsiveness. Yet it comes with the
challenge of maintaining national uniformity and accountability. Differentiated models may result in uneven
service quality, confusion among migrating workers, and difficulties in monitoring performance across
jurisdictions.
Each of these options carries a different vision of institutional identity. The hybrid model offers continuity with
innovation. The digital-first pathway aligns with modern governance philosophies. The enhanced physical model
reinforces the state’s presence in marginal geographies. And regional customisation reflects democratic
decentralisation and administrative autonomy. None is inherently superior; the choice depends on what EPFO
prioritises—inclusion, efficiency, adaptability, or scale.
What becomes clear is that no single model can serve all purposes in a country as diverse as India. Policymakers
must consider a staggered, multi-tiered strategy, perhaps beginning with a hybrid model, piloting digital-first
transitions in select urban clusters, and gradually developing a framework for regional adaptation. Any chosen
path must be accompanied by rigorous impact assessment, capacity building, and digital literacy campaigns to
ensure that innovation does not come at the cost of equity.
In the final analysis, NAN 2.0 has opened a window of opportunity—not only for EPFO but for all public
institutions—to reimagine service delivery in a way that is both modern and humane. The real policy question is
not which model to choose, but how to preserve the spirit of listening and accessibility that NAN 2.0 has come to
symbolise, while preparing for the digital future. It invites public administrators, scholars, and decision-makers
to reflect on a timeless truth in governance: delivery is not only about systems, but also about relationships.

Case Study Title:
Integrated Command and Control Centre:
A Holistic Approach to Tackling Environmental
Challenges in Chandigarh, India
Case Study Description: Chandigarh's ICCC was conceived to combat growing environmental issues such as air pollution, traffic congestion, water scarcity, and poor waste management. With strong leadership and support under the Smart Cities Mission, the city implemented a technology-driven, data-integrated command center to monitor and optimize urban operations across 25+ services. It evolved through four phases: planning, infrastructure development, real-time integration, and community engagement. The case presents both achievements and challenges—ranging from institutional resistance, financial limitations, and privacy concerns to remarkable successes in traffic management, pollution control, and citizen participation.
Case Text:
Setting the Stage: A City at the Crossroads
It started with a cough. A small, persistent irritation in Aarav’s throat as he cycled to work one morning.
He shrugged it off—maybe just the winter air. But as days passed, the cough did not go away. The air
felt heavier, the skyline hazier, and his usual refreshing ride to the office had turned into a battle against
pollution. Aarav was not alone. Across the city, parents worried about their children playing outside.
Sharma, a retired teacher, no longer took her evening walks because the air irritated her eyes. Rohit, a
college student, found himself stuck in traffic longer than ever, breathing in fumes from hundreds of
idling cars. Meanwhile, the city faced other looming crises—overflowing garbage, receding
groundwater levels, flash floods after sudden rains, and the relentless heat waves turning summer
months unbearable.
Chandigarh1

, once a model city of urban planning, was struggling. The very foundation that made it
“The City Beautiful”—its clean environment, efficient water management, and well-planned roads—
was now under threat.
By the early 2020s, Chandigarh faced growing urban challenges—traffic bottlenecks, inefficient waste
management, fragmented utilities, and rising safety concerns (Singh and Sharma 2016). Determined to
address these issues head-on, K.K. Yadav, commissioner of the Municipal Corporation and chief
executive officer (CEO) of Chandigarh Smart City Limited (CSCL), envisioned a real-time governance
hub that could streamline municipal operations and put citizens first.
This transformation aligned with the broader Smart Cities Mission, launched by the Government of
India in 2015, which aimed to foster sustainable urban living through technology-driven
infrastructure and citizen-focused services. As a centrally sponsored scheme, the mission allocated
₹48,000 crore ($5.78 billion) for 100 cities, with each receiving ₹100 crore ($12 million) annually, matched
by state and local contributions. Chandigarh’s Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC),
developed at a cost of ₹295 crore ($35.5 million), progressed in well-defined phases, steadily

incorporating new technologies. By November 2024, more than 7,350 projects had been completed
across 98 cities, all of which were operating ICCCs that played a crucial role in enabling data-informed

On 14 June 2020, the CSCL signed an agreement with Bharat Electronics Limited to bring this vision to
life. The ₹295 crore project aimed to build a high-tech ICCC with advanced surveillance, centralized
dashboards, data analytics, and SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems for utility
monitoring. The facility also housed a police command center and an on-site data center that provided
real-time insights across departments. This infrastructure enabled the real-time integration of services
through application programming interfaces, SCADA systems, and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors
deployed across the city. By its formal commissioning on 27 March 2022, the ICCC had become the
operational brain of the city (Chandigarh Smart City, n.d.). It integrated more than 25 urban services,
including:
• Intelligent traffic management system using artificial intelligence (AI)–based automatic number
plate recognition, red light violation detection, and speed violation detection at 45 junctions;
• Smart water and power monitoring through SCADA, tracking real-time consumption, leakage,
pressure anomalies, and grid load balancing;
• Geographic Information System–based solid waste monitoring, integrating data from 489 waste
collection vehicles and smart bins enabled by Global Positioning System or GPS to generate
optimized routes and alert dashboards;
• Smart parking and mobility platforms using license plate cameras and occupancy sensors to
manage more than 6,000 parking bays; and
• Real-time air and water quality monitoring through IoT sensors at pollution hotspots and surface
water points.
More than 2,000 intellectual property–based CCTV cameras were installed across 285 strategic
locations, feeding live surveillance into the ICCC’s video wall system, which provided a unified view
of traffic, law enforcement, and civic infrastructure. The video analytics module supported facial
recognition, crowd detection, object tracking, and thermal imaging—especially useful for managing
events and emergencies.
Technological Ecosystem
• IoT Platform. Handled data ingestion from thousands of field devices and supported protocols for
secured data-sharing for smart devices
• Analytics Layer. Used big data frameworks (e.g., Hadoop, Spark) for processing high-volume
datasets and providing visual dashboards to decision-makers
• Cybersecurity Framework. Included end-to-end encryption, biometric access control, log auditing,
and real-time threat detection aligned with the ICCC Maturity Assessment Framework (Indian
Institute of Technology Kharagpur 2023)
• Disaster Response Module. Integrated alerts from weather stations, flood sensors, and national early
warning systems to trigger automatic notifications to relevant departments
Following K.K. Yadav’s tenure, Anindita Mitra, who took over as CEO of CSCL, further refined ICCC’s
capabilities by integrating AI and machine learning–based forecasting for urban planning and
predictive maintenance. Under her leadership, Chandigarh’s ICCC was declared the top performer in
the ICCC Maturity Assessment Framework 2.0 in June 2024, with leading scores in cybersecurity, data
governance, and operational resilience.
This journey was not only about installing smart screens and dashboards; it was about bold leadership,
collaborative effort, and the courage to rethink how a city serves its people. The road, however, had its

Challenges

challenges. The early phases faced resistance from departments reluctant to share data, limited funding
that slowed progress, and public hesitation due to concerns over surveillance and privacy. However,
consistent dialogue, strong political support, and a commitment to citizen-first solutions gradually
broke down these barriers and kept the mission on track. Chandigarh did not just manage its
environment. It redefined how a city could thrive—one clean breath, one conserved drop, one recycled
bin at a time.
Tracing the Implementation Process
Chandigarh’s journey toward becoming a smart city required a structured, multi-phase approach. The
city administration recognized that simply deploying technology would not be enough; integrating
these solutions with existing infrastructure and ensuring public participation was equally crucial. The
implementation process evolved dynamically, requiring continuous assessment and adaptation to
emerging challenges. With sustainability as a core focus, the city leveraged a mix of technological
advancements and community-driven strategies to drive transformation.
Phase 1: Assessment and Planning
Chandigarh’s transition to a smart city began in earnest between 2016 and 2017, when the city
leadership took a hard look at growing environmental stress and infrastructure shortfalls (Chandigarh
ENVIS n.d.). Anindita Mitra, Indian Administrative Service,2 serving as municipal commissioner and
CEO of CSCL, spearheaded the effort (Chandigarh Smart City n.d.). Working alongside urban planners,
environmental experts, and community representatives, she led a structured assessment to identify
urgent urban challenges and set development priorities.
The team aligned their road map with existing efforts under the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and
Urban Transformation—launched in 2015—to ensure synergy between infrastructure upgrades, water
and sanitation improvements, and the expansion of green spaces (Government of India 2022).
To ground their strategy in real-world needs, the administration conducted rigorous environmental
monitoring and held consultations across sectors. These revealed critical issues that stemmed from
years of unchecked urbanization and environmental degradation—issues that directly threatened
public health, sustainability, and overall livability.
Through city-wide environmental monitoring and stakeholder consultations, several pressing issues
were recognized. High vehicular emissions, dust from construction sites, and industrial pollutants were
major contributors to deteriorating air quality, increasing respiratory diseases among residents. The
growing urban population led to a surge in waste generation, with landfills reaching their capacity and
improper segregation limiting recycling efforts. Overextraction of groundwater, coupled with
inadequate rainwater harvesting, had led to water scarcity, posing a threat to long-term sustainability.
As urban heat islands formed due to excessive concrete infrastructure and shrinking green spaces,
extreme heat events became more frequent, adversely affecting public health and energy consumption
(CPCB 2023, PSPCB 2023).
Strategic Road Map for Sustainable Urban Development
Recognizing these challenges, the city administration laid out a strategic smart city road map,
integrating technological advancements with environmental sustainability. The key focus areas
included:
• Introduction of electric public transport, expanding cycling infrastructure, and optimizing traffic
management systems to reduce congestion and carbon emissions.

• Strengthening waste segregation at source, upgrading processing plants, and integrating data-
driven waste collection systems to minimize landfill dependency

• Implementing city-wide rainwater harvesting, promoting treated wastewater reuse, and enforcing
stricter groundwater regulations
• Enhancing tree cover, expanding green corridors, and designing climate-resilient infrastructure to
mitigate heatwave effects

• To support these initiatives, Chandigarh adopted AI-driven environmental modelling and GIS-
based tools. These technologies enabled precise tracking of pollution hotspots, forecasting of urban

flooding patterns, and real-time monitoring of air and water quality.
Phase 2: Infrastructure Development
Chandigarh’s commitment to evolving into a smart city was exemplified through a series of strategic
infrastructure developments aimed at enhancing urban mobility, waste management, water
conservation, and environmental monitoring.
Smart Mobility Initiatives
To drive sustainable urban transport, the Chandigarh Transport Undertaking, under the leadership of
the CSCL, introduced 80 electric buses into the city’s public transport fleet. This move reduced both
carbon emissions and reliance on fossil fuels. At the same time, the CSCL and the Municipal
Corporation of Chandigarh (MCC) expanded the city’s cycling infrastructure by establishing over 600
bike stations and deploying 5,000 bicycles, including e-bikes (Chandigarh Smart City n.d.). These
initiatives encouraged residents to adopt non-motorized transport options, helping to ease traffic and
cut emissions. To further improve urban mobility, the engineering department and the CSCL
implemented a traffic light optimization system. This system synchronized signals across key
intersections, reducing traffic congestion, vehicle idling time, and fuel consumption, thereby
contributing directly to better air quality and smoother traffic flow.
Waste Management Overhaul
To tackle growing solid waste challenges, the MCC, with support from the CSCL, modernized waste
collection systems across the city. They deployed 489 GPS-enabled vehicles, each fitted with separate
compartments for wet, dry, and household hazardous waste, ensuring segregation at the source and
improving operational efficiency (Smart City Indore 2023). In commercial and residential zones,
authorities installed color-coded bins to promote easy and responsible waste disposal. These efforts not
only streamlined waste collection and processing but also increased citizen participation and
satisfaction with municipal services.
The Dadumajra Waste Processing Plant also saw major upgrades, enabling it to convert collected waste

into refuse-derived fuel—a shift that not only reduced landfill dependency but also promoted waste-
to-energy conversion. Back in 2017, only 30% of the city’s daily 450 metric tons of waste was being

scientifically processed.

The turning point came in 2018, when the MCC, backed by the ICCC, launched an aggressive door-to-
door waste segregation campaign. Color-coded bins were distributed to households, and although

many residents were initially resistant, sustained outreach changed the game. School-based awareness
programs, creative storytelling, and the celebration of local champions helped drive community
participation. One neighbourhood even achieved 100% segregation, becoming a citywide inspiration.
The ICCC played a crucial role by integrating smart bins and real-time tracking of garbage trucks.
Sanitation teams used live data to optimize collection routes, leading to a 50% reduction in landfill
overflow within a year. Neighbourhood-level dashboards identified low-performing areas, prompting
targeted awareness drives and stricter enforcement where needed. A major milestone in this journey
was the launch of the Pink Material Recovery Facility in Sector 25 near Dadumajra2

not just about better waste recovery; it was also a story of women’s empowerment. Operated mainly
by women, the facility boosted segregation and recyclable recovery while creating employment and

By 2023, Chandigarh had achieved a remarkable milestone—surpassing a 70% waste segregation rate.
This success laid the groundwork for waste-to-energy initiatives, where organic waste was converted
into power, turning an urban challenge into a sustainable opportunity.
Behind this transformation was a clear, data-driven strategy led by the MCC in collaboration with the
CSCL. Moving beyond the standard practice of segregating waste into just wet and dry categories, the
city introduced a granular segregation model, dividing waste into 10 to 12 distinct streams. Each waste
type was linked with designated recyclers and processors, allowing for precise and efficient handling
(Smart City Indore 2025).
In an interview with Elets News Network, Anindita Mitra, IAS, former CEO of the CSCL and
commissioner of the MCC, shed light on this transformative approach:
For the past 2 years, we have moved beyond conventional waste segregation practices. Sanitary waste,
for example—where few cities have seen success—was a key focus. In November 2021, we began with
just 15 kilograms (kg) of sanitary waste collected per day. Today, we are managing nearly 500 kg daily,
all of which is properly processed and disposed of.
Mitra also highlighted several innovative community-centric programs. Among them was “Project
Arpan,” an initiative that repurposes temple floral waste into incense sticks, candles, and other useful
products. This not only addressed the issue of religious waste disposal but also demonstrated the city’s
commitment to creative reuse and circular economy practices (Elets Smart City, n.d.).
Another key innovation was the launch of a reduce, reuse, recycle center, designed to engage citizens
directly. The center became a hub where residents could drop off used clothes, electronics, and footwear
for repair, refurbishment, and redistribution—effectively reducing landfill loads and promoting
responsible consumption.
These efforts reflect Chandigarh’s commitment to building a cleaner, more sustainable city through
holistic waste management, citizen engagement, and policy innovation. As Mitra emphasized, “The
systems we have implemented here can serve as a replicable model for urban centres across the
country.”
Digital Surveillance and Air Quality Monitoring
To address escalating environmental pollution, the MCC and the Chandigarh Pollution Control
Committee (CPCC), under the leadership of Anindita Mitra, IAS, adopted a data-driven, multi-agency
strategy beginning in 2018. Their goal was to curb deteriorating air quality and promote sustainable
urban living.
The administration installed IoT-enabled air quality sensors across the city to monitor pollutants such
as particulate matter (PM) 2.5 and PM10 in real time. This data was integrated into the ICCC, enabling
timely alerts and targeted interventions—ranging from traffic diversion plans and industry-level
emission controls to public health notifications. Digital Air Quality Index (AQI) display boards were
placed at key sites, such as Sector 17 Plaza and prominent traffic intersections, to keep citizens informed
and encourage behavioural change (WHO 2021).
These efforts were reinforced by broader regional insights. Sushil Dogra, a scientist with the Pollution
Control Committee, emphasized that Chandigarh’s environmental challenges extended beyond city
boundaries. He noted that the Chandigarh Tricity—which includes Panchkula (Haryana) and Kharar,
Kurali, Mohali, and Zirakpur (Punjab)—with a combined population of nearly 3 million, was

experiencing a steady rise in pollution due to rapid urbanization and industrial activity. Situated in the
heavily polluted Indo-Gangetic Plain, the region was particularly vulnerable. Despite these
challenges, Dogra highlighted that continuous monitoring and policy enforcement were being carried
out to improve air and water quality, regulate emissions, and promote sustainable practices.
Chandigarh also expanded its green mobility initiatives. The Chandigarh Transport Undertaking
added 80 electric buses to its fleet, all tracked through the ICCC for route optimization, energy
efficiency, and predictive maintenance. Dedicated cycling tracks were developed citywide,
accompanied by large-scale awareness campaigns promoting clean mobility.
To reduce road dust, a major contributor to PM103

levels, mechanized sweeping vehicles were
deployed along high-traffic corridors. In parallel, the engineering department introduced an adaptive
traffic control system at major intersections like Tribune Chowk, using AI-enabled traffic sensors to
adjust signal timings dynamically. These systems helped reduce congestion, minimize idling, and
lower vehicular emissions.
By 2021, CPCC data recorded a 15% reduction in air pollution levels. For the first time in years, residents
reported bluer skies, cleaner air, and an improved sense of urban liveability (CPCB 2023).
Water Resource Management
Water scarcity became one of Chandigarh’s most pressing environmental challenges, with depleting
groundwater levels and increasing demand for water threatening the city’s long-term sustainability.
To address this, Chandigarh’s ICCC, along with the Public Health Department, CPCC, and the MCC,
led a comprehensive transformation in water resource management, prioritizing efficiency,
conservation, and sustainable practices.
The city installed smart water meters across all sectors, allowing real-time monitoring of water usage
and detection of leaks. Within a year, this initiative helped reduce water wastage by 20%.
Simultaneously, the city revamped its wastewater management strategy: treated wastewater was no
longer discharged into drains but was instead reused for irrigating parks, gardens, and green belts,
conserving fresh water for critical needs.
To further tackle water scarcity, Chandigarh launched a citywide rainwater harvesting campaign. The
Public Works Department and the MCC constructed recharge pits and storage tanks at schools,
government buildings, residential colonies, and commercial zones. The ICCC tracked these efforts
meticulously, ensuring their widespread implementation and facilitating efficient water management.
As a result, aquifers gradually replenished, contributing to a significant shift toward water
conservation.
Through these initiatives, Chandigarh achieved a 30% reduction in groundwater use, underscoring its
commitment to sustainable water management. By promoting rainwater harvesting and treated
wastewater reuse, the city enhanced its resilience against drought and set the foundation for a more
sustainable and resource-efficient urban future (PSPCB 2023).

Phase 3: Data Integration and Real-Time Operations
The ICCC was central to Chandigarh’s smart city transformation, consolidating data from multiple
sources to enhance urban management and operations. The integration of smart meters, traffic cameras,
environmental sensors, and IoT-based infrastructure fundamentally changed how the city addressed
its growing challenges. Through real-time data analysis, the city not only optimized its resource
allocation but also improved its ability to predict and manage environmental hazards, traffic, waste,
and public safety.
1. Centralized Data Aggregation and Monitoring
ICCC consolidated citywide data into a unified dashboard, offering real-time insights for municipal
authorities. It enabled monitoring of air quality through IoT-enabled pollution sensors, waste collection
and sanitation via GPS-enabled trucks and smart bins, traffic flow through an AI-powered surveillance
network, and water distribution and leak detection using smart meters. By aggregating and visualising
this data, the ICCC supported quick, data-driven decision-making to improve service delivery and
respond effectively to emergencies. For instance, during periods of high pollution, officials used air
quality data to impose targeted traffic restrictions in high-emission zones and deploy anti-smog water
sprinklers in critical areas.
2. AI-Driven Predictive Analytics for Environmental Management
AI and machine learning algorithms played a central role in forecasting and preventing potential
environmental hazards through predictive analytics. Historical traffic data was used to anticipate
congestion and suggest dynamic diversions to prevent bottlenecks during peak hours. Similarly, AI
models forecasted spikes in air pollution, particularly during stubble-burning seasons, enabling early

warnings and preventive measures. Waste collection processes were also optimised through AI-
powered routing systems, ensuring timely garbage collection, reducing delays, and minimising fuel

consumption. For instance, in November 2024, AI-driven models predicted a 30% rise in air pollution
due to stubble burning in neighbouring regions. This allowed authorities to restrict generator usage in
advance, which helped reduce emissions (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi 2022).
3. Intelligent Traffic and Public Transport Management
The ICCC integrated advanced traffic control systems that streamlined traffic management and
enhanced public transport efficiency. Adaptive traffic signals were dynamically adjusted in response
to real-time vehicle flow, helping to ease congestion and improve overall traffic movement. Automated
AI-based cameras detected violations and issued e-challans instantly, which not only improved
compliance but also reduced accidents. In addition, GPS-enabled trackers installed in electric buses and
other public transport vehicles provided passengers with real-time location updates, improving
reliability and commuter experience. For example, during peak office hours, AI-powered monitoring
on Madhya Marg and Sector 17 helped reduce congestion and cut average travel times by nearly 15
minutes.
4. Real-Time Crisis Response and Disaster Mitigation
The ICCC’s integration of real-time monitoring systems greatly enhanced the city’s capacity to respond
to crises such as extreme weather, floods, and other emergencies. Drainage monitoring systems
detected blockages and potential water-logging, enabling authorities to intervene before problems
escalated. Temperature sensors identified high-risk heatwave zones, prompting the activation of
cooling stations and misting systems. In addition, emergency alerts on floods, accidents, and pollution
spikes were disseminated instantly through mobile apps and electronic billboards, ensuring residents
remained informed and safe. For instance, during the 2023 monsoon floods, drainage monitoring
systems flagged waterlogged roads in Sectors 22 and 43, enabling traffic diversions and the rapid
deployment of emergency responders, which helped minimise disruptions.

Challenges

9

Phase 4: Community Engagement and Capacity Building
Public participation was a cornerstone of ICCC’s success. While technology and infrastructure
provided the backbone for smart city initiatives, long-term sustainability depended on active
engagement from citizens, schools, and local organizations. The administration recognized that
fostering a sense of community ownership was crucial for ensuring behavioural change and the
successful adoption of new initiatives.
Awareness Campaigns and Behavioural Change Programs
A major challenge was shifting public attitudes toward waste segregation, sustainable commuting, and
water conservation. To address this, the municipal corporation launched a series of targeted awareness
campaigns:

• Cycling and sustainable mobility initiatives. Public awareness drives encouraged cycling as an eco-
friendly alternative. The administration, along with local cycling clubs and resident welfare

associations, organized community bike rides and “car-free days” to promote non-motorized transport
(The Hindu and ENN, n.d.).
• Waste segregation and reduction programs. The municipal corporation partnered with
nongovernment organizations (NGOs) and school eco-clubs to launch door-to-door awareness
campaigns on waste segregation. Workshops were conducted in residential societies, emphasizing the
importance of separating wet and dry waste at the source.
• Water conservation awareness. The administration worked with local community leaders to promote
rainwater harvesting and water-efficient practices in homes and offices. Special drives in schools
educated children on the importance of water conservation, encouraging them to act as “water
warriors” in their communities.
• Role of NGOs and citizen groups. Local NGOs and citizen action groups played a vital role in
mobilizing communities and bridging the gap between the administration and the public. Their
involvement ensured that smart city initiatives were not just government-driven but had grassroots
support.
• Waste management partnerships. NGOs assisted in managing community composting sites and
Project Arpan, which repurposed floral waste into incense sticks and organic dyes (Elets Smart City,
n.d.).
Capacity Building for Municipal Staff
For the ICCC to function effectively, municipal staff required extensive training in smart technology,
real-time data analytics, and emergency response systems. Specialised workshops and hands-on
sessions were organised to equip employees with the necessary skills. Field engineers and municipal
workers received technical training on monitoring IoT sensors, CCTV networks, and air quality
dashboards, enabling them to respond proactively to environmental hazards. In parallel, emergency
response teams participated in disaster management drills, where they learned to use real-time flood
monitoring tools and evacuation mapping systems, strengthening the city’s preparedness for extreme
weather events.
Crisis Management and Adaptive Strategies
The ICCC played a crucial role in managing crises such as flash floods, extreme heatwaves, and rising
pollution levels (UNDP 2023). The administration had to adopt dynamic strategies to respond to these
recurring environmental threats effectively.

Challenges

10

Urban Flooding and Flash Flood Monitoring
Unpredictable heavy rainfall events frequently overwhelmed Chandigarh’s existing drainage system,
leading to urban flooding in several areas. To address this, the city refined its drainage monitoring and
flood prediction systems. Real-time data from water level sensors, weather forecasting models, and
urban runoff analysis enabled pre-emptive actions, such as opening alternative drainage pathways and
issuing early warnings to residents. In July 2023, Chandigarh witnessed unusually heavy rainfall,
causing waterlogging in key commercial areas. The ICCC used real-time flood mapping to redirect
traffic and deploy emergency response teams, significantly reducing damage and disruptions
compared to previous years.
Pollution Control and Air Quality Management
With vehicle emissions, dust pollution, and crop residue burning contributing to poor air quality, the
ICCC played a proactive role in pollution mitigation. Real-time air quality data enabled authorities to

implement anti-smog measures when pollution levels spiked. Mechanized street sweepers and water-
sprinkling machines were deployed to reduce particulate matter levels in high-traffic zones and

construction areas. For example, in November 2024, when air pollution levels surged due to regional
stubble burning, the ICCC identified high-risk zones and coordinated targeted water-sprinkling efforts.
The initiative led to a 20% reduction in particulate matter levels within 3 weeks.
Smart Energy Solutions for Climate Resilience
To reduce dependence on non-renewable energy sources and enhance sustainability, Chandigarh
focused on smart energy solutions. Solar panel installations on government buildings and public
institutions were scaled up, aiming to meet at least 20% of the city’s electricity needs through renewable
sources. Smart grid systems were introduced to optimize energy consumption and reduce wastage. For
example, by 2023, Chandigarh successfully converted 50% of its municipal buildings to solar energy,
reducing carbon emissions and setting an example for other urban centers (Indian Institute of
Technology Kharagpur 2023, Times of India 2024).
Delivery Challenges
The implementation of the ICCC in Chandigarh faced numerous challenges, ranging from financial
constraints to technological and behavioral resistance. While the Smart City initiative brought a vision
for a cleaner and more efficient urban environment, executing that vision required overcoming
significant obstacles (Singh and Sharma 2016).
Financial Constraints and Bureaucratic Hurdles
One of the most critical challenges in Chandigarh’s smart city transformation was the shortage of
adequate funding. While the Smart Cities Mission had provided an initial financial boost— allocating
₹500 crore per city—the required matching contributions from the state government and the MCC often
fell short of actual infrastructure needs. This funding gap significantly slowed down the pace of
implementation across several components of the project. According to a comprehensive study by the
IIT Kharagpur titled “Evaluation of Integrated Command and Control Centres (ICCCs) under the Smart
Cities Mission” (2023) (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur 2023), most smart cities across India,
including Chandigarh, struggled with delays and limited functionality in their ICCCs due to
insufficient and inconsistent funding. These financial constraints restricted the rollout of key systems
such as smart traffic signals, surveillance networks, and predictive environmental tools.
In Chandigarh, the installation of AI-powered traffic lights and violation detection systems faced
repeated postponements because of delayed fund disbursement. Although these systems had been
approved and planned early in the mission, conventional traffic lights remained in use much longer
than expected, reducing the effectiveness of traffic decongestion and pollution control strategies.
Administrative hurdles further compounded these issues. Delays in approvals, lack of

Integrated Command and Control Centre: A Holistic Approach to Tackling Environmental
Challenges

11
interdepartmental coordination, and slow procurement processes created a noticeable gap between
planning and execution. These obstacles not only disrupted project timelines but also eroded public
confidence in the mission’s progress.
The IIT Kharagpur report recommended that, to address such setbacks, governments adopt more
flexible funding frameworks, improve financial autonomy of urban local bodies, and invest in
institutional capacity-building for better project management.
Infrastructure Deployment Issues
Setting up a robust technological framework required extensive infrastructure. Installing a fiber optic
network, IoT-enabled sensors, and CCTV surveillance cameras ran into several obstacles. High
installation costs, delays in regulatory approvals, and interference from existing underground utilities
disrupted progress. At one point, only 22 out of 710 planned cameras were operational due to technical
and logistical challenges, reducing the effectiveness of surveillance and data collection efforts. During
peak pollution seasons, the ICCC attempted to use surveillance footage to track illegal burning
activities. However, the lack of functional cameras in key areas reduced the effectiveness of
enforcement efforts.
Public Scepticism and Behavioural Resistance
Engaging the public in smart city initiatives proved difficult. Residents hesitated to embrace waste
segregation, plastic reduction, and sustainable commuting. Many saw these measures as inconvenient
or time-consuming. Privacy concerns also arose regarding data collection through surveillance cameras
and digital tracking systems. Addressing these concerns required extensive awareness campaigns and
public engagement sessions. When the municipal corporation launched a campaign to promote cycling
as an alternative to motorized transport, office goers were reluctant to participate, citing safety concerns
and a lack of parking spaces for bicycles near workplaces (Duarte 2024, Hindustan Times 2023).
Technical and Cybersecurity Challenges
Integrating new technologies with existing infrastructure required careful execution. The transition to
digitalized city services raised concerns about cybersecurity. Unauthorized access, hacking threats, and
data breaches became pressing issues, necessitating a robust cybersecurity framework. Real-time
monitoring and predictive analytics depended on stable internet connectivity and uninterrupted power
supply, both of which faced occasional disruptions. In 2022, ICCC’s traffic management system
experienced a temporary outage due to a cyberattack attempt. Although it was mitigated quickly, the
incident highlighted the vulnerabilities in the system and the need for enhanced cybersecurity
measures.
Extreme Weather Events and Environmental Constraints
Unpredictable weather conditions, including heatwaves and sudden rainfall, posed additional
challenges. Flash floods after heavy downpours frequently disrupted city operations, making it crucial
to integrate climate resilience into ICCC’s strategy. The system had to adapt to changing environmental
conditions and respond efficiently to disasters, requiring ongoing technological upgrades. During the
2023 monsoon season, unanticipated heavy rainfall overwhelmed parts of the drainage system, causing
urban flooding. Although the ICCC monitored the water levels in real time, the lack of adequate
drainage infrastructure slowed response efforts.
Each of Chandigarh’s environmental missions supported the others. Electric buses and cycle tracks
reduced traffic emissions and urban heating. Rainwater harvesting and wastewater reuse eased
groundwater pressure and supported urban greenery. Efficient waste management cut pollution and
prevented waterlogging. Had these steps not been taken, Chandigarh might have seen toxic air, water
shortages, overflowing landfills, and unbearable heat—a perfect storm. But instead, the city embraced
change with tech-driven governance, grassroots participation, and forward-thinking policies.

Integrated Command and Control Centre: A Holistic Approach to Tackling Environmental
Challenges

12
Now, as the Smart City project completed its official timeline, the baton has passed to the MCC. But the
foundations have been laid. From dusty roads to clean streets, from leaking taps to smart meters, from
unmanaged garbage to energy recovery—the transformation is real, measurable, and replicable.
Environmental and Sustainability Outcomes: How Chandigarh Reinvented Its Urban Ecosystem
By 2025, Chandigarh had demonstrated that a city could modernize without sacrificing its
environmental integrity. The transformation was enabled by the ICCC, along with strong collaboration
among the MCC, Punjab Pollution Control Board, Department of Environment, NGOs, and an
increasingly engaged citizen base. These efforts created measurable improvements in urban resilience,
sustainability, and quality of life.
Stabilized Air Quality Amid Rapid Urbanization
Despite increasing vehicular density and expanding construction, Chandigarh succeeded in stabilizing
its AQI over the past decade (Exhibit 1). While there were no dramatic improvement, real-time
monitoring, dynamic traffic regulation, and community-led green initiatives prevented a worsening of
air pollution levels. The ICCC facilitated coordinated efforts across departments to reduce emission
hotspots and monitor pollution trends, averting the significant AQI spike that typically accompanied
urban growth.
Optimized Solid Waste Management
The MCC implemented an AI-based route optimization system and deployed sensor-enabled smart
bins across key zones. This resulted in a 40% reduction in landfill overflow, improved waste collection
frequency, and enhanced source (Exhibit 2). Public participation was central to this success—citizens
took part in door-to-door awareness drives, school-led cleanliness campaigns, and local composting
initiatives. These efforts not only reduced methane emissions and groundwater contamination but also
enhanced urban hygiene.
Strengthened Water Conservation
Beginning in the early 2020s, the city adopted a data-driven approach to water conservation. Smart
water meters were installed across residential and institutional sectors, and AI-powered leak detection
systems were used to monitor and minimize wastage. These interventions led to a 20% reduction in
non-revenue water losses. Additionally, treated wastewater was reused for landscaping and
horticulture in parks, traffic islands, and government institutions. A rainwater harvesting drive,
mandated by municipal bylaws, expanded across both public infrastructure and private housing,
contributing to groundwater recharge.
Reduced Urban Heat Island Effect
To combat rising urban temperatures, Chandigarh launched targeted greening initiatives from 2021
onward. These included afforestation drives, urban forests in vacant plots, incentives for rooftop
gardens, and the expansion of green corridors along major roads. Data from the ICCC helped identify
high-heat zones where tree plantation and heat-reflective surfaces were prioritized. Over time,
localized temperature drops were observed in these areas, demonstrating measurable success in
mitigating the urban heat island effect.
Promoted Low-Carbon Mobility
Chandigarh’s Public Bike Sharing program recorded more than 875,000 rides, directly resulting in a
reduction of 875 tonnes of CO2 emissions. Based on usage data, the city expanded docking stations and
added new cycling infrastructure in underserved zones. Fuel-efficient routes for garbage collection
vehicles, monitored in real time through the ICCC, further saved ₹25 lakh monthly in diesel costs and
reduced carbon emissions by 61 tonnes. These initiatives positioned Chandigarh as a pioneer in
integrating clean mobility with climate action.

Integrated Command and Control Centre: A Holistic Approach to Tackling Environmental
Challenges

13

Improved Disaster Response and Urban Safety
During the 2023 monsoon floods, the ICCC played a crucial role in ensuring public safety. It processed
real-time flood alerts, water level data, and traffic patterns, enabling emergency teams from the MCC,
Fire and Emergency Services, and Police Department to coordinate effectively. As a result, casualties

were avoided, rescue efforts were timely, and essential services remained operational, even in high-
risk sectors. This event demonstrated the critical value of data-centric disaster preparedness.

Reinforced Urban Resilience Through Community Engagement
Chandigarh’s resilience was not built by systems alone; it was driven by its people. Citizens embraced

digital platforms to report civic issues, adopt sustainable practices, and participate in local decision-
making. Community groups helped monitor waste segregation, maintain green belts, and promote

water-saving practices. Regular outreach by the MCC and CSCL ensured that residents remained
informed and involved. This created a feedback loop through which governance was continuously
improved based on community input.
A Model for Tech-Enabled Environmental Governance
By 2025, Chandigarh had become a model of adaptive and sustainable urban governance. The city
successfully integrated environmental protection, technological innovation, and inclusive planning.
Investments in green infrastructure, combined with real-time monitoring, enabled the city to not only
respond to climate challenges but to proactively shape its ecological future. With reduced emissions,
improved civic amenities, and an engaged citizenry, Chandigarh proved that digital transformation
and environmental stewardship could go hand in hand.
Lessons Learned
Chandigarh’s experience with the ICCC provided several critical insights:
• Technology and human-centric solutions must coexist: Data-driven governance improved efficiency,
but public engagement ensured lasting impact.
• Interdepartmental collaboration was essential: The ICCC enabled seamless coordination among
municipal bodies, leading to more effective service delivery.
• Community awareness and participation drove success: Behavioural shifts, such as increased waste
segregation and cycling adoption, played a crucial role in the initiative’s effectiveness.
• Adaptive governance strengthened resilience: The ICCC’s real-time crisis management capabilities
were instrumental during the 2023 monsoon floods, preventing widespread disruption.
• Environmental challenges know no boundaries: Despite Chandigarh’s efforts, air pollution, water
conservation, and urban heat island mitigation remained regional challenges. Neighbouring cities and
states needed to implement similar strategies for sustainable change.
Conclusion
Before the ICCC, Chandigarh’s residents faced frequent traffic jams, irregular waste collection, and
safety concerns. Ananya Sharma, a long-time resident, struggled with these daily challenges. Her
commute often took longer due to poorly managed traffic signals, and waste piled up in her
neighbourhood due to inconsistent collection. Safety in public spaces also remained a concern.
After the ICCC’s implementation, her experience changed significantly. AI-driven traffic systems eased
congestion, waste collection services became more reliable, and public spaces felt safer due to enhanced
surveillance and quick response teams. Like Ananya, many residents noticed tangible improvements
in their daily lives.

Integrated Command and Control Centre: A Holistic Approach to Tackling Environmental
Challenges

14
The ICCC transformed urban governance in Chandigarh, proving that integrated technology and
collaborative policymaking could drive meaningful environmental progress. The city tackled air
pollution, conserved water, improved waste management, and mitigated urban heat islands—all
through data-driven solutions and community participation.
However, no city can solve environmental challenges alone. Chandigarh made significant strides, but
its efforts could only succeed if neighbouring regions followed suit. Pollution and climate risks
transcend borders, demanding collective action. The ICCC provided a blueprint, but true progress
required a shared commitment from surrounding cities and states. Chandigarh’s experience
underscored the power of innovation, cooperation, and public engagement in building resilient urban
ecosystems for the future.

Case Study Title: From Rural to Digital Markets: E-Saras-ONDC partnership Ushers E-commerce Revolution for SHG Enterprises
Case Study Description: The Deen Dayal Upadhyay National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM) launched e-SARAS, a digital marketing initiative to expand market access for Self-Help Groups (SHGs) facing challenges like limited reach, poor quality control, and weak linkages. Through eSARAS.in, SHG women artisans showcased handcrafted products online. To strengthen this effort, NRLM partnered with the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) to enhance outreach and create stronger forward linkages. However, differences in institutional structures, policy shifts, and SHGs’ limited production capacity created challenges. While digital marketing improved visibility and demand, supply-side gaps persisted. The success of e-SARAS now depends on sustained NRLM–ONDC collaboration, capacity building, and stronger supply chain systems to ensure long-term growth and rural women’s economic empowerment.
Case Text:
‘All one needs is a computer, a network connection, and a bright spark of initiative and creativity to join
the economy.’
1

‘The COVID lockdowns in India established the significance of the digital economy. The pandemic was different for
those with access to digital marketing and payments than for those without,’ says Mr Saransh Agarwal, Chief of
Staff with the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC), a Government of India initiative that aims to
democratise e-commerce through an open, inclusive e-commerce ecosystem.2 This e-commerce network
serves to break down online monopolies and empower smaller businesses to participate in the digital
economy.
The ONDC has played a critical role in the success of e-Saras, the Government of India’s digital marketing
strategy under the Deen Dayal Upadhyay National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM or Mission)

under the Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD or Ministry). E-Saras, integrated with ONDCs open e-
commerce network, aims to empower rural artisans and women-led self-help groups (SHGs) in India by

leveraging digital marketing tools and forward market linkages as strategic solutions to their
entrepreneurial success.

This initiative was built upon the Missions efforts under its Livelihoods programme, to promote self-
employment, financial inclusion and women’s economic empowerment in rural India. The Livelihoods

programme was thus mobilising poor rural households into self-help groups (SHGs) and their federations.
However, some challenges persisted, like limited economies of scale, low-value enterprises, poor
marketing, limited market access, irregular supply chains, lack of forward linkages and inconsistent
product quality. E-commerce offered a promising solution.

From Rural to Digital Markets: E-Saras-ONDC partnership Ushers E-commerce Revolution for
SHG Enterprises

3

Around mid-2022, the Mission built strategic alliances and established partnerships to create an online e-
commerce platform called ‘E-Saras’ which was launched in October 2022 to connect SHGs and rural

artisans with a wider market for their products. However, perceiving a need for upscaling e-Saras, the
Mission partnered with ONDC in 2024 to establish e-Saras as an online multi-platform e-commerce system,
which expanded its reach to multiple buyer applications connected on the ONDC network, thus fostering
business growth for SHG enterprises. However, the Mission-ONDC collaboration faced some challenges
too, including differing organisational structures and goals, evolving ONDC policies, supply-demand
mismatches, quality consistency issues and internal changes within the Mission that led to monitoring gaps
and disrupted continuity.
E-commerce Solution for SHG Products
The Ministry of Rural Development was tasked with leading an ambitious initiative - called the Deen Dayal
Upadhyay National Rural Livelihoods Mission (Mission), a flagship programme for financial inclusion and
poverty alleviation in rural India. The goal was to create sustainable livelihoods and viable enterprises for
nearly 10 crore rural women connected with the programme through Self-Help Groups (SHGs).
‘Though ambitious, this goal of empowering SHGs was not unattainable,’ said Mr Charanjit Singh,
3
the driving
force behind the Mission. His optimism was grounded in evidence. Systematic reviews (Brody et al., 2015)
had highlighted the positive impact of community-based organisations on financial inclusion, employment
and women’s economic and psychological empowerment. Membership in SHGs had shown to improve
women’s confidence, financial autonomy, decision-making power, access to information, and social
networks (Pandhare et al., 2024; Raghunathan et al., 2023).
Mr Singh, however, recognised the persistent challenges in advancing women’s economic participation
and income enhancement, particularly unequal access to financial services, small-scale enterprises, poor
marketing of SHG products, fragmented supply chains, limited forward linkages, low economies of scale
and inconsistent product quality across clusters. He still remained undaunted while acknowledging the
substantial efforts already undertaken by the Ministry under the Livelihoods Mission that aimed to reach
100 million rural poor across 6 lakh villages in India.

Among the key interventions made to address the multi-faceted challenges faced by SHG enterprises, e-
commerce emerged as a promising solution for providing the marketing and forward linkages for SHG

products. Evidence from past studies had highlighted the significant impact of e-commerce on business
strategy in small and medium enterprises, enabling them to adapt and thrive in the digital economy (Chiani
& Adibpour, 2023). However, some research studies on business strategies of smaller enterprises also
indicated a conflict between strategies to reach local markets and expanding to global markets (Lewis &
Cockrill, 2002).

3 Mr Charanjit Singh, a 1990-batch veteran Indian Forest Service officer, from the Madhya Pradesh cadre had extensive
administrative experience in Central Government and State Government functioning before joining the Ministry of
Rural Development in 2018. In 2020, he served as Joint Secretary, Rural Livelihoods Division in MoRD where he was
promoted as Additional Secretary in 2022. He retired from here on December 31, 2024.

From Rural to Digital Markets: E-Saras-ONDC partnership Ushers E-commerce Revolution for
SHG Enterprises

4

The Mission recognised that sustained digital marketing of SHG-products would depend on the growth of
the SHG-led retail businesses, the popularity of the e-commerce portal and its outreach. Despite this
potential, SHG-enterprises remained underdeveloped with only 1% of the DAY-NRLM SHGs operating in
the manufacturing sector (NRLM Analytical Reports 2023),4 Also, only about 9.9% of weavers had SHG
membership while 2587 handloom-households out of 39,438 had received SHG loans (7th Economic Census
2019-20).
Existing studies highlighted the critical gaps in marketing by SHG enterprises in terms of limited scale,
weak branding, and inadequate skills and technology for product improvement and packaging (Tirkey et
al., 2024). Nonetheless, urban consumers showed a preference for SHG-products, largely due to perceptions
of affordability (Malar & Malar, 2008). With 97% of the 86.84 Lakh SHGs linked to functional bank accounts
(NRLM SHG analytical reports 2023), their integration in the digital economy appeared viable. It remained
to be seen, however, whether e-commerce could effectively address the marketing challenges and ensure
sustained consumer reach for SHG-enterprises. The stability of the e-commerce portal itself depended on
successful partnerships with implementing organisations possessing relevant expertise.
Phased Roll-out of Livelihoods Mission
The Deen Dayal Upadhyay National Rural Livelihoods Mission (2011) was implemented in three distinct
phases: social mobilisation, institution building, and livelihoods promotion, (see Exhibit 1) which worked
in tandem to empower poor rural households by organising them into self-help groups (SHGs),
strengthening community institutions, and providing access to financial resources and livelihood
opportunities.
As Mr Singh recalled, “Initially, in the mobilisation phase, we focused on identifying and organising poor rural
households, particularly women, into self-help groups. Households were categorised based on their poverty levels and
vulnerabilities. In the second phase of institution building, we worked to strengthen the SHGs and their federations
at the village and higher levels. We also ensured access to banking credit. SHGs revolving fund and community
investment fund was created to provide SHGs with a credit history. A set of standard practices were also
institutionalised (see Exhibit 2) to operationally stabilise the SHG enterprises. These efforts worked as most SHGs
were operating on auto mode.”
Performance data from the first two phases suggested that SHGs had accessed around ₹ 9.75 lakh crore of
bank credit (DAY-NRLM KPI data, Analytical Report 2024). Strict monitoring of loan repayments
encouraged SHG members to take up livelihood activities and avoid defaulting. These efforts ensured that
the number of defaulters in the programme remained low. The Mission could soon move into the third
phase of livelihoods promotion, where the focus was on creating higher order enterprises through
marketing and digital commerce interventions.

https://nrlm.gov.in/outerReportAction.do?methodName=showReportMaster)

SHG Enterprises

5

Livelihoods Promotion
The Mission undertook large-scale livelihood initiatives across both farm and non-farm sectors. It had
progressively federated SHGs into larger higher-order collectives of producer groups and producer
enterprises.

5 Through the start-up Village Entrepreneurship programme—a sub-scheme of the Mission to
create business ecosystems in villages—several one-stop facility centres and incubation centres were

established. One-stop facility centres provided professional business development services to nano-
enterprises run by women. These were operationalised on a large scale. Yet, SHGs across India faced some

systemic barriers. Key constraints included:
(i) Low scale of operations: While SHGs demonstrated high economy of scope with a large variety of
products, they often lacked economy of scale, resulting in operational inefficiencies, whereby it was not
possible for SHGs to tap into national or global markets.
(ii) Inconsistent quality: Many SHG members lacked technical and production skills necessary to meet
market standards for high-quality products.
(iii) Limited Marketing Skills: Most SHG participants lacked formal training in marketing, which limited
their effectiveness in setting competitive prices and promoting their products. This was a significant
challenge as branding and effective digital marketing tools and techniques are crucial to sustainability of
small businesses (Dumitriu et al., 2019).
(iv) Poor packaging: Poor packaging of products caused limitations in long-haul transportation, shelf-life
and branding.
(v) Unorganised markets: SHGs could only manage to sell in the local markets that were unorganised and
fragmented, thus limiting their sales potential.
Considering these limitations, Mr Singh recognised a shift in how consumers engage with markets and felt
the need for a physical retail outlet to promote sales, which could also act as an experience centre to build
brand engagement and consumer trust.
Birth of the Saras Gallery
To align with changing consumer behaviour and expectations, the Mission, in 2021, renovated its retail

sales outlet called SARAS-Gallery in Baba Kharag Singh Marg in New Delhi and transformed it into a state-
of-the-art Emporium.

5 Producer Groups refer to an informal collective of small and marginal producers, like farmers or artisans, who come
together to enhance their income by improving production, adding value to their products, and gaining better access
to markets – usually for a specific product or commodity. Producer enterprises are formal, legally registered
organisations owned and managed by primary producers to engage in business. Both groups and enterprises are higher
order entities enlisting members of multiple SHGs from multiple clusters.
