modernising India’s fertilizer subsidy framework, fostering a more sustainable and equitable agricultural
sector.
The implementation of this project marked a significant shift in the way subsidies were managed and
disbursed. Unlike typical DBT models, this DBT system credited subsidies directly to fertilizer companies
after completion of successful sales to farmers, with each transaction being authenticated through a
Aadhaar-enabled Point of Sale (PoS) device. It thus enabled real-time monitoring of sales at the retail level
besides fertilizer availability, enhanced efficiency of subsidy delivery, and established a comprehensive
beneficiary database. Serving as a digital hub, it connected a wide network of stakeholders, including 173
manufacturers, over 30,000 wholesalers, 2.36 lakh retailers, and approximately 14 crore farmers.v By linking
subsidies directly to verified sales at the correct rate—through PoS devices, the DBT system enhanced
transparency, reduced leakages, and ensured that subsidies reached the intended beneficiaries. By
eliminating intermediaries and directly linking benefits to beneficiaries, the system significantly reduced
corruption, enhanced transparency, and ensured timely disbursement of subsidies.
Recognised as a national success, the DBT initiative received the Digital India Award in 2020. It formed a
part of the broader effort to streamline subsidy distribution across sectors, ensuring targeted financial
support while strengthening accountability throughout the fertilizer supply chain.
DBT Implementation
A comprehensive framework was developed to enable the targeted delivery of fertilizers, and a Project
Management Unit was established to oversee the nationwide implementation of the DBT system. The DBT
system for the fertilizer sector was launched in October 2016. Following initial pilot projects, it was
implemented nationwide in a phased manner by March 2018. Under this system, all sales of subsidised
fertilizers to farmers were conducted through PoS devices installed at retail outlets. Farmers were
authenticated at the time of purchase using identification documents such as Aadhaar, Kisan Credit Card,
or voter ID. A web-based Integrated Fertilizer Monitoring System (iFMS) was employed to track sales and
process subsidy claims submitted by companies. Subsidies were released to fertilizer companies based on
actual sales transactions. The infographic below showcases the working of the DBT fertilizer system:

1. The Framework: The proposed framework for implementing the Direct Benefit Transfer system in the
fertilizer sector was founded on four core pillars—Identity, Need, Entitlement, and Leakage—each
supported by specific technological and institutional mechanisms (See Exhibit 2). Under the Identity pillar,
farmers were digitally authenticated using their Aadhaar credentials, through the UIDAI server, which
ensured that only genuine beneficiaries could access the subsidy. The Need component, aimed to promote
balanced fertilizer use by leveraging data from the Soil Health Card, which captured the nutrient
requirements of farmland. This soil information was stored and managed through the Soil Health Card
Server. The Entitlement pillar focused on determining the eligible quantity of subsided fertilizer based on
a farmer’s verified landholding, which was facilitated through integration with digitised land records,
accessed via the Web land server. To address leakages, the movement of fertilizers across the supply
chain—from production to the end user—was monitored and tracked in real-time using the Mobile
Fertilizer Management System server, thereby preventing diversion or black marketing. Overall, the

Transforming Digital Governance with Direct Benefit Transfer of Fertilizer Subsidy
framework was sought to ensure targeted delivery, promote efficient fertilizer use based on actual need,
and bring transparency and accountability within the subsidy management system.
2. The Project Management Unit: Following the design and development of the implementation
framework, the next step was the establishment of a Project Management Unit (PMU) to meet essential
Human Resource requirements. To ensure effective execution of the DBT scheme, the DoF established a
dedicated PMU comprising 43 members. This unit was tasked with overseeing the project from inception
to execution, and ensure its successful rollout nationwide. The PMU was headed by Mr Niranjan Lal, as
the Director, who provided strategic direction and overall leadership. He was supported by Mr Rahul
Singh as the Project Lead Manager, responsible for day-to-day planning, execution, and coordination of
activities among various stakeholders. The project was continually monitored by NITI Aayog, the Cabinet
Secretariat, and the Prime Minister’s Office (see exhibit 3). The PMU played a pivotal role in managing both
the operational and technical aspects of the DBT rollout. A key function involved close coordination with
24 State Coordinators, who served as the primary points of contact at the state level to bridge any gaps and
ensure effective communication and seamless implementation between central directives and field
operations. The project was thus ready to be rolled out.
3. Pilot Project: The DoF adopted a phased implementation strategy (see exhibit 4), beginning with a pilot
project to test the operational feasibility of the system on the ground. The pilot was launched in the Krishna
and West Godavari districts of Andhra Pradesh, selected for their readiness in terms of robust
infrastructure, reliable connectivity, and effective administrative coordination. This initial phase of the
project served as a live test for end-to-end operations including technology integration, retailer
coordination and field level execution. This pilot project provided critical insights into ground-level
challenges such as biometric authentication failures, PoS device performance in rural conditions, supply
chain tracking bottlenecks and coordination gaps between retailers, state authorities and fertilizer
companies. For instance, due to lack of digitisation of land records nationwide and delays in authentication,
the pilot design was adjusted before being relaunched. Three servers were established, one each for use of
soil health cards, Aadhar cards, and for the farmer’s land records database. Due to the lack of digitization
of land records nationwide and delays in authentication, the pilot design was adjusted and relaunched in
six districts. Following relevant refinements, the pilot project was expanded to 17 districts across various
states between October 2016 and August 2017. Building on the lessons from the pilot phase, the DBT system
entered its first wave of phased expansion in September 2017. It was progressively extended to additional
states and districts across the nation.
4. Pre Pan India-Rollout Actions: With the institutional and technical blueprint in place, the DoF initiated
pre–Pan India roll-out activities to ensure operational readiness. Fertilizer companies were provided with
detailed guidelines for procuring and deploying PoS devices at retail outlets, with the DoF closely
monitoring implementation, extensive training programmes and awareness campaigns were conducted for
retailers, wholesalers, and farmers to familiarise them with the DBT system and PoS operations. The PoS
devices were integrated with the central DBT system, supported by dashboards and reporting tools for
real-time monitoring and decision-making. Technical support was provided for device installation,
configuration, and maintenance.
A dedicated Project Monitoring Cell, interchangeably referred to as the DBT Cell, served as the
comprehensive oversight body and institutional mechanism responsible for the overall implementation
and monitoring of the DBT in Fertilizer project. Operating under this Cell, the DBT PMU provided
technical, operational, and analytical support to facilitate effective execution. Regular stakeholder

Transforming Digital Governance with Direct Benefit Transfer of Fertilizer Subsidy
consultations with fertilizer companies, state governments, and farmers’ associations fostered trust,
addressed implementation concerns, and strengthened coordination.
5.Nationwide Roll-out: The nationwide rollout of the DBT system commenced in September 2017. By
March 2018, the DBT system had achieved full-scale implementation across all states and union territories,
marking a transformative shift in India’s fertilizer subsidy delivery mechanism. A key milestone during
this phase was the large-scale deployment of more than 2.60 lakh PoS devices, installed at retail outlets
across the country, to enable Aadhaar-based beneficiary authentication and real-time transaction
recording. To ensure their effective use, the DoF in collaboration with Lead Fertilizer Supplier, conducted
more than 15,954 training sessions for retailers, wholesalers, and other stakeholders, supported by
continual on-ground technical assistance to address operational issues.
For effective oversight, the DoF introduced a suite of dashboards and reporting tools tailored to various
stakeholders. Among these, the most significant innovation was the launch of the Integrated Fertilizer
Management System also known as the ‘Urvarak’ Dashboard, which enabled state governments, district
administrations, fertilizer companies and marketing federations to track and monitor the supply,
availability, and movement of fertilizers in real time.
The Urvarak Dashboard provided customised access for various stakeholders:
• Farmers: A dedicated ‘KISAN Corner’ for farmers and the general public provided retailer listings in each
district; access to real time fertilizer stock positions at each retailer outlet; information about the maximum
retail price of fertilizers, which was available online and also integrated with the UMANG4 application,
enhancing transparency and accessibility across the system.

• State Agriculture Departments: Provided information about state-wise requirement vs. supply data, all-
India retailer sales, and purchase analysis of the top 100 buyers.

• District Collectors/District Agriculture Officers: Showed district-level fertilizer requirements, sales, stock,
material in transit, retailer/wholesaler details, expired licenses, and buyer analysis reports including top
and frequent buyers.
• Marketing Federations: Offered data on fertilizer availability at Markfed outlets and stock acknowledgment
reports.
Addressing Operational Challenges
The nationwide scale-up of the DBT system in fertilizers introduced significant operational and behavioural
challenges.
Capacity Building: Technological issues emerged as some of the most immediate challenges, especially in
rural and remote regions where poor network connectivity and PoS device malfunctions disrupted fertilizer
purchase transactions. Farmer awareness and acceptance also posed hurdles, as the DBT model represented
a major shift from traditional billing and subsidy disbursement methods. Many farmers were initially
hesitant to adopt the new digital process. Addressing these challenges required sustained efforts through
training programmes, awareness drives, and capacity-building workshops to build confidence and
facilitate adaptation. To improve connectivity and ensure smoother transactions, states were advised to

carefully select network service providers with maximum coverage. Retail outlets were equipped with
external antennas, and service providers were asked to realign them to strengthen signal availability. In
addition, PoS devices were enabled with multiple connectivity options such as Wi-Fi, LAN, and PSTN. In
areas with extremely poor connectivity—such as parts of Odisha—VSAT systems5 were deployed to
maintain stable digital operations.
Expense Management: Operational costs added another layer of complexity. The procurement and
integration of PoS devices within the system and the maintenance of these devices was a major expense.
The costs of device procurement were initially allocated amongst fertilizer companies based on their market
share. If a company failed to either procure the PoS devices or provide funds to a lead fertilizer supplier to
coordinate the procurement process, the devices were procured by a supplier and the DoF could recover
these costs from that company's subsidy payments. Subsequently, the government provided an incentive
of ₹50 per metric ton to retailers for acknowledging the receipt of fertilizers. This was the retailer margin,
which fertilizer companies were mandated to use towards purchase and maintenance of the PoS devices
and biometric scanners installed at retail shops. Infrastructure setup also represented a substantial financial
outlay. Carefully managing these expenses without compromising service quality was a constant balancing
act.
Strengthening Grievance Redressal: Recognising that these challenges could undermine the project’s
acceptance if left unresolved, the DoF embedded a multi-layered grievance redressal mechanism within
the DBT architecture. Designed to function as a proactive and responsive system, this mechanism aimed to
provide safeguards to sustain stakeholder trust and ensure farmer participation for smooth
implementation.
At its core was a dedicated toll-free helpline enabled farmers to report issues such as PoS malfunctions or
stock shortages. A network of call centres ensured timely responses to queries, while Kisan Centres
provided information about physical locations where farmers could receive in-person guidance and
troubleshooting support. To strengthen coordination among stakeholders, state-level WhatsApp groups
connected agriculture department officials, district collectors, and other key personnel for real-time
problem-solving.
Additionally, State DBT Coordinators acted as vital intermediaries between field operations and central
oversight, to provide timely resolution of technical and operational issues. For instance, in cases of PoS
device failure due to server errors, coordinators facilitated prompt escalation and rectification. By
integrating this grievance redressal framework into the rollout strategy, the DBT initiative ensured that
technical, operational and behavioural obstacles were addressed swiftly and transparently. This approach
not only minimised disruptions during implementation of the pilot projects but also laid the foundation
for smoother scaling during the nationwide rollout, thereby reinforcing the system’s credibility among
farmers and other stakeholders.

• Improved Transparency: The integration of PoS devices and Aadhaar-based authentication
enhanced transparency and accountability to the subsidy distribution process.
• Efficient Inventory Management: Real-time data on sales and stock positions enabled better
inventory management and minimised instances of stockouts or overstocking.
The DBT initiative in the fertilizer sector marked a significant step towards modernizing India’s subsidy
distribution framework. By leveraging digital technology and direct benefit transfers, the project
established a more efficient, transparent, and accountable system that continues to benefit millions of
farmers across the country.
Project Evaluation
Following the nationwide implementation of the DBT system in fertilizers, the DoF sought to evaluate the
programme’s performance and impact. To ensure an objective and comprehensive review, the DoF
engaged MicroSave Consulting (MSC), a reputed consultancy firm with expertise in evaluating large-scale
government programmes. The evaluation aimed to assess the DBT system’s effectiveness, identify
operational challenges and measure its success in modernising India’s fertilizer subsidy delivery
framework.
The study sought to answer some key questions—how had the DBT system affected fertilizer distribution
and subsidy disbursement? To what extent had it successfully enhanced transparency and reduced
leakages? What operational challenges persisted, and where were improvements still needed?
To address these questions, the MSC adopted a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative and
qualitative techniques. Surveys and interviews conducted with farmers, retailers, fertilizer companies, and
other stakeholders captured first-hand insights while field visits across diverse regions, provided
evaluators an opportunity for on-ground observations (See Exhibit 5). Transaction data from PoS devices
and central databases was also analysed to evaluate system performance and track trends in subsidy flows
and fertilizer availability. MSC submitted its report to Niti Aayog and the Cabinet Secretariat. The findings
presented a largely positive picture. Transparency and accountability in subsidy distribution had improved
significantly. By linking subsidy disbursal directly to verified sales recorded on PoS devices, the DBT
system drastically reduced diversion risks and ensured that benefits reached the farmers. Leakages—a
long-standing challenge in fertilizer subsidies—had notably declined, due to Aadhaar-based beneficiary
authentication, which minimised fraudulent claims.
Persistent Challenges
The evaluation also brought to light some persistent operational challenges. Network connectivity issues
in some remote areas continued to occasionally disrupt PoS device functionality. Many retailers still needed
ongoing technical support and refresher trainings to handle the system confidently. Farmer awareness,
though improved, remained uneven. Some farmers continued to struggle with the new processes,
highlighting the need for capacity building through sustained outreach and assistance.
The evaluation also noted the DBT system’s positive impact on fertilizer availability. Timely subsidy
payments to fertilizer companies ensured that supply chains remained stable, with minimal delays in
product flow to retailers and farmers. The evaluation underscored the importance of accurate data
management, including updating of beneficiary records through Aadhaar linkages, which was critical to
the system’s continued success.
Overall, the evaluation confirmed that DBT in the fertilizers sector had delivered on its core promises—

Transforming Digital Governance with Direct Benefit Transfer of Fertilizer Subsidy
reducing leakages, improving transparency and aligning subsidy disbursal with actual fertilizer sales—
while also highlighting the need for sustained training support, technological upgrades, and farmer
engagement to ensure its long-term sustainability and effectiveness.
Way Forward
The evaluation of the DBT system in the fertilizer sector underscores its effectiveness in transforming
subsidy delivery in India. By enhancing transparency, reducing leakages and improving fertilizer
availability, the DBT system has demonstrated significant progress in ensuring that subsidies reach the
intended beneficiaries. These outcomes illustrate the potential for replicating the DBT model across key

sectors to promote efficient and accountable resource distribution. However, sustaining the system’s long-
term impact requires addressing the challenges, particularly those related to subsidy design.

While the DBT initiative in the fertilizer sector has mitigated inefficiencies, the continued provision of
substantial subsidies under a no-denial policy to ensure farmer access, may inadvertently encourage
excessive fertilizer use, potentially leading to environmental concerns and diminishing returns.
Moving forward, a more sustainable subsidy approach—one that promotes balanced nutrient application
while safeguarding farmer access to essential inputs—is critical for achieving both agricultural productivity
and environmental sustainability. The core principles of DBT can be applied to other sectors thus rendering
DBT as a powerful model for more efficient and equitable delivery of government welfare programmes.

Case Study Title: Springs of Change: Tackling Water Scarcity in Ziro Valley
Case Study Description: This case examines the revitalization of spring water sources and the transformation of a tribal village—Sibbe, situated in Arunachal Pradesh's Ziro Valley—through integrated water resource management, community engagement, and the convergence of government schemes, including the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM). The protagonist, Smt. Tage Yani, a grassroots leader, mobilizes the community amid ecological stress and water scarcity, ushering in sustainable water governance practices. The narrative documents challenges including deforestation, declining spring flows, community resistance to water tariffs, and lack of technical expertise, and shows how they were overcome through participative planning, spring shed rejuvenation, capacity-building, and institutional innovations such as Village Water & Sanitation Committee (VWSC) empowerment and water pricing models.
Case Text:
Introduction
Nestled in the verdant folds of the Eastern Himalayas, the Ziro Valley in Arunachal Pradesh paints a picture
of serene beauty and rich tribal culture. Among the many villages dotting this landscape is Sibbe, a quiet
hamlet located 5,500 feet above sea level and home to around 600 residents, most of them from the Apatani
tribei. Historically, the villagers relied on natural springs that gushed through the terrain to meet their daily
water needs. But with time, what once flowed freely began to dry up.
The causes were many—unchecked deforestation, increasing population, and a rise in tourism brought on
by events like the Ziro Music Festival. These factors disrupted the delicate hydrological balance of the
region. Natural Springs that had sustained generations slowly dwindled. The women and children,
traditionally tasked with collecting water, had to walk longer distances to fetch it. There was no formal
purification system, and the community relied on small, often contaminated, naal1 (natural water channels)
for their daily needs.
A Leader Emerges
It was during this time of mounting crisis that Smt. Tage Yani stepped forward. A respected member of the
Gram Panchayat and an active participant in the Village Water and Sanitation Committee (VWSC), Yani
had witnessed firsthand the growing struggles of her people. Her leadership, grounded in a deep
connection to her land and culture, became the rallying point for change. She began raising her voice
against the felling of trees, arguing not just from an ecological standpoint but from a survivalist perspective.
"Water is our lifeline. When the springs began to dry up, it felt as if we were losing a part of ourselves," Yani would
often remind the villagers. Back in 2013, the VWSC had been constituted by the Public Health Engineering
i The Apatani are a tribal group from the Ziro Valley in Arunachal Pradesh, India, known for their unique sustainable
wet rice cultivation and integrated rice-fish farming
Springs of Change: Tackling Water Scarcity in Ziro Valley 3
Department (PHED). But it was only after the water crisis deepened that its true potential was realised.
With growing urgency, Yani mobilised the community, emphasising the connection between ecology and
water sustainability.
"Saving our forests is saving our water. And saving our water is saving our future," she told the youth groups
during one of her early meetings.
She reached out to youth groups, elders, and even reluctant neighbours, persuading them to participate in
the spring shedii rejuvenation programs. She emphasised transparency in decisions, which gradually began
to build trust.
Facing the Challenges
While the vision for water security was clear, the journey toward achieving it was anything but easy.
Financial limitations slowed the pace of infrastructure development, forcing the community and local
authorities to prioritise projects in phases rather than all at once. Technical expertise within the village was
limited, and small technical faults—such as leakages or pipeline damages—often caused significant
disruptions until external help could be mobilised.
Social challenges proved just as daunting. Convincing villagers to pay for a service they had historically
accessed freely was met with scepticism and occasional resistance. Some elders, recalling past government
schemes that had promised much but delivered little, were wary of investing time, labour, and trust again.
Building consensus among diverse sections of the community required patient dialogue, transparency, and
repeated assurances that this initiative would be different.
Moreover, the initial stages of the spring-shed rejuvenation projects required intensive community labour
through shramdaaniii and careful monitoring of catchment areas, which tested the villagers' stamina and
unity. Infrequent yet unpredictable changes in rainfall patterns, possibly linked to larger climatic shifts,
occasionally disrupted the careful rejuvenation efforts, adding another layer of uncertainty.
"At times, it felt like two steps forward, one step back," Yani admitted. "But we knew that real change would not
come overnight. We had to stay patient, stay united, and keep reminding ourselves why we started."
Overcoming these multifaceted challenges ultimately strengthened community ownership and resilience,
laying a stronger foundation not only for water security but for future developmental initiatives as well.
Turning the Tide: The Jal Jeevan Mission
When the Government of India launched the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in 2019, aiming to provide functional
tap water connections to every rural household, Yani saw an opportunity. Her village became one of the
early adopters in the region. With support from Public Health Engineering Department (PHED) and JJM,
a storage tank was built to capture and store spring water. Biofiltration systems were installed to ensure
water quality. For the first time, every household in Sibbe had direct tap water access—running 24/7.
Ms. Runje Pertin, a Junior Engineer with PHED, recalls the transformation:
ii Springs are formed when groundwater naturally flows onto the surface. This typically happens when
the ground water table reaches above the surface level, or if the terrain depresses sharply. Springshed is
the unit of land where rain falls (recharge area) and then emerges at discharge points of the spring. It is
the natural unit for revival and management of spring. According to the NITI Aayog report (2018), there
are five million springs across India, of which nearly 3 million are in the Indian Himalayan Region.
iii Shramdaan (Shram meaning "labour" and Daan meaning "donation") is a Hindi word which refers to the
voluntary contribution of physical labour for the welfare of the community. It is a practice deeply rooted in Indian
tradition, emphasizing selfless service and the dignity of labour as means to foster social development and harmony.
Springs of Change: Tackling Water Scarcity in Ziro Valley 4
“Earlier, people collected water from naalas with no purification. With the new system in place, we could assure clean
drinking water. But more than infrastructure, it was the community ownership led by Yani that ensured its success.”
The Jal Jeevan Mission recognised Sibbe as a ‘Har Ghar Jaliv’village. With all households covered, the focus
shifted to sustainability. A tiered pricing model was introduced to ensure the financial sustainability of the
system. New users paid an upfront fee of ₹500 per tap connection, while monthly charges were fixed at
₹100 per connection. For instance, a household with two tap connections would pay ₹200 per month. While
a more rational approach would be to adopt volumetric pricing based on actual water usage, this would
require installing metered connections in every household—something envisioned for the future as the
system evolves. These funds, managed transparently by the VWSC, covered routine maintenance and
minor repairs. Villagers contributed labour under the traditional practice of shramdaan3, reinforcing
community ownership.
From Scarcity to Sustainability
The results of the community's efforts became visible within a few years, validating the vision and hard
work that had gone into the transformation. Springs that had once dried to a mere trickle began showing
signs of revival. Water flow, though initially modest, steadily strengthened, breathing new life into the
natural ecosystems of Sibbe. Farmers noticed that their fields stayed greener for longer, and small kitchen
gardens, once abandoned due to water scarcity, began to thrive again.
Vegetative cover around the critical spring catchment areas improved significantly. Community patrols,
awareness campaigns, and a collective sense of responsibility led to a drastic reduction in deforestation.
Where barren slopes had once accelerated runoff and erosion, young saplings and native shrubs now
anchored the soil, slowly restoring the valley's natural water-retaining capacity.
The change in mindset regarding water tariffs was equally striking. In the beginning, many had resisted
the idea of paying for something they believed nature had provided for free. But as transparency in fund
usage grew and the villagers saw firsthand how regular maintenance prevented breakdowns and ensured
clean, reliable water, attitudes shifted. “Now we pay happily because we understand where the money goes and
how it helps us,” said a resident, reflecting the growing sense of ownership and accountability.
Reflecting on the transformation, Yani remained modest about her role.
"This is not just my achievement; it belongs to every resident of Sibbe. It is the success of an entire community, not
just one individual," she emphasized, highlighting the deep sense of ownership and unity that fueled Sibbe’s
revival.
The Village Water and Sanitation Committee (VWSC), once seen as a bureaucratic formality, evolved into
a vibrant center for planning, dialogue, and decision-making—not just about water, but also about broader
development goals. Discussions on sanitation, waste management, afforestation, and even tourism
regulation found a platform through the VWSC’s regular meetings.
Tourists continued to visit Sibbe, drawn by its scenic beauty and cultural richness, but now under the
watchful eyes of eco-guides and community-led awareness campaigns. New guidelines restricted activities
that could harm water sources or local flora, helping to strike a balance between welcoming visitors and
protecting the fragile environment.
The success story of Sibbe did not go unnoticed. Neighboring villages, facing similar challenges, began
reaching out to learn from Sibbe’s model of integrated water management, community ownership, and
iv As per Operational Guidelines of Jal Jeevan Mission, after making provision of tap connections to all rural households in a village,
Rural Water Supply Department of State declares the village as ‘Har Ghar Jal’ village (translates to ‘Water to Every Household’)
on the basis of work completion report of the field engineer associated with the project.
Springs of Change: Tackling Water Scarcity in Ziro Valley 5
sustainable development. What started as a response to a local crisis slowly blossomed into a regional
movement for ecological restoration and empowered self-governance.
Broader Lessons
Sibbe’s transformation offers a powerful and enduring message: sustainable change is most effective when
it begins at the grassroots. True resilience is built not by imposing external solutions, but by empowering
local communities to take ownership of their challenges and solutions. The case highlights the critical
importance of blending traditional knowledge—rooted in the lived experiences and wisdom of the
people—with modern scientific methods, technology, and policy frameworks. Neither alone would have
sufficed; it was their thoughtful combination that enabled the revival of Sibbe’s springs and social fabric.
While the infrastructure development and financial support provided by the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM)
served as the catalyst, it was the active community participation—ignited and sustained by the unwavering
leadership of Tage Yani—that turned ambition into reality. Her ability to bridge the old and the new, to
honor tradition while embracing innovation, helped the community overcome suspicion, inertia, and
logistical challenges.
For policymakers, development practitioners, and administrators, Sibbe’s story offers a compelling
argument for adopting hybrid models of development. Large-scale, top-down programs achieve lasting
impact only when rooted deeply in local contexts and steered by those they aim to serve. Local ownership—
ensured through genuine engagement, trust-building, and transparent governance—can transform even
the most complex interventions into sustainable success stories.
Moreover, community-based governance models create a virtuous cycle: when people see visible outcomes
of their efforts, participation deepens, social trust strengthens, and behavioral changes, such as willingness
to pay for services or protect resources, become self-sustaining. By nurturing these dynamics thoughtfully,
governments and organizations can overcome the common pitfalls of rural development projects and build
systems that endure beyond project timelines and funding cycles.
In essence, Sibbe teaches that when people are not just beneficiaries but partners in progress, development
is no longer a program—it becomes a movement.
Conclusion
The Ziro Valley, once teetering on the brink of ecological and social stress, stands today as a beacon of what
integrated, community-led water management can achieve. Where once there was fear of springs drying
up, forests vanishing, and traditions eroding, there is now a renewed sense of vitality and pride. Sibbe's
story is not merely about the construction of pipelines and storage tanks; it is about people rediscovering
their deep, almost sacred, connection with nature—one that had sustained them for generations and now
holds the key to their future.
At the heart of this transformation is the spirit of collective action, and the leadership of a woman who
chose not to accept decline as inevitable. Tage Yani refused to wait for solutions to come from outside;
instead, she mobilized her community, combined traditional wisdom with modern tools, and proved that
change is possible when courage meets collaboration.
The success of Sibbe is also a reminder that resilient systems are those built together—through shared
responsibility, mutual trust, and the belief that every individual’s contribution matters. It demonstrates
that real, lasting progress is not delivered to communities; it is created by them.
Springs of Change: Tackling Water Scarcity in Ziro Valley 6
For communities across India and around the world grappling with water scarcity and environmental
degradation, the story of Sibbe offers more than just a technical model—it offers hope. Hope that even in
the face of mounting challenges, grassroots leadership, community participation, and a respectful
partnership with nature can chart a path toward a sustainable and dignified future.

Case Study Title: Community-Based Forest Fire Preventionand Management in Bandipur TigerReserve, Karnataka, India
Case Study Description: This case examines the transformation of forest fire management at Bandipur Tiger Reserve (2020–2023) following devastating fires in 2019. The Karnataka Forest Department adopted an innovative community-based model that redefined local communities as conservation partners rather than threats. Addressing challenges such as climate vulnerability, invasive Lantana camara, limited resources, and strained community relations, the initiative combined volunteer fire watchers, early warning systems, indigenous knowledge, livelihood-linked Lantana removal, economic incentives, and capacity building. The results were significant: fire incidents fell by 63%, burned area reduced by 74%, response time dropped sharply, and alternative livelihoods were created for hundreds of families. The case demonstrates that sustainable conservation depends on community participation, shared economic benefits, and integrating local knowledge with modern governance tools.
Case Text:
Background
The Bandipur Tiger Reserve, located in the southern Indian state of Karnataka, spans approximately
1,036.20 square kilometres (km2), comprising 872.24 km2 of core area and 163.962 km2 as forested
buffer area. The forest type in the eastern part of the tiger reserve is scrub forest (dry deciduous scrub),
the central part consists of dry deciduous forest, and the western part comprises moist deciduous forest
within the ecologically significant Western Ghats. Established in 1973 as a tiger reserve under Project
Tiger, Bandipur is recognized for its exceptional biodiversity, hosting approximately 150 resident
tigers; 138 resident leopards; 1,116 elephants; 994 Indian gaurs; as well as numerous other endangered
species, including dholes (wild dogs) and sloth bears, according to 2022 data from the Karnataka Forest
Department. The reserve serves as a critical wildlife corridor connecting several protected areas,
including Nagarhole National Park, Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary, and Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary.
The region experiences a tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons. Annual rainfall averages
about 800 mm, concentrated between June and September during the southwest monsoon. The
prolonged dry season from January to May creates ideal conditions for forest fires, with temperatures
often exceeding 35°C and humidity dropping below 30%. These factors, combined with the
accumulation of dry leaf litter and grasses, create a high-risk environment for fire ignition and rapid
spread.
Historically, the reserve has experienced recurring fire incidents, with particularly severe episodes in
2012 (Swarajya Staff 2019), 2017, and 2019 (“Wildfire Destroys” 2019). The 2019 fire was especially
devastating, burning over 10,000 acres of forest habitat over 5 days. When the fire was finally doused,
a total of 3,160 ha had been lost, according to data provided by the Karnataka Forest Department. This
incident received national attention (Ananth et al. 2019) and prompted serious re-examination of
existing fire management approaches. Post-fire assessments revealed significant losses to biodiversity,
with damaged bamboo thickets, destroyed ground nesting sites, and depleted food sources for
herbivores.
“The devastating 2019 fire was a turning point,” explains Conservator of Forests (CF) Ramesh Kumar,
who has spearheaded initiatives within the Bandipur Tiger Reserve. “During our post-fire assessment,
we found that areas dominated by Lantana camara had experienced the most severe damage. In some
