sections of the tiger reserve, the fire had completely consumed the understory and damaged the canopy
as well.”
A recent study (Rastogi 2020) found that Lantana camara, a tropical American shrub, has invaded more
than 40% of India’s tiger range. The Shivalik hills, Central India, and the Southern Western Ghats are
the worst hit. With its ability to adapt to a changing climate, lantana can tolerate high temperatures and
humidity. The species now threatens about 300,000 km2 of Indian forests.
The human context surrounding Bandipur adds complexity to fire management. The reserve is
bordered by 149 villages with a combined population of approximately 137,980 people, many from
indigenous communities with centuries-old relationships with the forest. Traditional agricultural
practices, including the use of controlled burning to clear agricultural plots and stimulate new grass
growth for cattle, have sometimes contributed to uncontrolled fires when winds shift or conditions
change unexpectedly.
This complex ecological and social landscape necessitated a new approach to fire management that
could address both the environmental vulnerabilities and the human dimensions of the challenge.
The forest fire risk zonation map of the Bandipur Tiger Reserve was prepared using historical data on
forest fire incidents; land use and land cover maps; forest type and vegetation maps; and other historical
weather parameters such as temperature, rainfall, relative humidity, and wind speed. In addition, other
factors such as soil parameters, slope, and aspect of the area were also considered.

Challenges
The Bandipur Tiger Reserve faced a multifaceted set of challenges related to fire prevention and
management.
1. Environmental Vulnerabilities
The reserve’s dry deciduous forest ecosystem is naturally fire-prone, as the seasonal drying of
vegetation creates significant fuel loads. Climate change has exacerbated these conditions, with
meteorological data showing a 1.2°C rise in average summer temperatures over the past 3 decades and
increasingly frequent drought periods. These changes have extended the high-risk fire season by
approximately 3 weeks compared to historical patterns.
The topography of Bandipur, characterized by rolling hills and valleys with elevations ranging from
700 to 1,200 meters above sea level, creates fire behaviour complexities. Fires can spread rapidly
upslope and become difficult to contain in remote areas with limited access. Some sections of the
reserve have steep terrain that is nearly inaccessible to firefighting vehicles, necessitating manual
intervention.
A significant environmental vulnerability that exacerbated fire risks was the widespread invasion of
Lantana camara throughout the reserve. As conservator of forests, Ramesh Kumar explains, “Lantana
camara has been one of the most problematic invasive species in Bandipur for several decades now. It
was introduced during the British colonial period as an ornamental plant, but it spread aggressively
throughout the Western Ghats. What makes Lantana particularly dangerous from a fire management
perspective is its structure and composition. The plant contains volatile oils that make it highly
flammable, and it creates dense thickets that can reach up to 3 meters in height. This undergrowth
forms continuous fuel loads across the landscape.”
Kumar’s team observed that areas with high Lantana density were experiencing fires that spread up to
three times faster than areas without Lantana. Additionally, these fires burned more intensely and
caused greater damage to native vegetation. Ecological surveys indicated that approximately 40% of

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 4
the reserve was moderately to highly invaded by Lantana camara, creating a serious fire hazard. Other
studies support the findings of the survey conducted by the Karnataka Forest Department in
collaboration with The Shola Trust, which mapped the distribution of Lantana camara in the Bandipur
Tiger Reserve, Karnataka. The study concluded that 38% of the tiger reserve had a dense presence of
Lantana, 50% had a moderate presence, and 12% had a low presence. Forest areas with dense and
moderate Lantana presence were highly susceptible to forest fires, and the damage caused to the forest
was intense. These Lantana shrubs also posed a problem for tigers, as their dense structure restricted
movement and affected predation behaviour.
2. Resource Limitations
Prior to the community initiative (Exhibit 2), the Karnataka Forest Department was responsible for fire
management across the entire reserve with limited resources. The department maintained a staff of
approximately 145 forest guards and rangers, inadequate for comprehensive monitoring of the vast
area. Fire detection relied primarily on 15 watchtowers, many of which were in poor condition with

limited visibility. Firefighting equipment was similarly constrained, with only four dedicated fire-
suppression vehicles, insufficient water storage facilities, and outdated communication systems.

Response times to fire incidents averaged 45–60 minutes, allowing small fires to grow to unmanageable
proportions before intervention. A major portion of the annual budget allocation for fire management
was directed toward the maintenance of fire lines (cleared strips that function as a barrier to fire spread)
and payment for the fire watchers. These fire lines, while important, covered only 73% of the needed
areas and were often inadequately maintained.
3. Social and Cultural Dynamics
Historical tensions between forest authorities and local communities complicated collaborative
approaches to fire management. Restrictive conservation policies implemented in the 1990s had limited
traditional forest access and livelihood practices without providing adequate alternatives, creating
resentment among local populations. Many villages practiced traditional agricultural techniques that
included controlled burning during the dry season. While these practices had been managed
sustainably for generations, population growth and changing land use patterns had made them
increasingly risky. However, attempts to simply prohibit these practices without acknowledging their
cultural significance and practical utility had proven ineffective. Educational gaps regarding fire
ecology and prevention techniques existed within both forest department staff and local communities.
Scientific understanding of fire behaviour and management strategies was not effectively integrated
with traditional knowledge systems, leading to missed opportunities for synergistic approaches.
4. Infrastructural Deficiencies
The reserve’s fire management infrastructure was inadequate for the scale of the challenge. Cleared fire
break areas, designed to stop fire spread, covered only 2,807 km of the required 3,565 km. Water sources
for firefighting were limited, with only 47 artificial water holes and check dams accessible during the
peak fire season. Road networks for rapid fire response were incomplete, with approximately 40% of
the reserve more than 5 km from the nearest accessible road. This severely hampered the ability to
deploy firefighting resources quickly in remote areas. Communication infrastructure was similarly
deficient, with radio coverage reaching only 65% of the reserve area and cellular network coverage
limited to areas near the periphery. This created significant blind spots where fires could burn
undetected for hours or even days. These multidimensional challenges required a comprehensive
approach that could address environmental vulnerabilities, resource constraints, social dynamics, and
infrastructural deficiencies simultaneously.

Case Study Title: Community-Based Forest Fire Preventionand Management in Bandipur TigerReserve, Karnataka, India
Case Study Description: continued
Case Text:
Solution: Community-Based Fire Management Initiative
In response to the escalating fire-related challenges, the Karnataka Forest Department, in collaboration
with local nongovernment organizations and the National Tiger Conservation Authority, launched a
comprehensive community-based fire management program in 2021. This initiative represented a
paradigm shift from the traditional top-down approach to a participatory model that leveraged local
knowledge, capacity, and commitment.
“When we launched the comprehensive community-based fire management program in 2021–22, I
insisted that Lantana control be included as a core component rather than as a separate program,”
explained CF Kumar. “We could not effectively address fire risk without dealing with this invasive
species. The major challenge was to understand the existing link between forest fires and invasive alien
species, which remained very critical and was thus the real challenge in addressing the integrated
approach of handling fire with alien species. Once this linkage was understood, it became much easier
for us to develop suitable strategies to tackle them.”
Establishing authentic partnerships that positioned communities as key decision-makers rather than
mere program executors, the initiative fostered genuine local ownership and commitment. This
collaborative approach differed from conventional community engagement strategies by placing local
populations, particularly indigenous tribes, at the center as primary stakeholders. The program
framework was specifically designed to generate mutually beneficial outcomes for both tribal
communities and wildlife conservation, particularly in strengthening tiger protection.
Kumar’s team strategically engaged local tribes as principal partners in manually removing Lantana

camara, an invasive plant species, rather than employing mechanical methods. Although machine-
based removal would have been more cost-effective than hand removal, the team deliberately chose

the manual approach (Exhibit 3). This decision prioritized minimal soil disruption while
simultaneously creating job opportunities for tribal members within their ancestral territories,
preventing the need for them to seek work in distant districts or states.
The key innovation lay in transforming the traditional engagement model from one in which
communities simply implemented externally designed programs to one in which they actively shaped
and benefited from conservation initiatives alongside wildlife protection goals.
This integrated approach was novel, as invasive species management and fire management had
traditionally been treated as separate domains with separate budgets and teams.
Some of the initiatives taken to prevent and manage fire are as follows:
1. Fire Watcher Volunteer Program
The tribal fire watchers and tribal leaders volunteer group program formed the cornerstone of the
community-based initiative. This program recognized that residents possessed intimate knowledge of
the landscape, seasonal patterns, and fire behaviour that could significantly enhance monitoring and
early response capabilities. Each participating village established a fire prevention unit called a Static
Fire Protection camp and a Mobile Fire Protection camp, consisting of 8-12 tribal fire watchers selected
through a community-driven process. Preference was given to individuals with forest knowledge,
physical fitness, and commitment to conservation. These tribal fire watchers and tribal leader volunteer
groups received comprehensive training conducted by forest department officials and fire management
experts. The training curriculum covered fire behaviour principles and methods for anticipating spread
patterns; safe firefighting techniques appropriate for different vegetation types; the use of basic
firefighting equipment (such as fire beaters, petrol backpack blowers, knapsack power sprayers and
bill hooks); communication protocols and emergency procedures; first aid for fire-related injuries; and
global positioning system (GPS) navigation and mapping techniques.

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 6
Volunteers were organized into rotating patrol teams that monitored high-risk areas throughout the
fire season. Each team followed designated routes that covered fire-prone zones, with special attention
to areas with historical fire occurrences. Patrol schedules were designed to ensure continuous coverage
while accommodating volunteers’ other responsibilities.
Equipment provided to volunteer teams included distinctive uniforms for identification and safety;
communication devices (walkie-talkies and mobile phones); basic firefighting tools; first aid kits; GPS
devices for accurate location reporting; and protective gear including masks, gloves, and boots. The
budget for equipment, communication devices, and basic fire aids came from different schemes and
sources, including state government schemes; central government programs such as CAMPA,
corporate social responsibility funds from institutions such as ICICI Bank, and the Tiger Conservation
Fund of the Bandipur Tiger Conservation Foundation. Although there was a resource crunch, forest
fire control and the management of invasive species were treated as topmost priorities, and funds were
mobilized from different sources.
The program established clear protocols for volunteer authority and responsibility. Volunteers were
empowered to conduct initial suppression activities for small fires but were trained to request
immediate support for larger incidents. This tiered response system allowed for appropriate handling
of different fire scenarios. In 2023–24, the program had expanded to include 540 tribal fire watchers and
50 tribal leaders as active tribal leaders volunteer groups across all 136 villages, creating a human
monitoring network that effectively multiplied the forest department’s surveillance capacity. At
present, there are 540 trained forest fire watchers, 12 fire tender vehicles, 32 quick response vehicles,
and 54 vacuum blowers for preventing and managing fire.
2. Early Warning Systems
The initiative implemented a multilayered early warning system that combined traditional observation
methods with modern technology.
“Though the early warning system for the detection of forest fire was working very well, the local
traditional methods were working extremely well in the timely detection of forest fires through fire
watch towers. Our traditional fire watch towers with one or two fire watchers remain very efficient and
effective in the timely detection of smoke or fire and subsequently inform the field staff (static fire
protection camps) without losing any time. All field staff deployed at strategic places will spot the fire
immediately and extinguish it using minimal personnel and resources. This local and traditional system
of timely forest fire detection remains highly effective and efficient compared with satellite-based early
warning systems. Because of advance planning and advance preparation, resource mobilization and
capacity building were done meticulously on time without any lapses, ultimately yielding positive
results,” says Ramesh.
2.1 Watchtower Network
The existing network of 19 fire watchtowers was renovated, and 10 additional towers were constructed

at strategic locations identified through fire risk mapping. Each tower was equipped with solar-
powered communication systems, high-powered binoculars, weather monitoring instruments, and

emergency supplies. The towers were staffed during daylight hours throughout the fire season, with
observation duties shared between forest department staff and trained community volunteers. This
arrangement provided comprehensive visual coverage of approximately 85% of the reserve area.
2.2 Digital Reporting System
A custom smartphone application, Bandipur Fire Watch, was developed specifically for the initiative.
This application enabled volunteers and staff to report fire sightings with precise GPS coordinates,
upload photographs of fire conditions, receive real-time updates on fire status and response activities,
and access fire prevention resources and emergency contacts.

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 7
The application also incorporated offline functionality to support areas with poor network connectivity,
automatically syncing data when connections became available. In 2023, the application had been
downloaded by more than 600 users and had facilitated the early reporting of 78 fire incidents.
2.3 Satellite Integration
The program established a partnership with the Indian Space Research Organisation to integrate
satellite-based fire detection into the early warning system. Through this collaboration, the Forest Fire
Alert System 4.0 provided near-real-time alerts on thermal anomalies detected within the reserve
boundaries. These alerts were automatically routed to the central dispatch centre and to field personnel
operating near the detected anomaly.
2.4 Weather Forecasting
A localized fire weather forecasting system was developed in collaboration with the Indian
Meteorological Department. This system analysed temperature, humidity, wind conditions, and fuel
moisture to generate daily fire risk assessments for different sectors of the reserve. These forecasts
guided the deployment of additional resources to high-risk areas during critical periods.
2.5 Central Dispatch Centre
A modernized control room was established at the reserve headquarters, at the office of the Conservator
of Forests and Director, Bandipur Tiger Reserve. This facility served as the central hub for the early
warning system, with capabilities including 24/7 staffing during the fire season, real-time monitoring
of all fire detection sources, coordination of response resources, documentation of fire incidents and
responses, and analysis of fire patterns and trends. The multilayered approach ensured redundancy in
the detection system, significantly reducing the likelihood that fires would go unnoticed during the
critical initial stages when suppression is most effective.

3. Traditional Knowledge Integration
Rather than dismissing traditional practices, the program took a novel approach by systematically
documenting and integrating indigenous knowledge into the fire management strategy.
3.1 Knowledge Documentation
A comprehensive ethnographic study was conducted to document traditional fire management
practices among the communities surrounding Bandipur. This research, led by anthropologists in
collaboration with community elders, revealed sophisticated understanding of fire behaviour, seasonal
indicators, and suppression techniques that had been passed down through generations. Key insights
included traditional calendars for controlled burning that minimized ecological impact, recognition of
specific plant species as indicators of fire risk, local techniques for creating effective fire breaks using
minimal resources, and weather prediction methods based on observation of natural phenomena.
Every year, before the start of the forest fire season, workshops on forest fire management were
conducted with all stakeholders, such as frontline staff, Eco- Development Committee members, and

leaders of tribal communities. This process helped identify vulnerable fire-prone areas and fire-
sensitive spots, leading to the preparation of forest fire risk and vulnerability maps. These efforts

culminated in the development of an annual fire management plan, prepared before the onset of the
fire season, which helped frontline staff make early preparations and deploy available resources to
prevent and control forest fires.
In addition, fire lines and fire breaks were created and maintained before the start of each fire season,
which greatly contributed to preventing forest fires. Once the fire season began, daily weather
parameters were collected, monitored, and disseminated to field staff to ensure preparedness and rapid

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 8
response. For example, days with high temperatures, low humidity, and strong winds were taken very
seriously, and staff were cautioned accordingly to prevent and control forest fires. Frontline staff and
drones were deployed at strategic locations along the forest boundary to restrict people from entering
the forest and thereby reduce the risk of fire incidents.
3.2 Modified Controlled Burning
Based on the documented knowledge, the program developed a modified controlled burning protocol
that combined traditional timing and techniques with modern safety measures. These carefully
managed burns were conducted under the strict supervision of the forest department during suitable
weather conditions to reduce fuel loads in strategic areas.
The controlled burning program focused on creating buffer zones around vulnerable ecosystems,
reducing fuel accumulation in identified high-risk areas, maintaining grassland habitats for grazing
species, and demonstrating proper burning techniques to community members.
3.3 Knowledge Exchange Forums
Regular knowledge exchange forums were established to facilitate dialogue between scientific experts
and traditional knowledge holders. Conducted in local languages and with cultural sensitivity, these
forums created opportunities for mutual learning and collaborative problem-solving.
Topics discussed included changing fire patterns due to climate shifts; adaptation of traditional
practices to current conditions; integration of modern tools with traditional techniques; and
documentation and preservation of traditional knowledge. These forums fostered mutual respect
between forest officials and community members, transforming the relationship from one of suspicion
to one of collaborative partnership.
3.4 Curriculum Development
The insights gained through knowledge documentation were incorporated into a locally relevant fire
management curriculum used in community training programs. This curriculum acknowledged the
value of traditional knowledge while supplementing it with scientific concepts and modern techniques.
It was delivered through hands-on workshops in village settings, field demonstrations of integrated
techniques, peer-to-peer teaching by community experts, and illustrated manuals in local languages.
By 2023, more than 800 community members had been trained through this culturally appropriate
curriculum, creating a broad base of informed practitioners.

4. Lantana Camara Eradication Initiative
In recognition of the significant fire risk posed by the invasive Lantana camara, a dedicated eradication
initiative was integrated into the broader fire management program. As CF Ramesh Kumar explained,
“We recognized early on that manual removal of Lantana across the entire reserve would be impossible
with just forest department resources. The scale was too vast. We needed community participation, but
we also needed to make this participation economically viable.”
Cut-Root-Stock Method
The team developed what they called the cut-root-stock method for Lantana removal. This
approach involved cutting the Lantana at its base, extracting the root crown, and using the
removed biomass to create value-added products. Although labour-intensive, the method
proved more effective than chemical approaches, which could have harmed the ecosystem.

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 9
Dedicated Lantana removal teams were organized in each participating village, operating
separately from—but in coordination with—the fire watcher teams. These teams, typically
consisting of 10–15 individuals, received specialized training in species identification, safe
removal techniques, and utilization of plant material. They were equipped with proper tools, including
machetes, root extractors, gloves, and protective eyewear.
Economic Value Creation
Instead of treating Lantana as waste, the initiative developed several ways to convert it into valuable
products, creating economic incentives for removal. “We established a Lantana Crafts Centre in
Melukamanahalli, where community members learn to create furniture, household items, and
decorative pieces from Lantana stems,” reports Kumar. “The woody stems are surprisingly durable and
flexible when properly processed. We have trained over 90 artisans, through three self-help groups
(SHGs), who now produce chairs, tables, baskets, and other items that are sold to tourists and through
online platforms.”
Lantana removal and grassland development had a significant economic impact on the lives of local
tribal communities. Therefore, Kumar’s team developed an activity or program called “Generating
Wealth out of Waste: Win-Win Situation for Tigers and Tribes.” The activity was linked to the Lantana
eradication and grassland development program, under which local tribal communities were trained
to make handicrafts from Lantana stems—material previously regarded as waste generated through the
removal program.
Additionally, the program partnered with a biofuel company that can process Lantana biomass into
fuel pellets. The leaves and smaller stems, which were unsuitable for handicraft production, were
converted into these pellets. This partnership created an additional revenue stream while ensuring that
all removed materials are utilized.
Strategic Prioritization
The initiative adopted a strategic approach to Lantana removal based on fire risk assessment. The team
created detailed maps that overlaid Lantana density with historical fire incidents and other risk factors,
such as proximity to human settlements and roads. This analysis helped identify priority zones where
Lantana removal would have the greatest impact on reducing fire risk.
They began by creating 100-meter buffer zones around critical fire lines and access roads, ensuring that
these strategic areas remained functional during fire incidents. Then they focused on natural recovery
zones—areas where native forests had strong regeneration potential once Lantana was removed.
Wildlife corridors and grazing grounds for herbivores were also prioritized as ecologically significant
areas. By 2022, they had cleared approximately 1,293 hectares of high-density Lantana areas and treated
another 2,300 hectares of moderate-density areas.
Ecological Restoration
To prevent reinvasion, Lantana removal was integrated with ecological restoration efforts. “Removing
Lantana is only the first step; we need to ensure that native vegetation reclaims these areas. Otherwise,
Lantana or other invasives will simply return,” emphasized Kumar.
After Lantana removal, assisted restoration was carried out using native seedlings in areas where
natural regeneration was slow. The effort proved particularly successful with pioneer species such as
Terminalia tomentosa, Anogeissus latifolia, and native bamboos. Native grasses were also reintroduced to
reduce fire risk and provide grazing for wildlife, thereby maintaining the habitat for herbivores such
as deer and elephants.
5. Economic Incentives

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 10
Recognizing that sustainable involvement required tangible benefits, the program developed a
comprehensive economic incentive structure.
Fire Watcher Stipends
Active fire watchers received modest stipends during the high-risk season (January to May). These

payments, averaging ₹613 per day, supplemented household incomes during the agricultural off-
season when alternative job opportunities were limited. To ensure accountability, payments were

linked to performance metrics, including attendance at scheduled patrols, timely reporting of
observations, participation in regular training sessions, and contribution to community awareness
activities (Exhibit 4). The stipend program injected approximately ₹5.03 million ($44,000) annually into
the local economy while ensuring consistent monitoring coverage.
Community Development Fund
The Bandipur Tiger Conservation Foundation (TCF) Fund was used for the Eco-Development activities
of the local communities through the 44 Eco-Development committees (EDC) of the Bandipur Tiger
Reserve. Many dormant EDCs were revived into active EDCs and seven newly formed EDCs were
funded with ₹100,000 seed money each. These funds were directed toward community-identified
priorities, including water infrastructure improvements, educational facilities and materials, healthcare
services, agricultural enhancement projects, and community hall construction or renovation. Between
2020 and 2023, villages received community development grants amounting to ₹7.8 million ($104,000),
creating tangible benefits visible to all community members.
Ecotourism Opportunities
The program developed community-based ecotourism initiatives that created additional economic
incentives for forest preservation. Local youth were trained as nature guides, and villages developed
visitor experiences showcasing local culture, cuisine, and conservation efforts. Ecotourism
developments included home-stay accommodations in peripheral villages, cultural demonstration
centres, nature trails guided by community members, traditional cuisine experiences, and conservation
education programs. These initiatives generated approximately ₹5.6 million ($75,000) in revenue in
2022–2023, with 75% of proceeds flowing directly to community participants.
6. Capacity Building
Ongoing training programs built local expertise in fire management and related conservation skills.
The capacity building program adopted a tiered approach that allowed participants to progressively
develop their skills:
(a) Basic Level: Introduction to fire prevention concepts and simple suppression techniques (1-day
program)
(b) Intermediate Level: Advanced fire behaviour understanding and team-based response strategies (3-
day program)
(c) Advanced Level: Leadership skills, complex fire management, and training capabilities (5-day
program)
This system created pathways for community members to develop professional-level expertise, with
advanced trainees eventually serving as trainers for new participants.
Fire Line Maintenance
Community members received specialized training in fire line creation and maintenance techniques.
This training covered strategic placement of fire lines based on topography and vegetation; proper
width and clearing techniques for different vegetation types; maintenance schedules and methods;

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 11
integration of fire lines with natural barriers; and reduced-impact methods for sensitive areas. By
transferring these skills to community members, the program expanded the capacity for fire line
maintenance to 2,807 km by 2023.
Emergency Response
The comprehensive emergency response training thoroughly prepared community members to act
effectively during fire incidents. Participants learned crucial incident command principles and
established a clear chain of communication to ensure coordinated responses during emergencies. Safe
evacuation procedures were taught for both people and livestock, recognizing the importance of
protecting all living beings within the community. The training also covered triage approaches for
managing multiple fire outbreaks simultaneously, enabling communities to prioritize response efforts
based on severity and risk. Participants also learned effective coordination methods with professional
firefighting resources (Exhibit 5), creating seamless integration between community first responders
and official emergency services. Post-fire assessment and reporting techniques were included to ensure
proper documentation and learning from each incident. This training was continuously reinforced
through regular drills and simulations conducted under varying conditions, including nighttime
scenarios and challenging weather situations, building comprehensive readiness for actual emergencies
across different contexts and circumstances.
Ecological Monitoring
Select community members received specialized training in basic ecological monitoring techniques to
assess fire impacts and track ecosystem recovery over time. Participants learned vegetation sampling
methods that allowed them to document changes in plant communities before and after fire events.
Wildlife sign identification and recording techniques enabled forest staff to track the presence and
movements of animals returning to recovering areas. Photo point monitoring was established at
strategic locations to visually document landscape changes over time, creating a powerful visual record
of ecological transformation. Basic data collection and management skills were taught to ensure
accurate recording and preservation of observations for future analysis and comparison. Participatory
mapping techniques allowed forest staff to document spatial patterns of fire impact and recovery across
the landscape. This comprehensive training enabled meaningful community participation in post-fire
assessments and long-term monitoring of ecosystem recovery processes. The gathered information
created a valuable feedback loop that continuously informed adaptive management approaches,
allowing the program to evolve based on observed ecological responses rather than rigid
predetermined plans.
Leadership Development
The program made significant investments in developing local conservation leaders who could sustain
the initiative beyond the initial project period, ensuring long-term community ownership. Participants
received training in conflict resolution and community mobilization skills, enabling them to navigate
disagreements and build consensus within diverse community contexts. Project planning and
management training equipped local leaders with the ability to design, implement, and evaluate their
own conservation initiatives independently. Communication and advocacy techniques helped
participants to effectively share their work with wider audiences and to advocate for policy changes
when needed. Financial management training for conservation initiatives promoted transparent and
accountable use of resources, building trust among community members and external partners.
Networking opportunities with government and representatives of nongovernment organizations
created valuable relationships that supported ongoing work and opened access to additional resources
and collaboration. By 2023, more than 50 community members, including Tribal leaders, had
successfully completed the comprehensive leadership development program and were actively leading
various aspects of the fire management initiative, ranging from frontline fire prevention to policy
advocacy at the district and state levels.

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 12
Implementation Process
The initiative was methodically rolled out in carefully planned phases to allow for learning and
adaptation. During Phase 1 in 2021–22, five pilot villages were strategically selected based on their
location near high-risk zones and demonstrated willingness to participate in the program. This initial
phase established the foundation through comprehensive training, equipment distribution, and the
creation of effective communication systems. Phase 2, spanning 2022–2023, built upon the evaluation
of the pilot phase and expanded the program to 53 tribal villages, incorporating valuable lessons
learned and refining protocols based on field experience. During Phase 3, 2023– 2024, coverage
extended to all 100 villages bordering the reserve, implementing a system of graduated responsibilities
based on each community’s demonstrated capacity and commitment. This phased approach allowed
for organic growth of the program, building on successes and addressing challenges before full-scale
implementation.

Results
The initiative resulted in three tangible outcomes.
First, the Lantana removal and grassland development program benefited the herbivore and ungulate
populations by restoring grassland habitats, which in turn supported tigers and other co-predators.
Second, the waste material (Lantana stems) generated from the Lantana removal and grassland
development program was used as the basis for producing Lantana crafts through a skills development
program called “Generating Wealth out of Waste: Win-Win Situation for the Tigers and Tribes.” This
community development program formed SHGs among local tribal communities, training members to
make handicrafts and household articles out of the waste generated from the Lantana removal program.
Third, once Lantana camara was removed and grasslands for herbivores were restored, the area became
free from excess fuel material, making the wildlife habitat less prone to forest fires, as Lantana
previously accelerated their spread.
Fire Incidence Reduction
After three full fire seasons of implementation from 2020 to 2023, the program achieved remarkable
and measurable results in reducing fire incidents across the protected area. The region experienced a
significant 73% decrease in fire incidents compared to the baseline period of 2015–2019, dramatically
reducing ecosystem damage and economic losses. The total area burned decreased by 85%, preserving
vital wildlife habitat and protecting forest resources. The average fire response time decreased from 45
minutes to under 18 minutes, allowing for rapid containment of small fires before they could spread
into major conflagrations. As CF Kumar observed in his assessment, “In areas where we have
substantially reduced Lantana coverage, we have seen a 85% decrease in fire incidents compared to the
reserve average of 74%. More importantly, when fires do occur in these treated areas, they spread more
slowly and are easier to contain.” This observation highlights the interconnected nature of invasive
species management and fire prevention, demonstrating how ecological restoration contributes directly
to reduced fire risk.
Environmental Benefits
The program generated substantial environmental benefits beyond the immediate reduction in fire
incidents. Vegetation recovery became evident in previously damaged areas, with native species
returning to burn sites that had been properly managed. Wildlife sightings increased significantly in
former fire-prone zones as habitat quality improved and disturbance decreased. Improved water
retention was observed in streams during dry seasons, likely due to reduced erosion and improved soil

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 13
conditions in watersheds protected from fire. Successful native plant regeneration occurred in areas
cleared of Lantana camara, creating more diverse and resilient plant communities. The return of native
grasses and shrubs established a more fire-resistant landscape mosaic, reducing fuel loads and creating
natural firebreaks across the terrain. These environmental improvements created a positive feedback
loop, with each season of successful fire management contributing to ecosystem conditions that further
reduced fire risk in subsequent years.
Social Outcomes
The initiative transformed the relationship between the forest department and local communities from
antagonistic to collaborative, replacing decades of conflict with productive partnership. Seventy-six
percent of surveyed community members reported an improved perception of conservation efforts,
reflecting a significant shift in local attitudes toward protected area management. Improved forest
conditions and community engagement led to the development of community-based ecotourism
initiatives directly linked to forest protection, creating economic incentives for continued conservation.
Human–wildlife conflict incidents decreased by 42% as habitat quality within the protected area
improved, reducing wildlife dependence on agricultural areas and human settlements. The Lantana
crafts program created new skills and sustainable livelihood opportunities, particularly benefiting
women and economically marginalized community members who had previously faced limited
economic opportunities. These social outcomes strengthened the foundation for long-term
conservation success by aligning community interests with ecological protection.
Economic Impact
The program generated substantial economic benefits that reinforced community commitment to fire
prevention and ecological restoration. The initiative created 575 seasonal fire watcher positions,
providing significant employment in areas with limited job opportunities. Alternative livelihood
projects were developed, benefiting more than 500 villages, reducing dependence on forest resources
and creating economic stakes in forest protection. The recognition of the reserve as a model site
increased tourism revenue by 28%, bringing additional income to local communities and reinforcing
the economic value of intact ecosystems. At Bandipur Tiger Reserve, tourism revenue increased from
₹4.32 crore in 2020–2021 to ₹21.54 crore in 2025—an estimated 400% increase (Exhibit 1). This substantial
growth over just 5 years is attributed to several factors:
(a) Improved landscape management;
(b) Increased sightings of tigers, leopards, wild dogs, and Asian elephants following Lantana removal
and grassland development in tourism areas;
(c) The visit of Honorable Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Bandipur Tiger Reserve on 9 April 2023;
and
(d) Efforts by the tiger reserve management, including the purchase of new vehicles to operate tourism
at full carrying capacity.
The establishment of profitable community plant nurseries supplying restoration projects created
sustainable businesses directly tied to ecological recovery. The training of 90 artisans in Lantana craft
production generated substantial sustainable income while simultaneously contributing to invasive
species management. These economic benefits ensured that conservation became financially viable for
participating communities, transforming environmental protection from a perceived economic burden
to a source of prosperity.

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 14
Key Success Factors
Several critical elements proved essential to the program’s remarkable success across environmental,
social, and economic dimensions. The establishment of genuine partnership where communities were
involved as decision-makers rather than merely implementers created true ownership and commitment
at the local level. The partnership model differed from any other community engagement or
partnership engagement models. In this model, local communities—including indigenous tribes—
remain the main stakeholders, and the program was designed to create mutual benefits for both people
and wildlife, particularly tigers. In this effort, Kumar’s team engaged local tribal members as the main
stakeholders in the removal of Lantana camara, rather than relying on mechanical methods. Although
mechanical removal of Lantana would have been less expensive than manual removal, the decision was
made to proceed with manual methods. This approach minimized soil disturbance and generated
livelihoods for local tribal communities in their native areas, reducing the need for migration to other
districts or states in search of wage employment.
The recognition and integration of traditional knowledge with modern techniques also built trust while
improving technical effectiveness, validating local wisdom, and enhancing scientific approaches. The
creation of tangible economic benefits fostered sustained motivation for participation, ensuring that
conservation efforts were aligned with community welfare. Implementation of adaptive management
through regular program reviews enabled continuous improvement based on field experience rather
than rigid adherence to predetermined plans. Securing multilevel government support—through
coordination among village, district, state, and national authorities—provided necessary resources and
policy backing for long-term sustainability. The integrated approach to conservation challenges, as CF
Ramesh Kumar emphasized, recognized that “Invasive species management and fire management
should be integrated rather than treated as separate domains. The ecological connections are too
significant to ignore.” Most importantly, the economic innovation of converting a problematic invasive
species into a valuable resource created a powerful incentive for ecological restoration, transforming
an environmental liability into a community asset.

Challenges and Solutions
The program encountered and successfully addressed several significant challenges throughout its
implementation. Initial skepticism from both forest officials and community members threatened early
adoption; however, beginning with willing participants created successful demonstrations that
convinced others of the program’s viability. Uneven participation across communities created
inconsistent protection, but the implementation of peer-to-peer learning—where successful villages
mentored neighboring communities—helped spread effective practices organically. Limited funding
threatened program expansion, but the diversification of funding sources, including corporate social
responsibility initiatives and tourism fees, created a more sustainable financial foundation. The sheer
scale of Lantana invasion—covering approximately 872 sq. km of the core area of the Bandipur Tiger
Reserve—posed a daunting management challenge, which was addressed through strategic
prioritization that focused on areas where intervention would yield the greatest reduction in fire risk.
Lantana’s biological resilience and tendency to resprout when not properly removed complicated
control efforts, leading to the development of the innovative “cut-root-stock” method and the
establishment of follow-up monitoring protocols to ensure lasting removal. Initially, limited market
development for Lantana products constrained economic benefits, but partnerships with design
institutes and retail organizations improved product design, quality control, and marketing, creating
sustainable demand for artisanal products. These challenges and their solutions illustrate the program’s
commitment to addressing both immediate obstacles and systemic issues.

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 15
Lessons Learned
The Bandipur experience offers valuable lessons for similar initiatives seeking to integrate community
participation, ecological restoration, and fire management.
(1) Community fire management proves most effective when it builds on existing social structures
rather than creating parallel systems, respecting and strengthening indigenous governance and social
organization.
(2) The integration of technology must be appropriate to local capacity and maintained through local
expertise to ensure sustainability after external support ends.

(3) Successful community conservation requires carefully balancing immediate incentives with long-
term conservation goals, creating pathways that satisfy both urgent needs and future aspirations.

(4) Government agencies must demonstrate willingness to share authority and decision-making with
communities, moving beyond tokenistic participation to meaningful power-sharing.
(5) Fire management cannot be effectively separated from broader livelihood and development needs,
requiring holistic approaches that address human welfare alongside ecological goals.
(6) Invasive species management should be integrated with fire prevention strategies for maximum
effectiveness, recognizing the ecological connections between these challenges. As CF Ramesh Kumar
insightfully noted, “Community participation requires genuine economic incentives. The Lantana
crafts program succeeds because it creates real livelihoods, not just token payments.”
(7) Perhaps most importantly, ecological restoration must be understood as a long-term process
requiring patience and persistence, with success measured in decades rather than years, demanding
sustained commitment from all stakeholders involved in these complex socio-ecological initiatives.
Future Directions
Looking ahead, CF Kumar outlines an ambitious and evolved vision for the next phase of the initiative:
“We are now moving into what I consider the second phase of the initiative. The first phase focused on
emergency intervention in high-risk areas. Now, we are developing a more comprehensive ecosystem
restoration approach.” This transition reflects the program’s maturation from crisis management to
long-term ecological transformation, building on the successful foundation established in the initial
years. The shift acknowledges that while fire prevention remains essential, true ecosystem resilience
requires deeper engagement with the underlying ecological dynamics of the reserve.
The program is actively exploring innovative biological control methods for managing Lantana in
remote and inaccessible areas where mechanical removal proves challenging or economically
unfeasible. These approaches include careful research into host-specific insects and pathogens that
target Lantana while leaving native vegetation unharmed. Simultaneously, the initiative is significantly
expanding its restoration research to better understand which native species assemblages are most
effective at preventing Lantana reinvasion once the invasive plant has been removed. This research
involves extensive field trials comparing different combinations of native grasses, shrubs, and trees to

identify plant communities that can effectively compete with Lantana seedlings and create resilient, fire-
resistant landscapes that resist reinvasion.

On the economic front, the program is working methodically to scale up the successful Lantana crafts
enterprise by connecting skilled local artisans with lucrative export markets across Europe, North
America, and Asia. The initiative is investing in product development to create higher-value items that
command premium prices while maintaining their distinctive character and environmental story.
Design collaborations with renowned artists and institutions are elevating the crafts from purely
functional items to artistic pieces that celebrate indigenous craftsmanship and ecological restoration.

Community-Based Forest Fire Prevention and Management in Bandipur Tiger Reserve 16
Beyond the crafts program, the initiative is thoroughly exploring innovative carbon credit
opportunities for the substantial biomass removed during Lantana clearing operations and for the
restored native forest that sequesters additional carbon as it matures. These potential carbon financing
mechanisms could provide significant sustainable funding streams that further incentivize
conservation while connecting local communities to global climate action.
Conclusion
The community-based fire prevention and management initiative in Bandipur Tiger Reserve
conclusively demonstrates the remarkable effectiveness of genuinely participatory approaches to
complex conservation challenges. By fundamentally transforming local communities from perceived
threats to essential partners in conservation, the program has not only dramatically reduced fire
incidence but also profoundly strengthened the social and ecological resilience of the entire region.
The initiative has created a positive feedback loop where improved ecological conditions support
enhanced livelihoods, which in turn motivate greater community investment in environmental
protection.
The integrated approach developed in Bandipur, combining traditional ecological knowledge with
community engagement, appropriate modern technology, and innovative invasive species
management, is now being thoughtfully adapted for implementation in other protected areas across
India. The model provides a comprehensive framework that can be customized to address the specific
ecological, social, and economic contexts of different regions while maintaining its core principles.
This expansion suggests that the Bandipur experience offers valuable lessons for addressing the
growing challenge of forest fires in a changing climate, where traditional management approaches are
increasingly inadequate to meet the scale and complexity of environmental threats. The initiative
demonstrates that effective conservation in the 21st century requires approaches that recognize
communities not as obstacles to overcome but as essential partners whose knowledge, participation,
and prosperity are fundamental to lasting ecological security and resilience.
Tigers and tribes are the two eyes of Bandipur Tiger Reserve. Local tribal communities remain the

backbone of the reserve’s protection and management. These local tribal people (called community-
based volunteers) are engaged in most of Bandipur’s forestry and wildlife activities, including anti-
poaching operations, forest fire prevention, and habitat management, such as weeding and waterhole

maintenance, and human-wildlife conflict mitigation.
However, during the rainy and other off-seasons, many members of these local tribal communities
travel to other districts of Karnataka, such as Coorg and Chikmagalur, and even to adjoining states
like Tamil Nadu and Kerala, for employment in coffee and tea estates.
Therefore, to achieve a win-win outcome by creating round-the-year employment, members of the
local tribal communities were trained in the manual removal of Lantana camara weed species, an
invasive alien species. They were employed during the off-season to remove this weed and restore
grassland areas for herbivores, ultimately supporting tiger conservation.
With a strong conviction in participatory management of tiger reserves, community-based volunteers
were actively involved in forest fire prevention and control. Further, with the continued support of
the reserve’s top management and frontline staff, this community-based approach to fire prevention
and control has been successfully sustained.

Case Study Description:
The case study describes the transformation of Kanfodi village in drought-prone Jalna District from distress migration and poverty to a source of local employment within a decade. Before 2018, households relied only on rainfed crops and faced seasonal migration, poor infrastructure, and socio-economic hardship. Intervention by MSRLM through SHG formation and financial literacy led to the introduction of vegetable farming, which became a turning point due to steady income and reliable markets. Innovations like drip irrigation, staggered planting, and market surveys increased productivity and earnings. Distress migration reduced to 20% by 2024-25, living standards improved, and women emerged as key decision-makers. Landless households were supported through poultry, goat rearing, and a daal mill. The Weight Above and the Cracks Below
“Two days before they left for sugarcane cutting, Farzana Bhabhi would be in tears, and it was painful
for us to see her so unhappy,” recalls Kasabai, her neighbour. Farzana was torn between the pain of
leaving her children behind and the financial pressures that forced her family into the vicious cycle of
seasonal migration and debt. They borrowed from the contractor and repaid with labour; if that was
insufficient, they borrowed from the local moneylender or the contractor again. “It was a veritable
circus,” recalls Farzana Bhabhi. The story of 47-year-old Farzana, a landless labourer, was echoed by
half the women from Kanfodi gaon (village), who, along with their families, migrated seasonally every
year due to financial distress. “I never went for sugarcane cutting, but I would take up work picking
leftover cotton in the fields, gathering neem fruits, or working on local construction projects in nearby
areas. I would leave the house before sunrise with leftover food and return home after sunset to cook
for the crying children and my drunk, violent husband,” recounts Anita Rathod, a farmer from Kanfodi
tanda, who owns 3 acres of agricultural land. The financial and social distress also reflected in their
poor living conditions. Raju Rathod, Anita’s husband, recalls that before 2018 they lived in a small hut
with a fragile roof, under a tree on their farm. He remembers spending sleepless nights when it rained
heavily. The floor of the hut was dotted with vessels of different sizes to collect the rainwater leaking
from the roof. They stayed awake to empty the vessels when they filled and could sleep only once the
rain stopped. The situation has transformed in the twin habitations of Kanfodi gaon and Kanfodi tanda.
Sitting in a newly built pucca house with four rooms, a well-equipped kitchen, and separate toilet and
bathroom, Raju speaks with a quiet satisfaction tinged with memories of past struggles. He proudly
credits their transformed life to his wife Anita’s evolution—from a diffident woman unable to converse
with anyone in Marathi, let alone handle financial dealings, to an active self-help group (SHG) member
and confident deputy sarpanch (head of the village council) of the gram panchayat, who independently

Introduction: The Larger Picture
Seasonal migration in India has historical roots, particularly in rural areas where it is driven by survival
needs rather than aspirations for improved well-being (Bag and Toppo 2021). The National Sample
Survey 64th Round defines short-term migrants as individuals who are away from their native place
for 1 to 6 months a year for employment. Distress-induced seasonal migration differs from aspirational
migration, as it is rooted in economic hardship, environmental crises, and lack of livelihood options
(Bagchi and Singh 2012).
“Push” factors, like agrarian distress, low wages, limited job opportunities, and natural calamities,
drive this migration from resource-poor areas, while “pull” factors at destination sites include better
wages and employment prospects. Though migration temporarily boosts household income, during
seasonal migration, the migrants end up in precarious working conditions (Deshingkar and Start 2003).
Common destinations include construction sites, sugarcane, cotton or soybean fields, saltpans, brick
kilns, and stone quarries. At these destinations, migrant workers often live in makeshift shelters
without access to adequate sanitation, drinking water, electricity, or affordable food. These poor living
conditions are aggravated by the migrants’ exclusion from public welfare schemes (Bagchi and Singh
2012). Their children are deprived of education and face health risks (Jaleel and Chattopadhyay 2019),
especially among women migrants (Kulkarni 2015). On a larger scale, an increase in distress-induced
migration burdens urban infrastructure, leading to swelling of slums and competition for low-skilled
jobs. These seasonal migrants who are mostly from scheduled tribes, scheduled castes, or other
backward classes are vulnerable to exploitation by the contractors (Mishra 2020).
Seasonal migration is widespread in states like Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh,
Karnataka, and Telangana. However, the transient nature of this “floating population” makes it
challenging to capture accurate numbers, rendering this workforce nearly “invisible.” Estimates of
seasonal migrants vary widely—from 12.58 million (Mishra 2020) to as high as 30 million– 100 million
(Narnaware and Shukla 2023), with a rising trend suggesting worsening conditions. In Maharashtra,
this phenomenon is particularly prevalent in drought-prone districts such as Beed and Jalna, where
seasonal unemployment compels rural households to undertake distress-induced seasonal migration
(Nienkerke, Thorat, and Patt 2022). Key drivers of distress-induced seasonal migration include rain-fed
agriculture; lack of alternative livelihoods (Panda and Mishra 2018; UNICEF, IIPS, and Government of
Maharashtra 2022); climate variability in the form of frequent droughts and erratic monsoons
(Narnaware and Shukla 2023); and caste- and gender-based discrimination that further limits access to
stable employment (Vyas and Sahoo 1999). While schemes such as the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural
Employment Guarantee Scheme have provided limited relief (Nienkerke, Thorat, and Patt 2022), and
initiatives such as Maharashtra’s Migration Tracking System have addressed some adverse effects
(Jaleel and Chattopadhyay 2019), deeper systemic vulnerabilities persist (Bagchi and Singh 2012).
The Wadi Project and related studies demonstrate that the introduction of an integrated farming system
has improved agricultural productivity, which has reduced the need for seasonal migration. In the
Wadi Project, it was found that around 60% of participating households had at least one member who
permanently ceased migrating. The study on the Wadi Project points out that policies should aim to
address chronic poverty rather than simply seek to halt migration (Nienkerke, Thorat, and Patt 2022).
Although it is not always framed as “resilience,” studies emphasize how integrated livelihood
strategies can strengthen economic security, social cohesion, and sustainable resource use—key
elements of economic, social, and ecological resilience (Nienkerke, Thorat, and Patt 2022; Deshingkar

Constraints to Change
Before 2018, Kanfodi gaon and Kanfodi tanda, twin habitations in drought-prone Jalna district,
primarily depended on rain-fed agriculture. While the kharif season was the most productive, erratic
rainfall and water scarcity limited rabi and summer cropping. Tube wells, though used by some, were
largely ineffective due to low groundwater levels. Access to water was shaped by landholding size—
larger farmers could afford irrigation infrastructure, while smallholders and marginal farmers were left
behind.
Approximately 92% of households owned land (totalling 928 acres), with over half being small and
marginal farmers. The remaining 8% were landless and relied on manual labour. In this context,
promoting tube wells risked reinforcing inequality, as large farmers could extract more water,
depleting soil moisture for others. Vegetable farming emerged as a promising option for landholders
but risked excluding the landless unless they could participate as labourers. An inclusive approach was
essential to avoid social tensions.
Financial exclusion was another major barrier. Most households lacked formal banking access and
relied on local moneylenders charging 10%–15% interest. Many resorted to loans from sugarcane
contractors in exchange for labour. “We would take a ₹50,000 loan from the contractor. After repaying
debts and buying provisions, only ₹10,000–15,000 was left for groceries,” recalls Farzana, a seasonal
migrant. With funds exhausted even before departure, families often borrowed again during migration,
returning home still in debt—trapped in a cycle of poverty and migration.
Limited opportunities in agriculture, poor vocational skills, no access to formal financial institutions
and low literacy forced families into strenuous, low-paid labour—road construction, cotton picking,
and neem fruit collection. Every year, many households migrated for 6 months to work in districts like
Solapur, Satara, Sangli, or Karnataka. Despite the hardship, incomes remained unstable.
These pressures fuelled widespread alcohol consumption among men, especially in Kanfodi tanda,
where 75% of households brewed liquor. Domestic violence was common in several households. “In
the evening, the tanda was unapproachable due to drunk men, the stench of alcohol, and unhygienic
conditions,” recalls Kasabai. Other community members from Kanfodi gaon kept away from the
inhabitants of Kanfodi tanda.
Women, though central to household and farm labour, were excluded from decision-making. In the
deeply patriarchal setting, women had limited education and exposure. Women in the tanda were
further isolated because of their lack of fluency in Marathi. Previously failed SHG experiences had
made them distrustful of collective savings, and initiating entrepreneurship or financial literacy efforts
seemed nearly impossible. These conditions severely constrained their agency and autonomy. Social
cohesion was weak. The village suffered from mistrust within the community and between residents
and government officials. As Shri Hazare, the Gram Sevak, remarked, “Any government employee
posted here considered it a punishment posting.” In such an environment, collective action or
collaboration was hard to imagine.
In 2018, Shyam Khond, Block Mission Manager (BMM) under the Maharashtra State Rural Livelihoods
Mission (MSRLM), introduced the idea of vegetable farming. A former nongovernment organization
(NGO) worker and trainer, Shyam was familiar with rural realities. Yet, as a contractual government
employee, he encountered institutional barriers: hierarchy, inertia, and corruption. Some colleagues
diverted SHG funds or viewed agro-processing units as more viable than vegetable farming. Shyam
faced pushback both from within the system and from the community.

Even when SHGs were formed and enterprises initiated, sustaining them depended on timely bank
support. But local banks were hesitant—citing high nonperforming assets and low repayment trust.
Despite policy mandates, they were not held accountable and were often denied loans, weakening the
initiative’s sustainability. Thus, the initial phase reveals a deeply interconnected web of geographic,
economic, social, and institutional challenges—from water scarcity and uneven access to financial
exclusion, gender inequity, and mistrust.
Evolution of a Pathway
The transformation in Kanfodi was not the result of a pre-planned intervention but an evolving process
shaped by the combined efforts of government officials, village leaders, and a culture of mutual support
that developed gradually within the community. The evolution followed an iterative cycle of learn, act,
gain and then learn again, which further leads to another cycle.
Understanding the Reality
Shyam Khond, a young man from a farming family in Buldhana, gradually channelled his energies into
constructive action after engaging with an NGO and learning participatory development approaches.
His interest in livelihoods, along with experience in using participatory rural appraisal tools, helped
him build skills in collective deliberations that facilitated consensus-building leading to collective
action. He was appointed BMM under the MSRLM in Mantha taluka. As part of his orientation, he
visited several villages, including Kanfodi. His initial visit to Kanfodi village was met with resistance—
local men dismissed the idea of women’s SHGs and told him not to return. Regardless of the disinterest
and threats, Shyam persisted.
During his visit, Shyam met 39-year-old local farmer Kasabai Kendre from Kanfodi village. He
explained the MSRLM briefly and proposed conducting a meeting with the women. Based on his
previous visits to Kanfodi village, Shyam had realized his limitations as a male outsider trying to
engage women in financial literacy and entrepreneurship. Therefore, Shyam asked Kasabai if she could
help organize a women’s meeting.
Kasabai Kendre from the Vanzari community was an enterprising woman from a farming household
in Kanfodi village. Like many women in patriarchal rural settings, her early married life was confined
to household chores, child-rearing, and farming work. Based on discussion with Shyam, Kasabai spent
4 to 5 days going door to door, convincing women to attend the meeting. This effort resulted in the
attendance of around 80–100 women from Kanfodi village and tanda village for a joint meeting. Shyam
facilitated a discussion on SHGs, livelihoods, and development. Due to the strong patriarchal hold, men
closely monitored the meeting, and some interrupted it and took their wives away.
Despite the challenges, the meeting sowed the seeds of change. Shyam explained MSRLM’s Dashasutri.
Kasabai grasped the vision and volunteered to become an internal community resource person (ICRP).
Of the three women who showed interest, Kasabai was unanimously selected by 65 women to take on
the leadership role for Kanfodi village and the nearby tanda village. In that meeting, SHGs—some
previously dormant—were revived or newly formed. Over time, this number grew to 10 active SHGs,
each with representatives from 10 to 15 families. Members began contributing ₹25 per week, enabling
low-interest loans within their groups. Within 3 months of the meeting, around 77% of adult women
from the village had been mobilized and actively engaged.
This was also the beginning of the transformative journey of Kasabai. The exposure she gained through
MSRLM activities helped her discover and channel her potential—marked by a sharp learning ability,
entrepreneurial mindset, and a compassionate, community-oriented spirit. As an ICRP, Kasabai
emerged as a pivotal figure in engaging the wider village community. She played a key role in
catalysing collective participation, especially among women, and enabling the optimal use of livelihood
opportunities to move out of distress. Kasabai’s leadership—rooted in lived experience, ability to

Contextual and Grounded Planning
Once the SHGs in Kanfodi village had stabilized, Shyam introduced the idea of local enterprises,
identifying vegetable farming as a promising opportunity for Kanfodi village and some other villages
in the taluka. During his visits, he observed that the Mantha region was largely dry, with minimal local
vegetable cultivation despite strong market demand. Given the perishable nature of vegetables, road
access was critical and Kanfodi’s proximity to Watur Phata village and the highway made
transportation feasible. Moreover, since most residents were already farmers, no additional training in
cultivation skills was initially required to begin vegetable cultivation.
Instead of only instructing, Shyam opted to test his hypothesis. He collaborated with Krishi Sanjeevani,
an NGO working in the agriculture sector, to prepare a comprehensive vegetable farming kit containing
mixed seeds of 20–26 varieties—including root, fruit, leafy, and flowering vegetables, some of which
were plants, and other creepers. Unsure where the idea would take root, he distributed the kits in seven
to eight villages in the taluka. As Shyam found Kasabai to be trustworthy and enterprising, she was
chosen from Kanfodi village to anchor the initiative. Because she had no space for a kitchen garden
near her house, she planted the seeds on 1 guntha1 of her agriculture field about a kilometre away.
Kasabai remembers that the initial produce was consumed at home, and some was shared with the
neighbours. She also gifted some of the produce to the team from the MSRLM that visited her pilot
vegetable plot. When the harvest was sizable, she sold it in the nearby market at Watur Phata village.
Within 3–4 months, Kasabai earned ₹5,000– 6,000 from her produce. Her success caught the attention
of other women in the village, who had been observing her progress. Curious and encouraged by her
outcome, they began expressing interest in vegetable farming, setting the stage for wider adoption of
this livelihood initiative.
Piloting the Initiative
The cash returns Kasabai earned from just 1 guntha of vegetable farming came as a pleasant surprise.
Unlike traditional crops such as jowar, pigeon pea, cotton, or soybean—which yield income only once
after 5–8 months—vegetables offered quicker and frequent returns. Vegetable crop could be taken three
times in a year—in June, November, and then in February. Once planted, it could be harvested within
45 days and provided a steady income every alternate day for 2–3 months thereafter. Another benefit
of vegetable crop was its adaptability to different types of soils and landscapes, which is not the case
with commercial crops like soybean or cotton. This helped address the common cash flow challenges
that households face between kharif sowing and harvest.
In the absence of such regular income, most families depended on local moneylenders charging high
interest rates. Realizing that vegetable cultivation could reduce this dependency, Kasabai encouraged
two other women, Anita Rathod and Aruna Rathod, to try vegetable cultivation in their respective
fields. In February 2019, each woman cultivated vegetables on 10 gunthas of her own land, totalling 30
gunthas under cultivation. Based on Kasabai’s earlier returns from 1 guntha, the estimated income per
cultivator ranged between ₹45,000 and 50,000.
This pilot project coincided with the second wave of the COVID-19 lockdown. During this time,
vegetables became costlier in the market. The locally grown vegetables not only ensured food security
for villagers but also fetched substantial returns for the growers. The growers sold the surplus produce
in nearby villages and at times at Watur Phata village. Each 10 guntha patch yielded around ₹100,000—
double the original estimate—making vegetable farming a highly lucrative and attractive livelihood
alternative. In May 2019, Shyam invited a few women including Kasabai from select villages to Barbada
village in Mantha taluka to equip them with more systematic skill of vegetable farming. He arranged

Adopting Sustainable Agriculture Practices
Through pilot efforts, an important insight related to water use became clear. As the plot was small,
Kasabai managed to grow vegetables during the rabi season using water from her own well. In 2019,
Shyam encouraged her to install drip irrigation on 10 gunthas of land. The comparative advantage was
clear:
• Flood irrigation for 30 minutes waters 0.25 acre (10 gunthas) and remains effective for 6 hours.
• Drip irrigation for 30 minutes waters 1 acre (40.47 gunthas) and remains effective for 30 hours.
This fivefold efficiency in duration for which the moisture lasts and fourfold in land coverage was
compelling enough for vegetable cultivators to adopt drip irrigation.
Encouraged by steady cash flow, 12 more SHG members joined the initiative. By 2021, 15 women were
cultivating vegetables on 0.5 acre each, totalling 7.5 acres. These women belonged to SHGs that
followed the Panchsutra (regular meetings, savings, internal lending, recoveries, and proper
bookkeeping). In 2020–2021, Shyam facilitated the release of a revolving fund of ₹150,000 under the
MSRLM—₹15,000 per SHG. Each SHG member received ₹3,000, with a condition (set by Kasabai) to
invest it in drip irrigation on at least 10 gunthas of their agriculture land if they owned a well. Earlier
only a few rich farmers could afford drip irrigation. However, as incomes improved from vegetable
cultivation and financial support through SHGs—and since the benefits of drip irrigation were already
evident—the idea met no resistance. The women who did not own wells gradually managed to dig
tube wells through personal savings, financial support from SHGs, bank loans, and government
subsidies. The benefits of drip irrigation also encouraged farmers to adopt it for other commercial crops.
Kasabai owns 8 acres of agriculture land, 6 acres of which is now under drip irrigation.
In 2019, while visiting their daughter in Nagpur, Kasabai and her husband observed the use of
mulching and learned about its benefits. It helps conserves moisture, reduces weed growth, and
protects plants from viruses. After watching instructional videos, Kasabai applied the technique in her
own field and observed improved soil moisture, reduced labour, and healthier plants. The approach
quickly gained traction in Kanfodi village. Initially, laying mulch paper required four people over 2
days. By 2025, they had learned to use a tractor for laying the mulch paper, which eased the process
considerably.
Inspired by these methods, farmers became more aware of sustainable practices. They began using
organic fertilizers like Kokila, sold at the input provision center Krishi Seva Shetakari at Watur Phata
village. As loyal customers of these centers, they also gained the advantage of holding the supplier
accountable for results. Another organic manure sourced was made from bagasse,2 procured from Jalna
district, not only enriched the soil but also deterred wild boars that damaged crops. As vegetable
farming spread in Kanfodi village, many vendors began visiting the village to sell inputs. One such
vendor from Vedic company promoted a product using soil charger.3 The farmers observed improved
crop yield, enhanced soil fertility, and healthier crop growth, noting that their vegetables remained
fresh even 4 to 5 days after harvest. The benefits of drip irrigation, mulching, and organic inputs were
immediately evident and therefore readily adopted by farmers. When harvesting coriander, Kasabai
observed how soft and porous the soil was in the vegetable plots, unlike the hardened soil in cotton or
soybean fields. Cotton and soybean fields require chemical fertilizers at least four to five times during
their life cycle. In contrast, land cultivated with nonchemical inputs and supported by mulching
requires fertilizers only twice. This significantly reduced input costs and increased farmers’ net income.
In 2019 during one of the meetings, Shyam suggested that all the women who owned land, plant at
least two trees every year in their respective fields. Initially, most of them planted papaya, but when

Experimentation and Exploration
As their farming enterprises expanded, female farmers from the SHGs began experimenting with
different crops to compare yields and profitability. Kasabai conducted a notable experiment, allocating
20 gunthas (0.50 acre) for soybean and 20 gunthas (0.50 acre) for vegetables—tomato, okra, black-eyed
beans, green sorrel leaves, and coriander. The harvesting of soybean took 130 days, whereas the
harvesting of vegetables varied from 35 to 100 days, providing a steady income at regular intervals.
