This comparison clearly demonstrated the higher financial returns from vegetable farming. It also
highlighted the value of water, as better yields were closely linked to efficient water use.
Selling vegetables at the market exposed farmers to new crop varieties and price trends. They began
testing new crops on small plots and scaled up based on positive results. So far, they have not
experienced many failures in these trials. Today, Kanfodi village farmers grow a diverse range of
around 20 vegetables.
Some farmers also started exploring beyond vegetable plants and creepers. In 2022, Neelabai planted
moringa on a large portion of her land. Moringa tree yields drumsticks twice a year for at least 10 years,
and three farmers in the village now cultivate it. Kailas, who owns an acre of land near his house in
Kanfodi tanda, planted sandalwood intercropped with mahogany 5 years ago to enhance long-term
returns. Recently, Kasabai was introduced to turmeric by her son-in-law. Her research showed that
turmeric can earn more than ₹500,000 per acre. Encouraged by this, she and two others, Renuka Pandit
and Gokarna Kendre, planned to cultivate turmeric for the first time in Kanfodi village during the 2025
monsoon. Turmeric is harvested about a year after planting. While it offers good one-time returns,
farmers know it cannot replace vegetables, which provide regular cash flow. These initiatives reflect a
shift toward evidence-based, profitable, and sustainable farming driven by local experimentation and
growing market awareness.
Developing an Ecosystem
As the number of vegetable growers and the area under cultivation increased, the volume of produce
rose significantly. To manage the growing output efficiently, farmers collaborated to organize a reliable
transport system. Dnyaneshwar Chavan, who earlier transported crops like cotton and wheat, adapted
his operations to meet the logistical needs of vegetable farmers. He initiated a pickup service, making
trips every 3 days to markets like Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Jalna, Washim, Buldhana, Malegaon,
Yavatmal, and Amravati. Facing issues with hired drivers, he now personally handles all deliveries.
Though he owns farmland, transportation remains his main income source. In 2021, Ganesh Rathod,
another villager from Kanfodi tanda village, launched a second transportation service with a smaller
tempo, focusing on nearby markets like Mantha and Partur. By 2022, his business had grown
considerably, complementing Dnyaneshwar’s long-distance network. These developments highlight
the growth of allied services driven by vegetable farming.
To streamline logistics, farmers began coordinating harvest timings with local tempo schedules.
Vegetables were collected from three points in the village, usually in the late afternoon. As the journey
to the wholesale market required overnight travel, male farmers took turns accompanying the driver.
They left the village in the evening, traveling through the night to reach the market by 4 a.m. There,

they sold the produce, collected bills, and returned the same day to hand over receipts and earnings to
their fellow farmers. Initially, farmers explored different markets and learned that prices varied widely
across locations. Over time, they began choosing markets based on real-time information. Kasabai
noted that wholesalers’ contact details on payment slips could be used to inquire about current rates.
Farmers conducted a quick market survey over the phone, before dispatching the tempo and compared
prices to decide on the most profitable destination. Local demand patterns also guided marketing
choices. For instance, coriander fetched low prices in Risol while bitter gourd sold well in Mantha and
Partur. This market insight helped farmers make informed decisions about crop selection and where to
sell, optimizing both cultivation and profits.
As the area under vegetable farming expanded and the number of farmers increased, it got more
visibility and publicity in that region. Apart from the vendors selling agriculture inputs, many brokers
and buyers visited the village, and some offered to collect the vegetables from the farm itself. The banks
initially were sceptical of lending money to the SHGs in Kanfodi village due to some defaulters from
the village. Shyam intervened and explained that the defaulters were individuals, and the loan was
requested by SHGs who have developed financial discipline. Kasabai also assisted bank staff in
recovering loans from individual defaulters in the village. Her involvement helped strengthen the
banks’ trust in the SHGs, which now receive regular financial support and loans. This collaboration
between various stakeholders and local institutions has ensured sustainability of the initiatives that
took root through collective action in Kanfodi.
Vegetable farming required more regular care and manual labour for timely harvesting than traditional
or cash crops. This created steady employment for entire households as well as for landless labourers.
The village youth became enthusiastic about vegetable cultivation. They began taking greater
responsibility in farm work, and the experience started shaping their aspirations. Sharad, who helps
his mother Neelabai Pandit on the farm, now plans to pursue a bachelor’s degree in agriculture.
Vegetable cultivation has also created steady work for men who once spent their days idle, drinking,
or gossiping. The shift in work culture was evident. Raju Rathod from the Kanfodi tanda village, once
addicted to alcohol, has now quit drinking. “Earlier, I drank because I was stressed. Now I have work
that gives good returns. I don’t feel the need for alcohol anymore,” he says. Several women from
Kanfodi tanda village affirmed that domestic violence has significantly reduced because of this
transformation. Vegetable farming thus fostered an ecosystem that supported logistics, informed
decision-making, household employment, and domestic well-being—transforming lives with
livelihoods (see Loop 2 – VF Adoption, Loop 3 – VF Expansion, and Loop 4 – Local Employment in
Exhibit 3).
Awareness and Capacity Building
Financial literacy proved crucial for SHG members and their households in making informed decisions
for better returns from vegetable farming. Capacity building in handling money began with the
formation of SHGs, internal lending, and timely repayment. The financial discipline thus developed
was further strengthened due to orientation sessions organized by the MSRLM. Kasabai says that
earlier, whenever she would get money, especially after harvest, she would purchase gold and jewelry
for herself. Through the training sessions under the MSRLM, it became clear that investing in gold was
a dead investment. Through simple calculations, the women realized that their money would get better
returns if invested in quality farm inputs, improved technology, or the purchase of domestic animals.
As the women maintained financial discipline in both savings and repayments, they developed their
financial credibility that enhanced their creditworthiness, making them eligible for bank loans. Access
to formal credit sources such as banks provided them with financial security and allowed them to
borrow at much lower interest rates than those charged by local moneylenders. This bank linkage also
significantly boosted the women’s confidence. Women in Kanfodi village took turns each month to
deposit their SHG savings in the bank. Each month, one woman from a different SHG was chosen to

handle the bank transaction. This gave many women exposure to financial procedures and built their
confidence in handling money.
Under MSRLM norms, SHG members met weekly. These meetings, apart from managing savings and
repayments, became platforms to share personal experiences and challenges. Kasabai observed that
these interactions helped build trust, resolve misunderstandings, and foster cooperation— laying a
strong foundation for collective marketing and vegetable farming among women and consequently
their households.
Kanfodi village also had a village organization made up of representatives from the SHGs. The village
organization met once a month, often inviting government officials to share information about various
development schemes. This interaction proved valuable in helping women access public health
services. For example, Kasabai narrated how, in 2022, she accompanied a woman to the government
hospital in Watur Phata village for childbirth. The delivery service was free, and women in the Below
Poverty Line category received ₹500 as compensation for lost wages. This was a significant saving
compared to private hospital costs, which could range from ₹60,000–₹1,10,000 in complicated cases.
Following this experience, more than six institutional deliveries have taken place in government
hospitals, with earlier beneficiaries accompanying newer mothers, creating a strong support chain
among women. The village organization meetings also helped members access other government
schemes and services.
In the early stages of SHG formation, Shyam recognized the patriarchal constraints that limited
women’s participation in training sessions at the taluka place. Typically, women attended only if
accompanied by male family members, who often waited outside—unsure and sceptical of what was
being taught. Shyam responded by designating a space for the men and allocated part of the training
budget for their refreshments. He also engaged with them directly, explaining the training content and
MSRLM’s goals. This open dialogue gradually shifted men’s perspectives; they began supporting the
training and even sought Shyam’s guidance for their own agricultural ventures.
As financial literacy improved and a steady income stream developed, women’s confidence—and their
family’s trust in them—rose noticeably. Anita Rathod recalls how, 2 years ago, her uncle proposed her
name for the gram panchayat elections in Kathala Khurd. Anita recounts the moment she accompanied
him to file her nomination: “When I stepped up and signed the candidature form in English, my uncle
was completely taken aback.” This growing self-assurance was reinforced by increased support from
families. Kasabai remembers needing permission from her mother-in-law to step out, often explaining
every detail of her travel. Now, she travels to exhibitions and trainings without needing to justify her
movements. Her family trusts her completely. Women who were once restricted to domestic spheres
now started confidently participating in economic and social arenas. This transformation was
emblematic of shift in gender dynamics and community perception. This process is depicted by Loop
1 – Leadership, Loop 5 – Women Workforce, and Loop 6 – Financial Inclusion in Exhibit 3.
Enabling Equitable Livelihoods
While vegetable farming primarily benefited landholding farmers, landless labourers also gained due
to the steady rise in demand for labour in the fields within the village, reducing the need to migrate for
employment. However, relying on a single income source could make families vulnerable to shocks.
Therefore, for households with little or no land and who depended on manual labour, alternative
livelihood options such as poultry, animal husbandry, tailoring, and dal milling were introduced. These
helped diversify income sources and supported economic empowerment.

Restoring Roots of Resilience: Evolution of Seasonal Migrants into Employers 11
Diverse livelihood opportunities for marginal landholders and landless households were introduced,
as summarized in Exhibit 9. Further, a dedicated producer group for landless women was formed in
2024. This group received financial support and guidance to start small ventures such as goat and
poultry rearing, and dal (pulses) milling. Sakhubai Survase, separated from her husband, depended
largely on farm labour, earned ₹250–₹300 daily, and up to ₹500 during peak season. She also operated
a small dal mill in the evenings, earning around ₹5,000 annually. Besides income, the mill provided a
space for women to gather and connect, says Kasabai. The landless families who started animal
husbandry got substantial income from animal produce. For example, within just 6 months, one goat
can add about ₹20,000 to a household’s income. This additional income not only diversified their
sources of livelihood but also allowed them to take break from physical labour when needed.
By providing a diversified source of income, animal husbandry brought greater stability not only to
landless families but also to small landholders. Anita Rathod is one such example: she diversified her
income by combining vegetable farming and traditional crops such as cotton and soybean with
investments in goat rearing and poultry. This mix of activities helped boost her earnings.
Migration from Distress
The transformation in Kanfodi village was not an outcome of a well-designed blueprint; it evolved
organically, with each small success encouraging the next step. As vegetable farming took root in
Kanfodi village, it eventually addressed the issue of distress-induced seasonal migration. However,
this was neither a linear nor a simple cause-and-effect process. The case narrative explains, and Exhibit
3 depicts, the complex relationships between various factors and processes that contributed to the
destabilization of seasonal migration.
The process of capacity building, financial support, and the introduction of vegetable farming were
neither extraordinary nor unique but their impact in Kanfodi village was exceptional. Similar
interventions took place across other villages in the state, helping address the distress faced by
individual households, groups of families, or specific sections of the community. It rarely impacted the
whole village in such a short duration, especially by addressing a chronic multifaceted development

challenge. Some of the factors that contributed to the effectiveness of the initiative included the context-
specific and grounded identification of vegetable farming as a relevant livelihood strategy. This

intervention was further strengthened by Kasabai’s transformational agency that extends beyond a
limited quest for personal gains to encompass the development of her fellow villagers. The efforts of
Kasabai, supported by Shyam, were amplified by the cooperative spirit of the people of Kanfodi village.
This cooperative spirit was fostered by a culture of trust and interpersonal bonds that developed among
the SHG members through regular meetings, financial transparency, and emotional solidarity. This
cooperative spirit lay at the heart of the community’s collective action, nurtured by the support of
various stakeholders. These efforts helped Kanfodi village put an end to seasonal migration as a means
of survival.
This process did not ensure only economic gains over 7 years but introduction of a reinforcing cycle of
ecological, economic, and social resilience. Improved soil practices, better water management,
increased green cover and diversified crops enhanced ecological sustainability. Diverse and sustained
income sources brought economic stability, and when coupled with equitable livelihood efforts, further
strengthened the social cohesion initiated through SHGs. Those who once worked as labourers have
now become employers. Kanfodi’s experience reveals that when individual agency is channelled
toward collective action—and supported by relevant stakeholders and institutions—the shift from
distress to resilience becomes possible.

Restoring Roots of Resilience: Evolution of Seasonal Migrants into Employers 12
Reaping the Fruits of Labour
Reviewing the situation in Kanfodi village after 7 years of its journey reveals the initiative’s impact on
the village’s economic, social, and cultural dimensions. The graphs depicting contributory and
constraining factors in village development offer insights into the effects of the intervention, triggered
by the formation of SHGs and the adoption of vegetable farming among their members. Exhibit 10
highlights the reduction in factors previously detrimental to village development. The percentage of
households migrating has declined significantly, and a similar trend is seen among households that
earlier brewed local alcohol. In addition, five commercial alcohol brewing units that sold and served
liquor have now all been closed.
In contrast, the contributory factors depicted in Exhibit 11 demonstrate significant growth in these
indicators. Except for the increase in irrigated area—which has been moderate—all the other indicators
have shown two- to threefold growth.
Beyond improved statistics, these graphs indicate emergence of ecological, economic, and social
resilience. They also communicate the possibility of intangible changes that are seen in Kanfodi village.
Women’s active participation in agriculture and financial decisions reshaped household and
community dynamics, positioning them as drivers of change. The decline in alcohol consumption and
domestic violence has improved the living quality and social environment. In certain cases, gender
relations changed, and husbands assumed a more supportive role towards their wives’ initiatives.
Dattarao Kendre does not feel threatened by his wife getting the limelight, as her story was covered by
Doordarshan; in fact, he is an encouraging partner to Kasabai.
One concern—that the vegetable farming initiative would not be sustainable—was assuaged by
emerging innovations in the processes and tools of vegetable cultivation in the village. To make
planting more efficient, Kasabai’s son, Santosh, designed an iron tool to punch evenly spaced holes in
the mulching sheets based on the crop’s requirements. Kasabai’s household freely lent this tool to other
farmers in the village. Farmers also began experimenting with ways to optimize planting cycles. Based
on their understanding of cropping cycle, the farmers began planting the next crop diagonally opposite
on the same mulching mound about 15–20 days before the first crop ended. This overlapping method
reduced the gap between harvests, allowing continuous cultivation and minimizing the loss of time
and resources. As a result, land use was maximized, yields increased, and farmers’ incomes improved.
These innovations reflected the growing confidence and problem-solving ability of local farmers and
indicated that the community has taken ownership of the intervention.
The model in Kanfodi is now mirrored in villages like Lavani and Dhondi Pimpalgaon of Mantha taluka.
However, challenges remain in Kanfodi—water scarcity in summer and a shortage of farm labour are
emerging issues. Observing the proactive and effective management by Shyam, in 2024, he was
transferred to another taluka. SHG members in Kanfodi had a sense of security and confidence to take
risks with new initiatives when Shyam would reassure them with his words “go ahead with your
experiment, I am with you.” In Shyam’s absence. the women feared that they may not receive proactive
and reliable support from the block level functionaries of MSRLM.
Despite the roadblocks, the women are sustaining the momentum through SHGs and have formed the

Krishiseva Farmer Producer Company, aiming to develop moringa-based products and agro-
processing units. Plans include establishing a dairy enterprise and a turmeric powder unit that would

provide another livelihood alternative to Kanfodi village. The women have realized that they will need
to make additional efforts to advance their initiatives, even in the absence or lesser involvement of
facilitators like Shyam. Although some of her efforts were not successful, Kasabai remains optimistic.
She is thoughtfully preparing her next steps to ensure continued progress without setbacks.
Kanfodi’s experience offers valuable insights into the process of cultivating rural resilience through
contextual livelihood strategies, embedded local leadership, and an ecosystem of support that aligns

Restoring Roots of Resilience: Evolution of Seasonal Migrants into Employers 13
state programs with community initiative. Giving space and scope to the agency exercised by Shyam—
and activating agency among individuals like Kasabai—has proven to be key to collective action,
which, when strengthened through collaboration with relevant stakeholders and institutions, mobilizes
a reinforcing loop of ecological, economic, and social resilience. Therefore, there is a need to recognize
such women leaders, celebrate their agency, and study it further. The role of MSRLM functionaries
such as Shyam is critical to the success of these initiatives—at least until they mature and remain
sustainable for 3–5 years. This underscores the importance of identifying and nurturing such
champions.

Case Study Title: CCTNS - Lessons in Managing Large Technology Projects in  Indian Policing System
Case Study Description: This case study examines the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network Systems (CCTNS), conceptualised by the Ministry of Home Affairs in 2009 under the National e-Governance Plan to digitally connect all police stations in India, digitise crime records, and enable real-time information sharing and decision-making. While CCTNS aimed to replace fragmented, manual record-keeping with a unified technology-driven system, its initial implementation (CCTNS 1.0) faced significant challenges, including delays, design gaps, and coordination issues across Centre–State and multi-stakeholder arrangements. Despite repeated setbacks, the project was revived with renewed focus. The case highlights the ongoing need for police workflows that resolve criminal identity and enable data analytics—objectives now linked to the upcoming CCTNS 2.0.
Case Text:
Introduction
In 2009, Kolkata Police detained a man for petty theft, who gave the false name Md. Arshad. With no way
to confirm his identity, they released him with a minor fine. Later, the National Investigation Agency (NIA)
identified him as Yasin Bhatkal, a suspected Indian Mujahideen commander linked to terrorist attacks in
Pune, Bangalore, Varanasi, Delhi, and Hyderabad. A real-time, nationwide criminal database could have
flagged his identity, potentially prevented his release and averting future incidents. Manual systems and a
lack of interstate data sharing hindered effective policing at the time.
The Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS), launched in June 2009 by the Ministry
of Home Affairs after the 26/11 Mumbai attacks, aimed to address such gaps. Fully funded under the
National e-Governance Plan.

1 With ₹2,000 crore, CCTNS aimed to digitally connect all police stations,
create a centralised crime database, and enable instant data access nationwide. This technology-driven
system replaced outdated manual records, enhancing real-time policing and coordination to improve law
enforcement efficiency.

1 The National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) has been formulated by the Department of Information Technology
(DIT) and Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances (DAR&PG), comprising of 27 Mission
Mode Projects (MMPs) and 10 components on May 18, 2006. The NeGP aims at improving delivery of
Government services to citizens and businesses.

CCTNS - Lessons in Managing Large Technology Projects in Indian Policing
Ecosystems
The national edition of The Hindu2 On 18 December 2024, the headline:
"All 17,130 police stations in the country are linked through a centralised online platform."
The article noted that this project, launched in 2009 with a budget of ₹2,000 crore, had now become a key
enabler for the implementation of the three New Criminal Laws rolled out on July 1.
This piece was read by Mr Sanjay Mathur, IPS, currently serving as Joint Director, CCTNS. He remembered
how, a few years ago, a leading news daily had raised a critical question 3 "Can a project of such national
importance like CCTNS ever be completed on time?". But Mr Mathur, a seasoned officer, never allowed himself
to be distracted by headlines.
He had been part of this project from its early days as the nodal officer leading its implementation through
the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) on behalf of the Ministry of Home Affairs. He remained
focused on the work and the facts. Reading the recent news piece, he felt a quiet sense of accomplishment.
The journey of CCTNS had delivered results, belatedly though, but it had also offered lessons. As he now
guides the team working on CCTNS 2.0, a more advanced version developed based on user feedback and
consultations, he applies those hard-learned lessons there.
Overview
Policing or Law enforcement in India is a state subject. It has been traditionally a technology-challenged
domain. Introducing technology tools & systems through a top-down approach (federally driven but
decentralised execution) has an inherent risk of rejection or poor execution & apathy to adoption.
Police need workflows that resolve criminal identity and provide data analytics. Therefore, CCTNS 1.0 was
imperative as the need for pan-India criminal tracking. But real-world policing involves many complex
processes. It involves covering complaints and investigations to charge sheets, court procedures, data
recording, and mandated registers. These had to be process-engineered into a comprehensive police
application, which was a massive task. Key challenges included coordinating multiple stakeholders and
dealing with different levels of IT readiness.
Project management of e-governance projects of this magnitude, especially the central-state repercussions
and implementation profile, required an out-of-the-box approach, challenging traditional methods. One
would like to learn from CCTN 1.0 the adequacy of execution of the concepts generally encountered in
implementing large technology or IT projects like agile project management, design thinking, scenario
planning and possible futures, which are dealt in this case study.

2 https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/all-17130-police-stations-in-the-country-linked-through-centralised-
online-platform/article69000647.ece

3 2016; Mohd Ujaley; “What is causing the CCTNS delay? ” - https://www.expresscomputer.in/magazine/what-
is-causing-the-cctns-delay/15536/

CCTNS - Lessons in Managing Large Technology Projects in Indian Policing
Ecosystems
Background of IT Police Systems in India
Mr. Sanjay Mathur argues that CCTNS should be seen as a continuous process rather than a solo event, but
along with scale, implications & execution machinery. Earlier initiatives laid the groundwork, including
the National Crime Records Bureau’s (NCRB) Crime and Criminals Information System (CCIS) and
Common Integrated Police Application (CIPA), alongside state-led efforts like Andhra Pradesh’s e-COPS,
Karnataka’s Police IT, West Bengal’s Thana Tracking System, Tamil Nadu’s CAARUS (Crime Analysis
Automatic Record Updating System), and Gujarat’s IITS (Integrated Information Technology). Some states,
like Rajasthan, transitioned from static police portals to dynamic content management systems, allowing
district-level updates to crime data, though not in real time.
Launched in 1995, CCIS focused on creating a crime and criminal database for monitoring by NCRB, State
Crime Records Bureaus (SCRBs), and District Crime Records Bureaus (DCRBs). It supported statistical

analysis, online reports (e.g., Missing Persons), and NCRB’s annual crime report, but was limited to crime-
related data, excluding other police functions.

CIPA, introduced in 2004, advanced automation by enabling First Information Report (FIR) registration,
printing, and management of police station records, including databases of hardcore criminals. However,
CIPA lacked a centralised database, real-time data sharing, and advanced features like browser-based
access, role-based controls, and robust dashboards or analytics.
CCTNS represents a significant leap, addressing CIPA’s limitations by enabling centralised, real-time data
exchange and data-driven decision-making. Unlike earlier systems, CCTNS integrates police stations,
higher offices, and NCRB, offering features like alerts, document management, and comprehensive
reporting, revolutionising IT adoption in Indian policing with a focus on scalability and efficiency
Objectives of CCTNS
Mr Nirmaljeet Singh Kalsi, IAS, a career civil servant & a seasoned technocrat, who was Joint Secretary
(Police) in MHA during the conceptualisation and implementation of CCTNS, sees CCTNS as one of the
single most critical projects for India’s internal security. He explained that Networks like these are a
fundamental requirement of modern policing and security management.
It was felt that a standalone application like CIPA couldn't provide the enhanced outcomes in the areas of
Crime Investigation and Criminal Detection, like real-time outputs & analytical data. For this reason, MHA
decided to launch the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network System (CCTNS) program.
The objectives of the Scheme include enhancing police efficiency and transparency by automating police
station operations and leveraging ICT for improved citizen services. It equips investigating officers with
tools and technology to aid crime investigation and criminal detection. The scheme facilitates seamless data
collection, storage, retrieval, analysis, and sharing across police stations, districts, state/UT headquarters,
and other agencies. It supports senior officers in managing police forces and tracking case progress,
including in courts. Additionally, CCTNS reduces manual and redundant record-keeping, streamlining
operations and fostering a data-driven, interconnected policing system across India. Key deliverables have
been enumerated in annexure-1 in the appendix section.

CCTNS - Lessons in Managing Large Technology Projects in Indian Policing
Ecosystems
Implementation Philosophy of CCTNS
Mr Kalsi explained that CCTNS has been implemented in a way where the States are playing a major role.

The Crime and Criminal Tracking Network System (CCTNS) has been implemented under the National e-
Governance Program (NeGP) principle of "centralised planning and decentralised implementation." The

Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) lead planning, develop
core components, and monitor progress, while States and Union Territories (UTs) drive state-level planning
and execution.
The Core Application Software (CAS) includes four key modules—Registration, Investigation,
Prosecution, and Search and Reporting—along with a citizen interface portal, implemented progressively
across police stations and higher offices with varying comprehensiveness.
A hallmark of CCTNS implementation is the "bundling of services" approach, where each state appoints
a single System Integrator (SI) as the point of contact for all components, including customized
applications, hardware, networking, site preparation, capacity building, change management, and
maintenance. This integrated service model contrasts with procuring components separately, ensuring
cohesive implementation. Fully funded by the central government, CCTNS covers hardware, networking,
technical support, and training, easing states’ financial burdens. However, states must adhere to central
guidelines, posing challenges in adapting to prescribed procedures. This approach empowers states to
tailor CCTNS to local needs while maintaining a unified framework, with NCRB ensuring compatibility
and oversight.
Execution Strategy of CCTNS
The philosophy is ‘State Ownership with National Uniformity’: Ensures states manage their infrastructure
and data, while maintaining consistency across the country for seamless information sharing. To this
extent, NCRB (on behalf of MHA) would drive only a few components of the project, such as defining the
application core program review and monitoring. For the most part, the implementation would be led by
the States. This prevented overall incompatibilities while still maintaining adequate flexibility for states.
The felt need was to maintain the continuity and evolutionary path of police related information technology
systems in perpetuity. This was essential to have the application being technology agnostic as well as
neutral to the whims & fancies of executive machinery and having temporal awareness of the speed of
change in technology in the centre of execution philosophy.
The exercise begins with a site survey 4 at Police Stations and Higher Offices, which involve evaluating the
location (police station and higher offices) to ensure it meets the requirements for installing hardware and
communication systems.
Key Stakeholders & their stakes

4 Site Survey includes procuring, setting up and testing equipment like PCs, peripherals, network wiring,
switches and other infrastructure. It covers both the physical setup and the necessary network
infrastructure for seamless operation The process ensures proper deployment at police stations and higher
offices, ensuring everything is fully operational for daily use.

CCTNS - Lessons in Managing Large Technology Projects in Indian Policing
Ecosystems
The following are the key stakeholders in the Project at the State/UT level:
a) Home Ministry: Oversees project progress, monitors fund utilisation, issues policy directions, and
provides guidelines to ensure timely implementation.
b) State Police: Drives operational use of CCTNS, ensures system adoption, and provides feedback for
continuous improvements to enhance functionality.
c) System Integrator (SI): Acts as the state’s single point of contact, responsible for deploying and

commissioning all CCTNS components (application, hardware, networking) on time, meeting pre-
defined standards and Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

d) BSNL (ISP/TSP): Provides reliable connectivity to police stations and higher offices. Initial bandwidth
limitations in remote areas (e.g., North Eastern States, Jammu & Kashmir) caused connectivity gaps,
later addressed by allowing private TSPs (Airtel, Vodafone, Idea) with VPN tunnelling to improve
access.
e) State DIT (Department of Information Technology): Manages technical implementation, ensures
system compatibility with state IT infrastructure, and resolves technical issues during deployment and
operation.
f) SPMC/SPMU (State Project Management Consultant/Unit): Prepares Detailed Project Reports,

customises RFPs, supports SI selection through techno-commercial bid evaluation, and develops state-
specific functional specifications for CCTNS enhancements.

The major interests and concerns of the States and Union Territories (States/UTs) & other stakeholders in
the CCTNS project reflected a mix of technological, operational and logistical priorities. The Home
Department and State Police prioritised rapid CCTNS implementation, but delays arose from slow SI
engagement, hardware procurement, and deployment at police stations and state data centres.
BSNL’s initial sole role as a connectivity provider faltered in remote areas due to insufficient bandwidth,
later mitigated by private TSPs under Universal Service Obligations. State DITs provided technical and
manpower support, while some states leveraged existing networks or Bharat Net 5 for connectivity.
Diverse stakeholder priorities, including public expectations, caused delays and shaped CCTNS’s design,
with MHA’s monitoring via the Pragati dashboard ensuring accountability. These varying interests and
concerns also shaped the eventual design of the system.
Challenges in CCTNS Project Implementation
Interaction with Sh. Alok Ranjan, IPS, Director, National Crime Record Bureau, was revelatory in
understanding the contours that the project took during implementation. He explained that the CCNTS
project seems a simple project on face value. However, in reality, it is far different. It is a complex project
as there are multiple central and state agencies involved in it.
Police and Law enforcement a state subjects and systems across states are not uniform. Basically, a state
selects a system integrator, sets up a state data centre, usually with the help of NIC, and then connects all

5 BharatNet: https://usof.gov.in/en/bharatnet-project

Ecosystems
the police stations with this data centre with the help of connectivity providers. It finally syncs all the State
Data Centres with National Data Centres at New Delhi, Pune and Hyderabad, which function as disaster
recovery sites. And, on top of this, the NCRB provides a standard Core Application Software which police
stations use for lodging FIRs and for entering data.
The initial inter-state usage of crime data was tedious as the requests from police stations landed in state
headquarters, which were then routed to the national database and the downstream flow of data after
search completion. Also, different states had frameworks that existed on different operating systems, viz.
Linux, Windows and others. So, changes or patches to be incorporated had to be rolled out, keeping in
mind three different operating systems in the policing ecosystem.
Apart from these, there were a lot of unprecedented challenges in the project. A major concern was the
reluctance of police personnel to embrace new technology as many were accustomed to traditional methods
of operation. The Project spread over 20000+ locations, which was initially proposed to cover more than
16000 Police Stations and 6000 Higher Offices. Many Police Stations in the States/UTs were located at
remote locations where Road/Rail Transport was not available
The project had many stakeholders & many were not under the direct control of NCRB. There was and is
a shortage of trained manpower in the Police Force who can operate the computers efficiently. Power
outages, at times, last for 8 to 10 hours. Such outages prevent the batteries of the inverters from getting
charged. Due to low levels of intake of computer-savvy personnel, the absorption of the new system will
be time-consuming.
The States/UTs were the rate-limiting steps in the implementation matrix. There were huge differences in
the state of readiness in which they operated. Advanced States (like Andhra Pradesh, Telangana,
Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat) were already using their software for police functioning, and they
were quite ahead in implementation. Some states were not able to proceed due to their managerial and
financial conditions, like Rajasthan & Bihar, which were the last two states to be onboarded in the CCTNS
as late as 2017. The reasons for such late onboarding have been dealt with specific case study of Rajasthan
later in the discussions.
The performance of System Integrators selected by different States/UTs varied. While some System
Integrators successfully met their tasks and adhered to contractual conditions, others faced challenges in
fulfilling their responsibilities. In certain states, this led to a transition to new System Integrators, which,
although it introduced some delays, also provided an opportunity to bring in fresh expertise and drive
improved implementation of the project moving forward.
The decision was made to digitise 10 years of legacy data & while many physical records were successfully
digitised, some were incomplete or lacked essential information such as age, address, etc. Additionally,
certain older records contained irrelevant or outdated information. Despite these challenges, the process
provided valuable insights & efforts were made to improve data quality and accurate digitisation.

Ecosystems

THE CCTNS EXPERIENCE - THE HINTS OF AGILE PROJECT
MANAGEMENT
Agile project management is an iterative, flexible approach to managing projects, emphasising
collaboration, adaptability, and incremental delivery. It breaks projects into smaller phases called sprints,
allowing teams to prioritise tasks, incorporate feedback, and adjust to changing requirements. Key
principles include customer collaboration, continuous improvement, and delivering functional outputs
frequently. Agile methodologies typically focus on teamwork, transparency, and responsiveness,
contrasting with rigid, linear methods. The following aspects of CCTNS are worth analysing to arrive at a
finality on whether what gives a whiff of agility of the project is actually agile.
1. System Integration and Operationalisation
The CCTNS adopts a Core-Configurable-Customizable (C-C-C) approach, ensuring a modular, layered
architecture for seamless integration across India. The core system, CAS (Centre), operates nationally,
collecting and processing crime data from all states for nationwide information exchange.
The configurable and customizable layers, CAS (State), allow states to adapt the system to local crime
patterns, administrative processes, and existing police systems, balancing flexibility with consistency.
For Standardised Data Collection, NCRB collaborated with States/Union Territories (UTs) to
introduce Integrated Investigation Forms (IIFs) for uniform police processes. IIF1: Registration of FIRs;
IIF2: Scene of Crime details; IIF3: Details of arrested persons; IIF4: Property seized and recovered & IIF5:
Final Report/Chargesheets
States engage System Integrators (SIs) to customise CAS (State), with each SI as the single point of contact
for CCTNS components. M/s Wipro, selected via a Global Tender Process on June 21, 2010, developed the
core application software, distributed to all States/UTs except six advanced states—Andhra Pradesh, Goa,
Gujarat, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Telangana—using their own software because these States have
been using their own Police applications before introduction of CCTNS.
The fact that these six states used different software systems & not the CCTNS core software, did not hinder
nationwide integration due to the design of the CCTNS application. In fact, NCRB gave crisp guidelines
for such states to prevent any incompatibilities creeping into the process including aligning with CCTNS
core specifications, providing NCRB with required data per standards, procuring key CCTNS components
before requesting funds for advanced applications & obtaining MHA/NCRB approval for specialized
applications.
As an example, CIPRUS, 'Common Integrated Police Records Updation System’', is the Core Application
Software for Tamil Nadu Police which opted out of NCRB’s CAS and requested to use the legacy software
CAARUS as CAS for Tamil Nadu State. NCRB conceded to the request mandating certain services to be
included in the CAARUS software. The task of upgrading CAARUS software, to “State CAS” with
mandates of NCRB was entrusted to NIC, New Delhi. CIPRUS , was thus born out of CAARUS & CIPA
wedlock which embeds certain unique features.

CCTNS - Lessons in Managing Large Technology Projects in Indian Policing
Ecosystems
The CAS pilot launched on January 4, 2013, with States/UTs engaging SIs and State Project Management
Units (SPMUs) in 2012 for pilot implementation in two districts. Currently, CAS 5.0 (released February
2021) is implemented in 15 States/UTs, while CAS 4.5, with nearly all CAS 5.0 functionalities, is used
elsewhere.
After Wipro made an exit as SI, M/s CDAC, Pune has been engaged for Maintenance and Enhancement of
CAS (State) 5.0 under CCTNS 1.0 effective from 1st December 2020 in place of M/s Wipro as their project
tenure is complete.
2. Building A Reform Team: Project Planning, Evaluation & Monitoring
The CCTNS requires robust central coordination for its implementation across 35 States/Union Territories
(UTs). The Central Project Management Unit (CPMU) oversees progress, monitors fund utilization,
ensures training and infrastructure, maintains network connectivity, and resolves challenges.
The Operational Program Management Unit (OPMU) within CPMU engages stakeholders, while
the Technical Program Management Unit (TPMU) assists NCRB with technical issues involving States,
BSNL, Software Development Agency (SDA), System Integrators (SIs), and others. A dedicated team
supports the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) with daily project tasks.
State Project Management Units (SPMUs) aid nodal officers in States/UTs by Validating project plans
and charters for State/UT-specific CAS deployment; Monitoring SI’s project management, configuration,
and issue-tracking systems for compliance & Coordinating workshops among NCRB, SDA, SI, State Police,
and stakeholders.

Case Study Title:
Operation of Shramik Special Trains for Migrant
Labour amid Covid-19 Crisis
Case Study Description: The COVID-19-induced lockdown in March 2020 left millions of migrant labourers stranded in various Indian cities. In a historic response, Indian Railways launched "Shramik Special" trains to facilitate their return to their native places, particularly to Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state. This massive humanitarian and logistical operation, led by Sanjay Tripathi, DRM/Lucknow and nodal officer from Railways, involved coordination with multiple stakeholders—central and state governments. This case highlights the challenges of planning large-scale transportation during a public health crisis, including compliance with COVID-19 safety protocols, logistical hurdles in catering, transport, and staffing, and communication bottlenecks. It underscores leadership, real-time problem solving, delegation, and use of technology in public administration. The operation saw the successful movement of over 3 million labourers to Uttar Pradesh via 957 trains.
Case Text:
On 24 March 2020, the Government of India imposed a nationwide lockdown following confirmation of over
500 COVID-19 cases and indications of rapid community transmission. In compliance with the Ministry of
Home Affairs directive, the Ministry of Railways suspended all passenger train services.
This sudden and unprecedented suspension of economic activity left millions of migrant workers or shramiks
stranded across metropolitan centres such as Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, and Chennai. Deprived of employment,
food and shelter, many attempted arduous journeys covering hundreds of kilometres back to their home
states—on foot, or by bicycle—accompanied by their families, including infants and pregnant women. Their
distressing plight, extensively documented by the media, underscored the urgent necessity for government
intervention.
In response, the Ministry of Home Affairs, on April 29, 2020, authorised the transportation of stranded migrant
labourers on Shramik Special trains to be operated by Indian Railways, which daily carries 2.2 million
passengers across India. Indian Railways, known as India’s National Transporter, initiated the operation of
special trains to facilitate the safe return of migrant labourers to their home states.
Between 1 May and 31 August 2020, Indian Railways operated a total of 4651 Shramik Special trains,
transporting 6.31 million (63.19 lakh) passengers across the country. Of these, 1,726 trains terminated in Uttar
Pradesh, enabling the repatriation of more than 3 million migrant workers to their native districts across the
state. This operation of Shramik Special trains perhaps represents the largest evacuation exercise conducted by
a nation, using a single mode of transport and within the shortest duration. This case study examines this
initiative as an exemplar of large-scale crisis management, inter-agency coordination and leadership in mass
transportation, executed under stringent health and safety protocols during an unprecedented public health
emergency.
Preparing to Handle a Crisis
‘It was a highly challenging national-level project that required seamless coordination with multiple state agencies, disaster
management authorities, health departments, and railway operations across different zones,’ recalled Mr Sanjay
Tripathi, then the Divisional Railway Manager, Lucknow Division of Northern Railways. In April 2020, Mr

Tripathi was nominated as the nodal officer1

for Indian Railways in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state.
He was entrusted with the responsibility of arranging rail travel for millions of stranded shramiks from various
cities and districts across multiple states to their home districts in Uttar Pradesh. Despite his 28 years of
experience in railway operations, Mr Tripathi described this assignment as ‘unprecedented in scale and scope.’
The situation was grim. The nationwide lockdown imposed on March 24, 2020, had resulted in an abrupt
suspension of economic activity, including transport and rail services. Following the closure of factories and
workplaces, millions of migrant workers—majorly from Uttar Pradesh and Bihar—faced the loss of income,
food shortages and uncertainty about their future. The lockdown had thus triggered one of the largest internal
migrations in India’s history—comparable in magnitude only to the Partition of 1947—as millions of labourers
stranded in cities and towns, desperately sought to return home.
The media showed distressing images of migrant workers—many of them women and children—walking
hundreds of kilometres in the scorching heat, without adequate food, water, or shelter. Their hardships were
compounded by state border closures and heavy-handed enforcement of movement restrictions by the police,
which left thousands of shramiks stranded and vulnerable. In desperation, some resorted to walking along
railway tracks to avoid detection, leading to tragic accidents, including one heartbreaking incident, in which a
group of exhausted labourers, after walking for miles, fell asleep on the tracks and were run over by a passing
train.
Recognising the gravity of the situation, the Government of India, on 29 April 2020, issued an orderin which
Indian Railways was tasked with organising rail travel for stranded migrants through Shramik Special Trains’.
The order also directed the coordination of migrant transportation efforts between state governments and
Indian Railways. Additionally, it mandated that travel arrangements included the provision of food and water
to passengers, and strict compliance with COVID-19 safety protocols, including sanitation and physical
distancing measures.
Although Indian Railways, as the national transporter, had previously managed emergency rail transport
operations—such as despatching relief materials during national disasters like the Bhuj earthquake and
Kedarnath floods—this mission presented an unprecedented logistical challenge in both scale and complexity.
Unlike its earlier relief efforts—focused on limited destinations, this initiative required nationwide
coordination of train movements across nearly every state in India covering all railway zones.

Operational Challenges
The government’s decision to run Shramik Special trains offered a lifeline to migrants desperate to return home,

back home to their native districts in Uttar Pradesh.
Complex Multi-Agency Coordination

The foremost challenge was establishing effective coordination between Indian Railways and multiple state-
level authorities. For instance, district administrations had to assess the demand—the number of shramiks who

needed transportation; health departments were responsible for enforcing the Covid-19 protocols; state
transport corporations needed to arrange buses for transporting shramiks to railway stations. Based on this
information, Indian Railways needed to coordinate with the Indian Railway Corporation for Tourism and

This route congestion required seamless coordination across multiple railway zones within Indian Railways—
Western, Central, Northern, and North Western zones—and with state authorities. Uttar Pradesh, with its 75
districts, needed to receive trains arriving from multiple directions, which demanded large-scale mobilisation

Severe Time Constraints
The urgency of bringing back migrant workers home significantly heightened operational pressure. Directives
from the Union Minister of Railways and the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, demanded immediate action.
While the decision to run trains was finalised on 29 April 2020, the Ministry of Home Affairs mandated
commencement of operations on 1 May2020—International Labour Day—thusgiving Indian Railways just two
days to plan and launch services.
Different Standard Operating Procedures
Operations for the Shramik special trains were fundamentally different from regular passenger trains.
Standard train operations follow fixed timetables, pre-defined routes and scheduled stoppages, with rostered
railway staff in trains for management of catering arrangements by IRCTC. In contrast, Shramik Specials had
to be planned from different stations based on demand from district administrations; train stoppages required
real-time adjustments; catering norms had to be redesigned based on length of journey and passengers’ need
for food; and railway staff had to be mobilised at short notice despite the risks posed by the deadly Covid-19
virus. For Mr Tripathi and his team, ensuring the safety of railway personnel too was a parallel challenge.
Compliance with Pandemic Protocols
Observing COVID-19 protocols during the journey posed another challenge. The government clearly directed
that transporting migrant workers must not lead to the spread of COVID-19. Indian Railways thus had to screen
passengers to ensure that infected persons did not board the trains, social distancing norms were followed and
sanitation measures were being implemented. The guidelines, as prescribed by the Ministry of Health and
Family Welfare, required originating state authorities to bring passengers to the designated railway station in
sanitised buses and in controlled batches while following social distancing norms and other Covid-19
precautions. Implementation of these protocols demanded close coordination with state health officials, which
was a daunting task in an environment of fear, uncertainty and urgency.
Catering Challenges
Arranging food and distribution of meals for millions of passengers posed a significant challenge. The
guidelines mentioned that state governments were responsible for providing food packets and drinking water
at the originating points, while Indian Railways had to arrange one meal for journeys exceeding 12 hours. Mr
Ambar Pratap Singh, an official of North Eastern Railway responsible for managing Shramik Special trains at
Lucknow, Sitapur, Gonda, Basti, etc., recalled that, ‘Arrangement of catering was the biggest challenge. Unlike
routine operations, these trains required rapid contact-minimised food distribution mechanisms appropriate for pandemic
conditions.’

Last Mile Connectivity
Upon arrival in Uttar Pradesh, migrant workers needed safe transport to their home districts via buses. This
last mile connectivity had to be arranged by district officials at the destination stations. Each train generally
carried around 1500 passengers, while a single bus could only accommodate around 40 individuals. This meant
approximately 40 buses were required to transport the shramiks on each train. As the frequency of trains
increased in the later days, arranging sufficient buses posed an immense logistical challenge for the state
transport department.
Funding
Financing this operation posed a significant challenge. Unlike regular train operations, Shramik Specials were
mandated to run free of cost for passengers. Indian Railways was required to transport migrants without
recovering any fares. Consequently, the central and state governments had to conduct detailed negotiations to
determine cost-sharing arrangements for expenses on train operations, meals, and last-mile bus connectivity.
Tracing the Implementation Process
The key mandate for nodal authorities in each state and union territory was to register the demand of stranded
persons within their jurisdictions. Recognising the urgency for completion of this task, Mr Tripathi, convened
an emergency meeting with key railway officials. He understood that the success of this operation would
depend upon seamless coordination between officials of the Indian Railways and state agencies. Building a
capable and cohesive team was therefore essential.
Setting up the Team: Mr Tripathi thus selected a dynamic railway officer, Mr Siddhartha Verma, Assistant
Operating Manager of Lucknow Division, Northern Railway, to lead the entire Shramik Special operation in
Uttar Pradesh. Mr Tripathi granted Siddhartha complete autonomy to select his team and manage the
operation. Siddhartha appointed three railway officials to assist him, namely, Vikas Sinha, Chief Commercial
Inspector, Ankit Pathak, Chief Commercial Inspector and Deepak Srivastava, Controller. Their task was to
liaise with various districts and state authorities to coordinate the arrival of Shramik Specials arriving across
various districts in Uttar Pradesh.
Another crucial figure in the operation was Mr Awanish Kumar Awasthi, Additional Chief Secretary Home,
Uttar Pradesh, whose meticulous planning and direct involvement ensured strong state support. As Mr
Siddhartha Verma recalled: ‘Awasthi Sir was always available, round the clock. Even calls at midnight were answered
with the same urgency as during the day.’
Coordinating stakeholders: The Shramik Special train operations during the COVID-19 pandemic required
intensive, real-time coordination between Indian Railways and the Uttar Pradesh state government. To
facilitate this, Mr Tripathi established a 24-hour ‘Control Room’ near the Additional Chief Secretary’s (ACS)
chamber in Lok Bhavan, Lucknow. This facility served as the central hub for real-time coordination between
railway and state officials. It enabled seamless information sharingbetween district magistrates, zonal railways
and state departments, primarily relating to shramiks’ details and train operations, particularly crucial for
planning services like food supply. (See Exhibit 2)

Assessing the Outcome
The operation of Shramik Special trains was one of the most complexly challenging logistical exercises in the
history of the Indian Railways, demanding unprecedented coordination, strategic planning and rapid
execution. The authorities successfully executed the entire operation to facilitate the return of shramiks to their
native places while adhering to government guidelines and COVID-19 protocols for the movement of labourers
and providing all necessary arrangements during the journey.
Although initially, this task seemed daunting, the collaborative and coordinated efforts of officers across
multiple departments ensured the safe return of 3 million shramiks to their homes across various districts in
Uttar Pradesh. Given the extraordinary circumstances during the COVID-19 pandemic, the government bore
the cost of travel and food. While these trains were initially intended for shramiks, rising demand led to their
use by students, pilgrims, tourists, and others. Public concern about transmission of the COVID-19 virus was
high, but strict enforcement of COVID-19 protocols ensured safe travels.
The Ministry of Railways operated 4621 Shramik Special trains (See Exhibit 7), facilitating the return of 7
million shramiks across India to their respective states. About 40% or 1726 of these Shramik Specials terminated
in various districts of Uttar Pradesh, bringing home more than 3 million migrant workers to their native
villages. Almost 90% of these trains operated at speeds higher than regular mail express services. Initially, what
appeared to be a herculean task of managing heavy demand of Shramik Specials from the four states of Gujarat,
Maharashtra, Punjab and Delhi was managed successfully by running 1334 Shramik Specials from these states
(See Exhibit 8). Despite rising demand for more trains, severe time pressures and restrictive pandemic
conditions during Covid-19, the railways nodal officer, Mr Tripathi coordinated closely with officials across
multiple state and railway departments to deliver on the Ministry’s mandate.
However, despite adherence to Covid-19 protocols, some tragic passenger deaths occurred aboard the Shramik
Special trains. These incidents created panic and posed some administrative challenges regarding the handling
of bodies. Mr Ambar shared that initiallythe Government Railway Police (GRP) hesitated to take responsibility,
but the issue was soon resolved and all such cases were handled promptly and respectfully, with bodies being
covered in white cloth and arrangement of last rites.
Despite the challenges, the operation received appreciation from the public, the media, and the migrant
workers. Criticism was constructively handled and taken in a positive spirit as feedback. Railway authorities
also addressed complaints by either taking remedial measures or issuing clarifications.
As stated in a media brief, the Railway Board Chairman, Mr Vinod Yadav mentioned, ‘Nearly 80% of migrants
travelled to Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Indian Railways also resumed special passenger trains from May 12 and planned to

Reflections
The successful operation of Shramik Special trains across India underscored the collective and collaborative
efforts of multiple stakeholders, including Indian Railways, state governments, and countless individuals,
whose coordinated actions made an otherwise daunting task achievable. Numerous acts of generosity and
compassion also marked the operation. Retired railway employees, including a former staff member from
Lucknow Division, volunteered to cook meals for labourers free of charge. Despite the pervasive fear of virus
transmission, public officials demonstrated extraordinary commitment. Tragically, several railway and state
government employees lost their lives in the line of duty. Their sacrifice remains both an enduring inspiration
and a reminder of the need for railway officials to adopt stronger health and safety protocols for its staff in
future emergencies.
The success of this entire operation completed in a short span of less than 2 months can essentially be attributed
to the dynamic leadership of the nodal officer, the collaborative efforts of all stakeholders, the 24-hour
monitoring mechanisms, online tracking of train movements and strong political support.
Mr Sanjay Tripathi, the railway’s nodal officer for Uttar Pradesh, exemplified leadership qualities such as
accountability, resilience, and unwavering sense of ownership. He managed planning, coordination,
monitoring, and emergency responses. Reflecting on one incident, Mr Tripathi shared, ‘When I learned that the
catering arrangements were inadequate, I left my office immediately and addressed the issue so that such failures do not
occur in the future. The successful completion of this mission brought immense satisfaction. If a career’s crowning glory
lies in a national service, it leaves a lifetime of satisfaction.’
However, the operation also attracted criticism. The media once misreported that a Shramik Special train had
gone missing. The utter chaos resulted in trains being diverted far away from their supposed destinations,
inflicting immense misery on passengers’ Railway officials, upon enquiry, discovered that the train had taken
a longer, alternative route as shorter routes were congested, and immediately issued a clarification. As Mr Vikas
mentioned, ‘After this report, we realised the need to monitor routes more closely and ensure that news agencies did not
misinterpret the information.’ The confusion stemmed from communication gaps that railway officials
subsequently addressed.
The uproar about the ‘missing’ train became so intense that Railway Board Chairman Mr V.K. Yadav had to
address the media and issue a clarification that no trains had gone missing. He publicly stated that this report
was ‘fake news.’
The team efforts received recognition from senior officials, including Railway Minister Mr Piyush Goyal and
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Mr Yogi Adityanath. Mr Siddhartha’s dedication to the operation was
recommended for a Commonwealth scholarship, while ACS Mr Awanish Kumar Awasthi received praise for
his leadership, and following his retirement in 2022, he became the Chief Advisor to the Chief Minister.
